## 2026-09-29 -- Batches 33-35: arguments taken where they are sent

bh44 2728, bh45 2741 (+13, -0), bh46 2747 (+7, -1: `message_004`, which picks
at random). Batch 35 (bh47) carries the argument-order change.

- **A by-value argument is taken where it is sent** (`snapshotSends`). An
  argument naming a variable was carried to the call as the variable and
  read there, after every later argument: `f($a, $a = 1)` passed 1, `f($i,
  $i++)` passed 1, `f($x, g($x))` with `g(&$r)` passed what `g` wrote. Now,
  when an instruction later in the same block may write the variable -- its
  first operand and not one of the reads, or a by-reference or undecided
  send of it -- a `copy` is taken at the send's position, marked `share` so an
  array gets its own holder (the emitter already turns that attribute into
  `Value.Share()`). Only then: a copy for every argument would cost the int
  paths their facts. The TODO item is closed.
- **The engine's exception constructors coerce their arguments** as the
  internal functions they are, in a frame of their own, and name the class
  that declares the constructor: `Exception::__construct(): Argument #1
  ($message) must be of type string, stdClass given`. ErrorException's takes
  severity, filename and line before `$previous`, which the old arm read from
  the third position.
- **`self::`, `parent::` and `static::` forward the called class**, and so do
  their callable spellings (`pendingLSB`, consumed where the method is
  entered and cleared after the call either way); naming a class resets it.
- **A method named by a non-string** is `Method name must be a string`, for
  `$o->$m()` and `C::$m()` alike, before the receiver is looked at.
- **A return type separates a reference** in a by-value function (`bind_var`,

## 2026-09-28 -- Unboxed int entries and int frames

Ackermann after the dispatcher split was still ~70 ns a call. Measured on
hand-edited emitted code (Ack(3, 9), minimum of seven, load ~40): 0.78 s as
emitted; 0.61 calling the version directly; 0.34 with no frame push at all
-- so the version's boxed parameters and the frame were the two costs.

- **Unboxed entry.** When an int version assumes every parameter an int and
  never reads its own argument list, it is emitted as `php_f__i(ctx, a0, a1
  int64)`, and its `recv` of an assumed parameter is the int64 itself
  (IntReps now makes that recv an IntRep, not counted as a gain). The
  dispatcher calls it for exactly n plain in-range ints; more arguments go to
  the general body, whose trace shows them.
- **Direct calls.** A call to such a function tests its arguments inline --
  range for an int64, kind and range for a boxed value, nothing for an int
  literal -- and calls `callUserInt<n>(ctx, name, php_f__i, ...)`. An
  undecided send of a temporary (`preferref %9`, the inner `Ack(...)`) is a
  by-value send here: every parameter of an unboxed entry is by value.
- **Int frames.** `callUserInt<n>` pushes with `Ctx.PushCallInts`: the ints
  stay in the frame, pointer-free, and `Args` is built only when `Stack()`,
  `CallStack()` or `SwapCallStack()` reads the frames. The push is built in
  place, and `PopCall` reads the frame through a pointer.

Ack(3, 9): 0.78 -> 0.55 (unboxed entry) -> 0.377 (int frames); the engine
takes 0.87. The floor with no frame at all is ~0.21: the rest is writing the
~180-byte StackFrame. `framestack_test.go` fails if CallStack stops
materialising, but only once the stack has spare capacity -- its first cut
pushed onto an empty stack, where every push takes the general path, and a
mutation survived. `int_versions.php` covers extra arguments, call_user_func,
a variable function name, a float, a numeric string and an out-of-range int,
and func_get_args keeping a function off the unboxed entry.

## 2026-09-28 -- The general body was the cost of an int version's call

With the argument slice gone, ackermann's profile turned inside out: the
**general** entry `php_ack` was 31% flat against the int version's 21%,
although all it did on every call was bind names and hand over. It is the
general body, so it declares every value the body uses -- a large frame
zeroed per call (`memclrHasPointers`), which also made the deep recursion
grow the goroutine stack (`newstack`, `copystack`) -- and it holds the
conditional release `defer`, so the hand-off's return took Go's slow defer
path (`_panic.nextDefer`).

A versioned function is now three Go functions: `php_f` binds the named
arguments and dispatches, `php_f__int` is the version, `php_f__gen` the
general body; neither body binds again (`boundByCaller`). Ack(3, 9): 1.79 s
-> 0.78 s, where the engine takes 0.88. The lesson is general: a fast path at
the entry of a big function still pays for the function's frame.

## 2026-09-28 -- Calls borrow their argument slots

The last lever: every compiled call allocated its argument slice on the heap,
because the frame keeps it (`StackFrame.Args`, for traces) and `CallStack()`
copied frames shallowly, so an exception's trace pointed at the caller's
slice.

Now the Ctx keeps an **argument stack**. `PushCallArgs` copies a call's
arguments onto it and the frame's Args is that region, marked with where it
starts; `PopCall` clears and releases the region; `CallStack()` deep-copies
the Args of such frames, since a snapshot outlives the call. The emitted
`callUserArgs` takes its arguments variadically, so the `[]php.Value{...}`
literal at the call site stays on the Go stack. It is used only for a callee
whose body keeps nothing of the slice -- not a generator or a resumable body,
whose frame holds `args` for the life of the generator.

Safe because compiled code keeps `c.stack` strictly LIFO: a suspended body is
popped and re-pushed by the driver with its own stored arguments, and the
goroutine fibers that swap stacks are the interpreter's.

`borrowed_args.php`: traces printed after later calls reused the slots, a
40-deep recursion that grows the stack mid-call, debug_backtrace and
func_get_args after nested calls, by-ref/named/default/variadic, and a
generator's trace. Dropping the deep copy prints `inner(...)` with the wrong
arguments; letting a generator borrow prints `traced(NULL, NULL)` (checked by
editing the emitted call, because the harness's first-match mutation hit the
census copy of the table, not the emitter's).

0.24 -> 0.21 (0.21), zend_bench 1.04 against 1.19, zend_micro_bench 5.37
against 6.14. Batch 24 pending.

## 2026-09-28 -- Packed arrays store values only

The storage lever. An array's elements were one slice of `{key, value}`
buckets, 56 bytes each (a 32-byte `Key` -- bool padded to 8, int64, string --
beside a 24-byte `Value`); the engine's packed arrays are a bare 16-byte zval
each. Building a list was mostly allocating and copying keys nobody read.

Now `arrayBody` keeps `vals []Value` and `keys []Key`, position for position,
with **keys nil while the array is packed** -- a packed key is its position,
`keyAt(i)` answers `IntKey(i)` -- as `hashes` already was. A list costs 24
bytes an element; a hashed array costs what it did. Every new element goes
through one place, `add`, which ends the packed mode (`unpack`: keys, hashes
and table spelled out) the first time a key is not the next position; `Rekey`
unpacks before renaming. Everything else was a mechanical rewrite of bucket
reads to `vals[i]` / `keyAt(i)` / `deadAt(i)`. Developed in a scratch copy of
the module while batch 22 ran against the live runtime, then copied in.

The array model test (`TestArrayIndexAgreesWithAnOrderedMap`) passed at 60
seeds, not just its one; fixtures 347/347.

`hack/bench.sh -n 3` (load ~30, engine alongside): movewrite 0.47 -> 0.32
(engine 0.33), arrpass 1.64 -> 1.36 (1.39) -- its build phase 1.05 -> 0.63
against 0.64. ary3 is unchanged at 1.4x: it is the element read-modify-write,

The cheap levers from the gap analysis (per call 133 vs 78 ns, per foreach

  list is packed, unshared and has room.

  `x*y + z` and mandel2 drew three characters differently from the engine.
  `php2gotest -fused-math` (`hack/bench.sh -F`) emits them verbatim, for
  speed where the last bit does not matter; graded, it fails exactly there.
- **ints** box exactly, so they may go anywhere. `++`, `--` and `± literal`
  are native only under a branch fact bounding the same SSA value: the true
  edge of `a < b` or the false edge, `b <= a`, which is non-strict and so
  proves nothing with a variable bound. `%`, `&`, `|`, `^` and int
  comparisons are native.
- **Int versions** (`lower.IntVersions`): a plain function whose untyped
  parameter would unbox more gets a clone assuming it is an int within
  ±2^62, entered from the general body after a kind-and-range test. Call-site
  typing is unsound here (computed callable names everywhere, the bundled
  library included).

**An unsound join, older than all of this.** `inferTypes` read a value with
no fact as bottom at a merge, and an untyped parameter, an untracked read
and an unknown constant never get one. So `$x = $n; if (..) $x = 1.5;` was
proved a float: `"abc" + 1` answered `int(1)` where PHP throws (checked with
the new passes off), and FloatReps rounded PHP_INT_MAX. Now seeded unknown
(`unanswerable`); `untyped_joins.php`.

Two regressions of my own, both caught by the benchmark suite rather than the
corpus: versions missing the ownership facts (`issetor` 0.14 -> 4.6 s; a
version is now in `gogen.Bodies`), and an inlined `Value.Bool` pushing
`ToBool` over the inline budget (47% of mandel in the call). Smaller wins:
coercion returns a value already of the declared scalar type before parsing
the declaration; a return value is coerced once, not twice; `ReadDim` of a
packed list is tested at the call site (`php.PackedAt`).

| zend_bench | 2.21 | 1.39 | 1.21 |
| zend_micro_bench | 8.60 | 6.42 | 6.15 |

| ary3 | 1.07 | 0.79 * | 0.40 |
| issetor | -- | 0.080 | 0.19 |

## 2026-09-28 -- Diminishing returns on dynamic fast paths

The hot helpers (`Add`, `Sub`, `AcceptsArithmetic`, `IsSmallerValues`,
`IsSmallerOrEqualValues`, `LooseEqualValues`, `NotLooseEqualValues`,
`StoreVar`) are now a small wrapper with the two-int case and an unexported
`...Slow` body; `plainFloats` reads float bits directly and inlines. Only
`AcceptsArithmetic` and `plainFloats` fit Go's inline budget (the others cost
85-97 against 80); **profile-guided optimisation** was measured on zend_bench
and bought 1-4%, so inlining is not where the time is.

micro_bench 8.74 -> 8.60 s, `ary3` 1.15 -> 1.07, `fibo` 0.31 -> 0.27;
zend_bench 2.27 -> 2.21 (1.8x). `mandel`/`mandel2` did not move: what is left
is the shape every operation has -- a boxed `Value`, a kind test per operand,
a call, a pending-error check. The remaining 1.5-2.8x gaps are that shape,
and closing them is type specialisation (plan D1/D4: knowing `$x` is a float
and emitting `float64`), not another fast path.

## 2026-09-28 -- Releasing an object stopped asking about its class

`newfoo` after the release-at-overwrite work spent 42% in
`RunConfinedDestructor` asking whether `Foo` has a `__destruct` -- through
`hasMethod`, `isArrayBackedClass` and a recursive interface walk lowercasing
every name, per object. Two fixes:

- **`Object.NoDestructor`**, set by compiled constructors for a class with no
  `__destruct` in a chain made only of compiled classes; the release then
  only marks the object destroyed. `no_destructor_flag.php` (a destructor from
  a subclass, a trait, two levels up, and an engine-class chain) fails if the
  flag is set on every class.
- **`isArrayBackedClass` is memoized** per class name: the parent and
  interface tables are the program's own and fixed.

`newfoo` 1.26 s -> 0.74 s (engine 0.49); micro_bench 9.23 -> 8.74.

## 2026-09-28 -- Smaller buckets, packed appends, and a GC target

Allocation and collection were over half of `movewrite` and `arrpass`:

- **A bucket is 56 bytes, not 72.** The `deleted` flag (8 bytes with padding)
  is a sentinel kind in the bucket's value (`kindDeleted`); the cached hash
  moved to a parallel `hashes` slice that a packed list never allocates.
  Checked with the randomized index model at 30 more seeds.
- **Appending to a packed list is a push** (`Array.Append`): its next key is
  its length, which cannot be taken, so there is no lookup and no index.
- **Compiled programs collect at GOGC=400** unless `GOGC` is set. Measured on
  the built binaries: `movewrite` 1.09 s at 100, 0.65 s at 400; `arrpass` 4.34
  -> 3.59; peak RSS 13 MB -> 26 MB. The engine never traces, and Go's default
  of collecting each time the heap doubles is a poor fit for PHP loops over a
  heap of a few megabytes.

Medians of three: zend_bench 2.24 s (1.9x), micro_bench 9.23 s (1.5x),
`movewrite` 0.76 (2.4x), `arrpass` 3.55 (2.6x), `newfoo` 1.26 (2.6x),
`ackermann` 0.53 (2.2x).

## 2026-09-28 -- Objects released at overwrite in loops; no empty dynamic table

`newfoo` (`$x = new Foo()` five million times in a function) kept every
object until the function returned. The renamer leaves a `ReleasePrev` marker
where a promoted store dropped a local's previous object -- but only when it
knows that value, and a local that is only ever written reaches the loop
header with no block argument to carry it. Now every promoted store to a
local that may take an object (a `*obj` value) also leaves a **tracking**
marker (`ReleasePrev` with `track`) naming the value it *takes*; the emitter
keeps the local's last confined object in a Go variable and releases it at
the next store. `SettleReleaseTracks` marks a site `keep` where another value
stored to the local is still live after it. Handles now alternate as the
engine's do (`1 2 1 2` for `spl_object_id` in a loop).

The first version corrupted the IR: `apply()` filtered instructions in place,
which was safe at one marker per dropped store and overwrote unread
instructions at two -- the `echo` after the assignment vanished. Now a fresh
slice. `release_in_loop.php` fails if the tracked release is not emitted.

Then allocation was the cost: every structured instance made an empty
`Props` array (two allocations) for dynamic properties it almost never gets.
It is now made on the first dynamic write (`Object.dyn`); and constructors
write defaults straight into `o.Slots[k]` instead of through `Set`'s lookup.

`newfoo` 2.31 s -> 1.60 s (engine 0.49).

Found and not fixed: `both($x, $x = new D())` passes the new object twice --
the lowering reads `$x` for the first argument after the second argument's
assignment (TODO).

## 2026-09-28 -- A known callee settles an undecided send; int equality

`ackermann` (4.3x) showed two things:

- **Recursive calls boxed their arguments.** A call to a function not yet
  declared where it is written -- recursion, or a forward call -- is an
  undecided send (`SEND_VAR_EX`, lowered `preferref`), and a local sent that
  way went as a fresh reference box (`RefArg`) every call, turning the
  caller's variable into a reference as a side effect. The emitter has the
  callee's signature; a positional, by-value, non-variadic parameter now
  takes the value (`ReadVar`, which also gives the engine's `Undefined
  variable` warning for an unset local -- the box passed undef instead).
  `undecided_send_known_callee.php` fails if a by-reference parameter is
  treated the same way.
- `==`, `!=` and `===` allocated a recursion guard even for two ints (and
  `===` for two strings); scalars of one kind now compare directly.

`ackermann` 1.03 s -> 0.68 s (engine 0.24); zend_bench 2.47 -> 2.38.

## 2026-09-28 -- foreach walks a share; packed lists skip hashing

- **By-value `foreach` over an array** copied every key and value into slices
  before the first iteration. It now iterates a copy-on-write share of the
  array (`Iter.snap`) by bucket position and hands the share back at
  `iter.free`. Closer to the engine, too: an element holding a reference is
  read when the loop reaches it (`$r = &$a[1]; foreach ($a as $v) { $r = 9;
  ... }` prints 9 for it, as the engine does; the copy printed the old value).
  `foreach_snapshot.php` hangs if the walk iterates the array itself instead
  of a share. The **interpreter** has its own iterator, which reads the live
  array against a key snapshot and so stops early when the body unsets an
  element it has not reached -- older, recorded in TODO.
- **A packed list no longer hashes its keys** on append; the hashes are
  filled when it stops being packed. The randomized index model test caught
  the one place that trusted a packed source's hashes -- `clone`, whose copy
  can leave the packed mode part-way through because deleted buckets shift
  positions -- now `bucketHash`.
- `$a[] = v` on an array skips `writeDim`'s object and box questions, and the
  emitted `stepIncrement`/`stepDecrement` handle an int directly.

`arrpass` pass half 3.34 s -> 2.09 s (engine 0.73); zend_bench 2.81 -> 2.47.

## 2026-09-28 -- Array elements by int key; string offsets refuse assign-ops

zend_bench's array tests (`ary3` 4.9x, `sieve`, `hash2`, `matrix`) spent their
time in `readDim`/`writeDim` judging the offset and converting the key before
every lookup, and in `$a[$i] op= v` looking the key up twice:

- `readDim` and `writeDim` take an int key on an array directly: one lookup,
  nothing to convert or warn about. A missing key, or an element holding a
  reference (which may carry a typed property's constraint), takes the
  general path.
- A read-modify-write on an element keeps the element's `php.Slot` from the
  read (`place.dimFast`) and writes back through it; `SlotSet` refuses a slot
  whose array became shared or restructured, and the general path runs.

`ary3` 1.86 s -> 1.20 s (engine 0.41). `dim_rmw_fast_path.php` fails if the
reference exclusion or the shared-array check is dropped; SlotSet's own
reference check is defensive (only user code between the read and the write
could plant one, and that case -- a `__toString` that unsets or grows the
array mid-assignment -- corrupts the **engine's** heap, so there is no oracle
for it).

It also found an older wrong answer, fixed: `$s[0] .= "z"` on a string wrote
the offset (with `Only the first byte will be assigned`) where the engine
refuses the read-write fetch -- `Cannot use assign-op operators with string
offsets`, or `Cannot increment/decrement string offsets` for `++`/`--`.
`??=` is not a read-write fetch and still works.

## 2026-09-28 -- Calls and float arithmetic; floats rendered as the engine writes them

zend_bench's remaining gap was calls (`fibo`, `ackermann`) and float math
(`mandel`, `mandel2`). Fast paths, each for operands that need no conversion:

- `AcceptsArithmetic`: two ints never warn under any operator; two plain
  numbers never warn under a non-integral one (it was 20% of `fibo`).
- `Add`/`Sub`/`Mul`/`Div` and `<`/`<=`: two plain numbers with a float among
  them compute as doubles directly (`plainFloats`) instead of classifying
  each operand and converting through `Value.Float()`'s switch.
- `StoreVar` of a scalar into a slot that is not a box is a plain write, and
  `Value.Share` is split so its common case inlines.
- A releasable parameter's `defer php.ReleaseShared` is emitted only when the
  argument is an array; it was a deferred call per invocation of every
  function taking one.

zend_bench 4.57 s -> 2.86 s; micro_bench 12.05 -> 11.0; `mandel2` 2.38 ->
1.13 (engine 0.66); `fibo` 0.61 -> 0.47 (engine 0.21).

**NaN compared equal.** `compareNumeric` answered 0 for an unordered pair, so
`NAN <= 1`, `NAN <= NAN` and `max(NAN, 1)` disagreed with the engine, whose
three-way comparison answers 1 whenever NaN is involved. Fixed. `min(NAN, 1)`
and `sort()` over a NaN still disagree -- they were wrong before and follow
their own engine rules (TODO).

**Floats were rendered with Go's shortest 'G'**, which goes exponential far
sooner than the engine and pads the exponent: `var_dump(1e15)` gave
`float(1.0E+15)` for `float(1000000000000000)`, `json_encode(1e14)` `1e+14`,
`serialize(1.5e-5)` `d:1.5E-05;`. Found building the float fixture.
`php.ReprFloat` is zend_gcvt's layout over the shortest digits -- fixed
notation unless the decimal exponent passes 17 or drops below -3, `1.0` for a
lone mantissa digit, no exponent padding -- and var_dump, var_export,
json_encode and serialize all use it. `echo`'s 14-digit form kept Go's
padding (`1.0E-05`) and is fixed too. Fixtures `float_arith_fast_paths.php`
and `float_rendering.php`.

Corpus `bh17` identical to `bh16` (2616 / 912 / 379 / 1); fixtures 334/334;
interpreter corpus byte-identical to `base-0923` -- no corpus test exercised
the float layouts that changed.

## 2026-09-28 -- Objects as Go structs; Value from 88 bytes to 24

**Per-class structs.** Compiled classes allocate their instances as
`obj_C struct { php.Object; f [N]php.Value }` (the user's choice, over a slot
vector or fixed bucket offsets); declared properties live in the struct,
`Props` keeps the dynamic ones. The runtime reads properties through `Prop*`
accessors on `Object` that present the old single ordered table, and a
consumer that needs a live `*Array` demotes the object with `Table()`.
Interpreter objects never get slots, so `runtime/interp` was left on `Props`.
Throwables stay in table mode: their engine properties precede the class's
own. Details in OWNERSHIP-PERF.md.

On its own the struct moved `propinc` only 0.68 s -> 0.64 s: finding the
property was no longer the cost. The profile's other constant was copying
`Value`s.

**Value is three words.** It had a field per kind (88 bytes) and is copied
everywhere. Now a kind, a flags byte, one word (int / float bits / string
length) and one pointer (string bytes or the handle). All ~95 field uses were
inside `runtime/php`, behind guarded accessors that return the zero value for
another kind, as the separate fields did. `_ [0]func()` makes Value
incomparable -- the build found no `==` on it anywhere.

micro_bench 15.7 s -> 12.05 s (1.9x the engine), zend_bench 4.97 -> 4.57,
arrpass 9.8 -> 7.8, movewrite 2.2 -> 1.5, newfoo 3.1 -> 2.4, propinc 0.64 ->
0.43. Corpus `bh16` 2616 / 912 / 379 / 1 against `bh15`'s same totals (one
`random_int` test swapped for another, both `noreference`). Fixtures 332/332.
Interpreter corpus byte-identical to `base-0923`.

## 2026-09-28 -- Call sites that remember

micro_bench's largest remaining gaps were helpers re-asking, on every
execution, what a literal site had already been told: `$this->x++` found the
property's declaration and slot twice (read, then write); `self::$x = 0`
walked the class tables, lowercased the class through a map iteration
(`realClass`) and built two `owner+"::"+name` strings; `self::f()` and
`$this->f()` ran a dozen special-case checks and built the frame name per
call. Each literal site now keeps what its first **successful** access
resolved -- a property slot (`place.getMod`/`setMod` over the new
`php.Array.Slot`), `staticSite`, `staticCallSite`, `methodSite` (an inline
cache keyed on the receiver's class), `constSite`. Details and the
defensive-versus-load-bearing account in OWNERSHIP-PERF.md.

The fixtures built to break them (`static_property_sites.php`,
`call_sites.php`) found three older wrong answers, fixed: a write to a static
dropped a reference bound to it; and `C::$p`, `C::K`, `C::m()` answered for a
conditionally declared class before its declaration ran. A fourth is
recorded: the engine initializes every deferred static default of a class at
its first static access, compiled output one property at a time.

Also: `staticMethodFns` as a package-level map literal was an initialization
cycle (its methods reach sites that read it) -- three fixtures `errored`
before it moved into `init()`.

| | before | after | engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| `zend_micro_bench` | 24.7 s | **17.5 s** | 6.1 s |
| `propinc` | 1.38 s | 0.81 s | 0.14 s |
| `staticprop` (new) | 2.03 s | 0.50 s | 0.30 s |
| `methodcall` (new) | 1.04 s | 0.54 s | 0.31 s |
| `zend_bench` | 4.93 s | 4.97 s | 1.21 s |

## 2026-09-27 -- Superglobals are userland's to define

The entry below seeded the superglobals from Go. The user's call: most modern
programs read the request through a framework object rather than `$_GET`, so
what the superglobals hold is the embedding's business -- **userland code
defines them**, and a host's or application's definition wins over the
defaults. The Go-side defaults (`php.RequestGlobals`) are gone again.

- `register_superglobals_impl`, the bundled library's existing initializer,
  now defines `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_COOKIE`, `$_FILES` and whichever of
  `$_SERVER`, `$_ENV`, `$_REQUEST` the program names, with values built in
  PHP (`auto_global_impl`: `getenv()` and the clock leaf).
- Go keeps two leaves in `runtime/stdlib`: `auto_globals()` hands over the
  harvested list (`Ctx.SetAutoGlobals`), and `register_superglobal` became a
  shared builtin storing through `Ctx.SetSuperglobalDefiner` -- the
  interpreter's global table, or the compiled program's `globals` map.
  **First definition wins**, once per request.
- **Compiled programs now link and run the library's initializers** before
  the file body, through the same fatal/exit path. They had never run them.
- A registered name the engine does not define (`$_RESP_HEADERS`) stays out
  of `$GLOBALS` and `get_defined_vars()`; compiled functions bind a variable
  spelled like a superglobal to the global when one is defined, as the
  interpreter does at frame entry. That also fixes an older wrong answer:
  compiled `header()`/`headers_list()` read `$_RESP_HEADERS` as an undefined
  local (`headers_list(): Return value must be of type array, null
  returned`).
- An included file that is the first to name a just-in-time superglobal gets
  it when it runs; the interpreter asks `auto_global_impl` again. Verified in
  a bundle against the engine.

Tests: `TestLibraryDefinesSuperglobalsFirstWins` (interp),
`TestDefineSuperglobalFirstWins` (runtime/php, with and without a definer),
fixture `library_superglobal.php` (fails if the prologue binding is dropped);
the two superglobal fixtures still pass and still catch their mutations.

Not covered: `php2phpt` and `php2eval`'s interpreter arm install no userland
library, so there the superglobals are undefined, as they always were. And
nothing yet lets an *application* add an initializer of its own to a bundle;
the precedence rule is in place for when something does.

Measured: corpus `bh14` identical to `bh13` (2616 / 912 / 379 / 1, nothing
gained or lost); fixtures 330/330; interpreter corpus byte-identical to
`base-0923`. Each compiled program grows by three functions (~280 lines on a
13k-line hello-world); the corpus pass took 34 min against an inferred ~31 for
`bh13`, whose start time was not recorded -- not attributable either way.

## 2026-09-27 -- Superglobals exist because the compile said so

Profiling micro_bench's `$x = $_GET` (3.9 s against 0.19 s) found no copy at
all: 90% of the loop was `Ctx.Warn` formatting `Undefined global variable
$_GET` into the output buffer. **Neither back-end created any superglobal** --
a read warned and answered null, a confident wrong answer the corpus never saw
(seven tests touch superglobals, six `noreference`).

Asked of the engine: `$_GET`, `$_POST`, `$_COOKIE`, `$_FILES` always exist,
empty, first in the global table; `$_SERVER`, `$_ENV`, `$_REQUEST` exist only
when the file spells one, created in the order the compiler met them, with the
environment (plus `REQUEST_TIME_FLOAT`, `REQUEST_TIME`, `argv` `[]`, `argc` 0
in `$_SERVER`). And `$GLOBALS["_SERVER"]` compiles to **the identical
`FETCH_R`** as `$_SERVER` -- same operands, same extended_value -- without
creating it, so no reading of the op_arrays can say which exist.

So the harvester asks the compile: before each one it re-arms the three JIT
globals and removes them from `EG(symbol_table)`, and afterwards it reads back
what the compile created (`Unit.auto_globals`, new proto field 5). Both
back-ends seed from that list through `php.RequestGlobals`, once per request
(an include after `unset($_SERVER)` does not restore it). The interpreter's
file-scope `get_defined_vars()` now reads the global table rather than only
its own compiled variables, and `$GLOBALS` skips names bound but never
assigned.

`superglobals.php` and `superglobals_by_name.php` fail if the JIT list is
empty, if all three are always created, or if their order is fixed rather than
harvested; `TestCompileUnitReportsAutoGlobals` covers the read-back per file,
including the `$GLOBALS` and `$$n` spellings.

`$x = $_GET` 3.88 s -> 0.14 s net (engine 0.19 s); micro_bench 29.4 s -> 24.7 s
(4.0x). Corpus `bh13` against `bh12`: 2616 / 912 / 379 / 1, no losses (the one
gain is `message_004`, whose output is random). Fixtures 329/329. Interpreter
corpus byte-identical to `base-0923`. Left open in TODO: file-scope variables
all dump as `&` in the interpreter (older), and compiled file-scope
`get_defined_vars()` stays refused.

## 2026-09-27 -- Plain properties and integers skip the questions

`$this->x++` was the largest ratio left (18.7x), and a profile showed it asking
questions the compiler already knew the answers to. Now:

- The class's declaration table marks each property `Plain` (public, unhooked,
  not a shadowed private's slot) and `PlainWrite` (also untyped, not readonly,
  one visibility). The emitted `propGetMode` and `propSet` go straight to the
  slot for those when it holds a value -- and, for a write, when it is not a
  box carrying a typed property's constraint.
- `Increment`/`Decrement` and `<`/`<=` handle two ints before anything else.
  The general comparison asked about enums, booleans and objects first, and
  that was 22% of bench.php.

`property_fast_path.php` is built to break it: typed, readonly, asymmetric,
hooked (and a subclass of hooked), `__get`/`__set` after unset, a public name
shadowing a private, a lazy ghost and a lazy proxy, a typed box in an untyped
slot, a dynamic property, both ends of the integer range. Mutations dropping
the shadow test, the PlainWrite test, either undef test or the typed-box test
each fail it. Dropping `PlainAccess` or the `Lazy == nil` test does **not** --
hooks are per declaration, and a lazy object's unwritten slots hold undef -- so
those two are defensive and documented as such.

**Two older bugs found by the fixture, on the full path:** reading an unset
*untyped* declared property threw `must not be accessed before initialization`
(the typed rule) instead of warning `Undefined property` and asking `__get`;
and writing one skipped `__set` because the surviving undef slot looked
present. Measured against the engine and the interpreter, which were right.

| `arrpass` | 14.1 s | 10.3 s |
| `issetor` | 0.66 s | 0.16 s (engine 0.19) |

## 2026-09-27 -- P2 moves, and the cheap half of P4

**P2 changed meaning under P3b.** A store no longer clones; it shares -- and
sharing a fresh temporary that dies at the store left the body counted as
shared, so the variable's next write cloned an array nobody else held. The
trace's `Moves` now take `StoreVarShared`: `movewrite` (`$b = build(200);
$b[] = $i;`) 4.72 s -> 3.56 s. `move_stores.php` holds the shapes that are not
moves (a property's array, a function keeping what it returns in a static, one
returning its parameter); treating every store as a move breaks it.

**P4 started with what was in front of it.** Profiling `new Foo()` in a loop:

- a per-object Go map of property declarations, filled on every `new` --
  now the class's table, built once and shared copy-on-write;
- `callCtor`'s dispatch, walking the class's interfaces, for a class with no
  constructor -- skipped when no `__construct` exists in a chain of compiled
  classes (the destructor is still registered; treating every class as
  constructor-less breaks the new fixture);
- two maps that grew with every object that ever died (`Ctx.destructed`, the
  emitted `freeObjectSet`) -- flags on the object;
- the frame drain list holding every confined object a loop made -- now drops
  finished ones before growing.

`newfoo` 9.58 s -> 3.89 s (20x -> 8.2x); `micro_bench` 59.8 s -> 53.5 s.
Storage reuse, the rest of P4, is left: it turns a lifetime mistake into two
objects sharing state, and wants attack cases first.

The first pipeline run caught one thing: a class listing a name twice
(`parent_property_hook.php`) made a duplicate key in the generated declaration
table, which Go refuses; the last declaration wins, as it did with one
`Declare` call after another.

Gate clean; fixtures 326/326; compiler corpus `bh11` identical to `bh10`;
interpreter corpus 4306 / 208 / 173 / 29, byte-identical to its baseline.

## 2026-09-27 -- The array index is a table of our own, not a Go map

The user pointed out that a Go map inside the array container did not look
right, and every profile agreed: `build()` spent 34% in `mapassign`, lookups
hashed a three-field struct, and P3b's separation had to rebuild the map entry
by entry. `runtime/php/arrayindex.go` is the engine's shape instead -- packed
while every key is its position, otherwise open addressing over an `[]int32` of
bucket positions with cached hashes, deleted and renamed buckets as free
tombstones. A separation now copies two slices.

A randomized test against a plain ordered-map model covers set, unset, rekey,
clone and share, and fails if the tombstone check or the packed test is
removed. `zend_bench` 7.71 s -> 6.96 s (5.8x the engine), `arrpass`'s return
loop 9.60 s -> 7.47 s, `newfoo` 10.69 s -> 9.58 s -- object property tables are
arrays too.

The interpreter shares `php.Array`, so its corpus was run as well: 4966 tests,
**4306 passed / 208 failed / 173 unsupported / 29 errored**, and every chunk's
output byte-identical to the 2026-09-23 baseline. Compiler corpus `bh10`
against `bh9`: unchanged but for the two `random_int` flakes trading places;
fixtures 324/324.

## 2026-09-27 -- P3b: copy-on-write by holder, and shares handed back

**The design moved from a bit to a split.** A "shared" bit cannot separate: the
writer has to put a copy somewhere, and a writer holding a `*Array` does not
know the slot it came from. So `php.Array` is now a header -- the holder's
internal pointer and foreach cursors -- over an `arrayBody` that headers share.
`Share` gives a new holder a header; every mutator calls `own` first. Only
`array.go` touches the body, so the audit is one file, and a test lists every
mutator. The interpreter still `Clone`s and never meets a shared body.

**Asking the engine turned up a pre-existing wrong answer the design fixes.**
`$r = &$a[0]; $b = $a; unset($r); $a[0] = 7; echo $b[0];` is 1 in PHP and was
7 compiled: `zend_array_dup` decides which references survive when it
separates, and the eager Clone decided at the assignment. Separation now takes
references the way PHP does -- kept when a name still holds the box or when it
points back at the array itself, flattened otherwise.

The first corpus run lost three files, each a lesson about a body with more
than one header:

- `bug38469`, `gc_032` -- `$b[0][0] = $b` opens `$b[0]` for writing *before* it
  reads `$b`, so the share arrived in the middle of the write. `DimTarget` now
  counts open writes on the body, and `Share` snapshots while one is open. It
  was first counted in `DimRef`, which `$r = &$a[0]` never releases, and that
  left every array a reference was ever taken into snapshotting for good.
- `bug69376_2` -- a self-referencing array seen through two headers:
  `print_r`, which is userland PHP walking with `array_id`, recursed forever
  because `array_id` printed the header. Identity is the body's now, in
  `array_id` and in the runtime's own cycle checks.

Two more pre-existing aliasing bugs closed on the way: a **by-value parameter**
was the caller's own array (`Unbox` shares now), and a **promoted `$b = $a`**
lost the copy its store made (promotion marks the read `share`).

**Then the parameter fix made a loop quadratic**, which is what the user's
question about read-only containers was about: `passloop` -- append, pass to a
function that only counts -- took **26.15 s against the engine's 0.002 s**,
because receiving the parameter set a one-way flag and the caller copied on
every append after. The flag is a count of extra holders now, a writer that
separates takes its one away, and the trace hands back shares it proves dead:
`ParamReleasable` at the callee's exit, `ReleaseAfter` at a promoted copy's
last use. `passloop` 26.15 s -> **0.024 s**; `copyloop` 0.022 s, where the
engine takes 1.2 s.

Cost where nothing is written: `arrpass`'s pass loop is ~19% slower (5.36 s ->
6.36 s), a header and a deferred release per call. Skipping the share when the
callee cannot observe a write to the caller's array -- no calls, no global or
property writes -- would recover it.

Gate: build, vet, `go test ./...` clean (goldens regenerated for the `share`
mark); fixtures 324/324 (`array_value_semantics.php`, `read_only_params.php`,
mutation-checked). Corpus `bh8`/`bh9`: 2609/2608 passed against `bh6`'s 2607,
gained `bug67633`, lost nothing but the `random_int` flakes.

## 2026-09-27 -- P3a: literals built once, copies and stores not made

The trace now hands the emitter three facts that rest on one predicate,
**private** -- an allocation this body made, not borrowed, never written in
place, never leaving the frame, not even by a return:

- `SharedLiterals`: an inline array literal becomes a package-level array
  built once (`sharedLiteralN`), shared program-wide by text;
- `SharedCopies`: a `copy` of a private value is not made;
- `SharedStores`: a `write_var` of a private value calls `StoreVarShared`,
  StoreVar minus the copy. Found by profiling after the first two: the
  ternary's merge temporary was still copying the shared literal on every
  iteration. The destination is in the value's identity, so the same proof
  covers it.

`issetor` 16.35 s -> **0.73 s** (85x -> 3.5x); micro_bench's ternary line
13.02 s -> 0.11 s, level with the engine; micro_bench overall 83.9 s -> 61.1 s.
On Twig and CakePHP it reaches little (4 and 256 literals), because arrays
there leave their frame; that is P3b's job.

**The first fixture could not tell the rule from no rule.** Dropping the write
check or the escape check still passed, because the copy every store makes
protects every shape that goes through a variable. What sharing can break is a
write with no store in between -- `foreach ([1, 2] as &$v)`, and the same over a
call's result -- and with those added, each mutation fails. Worth remembering for
P3b: an attack case has to reach the array without passing a store.

Registering literal sites also turned up a gap in the trace: an intrinsic's
arguments were only visited at positions its rule names, so `count([1, 2, 3])`
had no site at all. Every argument is visited now.

**A second pre-existing aliasing bug, not fixed**: a by-value array parameter is
the caller's own array, since neither the call nor a promoted parameter copies
it, so `f($g)` with `global $g; $g[] = 2;` inside sees the write through `$a`.
Copying on entry would cost every array-taking call an O(n) clone; the fix that
does not is P3b's bit. Recorded in TODO.md.

Gate: build, vet, `go test ./...` clean (`StoreVarShared` listed as not an
intrinsic of its own in the catalogue test); fixtures 322/322. Corpus `bh5`
and `bh6` against `bh4`: unchanged but for the `random_int` flakes.

## 2026-09-26 -- P0 and P1: a benchmark harness, and strcat stops being quadratic

**P0.** `hack/bench.sh` times compiled output against `php2eval -raw` on the same
PHP, median wall clock, and keeps each program's own output and optionally a
CPU profile. It needed one new mode: `php2gotest -emit DIR` writes each
program as a buildable module and does not grade -- a benchmark prints timings,
so it never passes, and grading would run the engine twice. Inputs are
`hack/bench/*.php` plus the engine's `bench.php` and `micro_bench.php` with the
timezone block removed. The first version of that `sed` deleted the `if` line
with the call and left a stray `}`, so bench.php "ran" in 9 ms; worth checking
the outputs, not only the table.

Baseline: `zend_bench` 19.49 s vs 1.21 s (16.1x), `micro_bench` 13.9x, `strcat`
717x. Run to run noise is up to ~10%.

**P1.** `lower.StringChains` carries a loop-carried `.=` chain as `*strbuf`
(a `strings.Builder`), and every other use of a chain value reads an O(1)
snapshot. The proof is the trace's append fact, checked per **group** -- every
value one buffer can flow through -- because at run time they are all the same
builder, so at each append nothing else in the group may be live. A chain is
entered only from a string literal or a concatenation, so no conversion moves:
`$s = 0; while (...) $s .= "x";` must still return `int(0)` when the loop does
not run. Both of those are what `string_append_chains.php` breaks on when either
check is removed.

Snapshots made one rule of the trace unnecessary: an append no longer needs
"no other holder". What a container or a callee holds is a finished string, and
the builder never rewrites bytes it has handed out.

bench.php's own `strcat` line: 11.83 s -> **0.033 s** (engine 0.008 s).
`zend_bench`: 19.49 s -> **7.43 s**, 16.1x -> 6.2x the engine -- the dispatch
floor the plan predicted. Twig / CakePHP: 166 / 599 concatenations rewritten.

Gate: build, vet, `go test ./...` clean; fixtures 321/321. Corpus `bh4` against
`bh3`: 2607 / 921 / 379 / 1, gained 1 (`message_004`, the `random_int` flake),
lost 0.

## 2026-09-26 -- The trace learns writes and moves, and finds two miscompiles

The plan in `OWNERSHIP-PERF.md` needed five facts the ownership trace did not
have. It has them now (`lower.Trace`): array sites including inline literals,
**Written**, **moves**, **in-place appends**, **returns fresh** and
**parameter written**, on top of a new liveness pass (`ownership_live.go`).

Three things turned out different from the plan:

- **"Used once" is liveness, not a use count.** bench.php's loop-carried
  string has two uses on paths that never meet.
- **A dead value can still have a live alias.** `%2 = copy(%1)` names one array
  twice; a move of `%2` has to check `%1`. Written into a unit test built to
  fail without the check.
- **Written belongs on the identity partition, not the escape one.** Storing
  into a container copies, so writing through the container does not write
  what was stored. On the escape partition, every parameter a constructor put
  into `$this` was "written"; half of Twig's.

The last point assumes the runtime copies at every container store, so I
checked it against the engine rather than the code -- and **a property store did
not copy**. `$o->a = $arr; $o->a[] = 2;` grew `$arr`, in both directions, for
instance, typed, dynamic and static properties, at file scope too. The emitted
`propSet` and `staticSet` stored the pointer; `WriteDim` and `ArrayAppend`
copied. Fixed, `property_store_copies.php`.

The write rules' own tests found the other: **`foreach ($a as &$v)` over a
local, in a function, lost every write.** The loop opens `$a`'s box, but
`ExplicitReads` had turned the argument into `read_var($a)`, so promotion never
saw the address taken and promoted `$a`. Fixed in `mem2reg.go` by following
the read back to its place; `foreach_by_ref_local.php`. The file body was fine
-- it is never promoted -- which is presumably why nothing caught it.

**Parameters written was 49% on a Twig sample until the `preferref` sends were
answered.** Every method call passes `preferref`; the trace now asks
(`ByRefArg`) whether the callee's parameter is by reference -- compiled bodies,
builtin signatures, methods by name, unknown means yes. 15.7% after.

Measured on Twig / CakePHP: appends in place 52% / 37% of concatenations;
arrays never written 76% / 72%; moves 1.1% / 2.8% of stores; bodies returning
fresh 62% / 42%. Moves are the small lever one file at a time -- a store's
value is usually borrowed.

Gate: build, vet, `go test ./...` clean; fixtures 320/320. Corpus `bh3` against
`bh1`: 2606 / 921 / 379 / 1 against 2608 / 921 / 379 / 1, and the two files
that moved are the two `random_int` tests TESTING.md already names
(`value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`, `message_004`) -- both read `random_int`,
and both gave a different outcome on rerun with the same binary.
Neither fix moves a corpus file; both are graded by their fixtures.

## 2026-09-25 -- Where compiled output's time goes

Asked for a plan to get speed out of the ownership trace, so I measured first.
Plan in `OWNERSHIP-PERF.md`; inputs in `.agents-workspace/tmp/bench/`.

**`php2go bundle` runs the interpreter.** The first profile of a bundled
`bench.php` was all `interp.execFrame`. Compiled numbers need the `gogen` path:
`php2gotest -keep`, the kept file built against the local runtime.

**Compiled `bench.php` is 18.1 s; the engine is 1.19 s.** 10.98 s of it is
`strcat` -- `$str .= "hello\n"` -- which is quadratic in `concatstrings`. The
builder pass that exists for it reports zero candidates, because promotion
had already turned `$str` into a loop-carried SSA value. Without strcat the gap
is 6x, and that 6x is operator dispatch (`IsSmallerValues` 22%, object and
enum checks on integer compares), which ownership does not touch.

**The largest ratios are all copies of something nobody else holds.**
`$x = $val ?: null` over a 10-element literal is 93x the engine: the lowering
folded `$val` into its literal, and the emitter rebuilds the literal every
iteration and then deep-copies it. `$x = $_GET` is 18x (a deep copy per store);
`$b = build(100)` spends 12% cloning the array it was just handed. `new Foo()`
in a loop is 18x, mostly allocation and the GC.

One non-finding worth keeping: passing an array into a function copies
nothing today. Promotion removed the parameter's store, so the eager copy never
runs. The cost of `sum($a)` is iteration.

`perf` is not permitted on this box (`perf_event_paranoid`); a small file in
the build directory starting Go's CPU profiler over a time window works, and a
window has to end before the program does or the profile is never flushed.

## 2026-09-25 -- Ownership tracing through containers, and a constructor-argument bug

The escape measurements said ~95% of library allocations escape, and the
container-fate table said why: the object rarely goes anywhere on its own, the
**container** does. So the question became who owns an object, through which
containers, and whether ownership is ever shared or only moved. Written up as
`OWNERSHIP.md`; implemented as `lower.TraceOwnership`.

**A soundness bug in the shipping escape analysis came out of writing the note.**
`escapes.value` read every mention in a `call.ctor` as the receiver, so
`new Holder(new X)` confined `X` -- and the compiled program printed `X`'s
destructor when `make()` returned, while the returned `Holder` still held it.
Fixed: a constructor argument escapes unless `argKept("__construct")` says the
constructor keeps nothing, which no compiled one does yet.
`ctor_argument_lifetime.php` fails without the fix and passes with it.

The fixture keeps both holders alive to the script's end on purpose. Releasing a
holder earlier needs its part to die with it, which is a refcount question: with
the fix, an escaping part dies at script end, not with its holder. A first draft
of the fixture unset the holder and could not pass for that reason -- the
direction is now late rather than early, which is the safe one, and it is
D3.3's to close.

**The fix erased most of what the escape rate had claimed.** Twig's confined
count went from 34 to **1**, CakePHP's from 19 to **14**. 33 of Twig's 34 claims
were the bug, so the "5.1%" quoted in the entry below was not a floor; it was
mostly wrong.

The tracer, in outline (the note has it in full):

- **Seven edge classes** -- forward, alias, contain, splice, extract, part-of,
  sink -- declared per intrinsic in one table. Unknown means sink, and
  `TestOwnershipRulesAreComplete` holds the table to the catalogue in both
  directions. The ad-hoc classifier in php2gotest missed a forwarding edge three
  times, each time towards the unsafe answer; the table is the answer to that.
- **Two union-finds**: Steensgaard's for fates, one node of contents per
  container; and a forward-only identity partition for counting owners, because
  counting on the first makes the elements of a container owners of each other.
- **Moves versus shares**: a terminal sink moves; a second local, a second
  container or a kept argument shares.

**The catalogue's `ReEnters` misses ArrayAccess.** `dim.get` and `dim.set` are
unmarked, though on an object they are `offsetGet`/`offsetSet` with the object as
`$this`. The ownership table declares it itself; the catalogue flag drives
diagnostic ordering, so changing it there is its own question (TODO).

Measured on the same Twig and CakePHP trees:

- **75% (Twig) and 79% (CakePHP) of escaping objects are only ever moved.**
  A refcount on them never exceeds one. That is D3's premise in another form:
  not "most objects do not escape" but "most escaping objects are not shared".
- **`throw` is CakePHP's largest single reason: 382 sites, where it is the only
  reason.** The old classifier never counted it, because it only looked for
  `ret`.
- 149 of the 167 Twig sites that escape only through a container escape
  because that container is returned.
- Every disagreement with `ConfinedNew` is in the trace's favour (1 and 6), and
  none goes the other way.

Gate: build, vet and `go test ./...` clean; fixtures 318/318. Corpus run `bh1`
against `bg6`: **2608 / 921 / 379 / 1 both, gained 0, lost 0.** The fix moves no
graded file, which fits what it changes: it withdraws claims whose early
destructor the corpus never observed. `internal/lower/BUILD.bazel` had drifted
by seven files; it now lists every Go file in the package.

## 2026-09-25 -- The escape rate, on the corpus and then on Twig

Phase A's item 6, asked because it bounds what selective refcounting can buy
before any of it is built. Counted per **`new` site**, which is what an emitter
can act on, as a by-product of the compile pass -- so it is free to reproduce.

**`Zend/tests` (4 of 12 chunks, 1,761 sites): 5.0% claimed.** And the headline
was not that: **62.9% of sites are in the file body**, where frame confinement is
not asked at all, because `{main}`'s locals are globals and `markConfined` skips
it. The 5% is measured almost entirely against the other third.

So the corpus was the wrong instrument, which the user named directly: the first
real target is Twig. Shallow clone at `9d33a10`, `src/` only, 284 files.

**Twig: 669 sites, 5.1% claimed, and 0% in the file body.** The inversion is
exactly what the shape of the code predicts -- a library puts every allocation in
a method -- and it *barely changes the answer*. Under today's analysis **about
95% of object allocations on the real target would need a refcount.**

That is the opposite of the plan's premise. D3 was scoped on "refcount only what
escapes", with the non-escaping majority carrying no refcount at all. On Twig the
exempt set is the minority.

Two more facts worth keeping:

- **`disposable` and `discarded` fire on Twig zero times.** Both claim shapes
  that occur in test scripts -- an object handed to a call and dropped, an object
  nothing looks at -- and apparently not in library code.
- **5.1% is a floor, not the number.** `php2gotest` compiles one file per
  program, and `leaksThis` treats a method this unit never declared as leaking;
  Twig's classes reference each other across files, so every cross-file call is
  counted pessimistically. The whole-program figure is the one that should decide
  D3, and it needs the bundle path -- which does not yet run even the call-graph
  wiring the fiber work added.

Written up with the three readings it supports in
`.agents-workspace/tmp/TWIG-ESCAPE.md`. I am not proposing which to take: the
honest position is that the premise D3 rests on did not survive its first
contact with real code, and the next measurement -- whole-program -- is cheap
compared to building on a number that may be off by a lot in either direction.

**Two shells died to the same mistake while doing this**, both now in TESTING.md:
`pkill -f` and `pgrep -f` match the command doing the matching, and the recorded
bracket trick does not help when the same command *writes a file of that name* --
the pattern matches through the heredoc text. It left a launcher truncated at 294
bytes that exited 0 and did nothing.

## 2026-09-25 -- A generator parks instead of breaking, and a driver call can be resumable

Censusing `bg3`'s refusals leaves one real gap standing above the rest. Setting
aside `include or eval` (141, refused by design), the top entry is **`a fiber
suspension crossed a generator driver` -- 26 files**, and every smaller one is
3-7. That is where the fiber arc converges, and it is the caller question in its
last form: `$g->next()` is an ordinary call, and a suspension inside the body has
to travel out through it.

This tick is the **runtime half**, which everything else rests on.

A generator whose body suspends is now **parked** rather than only stuck: its
body is stopped mid-step and the value it suspended with is kept. `GeneratorDrive`
performs one driver call as a `Resumable`, so a frame that was rewritten into a
state machine can make the call, hand the suspension out to the fiber, and
resume the body exactly where it stopped. The advance loop is what continues on
resume -- not the driver call, which has already had its effect on the
generator's state, and re-running it would hand the body a second resumed value.

Unchanged for everyone else: a driver call from a frame that is *not* resumable
still reports the gap, because nothing there can resume it. The two are told
apart by who is asking, not by what the body did.

Three tests: the drive carrying a suspension out and back with the body
continuing past it, the ordinary advance still refusing, and the existing
"reported, not faked" test still passing unchanged.

**A test bug worth noting**, because it read as a code bug: `if err := g.Next(ctx);
!errors.Is(...)` scopes `err` to the `if`, so a later `IsUnsupported(err)` in the
same function silently read the *outer* `err`, which was nil from
`StartGenerator`. The failure said the error was unclassified when there was no
error in hand at all.

Gate clean.

**The emitter half, same day.** Four pieces, and each one taught something:

- **Typing the receiver.** `$g = gen(); $g->next()` is a call on a Generator, and
  saying so is what lets the rewrite treat it as a suspension point. Calling a
  generator function makes a Generator whatever it declares, so `World` now
  carries `Generators` and `resultClass` answers from it. `InferReceivers` had
  only ever run in `php2lower`'s report; the compile path runs it too.
- **A driver call splits whether or not the receiver was resolved**, because it
  usually is not -- `$iterable` is a closure `use` variable, a property, anything
  the inference does not reach. That is safe because a receiver with **no frame
  of its own now gets one that performs the ordinary call** (`php.CallOnce`), so
  an over-eager split costs a resumption and changes nothing. Refusing instead
  would have turned every conservatively-split call on an ordinary object into a
  gap.
- **An empty reach set does not mean nothing splits.** A generator that suspends
  is deliberately *not* in the set -- calling one suspends nobody -- but driving
  one does, and `suspendingCallee` was short-circuiting on the set alone. The
  predicate was never consulted; the debug print that showed nothing at all is
  what found it.
- **Inference made the analysis worse before it made it better.** With a receiver
  inferred, `Sub extends Direct` looks up `sub::work` and misses, because the
  method is declared in the parent -- so a call that used to split by name
  stopped splitting. The exact key is now tried *and* the name is the fallback.
  A fixture caught it; the corpus would have reported it as a fiber losing its
  body.

**And a latent bug in my own earlier work, found by a fixture asserting three
calls in one expression.** `demoteAcross` recorded a **block parameter** as
crossing a suspension and then emitted no store for it, because it walked only
instruction results -- and a parameter is the previous split's result, arriving
through `frame.resumed`. `f($a->next(), $b->next(), $c->cur())` printed null for
everything but the last. It had been there since the first suspending call
landed; nothing exercised two in one expression until now.

A `Fiber::suspend()` inside a generator now travels out through `$g->next()` and
back in. What does **not** work yet is the `yield from` chain through an
`IteratorAggregate`: `NewDelegate` resolves one to a `traversableDelegate`, not a
`generatorDelegate`, and `parkedInChain` only follows the latter. All 26 corpus
files in this family are that shape, so the corpus may not move at all -- the
capability is real and fixture-covered, and the files need the Traversable hop
to park too.

Fixtures 315 -> 316, userland probe 328/331 with 0 failed, gate clean.

**`bg4` 2600 / 920 / 388 / 1: gained 6, lost 0**, and I had predicted possibly
nothing. `gh15108-004`, `gh15330-002` and four `gh9916-*` were the direct shape
after all. Wrong in the pessimistic direction, which is worth recording next to
the two optimistic misses.

**Then the Traversable half, same day.** `yield from new It()` over an
`IteratorAggregate` resolves to a Traversable wrapping what `getIterator()`
returned -- usually a Generator -- so the body that parks is not the one being
driven. `runtime/php` cannot name the wrapper, so it declares `GeneratorSource`
and the emitted `methodTraversable` answers it: the same "declared here,
supplied from above" shape as `CallValue` and `ObjectProperties`. The chain walk
follows both delegate kinds through one `delegatedGenerator` helper.

One more thing was stale: a Traversable delegate **caches `valid`** and
refreshes it in `Advance`, and resuming a parked body goes straight to the
generator instead. Without re-asking, the chain reported the element it was
parked on for ever.

Of the 16 files still refused before this, **8 now pass**.

`bg5`: **2607 / 921 / 379 / 1, gained 8** -- the whole `gh15108` family plus
`gh15275-001` and `gh15330-001`, losing only the non-deterministic
`message_004`.

**And then the half that was still wrong, which two unit tests found and the
corpus could not.** A generator that *resumes and then yields again* answered
the element it was parked on. The direct case was fine; the delegate chain was
not, and the difference is why the corpus said nothing: every file that passes
today suspends and never produces another element.

`parkedInChain` returned the **first** parked generator, and every generator in
the chain is marked parked -- each of them is stopped. So it found the
*outermost*, whose body is sitting at its `yield from` rather than at the
suspension, and resuming handed the fiber's value to the wrong body. It has to
be the innermost.

Two tests over transcribed frames pinned it: one for a direct generator that
yields again after resuming, which **passed** and so ruled out the drive itself,
and one through a `Traversable` that failed with `the drive gave suspended, want
returned`. Isolating at the runtime level is what separated the two; from the
emitter side both looked like "the chain answers a stale value".

The fixture is back to the full shape -- suspend, resume, yield again, through
both an `IteratorAggregate` and a plain `yield from`.

Fixtures 316 -> 317, userland probe 328/331 with 0 failed, gate clean.

**`bg6` 2608 / 921 / 379 / 1: the only gain is the non-deterministic
`message_004`, so +0.** The innermost-parked fix is corpus-neutral, and that is
the honest reading rather than a disappointing one: no corpus file resumes a
parked chain and then yields again. It is a real correctness fix with a fixture
and two unit tests behind it, and it bought nothing measurable. Both halves of
that sentence are worth keeping.

## Where the gaps are after the fiber work

Re-censused rather than assumed. The **refusal** tail is flat: excluding
`include or eval` (141, refused by design), nothing is above 7, and the largest
items are unimplemented library functions -- `stream_wrapper_register`,
`preg_match`, `highlight_string` -- rather than anything architectural. The
fiber/generator family went **396 -> 379 refusals with +13 passes** over three
runs and what is left of it is four files.

The **failures** are where the work now is, and they are not a long tail:

- **212 of 921 are the same size** -- the output's shape is right and a value is
  wrong.
- Of those, roughly **100 are object identity or destruction ordering**:
  `object(C)#N`, `lazy proxy object(C)#N`, `C::__destruct` and the `int(N)` that
  is a `spl_object_id`. A handle number is a statement about when something
  died.
- The stack-frame family, which this session took from 47 divergences to a

## 2026-09-24 -- Suspending outside a fiber is a message, not a gap

Sizing the remaining refusals **by mechanism** this time, after the last entry's
estimate missed by twenty: `runtime:` refusals split into `getIterator` (13),
`{main}` (8), runtime-invoked closures (12) and `rewind` (3).

Opening one `{main}` case answered it: `Fiber::suspend(1)` at top level is not a
capability at all. It is `FiberError: Cannot suspend outside of a fiber`, and we
were reporting a missing feature where PHP has a diagnostic -- the exact shape
`unsupported-versus-php-errors.md` warns about, on the other side.

So the ordinary entry point of a suspending body no longer refuses. It drives
its own frame, and `RunUndriven` keeps the refusal for the one case that still
is one: arriving there from **inside** a fiber, which means the call came by a
path the rewrite could not see.

Two corrections while getting it right, both found by the fixture and both about
*where* something happens rather than whether:

- **The error is raised at the suspension point, not in the driver.** Raised
  after the body had already handed `Suspended` out, it landed outside every
  handler the body has, so `try { Fiber::suspend(1); } catch` did not catch it.
  The engine raises it where the call is written. `SuspendOutsideFiber` is now
  the check the suspension site makes before giving control up.
- **An exception unwinds frame by frame.** `callStack` abandoned the whole stack
  on an error from an inner frame, so an exception from a suspending callee
  sailed past a `try` written around the call. Each caller now gets it raised at
  its own suspension point -- `ResumeThrowing` on the frame below -- which is
  what lets its `try` catch and its `finally` run. That was a stated shortcut in
  the original `callStack` comment and it was wrong; PHP unwinds, it does not
  abandon.

## 2026-09-24 -- Suspending callees reached as methods, and what that did not fix

Censusing `bf8`'s refusals put the largest remaining "suspends into its caller"
group on **`getIterator` -- 12 files** -- with `__invoke` (2) and closures (9)
behind it. All method-shaped, and the split matched only a bare function name
while the graph keys a method `class::method`. So: widen it.

`SuspendingCallee` now takes the call's **kind** as well as its name, because a
method site carries a bare name and a receiver class inference may not have
supplied. With a receiver the answer is exact; without one every method of that
name is a candidate, which is the same conservative reading `Reach(methods:
true)` gives the graph's own edges and the one the earlier measurement priced at
0.0% against the exact answer.

The call side needed a run-time table, `methodFrames`, keyed class -> folded
method: which `__invoke` runs is a run-time fact. `frame.of.method` looks the
constructor up through the receiver's class chain exactly as the dispatcher
looks up the body; `frame.of.static` resolves at emit time. Method and closure
bodies already had `_frame` constructors -- the branch that emits them was
generic all along -- so only the call side was missing.

**And then it did not move `getIterator`.** The refusal there is a *runtime*
one, not an emit-time one, and that distinction is the whole finding: in
`gh15108-001` nothing in the IR calls `getIterator`. The delegate machinery
behind `yield from new It()` calls back into user code through a hook, so there
is no call site to split. Same for `new Fiber($obj)` reaching `__invoke`.

That is a different mechanism -- **the runtime entering user code resumably** --
and it is where those ~14 files live. One half of it is now done, because
`resumableOf` can build an `__invoke` frame out of the same table: a fiber over
an invocable object works, and `backtrace-object` passes. The other half is the
delegate machinery, which still enters `getIterator` as an ordinary call.

## 2026-09-23 -- Frames for a suspending call, which step 3 owed

A call performed as `Called` is entered by the driver rather than by a Go call,
so nothing at the call site was left to push a frame for it. A backtrace through
one was two frames short:

    #0 [internal function]: suspend_fiber()      <- missing entirely
    #1 [internal function]: {closure:...}()      <- missing entirely
    #2 file(15): Fiber->resume()

**Where the identity comes from.** A generated frame now answers `TraceName()`
and `TraceArgs()`; `callStack` asks. The name is the declared spelling, as
everywhere else, and for a closure it goes through the same absolute-to-relative
path substitution `diagName` and `closureMeta` make -- the harvest bakes the
engine's absolute path into `{closure:FILE:LINE}` while every position the
program reports is the path it refers to itself by, and a trace naming a closure
has to agree with the rest.

**The frames are pushed per step, not once.** A CPS frame is entered many times
and the Go stack that held it is gone by the time control comes back, which is
the whole reason it is explicit here.

**The body's own frame is the fiber driver's, and only the fiber's.** A
generator's driver already pushes one -- it knows the name, the arguments, and
the line that drove it -- so `callStack` pushes the root only when asked, which
`NewFiber` does and `StartGenerator` does not. It is located at
`[internal function]`, because the engine enters the body from inside `start()`
or `resume()`.

**The bug worth keeping: `PopCall` restores the position.** Reading
`ctx.Location()` to capture a call site *after* undoing the frame pushes gave
the driver's position, so every called frame was located at
`[internal function]` instead of at the line that called it. The position has to
be read before the undo. Nothing about the code looked wrong -- `PopCall` is
named for what it removes, not for what it restores -- and the symptom was one
correct-looking frame with the wrong location.

## 2026-09-23 -- Step 3: a fiber suspends through a call

`bf5` first: **2586 / 910 / 412 / 1, gained 0 lost 0** -- step 2 was exactly
corpus-neutral, and the 45 refusals changed their reason without changing their
bucket, which is what it was supposed to do.

Then the emission, and it works: a `Fiber::suspend()` two frames down now
suspends and resumes correctly, through a named function and through a closure.

**The protocol.** A new outcome, `Called`, carries the callee's frame -- built
and not entered. `callStack` holds those frames and is itself a `Resumable`, so
both drivers wrap their body in one and are otherwise untouched: a `Called`
never escapes, and what a driver sees is whatever the innermost frame produced.
The generator and fiber drivers disagree about what a suspension *means* and
neither needs to know a call is in progress underneath. The stack is explicit on
purpose -- it is the thing a goroutine would have made implicit, and the thing a
byte-exact backtrace has to be read off.

Three bugs on the way, each instructive:

- **The terminator carried the whole call.** Rendering an argument list is the
  call machinery's job and a terminator has none of it, so the split now leaves
  the call an *instruction* -- `frame.of.fn`, which builds the frame and runs
  none of it -- and the terminator carries only the frame value.
  `ret.yield_from <src>` had this shape all along.
- **`Frame: %7`.** The terminator rendered the raw IR operand because I reached
  for the value unrendered; `operand` was wrong too, since it renders a zval and
  this is a `php.Resumable`.
- **The graph had no edges.** `Reach` answered `{inner}` and not `{outer}`, so a
  caller one level up never split. `CallGraph.Link()` resolves sites into edges
  and is a separate step because a site can only be resolved once every
  definition is known. I called `Add`, `PropagateMarks` and `Reach` and skipped
  the one in the middle.

**And one that was silent, which is the one worth keeping.** `$a = strlen($v);
return $a . inner($v);` came back `"R!"` where the engine says `"2R!"` -- `$a`
simply gone, no error anywhere. The IR's rule is that no SSA value is used
outside its defining block and the frame holds exactly the places; `mem2reg` had
already promoted `$a` to a value because the call was not a boundary when it
ran, and the split made it one. Values crossing the new boundary are demoted
back to places, which puts them in the frame. A wrong answer with nothing to
catch it: the fixture is what caught it, and only because it kept a value across
the call.

Measured on `Zend/tests/fibers`: refusals **28 -> 15**, passes 23 -> 25, failures
27 -> 37. Refusals becoming attempted behaviour is the point, and failures rising
alongside is the expected shape -- read together, not separately. Of the new
failures ~11 are destructor ordering (the refcount family, untouched by this) and
**~4 are stack frames through the new call stack**, which this change owes: a
call performed as `Called` pushes no frame, so a backtrace through one is short.
That is the next piece.

Fixtures 311 -> 312, gate clean.

**Measured.** `bf6` 2588 / 920 / 399 / 2, then `bf7` 2587 / 921 / 399 / **1**
after the fix below. Against `bf5`'s 2586 / 910 / 412 / 1 that is **unsupported
-13** and passed +1, with the +/-1 on `message_004` being the known
non-deterministic file. Thirteen files stopped being refused; two of them --
`fibers/gh10496-002` and `fibers/suspend-in-nested-function` -- went all the way
to passing, and the rest now fail on behaviour rather than being declined.

**`errored` ticking 1 -> 2 is what caught the last bug**, and it is worth saying
why that mattered: the headline was +2 and underneath it was a generated program
that did not build. `ctx.EndSilence(int64(v$__cps0))` -- not an identifier. Four
emitters render an operand with `val` rather than `operand`, because their
operands are not zvals at all: they are places and iterators, called as
`x.unset(ctx)` or `x.get(ctx)`. Demotion can now turn any of them into a place,
and `val` on a place produces garbage while `operand` on a non-zval is wrong the
other way. `frameOf` gives the slot the value's own Go type, so one renderer
answers both -- `f.p___cps0.unset(ctx)` and `v3.unset(ctx)` are the same thing.
That file now compiles and runs, failing on behaviour (a silence spanning a
suspension), which is the honest direction.

A capability change that converts refusals into attempts will raise `failed` and
can hide a build failure inside the gain. Reading all four buckets is what the
quality gate asks for, and this is the run that shows why.

## 2026-09-23 -- Step 2: the call graph reaches the compile path

`Reach` existed only inside `cmd/php2lower`'s `-callgraph` report, so the set a
body must be judged against was not available where the lowering runs. Now it
is.

**The compile path had to become two phases.** Every site was
`lw.Lower(...)` -> `resumable(fn)` -> `specialize(fn)`, inline, which cannot
work once the rewrite needs a whole-unit answer: a graph needs every body first.
Lowering now `record`s bodies and `finishBodies` runs the two passes afterwards,
in the order they used to run. The graph is built **before** anything is
rewritten, and the reason that matters is not the obvious one -- yes, a
suspension terminator becomes `ret.suspend`, but the one that actually bites is
that a suspending *call* becomes a terminator, so the call instruction the graph
reads its edges from is no longer an instruction.

**A bug the fixtures caught immediately: generators are not fiber suspensions.**
Seeding from `CallGraph.Reach` dropped the fixtures 311 -> 297, and all 14
refusals were *generator* files. `Reach` seeds from `cgNode.suspends`, which
counts `yield` -- correct for the question it was built for, "how far can a
suspension of any kind be from the top of the stack", and wrong for this one.
Calling a generator function returns a Generator object and suspends nobody, so
`yield` says nothing about a function's callers; `cps.go` states exactly this
and I wired past it. `ReachFiber` seeds from `fiber.suspend`/`ret.suspend` only.
`Reach` is left alone so the php2lower report keeps measuring what it measured.

Verified end to end: a chain of `Fiber::suspend()` inside `inner()` called from
`outer()` now refuses with **`emit: terminator ret.call`** where it used to
refuse with `call to inner, which suspends into its caller`. The caller question
is answered in the lowering; what is left is emission, which is step 3.

One trap worth noting: `bodies` is package-level and this binary compiles
thousands of files in one process, so it is cleared per unit. Left accumulating,
the second file would rewrite the first file's bodies a second time -- a CPS
rewrite over an already-rewritten body, with nothing to say so.

Fixtures 311, userland probe 328/331 with 0 failed, gate clean. `bf5` is in
flight to confirm the corpus is unmoved; the 45 refusals should keep their
bucket and change their reason.

## 2026-09-23 -- Step 1 of the fiber plan: a call becomes a suspension point

The first piece of the plan that was already written down, rather than a
mechanism of my own. `internal/lower/cps.go` split a block only at a direct
`fiber.suspend` terminator, so a *call* to a suspending function handed an
`Outcome` back to a frame with nowhere to put one -- which is why gogen refuses
those calls outright and why 45 corpus files sit in `unsupported`.

**The shape is `yield from`'s, not `yield`'s.** Control leaves at the call, the
callee's frame runs, and this function resumes with the callee's **return
value** rather than with anything it yielded. So the call's result becomes the
continuation block's first parameter, which is exactly where the existing
rewrite takes the resumed value from -- no new resume machinery, just a block
split and a terminator.

`Resumable` now takes a `SuspendingCallee` predicate. It is supplied rather than
computed because "can this callee suspend" is a whole-program property
(`CallGraph.Reach`) and the pass sees one function. Every caller passes `nil`
today, so nothing splits and the corpus is unmoved: fixtures 311, gate clean.
Wiring the graph into the compile path is step 2, and `Reach` is currently
computed only in `cmd/php2lower`'s report.

A split also marks `SuspendsToCaller` on the splitting function, since control
now leaves it for the driver and its own callers are in the same position.

**The test passed before the code was right.** Asserting the split happened, the
state machine formed, and `frame.resumed` appeared -- all true -- while the
terminator read `ret.call call.fn "App\inner"` with **no arguments**. A call's
`ArgList` is deliberately kept out of `Operands` so it can attach to the callee,
and joining only the operands dropped every argument and the `fallback=`
attribute with them. Nothing downstream reads them yet, so nothing failed; it
would have broken the first time something tried to perform the call, a step
later and with no obvious cause.

Dumping the IR is what caught it, and that is the lesson worth keeping: for a
pass that rewrites structure, assert on the **rendered** result, not only on
counts and flags. Both facts now have their own assertions.

Corrected by the user, and the correction is right. I spent a tick "settling"

**The recorded reason is better than mine and defeats it.** A goroutine gives

ordering, so the suspension has to stay explicit data the emitter can see and
order. I had just spent eleven corpus runs making backtraces byte-exact and

that `gh15108-004`'s delegate-as-a-parameter defeats static analysis is answered

read `TODO.md` only where it touched the family I was already in. A settled
decision with a plan sat 300 lines further down the same file. The lesson is
narrow and worth keeping: *before choosing a mechanism, grep TODO.md for the

- `newLazyGhost` / `newLazyProxy` allocation order on its own: **matches**.
- A failed `clone` of a lazy object, ghost and proxy: **matches**.
- Reassignment release, function-local death, catch-variable rebinding:

exactly what the plan means by "static liveness matches refcount timing only

## 2026-09-23 -- A generator body's frame, and one fix left on the floor

The generator cluster was three defects behind one symptom, and the third is
the interesting one because it is **not** landed.

- **The Generator driver's frame was not internal.** A body resumed by
  `$g->next()` is entered from inside the engine and renders
  `#0 [internal function]: g2()`. Marking `Generator->next()` internal is the
  whole fix -- `PushCall` already carries the rule -- and a `foreach`, which
  drives without one of those frames, correctly keeps the loop's own location.
- **Neither frame carried arguments.** `Generator->send('x')` read
  `Generator->send()`, and the body's frame read `gen()` where the engine says
  `gen(Object(stdClass))`. The driver's are to hand at the push; the body's had
  to be kept on the generator, because the frame is pushed fresh on every resume
  and names the original call each time.

- **`yield from` loses the delegating frame, and the fix is reverted.**
  `resume` advances the delegate without the delegating generator's frame on
  the stack, so a throw two levels down traced `#0 from(2)` then `{main}` where
  the engine has `#1 outer()` between them. Pushing it produced the right
  *structure* -- and the wrong lines: the engine locates the delegate's frame at
  the `yield from` site **inside the delegating body**, and ours used the
  driver's line, so both frames came out at the `foreach`. The body moves the
  reported location as it executes, and the driver call has already restored it
  by the time the delegate advances.

  A structurally-right, positionally-wrong trace fails the same files the
  missing frame did, so the change bought nothing and added a live push to a
  resume path. Reverted. What it did buy is the diagnosis, which is filed:
  the delegating body's suspended position has to be restored before the
  delegate is advanced, and the Generator does not currently keep it.

clean.
