**+6** -- all generators: `backtrace`, `bug63066`,
`errors/resume_running_generator_error`, `finally/yield_throw`,
`throw_rethrow`, `yield_from_backtrace`. `bd4` 2551 -> `bf4` 2586, **+35**.

## 2026-09-23 -- A property hook's frame, and the table that sat above the push

A hook's frame is spelled unlike anything else in a trace: the declaring class,
an arrow, the property **with its `$`**, then `::` and the hook --
`A->$prop::set('x')`. Arguments are the hook's own, so a `set` names the value
and a `get` names nothing. `runtime/interp` had it; compiled output pushed
nothing at any of the four hook call sites.

The declaring class again, not the receiver's -- a hook declared in `A` reached
on a `B extends A` still renders `A->$prop::set(...)`. `propHooks` is keyed by
the *instance's* class, so an entry could not say who declared it; `Prop.Class`
already knew, and now rides on the entry.

**The probe earned its keep on the last line.** `get_object_vars($c)` on a
hooked object wants `#0 [internal function]: A->$prop::get()`, and gave the call
site instead. The hook frame was right; what was missing was the frame *beneath*
it. `get_object_vars` is scope-sensitive, and `callBuiltin` dispatched the
scope-sensitive table in its first four lines -- **above** the push it added for
every other builtin. So those builtins had no frame of their own, and nothing
they called could be located against one.

The comment there still read "One builtin is scope-sensitive", naming
`property_exists`. The table had grown to include `get_object_vars` and the
comment had not, which is what made the early return look deliberate rather than
stale. Both fixed.

That is the second time this session a frame turned out to be missing *under*
the thing being fixed rather than at it -- the first was the callback whose
`array_map` frame was fine and whose own was absent. Worth checking the frame
below before concluding a frame is mislabelled.

Three corpus files wanted a frame named literally `[constant expression]()`.
A deferred initializer is evaluated with the reported position moved to where it
was **written**, and a trace taken under that override gains a synthetic entry
recording where the program actually was: forcing `const K = 1 %% 0` from line 15
gives `#0 file(15): [constant expression]()`.

`runtime/interp` had all of this already, probed, in `enterConstExpression` --
including that the frame appears only when the two positions differ and only for
the outermost evaluation, so a constant reaching through another moves the
position again and adds no second frame. Compiled output had `constAt`, which is
the same function with the frame half missing: it moved the position and stopped
there. The depth counter went on `Ctx` so both back-ends can ask; the
interpreter keeps its own on the Unit and is untouched.

The part that needed the fixture to find is the exception. **A bare constant
fetch is not evaluated in its own frame at all**: `const K = SOME_CONSTANT;`
reports an undefined constant against the *use* site and adds nothing, while
`SOME_CONSTANT + 0` in the same place reports against the declaration and does.
`runtime/interp` calls this `evaluatedInOwnFrame` and had probed it both ways;
gogen now gates on the same expression kind. Without it the new frame appeared
on a case the engine leaves bare -- a regression introduced by the fix, caught
only because the fixture asked for both spellings side by side.

Found on the way and **not** fixed: re-reading a class constant whose
initializer already threw answers `NULL` instead of raising again. The engine

## 2026-09-23 -- Constructors, and a dimension that only looks like a method call

Two ends of the engine-frame family, and they pull in opposite directions.

**Constructors needed a frame added.** `new ReflectionClass("Nope")` and
`new WeakReference()` never reach `callMethod` -- construction is its own path
-- so `engineFramed` never saw them and both opened their trace at the `new`.
`runCtor` splits: the user-class switch stays, then an engine class that claims
`__construct` gets the same framed call the methods get, and `runEngineCtor`
holds the remainder.

The comment already in `runCtor` is what made this safe to do, and it is worth
restating because it is a trap: PHP captures a throwable's trace **at `new`,
before the constructor runs**, so a frame around the exception-class arm would
put `__construct` into every exception's own trace. The exception classes are
not in the modelled engine set, so nothing claims their `__construct` and the
new push cannot reach them -- but that is a property to keep, not a coincidence
to rely on silently, so the fixture now asserts it.

**And one needed a frame taken away.** `$map[$k]` on a WeakMap is not a method
call: the engine reads it through the object's own handler and pushes nothing.
`arrayAccessCall` routed every `ArrayAccess` dimension through `callMethod`, so
the moment `weakCall` got framed, every WeakMap dimension read grew a
`WeakMap->offsetGet(...)` frame the engine does not have. Written out as
`$map->offsetGet($k)` it **is** a call and does get one -- so the two spellings
genuinely differ, and the fix is a direct route for the store rather than a
narrower frame. A subclass declaring its own body still runs it.

That is the shape worth remembering: adding a frame in a shared dispatcher adds
it to every caller of that dispatcher, including the ones that reach it for
syntax rather than for a call. The probe caught it only because it read a
WeakMap dimension; a fixture built around the methods alone would have shipped
it.

Fixtures 308 all passing, userland probe 328/331 with 0 failed, gate clean.
**`bf1` is not a result.** I edited `runtime/php/ctx.go` while it was in
flight -- the hazard TESTING.md documents twice, under two headings -- and 384
files failed to build. `tally.sh`'s guard caught it and refused to compare, so
no wrong number reached the record. The rule is that `internal/gogen` edits are
safe mid-run because the harness binary is frozen, while `runtime/php` edits are
not, because each generated program links the live tree. Knowing the rule is
evidently not the same as remembering it at the moment of typing; the guard is
what actually held.

`weakrefs/weakrefs_005`). Across the frame work, `bd4` 2551 -> `bf2` 2577,
**+26**.

## 2026-09-23 -- Who declares an engine method, asked of the same harvest

The spelling table wanted one more column. A frame names the **declaring engine
class**, not the receiver's: `class MyRef extends ReflectionClass` failing in
`getMethod` renders `ReflectionClass->getMethod('nope')`. Probed; the engine is
unambiguous.

The table could not answer that, because it carried only the methods whose
declaration is not already lower-case -- enough to spell a name, useless for
deciding who owns one, and `__construct` was absent from it entirely. Carrying
every method fixes both questions with one table: the spelling is the value, and
the *presence of the key* is the ownership. `engineMethodOwner` then walks the
receiver's parent chain until a class claims the folded name, which is what
turns a user subclass into its engine ancestor.

With that in hand, `weakCall` and `reflectorMethod` get frames through one
shared `engineFramed` rather than a copy each. Two things it does **not** do,
both deliberate:

- **It does not mark the frame internal.** The Fiber frame does, because the
  engine enters a body the program wrote from inside `start`. These methods
  answer for themselves; nothing is pushed on top that would need a location.
- **It pushes nothing when no engine class claims the name.** There is no
  declaration to name a frame after, and the call is about to be refused anyway.

Still unframed and now clearly separate: the engine **constructors**.
`new ReflectionClass('NoSuchClass')` and `new WeakReference()` raise with the

## 2026-09-23 -- An engine class's method needs a frame, and a fiber body is entered from inside one

one `PushCall` already states, and it applies here the moment the Fiber method's
own frame is marked internal, which it is: the engine enters the body from
inside `start`, not from a line of PHP. So `MarkInternalCall` on the Fiber frame

## 2026-09-23 -- A stack frame names a method as it was declared

Follow-on from the callback frames above, and the same shape a sixth and
seventh time: a rule implemented in the static dispatcher and not in the
instance one, and a decision made before the push on one path and after it on
the other.

**The spelling.** The engine names a frame by the **declaring class and the
declaration's own spelling**: `(new B)->instmeth()` on `A::InstMeth` renders
`A->InstMeth()`, and `B::statmeth()` renders `A::StatMeth()`. Neither the call
site's spelling nor the folded name appears. `methodOwnerOf` has returned the
declared spelling as its second result all along -- the static dispatcher takes
it for the refusals it quotes -- and the instance dispatcher discarded it with
`_` and built the frame from `lower`. So every trace naming a method whose
declaration is not already lowercase was wrong: `It->getiterator()`,
`Bad->__tostring()`, `Fiber->getreturn()`. The static push had the value in
hand and used the *call site's* `name` instead, which is wrong for a
differently-spelled call.

The call site's own spelling still matters in exactly one place, unchanged:
`__call` and `__callStatic` receive it as their first argument.

**The spurious frame.** A name that is not a method gets no frame of its own.
`A::nope()` on a class with `__callStatic` renders
`A::__callStatic('nope', Array)` and nothing else, and without one the
undefined-method Error names no frame either. The instance dispatcher already
decided this before pushing -- there is a comment there saying so -- and the
static dispatcher pushed unconditionally and put `A->nope()` underneath. Guarded
on `known`, which `methodOwnerOf` already answers.

Both found by probing the 43 frame-line divergences that survived `be4`, after
the callback fix moved only 4 of the census family's 25. The census names a
file's *first* divergence, so a family counted by symptom held two causes.

**And a trait alias renames the method for the trace.** `be5` measured the two
fixes above at **2557 / 939 / 412 / 1**, gaining 5 and losing 3 -- and the three
losses named the cause exactly: `bug64239_4`, `bug70156`,
`bug69180-backtrace`, all trait aliases. `use T { t2method as Bmethod; }` gives
one body two names, and a frame names the one that was *called*: `A::Bmethod()`
and `A::t2method()` both appear. The function keeps the trait's own `Name` --
the body is shared with every class that composes it -- so the alias clause is
the only place that spelling exists, and taking `fn.Name` for it named every
aliased call after the trait's original. `zend_find_alias_name` is the engine
doing the same lookup, and it is in bug70156's own title.

The IR already carried `Class.TraitAliases`; gogen's class model carries it
forward and had it in hand. `methodOwnerOf`'s spelling table now walks the class
chain applying aliases last, so a composed name inherited from a parent keeps
the parent's clause and the alias wins over the declaration it renames. The
three files pass.

Worth keeping: the old spellings were wrong in *compensating* ways. The instance
dispatcher's folded name matched an all-lowercase alias, and the static
dispatcher's call-site spelling matched an alias called as written -- so both
regressions only appeared once the declaration became the source of truth. A
fix that is right in general can lose files that a wrong rule happened to cover.

Fixture `method_frame_spelling.php` covers twenty shapes: both dispatchers, an
inherited method, a differently-cased call, a dynamic method name, both magic
fallbacks, a class with neither, both callable forms, and seven trait-alias
cases including an alias reached through a subclass and one called in the wrong
case. Fixtures 305 -> 306, all passing; userland probe unchanged at 328/331 with
0 failed.

Corpus: **`be6` 2563 / 933 / 412 / 1**, gaining 6 and losing 0 against `be5`.
One is the non-deterministic `message_004`, so +5: the three alias regressions
recovered plus `bug64239_2` and `bug64239_3`. Across the two changes the frame
work is `bd4` 2551 -> `be6` 2563, **+12**.

## 2026-09-23 -- A callback reached from a library function had no frame at all

`getTraceAsString` on an exception thrown inside `array_map('boom', ...)` was one
line short in compiled output: the engine opens it at
`#0 [internal function]: boom(1)`, and compiled output opened it at the
`array_map(...)` call site instead. Two separate defects, found by instrumenting
`PushCall` rather than by reading the renderer -- the renderer already handled
`InternalFrameFile`; the frame simply was not there.

1. **`callValue`'s named-function branch pushed no frame.** `userFuncs[name]`
   resolved to the body and was called as `fn(ctx, args)` directly, so the callee
   was absent from every backtrace taken inside it. The closure and method
   branches beside it both pushed one. A check living in one branch only --
   this session's most common bug shape, now five instances.
2. **`callBuiltin` pushed its frame after `verifyBuiltinArgs`.** The argument
   check raises, so an `ArgumentCountError` against a library function named the
   *caller* as its innermost frame. The engine raises it inside the function:
   `#0 [internal function]: strtoupper('ab', 9)`.

The location rule is the engine's own and is now stated once, in `PushCall`: a
frame pushed while the frame below it is marked `Internal` is located at
`[internal function]`, unless `Ctx.CallSite()` names a place in the script -- an
error handler runs where the diagnostic was raised and says so. `runtime/interp`
already set `InternalFrameFile` explicitly at its two callback sites and reads
the same `CallSite` field, so it is unaffected; putting the rule in `PushCall`
covers the compiled closure, method and static-callable branches without
touching any of them.

The frame carries the **declared** spelling, not the callable's:
`array_map("BOOM", ...)` reaching `function Boom()` reads `Boom(1)`. `userFuncs`
is keyed on the folded name, so a `userFuncNames` table now recovers it, emitted
only for the functions whose declaration is not already lowercase.

`call_user_func('Boom', 7)` needs none of this -- Zend's own compiler folds a
literal one into a direct call, so there is no callback frame and the callee
names the real call site. That was already right and stays right.

Measured: the userland probe went 327/331 passed with 1 failed to **328/331 with
0 failed** (3 unsupported: `array_filter`, `instanceof Generator`, `eval`), which
retires the `c0016` remainder. Fixtures 304 -> 305, all passing.

## 2026-09-20 -- The undecided send, and a regression the fixtures could not see

`bb4`: 2542 / 945 / 412 / **8** -- a net **regression** against `ba4`'s 2545,
gaining 4 and losing 7, with `errored` up from 1 to 8. `bc4`, after the fix:
**2549 / 946 / 412 / 1**, so the change is +4 once it works.

**The change.** `ZEND_SEND_FUNC_ARG` -- the engine's send for an argument
*fetched* as a write target, where only the callee knows whether it wanted a
reference -- was lowered as `byval`. So `$f = "byref"; $f($a["k"])` read the
element instead of binding it: a warning about an undefined key, and an array
left untouched where the engine autovivifies and binds. Fixing the mode alone
would only have converted wrong answers into refusals, so the send is now
actually decided: a **static** callee settles it at compile time from the
signature in hand, a **dynamic** one asks `calleeWantsRef` at run time (strings
through `namedCallableParams`, closures from their own body), and unknown means
by value -- the safe direction, since reading an absent element warns while
binding one autovivifies storage the program never asked for.

**The regression, and why it matters more than the fix.** The by-value branch
next door has always asked **two** questions -- `e.vtypes` for a value and
`e.ptypes` for a slot holding one. My branch asked only the first, so a
slot-typed place went into the argument slice as a `place` struct. That does not
compile.

Seven corpus files failed to build, and **every one failed inside the linked
userland library** -- `parse_ini_string`, not the test's own source. So:

> `go test ./...` passed. All 303 fixtures passed. Neither suite mentions the
> code that failed to build, because the generated program *contains* the 274
> PHP functions of `internal/userland` and no test file names them.

The userland probe built two ticks earlier covers exactly that class, and I did
not re-run it before spending a 45-minute corpus run. It reports 297/300 with
**0 errored** now and would have shown this in ten minutes. The ordering is
written into TESTING.md: build/vet/test, fixtures, **probe**, corpus -- with
this failure as the worked example of what the probe catches that the other two
structurally cannot.

**`bd4`**: 2551 / 944 / 412 / 1, +2 clean, fixing the nested by-reference
target the undecided-send fixture had stopped short of.

The diagnosis was **lifetime ordering**, not a missing feature. `$a["k"]["j"]`
opens `$a["k"]` as a box and builds the inner place inside it; that box is a
mechanism the program never asked for and must be collapsed again -- but the
emitter ran the release where the place was *built*, not where it is *used*. The
storage was gone before anything wrote through it, so `byref($a["k"]["j"])` gave
`["k"] => NULL`. The release now travels on the place and is composed into
whatever release its user already returns, so the outer box collapses after the
inner write. That the engine shows no `&` on `$a["k"]` afterwards is what proves
the box must still be collapsed -- only later.

This tick also followed the TESTING.md ordering written the tick before --
build/vet/test, fixtures, **probe**, corpus -- rather than skipping to the run.

Session so far: 2211 -> 2551.

## 2026-09-20 -- An array copy keeps its internal pointer

`az3`: 2544, +2 real -- but it carried a **regression**, `bug38808`, and that
was the whole tick. `ba4`: **2545 / 951 / 412 / 1**, restoring it and gaining
`bug73753` as well.

**What broke it.** Routing callable builtins through `callBuiltin` (previous
entry) means a boxed argument is now unboxed for a by-value parameter --
`a.Deref().Copy()`. That exposed a bug that had been sitting underneath:

> **php2go's array copy dropped the internal pointer.** So `$f = "current";
> $f($a)` always answered the *first* element, however far `next()` had
> advanced.

Asked the engine rather than reasoning about it. After `next($a)`, **both**
`$b = $a` and a by-value `array $x` parameter see `current()` as the advanced
element: PHP's copy is refcounted and the pointer belongs to the array, so it
travels. Fixed in `Array.clone`, mapping the position through the first live
bucket at or after it -- the index cannot be carried across directly, because
deleted buckets are skipped while copying and every position after a hole
shifts.

**Two process notes, both corrections to my own method:**

- My first four reconstructions of the failing case all **passed**. The
  difference was that the real test's *final* read was also dynamic. I had
  recorded "run the failing case's exact text first, and vary it afterwards"
  two ticks earlier and then did not follow it. Going back to `bug38808.phpt`
  itself and bisecting from there found it immediately. A rule written down is
  not a rule followed.
- This is the same shape as `gh10043-011` earlier in the session: a correct
  change **surfacing** a latent bug rather than causing one. The tally cannot
  tell those apart -- a lost file looks identical either way -- so a loss is a
  reason to read the file, never a reason to revert on sight.

Session so far: 2211 -> 2545.

## 2026-09-20 -- `*RECURSION*` was two bugs pointing opposite ways

`aw3`: **2540 / 955 / 412 / 1**, gained 2 lost 0. The fixture suite is **298/298
-- fully green for the first time this session**, closing a failure that had
stood since the first tick.

`print_r_library.php` wanted `*RECURSION*` where we printed a nested array, and
the userland probe's `$a = array(); $a[0] = $a;` wanted a nested array where we
printed `*RECURSION*`. Opposite symptoms, two unrelated causes:

- **Assignment copies, and the dimension write did not.** `$a[0] = $a` must
  store what `$a` *was*; `writeDim` stored the value uncopied, so the element
  held the same `*Array` and every dump saw a cycle. `ArraySet` -- the
  array-literal path -- had been copying all along. One of two write paths was
  right, which is why no test of *construction* ever caught it.
- **`print_r`'s recursion guard rests on array identity, and its entry point
  destroyed it.** `print_r_render_impl` is careful: it takes its subject by
  reference precisely because php2go copies eagerly, and `array_id` is in
  `internalRefArgs` for the same reason -- the comment there says it is "the
  whole reason the table exists". But `print_r_impl`, one frame above, took
  `mixed $value` **by value**. So the render got a clone whose identity differs
  from the array the program holds, while an element bound with `&$a` still
  points at the original; the guard saw two identities for one array and fired a
  level too late.

The second is the more interesting failure. Every part of the mechanism was
built, documented and correct -- and the value was copied one frame before any
of it ran. A guard that depends on identity is only as good as the *shallowest*
frame that still holds the original.

**`ax3`** then measured the next probe finding: 2542 / 953 / 412 / 1, +2. A
compound assign through a variable variable did not warn -- `$$n .= "x"` on an
unset name owes `Warning: Undefined variable $a`, exactly as `$a .= "x"` does.

The cause inverts the usual one. Normally something is missing when a read needs
it; here the **storage was created too early**: `dynvarSlot` creates the slot
before the read, so by the time the read runs there is storage holding undef and
nothing left to notice. The name had to travel on the `place` for the read to be
able to say it.

Scoped to local variables on purpose. `$GLOBALS["nope"] .= "x"` has its own
wording ("Undefined global variable") and was not measured in the *compound*
position; assuming it matches is the same move that went wrong earlier with the
`.phpt` resource expectations.

**`ay3`**: 2542 / 952 / 412 / 1, +1 real (`ArrayAccess_indirect_append`).
`f($undef[])` with a by-reference parameter created **two** elements: reaching
an append target on a variable that is not yet an array runs an autovivifying
placeholder write, which creates the array *and* its first element, and the
append branch then made a second.

Worth recording how nearly it was missed. My first isolated probe **passed**,

## 2026-09-20 -- Compiled output never counted arguments

`au3`: **2538 / 958 / 412 / 1**, +2 real against `at3`'s 2535.

The probe's `ob_start("strtoupper")` case looked narrow -- PHP calls an output
callback with **two** arguments, so `strtoupper` raises `ArgumentCountError`.
Chasing it found something much wider:

> **Compiled output never checked argument counts at all.** The emitted
> `verifyBuiltinArgs` verified argument *types* and stopped, so
> `strtoupper("a","b")` quietly answered `"AB"`, `strtoupper()` answered `""`,
> and `count([1],0,9)` simply counted.

The interpreter had a correct implementation the whole time
(`verifyBuiltinArity`). That is the fourth instance this session of a check
living in one back-end only, so the rule went to `runtime/php` and the
interpreter now calls it too. It returns the **message** rather than raising,
because the interpreter attaches a frame the compiled program does not have --
the shared part is the rule and its wording, not the throw.

Three wordings, measured rather than guessed, because the choice is not obvious:

    strtoupper("a","b")   exactly 1 argument, 2 given
    substr("abc")         at least 2 arguments, 1 given
    count([1],0,9)        at most 2 arguments, 3 given

`exactly` is used **only** when the parameter list is fixed and fully required;
otherwise too few is `at least` and too many is `at most`. The number named is
the bound that was missed, not the count given, and it is singular for 1.

**A second half that is easy to miss.** `str_pad` and `ucfirst` are among the
274 functions reimplemented in PHP under `internal/userland`. Their generated
prologue checks for too *few* arguments and ignores extras -- which is right for
an ordinary PHP function and wrong for one standing in for a builtin, because
`str_pad("a",2,"b",STR_PAD_RIGHT,9)` must say `str_pad() expects at most 4
arguments, 5 given` rather than accept them. A body that impersonates a builtin
inherits the builtin's refusals, not PHP's ordinary ones.

**`av3`** then measured the namespaced-name fix: 2538 / 957 / 412 / 1, gaining
`bug77376` and losing the non-deterministic `message_004`, so +1 real. An
unqualified call inside a namespace compiles to the namespaced name with the
global one as `fallback=`, and the emitter substituted the fallback *before*
raising -- so `namespace Ns; nope();` named `nope()` rather than `Ns\nope()`,
a function the source never wrote. The substitution is right whenever the
fallback exists, which is exactly why it was applied unconditionally.

## 2026-09-20 -- The probe pays: a bug found outside the corpus fixes four inside it

`at3`: **2535 / 960 / 412 / 1**, gained 4 lost 0 against `as3`. All four are
string-offset tests -- `bug49866`, `list_assign_ref_string_offset_error`,
`string_offset_optimization`, `str_offset_002` -- and none of them was what I
was looking at. The bug came from the userland probe, not the corpus.

That is the result worth recording about the probe: **a defect it finds is not
worth one file.** The corpus covers these behaviours in several places, so
fixing the behaviour moves several tests at once; the probe just happens to
show the behaviour more directly than any single `.phpt` does.

**The bug.** `&$s[0]` on a string threw
`TypeError: Cannot access offset of type on string` where PHP throws
`Error: Cannot create references to/from string offsets` -- wrong class as well
as wrong words. The cause was **ordering**: `DimRef` ran a placeholder write
first and then reported whatever *that* refused on, so the diagnostic described
a different operation than the one the program performed.

Three neighbouring errors had to be separated, and the rule is not the obvious
one:

> The refusal follows the **type, not whether the offset exists**. `$a = "";
> &$a[0]` refuses exactly as a populated string does, while `$a = null; &$a[0]`
> **autovivifies** an array and succeeds. A non-string scalar says `Cannot use a
> scalar value as an array`; appending to a string says `[] operator not
> supported for strings`.

Guessing any one of those from the others would have been wrong. All three are
in the fixture beside the cases that must keep succeeding, plus five
differential cases so the interpreter is held to the same rule.

## 2026-09-20 -- Turning the userland library into a miscompilation probe

`as3`: **2531 / 964 / 412 / 1**, +1 against `ar3`. The number is not the point
again; the method is.

The previous entry's bug -- a short-circuit `&&` answering its left operand --
was found by accident, because a duplicate implementation forced the userland
one to run. That is not a repeatable way to find miscompilations, so this tick
built one:

> `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` holds 311 cases for the functions
> reimplemented in PHP under `internal/userland`. They run **interpreter-only**.
> But the compiled back-end has to execute those same 274 PHP functions, and the
> engine has a native implementation of every one -- so running the same cases
> through `php2gotest` is a ready-made differential for the *compiler*, over
> several thousand lines of real PHP that no corpus test covers.

Extracted as single-line cases into `.agents-workspace/tmp/ulprobe` and run:
**289 of 300 pass, 9 fail, 2 unsupported.** Each of the nine is a real defect the
4,986-file corpus had not surfaced. They are listed in TODO.md.

The first one fixed: **`$GLOBALS["nope"]` has its own diagnostic wording** --
`Undefined global variable $nope`, not `Undefined variable $nope`. The wording
follows the **syntax, not the table**: `$$n` at file scope reads the very same
globals array and keeps the ordinary wording, so no scope test can separate
them, which is exactly how the two came to share one emitted path. The
interpreter had it right already (`interp.go:3349`).

emission printed `$%!!(string=nope)s(MISSING)`. `e.p` is Printf-style, so a `%s`

## 2026-09-20 -- A silent miscompilation, found by writing a function that already existed

`ar3`: **2530 / 965 / 412 / 1**, +2 against `aq3`'s 2529. The two files are not
the point of this entry.

**The route there was a mistake, and the mistake was the useful part.** The
`unsupported` census listed `ucfirst`. I checked both back-ends: the compiled
one refused it, and `php2eval` answered `unsupported opcode call to ucfirst` for
the interpreter. So I implemented `ucfirst`, `lcfirst` and `ucwords` in
`runtime/stdlib`, where both back-ends would get them.

A test I had never seen rejected it: `lcfirst has conflicting userland
disposition`. All three already exist -- as **PHP**, in
`internal/userland/ext/standard.php`, among 274 functions catalogued that way.

> **`php2eval`'s interpreter arm does not link the userland library.** So
> "the interpreter does not support X" from that tool is not evidence, and I
> had taken it as evidence. `cmd/php2gotest` and `runtime/interp`'s own test
> harness both link it; the interactive oracle does not.

Removing my duplicate let the real implementation run, and it was wrong:
`ucwords("hello")` returned `"HELLO"`. The PHP source was correct, so the fault
was in what it compiled to. Tracing the generated Go found this:

> **A short-circuit `&&` or `||` assigned to a variable inside a function
> answered the LEFT operand.**

The lowering lands the result in a compiler temporary and writes it at the merge
block -- `write_var($atWordStart, $__t20)`. `liveIn` treated a store as a
definition of its place and `continue`d, so the **stored value**, itself a
tracked place, never counted as a use. Pruned SSA placed no block parameter at
the merge, and the promotion read whichever version reached first. One `continue`
skipping one operand.

Three properties made it survive this long, and they are the lesson:

- **Invisible at file scope.** `{main}` is never promoted, so every probe
  written at the top level of a script answers correctly. Four of mine did,
  before I thought to put the same expression inside a function.
- **`-no-mem2reg` passes.** That flag turned a mystery into a located bug in one
  run, and it is the first thing to reach for when compiled output disagrees
  with the interpreter on a *value*.
- **It produces a wrong value, not a diagnostic.** Nothing refuses, nothing
  warns; the boolean is simply the wrong one. That is the class of bug a pass
  count is worst at finding -- and the corpus moved by 2, which is no measure of
  what was fixed.

The session's other lesson, restated: I would not have found this by looking for
it. It surfaced because a *duplicate* implementation forced the original to run.

## 2026-09-20 -- Two functions that agreed with each other and not with PHP

`ap3`: **2528 / 968 / 412 / 1**, gained 4 lost 0 against `ao3`'s 2524. Note the
**`unsupported` column moved** -- 416 to 412, the first movement in that bucket
across this whole run of ticks.

The uniform-delta seam had saturated (the remaining same-delta groups are
coincidence, not one cause), so I censused the bucket nobody had looked at:
`unsupported`, pinned at 416 for a dozen measurements. It is mostly honest
refusal -- 141 `include or eval`, by design -- plus the known suspension gap.
`trait_exists` stood out as an ordinary class-table query being refused.

**Measuring the family first found something worse than the missing function.**

> `class_exists` and `interface_exists` had **identical bodies**. They agreed
> with each other everywhere, and with the engine only by accident: an interface
> answered true to `class_exists`, and a class answered true to
> `interface_exists`.

The engine's rules, measured over a class, an interface, a trait, an enum, a
backed enum, an abstract class, a final class and a name that does not exist:
`class_exists` covers classes, enums and abstract classes but **not** interfaces
or traits; `interface_exists`, `trait_exists` and `enum_exists` are exact to
their kind. All four now share one `existsAsKind` that is told which kind it is
answering for -- one place to be right rather than four to drift.

**The fixture then forced out two pre-existing bugs**, which is the argument for
writing the exhaustive case rather than the motivating one:

- `class_exists('Exception')` was **false**. `knownClass` answers only for
  classes the program itself declares, so every engine class arrived at the
  predicate as the empty string. Fixed by asking about the *name* rather than a
  resolved one, and by consulting `php.IsThrowableClass`, which already draws
  exactly the line needed -- it is false for `Throwable`, an interface that
  cannot be constructed.
- Engine interfaces that are neither throwable nor iterator-shaped --
  `Countable`, `ArrayAccess`, `Stringable` -- still fall through to the class
  arm, so both answers about them are backwards. Filed with the fix's shape:
  `interfacesOf` holds the names but cannot say which of its keys are
  interfaces, which is the whole distinction.

**The follow-up measured flat.** `aq3`: 2529 / 967 / 412 / 1, gained 1 -- the
non-deterministic `message_004` -- so no real movement from making every
harvested engine interface kind-aware. The fix is right (checked against the
engine for `Countable`, `ArrayAccess`, `Stringable`, `Traversable`, `Iterator`,
`JsonSerializable`, `Throwable`, `Exception`, `ArrayObject`, all nine of which
answered *both* questions backwards before) and simply nothing in `Zend/tests`
asks `interface_exists('Countable')`. Worth keeping, worth not claiming credit
for.

The tick's three bugs share a shape worth naming: each was **a table that was
right for the job it was written for and wrong for the one it got reused in** --
`class_exists`/`interface_exists` sharing a body, `knownClass` answering only
for program-declared classes, and `engineInterfaceNames` sized for *ordering*
`interfacesOf` rather than for membership. None was a wrong algorithm; each was
a correct answer to a different question.

## 2026-09-20 -- The one bitwise operator that could not reach the guard

Following the same method as the comparison fix -- group failures by *uniform
byte delta*, on the theory that a constant difference repeated across unrelated
files is one missing thing -- five files sat at exactly -131, led by
`float_to_int/warnings_float_vars`. The missing thing:

    Deprecated: Implicit conversion from float 1.5 to int loses precision

Probing all six bitwise operators showed `|`, `&`, `^`, `<<` and `>>` were
**already right**, and only `~` was silent. The reason is structural rather than
an oversight:

> The binary integral operators reach the deprecation through
> `AcceptsArithmetic(ctx, symbol, a, b)`, which the emitter runs as their
> `Guard`. It takes **two operands**, so a unary operator cannot use it -- and
> `~` was the only unary member of the group. The catalogue said so without
> anyone noticing: `BitNot` was the one entry whose `Effects` lacked
> `Deprecates`, while every sibling carried it.

That is the second declaration-versus-implementation mismatch in two ticks, in
opposite directions. The comparison intrinsics *claimed* `Warns` and could not;
`BitNot` *did not claim* `Deprecates` and should have. Both were readable in
`catalogue.go` before either was measured.

**The fixture earned its place immediately.** My first version deprecated
`~"1.5"` too, by reusing the shared `warnPrecisionLoss` -- which handles a
float-shaped string because the *binary* operators genuinely convert one. `~` on
a string is **bytewise**: it complements three bytes and converts nothing, so
there is no precision to lose. The engine returns `"\xce\xd1\xca"` and says
nothing. That made the shared helper exactly the wrong thing to apply unguarded,
and only a case that tried it would have shown that.

`float_to_int`: 17 -> 19 of 19. Measured as `ao3`: **2524 / 967 / 416 / 1**,
gained 5 lost 0 against `an3`'s 2519 -- one gain is the non-deterministic
`value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`, so +4.

## 2026-09-20 -- An object is 1, and the engine says so

`an3`: **2519 / 971 / 416 / 1**, gained 11 lost 1 against `am3`'s 2509 -- the
loss is the non-deterministic `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`, so **+11**.
Targeted four files; got eleven, the whole `compare_00N` family (001, 003, 004,
005, 006 and their `_64bit` twins) plus `objects_001`.

**How it was found.** The previous entry concluded that the handle seam is
bounded by static confinement, so this tick looked elsewhere: at files whose
*output length* diverges sharply, on the theory that a large uniform difference
is one missing thing repeated. Four `compare_00N` files were short by exactly
2983 bytes each. The missing thing was a diagnostic:

    Notice: Object of class stdClass could not be converted to int

**Two bugs, and the notice was the smaller one.** The engine raises it because
it is *announcing a conversion it performs*: against a number, an object stands
in as **1**. We were applying the "an object outranks everything" rule instead,
so `$o > 1` was true where PHP says false. The notice was the visible half of a
value bug.

Measured before writing anything, which paid three times:

- The notice names the type converted **to** -- `int` for an int operand,
  `float` for a float -- and fires for no other type. String, bool, null, array
  and another object all compare without conversion and say nothing.
- A `__toString` does not excuse it. The conversion attempted is to a number,
  not a string, so `1 > new S` notices exactly as `1 > new T` does.
- **An enum case is never converted.** It is uncomparable against a number --
  every relation false both ways -- and silent, *including a backed enum whose
  value is literally 1*. I missed that and `enum_identity` caught it, which is
  the fixture suite doing its job.

Two things had to change underneath, both of the same kind: a declaration that
described behaviour nothing implemented.

> `catalogue.go` has carried `Effects: Warns` on the comparison intrinsics all
> along, while `php.Compare` and `php.LooseEqual` take no `*Ctx` and so had
> nowhere to warn from. An effect annotation is a claim about the
> implementation, and this one had been false since it was written.

And the emitter's `GoScalar` wrap was applied *around* the call rather than to
its result, so a binding returning both a Go scalar and an error produced
`php.Bool(f(ctx, a, b))` over a two-value call. Not a bug anyone could have hit:
the combination had no user until a comparison needed a `Ctx`.

This also unblocks the lazy-object `==` trigger filed earlier, which was waiting
on exactly this signature change.

## 2026-09-20 -- Release points: the machinery works, and it bounds itself

`al3`: **2507 / 984 / 416 / 1**, identical to `ak3` -- the function-body
extension of the reassignment release was inert and safe, as predicted.
`am3`: **2509 / 983 / 416 / 1**, gained 3 lost 1, two of those four being the
known non-deterministic files. So **+2** from the largest change of the session.

**What was built.** Promotion removes the store PHP destroys at, so the renamer
-- the last pass that still knows, walking in order with the outgoing value in
`cur[place]` -- now leaves a `release_prev` marker where the store was. The
emitter claims it only for values `ConfinedNew` already proved cannot leave the
frame, which also proves at most one local binds them (`confinedValue` refuses a
value bound to two). Three things it turned on:

- **`unset` needed no marker but did need the escape walk.** It survives
  promotion -- being unset is what disqualifies its local from promotion -- yet
  `local()` read it as an unrecognised use, so an unset local was not even
  *confined*, let alone released. Unsetting a local is the opposite of letting
  the object escape.
- **The marker must not count as a use.** Every lifetime walk skips it and
  `useCounts` excludes it; counting it would change every disposable claim about
  that value, in the wrong direction. This hazard was written down before the
  work started and was real.
- **A golden IR test caught noise that would have shipped.** The first version
  marked rope accumulators and loop counters (`$__iter5`, `$sum`). Filtered now
  to non-temporary locals holding values the IR types as possibly-object.

`reassign.php` -- failing since the first tick of this session -- passes, with
reassignment, `= null`, `unset` and read-between-writes.

**Why +2, and this is the part worth keeping.** The handle-number family did not
move at all: 125 before, 125 after. Reading one (`cast_to_object`) says why --

    $o = new test;
    $vars = array( ..., $o, ... );

the objects go **into a container**, so confinement refuses them, correctly. The
release machinery is complete for *frame-local* objects, and frame-local objects
were not what the remaining failures are made of.

> Static confinement can only reach objects that never leave the frame. The
> corpus's remaining handle failures are overwhelmingly objects that do -- into
> arrays, properties, closures. No amount of polishing the confined path
> reaches them; that is the tier-2 refcounting work, and it is a different
> project rather than a further increment of this one.

That is a boundary, not a defeat: the tier-1 path is now correct and its limit
is known. It also means the next tick should pick a different seam rather than
push here.

the sixteen is the non-deterministic `message_004`, so +15 -- from changing one

constant, not a bug in any of them.

**The constant, and the part worth keeping.** `firstScriptResource = 5` carried
this justification:

> the id the first resource a script opens receives under the CLI, which is the
> SAPI the corpus's expected output was recorded with

I checked two `.phpt` files, found `resource(%d)`, and concluded the corpus
wildcards the number -- so the comment was simply wrong and 5 was answering
nobody's question. **That conclusion was my own too-quick generalisation from
two files.** Changing the constant to 2 fixed nine compiled files and broke two
interpreter ones, because some expectations spell `resource(5)` literally.

Both harnesses were right, about different hosts:

- `php2phpt` grades against `.phpt` text recorded under the **CLI**, which holds
  the three standard streams plus one more before a script runs -> first id 5.
- `php2gotest` grades byte-exact against the **embedded engine running in this
  process**, where `fopen('php://memory','r')` is `resource(2)` -> first id 2.

and it is now a `Ctx` setting rather than a constant. The default matches the
engine we actually run -- which also keeps the `php2eval` engine-versus-
interpreter differential clean -- and `php2phpt` asks for 5 because reproducing
the CLI is its job. Checked both ways: `php2phpt` 14/14 before and after,
`php2gotest` 9 failures -> 0.

Two things this tick taught that generalise:

> **A comment that asserts something checkable is worth checking.** This one had
> stood for a long time and was wrong in a way a single `grep` disproves. But
> the disproof was also too fast: "the corpus records `%d`" was true of the two
> files I looked at and false of the corpus.

> **The census undercounts.** It named nine files; the fix moved fifteen.
> A census keys on each file's *first* divergence, so a family that appears
> mid-output anywhere is invisible behind whatever differs earlier. Expect the
> real size of a uniform-delta family to exceed its census count.

**What could not be done honestly.** This change has no fixture. Every portable
source of a resource is `unsupported` in compiled output -- `tmpfile()`,
`php://memory`, `php://temp`, `php://stdout`, `tempnam` -- and `fopen(__FILE__)`
is environment-dependent, because the compiled program runs from a different
working directory than the fixture lives in. That is a deliberate exception to
"a differential case for every behavioural change", recorded in TODO.md with the
thing that would close it (supporting `php://memory`), and the evidence in its
place is the fifteen corpus files plus the two-harness check above.

doc comments say they reach "the same storage" are still two code paths, and a
fix in one of them is not a fix.

The table also settles the rest of the surface as *correct*, which is worth as
much as the fixes: `print_r`, `var_dump`, `(array)`, `array_walk` and `count`
deliberately do **not** initialize, and we match the engine on all five. Only
`==` still diverges, and it is filed with its mechanism rather than as a
mystery -- `php.LooseEqual` takes no `*Ctx`, and `catalogue.go` already supports
`Ctx: true` variants.

**The method generalises past lazy objects.** A census counts symptoms; a probe
table establishes a *surface*. The census had said "113 lazy failures" for
several ticks and pointed at no particular thing. Fourteen probes, run once,
said which two operations were wrong and proved the other twelve right.

Session so far: 2211 -> 2481.

## 2026-09-20 -- `unpack` is a read, and a pass-through that was sound one way only

`af3`: **2475 / 1016 / 416 / 1** (+3 real, the `return_types` files the previous
entry predicted, and one real loss). `ag3`: **2479 / 1012 / 416 / 1**, gained 5
lost 1 -- two of the six are the known non-deterministic files, so +4.

**The loss in `af3` was mine, and the shape of the mistake is worth keeping.**
Seeing through `coerce_return` is sound for *"is this object fresh"* and wrong
for *"does this object leave the frame"*. With the check transparent,
`return new A()` in a typed function makes the terminator mention only the
checked value -- so the `new` looks frame-local, gets claimed as confined, and
the frame drain destroys an object the caller is about to receive.
`added_interface_intersection_type` caught it.

> One relation, two questions, opposite safe answers. Pass-through is now gated
> on the walk that asked for it (`allowReturn`), not asserted about the
> instruction. A fact about an instruction is not automatically a fact for every
> analysis that meets it.

**Then off the handle seam, which the census said was only the fourth-largest
family.** Probing one file from `missing output` -- `access_modifiers_011` --
found a lowering bug with real reach:

> **An `unpack` send is a read.** `f(...$args)` and
> `call_user_func_array($cb, $args)` both compile to one, and all three places
> that enumerate send modes -- `readSendArgs` plus two in `mem2reg` -- listed
> `byval`/`byref`/`preferref` and stopped. The argument stayed a bare place
> nothing read, so the local was promoted away as unused and the call reported
> `Undefined variable $args`.

The symptom is why it took bisecting rather than reading: the failure appears
*inside* a body whose `var_dump($args)` one line earlier prints the variable
perfectly well, which reads as a `__call` bug or a defaults bug -- anything but
lowering. What located it was noticing that `call_user_func_array($cb, [])`
worked where `$cb, $args` did not. **When a variable is undefined only at one
use, suspect the use, not the binding.**

An enumerated set of modes in three places is the kind of thing that goes wrong
once per mode: `preferref` was already missing from `sentByValueAt` earlier this
session, for the same reason and with a different symptom.

Session so far: 2211 -> 2479.

## 2026-09-20 -- The fresh-return summary measured flat, and why

`ae3`: **2472 / 1018 / 416 / 1** against `ad3`'s 2473 / 1018 / 416 / 1. Gained 0,
lost 1, and the loss is `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001` -- one of the three
known non-deterministic files. So: **flat**.

The tick's work was the return-freshness summary -- teaching
`DisposableTemporaries` that a *call* can define a disposable value, so
`var_dump(Foo::make())` frees the returned object at the statement the way
`var_dump(new Foo)` does. It is correct and it bought nothing, and the reason is
worth recording because it is the third time this session a summary has been
right and inert.

Following this journal's own rule -- a flat measurement is not proof nothing
changed, go look at the targeted files -- `return_types/inheritance004` was
byte-identical before and after. Instrumenting the refusal (rather than guessing
at the rule, which is the lesson from the previous entry) named it in one run:

> **A declared return type puts a check between the value and the `ret`.**
> `function t(): self { return new Foo; }` returns the *checked* value, whose
> definition is `coerce_return`, not the `new`. The summary saw a body handing
> back something it had not made and refused it. Most factories in the corpus
> are typed, so the summary fired almost nowhere.

Two spellings had to be matched, which is its own small trap: the lowering emits
`verify_return` and the specializer rewrites it to the intrinsic
**`coerce_return`**. The summary runs after specialization, so matching only the
pre-specialization name found nothing -- and "found nothing" and "nothing to
find" look identical from the outside. With both matched and the check treated
as pass-through (for an object it is: the only coercion it performs is
int-to-float widening), `inheritance004` passes.

Honest scale: this is worth about 3 files of the 49 in the `+1`/`+2` handle
clusters, not 49. The handle seam is thinning -- `ad3` +30, `ae3` +0, this one
~3 -- so I censused all 1018 failures instead of grinding it further:

    value/format differs              377
    extra output (want empty line)    263
    missing output (got empty line)   218
    handle number                     136
    fatal error text                   18

Handle numbering is no longer the largest family; it is the fourth. The two
output families are bigger than it together, and neither has a single visible
cause in the first-divergence line -- which is exactly what this journal already
says about censuses: they name a file's *first* refusal, so the next step is to
probe those surfaces, not to count them again.

## 2026-09-20 -- One missing `continue`: 2443 -> 2473

`ad3`: **2473 / 1018 / 416 / 1** against `ab3`'s 2443 / 1046 / 416 / 3. Gained
30, lost 0; `errored` back to 1 and `unsupported` back to 416. Twenty-eight of
the thirty are `lazy_objects`. The `+2` handle cluster went **0/50 -> 26/50**.

The cause was one line, and how it was found matters more than what it was.

**First, the regression.** `ac3` measured 2441 -- *worse* than `ab3` -- gaining
0 and losing 2, with `errored` 3 -> 6. Entirely self-inflicted: the reassignment
release emitted `prevHeld1 := ...` at statement level, and Go refuses a `goto`
that jumps over a variable declaration. These bodies use `goto` for basic
blocks, so five files became **build failures** rather than wrong answers, which
is also why `unsupported` moved -- two of them had been `unsupported: include or
eval` and could no longer get far enough to say so. Block-scoping the release
fixed all five. A `{ ... }` is jumped over harmlessly; a declaration is not.

So the entire previous tick's reassignment work measured **zero gain**.

**Then, the method.** I had spent several rounds guessing at this cluster --
`clone` is a read, `class_name` is a read, the method-argument allow-list, the
`slot.set` write shape -- each plausible, each changing nothing measurable. What
finally worked was three minutes of instrumentation: print *which instruction*
made the walk refuse, and for which value. The answer was somewhere I had not
looked at all:

> **`derived()` was missing its mention guard.** Its `call.method` arm fired for
> **every** method call in the body, receiver or not -- so a body containing a
> single method call refused every value read out of a local, whatever that call
> was about. `value()` and `local()` both open by skipping instructions that do
> not mention the value; only this third walk did not.

The fix is a `continue`. The rule it teaches is not:

> When a conservative analysis refuses more than it should, do not guess at
> which *rule* is too strict -- ask it which *instruction* it refused on. Three
> of the four things I changed while guessing were correct and still moved
> nothing, because none of them was the one refusing.

The guesses are kept, all of them measured-or-reasoned rather than assumed:
`clone`, `class_name` and `instanceof` really are reads of their operand;
`initializeLazyObject`, `isUninitializedLazyObject` and
`markLazyObjectAsInitialized` really keep no reference to their **argument** --
measured with a negative control (`$sink->keep($g)`), which is what makes the
probe mean anything, since a probe that cannot detect retention proves nothing
by failing to find it. That list is deliberately separate from the receiver
list: a method can store an argument without storing `$this`. For a *compiled*
method the answer is "assume it keeps" -- reusing the `leaksThis` summary there
was the tempting move and would have been wrong, because that summary answers a
different question.

## 2026-09-20 -- Handle numbering: clone, the reflector receiver, and the frame drain that forgot half its job

Two runs. `zz2`: **2439 / 1052 / 416 / 1**, gained 5 lost 2 against `zy2` -- but
two of those seven are the known non-deterministic files, so really 4 gains and
one real loss. `ab3`: **2443 / 1046 / 416 / 3**, gained 4 lost 0.

**Read the `errored` column.** `ab3` gained four and lost none, and still is not
a clean win: `errored` went 1 -> 3. Both new ones are `object_gc_in_shutdown`,
timing out at 30s -- a **hang**, which is worse than a wrong answer and is
invisible in the pass/fail counts. Cause below. With it fixed the two go back to
`failed`, so `ab3` reads 2443 / 1048 / 416 / 1.

**The loss in `zz2` was a bug I exposed, not one I wrote.** `objects_028` broke
when a bare `new foo;` started being claimed. `SetDestructorRun` called
`callMethod(o, "__destruct")` unguarded, and `callMethod` falls through to
`__call` for any name a class does not have -- so destroying an object of a
class with a `__call` and no destructor *called the accessor with the name
`__destruct`*. Confirmed pre-existing: a frame-local of such a class already
printed `call:__destruct` before any of this tick's work. PHP does not route
`__destruct` through `__call`; the hook now asks `hasMethod` first.

**Then I clustered instead of picking.** 135 same-size handle failures remained;
by delta the buckets are +1: 31, **+2: 63**, +3: 15, +4: 12. Of the 63, **42 are
`lazy_objects`**. Tracing one against the engine found three gaps, each settled
by measurement:

- **`clone` was never claimed.** It makes a fresh object the frame owns, but
  `makesFreshObject` knew only `new`. Gated on `__clone`, because the engine
  runs it on the copy and that call is implicit in the opcode rather than an
  instruction the walk can see. The gate then misfired in a way worth naming:
  `leaksThis` answers `!nonRetainingEngineMethod(m)` for a method no compiled
  body declares, so in a program where no class declares `__clone` the question
  "does `__clone` store `$this`" came back **yes**, and every clone site was
  refused. "Unknown" and "dangerous" are the same value in that predicate.
- **The reflector receiver was never released.** Measured all sixteen
  `ReflectionClass` methods the corpus uses with
  `$o = new C(); (new ReflectionClass(C::class))->m(...); echo spl_object_id(new C());`
  -- every one answers 2, so every one hands its receiver's handle straight
  back. They are on the allow-list now.
- **A confined local never returned its handle at all.** The frame drain ran
  destructors and stopped; `releaseObjectID` was only ever emitted by the
  *disposable* path. So a confined local died at exactly the right moment and
  still pushed every later object's number up by one -- correct timing, wrong
  numbering, which is why it survived so long.

**The thing worth keeping.** Adding the release to the drain regressed a case,
and the reason is the sharpest finding of the tick:

> **After slot promotion, a local and a true temporary have the same shape.**
> PHP frees a statement temporary at the end of its statement and a local when
> the frame dies. `$c = clone $o; f($c);` with `$c` read once loses its slot and
> becomes indistinguishable from `f(clone $o)` -- so releasing at the last use
> is right for one and early for the other, by exactly the objects allocated in
> between.

I had already hit this once this tick, with `discarded_new`, and worked around
it by restricting the claim to the file body. That was a patch on a symptom.
The cause is fixed now: `Mem2Reg` records which SSA values are promoted
user locals (`Function.FrameBound`), and the disposable path declines them. A
question the compiler destroyed the answer to has to be recorded where it is
destroyed; no later pass can recover it.

Also settled against the engine, since the design depended on it: the free list
is a **LIFO stack**. Free 2 then 4 and the next two objects take 4 then 2.

**The hang.** `releaseObjectID`'s duplicate check was a linear scan of the free
list. Harmless while only the disposable path called it -- the list is normally
near-empty -- but the frame drain calls it once per confined object, and
`object_gc_in_shutdown` allocates a million in one frame. O(n^2), 30s timeout.
Now a set beside the list. The check itself has to stay: pushing a handle twice
hands one number to two live objects.

Fixtures: `destruct_not_via_call.php`, `frame_bound_handles.php` -- the latter
built around the distinction above, with a temporary that must reuse a handle
and a local that must not, each followed by an allocation so getting it wrong
shows. Suite 280/281, the one failure pre-existing.

## 2026-09-19 -- The parameter-escape summary, and what it did not buy

`zy2`: **2436 / 1055 / 416 / 1** against `zx2`'s 2418 / 1074 / 416 / 1. Gained
19, lost 1, and the loss is `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001` -- one of the
three files known to be non-deterministic, so no real regression.

**Read the gains, not the total.** Eighteen of the nineteen are `lazy_objects`,
from the magic-guard fix and the lazy-resolver binding in the previous entry.
The parameter-escape summary -- much the larger piece of work -- moved exactly
**one** file, `typed_properties_088`. Recording that plainly because the
temptation is to let a good headline number cover for the half of the tick that
did not pay.

**What was built.** `DisposableTemporaries` could release `var_dump(new P())`
because `var_dump` is on a hand-written allow-list; a call to a *compiled*
function had no answer, so `test(new A); test(new B)` printed `#1, #2` where the
engine prints `#1, #1`. `lower.RetainedParams` now derives that fact by escape
analysis over the parameter locals, run to a fixpoint over the call graph. Three
things it turned on, each of which had the analysis answering confidently and
wrongly first:

- **The walk knew only `slot.set`.** A parameter never survives promotion as a
  slot: it arrives as `recv` and is written into its local by
  `call.intrinsic "write_var"`. The walk treated that as an unrecognised use and
  refused every parameter -- and then refused again at the local's own binding
  site, for the same reason one level down.
- **Per parameter, not per body.** `function f($o, $n) { return $n; }` returns a
  parameter, so "does `f` keep any argument" is yes, and the object in the
  *other* position lost its release for a reason having nothing to do with it.
  Returning a parameter is ordinary PHP, so the coarse question gave up on most
  real callees. This was the single biggest precision defect and it was invisible
  until a fixture with a two-parameter callee existed.
- **The fixpoint runs from the optimistic end.** Escape is a reachability
  property: an argument passed around a cycle of bodies none of which *stores*
  it has gone nowhere. `f($o) { f($o); }` keeps nothing, and a pessimistic
  iteration -- which only adds proofs -- can never supply a recursive body's own
  premise. Anything that does store propagates outward monotonically, so the two
  ends agree wherever a proof exists at all.

**Why the yield was one file.** 135 same-size handle failures remain, and
sampling them says the shape I built for is not the common one. The commonest is
simpler than a call: `new foo;` as a **bare statement**, a `new` whose result is
used by nothing at all. It dies at once, and nothing claims it -- it is in the
file body, where `markConfined` is deliberately skipped because `{main}`'s
locals are globals, and `DisposableTemporaries` only claims a value some
non-retaining call consumes. A value consumed by *nothing* falls between the
two. That is the next tick.

The lesson is one this journal has recorded before in another costume: I sized
the family by its *name* ("handle numbering, 271 files") and built for the
mechanism I already had a partial answer to, rather than sampling the members
first. Sampling took four minutes and would have reordered the work.

Fixtures: `param_escape_summary.php` and `param_escape_attacks.php`, the second
written as an attack -- eight escape routes (static local, closure `use`, method
store, return, nested array, property, global array, throw) that must all be
refused, because being wrong in that direction reuses a *live* handle and prints
as some other object. Suite 276/277, the one failure pre-existing.

## 2026-09-19 -- A dead hook found by audit: the lazy resolver, and the guard it exposed

`zx2` measured 2418 / 1074 / 416 / 1 against `zw2`'s 2416 / 1076 / 416 / 1 --
net +2, but the diff read **gained 8, lost 6**, and all six losses were
`lazy_objects` tests I had passed the tick before. A net gain hid a regression
of my own making. Read the diff, not the total.

**The audit that started it.** The previous entry ended on "a dead hook is
invisible in a way a dead *branch* is not". So I enumerated all 39
`func (c *Ctx) Set*` hooks in `runtime/php` and asked which
`internal/gogen/gogen.go` installs. Eleven it never does; seven of those the
*interpreter* installs, so each was a behaviour compiled output silently lacked.

That framing was half wrong, and the correction is the useful part:

> **An unbound hook is not automatically a gap.** `SetErrorReporting` is unbound
> and `error_reporting(0)` works in compiled output anyway, because the
> behaviour is supplied elsewhere. Probe each one; do not count them.

Two of the seven were real, in opposite ways:

- **`SetLazyResolver` -- a genuine gap, and its own doc comment said so.**
  `Ctx.Materialize` applies the hook and is the identity when nothing installs
  one. `runtime/stdlib/serialize.go:37` and `json.go:23` *already called it*.
  So `serialize` on a lazy object serialized an empty shell. I had filed this in
  `TODO.md` as needing runtime work; the mechanism had been sitting there
  complete and unplugged. Its comment even names its own expiry -- the identity
  holds *"until `ReflectionClass` reaches"* the compiled back-end -- which it
  did, several ticks ago, without anyone revisiting the comment.
- **`SetWeakObserve`/`SetWeakRelease` -- unbound, but binding them fixes
  nothing.** WeakMap lifetime is wrong in compiled output (`$a = null` neither
  destructs nor drops the entry), and the trigger is refcounting, which no hook
  supplies. Filed as blocked on the same lever as handle numbering, not as a
  hook.

**The regression the audit did not cause but did explain.** Last tick I bound
`SetMagicAvailable` as `hasMethod(o.ClassName, method)`. The interpreter's own
`magicAvailable` (`runtime/interp/magic.go:62`) answers a strictly narrower
question: the class has it **and it is not already running for that name on that
object**. I had implemented half a predicate. Worse, the generated program keyed
its in-flight set on `o.ID` while the interpreter keys on `guardOf(object)` --
`Object.Guard` when set, falling back to the handle. `Guard` is precisely what a
lazy proxy and its real instance **share** (`lazyresolve2.go:229`), so keying on
the handle makes the accessor fire once for the shell and once for the instance.
That is GH-18038, "Lazy proxy calls magic methods twice", and we reproduced it.

Fix: key all nine guard constructions on `php.GuardOf(...)`, and give the
availability hook the in-flight check it was missing. All six lost tests came
back with the four magic-related gains kept, and `lazy_objects` went **48 -> 66**
(+18) once the resolver hook landed too.

**The generalisable bit.** Both defects are the same shape: a predicate that
exists in full in one back-end and in truncated form in the other. `hasMethod`
was a plausible-looking answer to "is magic available", and nothing failed to
build. The interpreter is the specification for any predicate both back-ends
need -- when binding a hook, read the interpreter's implementation of the same
hook first and port it, rather than writing what the hook's *name* suggests.

Fixtures: `lazy_serialize.php`, `magic_guard_shared.php`. Gate clean; `zy2` in
flight.

## 2026-09-19 -- a dead hook, found because something finally asked it

Corpus `zw2`: **2414 -> 2416**, and it **lost** `unset_magic_may_not_initialize`
-- a real regression from the `unset` trigger added in the same tick. The
filename states the rule I broke, which is twice now that a `lazy_objects` test
has been named after exactly the mistake.

The cause was not the new code. `ResolveLazy` has always had the guard:

    if magic != "" && !c.DeclaresProperty(...) && c.magicAvailable != nil &&
        c.magicAvailable(object, magic, property) { return object, nil }

and **nothing in the emitter ever installed `SetMagicAvailable`**. The hook was
nil, so that branch could not fire in compiled output at all. It cost nothing
for as long as no compiled path passed a `magic` argument, and the moment one
did it read as the new code being wrong.

A dead hook is invisible in exactly the way a dead *branch* is not: nothing
fails to build, nothing refuses, and the behaviour it guards simply never
happens.

Installing it fixed the regression and, with `__isset` now reachable, exposed a
second gap that has nothing to do with lazy objects:

    class M { public function __isset($n) { ... } }
    isset($m->nope);     // engine calls __isset; php2go answered false

`existsProp` called `__isset` only for a property visibility **hides**, never
for one the object simply does not have -- which is the commoner spelling. And
`empty()` on a true answer has to go on to `__get`, which is the one place the
two questions differ.

Also this tick: **a lazy object never ran its destructor.** `ConfinedObjects`
only ever claimed values defined by `new`, and a lazy object arrives from
`newLazyGhost` -- a method call -- so there was no definition to claim and the
object fell through to script-end teardown, far too late for a frame local. It
now recognises a small measured set of **object factories** as fresh-object
sites, and the emitter appends their results to the frame list the way it does
after a constructor.

## 2026-09-19 -- a behavioural bug hiding inside a numbering cluster

Grouping the 25 still-failing `lazy_objects` files by their first diff separated
two kinds of thing that the cluster's headline -- "handle numbering" -- had been
hiding:

    14  an object handle number
     3  want "initializer", got NULL or the wrong value

The three are not numbering at all. **Cloning a lazy object initialises it
first**, and we were copying the empty shell, so the initializer never ran.
Measured for both kinds:

    $c = clone $ghost;   // initializer, then __clone
                         // *both* the original and the copy end up initialised

so the state is produced once and copied, rather than deferred into the clone. A
proxy behaves the same and the clone copies the instance it forwards to.

Three lines in `cloneObject`, and all three files now fail on a handle number
alone -- the behaviour is right.

The fixture prints **no object handles at all**, deliberately: the numbering of
a lazy proxy is a separate and still-open question, and pinning it here would
make a numbering bug look like a clone bug. It covers a ghost, a proxy, a second
clone proving the initializer runs once rather than once per clone, an
already-initialised object, and an initializer that throws at the clone.

The general lesson is the one about census granularity again, from the other
direction: a cluster named for its commonest symptom will hide anything whose
symptom is rarer, and the way to find those is to group the cluster's own
members rather than trust the name.

Applying that to the whole corpus found the cluster is **166 files, not 30** --
I had been sampling `fetch_*`. Grouped: 80 handle numbers and ~86 behavioural,
in many small families. So the next question was not "which file" but **which
operations initialise a lazy object**, enumerated in one probe over fifteen:

    initialise:  read, write, clone, serialize, json_encode,
                 get_object_vars, foreach, isset, unset, ==
    do not:      var_dump, print_r, (array) cast, count

php2go did **none** of them. The split is the interesting part and is not
guessable: reading properties *for their values* initialises, while the dumps
deliberately do not -- which is exactly why the fix went in
`visibleProperties`, the path that reads values, and not in
`objectProperties`, which is what the dumps walk. One edit there fixed
`json_encode`, `get_object_vars`; a second in `newIterator` fixed `foreach`.

`isset` followed, in `existsProp`, and `unset` in `place.unset`. That leaves
`serialize` and `==`, and the reason those two lag is worth naming: they are
the only ones that live in **`runtime/php`** rather than in emitted code, so
they cannot be touched while a corpus run is in flight. The comparison in
`ops.go` would also need a `*Ctx` it does not currently take. Both are filed
rather than asserted -- the fixture holds the settled half plus the four that
must stay lazy, because a fixture that always fails stops being a signal.

Corpus `zu2` for the clone fix: **2408**, flat -- one lazy file gained and one
**lost**, and the loss was a real regression of my own making.
`clone_preverves_object_class` is named after exactly the mistake I made:
resolving a proxy and then cloning the *resolved instance* gives the clone the
instance's class. Fixing that by cloning the shell instead broke the other
file, which wants independent state. Both halves are one rule -- a proxy's
clone keeps the proxy's class **and** gets its own copy of the instance -- and
each half was broken in turn while fixing the other. Both files pass now, and
the fixture pins both.

Corpus `zv2`: **2408 -> 2414**, 7 gained against the flake. Six are the trigger
table -- `init_trigger_get_object_vars`, `init_trigger_json_encode`,
`init_trigger_json_encode_hooks`, `serialize_props_ht`, `gh15823`,
`oss_fuzz_71382` -- and the seventh is `clone_preverves_object_class`, the file
whose regression is described above.

## 2026-09-19 -- handing an object over, and the measurement that forced a proof

The largest identified remainder is object handle numbering -- 128 of the
failures, against nothing else above single figures -- and its largest
sub-cluster is 33 `lazy_objects` files turning on one fact:

    $g = $r->newLazyGhost(function ($o) { ... });
    spl_object_id(new P());   // 4  -- the closure is alive
    $g->a;                    // initialises
    spl_object_id(new P());   // 2  -- the closure's number came back

**Initialising a lazy object releases its initializer.** The obvious
implementation is to release unconditionally, and the first thing I did was
measure whether that is safe. It is not:

    $f = function ($o) { ... };
    $g = $r->newLazyGhost($f);   // closure is #2
    $g->a;
    spl_object_id(new P());      // 4, not 2 -- $f still holds it

So the release has to be gated on a **proof of sole ownership**, and that
settles the design rather than leaving it to taste.

Three pieces, each in the place that can answer its own question:

- `lower.SoleUseClosures` proves it: a closure created for one call, sent by
  value, mentioned nowhere else. Deliberately narrower than
  `DisposableTemporaries`, which also decides *when* the object dies -- for an
  initializer that is not at the call at all, but whenever the object first
  initialises, if ever.
- The proof travels on the value as `Object.SoleOwned`, so the callee reads a
  fact rather than the caller reaching into it.
- `runtime/php` knows **when** -- initialisation drops the initializer -- and
  the generated program supplies **how**, through a `SetReleaseHandle` hook,
  because the free list is the program's. The same "declared here, supplied
  from above" split every other cross-layer question here uses.

The fixture covers the inline closure, the same closure kept in a variable, a
proxy factory, and a lazy object that never initialises. Only the first gives
its number back.

Corpus `zt2`: **2408, unchanged**. 0 gained, 0 lost.

The mechanism works and was verified directly --
`lazy_objects/fetch_declared_prop_initializes` now numbers its proxy `#4` where
it had `#5`, matching the engine. The file still fails, on the **next** number
along: the proxy's instance is `#3` in the engine and `#5` here, because the
ghost died when `$obj` was reassigned and gave its number back.

That is the honest shape of this family. Each file has more than one numbering
cause, so fixing one moves the diff without moving the bucket, and a tick aimed
at 33 files can be correct, verified, and score zero. The next cause is a local
reassignment dropping its object -- which is general refcounting, not another
ownership proof.

## 2026-09-19 -- the same refusal twice, and only one copy was fixed

`zr2` measured the named-unpacking work as **flat**, one gain and it the flake.
The useful move was not accepting that: the eight files in the cluster were

There were two copies. `unpackArgs` handles an array and a Traversable in
