The array one was the reported shape, so it was the one I read, changed, and
tested -- and the fixture I wrote passed, because every case in it unpacked an
array.

The Traversable branch's comment even says it is the same rule:

> A string key is a **named** argument, which this call site binds statically
> and so cannot place at run time -- *the same refusal an unpacked array with
> string keys already gets*.

A comment pointing at its twin, and I still only fixed the twin it pointed at.
The fixture now unpacks a generator with string keys and a generator mixing
both, so the two branches are pinned together.

Corpus `zs2`: **2408**, one real gain (`named_params/unknown_named_param`)
against the flake, and `unsupported` 422 -> 416. Six files stopped refusing;
one of them now passes.

The cluster is 5 refusals down to 1. Also landed: the combination case
`f(...$arr, c: 30)`, deferred last tick. The known-callee path places names into
positions at emit time and genuinely cannot when an unpack is present -- but the
*unknown*-callee path already sends names trailing for the prologue to permute,
which is exactly right, so a mixed call now takes that path. Only for a compiled
callee: a library function has no prologue of ours.

The ordering there is the part that bites, and the first version got it wrong.
Names must line up with the **trailing** values in the same order, and an unpack
contributes its names at run time, after everything written before it -- so the
emitter's names have to be appended rather than prepended. Prepending gave
`f(...["b" => 20], c: 30)` the names `c, b` against the values `20, 30`, and
each bound the other's.

## 2026-09-19 -- the refusal was right and the machinery was already there

`f(...["b" => 20])` was refused as `named argument from unpacking`, and the
comment beside it argues its own case well:

> a string key is reported as the gap it is rather than quietly bound by
> position. `f(...["b" => 5, "a" => 4])` binds by name in the engine, which is
> what makes the quiet version a wrong answer.

Entirely right, and it had been true for as long as there was no way to bind by
name. There is: `ctx.SetArgNames` and `php.BindNamedArgs`, which is how an
explicitly written `f(b: 20)` has worked all along. The unpack just never fed
them.

One thing was genuinely missing, and it is the sort of absence that quietly
decides a design: `SetArgNames` **replaces**, and there was no way to read the
list back. So two sources of names -- an unpack and a written named argument
beside it -- would have silently overwritten each other, and the only shape that
could be implemented without noticing is the one with a single source. A
four-line `ArgNames()` getter makes the combination expressible.

The fixture covers positional-then-unpack, a variadic collecting named keys, a
method, a builtin taking three names, and `f(...["c" => 3, 0 => 9])` -- a
positional key after a named one, which the engine refuses and which the unpack
now refuses in the same words.

`f(...["b" => 20], c: 30)` is still refused, by a **different** check -- `named
argument with unpacking` -- which is where the combination case will be picked
up. Left alone deliberately: this tick measured what a string key means, not
what two sources of names mean together.

Corpus `zr2`: **2407 -> 2408**, and the one gain is the flake. **Flat.** The
cluster it aimed at was still refusing, which is what sent the next tick looking
-- see below.

## 2026-09-19 -- eight producers, and the guess that three had given me

Two ticks ago I filed the `dim.ref` refusal with a rule inferred from the three
containers that happened to be reported -- "a real call's result has storage, a
constant's or an intrinsic's does not" -- and wrote that it must not be
implemented on that basis. Settling it properly took one probe over eight
producers, and the guess was wrong:

    byRef($o->m()[0])           silent      byRef(C[0])                Error
    byRef(f()[0])               silent      byRef(func_get_args()[0])  Error
    byRef($o->arr[0])           silent      byRef([1,2][0])            Error
    byRef(C::$sarr[0])          silent
    byRef($local[0])            silent

A **property read is storage-bearing and is an intrinsic call**, so "intrinsic
means no storage" would have refused four correct cases. The real question is
whether the producer yields a slot, and the IR's shape does not answer it --
`prop.get` and `func.args` are the same kind of node.

Two things fell out of implementing it.

`separate` sits between the producer and the consumer for a call result --
`%1 = call.method`, `%2 = separate %1`, `%3 = dim.ref(%2, 0)` -- so recording
the call's storage against `%1` left the consumer asking about `%2` and still
refusing. The property cases worked immediately and the call cases did not,
which is what pointed at it.

And the const and array-literal spellings turn out to be **compile-time** errors
in their direct form: the engine bails rather than raising something catchable,
so they never reach this path at all. They are reachable only through the
indirection `gh12102` uses, and those producers stay refused.

Corpus `zq2`: **2404 -> 2407**, 3 gained and **0 lost**; two real, `bug52041`
and `bug79108`.

Five of the six corpus files in this cluster still refuse; one passes. The
refusal is now on the shapes the engine genuinely makes an Error rather than on
everything that is not a reference.

## 2026-09-19 -- a unit test that was protecting the wrong rule

The engine-class list applies to `instanceof` exactly as it does to `new`, and
for a sharper reason: `$x instanceof Nope` is plain **false**, and measured, it
does **not** autoload -- so there is nothing deferred about the answer at all.
Refusing it replaced an answer with a gap. 7 files.

The same holds for `catch (Nope $e)`: the arm simply never matches.

`go test` then failed on `TestACatchOfAnUndeclaredClassIsRefused`, which asserts
the coarser rule this replaces. The test was doing its job -- a catch of a class
**PHP has and this emitter does not** must still be refused, or the arm silently
never fires where the engine would catch. What it could not express was the
distinction, because it built a `Program` with no engine class list at all.

So it now emits the same source **twice**, against two different lists: refused
by name when the engine has the class, emitted and non-matching when nobody
does. That is a stronger assertion than the one it replaces, and the reason is
written where the old one was -- a test whose premise has been superseded should
say what superseded it, or the next reader restores the old behaviour.

Corpus `zp2`: **2399 -> 2404**, 6 gained against the flake. A new high-water
mark: `instanceof`, `catch`, `bug55086`, `try/bug74444`,

Worth being explicit about the judgement, since "a test failed so I changed the
test" is usually the wrong move: the test encoded a *policy*, the policy was
measured against the engine and found too broad, and the replacement keeps every
case the old one actually protected.

## 2026-09-19 -- asking the engine which classes it has

`new DoesNotExists()` was refused at emit time as `new of undeclared class`,
where PHP raises `Class "DoesNotExists" not found` at run time. The refusal was
not careless -- the comment beside it says exactly why it is there:

> Gated on the program registering an autoloader at all, so that
> `new ReflectionClass` in a program with none keeps its honest refusal rather
> than becoming `Class not found` -- which would be a wrong answer replacing a
> named gap.

Two cases that look identical to the emitter, and only one of them is an answer:

    new DateTime()       PHP has it, php2go does not: a gap
    new DoesNotExists()  nobody has it: the engine's own run-time Error

Telling them apart needs the list of classes the engine provides, and I had
noted twice before that no canonical list exists -- which is true of anything
written down, and irrelevant, because **the engine has one and will hand it
over**. `zend.InternalClasses()` already existed and was already used by four
other commands; `cmd/php2gotest` was simply never wired to it. The list is not
transcribable in any case: it depends on which extensions the build links.

So the refusal now fires only when the engine *does* have the class, and
everything else compiles to the run-time lookup that raises properly.

A second effect worth noting. `try_multicatch_002` gets its `Exception1` from a
`require_once`, and was refused as `new of undeclared class Exception1`. It now
compiles, runs, and reports `unsupported: require once` -- the same bucket, but
naming the gap that is actually there. An emit-time refusal on the *later*
construct was hiding the real one.

`include` is a **run-time** refusal here, deliberately, so a program that never
reaches the include still runs: that design is what makes this improvement
rather than a regression.

## 2026-09-19 -- what the handle family is actually blocked on

With the method-consumer shape landed, the handle family is 129 files and worth
knowing the composition of rather than chipping at. Splitting the 61 that are
off by exactly +1:

    33  lazy_objects/*
     3  function_arguments/sensitive_parameter*
    25  everything else

The lazy cluster is one mechanism, and measuring it settled what the current
approach can and cannot reach:

    $r = new ReflectionClass(C::class);            // #1
    $g = $r->newLazyGhost(function ($o) { ... });  // closure #2, ghost #3
    spl_object_id(new P());                        // 4  -- closure alive
    $g->a;                                         // initialises
    spl_object_id(new P());                        // 2  -- closure released

**Initialising a lazy object releases its initializer's handle.** That is not
general refcounting -- it is one drop at one point, the same shape as the
constructor-throws release. What makes it different from everything
`DisposableTemporaries` handles is that the release point is **later than the
call that consumes the closure**: the analysis can prove the closure is a
temporary handed to `newLazyGhost` and stored nowhere else, but the release has
to happen when the lazy object initialises, which may be anywhere or never.

So the shape it needs is "hand ownership to the callee" rather than "release
now". Filed with the measurement; it touches `runtime/php`, so it waits for a
tick with no run in flight.

The `sensitive_parameter` three were reachable and are done: they are
`(new Exception)->getTrace()`, an **engine** class method with no compiled body
to summarise. Eleven such methods were measured the same way the function
allow-list was, and consulted **only** when no compiled method of that name
exists -- so a program declaring its own `getTrace` is still summarised from its
own body.

That last point is not hypothetical. The first test I wrote for it put a class
with a leaking `getMessage` in the same file as `(new Exception)->getMessage()`,
and both were refused: the summary is keyed by method *name*, so a user class
shadows the engine one everywhere. That is the conservative direction and
correct, but it means the engine list only helps in files that do not collide
with it.

Corpus `zl2`: **2392, flat** -- one flake in, one flake out. The engine-method
list bought nothing measurable. It is kept because it is measured and correct,
not because it paid.

## 2026-09-19 -- the method summary finally pays, and a miss worth keeping

With `zj2` at 2388, the failure census is still dominated by one cause: **129
files whose first divergence is an object handle**, against a long tail where
nothing else reaches double figures.

`DisposableTemporaries` only ever claimed one shape -- a temporary handed to a
non-retaining *library* call. The other obvious shape is a temporary consumed by
a **method** call, `(new M)->read()`, and it could not be claimed before because
deciding it needs to know whether the method hands `$this` anywhere. That is
`LeaksThis`, built two ticks ago, which bought nothing at the time and is what
makes this possible now. Worth recording: the summary's value was not in the
tick that added it.

It also forced `markDisposable` into the whole-unit post-pass beside
`markConfined`, for the reason that pass exists -- the method being called may
not have been lowered yet when the `new` site is examined.

The fixture is six methods chosen to pull in different directions: one that
keeps nothing, one that touches only its own property, and four that let the
receiver out -- into a global, by returning it, by passing it to a function, and
by storing it in an array. All six are right.

Corpus `zk2`: **2388 -> 2392**, 5 gained and 1 lost (the flake). A new
high-water mark -- and the five are `type_declarations/variance/
class_order_autoload1` through `5`, **not** the handle files this was aimed at.
Worth saying: a change measured against the family it was designed for can pay
somewhere else entirely, and reporting only the intended family would have
called this flat.

A seventh case was **removed** from the fixture, and the reason is the
interesting part. A method
whose only use of `$this` is a closure capturing it:

    public function capture() { $f = function () { return $this; }; }

The engine **frees** the receiver there -- the closure is itself a temporary
that dies at once -- while `LeaksThis` refuses every closure outright, so we
keep the handle. That is a *missed* claim, which is the safe direction, and the

## 2026-09-19 -- a run that looked like a catastrophe, and was my own edit

`zi2` came back as **2383 -> 2238, 147 files lost**, the losses alphabetically
contiguous from `bug52484_2` to `closure_017`. That is not what a regression
looks like, and two checks said so before any code was examined:

- **The buckets did not add up.** `passed + failed + unsupported + errored` was
  3,658 against `files 4986`.
- **`noreference` said why.** 248 of them: `the runtime failed to build:
  runtime/php/coerce.go: src.Declared undefined`.

A correction belongs here, because my first reading of this was wrong in a way
that would have built the wrong guard. I took `noreference` to be normally
**zero**. It is not: every recent run has ~1,078 of them, from tests the engine
itself bails on and from `.phpt` skips, and that has always been part of the
4,986 denominator. `zh2`, the run I had just accepted as the baseline, has
1,078. The buckets have *never* summed to the file count; the tally command
simply never printed that column, so I had never looked.

So the signal is not "noreference is non-zero" -- that would refuse every run --
it is **the reason**. `the runtime failed to build` is the one that means the
measurement is void. `.agents-workspace/tmp/seg/tally.sh` now does the sum, and
refuses a comparison on that reason alone.

That was mine. A corpus run builds each generated program **against the live
tree**, and I had spent the minutes after launching it writing `CheckRefStep`
with the wrong field names. Editing `internal/gogen` mid-run is safe -- it is
compiled into the harness binary the run already holds -- but `runtime/php` is
linked at *test* time, so a file that does not compile for two minutes takes
out every file still to be graded.

The harness classified it correctly and said so in plain words, which is the
only reason this cost twenty minutes rather than a day. The comment at its
`go build` step was written after the same thing happened to a half-written
`iter.go`: *"a compile error inside the runtime is not an emitter bug at all --
and on a shared tree it happens"*. It was right then and it was right here.

The other 845 were `engine bailed`, from a box running fourteen graders plus my
builds. Also not a regression, and also not a result.

Recorded in TESTING.md as a rule: rebuild before launching, leave `runtime/`
alone until the run finishes, and **sum the buckets before believing a large
loss**.

The tick's actual work, measured properly by `zj2`: **2383 -> 2388**, 5 gained
and **0 lost** -- `typed_properties_019`, `_023`, `_044`, `_063`, plus the
flake. That covers the typed-static coercion and both halves of the overflow
wording. The reference half of the latter: `$r++` on a reference bound to `public int $n`
lowers to `increment` and then a plain `write_var` with nothing marking it as a
step, so the store cannot tell one from an assignment -- but the emitter can,
having just rendered the increment. It records the step's result value and emits
a `CheckRefStep` guard **ahead of** the store, because the refusal replaces the
write: the property keeps the value it had. The recording had to move to the top
of the intrinsic emitter, since the step variants are fallible and return
through their own branch before the call is assembled.

## 2026-09-19 -- the fourth container, and it was a static

`typed_properties_070` survived the array-element fix from the previous entry
and was worth chasing on its own, because it said the bug was not what I had
just fixed:

    class Foo { public static string $s = "1"; }
    Foo::$s .= "1";   // string("11")  -- right
    Foo::$s += 2;     // engine string("13"), php2go int(13)

`.=` was right by accident -- concatenation already yields a string, so no
coercion was needed. `staticSet` wrote `*slot = v` with **no coercion at all**,
so a typed static never coerced anything, and the TypeError for
`Foo::$i = "x"` never fired either.

Two write paths, both needing it, and the lowering shows them plainly:

    Foo::$s = 42   ->  call.intrinsic "sprop.set"(...)
    Foo::$s += 2   ->  %0 = sprop.ref(...) ; store %0, %2

The second goes through `place.setVerb`, whose `direct` branch is the static
one. The `place` struct already carried `sclass`/`sname` with a comment saying
why -- *"a static slot is a plain \*php.Value with nothing on it saying what
declared it"* -- so the plumbing for this existed and only the coercion was
missing. One helper, `coerceStatic`, called from both.

It has to **walk the chain**: a subclass shares its parent's slot, and the
parent's declaration is the one that governs, including in the message. The
fixture pins that, along with `++`/`--` through the same place and an untyped
static that must keep taking anything.

Corpus `zh2`: **2380 -> 2383**, 4 gained -- exactly the four negative-zero files
from the entry below -- against the flake. A new high-water mark.

Then the overflow wording from the same file, which took two wrong designs to
get right and is the more interesting half.

Overflowing a typed property has its own message -- `Cannot increment property
C::$n of type int past its maximal value` -- where we gave the generic `Cannot
assign float to ...`. The *shape* was already correct: a TypeError, value
unchanged. Only the wording differed, on 13 occurrences in the corpus, with
another 28 for the through-a-reference variant.

**First design, wrong:** test `d.Type == "int"`. The corpus wants this message
for `?int` and `int|bool` too, and a hand-kept list of which declarations refuse
a float is a list that will drift.

**Second design, also wrong, and instructively so:** ask `CoerceProperty` and
reword its refusal -- let the type rule decide and only supply the words. That
is the right instinct and it fails on the decrement, because
`PHP_INT_MIN - 1` is **exactly representable as a float**: assigning it to an
`int` property succeeds and stores `PHP_INT_MIN` again. Measured directly --
the same value assigned plainly is accepted while the step is refused -- so the
rule is about the *operation*, not about the value, and no amount of asking the
coercion will see it.

**What it is:** does the declaration admit a float at all. `php.StepRefusesOverflow`
lives beside the coercion rules because that is what it reads, and the
project's own catalogue test made me say so out loud -- an exported
`runtime/php` function must be an intrinsic or an explicitly excused shared
rule, and writing the excuse is what forced the distinction between "a property
of a declaration" and "an operation with a home".

The direction still needs no opcode: only an increment can leave a positive
float there.

The reference variant is the larger half and is **not** done -- that write goes
through `write_var`, which carries no step marker, so it needs the producing
`increment`/`decrement` tracked at its def site. Filed.

## 2026-09-19 -- negative zero is a valid Go literal, which is the problem

`float(-0)` against `float(0)` was four files in the failure census, and the
cause is a nice one: the emitter rendered the literal as

    php.Float(-0)

which **compiles**, and is positive zero. Go has no negative-zero constant --
`-0` is an untyped integer and `-0.0` folds the same way -- so only
`math.Copysign(0, -1)` carries the sign. The renderer already special-cased
`Inf` and `NaN` there, with a comment saying they "are not Go literals"; this is
the fourth member of that family and the one that does not announce itself,
because nothing fails to build.

It reaches more code than it looks like it should, because **Zend constant-folds
the arithmetic**: `0.0 * -1`, `0.0 / -1` and `1 / -INF` all arrive as this
literal.

The **interpreter was right throughout**, and that is what localised it: both
back-ends share `runtime/php`, so a disagreement between them cannot be about
value semantics. Running the same snippet through `php2eval` without `-raw` --
which runs engine and interpreter side by side -- was a two-second test that
said "this is the emitter" before any code was read.

Building the fixture turned up two more, because a fixture written to cover
*every way the value can arrive* asks questions the reported case did not:

- `abs(-0.0)` kept the sign. `if f < 0 { f = -f }` is false for negative zero;
  `math.Abs` is not. Shared with the interpreter, so this one was a real
  runtime bug rather than an emitter one.
- **`min` and `max` break ties differently with two arguments than with
  three** -- `min(-0.0, 0.0)` is the second and `max(-0.0, 0.0)` is the first,
  while `min(1, 1.0, "1")` and `max(1, 1.0, "1")` are both the first. PHP
  special-cases the two-argument call. **Filed, not encoded**: four
  measurements plus a guess at the mechanism is not a rule, and a tie-break
  written from a guess looks right until an array form disagrees.

All four corpus files pass locally.

Corpus `zf2` for the lazy-proxy `instance`: **2376 -> 2379**, 4 gained (all four
real lazy-object files) against the `message_004` flake. A new high-water mark.

     33  want string got string

      7  want int    got string      <- these two

    $arr[0] .= "5";     // engine: int(115).  php2go: string("115")

A reference bound to a typed property carries that property's declaration, and

array element. Writing through it stored a string in an `int` property and never
raised the TypeError the engine raises.

Worth noting how it was found. Not by reading the reference machinery -- that
code is correct and well-commented -- but by grouping failures on `(type wanted,
type got)` and noticing that `int` vs `string` and `string` vs `int` are the
same bug seen from both ends. Eleven files, in a bucket that otherwise looks
like an undifferentiated long tail of wrong values.

Fixture `typed_ref_in_array.php` covers all three sites, both coercion
directions, the TypeError, `+=` and `--` as well as `.=`, an element holding no
box at all, and a nested array -- because the fix is a check on one container
and the obvious way to get it wrong is to check only the shape that was
reported.

and fails on a *different* missing diagnostic, `Cannot decrement a reference
held by property ... past its minimal value`. The eleven files each have more
than one problem; fixing the first one they hit moves the diff, not the bucket.
`typed_properties_070` is still wrong in the other direction and is not
explained by this fix -- a `string`-typed property taking an int, which the
fixture covers and passes, so its shape differs from the one I reproduced.

## 2026-09-19 -- four lazy states, and only one of them has an instance

`var_dump` of a lazy object was wrong in one of its four states, and the way to
find that was to enumerate all four rather than reason from the one in front of
me:

    uninitialized ghost   lazy ghost object(P)#7 (0) {}
    uninitialized proxy   lazy proxy object(P)#3 (0) {}
    initialized ghost     object(P)#9 (2) { a, b }        <- no prefix at all
    initialized proxy     lazy proxy object(P)#5 (1) { ["instance"] => ... }

Only the last has an `instance`, and it is the only one still labelled lazy
after initialization -- a ghost becomes an ordinary object. Any of the other
three would have been a plausible guess about the fourth.

php2go fell through to the proxy shell's own property table, which is empty, so
an initialized proxy dumped as `(0) {}`. Two lines to fix once the rule was
known.

Fixture `lazy_proxy_dump.php` uses **`print_r`** rather than `var_dump`, and for
the same reason the Closure fixture binds its closures to variables: `print_r`
shows the property set without an object handle, so the fixture pins the layout
and not the numbering. The first draft, with `var_dump`, failed on a handle
number one byte away from correct -- which is exactly the way a numbering bug
gets mistaken for a layout bug.

## 2026-09-19 -- Zend keeps a closure's captures where its statics live

Corpus `zd2` for the lazy `__debugInfo` fix: **2372, identical to `zc2`** -- 0
gained, 0 lost. Checked rather than shrugged at, and the same pattern as the
Closure work above it: `init_trigger_var_dump_debug_info_001` now differs from
the engine by an **object handle alone**, byte-identical otherwise. The fix
worked and moved the file into the numbering family. A tick that measures flat
is not always a tick that changed nothing, and the only way to tell is to look
at the files the change was aimed at.

Then the `static` half of the Closure layout, and it turned into the sharpest
lesson of the session.

The engine shows `static` for **three** different things, which took three
probes to separate:

    function () use ($cap) {}          // static => ["cap" => 7]
    function () { static $sv = 1; }    // static => ["sv" => 1]
    func(...)                          // static => the callee's statics

and a closure with both a capture and a static shows **one merged array**,
captures first. A static that has run shows what it holds now; one that has not
shows its **declared initializer**, not NULL -- `static $sv = 1` is `int(1)`
before the first call.

Building that broke my own fixture: a by-reference capture printed `&NULL`. The
cause is worth recording because it is a fact about the engine, not about this
code. **Zend stores a closure's `use` bindings in the same `static_variables`
table as its `static $x` declarations** -- that is how closures are implemented
-- so `fn.Statics` contains both and nothing in the harvest tells them apart.
Registering both put `use (&$literal)` into the closure's own static list, where
it overwrote the capture with the fallback slot's NULL.

Two attempts at the fix, and the first was wrong in an instructive way: filter
the captures out at **registration**, using `fn.Statics` as "the authority on
which names are really `static $x`". It is not the authority, because the engine
does not draw that line there. The separation only exists where it is actually
knowable -- at display time, where a capture is **bound** and a static is not.
When a table cannot answer a question, the answer is not a better filter on that
table.

Corpus `ze2`: **2372 -> 2376**, 4 gained and 0 lost -- the three the work was
aimed at (`gh8083`, `bug79778`, `call_user_func_003`) plus
`value_unknown_at_compile_time_001` landing favourably. A new high-water mark. `bug81076` is filed instead of fixed: an arrow function
auto-captures only variables that **exist**, while an explicit
`use ($undefined)` warns and lists NULL -- two different rules that lower to the
identical `bind_lexical ... use=value`, so separating them needs
`ZEND_ACC_ARROW_FUNCTION` harvested onto the closure.

## 2026-09-19 -- two layouts for a Closure, and a census cut that found them

`zb2` confirmed the `bind_ref` half: **2370**, one real gain
(`type_declarations/intersection_types/typed_reference`) against one flake loss
(`anon/004`). The narrowed-place family is closed for now -- the remaining
narrowing shapes were probed directly (stores that disagree, a place reassigned
across types, `unset` then reuse, `list()` destructuring, in-place concat) and
all are correct. Narrowing itself is sound; only a place whose storage is held
elsewhere was ever at risk.

With `unsupported` at 447 and mostly refusals by design, the failures were cut
again by the shape of their first diff. Splitting the object-header ones by
*which* number differs separated two families that look identical in a diff:

    122  object handle number   (the refcount family, still the largest)
     34  object property count

and the second turned out to be mostly one thing: **`var_dump` of a Closure**.

The engine has **two layouts**, not one:

    $f = function ($x) {};       // name, file, line, parameter
    $g = strlen(...);            // function, parameter    -- no file, no line
    $h = $obj->m(...);           // function, this, parameter

php2go emitted name/file/line for all of them. The comments in both
`closureFromCallable` and the debug-info builder already **described** the right
behaviour -- *"a literal shows name/file/line, a first-class callable shows
`function`"* -- and the code did the other thing. A comment is not a test.

Three pieces were needed. A `function` field on `closureMeta`, so the two
layouts are two shapes rather than one with a field missing. A runtime
`namedCallableParams` table, because a named closure has to look its callee's
parameters up where a literal carries its own -- built from compiled functions,
compiled methods and the harvested builtin signatures, and the same table
`ReflectionFunction::getParameters` will want. And `this` for an array callable:
`$o->m(...)` set the receiver on the way back out, but a `[$o, "m"]` reaching
`closureFromCallable` directly had nobody to set it.

Fixture `closure_debug_info.php` binds each closure to a **variable** rather
than dumping a temporary, so it tests the layout and not object-handle reuse --
the first draft failed on a handle number with the layout already correct, which
would have made a numbering bug look like a layout bug.

Corpus `zc2`: **2370 -> 2372**, 2 gained and 0 lost -- and one of the two is
`message_004`, so **one** real file where the census pointed at eight. Worth
saying, because the census was not wrong: checked afterwards, two more
(`first_class_callable_optimization`, `gh8962`) now differ from the engine by an
object *handle number* alone, with byte-identical output otherwise. They moved
from the layout family into the numbering one and will come back with it. A
census that counts a file's **first** difference cannot tell "fixed" from "fixed
one of two problems", and the honest way to read a small gain against a large
cluster is to go and look.

Three more are genuine remainders and are filed: a named callable must also show
the callee's `static` variables, which our `static` carries only for a closure's
`use` captures.

The same tick also found `__debugInfo` never reaching a **lazy** object: the
dispatch sat after the lazy branch, so a ghost dumped its deferred slots instead
of what the class declared `__debugInfo` to show. Asked of the engine first,
because the obvious worry is that calling a method initializes the object -- it
does not: the method runs, the initializer does not, and
`isUninitializedLazyObject` still answers true afterwards. Fixture
`lazy_debug_info.php` pins all three of those, and keeps a class **without**
`__debugInfo` beside them so the deferred-slot path stays covered.

## 2026-09-19 -- a summary that bought nothing, and the bug it led to

`ConfinedObjects` has always been handed **nil** for its method summary, which
makes every method call on an object count as an escape -- the measured
difference between claiming 9% and 26% of `new` sites. Three separate TODO items
wanted it, so this tick built it.

The lowering makes the question unexpectedly easy, and that is worth writing
down because it is invisible from the PHP. Reaching your own properties leaves
the receiver a **literal token**:

    call.intrinsic "prop.set"($this, "x", 1)
    isset $this, "x", on=prop

while every way of letting it out first materialises it as a value:

    %0:*obj = this

So the summary is close to "does the body contain a `this` instruction".

The test for it is 16 attempts to get a **false** out of a method that really
does leak, because a wrong false frees a live object while a wrong true only
costs a claim. **It caught one, and it was not one I would have found by
reading:** a closure captures `$this` implicitly, so `function () { return
$this; }` inside a method lowers to a bare `closure` instruction and *nothing in
the body mentions the receiver at all*. Every rule passed it. Closures are now
refused outright.

Two structural notes. It had to become a whole-unit **post-pass**, because
`ConfinedObjects` asks about a method *name* and that body may not be lowered
when the first `new` site is examined. And because it gets only the name, two
classes sharing one fold together as "leaks if either does" -- with a separate
per-**class** table for `__construct`, since every constructor shares one name
and folding them would have refused every one.

Corpus `zz`: **2364 -> 2363**, 0 gained, 1 lost -- the flake. **Nothing.**

That deserves stating plainly rather than being buried. The 9%-to-26% figure is
about how many `new` sites an analysis can *claim*; `ConfinedNew` spends those
claims on one thing only, destructor timing at frame return, and the objects it
newly claims mostly have no destructor to time. A coverage number is not a
behaviour number, and this one has been cited twice in these notes as though it
were the second. It is not, and the summary should be kept for what it unlocks
next rather than counted as a win.

What the tick is actually worth is a bug found on the way. Probing whether a
constructor that throws gives its handle back needed a "leaks `$this`" case to
compare against, and the obvious one -- `global $k; $k = $this;` -- **did not
work at all**:

    function m() { global $k; $k = $this; }   // $k stays null
    function m() { global $k; $k = 7; }       // fine

`storeVariant` refuses to treat a store as a variable write when the place's
representation is narrower than `zval`, on the grounds that such a place is a
frame slot -- an iterator handle, a rope buffer. But representation inference
had narrowed `$k` to `*obj` from its only store, so a perfectly ordinary PHP
variable was written as a frame slot, **replacing** the box `bind_global` had
put there instead of writing through it.

`placeRepresentation` already carried this exact fix for closures captured by
reference, with a comment describing the identical failure. `bind_global` and
`bind_static` were simply never added beside it. One line each.

It stayed invisible because it needs a value narrower than `zval` to appear at
all: every scalar store takes the correct path. Fixture
`global_object_store.php` covers an object, an array, a string and a static, and
keeps a scalar beside them as the case that always worked.

Treating it as a **class** of bug rather than one bug then paid again. Probing
the five shapes that bind a box found one more: `$b = &$a; $b = new C();` leaves
`$a` null, because `bind_ref` was missing from the same set. Both operands are
boxed now -- the two names share one box, so neither may be narrowed. The
by-reference *parameter* shapes were probed too and are fine, so `bind_var` is
deliberately not in the set: there is no evidence of a bug there, and adding
untested handling is how one gets introduced.

Corpus `za2`: **2364 -> 2370**, 7 gained and 1 lost -- the loss being the
`value_unknown_at_compile_time_001` flake. One of the gains, `anon/004`, is
itself one of the three known non-deterministic files, so the honest count is
six solid. `bug30162` is among them, which is the constructor-throws handle
release working: a constructor that throws gives its number back, gated on
`LeaksThis` saying it did not hand `$this` out first. So the method summary
bought nothing through `ConfinedNew` and something through this, which is the
argument for keeping it.

## 2026-09-19 -- the biggest failure family is a number, and it is the refcount

With `unsupported` down to 449 and `failed` at 1102, the work has moved into the
failures, so this tick cut them by the **shape** of the first diff rather than by
its text. The shapes:

    687  value or ordering differs
    257  MISSING output, engine printed something
     79  EXTRA output, engine printed nothing there
     73  MISSING diagnostic

and inside the first of those, one family dominates: **131 files whose first
divergence from the engine is an object handle number and nothing else** --
larger than any refusal cluster, including the 132 compile-error files closed
earlier today. Splitting them by offset:

    got - want:  +1: 65   +2: 22   +4: 20   +3: 10   other: 14

php2go's handles run **high**, which is the signature of reuse it does not do.
The cause is one line of PHP:

    var_dump(new Point(1));   // engine: #1
    var_dump(new Point(2));   // engine: #1 again -- the first is already gone

PHP hands out the lowest free handle; php2go counted monotonically. This is the
refcount gap, and the handle is *printed*, so it is a wrong answer rather than a
slow one.

`lower.DisposableTemporaries` now claims the `new` results that provably die at
the call consuming them. It is deliberately stricter than `ConfinedObjects`,
which answers "cannot outlive this frame" -- enough to time a destructor, not
enough to time a *number*. A site is claimed only when every use is recognised,
one call is the sole consumer, the value is sent by value exactly once, and the
callee is known to keep nothing. The emitted program allocates from a free list,
lowest first.

Four things worth recording.

**It has to run on the file body, and `markConfined` deliberately does not.**
`{main}`'s locals are globals, so frame confinement says nothing there -- but a
temporary handed to `var_dump` dies at the call whatever frame it sits in, and
the file body is exactly where such statements are written. Wiring it only to
named functions and methods made it fire on nothing at all, which is how the
first version measured as a no-op.

**Every allocation site has to share the allocator.** Sixteen places called
`nextObjectID++`; one left behind would skip a freed handle and print the wrong
number somewhere else. That included a save/restore whose comment says a
throwaway instance "must not cost a handle" -- which now has to restore the free
list too, since popping one and putting the counter back still loses it.

**A class with `__destruct` is excluded on purpose.** Its death is observable, so
recycling the handle without also moving the destructor would fix the number and
keep the wrong output -- a file that goes from wrong-in-two-ways to
wrong-in-one-way, which grades the same and hides the remaining bug. Confirmed
by writing that case and watching it fail on the pre-existing timing gap, then
taking it out of the fixture rather than letting it mask the claim under test.

**The allow-list was asked of the engine, not written from memory.** Each name in
`nonRetainingCallee` was checked with

    f(new P()); $x = new P(); echo spl_object_id($x);

which answers 1 when the argument was released and 2 when it was kept. Fourteen
answered 1. Three more were **dropped for being unmeasurable** rather than for
answering wrongly -- `strlen` and `intdiv` refuse an object outright, `echo` is
not a call in the IR -- because an entry that cannot be measured does not belong
in a list whose whole safety property is that it fails closed.

Fixture `object_handle_reuse.php` is five attempts to break the claim, not five
confirmations of it: kept in a local, stored by a callee through `global`, held
by another object's constructor, returned from a function. All correct. One case
it gets conservatively wrong is `var_dump([new P(), new P()])`, where the engine
frees both and the analysis sees the values enter an array construction and
refuses -- a miss, not an error, which is the designed direction.

A follow-up tick extended this to groups -- `var_dump([new P(), new P()])`,
where the objects reach the call through an array -- and that extension caught a
**wrong assumption already shipped**. The TODO note it was built on said the
engine reuses the *lowest* free handle. It does not:

    $a = new P(); $b = new P(); $c = new P();
    unset($a); unset($b);   // freed 1 then 2
    new P(); new P();       // -> 2 then 1, not 1 then 2

and reversing the unsets reverses the answer. **The free list is a stack.** The
two disciplines agree whenever only one handle is outstanding, which is exactly
why `zx` passed 4,986 files without distinguishing them -- a whole corpus run is
not evidence for a rule it never exercises. Two further notes from that work: the
order releases are emitted in is now *observable* (for an array, its elements in
array order), and an element that cannot be claimed is **skipped rather than
fatal**, since `[new P(), $held]` frees the temporary and leaves `$held` alone.

Corpus `zy` for that follow-up: **2364 -> 2363**, 0 gained, 1 lost -- the loss
being `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`, the flake. **Flat.** The LIFO fix was
correctness insurance rather than progress, and the array shape is rarer in the
failing set than the fixture made it look. Recorded as flat rather than folded
into the +8 above it.

Corpus `zx`: **2356 -> 2364**, 8 gained and **0 lost**. Eight of 131 is a small
share of the family, and the zero is the part that matters: the conservative
rules held across 4,986 files, so widening them is now an incremental job rather
than a gamble. The remaining shapes are in TODO.md.

## 2026-09-19 -- writing through a temporary, and choosing four passes over five

`refSlot` refused every write through a non-reference, on this reasoning:
*"a value that is not a reference has no storage behind it, and writing to a
copy would be a change nothing can observe -- so it is reported instead."* The
mechanics are right and the conclusion is backwards. **A change nothing can
observe is exactly what the engine does.** On a method call returning an array,
all four write modes are silent:

    $o->m()[0] = 99;     $o->m()[0] += 5;
    unset($o->m()[0]);   $o->m()[] = 3;      // all print nothing, all run on

So the writer now gets scratch storage and carries on. Fixture
`temp_dim_write.php`.

That is not the whole cluster, and the interesting part is what happened next.
With scratch handed out *everywhere*, the ten-file cluster went 10 unsupported
-> **5 passed, 5 failed**. Three of those failures are the same message:

    byRef(func_get_args()[0])   // Cannot use temporary expression in write context
    byRef(C[0])                 // same, for a const array
    byRef($o->m()[0])           // silent

Same syntax, same intrinsic (`dim.ref`), opposite answers -- and `refSlot` sees
only a `php.Value`, so it cannot tell them apart. Handing out scratch there
answers **silence where the engine throws**, which is the precise failure mode
the 2026-09-18 backouts were about, arrived at from the other direction: there
it was a refusal replacing a right answer, here a right-looking answer replacing
an error.

So `dim.ref` keeps refusing and everything else takes scratch. The cluster ends
at **4 passed, 0 failed, 6 unsupported** -- one *fewer* pass than the blanket
version, and the right trade. A refusal says "we know we cannot"; a silent wrong
answer says nothing at all, and is the kind of thing found three ticks later by
bisecting.

The discriminator does exist, and it is in the lowered IR at the container's
**def site**:

    %1:zval = call.method %0, "b"()          -> silent
    %4:zval = call.intrinsic "func.args"()   -> Error
    %7:zval = const.fetch "C"                -> Error

which reads as IS_VAR versus IS_TMP_VAR/IS_CONST -- a real call's result has
storage, a constant's or an intrinsic's does not. **Filed rather than
implemented**, and deliberately: that is a rule generalised from three samples,
and AGENTS.md's founding rule is that reasoning about Zend operand encodings has
been wrong more often than right. It is worth ~6 files and it needs `php2eval`
across the producers first. The earlier note in TODO.md carries the evidence.

## 2026-09-19 -- a file the engine cannot compile is an answer, not a gap

The largest single refusal cluster in the corpus is **132 files** -- larger than
`include or eval` at 120 -- and every one of them is `compile: zend: ... Parse
error` or `... Fatal error` at compile time. They had been sitting in
`unsupported` since the harness was written.

They do not belong there, and the reason is already written down in this tree.
`Program.CompileDiagnostic` exists because *"some of PHP's diagnostics are
emitted at compile time, not run time ... php2go is unusually placed here,
because the engine emits the text while we harvest and the harvest already
captures it. Replaying it in the prologue is what makes the compiled program's
output match."* That is the case where compilation **succeeds** and still
prints. The case where it fails outright is the same principle with nothing
left over: PHP's behaviour for such a source is to print the diagnostic and run
nothing at all, so the artifact that reproduces exactly that **is** the correct
artifact. `compileFile` already says so in a comment -- *"a compile error is a
legitimate outcome, not a harness failure: many PHP tests exist precisely to
trigger one, and the message is their expected output"* -- and then the caller
threw the message away.

So: when `CompileUnit` returns a `*zend.CompileError`, emit a program with no
file body, no functions and no classes, whose whole behaviour is the diagnostic
prologue that already exists. 131 of the 132 now pass. The one that does not is
correctly still refused -- the arm is bounded to a **diagnosed** failure, and a
bailout or an empty diagnostic is the engine giving up rather than answering,
which is not something to replay.

**Why this is not a gap dressed up as a pass, stated plainly because the number
is large enough to deserve the question.** Three reasons, in increasing order of
how much they settle it:

1. php2go does not have a parser; it delegates parsing to the engine at harvest
   time by design. For unparseable source there is no php2go machinery being
   skipped -- there is no machinery that *could* run.
2. The principle was already established and documented for compile-time
   warnings. This extends it to the case where the diagnostic is fatal; it does
   not invent a new licence.
3. Decisively: **the mechanism cannot manufacture a false pass.** The oracle is
   the engine itself and grading is byte-exact on stdout, so a pass here means
   the compiled program printed precisely what PHP printed. A file whose
   expected output held anything beyond the diagnostic would grade `failed`, not
   `passed`.

What it does *not* prove is worth saying too: these 132 files exercise the
**parser**, and passing them says nothing about lowering, emission or the
runtime. The headline count moves by more than the compiler's coverage does, so
the number is reported on its own line rather than folded into a tick.

Mechanically this needed one refactor: the build-run-compare tail of `grade` is
now `buildAndRun`, because a diagnostic-only program is built, run and graded
exactly like any other. The first attempt at that extraction matched the wrong
`os.WriteFile(work/main.go)` -- there is a second one in `run()` seeding the
module -- and moved a 400-line span into the new function. Caught by the build,
not by reading. When cutting a span by a matched line, match on something that
occurs once.

Corpus `zv`: **2220 -> 2352**, `unsupported` 587 -> 456. 132 gained, **0
lost**. 131 of those are the cluster; the other is `message_004` landing on the
favourable side again. Reported here on its own because it is a parser result,
not a compiler one -- the compiler's own coverage did not move at all this tick.

Corpus `zu` (the ReflectionMethod predicates, dynamic properties and
`ReflectionException`): **2221 -> 2220**, 0 gained and 1 lost, the loss being
`message_004` flipping again. `unsupported` 592 -> 587 while `failed` rose 1094
-> 1099: five files stopped refusing and started giving wrong answers. That is
movement, and it is not progress in `passed` -- recorded as it happened rather
than folded into the reflection entry above it.

## 2026-09-19 -- probing a surface instead of counting refusals

The refusal census names a file's **first** refusal. So one missing method hides
every later one in the same file, and a surface with a hole in its entry point
looks like a surface with one hole. Probing `ReflectionClass` one method at a
time -- twenty small programs, each calling exactly one method -- found **19 of
the 20 missing** where the census had named three. The technique is worth more
than the result: *size a surface by probing it, not by counting reasons.*

Filled in one pass, all backed by tables the emitter already had
(`classConsts`, `classMethodOrder`, `classTraitOrder`, `parentOf`,
`interfacesOf`, `methodVisibility`, `finalClasses`, `enumClasses`):
`getConstants`, `getConstant`, `hasConstant`, `hasProperty`, `hasMethod`,
`getParentClass`, `isAbstract`, `isFinal`, `isEnum`, `isInstantiable`,
`implementsInterface`, `isSubclassOf`, `getStaticProperties`, `getTraitNames`,
`getConstructor`, `getMethods`. Three new tables were needed and only three:
`abstractClasses`, `classConstOrder`, `staticPropOrder`.

Four things the engine settled.

**A per-class table is not a flattened table.** `classConsts[c]` and
`staticPropOrder[c]` hold each class's *own* declarations; the flattening the
engine does in its own tables happens at **lookup** here. So `getConstants` and
`getStaticProperties` needed explicit walks -- the class, then each ancestor,
then the interfaces -- and `hasConstant`/`getConstant` needed the same walk
rather than one map lookup. Each was caught by the fixture in turn, one line at
a time: 3 constants wanted, 1 given; then `getConstant("BK")` false; then 2
static properties wanted, 1 given.

**`$m->class` is where a method was declared, which is not where it was
found.** An **ancestor's** method reports the ancestor; a **trait's** reports
the composing class, because the engine copies a trait method in rather than
inheriting it. From the walk they look identical, so `getMethods` carries a
separate `reportAs` alongside the owner it is reading.

**`methodVisibility` records only the non-public methods.** An entry's mere
presence is the whole answer for `isInstantiable`; reading a field out of it
reads the *owner*. The first version did read a field, and passed the fixture
by accident -- the owner string is neither empty nor `"public"`, so the test
that was meant to ask about visibility happened to give the right answer for
the wrong reason. Fixed to the presence check.

**A dynamic property is reflectable from the object and not from the class.**
`new ReflectionProperty($o, "dyn")` succeeds; `new ReflectionProperty("P",
"dyn")` is a ReflectionException; `ReflectionClass::getProperty("dyn")` throws
and `ReflectionObject::getProperty("dyn")` does not. This is the same shape as
the refusals backed out on 2026-09-18 -- a check that needs to know what it is
looking at -- and it was safe here for one reason worth stating: **the
distinction is still visible at the site that needs it.** The constructor can
see whether its first argument was an object; `getProperty` can see its own
kind. Where that is true, a check is safe; where it is not, the last two ticks
say do not write one.

`ReflectionException` was missing from `throwableParents` entirely, so any
program that *caught* it refused at emit time -- `instanceof undeclared class
ReflectionException`. Found by writing a fixture that catches one. The table's
own header says every relationship in it came from asking the engine; this one
was asked the same way before being added.

Corpus `zt` (the ReflectionNamedType and ReflectionClass batch): **2218 ->
2221**, `unsupported` 596 -> 592, 3 gained and 0 lost. Two are real --
`enum/value-property-type` and `type_declarations/typed_properties_018` -- and
the third is `message_004`, the flake, coming back. The ReflectionMethod,
dynamic-property and ReflectionException work landed after `zt` started and is
not in that number; `zu` measures it.

Fixtures: `reflection_type.php`, `reflection_class.php`,
`reflection_method.php`. 256/257 passing, the one failure being the
long-standing `print_r_library.php`. Gate clean.

## 2026-09-19 -- ReflectionProperty's value surface, and the order it lists in

After two ticks lost to refusals that needed a classification the emitter could
not make, this one deliberately took the opposite risk profile: **adding a
capability** rather than adding a check. A capability that is wrong shows up as a
failing fixture on the way in; a refusal that is wrong shows up as a working
program that stopped working, three chunks into a corpus run.

The gap, from the `zr` refusal census: `ReflectionProperty::setValue` (5 files),
`ReflectionClass::getProperties` (4), `ReflectionProperty::getValue` (3). The
class could be *constructed* and nothing else -- none of the predicates existed
either. Added: `getValue`, `setValue`, `isInitialized`, `getProperties`, and the
cheap predicates `isStatic`, `isReadOnly`, `isPublic`, `isPrivate`,
`isProtected`, `isVirtual`, `hasDefaultValue`, `getDefaultValue`. Deliberately
**not** added: `getType`, which needs a `ReflectionNamedType` that does not
exist, so it stays `unsupported` rather than becoming a plausible string.

Three things the engine settled that reading the class would not have.

**Reflection bypasses visibility and nothing else.** `setValue` reaches a private
property from global scope, but a readonly one still refuses a second write
(`Cannot modify readonly property P::$r`) and a typed one still coerces or
throws (`"7"` stores `int(7)`; `"z"` is a TypeError). So the arm skips the
visibility check and keeps `CheckPropertyWrite` and `CoerceProperty` -- passing
the *declaring* class as the scope, which is what lets the readonly first write
through while leaving the once-only rule in force.

**`setValue($v)` and `setValue(null, $v)` are the same call for a static.** The
first parameter is the object only when there is a second. Reading argument 0
unconditionally wrote `null` into `P::$st` and the fixture caught it on the first
run.

**`getProperties()` lists in declaration order, not slot order, and drops an
inherited private.** Two separate facts, each worth its own note:

- A static property has no slot among the instance ones, so concatenating the
  two lists gives `a s untyped st` where the engine says `a s st untyped`. The
  IR already carries `Property.order` -- harvested for exactly this, with a
  comment saying so -- and the sort happens at emit time rather than in the
  emitted program.
- `Base::$hidden`, a private of the parent, is **absent**. The subclass cannot
  reach it, so reflection does not offer it; only `Base`'s own reflector has it.
  Found by diffing the fixture, not predicted.

One structural choice worth recording. Statics went into a **new**
`declaredStaticProps` table rather than into `declaredProps`. Every consumer of
`declaredProps` is lazy-object machinery that skips a static anyway, so widening
it would have changed four unrelated algorithms to serve one new caller -- the
same shape as the WeakMap extraction that lost behaviour by omission. A second
table costs nothing and keeps the blast radius at zero.

Fixtures: `reflection_property.php`, 253/254 passing (the one failure is the
long-standing `print_r_library.php`). Gate clean.

Corpus `zs`: **2211 -> 2218**, `unsupported` 609 -> 596, 8 gained and 1 lost --
the loss being `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`, one of the three known
non-deterministic files. A new high-water mark. What the eight are is worth
recording, because only two of them are *about* reflection:
`attributes/009_doctrine_annotations_example`, `bug72177`, `bug78921`,
`lazy_objects/rfc/rfc_example_011`, `lazy_objects/use_case_002`,
`property_hooks/bug001`, `property_hooks/cpp`,
`property_hooks/find_property_usage`. Property hooks and lazy objects reach for
`ReflectionProperty::setValue` as a *tool*, not as the thing under test -- which
is the general shape of the reflection gap and the reason the census undercounts
it.

## 2026-09-18 -- two more refusals backed out, and what they have in common

Corpus: the run that measured these, `zq`, was **2212 -> 2211**: 3 gained, 4
lost. The confirming run after the reverts, `zr`, is **0 gained and 1 lost**
against `zp` -- the loss being `message_004`, the known flake -- so the
reverts restored the baseline exactly. Two losses were the known non-deterministic files; **two were real** --
`named_params/basic` and `named_params/runtime_cache_init`. Both changes are
backed out, so the tree is where `zp` left it at 2212.

A tick that ends at zero. The reason it ended there is the part worth keeping.

### What was attempted

**An unknown named argument to a library function.**
`array_merge([1], nope: [2])` is `ArgumentCountError: array_merge() does not
accept unknown named parameters`, where a *user* variadic keeps the name under a
string key. Implemented for every internal variadic. Broken by
`call_user_func(['C','m'], b: 0)`, which **forwards** the name to the callee --
and nothing in the harvested signature tells a forwarding variadic from a
collecting one. Both are `...$args`.

**A by-reference parameter given a literal.** `br(1+1)` on `function br(&$r)`
is `br(): Argument #1 ($r) could not be passed by reference`. Implemented as a
positional scan of the argument list. Four attempts:

1. Wrong return shape -- the refusal belongs in the prelude.
2. Matched a **named** argument against a positional slot.
3. Tested `CutNamedSend` on the operand when the name is on the whole item.
4. Used the right helper, `cutNamed`, and it *still* failed.

Each fixed one shape and broke `named_params/basic`, which exercises five
orderings of the same call.

### What they have in common

Both are refusals whose safety depends on classifying something this code cannot
reliably classify.

- The named-parameter one needs to know **which internal variadics forward**,
  and the signature does not say.
- The by-reference one needs to know **which items are positional**, and by the
  time it runs the list carries a send mode, an optional name, and a position
  the named-argument pass may already have reassigned.

That is the same shape as the `Interface "X" not found` check two entries back,
which needed to know every interface the engine provides. Three refusals, three
different missing classifications, and in every case the failure mode is the
same: a **working** program is refused.

The principle from the previous entry, now tested twice more and holding:
*a refusal is only as safe as the completeness of what it accepts* -- and its
corollary, *a refusal is only as safe as its ability to tell what it is
refusing.*

Both `php.ThrowNoUnknownNamedParameters` and
`php.ThrowArgumentNotByReference` are kept, with the reasoning written where each
check would go. Neither is hard once the missing fact exists; both are unsafe
until it does.

### The cost, stated plainly

Four attempts at one check is too many. The signal to stop was available after
the second -- the first two failures were already *different* shapes, which is
what distinguishes "one more edge case" from "cannot classify the input". That
is the judgment to make earlier next time.

## 2026-09-18 -- nested unset, and a check that had to be backed out

Corpus: **2211 -> 2212 passing**, unsupported 609 unchanged, failed 1088 ->
1087, errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zo`: **1 gained, 0 lost**.

One file landed. The change that did **not** land is the more useful record.

### Nested unset through a non-container

`unset($a["x"]["y"])` was a silent no-op whatever `$a` held. Single-level unset
was already right; only the nested form went through `refExisting`, which
returned a scratch value for anything that was not an array or object. Measured
over every container:

| container | engine |
|---|---|
| `null` | nothing, and no diagnostic |
| `false` | the deprecation, then nothing |
| `string` | `Cannot unset string offsets` |
| int / float / `true` | `Cannot unset offset in a non-array variable` |

**Three of the six were being swallowed.** Only null and false are silent, and
the code had generalised from those two to all of them.

### The link check, and why it is not in the tree

A class naming an interface nothing declares is a fatal in the engine --
`Interface "X" not found` -- and compiled output bound it happily and printed
nothing. The check looked small. It worked on its own cases, then broke **30 of
253 fixtures** on `implements ArrayAccess`. Adding `ArrayAccess` to the
engine-interface set fixed those and it broke again on `JsonSerializable`.

That is when the shape became clear: the check needs to know **every interface
the engine provides**, `realClass` answers nothing for any of them, and no
canonical list exists anywhere in this tree. Each name missed from a
hand-written set turns a *working* `implements` into a link failure -- a wrong
answer replacing correct behaviour, which is the one trade the quality gate
forbids.

Two misses in two attempts is what makes the set **unenumerable rather than
merely incomplete**, and that is the difference between "try harder" and "do not
do this yet". Backed out, with the reasoning written where the check would go so
the next attempt starts from why it failed rather than from how it looked.

The general form, worth keeping: *a check that refuses is only as safe as the
completeness of what it accepts.* A refusal built on a set you cannot enumerate
is not conservative -- it is a wrong answer waiting for the first name you did
not think of.

## 2026-09-18 -- two bugs in six lines of ArrayUnpack

Corpus: **2207 -> 2211 passing**, unsupported 609 unchanged, failed 1091 ->
1088, errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zn`: **5 gained, 1 lost**.

### The cluster needed re-screening first

The previous entry reported "80 files that print nothing". Screened for
lifetime, as every other cluster this session has been: **13 of the 77 are
lifetime-bound** and 64 are reachable. `exception_026` is the instructive one --
a recursive `__destruct` cascade that only *looks* like an undefined-constant
test. The screen should have been applied when the cluster was first named.

### Two bugs, same six lines

`ArrayUnpack`'s Traversable arm:

- **No key-type check.** A generator can `yield [] => 1` -- legal to write, and
  it only fails when something unpacks it. Measured across all of them: `null`,
  `true`, `false`, a float and an array are each
  `Error: Keys must be of type int|string during array unpacking`. Non-string
  keys were being silently appended.
- **Integer-like string keys were not renumbered.** `yield "42" => 1` unpacks to
  `[0 => 1]`, not `[42 => 1]`: the key normalises to an integer, and integer
  keys are renumbered rather than preserved. This closes `string_keys.phpt`, a
  gap filed several ticks back when the ArrayIterator work first made that file
  compile.

### The file that was passing by accident

`generators/gh11028_3` went from passing to failing, and the diagnosis is worth
keeping because the fix is still right:

    function generator() {
        try { yield null => 0; }
        finally { throw new Exception("exception"); }
    }
    var_dump([...generator()]);

The engine prints `exception`. Its key error aborts the unpack, **destroys the
generator, runs its `finally`, and that throw supersedes**. Before this tick the
file passed because the null key was silently accepted, the generator ran to
completion, and the `finally` threw anyway -- the right output by the wrong
route. The key check is now correct and the file fails on what was always
missing: generator destruction running `finally`. That is the lifetime work
again, and it is filed rather than papered over by reverting a correct check.

### Two hypotheses that were wrong before any code was written

`Undefined constant "X"` and `Constant X already defined` were both earmarked as
sub-clusters worth fixing. Both **already work** -- tested in isolation before
building anything. Those files fail for unrelated reasons. Checking first cost a
minute and saved the tick.

## 2026-09-18 -- the files that print nothing

Corpus: **2207 -> 2207 passing**, failed 1091 and unsupported 609 both

Net zero. The tick's value is the **cluster it identified**, not the one file it

### A different cut through the failures

Refusals are exhausted, and clustering failures by *reason* had already been
tried and given nothing above six. Cutting them by **output size** instead:

    got 0B against a non-empty want      80 files
    want 0B against a non-empty got       0 files

Eighty files where the compiled program prints **nothing at all**, and none the
other way round. That asymmetry is the finding: the shape is single even though
the fixes are not. **PHP raises where compiled output silently continues**, and
since such a test's whole output is the caught message, producing no diagnostic
produces no bytes.

Sampled causes -- array-unpack key types, undefined constants, a magic method's
return type, `define()` argument validation, by-reference argument errors. Each
its own small missing diagnostic, and none of them needing a refcount, which
makes this the most tractable seam left.

### The one fixed, and the mistake worth keeping

`#[Attribute(Attribute::TARGET_CLASS)]` used on a function must refuse at
`newInstance()`. It did not, and two hypotheses were wrong before the third was
right:

1. *The constant argument had not folded.* It had -- `KIND_INT text="1"`.
2. *The emitted table was missing it.* It was not.
3. `newInstance()` runs on a **ReflectionAttribute**, whose `kind` is
   `"ReflectionAttribute"`. It had no idea what it had been found *on*.

The reflector carries an `origin` beside `kind` now. "What am I" and "where was
I written" are different questions and one field was doing both -- which is the
kind of conflation that only shows up when a rule finally needs the second one.

## 2026-09-18 -- WeakMap moves down, and handle reuse turns out not to be cheap

Corpus: **2193 -> 2204 passing**, unsupported 651 -> 622, failed 1063 -> 1081,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zk`: **11 gained, 0 lost**. The WeakMap
subset, 28 files: **0 -> 6 passing**.

Eleven against a subset that gained six: the extraction also reached files that
use a WeakMap incidentally rather than as their subject.

### First, a claim from the previous tick that was wrong

I wrote that handle reuse "needs no lifetime analysis at all" and would be the
cheap thing to try next. Asserted without asking the engine. Measured:

    $a = new P(); unset($a); $b = new P();          // $b is #1
    $c = new P(); $d = new P(); unset($c);
    $e = new P();                                    // $e is #2, the lowest free

and `class P {}` has **no destructor**. The free list therefore tracks refcounts
for *every* object, which is a strictly larger population than destructor timing
needs. Handle reuse is the same problem in a cheaper-looking hat.

**So D3's remaining work is one thing, not two: the refcount.** Both destructor
timing and handle numbering fall out of it and neither is reachable without it.

### WeakMap, the most extractable piece yet

302 lines and **5** coupling points -- against 4 for the array store, 14 for the
fiber driver, 19 for lazy objects and 56 for reflection. `WeakMapStore` and
`WeakRefStore` are in `runtime/php` now, with two hooks for the questions a weak
container cannot answer for itself: when a key has died, and what letting go of
a value implies.

The interpreter installs both -- it can compute reachability, so it sweeps
before answering, and releasing a value may run a destructor there and then.
Compiled output installs **neither**, and that is the honest limitation written
into the code and the fixture: **the weakness itself is not modelled**. Entries
persist, because knowing a key died is the refcount that does not exist yet.
Right for every use of a WeakMap except the one that makes it weak, and the same
lifetime gap rather than anything particular to weak maps.

### What the differential suite caught

- **The hooks were unbound.** Moving the code without installing the hooks
  silently stopped destructor-on-overwrite from firing -- a behaviour the old
  code had inline. An extraction can lose behaviour by *omission* as easily as
  by mistranslation, and only the suite says so.
- **`WeakReference::create` has no parentheses** in the engine's refusal for the
  `new` path. I wrote `create()`. One character, and the kind of thing that is
  only ever found by diffing against the engine.

`count()` also had to learn the class: it gates on `hasMethod`, and a WeakMap
that does not answer it is not Countable.

## 2026-09-18 -- the escape analysis, and where a local dies

Corpus: **2194 -> 2193 passing**, failed 1063 and unsupported 651 both
unchanged, errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zj`: **0 gained, 1 lost**, and
the loss is `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001` -- one of the three known
non-deterministic files.

**Zero movement.** The behaviour is correct and the fixtures prove the timing is
exact; it simply does not reach enough sites to show. The escape-rate
measurement predicted this and the number was already written down: 9% of `new`
sites are claimable without a method summary, and the destructor-bound failures
are not where they are.

D3's second increment: an object the compiler proves cannot outlive its frame is
destroyed when the function returns, instead of waiting for script-end teardown.

### Why this is exact rather than approximate

PHP destroys a local when the **frame** is destroyed, which is at return. So for
an object that provably was never stored anywhere else, "destroy it at function
exit" is not an approximation of the engine -- it *is* the engine's timing. That
is what makes the increment worth having despite the analysis claiming only a
minority of sites.

### Two orderings, and they disagree

Measured, not assumed, and the second is the one that surprises:

| | order |
|---|---|
| function locals at frame end | **creation** -- `dx, dy, dz` |
| globals at script end | **reverse** -- `dC, dB, dA` |

So a `defer` per object -- the obvious emission -- is wrong twice over, since
LIFO gives the second order everywhere. The emitter keeps a frame list and
drains it forward from a single deferred call, which also covers every exit path
including the ones an error takes.

### The tests were written to break the claim, and two of them did

`ConfinedObjects` has fifteen adversarial cases. The obligation here is stronger
than `QUALITY_GATE.md`'s usual one: the analysis is safe only if **every** way an
object can outlive its frame leaves it unclaimed, so the cases have to be the
ones that fail if the claim is wrong, not the ones that fail if the feature is
absent.

- **`$$n` does not survive lowering as `$$`.** It becomes a `dynvar` place. The
  text check this replaced passed a body that can write through any local,
  including the one holding the object.
- **The method case had no local at all.** `mem2reg` promotes the slot away when
  nothing reads it again, so keying the analysis on a local missed the object
  entirely. Rekeyed on the `new` result, which also picks up the sites the
  throwaway analyser had counted as "never stored" -- 202 of them.

A third case was the *test* being wrong: `$b = $a` with neither read afterwards
vanishes in lowering and the object genuinely is confined, so claiming it is
correct. Rewritten as a real escape rather than weakened to match a bad
expectation.

### The wrong answer it shipped, and how it was found

The destructor-bound subset went 11 -> 10. One file, found by building a variant
with the analysis disabled and diffing the passing sets rather than reading
diffs: `bug36268`.

The cause was principled. **`{main}`'s locals are globals.** They are destroyed
at script end in reverse order, not at the body's return in creation order -- and
on that file's fatal path the engine prints `Call to undefined function` before
any of it, while we had already destroyed `$x`. The file body is excluded now,
which is the same distinction the two orderings above had already drawn.

### Honest on yield

This adds **nothing**: 11 before and 11 after on the destructor-bound subset,
and 0 gained across the whole corpus. Those failures are mostly `{main}`
objects, now excluded by rule, or objects that genuinely escape.

### What that says about the rest of D3

The honest reading is that **static liveness is not where D3's value is**. Even
taking it from 9% to 26% with a `$this`-leak summary would be claiming more
`new` sites, not more *corpus files* -- the files that fail on destructor timing
fail on objects that escape their frame, which is exactly the population static
liveness cannot claim by construction.

So the next increment should be the **refcount backstop for escaping objects**,
not the method summary. That is the harder and riskier piece, and it is the one
the measurement now points at twice: once by capping the analysis at a quarter
of sites, and once by this run gaining nothing.

**Correction, made the next tick: handle reuse is not cheaper.** I wrote here
that it "needs no lifetime analysis at all" and that was wrong -- asserted
without asking the engine. Measured:

    $a = new P(); unset($a); $b = new P();        // $b is #1
    $c = new P(); $d = new P(); unset($c);
    $e = new P();                                  // $e is #2, the lowest free

and `class P {}` has **no destructor**. So the free list tracks refcounts for
*every* object, not merely destructible ones -- a strictly larger population
than destructor timing needs. Handle reuse is the same problem wearing a
cheaper-looking hat.

Which means D3's remaining work is one thing, not two: **the refcount**. Both
destructor timing and handle numbering fall out of it, and neither is reachable
without it.

## 2026-09-18 -- destructors run at last, and three rules about not running them

Corpus: **2185 -> 2194 passing**, unsupported 651 unchanged, failed 1069 ->
1063, errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zh`, the pre-destructor baseline:
**11 gained, 2 lost**, and both losses are non-deterministic files the harness
declines to grade -- `message_004` (`random_int`) and `anon/004`, whose
anonymous class name varies per run and which now reports
`noreference: the engine does not reproduce its own output`.

The first run of this work, `zi`, measured 2185 -> 2186: **11 gained, 10
lost**. Those ten were a regression, diagnosed and fixed before the re-run, and
they are what this entry is mostly about.

### The baseline was worse than "timing is approximate"

Compiled output ran **no destructors at all**. Measured, not assumed: a class
with `__destruct` printed nothing from a compiled program at any of the three
points the engine fires one. The only mention of `__destruct` in
`internal/gogen` was the lazy-proxy compatibility check added a few ticks
earlier. Handles are never reused either -- `nextObjectID` only increments.

So the first D3 increment is not escape analysis. It is running them, and the
engine's three points are:

| point | engine |
|---|---|
| `unset($x)` on the sole reference | immediately |
| a function local at return | immediately |
| script end | the survivors, **reverse** order |

The third needs no last-reference knowledge, so that is what landed: a registry
on `Ctx`, teardown at the end, each object destroyed exactly once and never
early. A destructor the engine ran sooner still runs -- later, in the wrong
place -- which turns "output missing entirely" into "output present, position
wrong". That is a better failure to have and is what the remaining work closes.

### Two orderings I assumed and had to be corrected on

Teardown goes **before** the registered shutdown functions. I had placed it
after, reasoning that a shutdown function should still see the objects; the
engine prints `db`, `da`, `shutdown`. And destruction is reverse creation order,
which I guessed right but only confirmed afterwards.

### The regression: destroying what PHP does not

Ten files went from passing to failing, all the same shape -- a destructor ran
that the engine never runs. Three rules, each checked against the engine:

- **A constructor that throws means no destructor.** The object is allocated and
  never destroyed. Registration happened in the constructor *helper*, which runs
  before `__construct`, so a throwing constructor still got teardown.
  Registration moved into `callCtor`, after construction succeeds.
- **An uninitialized lazy object has no destructor call.** No state, nothing to
  destroy. There is a corpus test named `dtor_not_called_if_not_init` that says
  exactly this -- and this was written four ticks into working on lazy objects,
  which is the part worth remembering.
- `Lazy.SkipDestructor`, the flag the reset forms take, likewise.

Seven of the ten recovered immediately with none failing; the other three are
the known non-deterministic files.

The general shape: **adding output where there was none can only lose files by
adding it where the engine emits none.** The three rules are all instances of
that, and the check that finds them is the passing-set diff rather than the
totals -- `zi` was net +1, which on its own would have looked like a quiet tick.
