single structural lever by a wide margin, exactly as `.agents/docs/` predicted
when the compiler track opened. Of the reachable 689, the largest coherent named
cluster was `lazy_objects` at 41.

### The bug was mine, and the reasoning that produced it was plausible

Clustering those 41 files' diffs gave one dominant cause, 45 occurrences of
`want "[\"b\"]=>" got "}"`: a dump of an uninitialized lazy object showed
**nothing** where the engine lists its typed properties.

`newLazyGhost` built a bare object, on the reasoning that a lazy object "has a
class and a handle but no state" -- which is what the LTM note says, and is
still wrong here. It has no *values*; it does have its class's declared
**slots**, and those carry the declaration order and the types that a dump
names. The interpreter's `newLazy` instantiates and then strips, and skipping
the instantiate is what produced `{}`.

`StripLazyState`, `DropDynamicProperties` and `LazyVisibleProperties` are shared
now rather than interpreter-only. The no-properties case came along with it: a
class declaring none has nothing to defer, so the engine hands back an ordinary
object with no label and never calls the initializer.

### Four fixtures apart

`lazy_dump.php` is the fourth file split out because dead temporaries ahead of
it shift every object handle. That is written into its header now as a shape
rather than a surprise: a fixture that dumps whole objects wants nothing before
it.

## 2026-09-18 -- resetting an object back to lazy

Corpus: **2174 -> 2174 passing**, unsupported 675 -> 651, failed 1059 -> 1082,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `ze`: **1 gained, 1 lost** -- the loss is
`attributes/deprecated/message_004`, the `random_int` coin-flip, for the third
time. So the tick's real movement is **+1**, and the flake cancelled it.

The lazy cluster, 211 files: 27 passing (unchanged), unsupported **33 -> 12**.
Twenty-four files across the corpus stopped refusing and twenty-three of them
landed in `failed`. That is the honest shape of this one: `resetAsLazyGhost`
works, and the files that use it want more besides.

### The differential suite caught the extraction bug

The shared `StripStateForReset` read `object.Declared[name].Readonly`, on the
assumption that both back-ends record readonly on the instance. The interpreter
does not -- it reads the class table -- so `ResetRoFinal`'s readonly property was
cleared instead of kept and the engine's `Cannot modify readonly property` never
fired. One case, already in the suite, went red.

The fix was to take `Readonly` from the **descriptor** rather than from the
object, which is the better source regardless: the declaration is the authority,
and not every back-end mirrors it onto instances. That is the third field
`PropertyDesc` has grown -- `Visibility` for the proxy count, `Readonly` here --
each with the reason recorded on it, which is what keeps the type a deliberate
subset rather than a slow re-export of `pb.Property`.

### The rule, and its two halves

A readonly property holding a value survives the reset **only when the class is
final**: with no subclass able to reach it, nothing could legitimately write it
again, so the value stands and the reconstructing `__construct` is refused. A
non-final class clears it and `__construct` may set it once more.

And a kept property must **also** be marked non-deferred. Keeping the value alone
is not enough, because the ghost's restore pass wipes it on the way in. Marking
it gets the tail case free: reset a final class whose only property is kept,
nothing is deferred, the object is not lazy, and the initializer never runs.

Both halves are in a fixture -- `lazy_reset.php`, which is a **third** file split
out because dead temporaries ahead of it shift every object handle. That has
stopped being a surprise and is now a shape worth recognising: any fixture that
dumps whole objects wants nothing before it.

## 2026-09-18 -- the lazy raw writers and forced initialization

Corpus: **2163 -> 2174 passing**, unsupported 746 -> 675, failed 998 -> 1059,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zd`: **11 gained, 0 lost**. The lazy
cluster, 211 files: 14 -> **27 passing**, unsupported 104 -> 33.

Five methods: `initializeLazyObject`, `isUninitializedLazyObject`,
`markLazyObjectAsInitialized`, and both of `ReflectionProperty`'s raw writers.

### Deciding not to extract

`lazyReflection` is 143 lines and looked like the next extraction. It is not:
its dependencies include `destructAt`, `releaseCheck` and `destructed` --
interpreter lifetime machinery that compiled output does not have and should not
be given. Moving it wholesale would have dragged a destruction model across a
boundary it does not belong on.

What moved instead is the pair of rules that are genuinely subtle and would
drift if copied:

- **`AllLazySkipped`** -- an object with nothing left to defer *is not lazy*, and
  its initializer never runs. The note is explicit that counting what a reset
  cleared gets the common case right and the general one wrong, so the question
  is asked of the deferred set and not of the clearing.
- **`SkipLazyProperty`** -- the two writers differ in exactly one respect.
  `skipLazyInitialization` on a property that is already not lazy does *nothing*:
  writing the declared default a second time would clobber what the program has
  since put there. A raw write was handed a value, so it overwrites. Neither
  asks whether the object is lazy at all, because on an ordinary object the raw
  write is an ordinary write and skipping does nothing.

Both are in the fixture, including the second write that ends the laziness with
the initializer never printing -- which is the case that proves laziness is per
property rather than per object.

### Left deliberately

`resetAsLazyGhost`, 18 files. Its rule turns on class **finality**: a readonly
property holding a value survives the reset when the class is final, because
nothing can reach it to write it again. `php.Declaration` already carries
`Readonly`, but `gogen.Class` has no `Final` field and emits no table for it,
while the protobuf has one. Carrying it is the prerequisite -- the same shape
the property descriptor needed, and the same reason not to improvise it at the
end of a tick.

## 2026-09-18 -- the lazy-proxy rule gets one home

Corpus: **2160 -> 2163 passing**, unsupported 746 unchanged, failed 1001 -> 998,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `zc`: **3 gained, 0 lost**.

Three files is the whole visible yield, and the tick was worth doing anyway: it
removed a **wrong answer** the previous one shipped.

### What was wrong

`internal/gogen` installed `SetProxyCompatible` as
`strings.EqualFold(proxyClass, instanceClass)`. PHP allows a **subclass to proxy
its parent** when the two have the same number of `properties_info` entries and
neither overrides `__destruct` or `__clone`. So a legal proxy earned
`TypeError: The real instance class B is not compatible with the proxy class D`
where the engine simply works -- worse than the refusal it replaced, which is
the one trade the quality gate forbids. It was a placeholder shipped without the
rule being read, and the LTM note states the rule plainly.

### The fix was not the one-liner I predicted

I said last tick that everything the real rule needed was already emitted. Half
right. `declaredProps`, `extendsClass` and `methodOwnerOf` were all there, but:

- the count needs **visibility** -- a private property is its own
  `properties_info` entry per declaring class -- and `PropertyDesc` deliberately
  did not carry it, so adding the field was the kind of deliberate act that
  descriptor's own note asks for rather than a field appearing by accident;
- `ProxyCompatible` took no `Ctx` and so had nothing to compute a count with,
  so the hook's signature widened too.

### The part worth more than the bug

The count is now `php.PropertyInfoCount`, and **both** back-ends call it: the
interpreter's own 23-line copy is gone. That is the subtle half of the rule --
one entry per declared name, a private one per declaring class, and an override
sharing the entry it overrides, which is what makes a redeclaration free and a
new name not. `default_properties_count` is the wrong number by the engine's own
comment. Two copies of that would have drifted, and the drift would have shown
up as a proxy accepted on one back-end and refused on the other.

Verified against the engine and kept in the fixture: `Redeclares extends Base`
proxies a `Base`, `Adds extends Base` does not.

## 2026-09-18 -- the property descriptor that unblocks lazy objects

Corpus: **2147 -> 2146 passing**, unsupported 851 unchanged, failed 910 -> 909,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `za`: **0 gained, 1 lost** -- and the loss is
`attributes/deprecated/message_004` again, the `random_int` coin-flip, which this
run bucketed as `noreference: the engine does not reproduce its own output`. The
harness caught its own non-determinism rather than calling it a failure, which is
the first time that file has self-identified instead of needing to be recognised.

**A pure refactor, measured to say so.** No compiled behaviour changed, so zero
movement was the expected result and anything else would have been a regression
I introduced.

### What was in the way

Lazy objects are the largest remaining cluster -- 211 files, 69 clear of the
handle/`__destruct` screen, and that screen is conservative here because a
lazy-object test dumps the object almost by definition. `runtime/interp/lazy.go`
is 751 lines with 19 coupling points, which puts it on the *extract* side: the
algorithm is subtle enough that a second copy would be the worst outcome, and
`php.Lazy` already lives on the shared `Object`.

The blocker was narrow and structural. `unit.properties` hands back
`[]*pb.Property`, and `runtime/php` cannot see the IR -- emitted programs import
`runtime/*` and never `internal/*`. So the shared algorithm had no way to ask
what a class declares.

### The descriptor, and why it is small

`php.PropertyDesc` carries exactly five things the machinery reads: name,
declaring class, declared type, the static/virtual flags, and an
already-evaluated default. Not a translation of `pb.Property` -- a deliberate
subset, so that adding a field later is a decision rather than a side effect of
exposing a protobuf to a package that must not depend on one.

`DeclaredProperties` is a `Ctx` hook because the **hierarchy walk** is the part
the two back-ends do differently: the interpreter walks `ancestry`, compiled
output reads an emitted table, and neither order is `runtime/php`'s to assume.
Both supply it now, and `RestoreDeclaredDefaults` -- the ghost's "start from the
declared defaults" pass, with its three rules about statics, skipped properties
and the uninitialized/null distinction -- is shared.

### What is still missing, and it is the pervasive half

`internal/gogen` installs **no** `SetLazyResolver`. Compiled output has no
materialization path at all, so nothing a ghost does would be observable: every
property access has to ask first -- `propGet`, `propSet`, the three `propPlace`
variants, and `visible`/`objectProperties` for the dump. `resolveLazy`'s guard is
`object.Lazy == nil`, so the cost on an ordinary object is one nil check, which
is what makes that affordable. Filed with the rest of the surface rather than
rushed onto the end of this tick.

Corpus: **2137 -> 2143 passing**, unsupported 909 -> 863, failed 862 -> 901,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `z8`: **8 gained, 2 lost**.

Both losses are the documented `random_int` coin-flip --
`attributes/deprecated/message_004` and
`class_constants/value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`, which call `random_int(1,2)`
in their own source while the harness runs the engine and the compiled program
as two processes. Verified rather than assumed: three re-runs of the pair gave
0, 0 and 1 of 2 passing. So the real movement is **+8, nothing lost** -- but the
headline number is +6, and the two are worth stating separately rather than
quietly netting.

The reachable Reflection subset, 68 files: **0 -> 7 passing**, 23 failed, 38
unsupported, errored 0. Forty-six files left `unsupported` and thirty-nine
landed in `failed`, the same trade the last two ticks made.

### The count was not the cluster

Reflection is 308 files and looked like the obvious next target. Screened, it is
mostly something else:

| | files |
|---|---|
| total, distinct | 308 |
| lazy-object tests | 206 |
| non-lazy | 102 |
| non-lazy **and** free of `__destruct` / `object(X)#N` | **68** |

And the 68 are an **attributes** cluster rather than a reflection one:
`getAttributes()` 82 uses, `getName()` 48, `getArguments()` 33,
`newInstance()` 31. So the tick is `#[Attr]`, which is a far better-shaped
piece than "implement Reflection".

### This one does not extract

The previous two ticks moved an implementation down into `runtime/php` and
hooked out what was back-end-specific. That was right when the back-end-specific
part was small: `arrayobject.go` had four coupling points, `fiber.go` fourteen.
`reflection.go` has **56**, because reflection is almost entirely *ask the class
table* and the two back-ends have genuinely different tables -- `*Unit` there,
emitted Go maps here. So the rule the earlier ticks followed applies in reverse:
share what is **data** -- the attribute lists -- and write the table questions
per back-end. Nothing moved out of the interpreter this time.

The prerequisite was missing entirely: `internal/gogen` had **zero** references
to attributes. The harvest carries them, on op_arrays, arguments, classes,
properties and constants, with the arguments left *unevaluated* -- which is not
an omission but the semantics: an attribute is a declaration, and its
constructor does not run until `newInstance()`. That is exactly the shape
`newInstance()` needs, so the table holds argument values and builds nothing.

An attribute whose argument the compiler could not fold -- `#[A(self::X)]` --
has no literal text, and is left **out of the table** rather than given a
guessed value.

### Three mistakes worth keeping

**Named arguments cover the trailing slots only.** `SetArgNames` takes names for
the last N arguments, and I passed one per argument with `""` for the positional
ones. The binder duly went looking for a parameter called `$`:
`Unknown named parameter $`. PHP requires named arguments after positional ones
and an attribute is written the same way, so the split preserves the order.

**A subclass must be asked about first.** `reflectorMethod` dispatched on the
payload before consulting the compiled method table, so `class R extends
ReflectionClass` overriding `getName()` would have run the engine's body. The
array store already guards this way; I did not copy the guard until the
interpreter's version of the same bug pointed at it.

**The interpreter's message was wrong, and the fixture found it.**
`new ReflectionAttribute()` raises `Call to private
ReflectionAttribute::__construct() from global scope` -- an ordinary private
constructor refusal naming the calling scope. The interpreter said "Cannot
directly construct ReflectionAttribute, use ReflectionClass::getAttributes()
instead", which this engine does not say. Fixed in both arms, with a
differential case.

That case also exposed a **second** gap, which is filed rather than fixed: both
of the interpreter's reflection gates test an exact class name, so a subclass of
any Reflection class never routes to the engine body at all. Widening them needs
the override guard above first, so the case was narrowed to what this tick
actually changed rather than left failing.

## 2026-09-18 -- fibers reach compiled output

Corpus: **2122 -> 2137 passing**, unsupported 959 -> 909, failed 826 -> 862,
errored 1. Passing-set diff against `z7`: **15 gained, 0 lost** -- and this time
against a baseline from this session rather than one four days old, which is the
habit the previous entry asked for.

The fiber cluster alone, 103 files: **0 -> 14 passing**, 36 failed, 53
unsupported, errored 0. The fifteenth gain is elsewhere, from the `zeroReturn`
fix below. Fifty files left `unsupported` and thirty-six of them landed in
`failed`: that ratio is the point of the tick rather than a disappointment, because
a fiber test that now runs and prints the wrong destructor order is a gap you can
see.

### The design question, and who answered it

`internal/lower/cps.go` had left a decision open in a comment, naming four
options -- uniform CPS, dual entry, selective, or keeping goroutines -- because
emitting the suspending function is the common prefix of all four and commits to
none. **The user chose CPS, for fidelity**: a suspension stays explicit data
rather than a Go stack, which is the side that can be made byte-exact for
backtraces and destructor ordering.

I had recommended goroutines, and one of my two arguments was wrong. I wrote
that uniform CPS "taints the whole program", citing the comment at
`callgraph.go:302`. That is reasoning from the header, which is the one thing
this project forbids, and `Reach` exists precisely to answer it -- its own
comment says the fiber decision should rest on the number. Measured over the 70
suspending files, 196 functions merged: 63 suspend outright, the floor reach is
91 (46.4%), the sound reach 104 (53.1%). **Opaque calls cost 6.6%, not
everything**, and knowing a receiver's class is worth 0.0% here. Blast radius if
any one function suspended: median 0, p90 0, max 31.

### What was already built, and what was not

Nearly all of it existed. `cps.go` emits `ret.suspend`, the call graph
propagates `suspends`, there is a `fiber.php` lowering fixture, and
`runtime/php/resumable.go` carries a `Fiber` with `Start`, `Resume`, `Throw`,
`GetReturn` and five status predicates -- with **no caller anywhere**, because
the interpreter drives fibers on its own goroutine and never touches it. It was
written for this and then left.

What was missing was the emitter, and one idea inside it: a fiber body is not a
generator. `(*emitter).resumable` always ended in `php.StartGenerator` and a
`Generator` object, but calling a suspending function does not make an object --
it hands its **frame** to whatever drives it. So such a body now gets a frame
constructor beside its entry point, a closure carries that constructor on
`closureBody`, and `Fiber::start()` asks for it through a new `Ctx` hook. The
arguments belong to `start()`, not to the constructor, which is why the frame
cannot be built until then.

### The guard had to come first

`internal/lower/ir.go` states two rules -- never emit a direct call to a body
whose suspension escapes, never emit a driver call on one -- and `internal/gogen`
implemented **neither**. That was safe only by accident: `ret.suspend` refused,
so nothing reached them. The moment the terminator became emittable they were
load-bearing, because an ordinary call would read the `Outcome` as the
function's return value. Rule 1 landed first, verified to change nothing, and it
is what makes the 44 remaining refusals refusals instead of wrong answers.

Rule 2 is answered by refusal rather than by code: a body that both yields and
suspends still contains `ret.suspend` and still refuses, so the driver call the
rule warns about is unreachable. `ir.go` records that 26 of 95 marked bodies are
of that shape, so this is worth saying out loud rather than leaving implied.

### An `errored` is worse than a refusal

The first corpus run produced one: emitted Go that would not compile, because
the declared-return-type check spelled `return php.Value{}` inside a `Step` that
returns `php.Outcome`. `zeroReturn` exists for exactly this and its own comment
says three sites were missed once already; this was a fourth, pre-existing and
only visible because the body now compiles at all. A gap that stops the build is
a worse answer than one that says what it cannot do, so it is worth separating
in the count rather than reading `errored` as a rounding error.

### What the failures say

Three clusters, all honest. ~8 are a fiber suspended and never resumed, whose
`finally` blocks PHP runs when the object is destroyed and php2go has no
refcount to trigger -- the same Phase D3 lifetime problem WeakMap is. ~6 are
backtraces; frames for `Fiber->start()` and for the body (which PHP shows with
no file or line, because the engine made that call) are pushed now, but the
files that want them are mostly blocked behind rule 1 anyway. The rest are the
refusal we do not raise yet. All filed.

Writing the fixture found one more: `$f->getReturn(1)` is an `ArgumentCountError`
in the engine and is silently accepted here. The fixture had the stray argument
by mistake, and the mistake was the useful part.

## 2026-09-17 -- ArrayIterator and ArrayObject reach compiled output

Corpus: **2108 -> 2122 passing**, unsupported 987 -> 959, failed 812 -> 826,
errored 1. Fourteen gains, and the twenty-eight files that left `unsupported`
split exactly half and half -- which is the movement the quality gate describes,
not a wash: a file that now compiles and prints the wrong bytes is a *visible*
gap where before it was a refusal.

The passing-set diff could only be taken against `y9j` (2026-09-14, 2,057), the
newest run whose chunk files are still in `seg/`: 65 gained, **0 lost**. The
three ticks between left no `pass-*.txt`, so their sets could not be differenced
-- worth fixing as a habit, since "nothing lost" is the claim that needs the
evidence.

`new ArrayIterator(...)` was refused at emission -- 31 corpus files whose only
gap was that line, plus 5 more that extend one of the two classes. The
interpreter has had both since long ago, in `runtime/interp/arrayobject.go`, and
the thing worth recording is how little of that file was actually the
interpreter's.

### The payload moves, the hierarchy question stays

237 lines, of which the interpreter-specific parts were four calls: `findClass`,
`instanceOf`, `resolveMethod`, `instantiate`. Every one of those is now a `Ctx`
hook, so `arrayStore` became `php.ArrayStore` and `arrayStoreMethod` became
`(*php.Ctx).ArrayStoreMethod` with no behavioural change -- the same move
`SensitiveParameterValue` made, and for the same reason. What stayed behind in
`runtime/interp` is `isArrayBackedClass` and `plainArrayStore`, because both ask
*this back-end's* class table a question the other back-end answers from a
different table. The shared half is the data and the methods; the hierarchy hop
is not shared, it is supplied.

### An engine class in compiled output is five tables, not one

The refusal was at `new`, but making `new` work proves nothing on its own. What
`ArrayIterator` actually needs from emitted Go:

- `declaredClasses` and `classCtors`, so `class_exists`, `new $name` and the
  `Class not found` refusal all see it;
- `interfacesOf`, because `foreach`, `$o[$k]` and `count()` are each gated on an
  **interface** and a class that lists none answers none of them;
- `callMethod`, dispatching to the store *before* the compiled tables, but only
  when the receiver's class has no compiled body of that name -- which is what
  lets a subclass override `current()`;
- `callCtor` and `callStatic`, the second so that `parent::__construct($a)` and
  `parent::current()` from a subclass reach the engine body;
- the parent-chain walk, which now breaks at an engine class exactly as it
  breaks at `stdClass`: neither contributes anything to inherit.

`engineClassInterfaces` is the whole declaration. Adding the next engine class
is adding a row and a payload.

### The engine's own interface edges

`$c instanceof Traversable` answered **false** for a class implementing
`Iterator`, because `Iterator extends Traversable` is the *engine's*
declaration and no program's own table carries it. Emitting that edge --
`engineInterfaceParents` -- was needed for `ArrayIterator` and fixes the general
case at the same time. Six engine interfaces became testable rather than
refused.

### Two places the fix had to be told the difference

**var_dump and var_export disagree on purpose.** `var_dump` of an `ArrayObject`
shows one entry, `["storage":"ArrayObject":private]`; `var_export` shows the
contents *flat*, with no `storage` at all. The interpreter had the first and not
the second -- `\ArrayObject::__set_state(array(\n))` for a two-element object --
so the fix went into `php.Ctx.ExportProperties` where both arms get it.
`ExportPair` had no way to say "this key is an integer", since a property name
is always quoted; it has one now.

**An unimplemented method is not an undefined one.** `asort`, `exchangeArray`,
`setFlags` and the rest of the surface are real methods, and the first version
of the compiled arm answered `Call to undefined method ArrayIterator::asort()`
-- a wrong answer where the interpreter refuses. It refuses now, with the same
words. `seek` was the sharper version of the same mistake: listing
`SeekableIterator` among the interfaces made `$it instanceof SeekableIterator`
true while `$it->seek(2)` was undefined, so `seek` is implemented -- in the
shared layer, so the interpreter gained it too, `OutOfBoundsException` and all.

### What the newly-visible files say

Of the 36 files, 10 pass. Most of the rest fail on gaps that were **behind** the
refusal and are now visible, which is the `unsupported` -> `failed` movement the
quality gate describes: a numeric-string offset reaching a user `offsetGet` as
an int (`bug63217`), spreading a Traversable without renumbering integer-like
string keys (`array_unpack/string_keys`), and two that differ only in
`object(ArrayIterator)#1` versus `#2` -- the handle a dead temporary would have
freed, which is Phase D3 and not this. All filed.

### A failure that is not this tick's

`print_r_library.php` is the one compiled fixture of 242 that does not pass:
`$a = [1]; $a[] = &$a; print_r($a)` descends a level too far instead of writing
` *RECURSION*`. Demonstrated not to be mine by rebuilding with
`engineClassNames` emptied -- it fails identically. The object cycle in the same
file is fine, so it is the array identity through a reference specifically.
Filed rather than fixed, and named here because a fixture suite that is
"241/242" reads as passing if nobody says which one.

## 2026-09-17 -- the callee places a named argument the call site could not

Corpus: **2105 -> 2108 passing** against the pre-tick baseline, unsupported 992
-> 987, failed 809 -> 812, errored 1. Two real gains, nothing lost.

A call whose callee is unknown at compile time -- `$f(a3: "x")`, a first-class
callable, a `__call` trampoline -- has no signature to bind against, so it was
refused. It now sends its named arguments **trailing under their names** and the
callee's prologue permutes them: only the callee knows which position each name
claims. The channel is the one the variadic work already built.

### Two corrections to my own first version

**A hole was not a hole.** `recv` for a defaulted parameter checked only
`i < len(args)`, so the `undef` a skipped parameter leaves behind was read as a
*passed* null and coerced -- `Argument #1 ($a) must be of type string, null
given`. The static named path had filled gaps with undef since it was written,
and documented it as "the same 'not passed' the callee sees for a short slice";
the defaulted branch had simply never been told.

**The first binder silently did the wrong thing.** For a name no parameter
claims I returned the arguments unchanged, with a comment about leaving it to
the caller's check -- but there is no caller check; not knowing the callee is the
premise. `named_params/__invoke.phpt` printed `a: B, b: C` where the engine
throws `Unknown named parameter $c`. That is a **wrong answer where a refusal
used to be**, which is the trade the quality gate exists to forbid. The binder
throws now, and is emitted for bodies with no parameters at all, since a name
arriving at one of those claims nothing either.

### The regression worth naming

The first measurement lost `named_params/variadic.phpt` -- a file an earlier
tick had made pass. The callee-side binder reintroduced the exact bug the
call-side fix had removed three ticks earlier: **a name never claims the
variadic parameter itself.** `paramIndex` had learned it; `BindNamedArgs` had
not.

The differential case written for the call-side fix passed throughout, because
it only exercised the **static** path. So the lesson is not "remember the rule"
-- it is that a rule holding on two sides of an interface needs a case on each
side, and the second implementation is exactly where the first one's mistake
comes back. Both the fixture and the case now drive it dynamically.

### Left as it was

A **resumable** consumes its arguments when the frame is built and has no body
to permute, so a named argument to an unknown generator keeps the call-site
refusal. Said in the code rather than skipped silently.

## 2026-09-16 -- a library function gets a stack frame

Corpus: **2103 -> 2105 passing**, failed 811 -> 809, unsupported 992 unchanged,
errored 1. Two real gains, nothing lost.

### First, a correction

The 2026-09-16 serialize entry reported
`generators/errors/serialize_unserialize_error.phpt` as passing. **It was not.**
The path handed to `php2gotest` was wrong -- the file is under
`generators/errors/`, not the tests root -- and the harness **silently drops a
path that names nothing**, so the command reported three files instead of four
and the remaining passes read as covering it. The next measurement showed no
gain and the claim had to be withdrawn. The check is now in TESTING.md: compare
`^files N` against the list length whenever a path is hand-typed.

Run at its real path, the file showed the not-serializable fix was right -- the
message was correct -- and that one thing was still missing.

### The fix

    Exception: Serialization of 'Generator' is not allowed in %s:%d
    Stack trace:
    #0 %s(%d): serialize(Object(Generator))

Compiled code pushed **no frame at all** for a library call, so the throw
appeared to come from the caller and the trace opened at `{main}`. The
interpreter has had this since `MarkInternalCall`.

Pushing the frame was not enough, and the reason generalises: `AttachStack` runs
in the **caller's** error handler, by which point the frame has been popped. The
stack has to be attached inside `callBuiltin` while the frame is still live.
`AttachStack` keeps the first stack it is given, so the caller's later attempt is
harmless.

That benefits every library function that throws, not just this one --
`gh8810_5.phpt` came with it.

### A note on the fixture

It asserts the trace frame by **function name**, walking `getTrace()` rather than
matching `getTraceAsString()`: the rendered form carries the call site's line
number, which moves whenever the fixture is edited above it.

## 2026-09-16 -- unserialize

Corpus: **2094 -> 2105 passing**, unsupported 1021 -> 992, failed 793 -> 811,
errored 1. **Eleven real gains, nothing lost** -- the largest single tick this
session, and the `random_int` pair stayed quiet so there is nothing to subtract.

`unserialize` is the larger half of the serialization pair and the last big
library item. The hooks were **consolidated** rather than multiplied:

- `ClassFacts` -- one struct answering known, not-serializable, the two dynamic
  property policies, and why `new` would refuse. They are all the same lookup
  and a caller that wants one usually wants two.
- `PropertyFacts` -- declared, and whether the declaration is **virtual**, which
  there is nowhere to put an unserialized value in.
- `NewInstance` -- allocate **without** running the constructor, laid out as
  `new` would. `ObjectMaker` was not it: that one only numbers a bare object.
- `EnumCase` -- and it reports **which way** the lookup failed, because the three
  failures are reported differently.

That last one earned its keep immediately: six of the eleven gains are enum
unserialize tests, and they exist precisely because the engine distinguishes a
class that is not an enum, a name that is a constant but not a case, and a name
that is neither. Collapsing them into one "not found" would have passed none of
them -- which is the argument for reading the interpreter's version rather than
writing a reader from the format spec. The format is easy; the error attribution
is not.

### The fixture found a bug in both arms

`R:` says two positions share a box. By the time it is read, the earlier one has
already been **copied into its container** -- so boxing the recorded *value*
left the array holding an unrelated copy, and `$back[0] = 9` never reached
`$back[1]`. The container now registers how to box its own slot.

It also has to be marked as a reference the **program** can see. Assigning the
unserialized array copies it, and a copy keeps only the boxes the program asked
for: unmarked, the two elements flattened straight back apart.

Neither arm had this right, and no differential case covered it until now.

### Two mistakes worth recording

**A stale `php2eval` cost twenty minutes.** It still ran the interpreter's own
copy of `unserialize`, which had just moved to `runtime/stdlib`, so probes
through it showed a difference that was already fixed. The giveaway was
behaviour *unique to the new code* -- `unserialize("")` answering silently --
still producing the old warning. `go test ./runtime/interp` runs the interpreter
in process and is always current; the binary is not. Recorded in TESTING.md.

**A hand-written test string declared length 10 for a 9-byte payload**, which
made a malformed-input result look like an enum bug.

### Filed rather than faked

An `O:` naming a class the program never declared builds a
`__PHP_Incomplete_Class` in the engine; php2go answers `false` with an offset
warning in **both** back-ends. The fixture says so rather than asserting the
wrong thing.

`runtime/interp/serialize.go` is now entirely dead -- nothing references it --
and is left in place pending permission to remove it.

## 2026-09-16 -- serialize moves to the shared library surface

Corpus: **2091 -> 2094 passing**, unsupported 1027 -> 1021, failed 790 -> 793,
errored 1. Three real gains, nothing lost -- and the `random_int` pair was quiet
this run, so the diff is signal rather than noise to subtract.

`serialize` is the biggest remaining library item at 33 files. Two new Ctx
hooks, both class-table facts the writer cannot answer for itself:

- `HasMethod`, asked **without** running `__call` -- which is why it is not a
  call attempt;
- `NotSerializable`, the handful of engine classes whose state has no written
  form and that say so rather than writing an empty object.

Everything else was already in place from earlier ticks: `ctx.Call` runs
`__serialize` / `serialize` / `__sleep`, `InstanceOfClass` answers
`Serializable`, `Materialize` produces a lazy object's state, and
`MangledProperties` **is** the storage table serialize writes -- `"\0*\0name"`
for a protected property and `"\0Class\0name"` for a private, which is what
makes an unserialized private land back in the right class.

One nuance that would have been missed by writing it fresh: serialize must
**not** produce a lazy object's state when the class answers for serialization
itself, or when the object was made with `SKIP_INITIALIZATION_ON_SERIALIZE`.
`__serialize` decides for itself what to write; `__sleep` does not, because it
answers with property *names* and the values behind them still have to exist.
That check turned out to be expressible in `runtime/php` terms -- `object.Lazy`
plus `HasMethod` -- so it moved with the rest instead of needing a third hook.

**The differential case caught the move's one casualty.** The `__sleep()`
warning came out as `[internal function] on line 0`: running the hook through
`ctx.Call` moves the location and nothing puts it back. The engine blames the
`serialize()` call for a name `__sleep` invented, so the call site is captured
before the hook runs.

Of the 33 files, 3 pass and **24 want `unserialize`** -- the larger half, and
the obvious next tick.

### And the tick that was not taken

The object-handle cluster was investigated first and left alone. The drift is
genuine **reuse**, not a constant offset:

    function f() { return new A; }
    f();
    $a = new A;   // engine: #1, php2go: #2

The engine hands the dead temporary's handle to the next `new`. More to the
point, **the interpreter has the same bug** -- so this is not the compiled arm
lagging, it is behaviour php2go does not model anywhere. 69 corpus files fail on
it, 45 differing in nothing else, which makes it the dominant remaining failure
shape and squarely the Phase D3 ownership work rather than a tick.

## 2026-09-16 -- a sensitive parameter is the callee's own fact

Corpus: **2088 -> 2091 passing**, failed 791 -> 790, unsupported 1027 unchanged,
errored 1. **One** real gain -- the other two files in the column are the
`random_int` pair, both landing lucky this time.

`#[\SensitiveParameter]` keeps a password out of a backtrace. Compiled output
showed the value raw, and the plumbing filed last tick turned out to be the
small half.

**The callee records it, not the caller.** Sensitivity is a property of the
*declaration*, and the caller that pushed the frame has no way to know which
parameters carry it -- so `MarkSensitiveArgs` reaches back to the frame already
on the stack from the body's prologue. The attribute travels
`zend.ArgInfo.Attributes` -> `lower.Function.Sensitive` -> that prologue;
`Params` is a list of strings and has nowhere to put an attribute.

**The wrapper moved to `runtime/php`.** Both back-ends build a
`SensitiveParameterValue` -- the interpreter from its object store, a compiled
program from its own -- and neither should have its own idea of what it holds.
`runtime/interp/sensitive.go` is now a call into the shared constructor.

**A hider shows nothing to anything that walks a table**, which is the whole
point: the declared private `$value` really does hold the argument, and
`HidesProperties` is what keeps `var_dump`, `get_object_vars`, `var_export`,
a cast and `json_encode` out of it. Compiled output honoured it in *none* of
them; the fixture reporting `props=1` found the second and third.

### Where this stops, and it is the same place as everything else

Of the seventeen corpus files calling `getTrace()`, the ones still failing now
differ **only in the object handle number**. That cluster is the dominant
remaining failure shape: **69 files** whose first difference is
`object(X)#N`, 45 of them differing in nothing else at all. Compiled programs
never free a handle, so every one drifts by however many objects the engine
destroyed and reused. It is the Phase D3 ownership work and no amount of
library surface will move it.

### A harness trap

Differential cases are Go **raw** string literals, so a backtick inside one
terminates the case -- and the parse errors land nowhere near the edit. A prose
comment mentioning an attribute in backticks reported `illegal character U+0023`
ten thousand lines earlier. Backslashes are safe and need no doubling; only the
backtick is fatal. Recorded in TESTING.md.

## 2026-09-16 -- getTrace, and two closures on one line

Corpus: **2088 -> 2088 passing**, failed 792 -> 791, unsupported 1027 unchanged,
errored 1. One real gain, no real losses -- the file in the "lost" column is the
`random_int` pair landing the other way, and it is also why the total does not
move.

`Exception::getTrace()` was simply absent: `getTraceAsString` was wired to the
engine's exception surface and this was not, so the call was
`Call to undefined method`. Three lines, using `stdlib.TraceArray` -- the same
rendering the interpreter uses, and an exception's trace omits the receiver
where `debug_backtrace()` supplies it. `named_params/backtrace.phpt` passes.

### The fixture found a worse bug than the one being fixed

Written for convenience as an array of arrow functions:

    $pair = [fn() => "first", fn() => "second"];
    foreach ($pair as $i => $f) { echo $i, "=", $f(), "\n"; }   // compiled: 0=second

**Two closures written on one line share `{closure:file:line}`** -- that is the
name PHP gives them -- and `Program.Closures` was keyed by it, so the second
overwrote the first and *both* references reached the same body. The emitted
file confirmed it: four arrow functions in the source, two closure bodies.

`closureRef` now carries the **index** within the declaring op_array, which is
what actually distinguishes them, plus the parent's name so keys stay unique
across bodies. The display name is untouched: it genuinely is
`{closure:file:line}`, and only the key changes.

**The corpus does not cover it.** Forty files declare two closures on one line;
seven passed before the fix and the same seven pass after. So this is a
correctness fix with no measurable movement -- which is worth saying plainly
rather than folding into the tick's `+1`. A differential case and a fixture now
cover it, since nothing else did.

### Where the rest of getTrace goes

Seventeen corpus files call `getTrace()`. One passes; eleven now stop on
`#[\SensitiveParameter]` rendering, where the engine shows
`Object(SensitiveParameterValue)` and compiled output shows the value raw.
`php.StackFrame.Sensitive` and `IsSensitive` exist and the renderer honours
them; `internal/gogen` never sets the field, and the attribute -- harvested as
`zend.ArgInfo.Attributes` -- does not reach `.params`. Filed; it is the same
plumbing `Property.Order` needed.

## 2026-09-16 -- named arguments reach a variadic

Corpus: **2085 -> 2088 passing**, unsupported 1036 -> 1027, failed 785 -> 792,
errored 1. Two real gains and no losses -- the third file in the "gained" column
is the `random_int` pair landing the lucky way.

Read the two numbers together, as the gate asks: **nine refusals went away and
two of them became passes.** The rest are behaviour that was refused becoming
behaviour that is wrong, and the reasons are named below.

`v(1, x: "X")` against `function v($a, ...$rest)` leaves `$rest` holding
`["x" => "X"]`. The argument slice is positional and cannot carry the key, so
the names travel beside it -- and they are always the **trailing** arguments,
because a positional argument after a named one does not compile, so a count
lines them up with the tail.

`StackFrame.ArgNames` already existed for *rendering* a trace: "names the
trailing arguments that arrived under a name no parameter claimed". So the
names now go on the Ctx as a pending-call channel -- set immediately before the
call, taken once inside it -- `PushCall` copies them onto the frame, and the
variadic collection keys its trailing elements by them.

### Two rules the first attempt got wrong

**A name never claims the variadic parameter itself.** Against
`function test($a, string ...$extra)`, `test(extra: "x")` puts "x" into the
collected array under `"extra"`; the parameter has no single position to bind.
`paramIndex` matched it by name, sent the value to the wrong slot, and left the
whole array keyed by position.

**An extra named argument is not one of the call's arguments** to
`func_num_args()` and `func_get_args()` -- `named_params/variadic.phpt` says so
in a comment, and the engine answers 1 and `["a"]` for a call passing four
things. The frame records which trailing arguments arrived under a name, which
is exactly the set to drop, so both take a Ctx now and subtract them. The
catalogue entries needed `Ctx: true`, and the `Args` spec was wrong first time:
`iter.new` uses an empty first element to mean "the operand", but these have no
operands, so the empty string asked for an argument the IR does not carry.

### The differential case earned its keep

`nvTyped(1, bad: "x")` against `function nvTyped(int ...$nums)`: the engine
throws `Argument #2 must be of type int`, the compiled arm agreed, and **the
interpreter silently put "x" in the array**. Its variadic collection ran
`verifyArgument` over the positional elements and skipped it for the named ones.
Fixed, with the position taken from the argument's overall place in the list,
which is how the engine numbers it -- `#2` for `t(1, bad:)`, `#3` for
`t(1, 2, other:)`.

### Filed rather than bundled

`Exception::getTrace()` and `getTraceAsString()` are not implemented in compiled
output at all -- `Call to undefined method` -- and that, not the names, is what
leaves `named_params/backtrace.phpt` failing; `debug_backtrace()` itself keys
its args by name correctly now. Three `gh9750-*` files reach far enough to fail
on the known destructor-timing gap, and `internal_variadics.phpt` wants named
arguments to a **library** variadic, which harvested arginfo does not carry.

## 2026-09-16 -- a declared type on a by-reference parameter is verified too

Corpus: **2080 -> 2085 passing**, failed 791 -> 785, unsupported 1036 unchanged,
errored 1. Six real gains, no real losses -- the one in the "lost" column is the
`random_int` file that oscillates by construction.

Two changes, one behind the other.

**Null against a class type.** `function f(T $a) {}` given null was accepted
silently. `declaredClassRejects` abstained on null on purpose, and said so: "a
nullable type admits it, and so does the implicit nullability a `= null` default
gives a class-typed parameter. Deciding that here would need the default, which
this does not have."

But it *does* have it by the time it is called: the emitter folds a `= null`
default into a leading `?` before calling `CoerceArgument`, with its own comment
saying why. So the `?` is the whole truth about null there, and its absence is a
fact rather than a gap.

Tightened behind an explicit `nullIsDecided` flag rather than globally, because
the check's own guard rail is that "a false rejection turns a working program
into a TypeError, which is worse than the silent acceptance it replaces". True
for a user function's parameter, a return type, a property and the
typed-reference path; **false** for a library function's parameter, whose
nullability comes from harvested arginfo rather than from this string. Checked
first that the only callers are `internal/gogen`, so the blast radius is the
compiled arm.

**And the by-reference half was a second, larger thing.** `recv` returned early
for a by-reference parameter: "coercing or copying it here would break the link
the `&` exists to make." Half right. Copying would; writing *through* the box is
what the engine does:

    function f(int &$r) {}
    $s = "21"; f($s);   // the caller's $s is now int(21)
    $b = [1];  f($b);   // TypeError before the body runs

So the type is verified and the coerced value written back through the box. One
wrinkle the previous tick created: an argument reaching a by-reference parameter
is **not always a box** -- unpacking a Traversable passes by value, with a
warning -- so the type is verified either way and only a box gets the write-back.
That is what finally landed `unpack_iterator_by_ref_type_check.phpt`.

### Filed rather than bundled

Writing the fixture with a dynamic `$f(null)` showed the TypeError losing its
`, called in %s on line %d` suffix that the same call written statically keeps.
`CoerceArgument` builds it from `ctx.Stack()`, so the dynamic path is not
pushing a frame before the callee verifies. Separate gap, separate TODO; the
fixture uses static calls.

### Checking a long run early

A change that starts *rejecting* what was silently accepted wants a regression
signal before the full 75 minutes. The first attempt reported thirty-odd
`closure_*` files newly passing, which would be a nonsensical result from a
change to argument verification -- the passing set is built by subtracting the
files a chunk **listed**, and the chunk still being written has not listed what
it has not reached. Filtering to chunks carrying the `^files N` summary header
gave a true partial diff: nine complete chunks, one flaky regression, one real
gain. The full run then found five more gains in the later chunks, all in
`type_declarations`. Recorded in TESTING.md.

## 2026-09-16 -- unpacking a Traversable

Corpus: **2075 -> 2080 passing**, unsupported 1044 -> 1036, failed 790 -> 791,
errored 1. Seven real gains, no real losses -- the two in the "lost" column are
the `random_int` pair that oscillates by construction, and the net of five is
that pair landing the other way.

`f(...$traversable)` was refused, and the refusal's own comment named the fix:
"draining one here means running the iterator protocol, which this program can
do but nothing has needed yet". So it drains -- one left-to-right walk of the
protocol the emitted program already had. The nine files that needed it went
**0 -> 7 passing**.

The whole rule was probed before any of it was written, and one part of it is
not what reasoning would give:

| yielded | result |
| --- | --- |
| `yield 1; yield 2;` then `...[3]` | positional 1, 2, 3 -- a later unpack continues |
| `yield 5 => "x"; yield 9 => "y";` | **also positional**: an integer key is not a position, they append in order |
| `yield "c"=>"C"; "a"=>"A"; "b"=>"B";` | named, bound by name |
| `yield "nope" => 1` | `Error: Unknown named parameter $nope` |
| `yield "b"=>"B"; yield 0 => "A";` | `Error: Cannot use positional argument after named argument during unpacking` |
| `yield 1.5 => "x"` | `Error: Keys must be of type int\|string during argument unpacking` |
| a by-reference parameter | **Warning**, not an Error, and the call still happens |
| `new ArrayIterator([...])` | identical -- being Traversable is what matters, not being a Generator |

Two things the probes did not cover and the implementation found:

**A Generator is Traversable without the class table saying so.** The first
version asked `isTraversableClass` and sent every generator to `Only arrays and
Traversables can be unpacked`. It is the engine's own type, recognised by its
payload the way `newIterator` already recognises it.

**The by-reference warning names the callee and the position**, so it cannot be
raised where the drain happens. `unpackArgs` now takes the callee's diagnostic
name and its by-reference parameter indexes from the call site, where
`calleeSig` already lives.

### Two left refused rather than forced

`gh18581.phpt` yields **string** keys, which are named arguments the call site
binds statically and cannot place at run time -- the same refusal an unpacked
array with string keys already gets. Filed; it wants the run-time binding that
`named argument to an unknown callee` also wants.

`unpack_iterator_by_ref_type_check.phpt` gets its warning now, but not the
TypeError that follows it. Checked whether that was specific to by-reference
parameters and it is not: `function f(T $a) {}` then `f(null)` is accepted
silently in compiled code for a by-value parameter too. Filed as the broader gap
it is -- a declared type naming a class the program does not declare should be
provably rejected when there is a class table and no autoloader.

## 2026-09-16 -- a class chain may end at stdClass

Corpus: **2072 -> 2075 passing**, unsupported 1047 -> 1044, failed 788 -> 790,
errored 1. Read honestly that is **one** real gain, not three.

`class X extends stdClass` was refused at emission: the walk that builds the
effective method table refuses a parent the program does not declare, with one
exception for the Throwable hierarchy that `runtime/php` answers for. stdClass
earns the same break for a simpler reason -- it declares **no methods and no
properties**, so a chain reaching it is complete and the refusal has nothing
left to protect.

Everything a subclass needs from the name was already keyed off `parentOf`,
which is emitted whether or not the program declares the parent: `instanceof`,
`get_parent_class`, scope walking, and the dynamic-property exemption the engine
grants stdClass by name. That was checked before writing anything, and the
fixture -- `new`, the array cast, `json_encode`, `foreach`, comparison and a
two-level chain -- passed first try.

**The count needs reading.** Three files entered the passing set and only
`instanceof_002.phpt` is this change: `anon/004.phpt` moved from `noreference`,
where the randomness check had put it, and `value_unknown_at_compile_time_001`
is the other half of that oscillating pair. Two more files moved from
`unsupported` to `failed`, which is the expected shape and worth naming:

- `ns_074.phpt` differs only in `object(stdClass)#2` against `#3` -- the known
  handle-numbering gap, reached for the first time here;
- `property_hooks/foreach_002.phpt` is a **live** by-reference foreach over an
  object, and it is a real limitation of the previous tick's work rather than of
  this one.

### The limitation this unblocked

    foreach ($a as $k => &$v) {
        if ($k == "foo") { $a->bar = "baz"; }   // the engine yields "bar" too
    }

A by-reference foreach over a plain object is **live** in the engine: a property
added during the loop is walked. `foreachPropRefs` builds a snapshot array of
the object's boxes, so writes reach the object but late arrivals are missed.
`runtime/interp` iterates the object's own table with `it.backing` and filters
visibility per step; the compiled side needs the same, because a live array and
a visibility projection cannot both come out of one array. Filed rather than
bodged -- "live when nothing needs filtering, snapshot otherwise" is a silent
behavioural split.

## 2026-09-16 -- a by-reference foreach over a plain object binds to the slots

Corpus: **2066 -> 2072 passing** over two measurements, unsupported 1055 ->
1047, failed 785 -> 788, errored 1. Six gained, nothing lost.

`foreach ($o as &$v) { $v = 1; }` over a plain object was refused: the compiled
unit built a detached array from `foreachProps`, so the writes would have landed
in that and vanished -- a wrong answer that looks like a working loop. It now
builds the array from the object's **own property boxes**, and the iterator
walks those.

Three facts the engine settled first:

- the writes reach the object;
- only what the **calling scope** can see is walked -- from outside, a protected
  and a private property are untouched; from inside `$this`, all of them;
- the element still bound when the loop ends keeps its box and the ones the walk
  moved past collapse: `["a"]=> int(1)`, `["b"]=> &int(2)`.

Two things needed care. `iter.new.ref` had no `scope` argument where `iter.new`
did, for a question it turns out to need the same answer to; the catalogue entry
gained one. And the first attempt handed the boxed array to `php.NewIterator`
and the writes still vanished -- that is the by-*value* constructor, which
snapshots. `php.NewRefIterator` is the one whose fetch hands out each element's
box.

A **readonly** property has no reference to give, and the refusal is worded as
it is for `$r = &$o->readonly`.

### Reading `failed` and `unsupported` together, as the gate asks

The first measurement was `unsupported` down 8 and `failed` up 6, which is the
normal shape when a gap closes: behaviour that was refused becomes behaviour
that is wrong. So the six were read, and five were real. Two said the same
thing:

    Cannot assign array to reference held by property Foo::$p

**A reference bound to a typed property is itself typed**, and a loop variable
is such a reference: `foreach ($o as &$v)` over `public int $i` then
`$v = "x"` is a TypeError naming the property, not a string left in an int slot.
The constraint travels with the box, so it has to be registered on it.
`place.refBox` already did that with `ref.AddSource`; `foreachPropRefs` simply
was not calling it. A fix rather than a filed gap -- `gh15187_3` and
`typed_properties_045` followed in the second measurement.

`temporary_cleaning_009` still fails on an uncaught-exception path, which is a
different thread.

## 2026-09-16 -- property hooks run in compiled code, and four facts about declaring a property

Corpus: **2059 -> 2066 passing**, failed 788 -> 785, unsupported 1061 -> 1055,
errored 1, noreference 1077 -> 1079. Nine gained, nothing lost -- the two files
in the "lost" column are the `random_int` pair that oscillates between `passed`
and `noreference` by construction.

A hooked property was refused by the compiled back-end wherever something asked
what an object *presents*: `get_object_vars`, `json_encode`, `var_export`. Now
those walk the class's declaration order and put each name through `propGet` --
the same read an expression performs, hook, mangling and `__get` guard included
-- instead of reading slots. Four things had to be true first, and each was
wrong in its own way.

**Declaration order is not slot order.** The harvested property list arrives
sorted by slot offset and a virtual property has none, so it landed last however
early it was written. `Property.Order` -- the index in the engine's
`properties_info` -- was harvested already and reached the IR proto, then stopped
there. Plumbed into `gogen.Prop`.

But sorting the whole list by `Order` was wrong, and `typed_properties_059`
caught it: a trait's properties carry indices of their own, and the engine lists
**a class's own declarations first and a trait's after them**, which is already
the harvested order. Re-sorting put the trait's first. So `placeVirtuals` moves
only the virtuals, into the position `Order` gives them.

**A child never inherited a virtual property at all.** `inheritAncestorProps`
skipped `pr.Virtual` outright -- right when a virtual had no representation
anywhere, wrong once one was needed.

**A virtual property is declared without being stored.** `o.Declared` is a table
of its own, not a view of `o.Props`, so a name can carry visibility without
carrying storage. Without the declaration, asking whether a virtual property was
reachable from a scope answered "not declared, so public".

**`initialization cycle for scopedBuiltins`.** `get_object_vars` now reaches
`propGet`, a hook body reaches a builtin, and a builtin reaches that table. Go
rejects the cycle at package scope even though nothing runs at initialization.
Filled at start-up, exactly as `propHooks` already is. This is the pitfall
`LTM/builtin-and-userland-runtime.md` warns about, hit for real.

`var_export` needed its own rule rather than the `get_object_vars` walk with an
empty scope. Asked of the engine: it **runs the hooks and applies no
visibility** -- every declared property under its plain name, private and
protected alongside the public -- so it borrows each property's declaring scope.

### The regression that was an accidental exemption

Declaring virtual properties made them visible to the **write** path too, and
five `gh19044-*` files started failing. They had been passing only because a
virtual property had no declaration and the asymmetric-visibility check was
skipped entirely.

The tempting fix was to drop `SetVisibility` for virtuals and take the five
files back. The engine says no:

    class V { private $s = 0; public protected(set) int $p { get => $this->s; set { $this->s = $value; } } }
    Outside::bump(new V);  ->  Cannot modify protected(set) property V::$p from scope Outside

`protected(set)` **is** enforced on a virtual hooked property, so restoring the
exemption would have made compiled code accept a write PHP refuses. The real
bug, three probes:

| shape | engine |
| --- | --- |
| declared only in the grandchild, sibling scope | refused |
| declared in the shared parent, sibling scope | **allowed** |
| unrelated scope | refused |

So the question resolves against the **first** class to declare the name, not
the subclass that redeclared it. And `runtime/interp` already knew --
`Unit.protectedOwner`, with that sentence in its comment. The compiled arm had
never had it.

**Then the fix was wrong in a second way, found before measuring it.** Putting
the first declarer into `Declaration.Class` made the check right and the message
wrong: the engine names `Mid::$p`, the redeclaration, while permitting any scope
descending from `Base`. Two facts that disagree, both observable, one field.
Split into `Declaration.SetClass`. The in-flight corpus run was killed rather
than spend an hour measuring a state already known to be wrong.

### Two more, found by the one file the hook work left failing

`oss-fuzz-382922236` needed `$b = &$obj->b` on a missing property, which
produced nothing at all. Reaching a property as **storage** creates it where the
`&` is, holding **NULL** -- not the undef a fresh box carries, which is the
uninitialised state of a *declared typed* property and something a dynamic one
never is, so every reader that filters undef dropped it. The deprecation fires
at the `&`, not at a later write, and a readonly class refuses outright. That
logic already existed in `propSet`; it is now a shared `createDynamic` reached
from `place.ref` and `place.refBox` too.

Writing the fixture for it exposed a second, unrelated gap: `get_object_vars`
was flattening references. Two causes stacked -- the walk called `.Deref()`, and
`Array.Each` *itself* hands over the value behind the box (`EachRaw` is the one
that keeps it). Same fact as `get_defined_vars` over the symbol table: these
functions **duplicate** the table rather than read it, so `$r = &$o->x` leaves
the array element rendering `&int(9)` and tracking later writes. The interpreter
already had this right.

`property_hooks/dump.phpt` is now down to `object(Child)#1` versus `#2` -- the
known handle-numbering gap -- having entered this tick as `unsupported` and
passed through `errored` on the way.

## 2026-09-15 -- json_encode moves out of the interpreter, and gains nothing

Corpus: **2059 -> 2059 passing**, failed 788 unchanged, unsupported 1062 ->
1061, errored 1, noreference 1076 -> 1077.

`json_encode` left `runtime/interp/json.go` for `runtime/stdlib/json.go`, so the
compiled back-end has it. Everything it needs about an object it now asks the
Ctx for, through two new hooks in `runtime/php/lazyresolve.go`:

- `LazyResolver` -- a lazy object owes its initializer to any library function
  that looks at the real state. The **identity** when nothing installs one,
  which is not a gap papered over: a program that cannot make a lazy object has
  none to initialize.
- `VisibleProperties` -- what an object presents to a scope, hooks run and
  virtual properties in. `json_encode` asks with the empty scope, because the
  engine's encoder sees what global scope sees.

**And the move immediately found a hole it did not cause.** `ctx.SetSubclassOf`
was installed only by generated programs -- `runtime/interp` never installed the
hierarchy hop at all. Any shared builtin asking `ctx.InstanceOfClass` under the
interpreter was told "no class table" and had to answer as if nothing matched,
which is why `json_encode` of a `JsonSerializable` came back `{}` the moment the
function stopped being interpreter-aware. The 29 existing differential cases
caught it on the first run.

**The honest result: it gained no passing file.** The census listed eight files
whose only gap was `library function json_encode`; six of them now stop one step
later on `the properties C presents, which declares property hooks`, and two on
`include or eval`. The refusal it was asked to remove is gone -- no output in
the corpus still says `library function json_encode` -- and the files behind it
were never one fix away.

That is a limitation of the ranking, not of the census: **the census sees
compile-time refusals, and a run-time refusal behind one is invisible to it.**
A library function whose first use is on an object will keep over-promising this
way. Recorded in TESTING.md.

Two repairs travelled with it.

**A previously unreachable emitter bug.** `property_hooks/dump.phpt` calls
`json_encode($this)`, so until now the emitter refused the whole file and never
reached the bug: `Test` and `Child` each declare `private $changed` with a get
hook, and **a private is one slot per declaring class**, so `Child`'s table
carries both and naming each hook after the *instance* class declared one Go
function twice. `hookNameIn` brings the declarer into the name only where a name
actually repeats. The `propHooks` table, keyed by property name, now keeps the
class's own declaration where an ancestor's private repeats it -- two identical
keys in a Go map literal would have been the next build error. `errored` -> an
honest `unsupported`. Same fact as `slotKey` and `Unit.instantiate`, which is
three places now.

**A file that was never a result.** `attributes/deprecated/message_004.phpt`
builds its deprecation message from `random_int(1, 2)`. PHP's own harness never
sees the problem -- it matches one run against an `--EXPECTF--` carrying a `%c`
exactly where the randomness sits -- but a differential oracle compares **two
runs** and has nowhere to put a wildcard. The file was read once as a gain and
once as a regression. `php2gotest` now buckets such a file `noreference` under
two conditions that both have to hold: both arms satisfy the test's own
expectation, *and* the engine disagrees with **itself** across independent fresh
`php2eval` processes. Neither alone can excuse a real difference. A two-way
random is caught about seven times in eight, so such a file now oscillates
between `passed` and `noreference` rather than polluting `failed`. Eight corpus
files touch randomness or the clock at all, and at most four of those put it in
their output, so the residual noise is bounded.

## 2026-09-15 -- get_defined_vars, and a share with no matching release

Corpus: **2057 -> 2059 passing**, failed 790 -> 788, unsupported 1062 unchanged,
errored 1 (the known `concat_003` timeout). Two gained, nothing lost.

`get_defined_vars()` is answered by the **emitter**, not by a library function:
the generated program knows its own variable names, and that is the whole of
what the function asks. `internal/gogen` records the body's place list in
`body()` and renders an inline `php.NewArray()` builder at the call site.

What the engine settled first:

- inside a function it is the variables **assigned so far**, in CV-slot order.
  One declared in a branch that did not run has a slot and no value and is not
  in the array.
- at **top level** the answer opens with `_GET`, `_POST`, `_COOKIE` and
  `_FILES`, which php2go does not register. So `{main}` keeps being refused:
  producing the rest would be a wrong answer rather than a partial one.
- a by-reference parameter is in the array **as a reference** -- `&string(7)
  "changed"` -- and the element tracks a later write to the parameter. That is
  `zend_array_dup` over the symbol table preserving `IS_REFERENCE`, and it is
  what separates this function from an array literal or `compact()`, both of
  which deref. Probed all three in one case before writing any of it.

The interpreter needed the same correction: `runtime/interp/locals.go` was
copying with an unconditional `Deref().Copy()`. It now uses `php.CopyElement`,
which keeps the box only when the reference is one the program asked for. The
undef check still derefs, because at global scope an unassigned CV is a
reference holding undef rather than undef itself.

**The mistake worth recording.** Making the compiled prologue mark a
by-reference parameter `php.Shared` cost two files, and the reason is that
`php.Shared` is a *counter* (`runtime/php/ref.go:151`), not a flag. Every mark
owes an `Unshare`. The emitter already released the body's own `&` bindings in a
`defer` -- `boundLocals(fn)` -- but a parameter is not one of those, so the
binding the **argument** made outlived the call:

- `bug68215.phpt`: `test($arr[$i], $fruit)`, then `var_dump($arr)` printed
  `&array(5)` where the engine prints `array(5)`.
- `property_hooks/get_by_ref_virtual.phpt`: `inc($test->prop)`, then
  `var_dump($test)` printed `&int(44)`.

Both are the engine rendering `&` from `Z_REFCOUNT > 1` rather than from "is a
reference": when the call returns, the count drops and the marker goes with it.
Fixed by adding `byRefParams(fn)` to the same `defer`.

Two process notes, both of which cost time:

- the first measurement read `2056 / 791 / 1062 / 1` and the temptation was to
  call it noise. It was not: a *net* -1 hid two regressions and a gain. The
  regressions were settled by building a second binary with the one line
  reverted and running the eight candidates against both, not by reading the
  diffs and guessing which looked new.
- `php2gotest -v` lists only non-passing files, and the per-run summary block is
  printed **twice** (once including skips, once excluding). Summing every
  `passed` line across chunks doubles the count. The passing set is the corpus
  list minus every file listed with a status prefix.

What php2go still cannot do here is a share the callee hands back out: with
`function f(&$r) { return get_defined_vars(); }` the engine drops the `&` when
the returned array dies, and php2go's counter never decrements. Filed under
references and lifetime; it wants the returned container's own lifetime, which
is the Phase D3 ownership work.

## 2026-09-14 -- three introspection answers, and one that cannot be given

Corpus: **2054 -> 2057 passing**, unsupported 1066 -> 1062, errored 1. Three
gained, nothing lost.

`get_mangled_object_vars` and `get_resource_type` moved to `runtime/stdlib`:
both are questions about a value and nothing else. The mangled names are the
engine's *storage* keys -- `"\0*\0b"`, `"\0C\0c"` -- which is what makes this a
different question from `get_object_vars`, and why one needed a scope and this
one does not.

Two small facts followed them into `runtime/php` as shared predicates:
`HidesProperties` -- a `SensitiveParameterValue` shows no properties at all --
and `LazyState`, which follows an *initialised* proxy to the instance holding
the state. The first is an interface the interpreter's type satisfies, the same
shape as `InternalOutputFilter`.

`get_declared_traits` is emitted into the generated program, in declaration
order.

**And one that was worth measuring before attempting: `get_declared_classes`.**
The engine answers with **137** entries -- every internal class, then the
program's own -- and php2go models a few dozen. A compiled program could produce
the tail but not the list, so a file that prints it would fail whatever is
written. It stays a gap; the eight files are not reachable this way. Traits are
different for one reason: the engine supplies none of its own, so the whole
answer is the program's.

## 2026-09-14 -- a live cursor that never moved

Corpus: **2044 -> 2054 passing**, unsupported 1078 -> 1066, errored back to 1.
Eleven gained, one lost -- a `random_int` coin-flip.

Six more functions moved to `runtime/stdlib`: `array_shift`, `array_push` and
`array_unshift` -- the three that rewrite their argument, and pure `*php.Array`
work -- plus `file_put_contents`, `unlink`, `file_get_contents` and
`is_resource`. The `arrayBuiltins` map in the interpreter is gone with them.

The two program builders in `php2gotest` are one `fillProgram` now. Three
separate defects this session came from a step being added to only one of them,
and the third was enough.

**And the find: a by-reference `foreach` never moved its cursor.**

    $a = [1, 2, 3];
    foreach ($a as &$v) { if ($v == 2) { array_unshift($a, 0); } }

The engine ends after the three elements it started with -- a live walk holds a
*bucket position*, and rebuilding the array moves it. php2go's did not, so the
cursor stayed put, walked the new elements and then the old ones again, and the
loop never ended.

`Array.RegisterCursor` was written for exactly this and **had no callers**:
`Prepend` and the rest already shift every registered cursor, and nothing ever
registered one. `NewArrayRefIter` does now, and `Free` unregisters.

It was invisible until this tick because `array_unshift` could not be called
from compiled code at all -- the file was `unsupported`, then `errored` for
thirty seconds, and only then a bug. Two of the three timeouts this session were
that shape: a gap hiding a defect behind it.

## 2026-09-14 -- a by-reference variadic, and the closures a linked body brought with it

Corpus: **2040 -> 2044 passing**, unsupported 1088 -> 1078, errored back to 1
(the `concat_003` timeout, unchanged). Four gained, nothing lost.

`function f(&...$rest)` compiles now. Each collected argument keeps the **box**
the caller sent, so writing an element writes the variable the caller named;
`variadicArgs` copies, and the by-reference form needed its own. A declared type
is not applied to it, for the reason an ordinary by-reference parameter does not
take one: coercing would replace the value in the caller's storage.

It was 11 files by the census, and the number had **grown** from 6 the tick
before -- because the harvested library uses the form, and linking it made those
bodies reachable. Closing a compiler gap now pays twice.

**And the linker was not bringing closures.** A library body that declares one
references it by the name the `closure` opcode uses, and nothing else emitted it:
three files got a Go file naming a function that was never written, which is
`errored`. `buildProgram` has always called `collectClosures`; the linker had to
as well. That is the third thing this session that went wrong because a second
builder existed -- after `Opcodes` missing from the census's `Program`, and the
library linking having to be added to both program paths.

## 2026-09-14 -- six leaves, a source path, and a quadratic append

Corpus: **2037 -> 2040 passing**, unsupported 1091 -> 1088, **errored 0 -> 1**.
The errored one is not a regression and is the most interesting thing here.

`clock` and `read_file` moved to `runtime/stdlib`, the second through a new
`SourceReader` hook: a bundle serves its PHP from `go:embed`, where
`os.ReadFile` finds nothing, so the loader is supplied from above and the three
sources -- a `data:` URI, the loader, the host -- are shared. Four leaves are
left and are in TODO.md.

**A linked library body reports its own file now.** Every one of them claimed
the program's path, which broke the thing that finds where a library function
was *called*: `PHP2Go\Internal\warning` walks back to the nearest frame in a
different file, and in compiled code there was no different file. So
`parse_ini_file()`'s warning named a line eight thousand deep in the generated
Go. `Program.LibraryFile` carries the virtual path per body and `.line` emits
it; the interpreter has always worked this way, which is why the two disagreed.

**The errored file is `concat_003.phpt`, and it is newly visible rather than
newly broken.** It used to be blocked at compile time on `microtime`; now it
compiles, runs, and does not finish. The cause is the mutable-builder gap the
plan predicted, measured on the same shape:

| appends | engine | php2go |
|---|---|---|
| 20,000 | 0.001s | 0.35s |
| 40,000 | 0.003s | 2.0s |
| 80,000 | 0.007s | 5.1s |

Quadratic, because every `.=` allocates a new Go string where the engine mutates
in place at refcount 1. The ROPE lowering already builds `"$a$b"` through
`strbuf`; `ASSIGN_OP concat` does not, and cannot until something knows the
target is only appended to.

**I did not reclassify it.** A timeout is `errored` by a deliberate decision in
`php2gotest` -- "not a wrong answer, and not a gap the compiler declared" -- and
that reasoning is still right. Moving it to `unsupported` to keep the invariant
at zero would have been exactly the kind of bookkeeping QUALITY_GATE.md exists
to forbid. The number is 1, the cause is named, and the fix is filed.

## 2026-09-13 -- the harvested library, compiled in

Corpus: **2002 -> 2037 passing**, unsupported 1150 -> 1091, errored 0. Against
the baseline *before* `print_r` moved to PHP (2031): **+6, nothing lost**. The
29 files that move cost are back, and 273 harvested functions are reachable
from an emitted program for the first time.

A generated program is its own Go module and cannot import
`internal/userland`, so the bodies are **compiled into it** the way its own
functions are. `cmd/php2gotest/userlandlink.go` harvests the two libraries once
per process -- a second engine parse of twelve thousand lines, which per file
would have dominated the run -- and pulls in the transitive closure of what the
program actually calls. The libraries declare 792 functions between them;
emitting all of them into every file would be most of the build.

**A public alias is stored under the engine's spelling with the op_array
renamed**, which is the trick `InstallUserlandLibrary` already used: the body is
`print_r_impl`, and every diagnostic it raises names the function it is running,
so without the rename a TypeError from inside one reported a name no program can
call.

Four things had to be fixed on the way, each found by a body that would not
compile:

- **`array_id` takes its argument by reference and lives in `runtime/stdlib`.**
  Compiled code needs it for the same reason the interpreter does.
- **The three diagnostic leaves** -- `deprecated`, `notice`, `warning` -- moved
  too. Nearly every harvested function that refuses an argument warns on the
  way, so without them the library was unreachable in practice.
- **`foreach ($a as &$v)` over a place.** A by-reference reset was refused when
  its subject was a place, which is what a by-reference *parameter* is -- and
  `print_r`'s walk is exactly that. Reading the place would have walked a copy
  and every write through the loop variable would have vanished, so the
  catalogue gained `PlaceBox`: a place here is **opened**, not read. The
  by-value reset beside it keeps reading, because a snapshot is what it wanted.
- **A `place`-typed frame slot in a by-value call argument** rendered as a Go
  struct into a `[]php.Value` literal and the program did not build -- six files
  `errored`. The check was there but asked `e.vtypes`, which is keyed by SSA
  value and has nothing to say about a `$name`; `e.ptypes` is the same question
  asked of a slot.

Two things the linker has to know that were not obvious:

- **A namespace fallback is a second name.** `namespace Foo; print_r($x);`
  compiles to a call to `Foo\print_r` carrying `fallback="print_r"`, and reading
  only the operand pulled in neither -- one file passed everywhere except inside
  a namespace.
- **A missing `PHP2Go\Internal` leaf is php2go's gap, not the program's.** Left
  alone it reached the emitted program as `Call to undefined function
  PHP2Go\Internal\warning` -- a fatal php2go invented. The linker refuses the
  file instead. Six leaves still live only in `runtime/interp`; they are in
  TODO.md with their file counts.

## 2026-09-13 -- print_r is harvested PHP

Corpus: **2031 -> 2002 passing**, unsupported 1109 -> 1150, errored 0. **Minus
29, nothing gained** -- and the 29 are exactly the files that call `print_r` and
pass today, because compiled output cannot reach `internal/userland` yet. The
number was measured *before* the work started, so this is a chosen cost rather
than a discovered one.

`print_r_impl` in `internal/userland/ext/standard.php` owns the whole rendering
and the recursion walk. It asks one native question --
`\PHP2Go\Internal\print_r_object($object, bool $entries)` -- because a Closure
prints `[name]/[file]/[line]/[parameter]`, a Generator prints `[function]`, and
an enum case is labelled `S Enum:string`, all built by the engine and reachable
through no PHP function; `get_mangled_object_vars` answers *nothing* for a
Closure. The `$entries` flag exists so a cycle can be refused by label without
running `__debugInfo` a second time.

**`__debugInfo` is not the boundary it looks like.** A private one is a
compile-time warning and then treated as public, so PHP can reach it with
`method_exists` and a call. It is behind the leaf only because the hook already
applies it.

**The recursion walk takes its subject by reference, and that is load-bearing.**
php2go copies an array eagerly, so a by-value walk sees a fresh identity at
