every level and `$a[] = &$a` would recurse for ever. `\PHP2Go\Internal\array_id`
now takes its argument **by reference** for the same reason -- by value it
reported the id of php2go's own clone, so every userland recursion guard built
on it was dead, `http_build_query`'s included. That needed a second table:
`internalRefArgs`, because `builtinRefArgs` says of itself that it is the
engine's, read back through Reflection, and the engine has never heard of these
names.

Iterating by reference leaves **no mark** behind -- I expected it to, and
checked: a nested by-reference walk over an array holding a bound element leaves
`var_dump` reading exactly as it did before.

`php.PrintR` is deleted. What is left in `runtime/php/printr.go` is
`PrintRPropertyLabel`, which is a fact about a property's declaration rather
than formatting.

**One boundary got simpler on the way.** A `__debugInfo` that does not return an
array used to travel back as `*debugInfoFatal`, a private interpreter type each
caller unwrapped -- which stops working the moment a caller is PHP. It writes
its fatal and returns `php.Exit(255)` now, so every caller just propagates, and
`var_dump` and `debug_zval_dump` lost their unwrapping arms.

Two more differential-case hazards, both from the shared engine process: a case
must not leave a **cycle** standing, or a later `gc_collect_cycles()` counts it
(this one reported 4 against the interpreter's 0), and a self-referencing array
needs its element cleared before the name is unset or it is a cycle too.

## 2026-09-13 -- asking whether print_r could be userland, and finding a copy that was not made

The question was whether `print_r` can move to `internal/userland`. Answer:
**the arrays can, the objects cannot** -- and finding that out turned up an
interpreter bug worth more than the answer.

**The bug: a by-value element of an array literal was not copied.**

    $inner = [1, 2];
    $outer = [$inner, $inner];
    $outer[0][] = "x";      // engine: element 0 alone. php2go: both.

`addElement` stored what `f.fetch` returned, so both slots held the same
`*php.Array`. The **compiled** path was right all along -- `ArrayAppend` does
`v.Copy()` -- so this was the interpreter catching up with its own intrinsic.
It also made a by-reference `foreach` over such a literal write every element:
`foreach ($outer as $k => &$w) { $w[] = "t$k"; }` gave both elements both tags.
Fixed, with a differential case; the compiled corpus cannot see it, since that
harness grades compiled output against the engine and the compiled side was
never wrong.

**What the investigation established about print_r:**

- **Array recursion detection needs identity, and PHP-level code has none.**
  `===` is structural: `$outer[0] === $inner` is true for equal-but-distinct
  arrays, so a `===`-based cycle check prints `*RECURSION*` where PHP prints
  the array.
- php2go *does* have one -- `\PHP2Go\Internal\array_id()`, already used this
  way in `http_build_query` -- but only through a **by-reference** `foreach`. A
  by-value walk gets a fresh id at every level, because php2go copies eagerly;
  the by-ref element is the original. (Before the copy fix above, by-ref
  reported *the same* id for two distinct elements, which would have been the
  same false positive from the other direction.)
- **`__debugInfo` is not the blocker** it looked like: a private one is a
  compile-time warning and then treated as public, so `method_exists` plus a
  call reaches it from PHP.
- The real blocker is that **Closure, Generator and enums print entries the
  engine builds**: `[name]/[file]/[line]/[parameter]`, `[function] => g`, and an
  enum's `S Enum:string` header. `get_mangled_object_vars` answers nothing for
  a Closure, and no PHP function exposes those.

So a userland `print_r` would need exactly one native leaf -- "what does this
object show" -- which is `Ctx.ObjectProperties` under another name. That is a
single well-defined question rather than a multiplexer, so it is a defensible
split; not taken yet.

## 2026-09-13 -- streamcontext.go folded into stream.go

`runtime/stdlib/streamcontext.go` is gone; its 177 lines are in `stream.go`.
The split had made the same lookup exist twice -- `AsStreamContext(value)` in
one file and `contextOf(args, at)` in the other, differing only in how they were
handed the resource and in that one matched `*Stream` by name where the other
used the `contextHolder` interface. One function now, the interface one.

The two types reach through each other, which is what the file boundary was
fighting: every handle exposes a stream-local context, and a context is what
`fopen`'s fourth argument carries.

Pure relocation. `surface.tsv` and `shape.tsv` regenerate byte-identical, the
whole gate is green, and the stream fixtures still pass.

## 2026-09-13 -- an array element that holds the box

Corpus: **2018 -> 2031 passing**, unsupported 1135 -> 1109, errored 0. Fourteen
gained, one lost -- a `random_int` coin-flip. The six files the previous tick
gave up are back, passing for the right reason this time.

`[&$x]` binds a reference **into the element**. Two new intrinsics say so --
`ArrayAppendBound` and `ArraySetBound`, which keep the box where `ArrayAppend`
and `ArraySet` copy through it -- and the lowering picks them on
`extended_value`'s low bit. It is a second intrinsic rather than a flag because
the two do opposite things with the value they are handed, and the engine
decides which is meant per element.

**Then the same bug one layer out: unpacking dereferenced.** `f(...$a)` did
`e.Deref().Copy()` on every element, so a bound one arrived as a value and a
`&$x` parameter bound nothing. That is also how `call_user_func_array` reaches
a callee -- the engine compiles it to `SEND_ARRAY`, which is an unpack, which is
why the census never listed `call_user_func_array` as a gap at all. The unpack
reads raw slots now and passes a box on as a box; the callee's `recv` already
knew what to do with one, taking it for a by-reference parameter and unboxing
for a by-value one.

Finding that took building the generated program by hand and running it: a
`println` in the shared `call_user_func_array` never fired, which is what said
the compiled path was not going through the library function at all.

## 2026-09-13 -- named arguments to library functions, and a reference that went missing

Corpus: **2022 -> 2018 passing**, unsupported 1124 -> 1135, errored 0. **The
count went down on purpose**, and that is the tick.

**A named argument to a library function now binds.** `str_replace(subject:
"aaa", search: "a", replace: "b")` was refused as `named argument to an unknown
callee` -- the parameter names were in the harvested arginfo all along, they
just were not reachable from the emitter, which passed `nil` where the callee
signature goes. A skipped **required** parameter throws the engine's own
`array_slice(): Argument #2 ($offset) not passed`; a skipped **optional** one is
still refused, because a hole means something different for a library function
than for a compiled body -- `recv` reads an undef as "not passed" and applies
the default, while a library function reads `len(args)` and sees an argument
that was passed. `call_user_func` and `call_user_func_array` moved to
`runtime/stdlib` in the same pass.

**And the tick's real finding: `$a = [&$c]; $a[0]++;` left `$c` alone and said
nothing.** The lowering ignored the by-reference bit on `ZEND_INIT_ARRAY` and
`ZEND_ADD_ARRAY_ELEMENT` and treated `&$c` as an ordinary element -- a wrong
answer rather than a missing feature, which is the one outcome the project
forbids. The bit is `extended_value & 1`, read back from the engine: `[$c]` is
4, `[&$c]` is 5, and `[$c, &$d]` carries the 1 on the second opline.

It is refused now, and **six corpus files that were passing are `unsupported`
instead**. They passed because their output did not happen to depend on the
binding; the emitter cannot tell those from the ones that do. That is the trade
QUALITY_GATE.md asks for -- a gap must not masquerade as working behaviour --
and it is worth writing the cost down rather than only the rule. The feature is
filed with what it needs.

**A measurement bug, caught by its own guard.** A `.phpt` can expect output
containing a NUL, and a `-v` chunk file quoting one is a *binary file* to grep:
it prints `Binary file ... matches` and none of the lines, so the passing-set
diff counted every file in that chunk as passing. It read `gained: 381` on a
tick that gained two. `grep -a` everywhere, and the check that caught it --
the passing set's size against the run's own `passed` total -- is in TESTING.md
now.

## 2026-09-13 -- a census that lied, and two globals nobody set

Corpus: **2019 -> 2022 passing**, unsupported 1131 -> 1124, errored 0. **+3
gained, nothing lost** -- the smaller half of the tick. The larger half is that
two of the measurements and one of the boundaries were wrong.

**The census had a Program of its own, and it was missing `Opcodes`.**
`cmd/php2gotest` built `gogen.Program` in two places; the grading one filled the
engine's opcode table and the census one did not. `constOp` names a deferred
constant expression's operator through that table, so `const baz = bar + 1;` was
reported as `unrenderable operand <lit:0>` by the census while grading compiled
the very same file and passed it. Six files of gap that were not there, pointing
work at a bug that did not exist -- and I spent the first half hour of this tick
bisecting a PHP file that compiled perfectly well. One constructor now, named
for the hazard.

**`php.ObjectToString` and `php.CountObject` were package-level vars that only
the generated program ever set.** The interpreter converted objects through its
own path and never came this way, so the hole was invisible until a shared
builtin reached `php.ToString` with an object: moving `settype` to
`runtime/stdlib` made `settype($withToString, "string")` throw `could not be
converted to string` where PHP converts. Both are Ctx hooks now, set by both
back-ends -- which is also two fewer pieces of mutable package state in a
package whose rule is to have none.

`settype` moved with them, on a third new hook: **`Ctx.NewObjectOf`**, because
`settype($x, "object")` has to make a stdClass and handles are the *program's*
to number. `to.object` was already declared a **local** intrinsic for exactly
that reason; this is the same fact with a door in it.

Two fixtures had to be rewritten around the handle-numbering gap rather than
through it: `var_export.php` cannot dump an object in a file that declares an
enum, and `settype.php` had to do its object casts **before** anything throws,
because a caught exception is an object too. Both are noted in the files.

## 2026-09-13 -- ini_set, assert, and a string literal that said " as "

Corpus: **2007 -> 2019 passing**, unsupported 1151 -> 1131, errored 0.
**+12 gained, nothing lost.**

Two more pieces of **request state** moved to the Ctx, and their functions to
`runtime/stdlib` with them:

- **INI settings.** A script writes one and reads it back, which is the same
  reason the constant table and the error-handler stack live there. The
  *storage* is a hook, because a Unit carries the harvested registry and a
  setting the build declares has a value nothing below could know; the *rule* --
  which names php2go models, and the handful that refuse a write -- is in
  stdlib, so compiled code has it. `ini_get`, `ini_set` and `IniQuantity`
  followed.
- **`assert`'s options.** Five flags and a callback, with the engine's defaults
  for `zend.assertions=1`. The body needed `Ctx.Call` for the callback and
  nothing else, so it moved whole, along with the
  `php2go\internal\assert_options` leaf the userland facade calls.

Moving `assert` turned up a hole in the boundary: **`php.Throw(o)` had no way
back into the interpreter.** `assert(false, new RuntimeException("x"))` throws
the object it was given, and stdlib says so with `php.Throw`; the interpreter's
`materialize` knew `php.AsError` -- a class and a message -- but not an object
already built, so the throw travelled out as a plain Go error and nothing could
catch it. The generated program's `materialise` had the arm all along.

**And a real emitter bug, found by a fixture rather than looked for: any string
literal containing `" as "` failed to compile.** The IR renders a named send as
`byval <operand> as "<name>"`, and the emitter recognised one with a substring
search -- so `var_dump("thrown as given")` was refused as `named argument`, and
the whole file with it. `lower.CutNamedSend` now **parses** the suffix: a
candidate counts only when the quoted string it opens runs to the very end of
the text. Three sites searched for it; two were wrong the same way, and
`cutNamed` was accidentally safe because `strconv.Unquote` rejected the
fragment.

**The handle-numbering family is bigger than the TODO said.** Of 752 compiled
failures, **40 differ first on nothing but an `object(X)#N`** -- 25 of them by
exactly one -- against the "10" recorded earlier. The cause is what the plan
predicted: the engine frees a temporary and reuses its handle, and the generated
program never frees one. `f(new foo); f(new bar);` gives the engine `#2` twice
and compiled code `#2` then `#3`. The interpreter gets this right through
`releaseTemp` and a reachability walk; compiled code has neither, and the honest
fix is the escape analysis in the plan rather than a guess about when a
temporary dies.

One more way the shared engine process leaks between differential cases: an
`ini_set` a case leaves standing is still there for the next one. It surfaced as
a syslog case reading `syslog.filter` as `"raw"` -- reported against the case
that did not cause it. Cases restore what they change now; see TESTING.md.

## 2026-09-13 -- var_export, and when an enum case takes its handle

Corpus: **2001 -> 2007 passing**, unsupported 1162 -> 1151, errored 0. Seven
gained, one lost -- a `random_int` coin-flip.

`var_export` and `debug_zval_dump` moved to `runtime/stdlib`, along with
`spl_object_id`, `spl_object_hash` and `get_resource_id`. What kept the first
two in the interpreter is a **second** object hook: what an object shows under
`var_export` is not what it shows under `var_dump` -- plain names, duplicates
kept, a get hook **run**, and a virtual property listed though it has no slot.
So `php.ExportProperties` sits beside `ObjectProperties`, with a default that
reads the table; compiled code installs one that refuses a class declaring
property hooks rather than reading the storage behind them.

**A compiled string literal is interned.** The engine keeps every compile-time
string in its interned table, and the one place that shows is
`debug_zval_dump`, which prints `interned` where a request-allocated string
prints `refcount(N)`. The emitter was rendering every literal as an ordinary
string.

**The real find: an enum's cases are built on first access, all at once, and
before the instance that names one.** Three measurements, each correcting the
previous fix:

1. Touching one case materialises **every** case of that enum. On a three-case
   enum, `E::B` is handle 3 and the next `new` is 5 -- the interpreter was
   building one at a time and every later object had the wrong number. The same
   fact shows without counting: reading `Y::A` raises for the bad backing value
   on `Y::B`, a case it was never asked for.
2. **In declaration order, the requested case included.** Building the others
   first and the requested one last put it at the end of the run of handles
   instead of in its place.
3. The generated program built them at **start-up**, which is worse: every
   object in a program that declares an enum was off. Deferred behind an
   `enumInit` thunk that `enumCasesOf` runs once.

Deferring then exposed the fourth: **a property default is evaluated before the
object exists.** `class A { public $p = E::Value; }` makes the enum case object
#1 and `new A` object #2, because the engine resolves a class's deferred
initializers when the class is first used, ahead of allocating the instance. The
emitter evaluated them inline, after the handle was taken, so the two came out
swapped -- which cost a file that had been passing, and is why the tick's first
measurement read +7/-1 with a real regression in it.

**And one more oracle artifact.** The engine arm shares a single process across
every differential case in the file, so its object handles start wherever the
previous case left off. A case about handle *numbers* has to compare them
against a baseline it took itself -- and hold that baseline in a **variable**,
since a temporary is freed and whether its handle is reused is a separate
question.

## 2026-09-12 -- $GLOBALS, get_class_methods, and past 2,000

Corpus: **1990 -> 2001 passing**, unsupported 1176 -> 1162, errored 0.
**+11 gained, nothing lost.** Two thousand of 4,986 files now compile to Go and
produce the engine's bytes.

**`$GLOBALS` read whole** was a *lowering* gap -- `ZEND_FETCH_GLOBALS: not
lowered` -- and the cheapest twelve files on the board. It is deliberately not
an intrinsic: the symbol table it reads is not a value `runtime/php` can see,
since the interpreter keeps one on the Ctx and the generated program keeps its
own. So it lowers to a plain `fetch_globals` opcode, alongside the four others
that arrive that way, and the emitter builds the array from its own `globals`
map. **A snapshot, not a live view** -- since PHP 8.1 writing through the array
does nothing, and `$GLOBALS["x"] = v` is rewritten by the compiler into a plain
global fetch rather than reaching this at all. Six of the twelve pass; the rest
are blocked on `serialize` and `ArrayObject`.

The map could not answer what order `$GLOBALS` lists its entries in, so a
`globalOrder` slice was added beside it, appended to in both places a global is
created. A global with no value yet is **not there**: `global $n;` alone makes
the slot without putting the name in `$GLOBALS`.

**`get_class_methods` needed a declaration order the generated program did not
keep** -- `Class.Methods` is a map -- so `MethodOrder` now carries the class's
own methods as declared, abstract and static included. The engine's order took
three measurements to get right, and each correction was a thing the harvest
does differently:

1. **Own before inherited** -- a subclass's methods first, then each ancestor's.
2. **A trait's methods are not in the class's own list.** The harvest keeps a
   trait as a class of its own; the engine copies its methods into the composing
   class's table right after that class's own, so that is where they go.
3. **Then the interfaces'.** `abstract class A implements I` lists `im` last,
   after its own methods and its traits'. The interpreter was missing this one
   too, and is fixed.

A name is marked seen **whether or not it is visible**: a subclass's declaration
shadows the ancestor's, so the ancestor's must not reappear further down the
chain merely because the nearer one was private. The visibility rule itself is
the generated program's existing `methodReachable`, not a second copy.

Like `get_object_vars` and `get_class_vars` last tick, this is a `scopedBuiltin`
rather than a move to `runtime/stdlib`: the answer depends on who is asking, and
the library table cannot see that.

## 2026-09-12 -- get_object_vars and get_class_vars, and three orderings

Corpus: **1972 -> 1990 passing**, unsupported 1197 -> 1176, errored 0.
**+18 gained, nothing lost.**

Both functions answer for the **calling scope** -- from outside a class the
public properties only -- which is why they are emitted into the generated
program's `scopedBuiltins` beside `property_exists` rather than moved to
`runtime/stdlib`. The library table cannot see who is asking. The *rule* is
still shared: both call `php.CheckPropertyRead`, so the visibility decision has
one home even though the iteration does not.

**They order their answers differently, and that had to be measured.**

- `get_object_vars` uses the **instance's slot order**, which is parent-first:
  `a` (declared in the parent) before `d` (declared in the child).
- `get_class_vars` puts a class's **own declarations first**, then each
  ancestor's -- `d` before `a` -- and puts **every static after every instance
  property**, whatever order they were declared in.

The harvest flattens the property table parent-first, so the first is free and
the second needed a reordering pass. The interpreter had the own/inherited split
already and applied it to the instance properties only, so a child's static came
out after its parent's.

**A static reports what the class *declares*, not what the program has
written.** After `A::$s = "changed"`, `get_class_vars("A")` still answers `"S"`:
the engine reads the default static table and php2go was reading the live slot.
Both back-ends were wrong and are fixed differently, because the default is in
different places:

- the interpreter reads it from the **declaring class's** property record --
  an inherited copy does not carry the default, which is what made the first
  fix return null for every inherited static;
- the generated program records each static's value on its **first access**,
  which is safe because every read and write goes through `staticSlot`, so
  nothing can have changed it yet.

Two smaller facts, both from the engine: an **uninitialised typed property** is
null under `get_class_vars` and *absent* from `get_object_vars` -- one asks what
the class declares and the other what the instance holds -- and
`get_class_vars` on an unknown name is a TypeError quoting **the name as
given**, not its type.

Compiled code refuses `get_object_vars` on a class with property hooks rather
than reading the table behind them: a virtual property has no slot and a backed
one answers through its getter. `get_class_vars` needs no such refusal, since it
reports declared defaults and the engine omits virtual properties from it
entirely.

## 2026-09-12 -- array_map, the scalar readers, and two wordings read back from the engine

Corpus: **1961 -> 1972 passing**, unsupported 1217 -> 1197, errored 0. Thirteen
gained, two lost -- both the `random_int` coin-flips -- so eleven are real.

`array_map` moved to `runtime/stdlib`; `Ctx.Call` was the only thing it needed.
So did the scalar readers -- `strlen`, `gettype`, `intval`, `floatval`,
`strval`, `boolval` -- which were in the interpreter's private table for no
reason but where they were written. `doubleval` is **not** among them: it is
already userland PHP, and registering a native one was caught by
`TestGeneratedSurfaceIsCurrent` as a conflicting disposition, which is what that
test is for.

**Two engine-verified wordings, both pre-existing and both wrong here:**

**A variadic parameter is never named in a diagnostic.** `array_map` declares
`(?callable $callback, array $array, array ...$arrays)`, and the engine says
`Argument #2 ($array) must be of type array` for the declared one and
`Argument #3 must be of type array` -- position alone -- for the variadic, the
first slot included. php2go printed `($arrays)` for every one of them. It is the
**parameter** that decides, not whether the position ran past the declared list:
the first fix keyed off overflow and still named slot #3, because `arrays` is a
declared entry. Fixed in both argument checks -- the interpreter's
`verifyBuiltinArgs` and the generated unit's -- through a shared `php.ArgLabel`,
so the two cannot drift.

**`intval`'s base argument was ignored entirely.** `intval("42", 8)` answered 42.
What the engine actually does, all of it read back rather than reasoned out:

- The base applies to a **string** and nothing else: `intval(42.9, 8)` is 42.
- **Base 10 is not strtol at base 10.** It is the ordinary numeric-string
  conversion, which is why `intval("1e3", 10)` is 1000 where `intval("1e3", 0)`
  is 1.
- An **invalid base answers 0**, not a ValueError: `intval("10", 1)` and
  `intval("10", 37)` are both 0.
- At base 0 **or** 2, PHP strips a leading `0b` itself and then converts at base
  **2 regardless of the base asked for** -- so `intval("0B11", 0)` is 3, not 11,
  and `intval("0b0b1", 2)` is 1 because PHP removes one prefix and the
  conversion removes the other.
- Overflow **saturates** at PHP_INT_MAX / PHP_INT_MIN rather than wrapping.

A differential case runs all 31 strings against six bases; it matched on the
first run. Worth noting that the last rule is **glibc-version dependent** -- a
`0b` prefix at base 2 or 0 is accepted by strtol only since glibc 2.38 -- which
is the founding rule earning its keep: the linked build is the oracle, and no
amount of reading the PHP source would have settled it.

Also found, not fixed: **the interpreter cannot `fopen("php://memory")` or
`php://temp`**. A differential case reached for one and got
`unsupported: fopen of php://memory`.

## 2026-09-12 -- debug_backtrace, trigger_error, and an exit both back-ends can raise

Three more moves out of the interpreter, all following the same hook pattern.
Corpus: **1948 -> 1961 passing**, unsupported 1241 -> 1217, errored 0. Passing-set
diff **+13, nothing lost**.

`debug_backtrace` was held back by one thing: an argument marked
`#[\SensitiveParameter]` is replaced in the trace by a
`SensitiveParameterValue`, and building one needs an object store. That is
`Ctx.SetSensitiveHider` now, so the whole trace-shaping body -- `TraceArray` and
`SplitCallName` -- moved to `runtime/stdlib` and an exception's `getTrace` calls
the same code. With no hider installed the argument is left alone, which is what
a program with no sensitive parameters sees anyway; compiled code installs none,
so it shows the raw value where the engine shows the wrapper. Named, not hidden.

`trigger_error` and `user_error` moved with it. Their one interpreter dependency
was E_USER_ERROR, which ends the request -- so `php.ExitError` now lives in
runtime/php, and the interpreter's `exitTermination` is gone in favour of it.
`php.Exit(status)` is what a builtin returns; `php.AsExit` is what each back-end
recognises. Acting on it stays the program's: the interpreter unwinds to the top
of `RunUnit`, and the emitted program calls `runShutdown` then `os.Exit` -- which
`runtime/stdlib` must never do itself, since the interpreter shares it with a
caller it must not end.

**The E_USER_ERROR path in compiled code is unverified**, and saying so is the
point. The oracle runs the engine through `zend_eval_string`, which *bails out*
on a request-ending fatal instead of handing back output, so every file that
reaches one grades `noreference` -- six of the nine corpus files that mention
E_USER_ERROR do. There is no reference to compare a compiled program against.
The body is the interpreter's, moved unchanged, and the `AsExit` arm mirrors what
`phpExit` already did; that is an argument, not a measurement. Filed in TODO.md.

**Two more oracle artifacts, both found by cases that failed for the wrong
reason:**

- A trace frame's `file` is the harness's own path -- `php2go-eval` against a
  temp file -- and an object's handle number is the harness's own count. A
  differential case over `debug_backtrace` has to print the frames **key by
  key** with those two left out; printing a frame whole compares two things this
  oracle cannot make agree.
- `exit` does *not* bail the engine arm, but the shutdown functions it should run
  afterwards do not appear in the capture, while the interpreter runs them. So a
  `register_shutdown_function` after an `exit` mismatches for the harness's
  reason. (E_USER_ERROR is the other way around -- the engine printed the
  shutdown output and *then* bailed.)

## 2026-09-12 -- output buffering, and an oracle that buffers its own output

`ob_start` and the four functions that end a buffer moved from the interpreter
to `runtime/stdlib`, so **a compiled program can buffer its own output** --
including through a PHP handler, with a chunk size, nested. The Ctx has held the
buffer stack all along; what kept the functions in the interpreter was
`ob_start`'s callable argument and running that callable when the buffer ends,
and both are Ctx hooks now.

Corpus: **1940 -> 1948 passing**, unsupported 1259 -> 1241, errored 0. The
passing-set diff is **+8 gained, nothing lost** -- one of the eight is the
`message_004` coin-flip landing heads, so seven are real.

`SetBufferFlusher` is no longer required. `Ctx.RunBufferFilter` handles both
kinds of handler itself: a Go one through the new exported
`php.InternalOutputFilter` (the `output_add_rewrite_var` rewriter is the only
implementation), a PHP one through `Call`. The interpreter still installs a
flusher because it wants the call made at its own depth; compiled code installs
nothing and works. The chunk-overflow path was gated on a flusher being
installed, which is why a chunked handler never ran in compiled code -- it is
gated on *either* route now.

**Two engine-verified divergences, both pre-existing:**

- **A bad handler passed to `ob_start` is not a TypeError.** Every other
  builtin's callback parameter raises one; `ob_start` warns with the same
  reason text, adds `Notice: ob_start(): Failed to create buffer`, and answers
  false with no buffer opened.
- **An object with no `__invoke` is refused for its *shape*.** The engine's
  callback-argument check says `no array or string given` for `new stdClass`,
  exactly as it does for `1.5`. `Object of type X is not callable` is what
  *invoking* one reports, and `callableReason` was returning the invocation's
  wording from the argument check -- so `array_map(new D, [1])` and
  `set_error_handler(new stdClass)` both said the wrong thing.

**The oracle runs one output-buffer level deep.** `php2go_eval` captures with
`php_output_start_default()`, so under `php2eval` the engine reports
`ob_get_level()` as 1 where the CLI reports 0, `ob_get_contents()` at top level
answers `""` rather than false, and a script that ends more buffers than it
opened tears down the capture and appears to print nothing. Eight of the first
ob_* differential cases were measuring that and not PHP.

The buffer is invisible to anything that only *writes*, which is why this has
never shown up: no file in the 4,986-file corpus reads `ob_get_level`,
`ob_get_status` or `ob_list_handlers`. It is a real fidelity gap all the same,
and the fix is to capture at `sapi_module.ub_write` instead -- also in-process,
also no file descriptor, and not a buffer the script can see. Filed in TODO.md
rather than done here, because changing the oracle changes every number and
would have made this tick's +8 unreadable.

## 2026-09-12 -- a compiled program can open a file

The wrapper and filter registries moved from the interpreter's `Unit` to the
`Ctx`, and `fopen` followed them into `runtime/stdlib`. **An emitted binary
opens, reads, seeks and closes real files now** -- the fixture that could not be
written last tick is `file_functions.php`, and it passes.

The registries belong on the Ctx for the reason the constant table and the
error-handler stack do: registering a wrapper is something a *request* does.
What they hold is thin -- a class name, some flags, and an opaque `Class any`,
because what a class is belongs to the layer with a class table. The one part of
`fopen` that genuinely needs that layer, opening through a wrapper the program
registered, comes back through a new `UserStreamOpener` hook, installed at the
stream dispatcher's entry rather than at one arm -- `fopen` reaches the opener
without going near a callback, which is why `installCallValue`'s old placement
was not enough.

Corpus: **1927 -> 1940 passing**, unsupported 1290 -> 1259, errored 0. Fifteen
gained; the two lost are both known `random_int` coin-flips.

**And the fixture found three divergences, all pre-existing and all in the
interpreter too.** They were invisible because compiled code could not open a
file and the corpus never exercised these exact shapes:

- `fread($f, 100)` on a 3-byte file left `feof` **false**. PHP *fills the
  buffer*: a short read is not the end, so the engine reads again until the
  request is met or a read returns nothing, and it is that empty read which
  sets EOF. Fixed, guarded to skip sockets and user wrappers, where a short
  read is the answer and reading again would block or re-enter PHP.
- An unknown wrapper produced **one** combined warning where the engine emits
  two: `fopen(): Unable to find the wrapper "x" ...` without the path, then
  `fopen(x://y): Failed to open stream: No such file or directory` with it.
- An invalid mode raised a **ValueError fatal** where the engine warns
  ``fopen(PATH): Failed to open stream: `!!' is not a valid mode for fopen``
  and returns false.

**A correction about method, and it matters.** `php2eval -raw` implies
`-engine`: it runs the engine *only*. Several times this session I read its
output as "the engine and the interpreter agree" -- they were engine-only runs,
and the interpreter was never exercised. The conclusions drawn from them still
held, because a differential *case* was added each time and the suite verified
it, but the reasoning was wrong. Drop `-raw` to get both arms and the
`--- MATCH ---` / `--- MISMATCH ---` verdict; that is how all three divergences
above were confirmed to be the interpreter's as well.

Still not compiled-reachable: a **closed** resource. `fclose($f)` twice is a
TypeError from the argument check in the engine, and compiled argument
verification does not reject a closed resource yet.

## 2026-09-12 -- the file functions followed the type, and hit the next wall

`fclose`, `feof`, `fread`, `fgets`, `fwrite`/`fputs`, `fseek`, `ftell` and
`rewind` are in `runtime/stdlib/filefns.go`. With the stream type moved they
touched nothing but `stdlib.*`, so what moved was the registration rather than
any behaviour; the interpreter dispatches them through one delegating arm,
keeping them on the path `verifyBuiltinArgs` runs ahead of.

`ErrUserStreamOperation` went with them. It is the sentinel a user-space
wrapper's method returns when the PHP behind it **refused** an operation rather
than failing, and the library functions read it to tell that -- which is
`false` -- from something going wrong, which propagates. It crosses the
`UserStream` interface in both directions, so it belongs with the interface
rather than with either side.

Two did not move. `stream_get_filters` reads the *interpreter's* registry of
user-registered filters, and `stream_get_meta_data` also answers for a
**directory** handle, which is a resource `runtime/stdlib` does not have.

Userland blockers **29 -> 24**, and only five native ones are left:
`ini_get`/`ini_set`/`ini_get_all` and those two.

**The fixture could not be written, and that is the finding.** A compiled
program still cannot obtain a stream: `fopen` resolves a **wrapper** through
`unit.streamWrapper(scheme)`, a registry the interpreter owns because
`stream_filter_register` and `stream_wrapper_register` write to it. So the file
functions are reachable from compiled code and there is nothing to hand them.
That does not make the move pointless -- the userland library calls them
directly and its blocker count is what dropped -- but it does mean the next
piece is the **wrapper registry on the Ctx**, not more function moves. The
behaviour itself is verified: the differential suite covers all eight and
passes.

Corpus: **1926 -> 1927 passing**, failed 694 -> 693, unsupported 1290 unchanged,
errored 0, zero regressions.

## 2026-09-12 -- the stream type moved to runtime/stdlib

The last real obstacle to an emittable userland library. `runtime/interp`'s
`stream` -- 3,700 lines with the filter chain beside it -- is now
`stdlib.Stream`, because an emitted program has to be able to **open** one. The
`Stream` interface the multiplexer split introduced only let compiled code
operate on a stream somebody else had made, which is no use when `fopen` is the
thing that makes it.

**The cut is 118 declarations to `runtime/stdlib`, 29 staying.** What stayed
needs a class table or a loader: opening a user-space wrapper, resolving a
filter class or an include path, and the **directory** handles -- a different
resource that had merely shared the file. `UserStream` is the interface the one
remaining piece is reached through, and defining it first, *before* moving
anything, is what made the move mechanical: the `user` field went behind the
interface, the tests still passed, and only then did the type move.

Two things about method:

- **Brace counting cannot split Go.** Three attempts to find declaration
  boundaries by counting `{` failed on a brace inside a string and on a
  multi-line signature, and the last one silently truncated three map entries.
  A 60-line tool using `go/parser` did it correctly first time, and emitting
  `//@@DECL@@` between declarations rather than a blank line was necessary too
  -- a struct has blank lines inside it, and splitting on those tore `Stream`
  in half.
- **A blanket rename must never touch string literals.** `stream` -> `Stream`
  rewrote `"Argument #1 ($stream)"` into `($stdlib.Stream)`, `"supplied resource
  is not a valid stream resource"`, `"Failed to open stream:"` and the
  `"stream"` a resource reports its type as. The differential suite caught all
  of them. Restoring them then over-corrected: `"Stream filter failed"` and
  `"Stream is not writable"` are **capitalised in the engine's own wording**,
  and lowercasing them broke two bundle tests. The rule is not "be careful" --
  it is that a literal is data and a rename is about identifiers, so the
  substitution has to skip quoted text and then each PHP-visible string has to
  be checked against the engine rather than guessed.

Corpus: **1926 / 694 / 1290 / 0**, identical to before the move; the one file
that differs is the `random_int` coin-flip. A relocation should move nothing.

The seven functions this was for -- `fclose`, `fgets`, `fread`, `fseek`,
`fwrite`, `stream_get_filters`, `stream_get_meta_data` -- are **not** moved yet.
They are still arms of the interpreter's dispatcher, but they now touch nothing
except `stdlib.*`, so moving them is a separate and straightforward pass. The
blocker count is unchanged at 29 until then, which is the honest reading: the
prerequisite is done, the thing it unblocks is not.

## 2026-09-12 -- array_walk, which was waiting on the callback check

`array_walk` was the last native blocker on the userland library that was not a
stream or an INI setting, and it had been waiting on something specific: it
validates its callback, and until the previous tick `runtime/php` had no way to.
With `Ctx.CheckCallable` it moved to `runtime/stdlib/arraywalk.go`.

The order matters and the comment says so: the callback is refused **before the
walk begins**, because an unusable one is an argument error rather than a
failure part-way through a mutation that has already written some elements back.

Two helpers went to `runtime/php` on the way, both pure over `*php.Object` and
both used elsewhere in the interpreter, so they are exported rather than copied:
`MangledName`, the engine's storage key for a non-public property, and
`NotePropertyType`, which records a typed property's declaration on a reference
so a by-reference walk over an object still type-checks what it writes.

Corpus: **1923 -> 1926 passing**, unsupported 1294 -> 1290, failed 693 -> 694,
errored 0, one lost and it is the `random_int` coin-flip.

Fixture: `array_walk.php`. It first failed on `object(P)#1` against `#4` -- the
object handle-number cluster, nothing to do with `array_walk` -- which is the
case TESTING.md's own screening rule already covers: a fixture that is not about
object identity should not print objects. `print_r` shows the properties without
the handle.

Userland blockers **30 -> 29**, and the native ten that remain are now exactly
two groups: `ini_get`/`ini_set`/`ini_get_all`, which want INI state on the Ctx,
and `fclose`/`fgets`/`fread`/`fseek`/`fwrite`/`stream_get_filters`/
`stream_get_meta_data`, which all want the same thing -- the `*stream` type
itself in `runtime/stdlib`.

## 2026-09-12 -- compiled code verifies a builtin's arguments now

The wider gap behind the callback bug: **compiled code did not check a library
function's arguments against the engine's declared parameter list at all.**
`str_repeat("a", [])` answered `""` where the engine raises
`str_repeat(): Argument #2 ($times) must be of type int, array given`, and 18
corpus failures were exactly that.

The interpreter has done this since the start, in `verifyBuiltinArgs` over the
harvested `engineSignatures`. Compiled code could not, because the arguments are
only known at run time, so the signatures have to be *in the artifact*. They are
now: `Program.BuiltinSignatures` carries them from the harvest, and the emitter
writes a `builtinSignatures` table for the functions the runtime provides -- the
engine declares some 1,500 and a program can only call the ones that exist, so
the table is the ~180 that do.

`php.CoerceInternalArgument` already existed and does the whole coercion half,
including the parts that are not refusals: a numeric string converts, and
passing null to a scalar parameter is **deprecated and then coerced to the
type's zero** rather than being an error. A by-reference parameter is skipped --
the native implementation parses its own and may narrow the declared type -- and
a `callable` parameter goes to the callback rule from the previous tick, which
says why the value is not one rather than what type it is.

Two things went wrong, both worth keeping:

- **The table came out empty**, because `php2gotest` builds a `gogen.Program` in
  **two** places and I filled the field in one. That is the third time this
  session a duplicated literal has swallowed a change; the symptom here was a
  feature that silently did nothing rather than a build error.
- **A mixed-case method name broke seven passing files.** `methodOwnerOf` keys
  methods **lowercased**, because PHP method names are case-insensitive, and
  `methodCallableReason` passed the source spelling. So `[$this, "EH"]` in
  `bug32226` reported `class A does not have a method "EH"` -- and because a
  callback argument is checked *before* the call, that turned a working
  `set_exception_handler` into a fatal. The corpus caught it; the fixtures did
  not, because every method in them was already lowercase.

Corpus: **1917 -> 1923 passing**, failed 699 -> 693, unsupported 1294 unchanged,
errored 0, zero regressions. Fixture: `builtin_argument_types.php`, which covers
the refusals, the coercions, the null deprecation, and a by-reference parameter
that must *not* be checked.

Timing note: the emitted programs carry the signature table now, so each is
larger and slower to compile. Chunks `q01` and `q02` no longer fit the
ten-minute cap even four-at-a-time; `split -n l/2` and concatenate.

## 2026-09-12 -- a builtin checks its callback before calling it

The wrong answer found at the end of the last tick, fixed. Compiled
`array_reduce([1,2], "nosuchfunction")` said
`Call to undefined function nosuchfunction()` where the engine says
`array_reduce(): Argument #2 ($callback) must be a valid callback, function
"nosuchfunction" not found or invalid function name`. The difference is *when*:
a builtin validates its callback argument **before** invoking it, and reports
something an invocation never would.

`CallableReason` is CallValue's other half -- same shape, same boundary, same
place supplying it: a `Ctx` hook answering **why** a value cannot be called,
"" when it can. `Ctx.CheckCallable(function, position, name, v)` turns a
non-empty reason into the TypeError, and `Ctx.CallableReasonFor` asks the same
question for `is_callable`, which wants the verdict rather than a diagnostic.
The interpreter installs its existing `callableReasonQuiet`; the emitter grew a
`callableReason` mirroring the resolution `callValue` already does without
performing the call.

That made `is_callable` implementable, which the compiler refused outright and
which blocked **19 corpus files**. It is not the same question as the argument
check, and the two places it differs were both read off the engine:

- **`__call` makes any method name callable.** `is_callable([new C, "nope"])` is
  true when C declares `__call` -- and so is `[new C, "p"]` for a *private* `p`,
  which is the case that needed the fallback repeated at the visibility check
  rather than only where the method is missing.
- **the name is written even when the answer is false**, and for shapes that are
  not callables at all: `42` gives `"42"`, null gives `""`, `[new C, 5]` gives
  `"Array"` rather than `"C::5"`, and `new stdClass` gives
  `"stdClass::__invoke"` while answering false.

Three more things the engine had to settle, none of them guessable:

- A **plain object is refused for its shape**: `new stdClass` as a callback
  argument is `no array or string given`, the same words an int gets, rather
  than anything naming the class. The first attempt kept a "class I do not
  declare, so I will not judge" escape, which let stdClass through to fail later
  as `Call to undefined method`.
- `$syntax_only` does not reach an object. `is_callable(new stdClass, true)` is
  **false** and `is_callable($withInvoke, true)` is true -- there is no syntax to
  check, so the flag is ignored for that kind.
- `CheckCallable` with **no hook installed claims nothing at all**, not even by
  shape. `runtime/php`'s own boundary tests pass `php.Null()` as a stand-in
  callback precisely because the hook ignores it; refusing a shape there would
  have invented a diagnostic for a caller that never asked for the check.

Corpus: **1912 -> 1917 passing**, unsupported 1310 -> 1294, errored 0, zero
regressions. `bug63111`, `bug65108`, `closure_001` and
`is_callable_trampoline_uaf` gained; the fifth is the `random_int` coin-flip.
Fixtures: `callback_validation.php` (24 shapes) and `is_callable.php` (25).

A measurement note: running six corpus chunks at once now exceeds the ten-minute
tool cap, because `php2gotest` is serial within one invocation and `q01` is 551
files. Four at a time, or split `q01`, whose four quarters concatenate into one
file the tally reads correctly.

## 2026-09-12 -- array_walk could not move, and the reason was a wrong answer

`array_walk` was the last easy native blocker on the userland library -- it
needs a callback, and `Ctx.Call` has been the hook for that since
`array_reduce`. It did not move, and finding out why turned up something worse
than a blocker.

`array_walk` validates its callback through the interpreter's `callValueFor`,
which raises
`array_walk(): Argument #2 ($callback) must be a valid callback, ...`.
`Ctx.Call` does no validation, so the question was whether the already-moved
`array_reduce` had lost that. Through the interpreter it has not -- `php2eval`
agrees with the engine on all four probes. **Through compiled code it has**:

	engine / interpreter: TypeError: array_reduce(): Argument #2 ($callback) must be
	                      a valid callback, function "nosuchfunction" not found or
	                      invalid function name
	compiled:             Call to undefined function nosuchfunction()

The emitted `callValue` resolves a callable and, failing, reports the error for
`$f()` rather than the one for a builtin's callback argument. That is a wrong
answer rather than a named gap, which is the case QUALITY_GATE.md rules out, and
it has been there since `array_reduce` moved.

It is also the single prerequisite for three separate things: `array_walk`
moving, `usort` ever becoming userland, and **`is_callable`, which compiled code
refuses outright and which blocks 19 corpus files on its own**. So it is worth
more than its own fix.

Rather than start it at the end of a long session, the engine was asked for the
whole vocabulary, so the next pass is implementation and not discovery: ten
distinct reason strings, each tied to the shape that produces it, recorded in
TODO.md. `["C", "m"]` and `"C::m"` both answer `non-static method C::m() cannot
be called statically`; `[new C, 5]` is `second array member is not a valid
method` while `[null, "m"]` is `first array member is not a valid class name or
object`; a plain object with no `__invoke` is `no array or string given`, the
same as an int.

Tree state: gate green, corpus **1912 / 688 / 1310 / 0**, userland blockers 30.

## 2026-09-12 -- the is_* family is one operation, and two questions answered by asking

**`type_check` is a catalogued intrinsic now.** `is_int`, `is_float`,
`is_string`, `is_array`, `is_object`, `is_null`, `is_bool` and `is_scalar` are
not eight functions: the engine compiles every one to ZEND_TYPE_CHECK with a
type mask, and the mask is the only thing that differs. The lowering already
emitted `type_check`, but the emitter rendered it through a hand-written arm and
the catalogue test *excused* it -- "the operation is the opcode". It has a real
entry now, `intrinsicFor` maps it, and the bespoke arm is gone.

It needed one new argument shape. The mask is an integer the **instruction**
carries, and the catalogue had `lit` (renders a Go string) and `raw` (renders a
place) but nothing for an immediate. `int` parses the operand as a Go integer
literal and refuses a computed one, which is right: the engine folds the mask at
compile time and there is no such thing as a computed one.

`is_numeric` is deliberately **not** in the family -- it asks whether a string
would read as a number, which no type mask can answer -- and that turned out to
matter. The library entries stay for the dynamic call (`$f = 'is_int'; $f($v)`),
the same split `count` has, and they all go through `php.TypeCheck` now so the
mask is the only thing stated twice. Writing the fixture for that path found a
**bug**: `is_numeric` read `FirstArg` without a deref, and a dynamic call hands
the argument over as a reference, so `$f = 'is_numeric'; $f(1)` was false. The
rest of the family never showed it because `php.TypeCheck` derefs inside.

Two questions came up mid-tick and both were settled by asking rather than
arguing.

**Why are `usort` and its siblings not userland?** No good reason, and the
pattern already existed -- `natsort`, `natcasesort` and `array_multisort` are
PHP built on `\PHP2Go\Internal\unstable_sort`. So they were converted, with
that helper generalised to `sort_entries($array, $compare, $by_key, $stable)`
(PHP's user sorts have been stable since 8.0 and the internal ones are not, so
the flag is a difference in the answer, not a mode). The differential suite then
refused it, and the reason is the one `array_flip` hit:

	engine:      refCmp(): ... must be passed by reference, value given in php2go-eval on line 9
	interpreter: refCmp(): ... must be passed by reference, value given in .../standard.php on line 3094

A comparator declared with by-reference parameters earns that warning from the
**engine's own argument binding**, and the engine attributes it to the caller
while a diagnostic raised inside a userland body is attributed to that body.
`array_flip` had `\PHP2Go\Internal\warning` to route around it; this has
nothing, because no PHP code raises it. The three are native again. The
generalised `sort_entries` stayed -- it is a better helper than the one it
replaced. **This is the second conversion the same gap has blocked**, and it now
covers more than explicit warnings: any userland body that invokes a callback
can trip it.

**Would a combined key-value iterator intrinsic be better?** The engine says no,
and says it plainly. Over a user `Iterator`:

	foreach ($it as $k => $v)   ->  rewind valid current key ...
	foreach ($it as $v)         ->  rewind valid current ...

Two separate calls when a key is bound, and `key()` **never called** when it is
not. Our lowering already emits exactly that -- `iter.current` then `iter.key`,
and `iter.current` alone for the value-only loop. A fused intrinsic would have
to carry a "key wanted" flag and still make two method calls in order, so it
gains nothing and can only lose fidelity. For a plain array the engine does
fetch both in one opcode via FE_FETCH's OP_DATA, but nothing user-visible runs
between the two reads there, so the split cannot disagree.

Corpus: **1912 / 688 / 1310 / 0** against 1913 before -- the one file is the
`random_int` coin-flip, so the intrinsic conversion is behaviour-neutral, which
is what it should be.

## 2026-09-12 -- the type predicates, and the sorts that only needed a hook

Third batch, again chosen by `-census -top 0` rather than by eye.

**The type predicates and three named blockers.** `is_int`/`is_float`/
`is_string`/`is_array`/`is_object`/`is_null`/`is_bool`/`is_numeric`,
`get_class`, `max`/`min`, and `explode`, `array_pop`, `strcoll` came out of the
interpreter's own map into `runtime/stdlib/typefns.go`. Unlike `stringlib.go`
and `arraylib.go` these had no file of their own, so they moved one entry at a
time.

That cost two rounds of repair, and the cause is worth writing down because it
has now bitten three times. **Balancing braces from the start of a map entry
does not find its end**: the first `(`...`)` to balance is the *parameter list*
of `func(_ *php.Ctx, args []php.Value)`, so the cut takes one line and leaves
the body orphaned in the source it came from. gofmt guarantees the entry ends
at a line that is exactly `\t},`, and matching that is both simpler and right.
The first attempt left three half-entries in `builtins.go`; they were restored
whole and re-cut.

**The user-comparator sorts needed one thing from the interpreter, and it was
already a hook.** `usort`, `uasort`, `uksort` and
`php2go\internal\unstable_sort` all bottom out in `sortPairs`, whose only
interpreter call is `in.callValue(...)` on the comparator -- which is what
`Ctx.Call` is, the hook `array_reduce` proved. They moved with `zendsort.go`,
which turned out to contain **no `php.` references at all**: it is 282 lines of
pure Go implementing Zend's insertion/quicksort hybrid, and it exists because a
PHP comparator can observe how often and in what order it is asked, so Go's
`sort` package is not a substitute even where the final array agrees. The
interpreter's arms are now the three-line delegation `array_reduce` established:
install the hook, look the builtin up, call it.

Corpus: **1906 -> 1913 passing**, unsupported 1319 -> 1310, errored 0 -- eight
gained against the usual `random_int` coin-flip.

Userland blockers **39 -> 30**, and only **11 are native** now: `array_walk`,
the three `ini_*`, and seven stream functions. Everything else is either a
forward reference inside the library (14) or needs the class table or object
store (5). `shape.tsv`: 48 unreachable, down from 51 at its baseline.

## 2026-09-12 -- the string and array libraries, and what a census with no ceiling says

Continuing the split, this time by measurement rather than by picking. Two
findings before any code moved.

**The census was truncating at 30 rows.** Over a corpus that is a ranking and
the tail does not matter; over the two userland files it hid most of the answer,
because every count is 1 and the cut is alphabetical. `php2gotest -census` takes
`-top` now, mirroring `php2lower`, and `-top 0` prints everything. The real list
was 51 names, not the 26 the truncated view showed.

**14 of those 51 are not blockers at all.** They are functions the userland
library *defines itself* -- `str_pad`, `is_dir`, `stream_socket_client`,
`stream_context_get_options` and the rest -- forward references within one unit
that resolve the moment it is emitted with its aliases. Counting them as
blockers would have sent the next several ticks after work that was already
done. The genuine set was 30 native plus 5 outside `main`/`ext/standard`.

`runtime/interp/stringlib.go` (911 lines) and `arraylib.go` (394) then moved to
`runtime/stdlib` whole. Both were candidates for the same reason `mathlib.go`
was -- stringlib's own doc says "these are all pure functions of their
arguments" -- and the check that matters is the one in both directions:
stringlib reached outside itself for exactly three names, and **nothing outside
it used anything it defined**. Two of the three were already in stdlib
(`FirstArg`, `MapStringBuiltin`); the third, `compare`, turned out to be a local
variable at one call site rather than the package-level function of that name.
A grep for `func compare(` found the wrong one.

`htmlentities.go`, `html_translation_table.go` and its embedded `.bin` went
along, because the `ent*` constants moved with stringlib and the translation
table reads them.

One namer had to change. `arraylib` used the interpreter's `givenTypeName`,
which is `php.ValueName` except that it cuts an anonymous class's name at its
NUL. On paper that is a difference; asked of the engine it is not, because
`array_is_list(new class {})` prints `class@anonymous` either way -- verified
before the swap and pinned as a differential case after, alongside the string,
bool and null arguments that take the other branches.

Corpus, same command: **1894 -> 1906 passing**, unsupported 1336 -> 1319,
errored 0. Thirteen files gained -- `anon_class_name`, `foreach_reference`,
`call_with_refs`, `array_merge_recursive_next_key_overflow`, `gh9775_1/2`,
`gh12457`, `gh19280`, `xor_002` among them -- against one lost, which is the
second of the two known `random_int` coin-flips.

Userland blockers: **50 -> 39**. `runtime/stdlib` is now 15 files and 158
registrations. What is left is characterised rather than guessed: 20 native
(`array_pop`, `array_walk`, `explode`, `is_array`, `is_object`, `min`,
`strcoll`, the `usort` family, the three `ini_*`, and seven stream functions),
5 needing the class table or object store (`debug_backtrace`, `enum_exists`,
`get_object_vars`, `get_resource_type`, `spl_object_id`), and the 14 that are

## 2026-09-12 -- the four stream multiplexers, split

`stream_operation`, `stream_set_option`, `stream_context` and `stream_socket`
were one entry point each, switched on a string naming the operation -- the
shape `shape.tsv` was built to catch the day before. All four are gone:
**15 multiplexers -> 11**, and 20 of the 29 `stream_*` helpers are now reachable
from compiled code where **none** of them was.

The boundary turned out not to need a `Ctx` hook, which is what made this
tractable. `php.Resource.Payload` is `any`, so `runtime/stdlib` can declare an
ordinary Go **interface** -- `Stream`, with `Flush`, `Sync`, `Truncate`, `Stat`,
`SupportsLock`, `IsTTY`, `Lock` and the five setters -- and the interpreter's
`*stream` satisfies it. The library functions get real signatures here, the
3,883 lines of implementation stay where the streams are owned, and moving them
later changes neither the PHP nor these names.

Three things the split surfaced that the multiplexer had hidden:

- **The return types disagreed.** `stream_set_option`'s five operations answer a
  bool, a bool, an errno-ish 0/-1, the same again, and the *previous chunk
  size*. One entry point forced all five through `php.Value` and left the PHP to
  know which it had. `Sync` is the sharpest: it returns 0 committed, 1 cannot,
  2 tried and failed, and only 1 earns `Can't fsync this stream!` -- a
  distinction a bool would have lost.
- **The selector was in a different argument position for one of them.**
  `stream_context('create')` takes no context, so its selector is argument 0
  while every sibling's is argument 1. Invisible while the calls go through one
  name; obvious once they do not.
- **A second layer of the same shape sat in the PHP.** `stream_sync_impl` took
  `'sync'|'data_sync'` and passed it down, and `stream_socket_open_impl` took
  `'server'|'client'`. Both are booleans now -- the two branches take identical
  parameters, so the string only ever said which function to call.

`streamContext` moved **whole** rather than hiding behind an interface: it is an
options array, a callback and a flag, with nothing in it needing a class table
or an open file. Its `options` field was reached into directly by
`socketContextBacklog`; that became `Option("socket", "backlog")`, which is the
accessor the caller wanted anyway.

The four socket operations that **create** a stream -- server, client, accept,
pair -- stay in the interpreter, because building a `*stream` is that package's
business. They are named entries now rather than arms of a switch, and
`shape.tsv` reports them honestly as `reachable=no` instead of burying them
inside one helper that was equally unreachable. That is why the unreachable
total went 47 -> 50 while the multiplexer count fell: four helpers that always
existed are now *visible*.

Missing their registrations was the one mistake, and the bundle caught it:
removing the `stream_socket` stub from `builtins.go` took the name that made the
dispatcher reachable, so `stream_socket_pair()` was undefined at run time.
Four new stubs restored it. `go test ./runtime/...` did not see this --
`internal/bundlebuild` did, because it is the only suite that runs the userland
library end to end.

Corpus, same command: **1894 / 680 / 1336 / 0**, against 1895 before -- the
single file is the known `random_int` coin-flip, so the split cost nothing.

## 2026-09-12 -- a measurement for the shape of a userland conversion

A conversion can be complete and still be wrong, and nothing was counting the
way in which. The streams library is the case: every function has a PHP body,
and the bodies call one helper per *area* with a string naming the operation --

	\PHP2Go\Internal\stream_operation($stream, 'flush')
	\PHP2Go\Internal\stream_context('merge_options', $context, $options)

which is `php_stream_set_option(stream, option, value, ptrparam)` carried across
unchanged. In C the selector is a constant passed to one entry point; in PHP it
should be separate functions. That is not taste: a multiplexed helper has no
signature to type, its Go side is an arm of a switch rather than a function, and
every caller pays for the union of what any caller needs.

`internal/userland/shape.tsv` now measures it, generated and checked in beside
`surface.tsv`, with two numbers per helper:

- **selectors** -- the largest number of distinct string literals in any one
  argument position. 0 means the helper takes data; 2 or more means it takes an
  opcode.
- **reachable** -- whether compiled code can call it at all.

The baseline it establishes: **51 helpers, 15 multiplexers, 50 unreachable from
compiled code.** Only `formatted_print` is reachable. That last number is the
one that matters most, and it was not visible before: *no* userland library that
touches a helper can ever be emitted, however good its PHP is. Worst
multiplexers: `network_database` 8 selectors over 8 calls -- every call a
different operation, so it is a dispatch table with no dispatcher --
`stream_socket` 7, `stream_operation` 6, `directory_operation` 6,
`stream_context` 5 over 13 calls, `stream_set_option` 5.

Calibrating the heuristic took two corrections, both worth keeping:

- `\PHP2Go\Internal\warning` came out top at 39 "selectors" over 83 calls. Its
  argument is the message. A selector is an **identifier** and data is not, so
  only literals matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_-]*$` and at most 32 bytes count. That
  dropped `warning`, `notice` and `deprecated` to 0, which is right.
- The first version of that pattern had no hyphen, and `network_database` --
  the worst multiplexer in the table -- fell to 1 because its selectors are
  spelled `host-by-address`. A false negative on the worst case is how a
  measurement quietly stops measuring.

`TestGeneratedShapeIsCurrent` keeps it honest the way its surface twin does. Two
kinds of diff are the point: a helper's selector count rising above 1, meaning
an operation was added by widening a string switch instead of writing a
function; and a new `reachable=no` row, meaning another userland function just
became impossible to emit.

## 2026-09-12 -- eleven functions moved from Go to PHP, and the harness that was not testing them

Following the correction: the standard library should be PHP under
`internal/userland` wherever it can be. Converted `str_shuffle`, `ucfirst`,
`lcfirst`, `ucwords`, `nl2br`, `quotemeta`, `strrev`, `str_pad`, `array_sum` and
`array_product`, deleting each Go implementation so there is one of each.

Every edge was **asked of the engine first**, and several were not what a
reimplementation would have guessed: `ucfirst` is ASCII-only, so
`ucfirst("\xe9tre")` comes back untouched; `ucwords`' separator argument
*replaces* the default set rather than adding to it, so `"hello world-foo bar"`
leaves `foo` alone; `nl2br` keeps the original bytes **after** the tag and
treats a CRLF pair as one break; `quotemeta` does not escape braces; `str_pad`
with `STR_PAD_BOTH` puts the odd byte on the right, and with an empty pad string
raises a ValueError the previous Go version silently ignored -- a bug the
conversion fixed by accident.

`array_sum` and `array_product` are the argument for the whole direction in
miniature: the body is `$sum += $value`, so the coercions and the diagnostics an
unsupported element earns come from **the language's own operator** instead of
being restated in Go.

**The finding that mattered more than the conversions.** The differential suite
does not install the userland library, so the moment a function's body became
PHP the harness reported `not yet supported: needs call to ucfirst` and skipped
it. That bucket is honest and it is also a silent loss of verification: every
conversion would have traded a Go implementation under test for a PHP one that
is not. `runWithSources` now installs both libraries, harvested once per test
binary behind a `sync.Once` -- `ext/standard.php` is 10k lines through the
engine and per-case harvesting would dominate a suite of 1,108. With that,
**1106/1108 cases match the engine**, and the userland library is under test for
the first time.

That immediately caught the one conversion that was wrong. `array_flip`
**warns**, and `trigger_error` from a PHP body attributes the warning to that
body:

	engine:      ... entry skipped in php2go-eval on line 1
	interpreter: ... entry skipped in /tmp/.../standard.php on line 5216

I first concluded no mechanism existed for raising a diagnostic at the **call
site**, and reverted `array_flip` to Go. That was wrong, and the way it was
wrong is worth recording: the mechanism is `\PHP2Go\Internal\warning`, used
**72 times in `standard.php`**, and the grep that missed it searched for the
lowercase `php2go\internal\` while the source spells it `PHP2Go\Internal\`.
`internalDiagnostic` in `builtins.go` re-attributes to
`libraryCallerLocation`, which is exactly the engine's behaviour. `array_flip`
is userland, with that helper, and the differential case passes.

Throwing needed no helper and was verified separately: the trace shows
`#0 php2go-eval(5): str_pad('ab', 6, '', 0)` -- the public name and the caller's
line.

Corpus, same command: **1894 / 680 / 1336 / 0**, passing unchanged. The exact
cost of moving ten functions out of compiled reach was **one file** --
`generators/send_returns_current.phpt`, now `emit: library function strrev` --
offset by one of the two known `random_int` coin-flips landing the other way.
It comes back when userland linking lands.

Also: two differential cases had to drop their non-UTF-8 literals.
`Literal.string_value` is a proto3 `string` and cannot carry `"\x00\xff"`, the
defect TODO.md has recorded since the start; the non-ASCII `ucfirst` edge is
covered by a `php2eval` probe instead.

## 2026-09-12 -- the library surface has a home now: runtime/stdlib

Course correction, on the user's instruction: **standard functions do not belong
in `runtime/php`**. The five ticks before this had been moving them there from
`runtime/interp` so compiled code could reach them, which fixed the symptom in
the wrong place.

Triaged first, because the stated reason -- "it is already available in
`internal/userland`" -- turned out to hold for less than it looks. Of the 470
first-blocker library refusals in the y6p run, over 99 distinct names:

| where the name lives | names | files |
|---|---:|---:|
| `internal/userland`, body is PHP | 14 | 38 |
| `native`, Go in `runtime/interp` | 53 | 309 |
| neither, outside main+ext/standard | 32 | 137 |

`surfacegen` **errors** if a name is both native and userland, and it passes --
so there is provably zero overlap, and nothing the earlier ticks moved
duplicated a userland function.

The decisive measurement is the next one. **The userland library lowers
completely -- 444 of 444 op_arrays -- and still cannot be emitted**, because its
own PHP bodies call 26 library functions it does not define: `fwrite`,
`ini_get`, `md5`, `explode`, `is_array` and the rest. A standard library that is
mostly PHP still rests on a native core, and `internal/` is unreachable from an
emitted program anyway -- it is its own Go module (`module php2gotest` with a
`replace`), so Go's internal rule forbids the import outright.

So the core needs a home both back-ends can import, and it is now
`runtime/stdlib`. This tick created it and moved everything the earlier ticks
had put in `runtime/php`: the byte strings, the maths, the paths, the process
odds and ends, the scalars, the array operations, the array pointer, the frame
readers, and `print_r`'s registration. Registration still goes through
`php.RegisterBuiltin`, so the **table stays one mechanism in one place** and
this package only supplies entries; a consumer links the surface with a blank
import, which is what the emitted program now carries.

Corpus, same command: **1894 / 684 / 1332 / 0 -- byte-identical to y6p.** A
relocation should move nothing and it moved nothing, which is the only result
that would have justified it.

Three things learned on the way:

- **`surfacegen` reads `RegisterBuiltin` as a string-literal call**, and from
  `runtime/stdlib` the call is spelled `php.RegisterBuiltin`. Matching only the
  bare identifier reported the entire new package as registering nothing. Fixed
  with `isRegisterBuiltin`, which accepts both spellings; `surface.tsv` then
  regenerates byte-identical, which is the proof the move was pure.
- **`mathfns.go` was a lie inherited from `mathlib.go`.** The user asked why
  `basename` was declared there. It was because that interpreter file had always
  held "the maths, the path helpers and the odds and ends that answer about the
  process" -- its own words -- and moving it wholesale carried the grouping
  across under a name that claimed otherwise. Split into `mathfns.go`,
  `pathfns.go` and `processfns.go`; `str_shuffle` went to the strings (it sat
  with the maths only because it needs a random source) and `is_scalar` to the
  scalars.
- **`strlen` is already an intrinsic**, end to end: the engine gives it
  `ZEND_STRLEN`, the lowering emits `call.intrinsic "strlen"`, and the catalogue
  and `php.StrLen` were already there. `count` is deliberately both -- the
  opcode serves `count($x)` and the library entry serves `$f = 'count'; $f($x)`.

## 2026-09-12 -- print_r, on var_dump's one hook

`print_r` was the largest single library blocker left after `fopen` -- 37 corpus
files -- and it needed nothing new. `var_dump` had already settled the boundary
at one question, *what should this object show?*, asked through
`Ctx.SetObjectProperties`; `print_r` asks the same question and formats the
answer differently. So `php.PrintR` sits beside `php.VarDump` in the shared
package and the interpreter's arm became the same three lines `var_dump`'s
already was: install the hook, call the renderer, turn a `__debugInfo` fatal
into the termination that `runtime/php` has no way to express.

**One fact had to come down with it.** `print_r` writes `Suit Enum:string`
where `var_dump` writes `enum(Suit::Hearts)`, so an enum's **backing type** is
observable in this renderer and was not in that one. The interpreter read it off
the class table; the shared package has none. Rather than open a second hole in
the boundary for one string, `Object` gained `EnumBacking`, set at the two
places an enum case is constructed -- `runtime/interp/enum.go` and the emitted
case table. Carrying the fact on the value keeps the boundary at one question.

The old `printR`, `objectKind`, `printRPropertyLabel` and the dumper's `fatal`
field are gone from the interpreter. A move is not finished while the old
implementation is still there: the bridge skips a name the interpreter's own
table already holds, so two renderers of one byte-exact format would have
diverged on whichever consumer was exercised less.

Corpus, same command: **1874 -> 1894 passing**, unsupported 1361 -> 1332,
failed 675 -> 684, errored 0. 22 files started passing. Two stopped, and
neither is a regression: `attributes/deprecated/message_004` and
`class_constants/value_unknown_at_compile_time_001` both call `random_int(1, 2)`
in their own source, and the differential harness runs the engine and the
compiled program as two processes -- so they agree half the time. Six repeats of
each flipped both ways. Recorded in TESTING.md.

Fixture: `print_r_library.php` -- the three enum shapes, the visibility labels
through an inheritance chain, an array cycle, an object cycle, and
`__debugInfo`.

Five ticks of extraction: **1790 -> 1894**, unsupported 1495 -> 1332.

## 2026-09-11 -- a frame now says whether it is an engine function's

The block found in the previous tick, removed. `StackFrame` gained `Internal`,
and `php.CallerStack` drops **trailing** internal frames rather than exactly
one. That is right for both consumers -- the interpreter pushes a frame for
every call including library functions, compiled code pushes none for a builtin
-- and right for the case that makes the loop necessary: a callback invoked by
`array_reduce` sees `array_reduce`'s frame, which is not trailing and must
survive. With that, `func_num_args`, `func_get_args`, `func_get_arg` and
`debug_print_backtrace` moved to `runtime/php/framefns.go`.

Two things about the mark, both learned by getting it wrong:

- **It is self-checking, and has to be.** `Ctx.MarkInternalCall(name)` marks the
  top frame only if that frame's function *is* the name. A frameless ICALL
  pushes no frame at all, so the top one there belongs to the caller, and an
  unguarded mark would flag an ordinary PHP frame as internal.
- **A userland builtin is an engine function whose body is PHP, and its frame is
  a PHP frame.** The mark went in at "everything below here is an engine
  function" -- one branch too early, above `unit.userlandBuiltins`.
  `http_build_query` is one of those: its PHP body reads
  `debug_backtrace(DEBUG_BACKTRACE_IGNORE_ARGS, 2)[1]['class']` to find the
  **caller's scope**, and skipping its own frame shifted that by one, so an
  object's private and protected properties vanished from the query string.
  `TestEmbeddedProjectMatchesEngine` caught it: `public=u` against
  `private=p&protected=r&public=u`. Moved below the branch, where the call is
  known to be answered in Go.

The second one is worth keeping as a rule: **"internal" is a property of the
implementation language, not of the name.** The engine's own
`http_build_query` frame is internal; ours is not, because ours is PHP -- and
the userland body is written to see itself exactly where the engine's would be.

Corpus, same command: **1866 -> 1874 passing**, unsupported 1379 -> 1361,
failed 665 -> 675, errored 0. Zero regressions. Fixture: `frame_library.php`,
which takes a backtrace from inside a callback so the non-trailing internal
frame is under test, not just the trailing one.

Four ticks of extraction: **1790 -> 1874**, unsupported 1495 -> 1361.

## 2026-09-11 -- the array functions moved; the frame readers could not

Third extraction tick. Moved into `runtime/php/arrayfns.go`: `array_fill`,
`array_fill_keys`, `array_slice`, `array_splice`, `array_merge`,
`array_key_exists`, and the sort family `sort`/`rsort`/`ksort`/`krsort`/
`asort`/`arsort` with `sortTarget`, `replaceList`, `reorder` and `sliceBounds`.
`sortTarget` and `replaceList` are exported, because the interpreter's own sorts
-- the ones that call back into user code and so could not move -- still need
them. `phpTypeName` became `php.KindName` the same way.

**`array_key_exists` turned out not to be a library function at all.** The
engine gives it its own opcode, the lowering emitted `array_key_exists` as an IR
instruction, and the emitter had no arm for it -- so every file using it was
`unsupported` for a reason the library histogram never showed, because it is not
a `call.fn`. It is now an operation with one home: `php.ArrayKeyExists`, a
catalogue entry, an `intrinsicFor` mapping. The opcode and the dynamic call
differ and both are right: the call is verified against the engine's arginfo
before it runs, so the opcode has to raise
`array_key_exists(): Argument #2 ($array) must be of type array, %s given`
itself.

**The frame readers were moved and then moved back.** `func_num_args`,
`func_get_args`, `func_get_arg` and `debug_print_backtrace` all read
`callerStack`, which is `ctx.CallStack()` minus one -- because the interpreter
pushes a frame for *every* call, engine functions included, and PHP's backtrace
starts one further out. Compiled code's `callBuiltin` pushes no such frame, so
the same subtraction there drops the **caller's own** frame and reports the
global scope. The compiled probe said it plainly:

	Fatal error: Uncaught Error: func_get_arg() cannot be called from the
	global scope

Shipping it would have replaced an honest `unsupported` with a confident wrong
answer, which is the one thing the measurement rules forbid, so all four went
back. The shared package cannot tell the two shapes apart until a `StackFrame`
says whether it is an internal function's -- recorded in TODO.md. The lesson is
narrower than "be careful": **a helper that compensates for its caller's
convention is not portable, however pure its body looks.** `callerStack` reads
as five lines of arithmetic and is really an assertion about who pushes frames.

Corpus, same command: **1858 -> 1866 passing**, unsupported 1394 -> 1379,
failed 658 -> 665, errored 0. Zero regressions. Fixture: `array_library.php`,
which sorts and splices through a variable because what those rewrite has to be
the caller's own array -- the half a move can silently break.

Three ticks of extraction: **1790 -> 1866**, unsupported 1495 -> 1379.

The second extraction tick. `runtime/interp/mathlib.go` opened with its own

With it went the internal array pointer -- `current`, `pos`, `key`, `next`,

Three things worth keeping:

- **`first` does not deref and `second` does.** They are the interpreter's two
  argument readers, 368 call sites between them, and that asymmetry is
  load-bearing: the first argument of a by-reference library function arrives as
  a Ref and the callee needs the box. Exported as `php.FirstArg`/`php.SecondArg`
  preserving the difference exactly, with the interpreter's names left as
  one-line wrappers so no call site moved.
- **The move broke a generated table, and the table was right to complain.**

  regenerate past: the surface generator reads `RegisterBuiltin("name", ...)`

  `RegisterBuiltin` twin was missing. With `registersBuiltin` added,
  `surface.tsv` regenerates **byte-identical to before the move** -- which is
  the right outcome for a pure relocation, and the proof that it was one.
- One deliberate deviation from verbatim: `str_repeat` now derefs its arguments.

  interpreter's argument verification and not obviously fine on the compiled

## 2026-09-11 -- the compiler's standard library was the gap

Screening the y6i corpus run for the next cluster turned up something larger
