to**, and 239 more on `new of undeclared class ReflectionClass`. The cause is
one number -- `runtime/php` registered **28** library functions against the
interpreter's ~192. The emitter refuses a call to anything outside that
registry, correctly, as a named gap. So the compiler had a standard library of

The head of the histogram, by files blocked: `fopen` 51, `str_repeat` 38,
`print_r` 35, `debug_print_backtrace` 33, `serialize` 31, `ob_start` 29,
`is_callable` 19, `array_map` 19, `range` 18. Full list in TODO.md.

This tick moved the byte-string batch -- `strtoupper`, `strtolower`, `trim`,

Two things it turned on:

- **Five helpers were shared with interpreter files that stay behind**
  (`toUpperASCII`, `toLowerASCII`, `mapString`, `twoStrings`,

`affordable` came across as exported `php.Affordable` with its ceiling: an

## 2026-09-11 -- a folded magic constant is a path arriving by a back door

`__FILE__`, `__DIR__` and `__METHOD__` inside a closure are folded by the Zend
compiler into **string literals**, so by the time the IR exists there is no node
left saying where the text came from. The path baked into them is the one the
engine was handed at harvest time -- absolute -- while every position the
emitted program reports uses `Program.Filename`, the path the program refers to
itself by. `diagName` and the `closureMeta` table already reconciled those two
spellings; a folded literal is the same fact arriving by a different route, and
nothing reconciled it.

The visible symptom was small and misleading: `$e->getFile() === __FILE__` was
**false** in compiled output, and `class_exists` inside an autoloading closure
printed `{closure:/abs/path:3}` where the engine printed the relative spelling.

`emitter.selfPath` now rewrites a string literal that contains the harvest path.
Two things it had to get right:

- `__DIR__` folds to the *directory*, which does not contain the file path, so
  it needs its own substitution. The two are **alternatives, not a sequence** --
  the relative spelling of the file ends with the absolute directory as a
  suffix, so running the directory rule over the output of the file rule
  rewrote the same text twice and produced `../../../..` doubled.
- The key of an **array literal** never passes through `operand()`; it is
  emitted straight from `ParseArrayLiteral`. `[__FILE__ => 'foo']` therefore
  kept the harvest path in its key while the lookup beside it got the
  program's own path, and the value could not be read back. That cost
  `gh11320_2` on the first measurement and was fixed before the second.

Corpus, same command: **1784 -> 1790 passing**, failed 631 -> 625, unsupported
1495 unchanged, errored 0. Six gained, none lost -- `assign_coalesce_006`,
`bug26697`, `constants_006`, `enum/magic-constants`,
`function_arguments/call_with_trailing_comma_basic`,
`magic_const_in_global_scope`. Fixture: `folded_path_constants.php`, which
prints no path at all: it asserts only that the spellings *agree with each
other*, which is exactly what breaks when one route is reconciled and another
is not. Verified to fail with the substitution stubbed out.

## 2026-09-11 -- a closure's name in a trace is three names

`getTraceAsString` and the frames `debug_backtrace` reports name a closure by
its own compiled name, `{closure:FILE:LINE}` -- and prefix it with whatever the
closure carries:

```
#0 php2go-eval(7): Host->{closure:Host::make():2}()     // bound $this
#0 php2go-eval(9): Host::{closure:Host::smake():3}()    // scope, no $this
#0 php2go-eval(11): {closure:php2go-eval:10}()          // neither
```

The engine was asked for all three; none of it was read off a header. php2go
pushed the literal `{closure}` for every closure frame, which is what PHP wrote
before 8.4 -- so the compiled output was byte-correct against an older engine
and wrong against the pinned one.

Both `PushCall` sites for a closure (`invokeClosure`, and the KindObject arm of
`callValue`) now go through an emitted `closureFrameName` helper that takes the
closure's harvested name from its `closureMeta` and picks the prefix from the
receiver, then the scope. Both sites also set `This:`, which they had not.

Corpus, same command: **1777 -> 1784 passing**, failed 638 -> 631, unsupported
1495 unchanged, errored 0. Seven files gained, none lost -- `bug49908`,
`bug75079_2`, `exception_023`, `gh8810_3`, `match/029`, `match/030`,
`return_types/013`. Fixture: `closure_trace_names.php`.

The screening rule found this: after dropping the handle-number and `__destruct`
clusters, `#N ...(N): {closur` was the largest remaining signature at nine
files. Two of the nine still fail on something else.

## 2026-09-11 -- a keyword can be the class of a callable too

	1777 passed / 638 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.5%   (+4 / -4)

Baseline `y6e*` 1773 / 642 / 1495 / 0; this run `y6f*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+4, -0**.

**Picked differently, and that is the point of the tick.** Two measurements in a
row had moved nothing because both areas ended at an object handle number. So
the candidate list was screened first: drop every failing file whose expected
output contains `object(...)#` or whose source defines `__destruct`, and 642
failures become 464 that can reach a pass. Clustering *those* put
`Deprecated: Use of "X" in callables` at five files.

The previous entry on callables handled a keyword in the **method** half
(`["C", "parent::func"]`). This is the other half: the keyword as the **class**,
in both spellings, which the engine deprecates and then resolves:

	call_user_func('self::s')      call_user_func(['self', 's'])
	call_user_func('static::s')    call_user_func(['static', 's'])
	call_user_func('parent::s')    call_user_func(['parent', 's'])

Both spellings funnel through `callStaticCallable`, so the rule lives in one
place. `self` and `parent` come off the calling scope, which `callerScope`
already read off the stack.

### `static` is late static binding, and the frame had to learn it

`Test2::test()` on a `test` declared by Test1 resolves `static` to **Test2** --
the class the *call* named, not the one that declared the running body. A static
method body already takes `lsb` as a parameter, but nothing reachable from a
callable could see it, so `php.StackFrame` gained an `LSB` field that
`callStatic` fills with the class it was asked for.

Not fixed, one file (`lsb_022`): `parent::m()` **forwards** the current LSB
rather than setting it to the named class, so `static` inside a method reached
through `parent::` still means the original call's class. Recorded in TODO.

**Method note, third time.** An edit to `gogen.go` silently did not apply
because the target text had been reformatted by a previous `gofmt -w` -- and
this time there was no assertion, so it failed quietly and the generated file
just lacked the branch. Every patch of emitter text needs an assert, or a line
range; a `replace` with no check is how a change becomes a no-op that still
builds.

## 2026-09-11 -- linking a class loads what its overrides name

	1773 passed / 642 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.4%   (unchanged)

Baseline `y6d*` 1773 / 642 / 1495 / 0; this run `y6e*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+0, -0**. Second measurement in a row with no movement, and
the reason is worth more than the number.

The piece the previous entry recorded as missing. Linking a class
variance-checks each override against what it overrides, and that resolves the
class names in **both** signatures. Probed:

	class Kid extends P { public function m(): R {} public function other(): S {} }
	// P declares m(): Q, and Q is a parent of R
	autoload Kid, autoload P, declared P, autoload R, autoload Q,
	declared Q, declared R, declared Kid

Three facts in that trace, all measured rather than assumed:

- A return type in a declaration does **not** force a load -- `P` was declared
  with `m(): Q` and Q was not loaded then. Only the *check* loads it.
- The **child's** type loads before the parent's. Sorting the names
  alphabetically gave Q before R, which is the same set in the wrong order.
- A method the parent does **not** declare is never checked, so `other(): S`
  leaves S unloaded for good -- `class_exists('S', false)` is false at the end.

### The five files are now correct except for one number

`class_order_autoload1` through `6` produce the engine's autoload order,
declaration order and output, and differ only in `object(B)#2` against
`object(B)#3` -- the handle a temporary's death would have freed. So they have
moved from "wrong about autoloading" to "waiting on the destruction gap", which
is a better place to be and shows as nothing in the count.

The handle-only cluster is now **47 of the 642** remaining failures, measured
the same way as before: same class on both sides, different number.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/conditional_class_autoload.php`, extended with
the variance-linking trace and the negative case.

## 2026-09-11 -- a class declared in a closure was bound before the program ran

	1773 passed / 642 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.4%   (unchanged)

Baseline `y6b*` 1773 / 642 / 1495 / 0; this run `y6d*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+0, -0**. The behaviour is more correct and the corpus does
not show it yet; the reason is at the end.

`allBodiesOf` -- the scan that decides which classes the program declares
**conditionally** -- walked the file body, the named functions and the methods,
and not the **closures**. An autoloader is a closure, so every class declared
inside one was listed as bound before the program ran, and `new B` took the
static path and never called the autoloader at all:

	spl_autoload_register(function ($c) { if ($c === 'B') { class B extends A {} } });
	new B;   // engine: autoload B, autoload A, declared A, declared B
	         // php2go: object(B)#2 -- no autoloader involved

Three things follow from the fix, and the third was a regression the
passing-set diff caught:

- **`new` of a conditional class goes through the run-time lookup** whether or
  not an autoloader exists. Gating that on `e.autoloads` turned three files from
  `failed` into `unsupported` -- a class the program plainly declares is not a
  gap, and the refusal there is for a genuinely undeclared name.
- **A conditional class links at its declaration point**, and linking autoloads:
  `class B extends A` inside the autoloader loads A from inside the load of B.
  `classNeeds` carries the parent and interfaces of conditionally declared
  classes for exactly this.
- **`class_alias`'s third argument is autoload, defaulting to true.** With `foo`
  now conditional, `class_alias('foo', 'bar', 1)` stopped finding it --
  `class_alias_007` was the one file lost on the first measurement, and it is
  the same fact from the other side: the alias has to load what it aliases.

### Why the corpus does not move

The five `class_order_autoload` files need one more thing. The engine links a
class by **checking its method signatures against the parent's**, and that
resolves the types named in them -- so `class B extends A` with
`public function method(): C` loads C as well, from inside the load of B.
php2go loads the parent and the interfaces and stops. Recorded in TODO: the
missing piece is the set of class names in the signatures of methods the parent
also declares.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/conditional_class_autoload.php`.

**Method note.** The fixture first used `var_dump(new B)`, which made it fail on
an object handle number -- the one gap this work is guaranteed to trip over. A
fixture for anything other than object identity should print `get_class()`, not
the object.

## 2026-09-11 -- four modes of a property fetch, and they disagree about nothing

	1773 passed / 642 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.4%   (+7 / -7)

Baseline `y5z*` 1766 / 649 / 1495 / 0; this run `y6b*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+7, -0**.

The dimension split from the previous entry, applied to properties -- and the
four modes turn out to disagree about exactly one thing, an **uninitialized**
property, in four different ways:

	$t->prop->prop = 0     W      Cannot indirectly modify readonly property
	$t->prop->prop += 1    RW     Typed property Test::$prop must not be accessed
	                              before initialization  -- it reads first
	isset($t->prop->prop)  IS     silent, false
	unset($t->prop->prop)  UNSET  done -- nothing there to remove

Each of those took its own round: the fixture was the two `variation_nested`
corpus files run after every change, and each round fixed one line and broke the
next. That is the shape of a rule with four cases being discovered one case at a
time, and it is worth reading as a whole rather than as four fixes:

- **W refuses before reading.** Reading first reported the property as
  uninitialized, which is a true statement about a different question.
- **But only when the property does not already hold an object.** Reaching
  *through* an object does not modify the property -- an object is a handle -- so
  an initialized `readonly Inner $p` allows `$t->p->x = 1` where an initialized
  `readonly array $a` refuses `$t->a[0] = 9`.
- **RW reads out loud**, which is the same fact as `$k->p .= "s"` warning about
  an undefined `$k`.
- **IS answers not-set**, and `propGetMode`'s silent path was refusing -- a
  separate defect the mode split exposed: `$t->prop ?? "d"` was a fatal.
- **UNSET refuses nothing anywhere on the chain**, including a non-object
  container: `unset($t->prop->array[0])` on an uninitialized `$prop` is a no-op,
  not `Attempt to modify property "array" on null`.

One regression, caught by the passing-set diff and fixed before the second
measurement: a **hooked** property has no backing slot, so "the property is
absent" is not "there is nothing there" -- `unset($c->prop['foo'])` on a
`get => $this->collection` property must still reach `offsetUnset`.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/property_fetch_modes.php`, which is the whole
cross -- six operations against an initialized and an uninitialized property.

## 2026-09-11 -- a fetch has three modes, and they are three operations

	1766 passed / 649 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.1%   (+1 / -1)

Baseline `y5x*` 1765 / 650 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5z*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+1, -0**. Small, and the work behind it is the design change
the previous entry said was owed.

A place fetch is not one operation with a mode flag. Measured, the three differ
in what they say and what they leave behind:

	$w["a"]["b"] = 1      W       silent, creates
	$y["k"] .= "s"        RW      Undefined variable $y, then Undefined array key
	                              "k" -- and creates
	unset($m["a"]["b"])   UNSET   Undefined variable $m, and creates **nothing**

So `prop.ref.rw`, `dim.ref.rw` and `dim.ref.unset` are now their own
operations. The mode cannot carry this: `IntrinsicCalls` strips `mode=` once it
has chosen the callee, deliberately, and every pass that needs the distinction
runs after -- `ExplicitReads` for the container's loudness, the emitter for
which opener a nested fetch uses.

Four things had to be got right, and three of them were only visible in the
**order** of output:

- **The container warning is its own instruction.** Emitting it inside the place
  builder, or in the call's argument prelude, put it second: `$a[$b] += 1` warns
  about `$a` and then `$b`, and the key's read is hoisted ahead of the fetch that
  consumes it. So it is `warn.undefined_container`, emitted before the place.
- **The RW fetch autovivifies before the read that follows**, which is what turns
  `Trying to access array offset on null` into `Undefined array key "k"`.
- **A nested RW fetch warns about each missing key on the way in** -- three
  warnings for `$n["a"]["b"] .= "s"`, not one.
- **A nested UNSET fetch creates nothing**, which closes a TODO the autovivifying
  `ref` had kept open. It still runs the fetch's *conversion*, though:
  `$q = false; unset($q[0][0]);` prints the false-to-array deprecation and leaves
  `$q` as `bool(false)`. Missing that cost `falsetoarray.phpt`, caught by the
  passing-set diff on the first measurement and fixed before the second.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/rw_and_unset_dim_fetch.php`, which covers all
three modes at one and two levels, plus the two conversions.

**Method note.** Two edits to `gogen.go` failed their exact-match assertions
because a previous `gofmt -w` had rewritten `\t` escapes inside the emitted
strings into literal tabs. The emitter's own text is not stable enough to patch
by matching it; patch by line range, and check the assertion fired rather than
assuming the write happened.

## 2026-09-11 -- a write fetch reads quietly, and refuses where it stands

	1765 passed / 650 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.1%   (+2 / -2)

Baseline `y5w*` 1763 / 652 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5x*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+2, -0**.

Two facts about a **write** fetch, both from probing every shape of
`$undefined->p... = 1`:

- **It reads its container silently.** `$d->p["x"] = 1` on an undefined `$d`
  warns about nothing; php2go added `Warning: Undefined variable $d`. The
  dimension form was already right, and for an uninteresting reason -- `dim.set`
  takes the place itself, so there is no read to be loud. A property fetch needs
  the container as a *value*, which is where the read came from. `SilentReads`
  on the `prop.ref` variant is the whole fix.
- **It refuses at the fetch that found the non-object**, not the one after it.
  `$ee->p->q = 1` is `Attempt to modify property "p" on null` -- the *outer*
  property, with `modify` -- while `$h["x"]->p = 1` is `Attempt to assign
  property "p" on null`, from the inner one. Two shapes that look alike and
  refuse in different places; a property place read as a container now refuses,
  a dimension one still answers null.

### The mode is spent before the read pass runs, and that is deliberate

`$k->p .= "s"` **does** warn `Undefined variable $k`: the RW form reads the
container before writing it, and that read is the ordinary loud one. So
`prop.ref` wants `SilentReads` for W and not for RW -- which cannot be written
where I first tried it, because `IntrinsicCalls` strips `mode=` once it has
chosen the variant, and `ExplicitReads` runs afterwards. The stripping is
deliberate and documented: *"the access mode is spent: it has just chosen the
callee, and the callee is where it now lives."*

So the honest shape is an **operation split** -- a distinct intrinsic for the RW
place fetch, per the catalogue's own rule that a distinct behaviour is its own
operation rather than a mode flag. Not done here; recorded in TODO with the
one-line probe that shows it.

Measured before keeping the change: W-silence is worth two corpus files and the
RW case costs none, so the net is positive and the remaining gap is one
diagnostic on a shape no corpus file exercises.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/write_fetch_diagnostics.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- a constant's `self::` means where it was written

	1763 passed / 652 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   73.0%   (+2 / -2)

Baseline `y5u*` 1761 / 654 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5w*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+2, -0**.

A class constant's initializer resolves `self::` and `parent::` against the
class that **declared** it, not the one it is read through:

	class P { const N = 'P'; }
	class A extends P { const selfN = self::N; const parentN = parent::N; const N = 'A'; }
	class B extends A { const N = 'B'; }
	B::selfN    // "A", not "B"
	B::parentN  // "P"

The engine flattens inherited constants into every subclass's table, and php2go
copied the *scope* along with them -- so every inherited initializer re-resolved
against the subclass. `ClassConstant.declaring_class` was already harvested and
already carries a comment in `ir.proto` saying exactly this; it just was not
plumbed through `gogen.ClassConst`. It is also the right `owner` for a typed
constant's refusal, which had the same defect.

### A trait's constant belongs to the composing class

The first measurement was **+2 / -2**: `traits/constant_001` and
`enum/traits-constants` broke, because a trait's constant harvests with the
*trait* as its declaring class, and `self::PRIVATE` inside a method of the using
class then failed a visibility check against the trait. The engine copies a
trait's constants into the user, so the user owns them. The harvest is right
about where the constant was written and wrong about who owns it -- two
different questions that `declaring_class` answers with one string.

Fixtures: `class_constant_scope.php`, covering inheritance, an interface
constant reached through an implementor, a typed constant, and the trait case
that the first attempt broke.

## 2026-09-11 -- three verbs again, and a callable that names a keyword

	1761 passed / 654 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   72.9%   (+3 / -3)

Baseline `y5s*` 1758 / 657 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5u*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+3, -0**.

### Reaching a property of a non-object refuses with three verbs

The same shape `private(set)` has, and measured the same way -- every operator
against every non-object kind, which all agree:

	$v->d = 1   $v->d += 1   $v->d .= "x"    Attempt to assign property
	$v->d++     $v->d--                      Attempt to increment/decrement property
	$v->d[] = 1   $r = &$v->d                Attempt to modify property
	$v->d (read)                             the warning, and null

php2go said `assign` for all six. `+=` being an assign and `++` not is the
distinction that costs something: both lower to the same read-step-write triple,
so the store cannot tell them apart from where it stands. `expandIncDec` marks
both halves `op=incdec`.

The read had to be marked too, and finding that out is the useful part. Marking
only the store gave `$v->d--` on a null an extra
`Warning: Decrement on type null has no effect` first -- because the engine
refuses at the **fetch**, before the step runs, and we were refusing at the
write. A `getStep` that checks the receiver up front is what puts the two in the
engine's order.

### `["C", "parent::func"]`

A callable whose method part names `parent::`, `self::` or `static::` is
**deprecated, not refused**, and resolves against the class of element 0 -- so
`[$this, "parent::func"]` reports `["C", "parent::func"]` using the object's
class, and `parent` means the parent of *that* class rather than of the calling
scope. php2go took the whole string as a method name:
`Call to undefined method C::parent::func()`.

Two things it needs that nothing on the callable path carries, both read off the
stack rather than threaded through six call sites:

- **The caller's `$this`**, when element 0 is a class name. `["C",
  "parent::func"]` written inside a method of C calls a non-static parent method
  on that receiver.
- **The calling scope**, for accessibility. `[$this, "parent::func2"]` inside
  `B::func` reaches B's *private* `func2` while the object is a C; passing the
  callable's own class refused it as `Call to private method B::func2() from
  scope C`. The frame carries the declaring class because that is what pushed
  it, so `callerScope` reads it back.

Not done: the two remaining `bug48770` files want the **callable-validation**
TypeError family -- `call_user_func_array(): Argument #1 ($callback) must be a
valid callback, cannot access private method B::func22()` -- raised by the
builtin before the call rather than by the call itself. Four corpus files want
it and each wants a different reason string, so it is a feature rather than a
message fix.

Fixtures: `property_on_non_object.php`, `keyword_callables.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- the name `__call` is given, and who it is given to

	1758 passed / 657 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   72.8%   (+5 / -5)

Baseline `y5q*` 1753 / 662 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5s*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+5, -0**. Found by continuing to read the flat
`Zend/tests` failures file by file -- eight of them are about magic-method
dispatch, and two rules cover them.

**The name keeps the case the program wrote.** `$o->getFoo()` on a class with
`__call` calls it with `"getFoo"`, not `"getfoo"`. PHP method names are
case-insensitive, so `callMethodFrom` folded the name once at the top and passed
the folded form everywhere -- which is right for every lookup and wrong for the
two places the name is *data*: the argument handed to `__call`, and the
diagnostics. The written name now travels and `lower` does the looking up.

**`__call`, not `__callStatic`, when a compatible `$this` is in scope.**
`A::m()` written inside an instance method of `A` is an instance call in
everything but spelling: the engine hands it to `__call` with the receiver.
Only a call with no `$this`, or one whose `$this` is unrelated to the named
class, reaches `__callStatic`. Probed across five positions -- outside, inside
the class, from a subclass, from an unrelated class, from a plain function.

### A -57 regression, and the shape of the mistake

The first measurement of this change was **1696 / 721**, 57 files *worse*. The
cause: folding the name meant rewriting every lookup in the emitted `callMethod`
to use `lower`, and I did it by matching emitter lines exactly -- which caught
two `switch name {` and missed a third, the **per-class method dispatch table**.
Every declared method stopped being found, so `Ext::someMethod()` became
`Call to undefined method`.

Two things made it survive to a full corpus run. The probe that drove the change
only exercised classes whose methods do *not* exist -- that is what `__call` is
for -- so the dispatch table was never consulted. And the fixture built from it
inherited the same blind spot.

The lesson is about the edit, not the feature: **a rename that must reach every
use is not a find-and-replace over emitter text.** Three lines emitted the same
`switch name {` at three depths and two survived the replace. A count of
substitutions was printed and read as success at 6 without asking what the
expected number was.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/magic_call_dispatch.php` -- and it now calls a
**declared** method too, which is the case the original probe lacked.

## 2026-09-11 -- calling with too few arguments was not an error at all

	1753 passed / 662 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   72.6%   (+11 / -11)

Baseline `y5p*` 1742 / 673 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5q*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+11, -0**.

Found by reading the flat `Zend/tests` failures file by file rather than
ranking them -- `001.phpt` and `003.phpt`, the first two files in the corpus,
both want `Too few arguments to function test2(), 0 passed ...` and printed
nothing at all.

There are **two** messages for a missing argument, and which one applies depends
on how it went missing:

	f(b: 2)   a named call leaving a hole   f(): Argument #1 ($a) not passed
	f()       a short positional call       Too few arguments to function f(),
	                                        0 passed in t.php on line 3 and
	                                        exactly 1 expected

Only the first was implemented, and the guard it was written with --
`else if pos < len(args)` -- meant a call with **no** arguments took neither
branch: the parameter bound null and the program carried on. The emitter's own
comment said so ("too few *positional* arguments still bind null, which is the
older gap this does not close"), which is how a known gap survives: it is
recorded where only someone already looking at it will read it.

Two details of the message, measured:

- `exactly N expected` when every non-variadic parameter is required, `at least
  N` when any has a default -- and a **variadic does not make it `at least`**:
  `function b($x, ...$r)` reports `exactly 1 expected`. The variadic count comes
  off the body (`recv.variadic`), since `Function.Params` carries the type and
  the by-ref flag and not this.
- The position is the **call site**, which is the top stack frame -- the same
  frame `CoerceArgument` reads for its `called in` clause, because a callee's
  frame records the line that drove the call.

### A closure's name carries the harvest's absolute path

The fix surfaced it: `{closure:FILE:LINE}` inside a diagnostic used the path the
engine was handed at compile time, where the rest of the program uses the path
it refers to itself by. `closureMeta` already substituted one for the other for
`var_dump`; `diagName` did not, so the two disagreed. Now both read one
`srcAbs`/`srcRel` pair on the emitter.

That substitution took three attempts for a reason worth recording: the two
`&emitter{...}` literals -- the census one and `Emit`'s -- are **identical
text**, so a blind single replace patched the census path and left the emitter
untouched. The generated file kept the absolute path and nothing looked wrong in
the diff.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/too_few_arguments.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- an enum case is a singleton, and 45 files wait on a dead handle

	1742 passed / 673 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   72.1%   (+2 / -2)

Baseline `y5n*` 1740 / 675 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5p*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+2, -0**. On the `enum` subset (139 files): passed 57 -> 59,
failed 7 -> 5.

Two consequences of one fact, in places with nothing else in common.

**Cloning a case is refused.** `clone Foo::Bar` is `Trying to clone an
uncloneable object of class Foo` -- a case is a singleton, so there cannot be a
second of it. It is the only member of the uncloneable set that is a
user-declared class rather than an engine one.

**Two cases are uncomparable, not ordered.** They are the same class with
different `name` properties, so the ordinary object comparison ordered them --
`Foo::Bar < Foo::Baz` because "Bar" < "Baz". The engine answers false to all
four relational operators. 1 in **both** directions is what "uncomparable" is:
`>` is `is_smaller(b, a)` and `>=` is `is_smaller_or_equal(b, a)`, so a compare
that answers 1 whichever way round it is asked makes every operator false.

The second half took two attempts, and the miss is the interesting part. Putting
the rule in `compareObjects` fixed case-versus-case and did nothing for
`Foo::Bar >= true`, because `compareAt` answers a **boolish** operand before it
ever looks at objects -- and for a plain object that is right: `$c >= true` is
`true == true`, so `>=` and `<=` are both true. An enum case differs there too,
which only showed up because the corpus test compares against `true` after
comparing against another case.

### The handle-number cluster is 45 files, and the mechanism is now known

Measured on this run's failure side: **45 of the 673** have a first difference
of the form `object(X)#N` versus `object(X)#M` -- same class, different handle.
A probe settles what it is, and it is not an off-by-one:

	function f() { return new stdClass; }
	var_dump(f());   engine #1, php2go #1
	var_dump(f());   engine #1, php2go #2
	$x = new stdClass; var_dump($x);   engine #1, php2go #3

The engine **reuses the handle of a temporary that died**. php2go frees nothing,
so it counts up forever. So this is not a numbering bug to be fixed on its own:
it is the destruction gap seen from another angle, and the narrowest decidable
slice of it -- an object created in a function, consumed by one by-value call,
never stored -- is exactly the escape analysis the plan's Phase D3 describes.

Also measured, for whoever picks up the long tail: of 673 failures, 151 print
**nothing** where the engine prints something and 54 print something where it
prints nothing. Both sets are long-tailed -- the largest single `want` shape
among the 151 is `int(N)` at 17 -- so neither is a cluster.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/enum_identity.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- a leading backslash is not part of a class name

	1740 passed / 675 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   72.1%   (+10 / -10)

Baseline `y5m*` 1730 / 685 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5n*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+10, -0**. Six of the ten are outside `varSyntax`, where the
three defects were found -- the same spread-thin pattern the previous entry
noted for a rendering defect.

Three defects, all from reading the `varSyntax` failures file by file.

### `'\A'` and `'A'` are the same class

A fully-qualified class name written as a string carries a leading backslash and
the engine strips it. php2go put it in the tables verbatim, so
`$n = '\A'; $n::$b` was `Access to undeclared static property \A::$b`. The
strip goes in **two** places, and finding only one would have left half the
paths wrong: `resolveAlias`, which every name-taking path in the generated unit
goes through -- `realClass`, `classConst`, `knownClass`, and so
`class_exists('\A')` -- and `php.ClassNameOf`, which is where a *value* naming
a class becomes a name.

### A class expression that is not an object or a string is refused

	$n = 1; $n::$b    Error: Class name must be a valid object or a string

Not `Access to undeclared static property 1::$b`, which is a different error
about a different thing. `fetch_class` became fallible for it -- it is a
standalone instruction, which is what made this a two-line change rather than
threading an error through `classRef`'s expression result.

### `->` on an array is not `[]`

	isset(["a" => "b"]->a)    bool(false)

Both forms lower to the same two-operand `isset`, and the emitter answered from
the container's **shape**: an array container plus a string key looked exactly
like an array offset, so it found the key and said true. Only the opcode knows
-- `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_PROP_OBJ` versus `_DIM_OBJ` -- so the lowering now marks
the property form `on=prop` and `existsIn` splits on it. The property half moved
out into `existsProp`, which the `[]` path still falls through to when the
object is not an ArrayAccess.

That also closes the TODO note sitting in `existsIn`'s own comment: an
ArrayAccess object answered `isset($o->p)` through `offsetExists`.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/dynamic_class_names.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- one opcode operand carrying two facts about a `?->` chain

	1730 passed / 685 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   71.6%   (+5 / -5)

Baseline `y5l*` 1725 / 690 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5m*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+5, -0**. On the `nullsafe_operator` subset (42 files):
passed 20 -> 24, failed 8 -> 4.

`ZEND_JMP_NULL` lowered to a branch and nothing else, which got two things
wrong at once:

- **The short circuit writes the chain's result**, and php2go never did, so the
  result temp was undefined on the null path. `isset($b?->bar)` printed `NULL`
  where the engine says `bool(false)`.
- **The guard read its operand loudly.** `$a?->p` on an undefined `$a` does warn
  -- but `$a?->p ?? "d"`, `isset($a?->p)` and `empty($a?->p)` do not, and all
  three got a warning the engine never emits.

Both answers are in `extended_value`, and reading it off the engine was much
quicker than deducing it. Four probes, one per form:

	$a?->p            0    null,  loud
	$a?->p ?? "x"     4    null,  silent
	isset($a?->p)     5    false, silent
	empty($a?->p)     6    true,  silent

So the low two bits are the **chain kind** -- expression, isset, empty -- and
bit 2 is set exactly when the chain is read silently. A first attempt scanned
the oplines being jumped over for an `_IS` fetch to decide the silence half;
the operand says it directly, and the scan would have been wrong for any form
not in the probe.

Writing the short-circuit result **before** the branch rather than on the taken
edge is the same thing and needs no extra block: the value path always
overwrites it.

The `silent` attribute is new on an instruction: `silentReads` used to ask only
the *variant*, and silence here is a property of the **chain**, not of `is_set`.

### `on false`, not `on bool`

	Call to a member function bar() on false
	Attempt to read property "p" on false

Both used `TypeName`, which says `bool`. The engine names a bool **by value** in
these two as it does in the three type-declaration messages -- asked again here
rather than carried over, since agreeing was not a given.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/nullsafe_short_circuit.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- two renderings only an uncaught throwable shows

	1725 passed / 690 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   71.4%   (+13 / -13)

Baseline `y5k*` 1712 / 703 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5l*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+13, -0**, from two changes of a few lines each. On the
`object_types` subset (11 files): passed 3 -> 6, failed 3 -> 0.

Both were invisible to every probe written so far, because both only appear in
the **uncaught** block -- `getMessage()` shows neither, and the differential
cases all caught their throwables.

### `and defined in`, not `in`

	a(): Argument #1 ($obj) must be of type object, int given,
	called in t.php on line 7 and defined in t.php:4

A userland argument TypeError's message already names the *call site*, so the
position appended after it -- where the function was **declared** -- is joined
with `and defined in`. A return-type TypeError, an internal function's argument
error and every ordinary throw carry no call-site clause and take the plain
` in`. The message is what decides, which is also how the engine decides it.

### An anonymous class's method keeps its `::a`

A diagnostic reaches this package with the function already joined:
`Two@anonymous\0FILE:11$1::a`. `DisplayName` cuts at the NUL, which is right
for a *class* and drops the `::a` for a **function** -- and the engine keeps it,
because it never joins the two: it interpolates the class (cut at its NUL) and
the method separately. `DisplayFunction` puts the halves back together, for
`->` as well as `::` since a trace frame names an instance method with the
arrow. Used in the argument and return diagnostics and in the backtrace
renderer.

The two compose: `Two@anonymous::a(): Return value must be of type object, int
returned` had *both* defects at once, which is why the `object_types` files
needed both fixes to move.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/uncaught_argument_type_error.php`, which ends
with a deliberate uncaught fatal -- the only way to see either rendering.

**Method note.** Six of the thirteen files are outside the families these two
were found in (`bug39003`, `ns_071`, `variadic/typehint_error`, ...): a
diagnostic *rendering* defect is spread thin across the whole corpus rather than
clustered, so it will not show up in a per-directory ranking. It surfaced only
because the `object_types` cluster was small enough to read file by file.

## 2026-09-11 -- a reference bound to a typed property is itself typed

	1712 passed / 703 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   70.9%   (+5 / -5)

Baseline `y5i*` 1707 / 708 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5k*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+6, -1** -- and the one lost is worth reading, below. On the
`type_declarations` + `union_types` subset (460 files): passed 131 -> 136.

`php.Ref.sources` and `AddSource`/`ConsumeReinit`/`DropSource` were already in
`runtime/php` for the interpreter. The compiler registered **nothing**, so a
reference bound to a typed property was an untyped box and a write through it
left whatever it liked in the property: `$r = &$t->i` on `public int $i` then
`$r = "21"` stored the *string*.

Four places had to learn about it, and they are four different operations:

- **`refBox`** registers the source when the place is a typed property -- which
  is where `&$t->i`, a by-reference argument and `$o->a[] =` all arrive.
- **`StoreVar`** -- `write_var` -- became fallible. Its catalogue variant is now
  `Ctx: true, Ret: "errno", Args: {"ptr", "", "strict"}`: `errno` rather than
  `err` because the operation has no result, only a refusal. `Effects` moved
  from `Pure` to `Throws` with it.
- **`propSet`**, for the box reached through *another* property:
  `$a->_ = &$a->foo` leaves the untyped `$a->_` sharing foo's box, and
  `$a->_ .= "e50"` is a TypeError naming foo. It reads the slot with
  `Props.Raw`, not `Get` -- Get derefs, and the box is the whole question.
- **Static properties**, which needed a new `staticTypes` table: a static slot
  is a bare `*php.Value` with nothing on it saying what declared it, so `place`
  gained `sclass`/`sname` for `staticPlace` to fill in.

And the constraint has to be able to **leave** a box again, which is two more
operations: rebinding (`Test::$x =& Test2::$y` frees the box a name still
holding Test::$x's former storage) and `unset($this->prop)` (after which the box
is no longer that property's storage). Both are `DropSource`.

One widening in `declaredClassRejects`: the `?` prefix used to exempt the whole
declaration, one step too conservative. `?Type` admits *null*, not an array, and
`$ref = [1]` through a reference held by `public ?Type $prop` is a TypeError
with nothing about the value in doubt.

### The lost file is a gap that was masquerading

`typed_properties_094.phpt` passed before and fails now. It does

	$r =& $b->prop;   // public int $prop
	unset($b);        // the object is freed, so its sources go with it
	$r = "foo";       // ok

and it passed only because the constraint did not exist at all. php2go frees no
objects, so the source outlives the object and the write is refused. That is the
destruction gap showing through, not a regression in this work -- and it is the
honest state to be in: one file that used to be accidentally right is now
visibly blocked on something named in TODO.

Not fixed, same family: `++`/`--` through a typed reference past the type's
limit is `Cannot increment a reference held by property C::$p of type int past
its maximal value`, which wants the same place-level step operation the
non-reference case does.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/typed_references.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- the implicit parent accessor is an internal function

	1707 passed / 708 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   70.7%   (+10 / -10)

Baseline `y5h*` 1697 / 718 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5i*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+10, -0**, every one of them in `property_hooks`. On that
subset (199 files): passed 86 -> 96, failed 17 -> 7.

`parent::$p::get()` and `::set()` reach the parent's hook when it has one --
that half already worked -- and otherwise PHP's **implicit accessor** for a
plain or backed property. php2go modelled the second as "read or write the
backing slot and answer null", which is wrong in five ways, and the reason is
one fact:

> The implicit accessor is an **internal function**, where a real parent hook is
> a user function.

So `parent::$backed::get(42)` is `A::$backed::get() expects exactly 0 arguments,
1 given` while `parent::$virtual::get(42)` -- a genuine hook -- takes the extra
argument happily. `parent_superfluous_args.phpt` puts both in one file and says
so in a comment.

Four more, all measured:

	parent::$p::set($v)   returns the value it stored, not null -- which is what
	                      makes var_dump(parent::$p::set($value)) print int(42)
	no parent             Cannot use "parent" when current class scope has no parent
	not declared there    Undefined property Q::$p      -- the **immediate parent**
	private in the parent Cannot access private property A::$prop -- the **declarer**
	uninitialized typed   Typed property C::$prop must not be accessed before
	                      initialization -- the **child**, when it redeclares it

Three different classes name the property across three refusals, and each had to
be asked separately. The declaration is looked up in `classFields[parent]` rather
than on the object, because a private parent property lives in its own slot and
the object's own `Declared` entry is the child's redeclaration.

### A set hook is not a way around private(set)

`public private(set) string $prop1 { set => $value; }` written from global scope
ran the hook: the asymmetric check sat on the backing-store path, below the hook
branch. It belongs above it -- the hook is what happens once the write is
allowed. A write from inside the hook carries the declaring class as its scope,
so it still reaches the store.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/parent_property_hook.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- readonly is unlocked by __clone, and a bind is a modification

	1697 passed / 718 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   70.3%   (+5 / -5)

Baseline `y5g*` 1692 / 723 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5h*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+5, -0**. On the `readonly_props` subset (40 files): passed
10 -> 14, failed 15 -> 11.

Clustering the failures with the destructor-blocked files removed -- 647 of the
723 -- put `property_hooks` at 17 and `readonly_props` at 15, both untouched.

### __clone may write a readonly property once

PHP 8.3's amendment, and `php.Object.Reinitable` with `AllowReinit` /
`ConsumeReinit` / `EndReinit` was already there for the interpreter. The
compiler never granted the permission, so `__clone` reinitializing a readonly
property was an uncaught `Cannot modify readonly property`. Three parts of the
rule were measured rather than assumed:

- **The scope test is the `protected(set)` one**, not the declaring-class one a
  readonly *initialisation* uses. A subclass's `__clone` may reinitialize a
  property its parent declared; a foreign scope reached from inside the hook is
  refused with `Cannot modify protected(set) readonly property A::$p from global
  scope` rather than the plain readonly message.
- **The permission is per object.** Another instance of the same class,
  constructed inside `__clone`, is refused normally.
- **`unset` reads the permission without spending it.** Unsetting and then
  writing both work in the same hook, and so does unsetting twice -- so the
  unset path consults `Reinitable` where the write path consumes it.

Indirect modification stays refused throughout: `$this->a[] = 2` inside
`__clone` is still `Cannot indirectly modify readonly property`.

### Binding a reference **to** a property is an indirect modification

`$this->bar = &$b` reaches the property through `bindPlace`, which is a
different path from the place-ref the write and append forms use -- and it asked
neither the readonly question nor the asymmetric one. So a constructor could
bind a reference straight into a readonly property with no diagnostic at all,
where the engine says `Cannot indirectly modify readonly property Foo::$bar`;
the same for `private(set)`, which names its own modifier. Both checks added in
the place-ref path's own order.

### Measured but not fixed

`unset($this->a[0])` on an **uninitialized** readonly array property is allowed
-- there is nothing to modify -- while `$this->a[0] = 9` on the same
uninitialized property refuses. Same place, two answers, and the operation
decides again. The IR already carries `mode=UNSET` on the `prop.ref`
instruction; `propPlace`'s catalogue variant does not take it, so the emitter
cannot see it. Folded into the existing TODO item about carrying the mode into
the place, which the nested-`unset` autovivification case needs for the same
reason.

Several `readonly_props` tests now differ **only** in object handle numbers
(`#2` where the engine says `#3`), which is downstream of the destruction gap:
PHP reuses the handle of a temporary that died.

Fixtures: `readonly_reinit_on_clone.php`, `bind_reference_to_property.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- a catch body is outside its region, but not outside its finally

	1692 passed / 723 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   70.1%   (+2 / -2)

Baseline `y5f*` 1690 / 725 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5g*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+2, -0**. On the try/finally subset (74 files): passed
28 -> 30.

A probe over eight finally shapes -- return in finally, break and continue
through one, a finally that throws over a pending exception, a nested inner
finally, return in try with a returning finally -- found exactly **one** wrong:

	function a() {
	    try { throw new Exception("t"); }
	    catch (Exception $e) { throw $e; }
	    finally { return "R"; }
	}

The engine runs the finally, and its `return` discards the exception in flight,
so `a()` is `"R"`. php2go let the exception leave the function without running
the finally at all.

The cause is in `regionOf`, which maps an opline to its try region over
`[try_op, catch_op)` -- the try body only. A catch body is deliberately *not* in
the region it belongs to, and it has to stay that way: `catch (E) { throw; }`
must not re-enter its own clause. But the region's **finally** still covers it,
and nothing in the block model could say "this block's catch cannot help it, its
finally can": `Region` is the enclosing try, which for a catch body is the outer
one or none.

`Block.InCatchBodyOf` says it, stored as region+1 so the zero value means none
-- a plain -1 default would have had to be written at every Block literal in the
lowering, and missing one would silently make block 0 a catch body.
`handlerForBlock` then takes the region's finally directly instead of walking,
because `handlerFor` prefers a catch over a finally within a region and would
have sent the throw back where it came from. By the time the emitter runs,
`Regions[r].Finally` already names the **unwind copy** -- `unwindPaths` rewrote
it -- which is the copy that runs with an exception in flight.

Second, smaller: an exception raised inside that unwind copy by a **called
function** did not chain the interrupted one. The literal `throw` terminator
already chained (`blk.Unwind` -> `ChainInFlight`); `onError` did not, so
`finally { throw_exception("finally"); }` produced an exception whose
`getPrevious()` was empty where the engine gives the whole chain. The emitter
now carries `blk.Unwind` as per-block state so both paths chain.

The rest of the `tests/try` failures are destructor-bound -- `__destruct` that
throws, from a foreach over an object -- and wait on the gap recorded in the
previous entry.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/finally_over_a_catch_body.php`.

## 2026-09-11 -- a generator's refusals, and the destructors that never run

	1690 passed / 725 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   70.0%   (+9 / -9)

Baseline `y5e*` 1681 / 734 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5f*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+9, -0**. On the generators-and-fibers subset alone (259
files): failed 54 -> 47, passed 69 -> 76.

### getReturn() primes

`function g() { return 42; yield 24; }` has returned by the time it first
suspends -- which is never -- so `g()->getReturn()` is `int(42)` on an untouched
generator. The engine calls this auto-priming. `GetReturn` took no ctx and so
could not prime, and answered `Cannot get return value of a generator that
hasn't returned` for four corpus files. Priming is not advancing: a generator
already parked at a yield stays there and is still refused.

### Five refusals a Generator makes, and none of them were guessable

	clone $gen              Error: Trying to clone an uncloneable object of class Generator
	$gen->prop = 1          Error: Cannot create dynamic property Generator::$prop
	foreach over finished   Exception: Cannot traverse an already closed generator
	$gen->rewind() ditto    Exception: Cannot rewind a generator that was already run
	resume while running    Error: Cannot resume an already running generator
	yield from $itself      Error: Impossible to yield from the Generator being currently run

Three notes, each of which had to be asked rather than reasoned:

- **The class of "already running" is `Error`**, where its two neighbours in the
  same sentinel table are `Exception`. We had it as Exception, in line with them.
- **Traverse and rewind are different refusals for the same state.** Opening a
  `foreach` over a finished generator and calling `rewind()` on that same object
  give different messages; the *operation* picks it, not the state. The foreach
  path answered an empty loop.
- **Cloning and dynamic properties are two different tables.** Closure and
  WeakMap clone fine but seal; every Throwable refuses to clone -- user
  subclasses included, and the message names the instance's own class -- while
  Exception seals nothing. One table would have been wrong four ways.

`yield from` the running generator was not a wrong answer but a **stack
overflow**: the delegate resumed the generator delegating to it, forever. The
guard walks the delegation chain rather than comparing identity, because `A`
yielding from `B` while `B` yields from `A` is the same cycle one hop out.

### The compiled output runs no destructors at all

Found while probing the `gh9750-*` cluster (8 files, identical shape). It is not
that abandoned-generator teardown is imprecise -- `__destruct` **never runs**,
for any object, in any position, including at script end:

	$a = new C(1); $a = null;      engine: destruct, then "after a"
	$b = new C(2); unset($b);      engine: destruct, then "after b"
	function f() { $c = new C(3); }  engine: destruct at the return
	$d = new C(4); /* end */       engine: destruct at shutdown

php2go printed the four echoes and nothing else. `grep -n __destruct
internal/gogen/gogen.go` returns nothing: the emitter has no destructor call in
it. **76 of the 725 remaining failures are in files that define `__destruct`**,
which makes this the largest single identified cluster left, and it is the gap
the plan names as the compiler's to close (static liveness for the non-escaping
majority, refcounts only for what escapes).

The TODO items about destruction timing all describe *refining* the
interpreter's reachability walk, which reads as though the compiler had a coarse
version of the same thing. It does not have one. Recorded as its own item.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/generator_refusals.php` -- every refusal above
with its class, the two engine-class tables, a Throwable subclass, and the three
getReturn priming shapes.

## 2026-09-11 -- a union type was not applied at all, and `(set)` refuses three things

	1681 passed / 734 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   69.6%   (+8 / -8)

Baseline `y5c*` 1673 / 742 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5e*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+8, -0**. (`y5d*` is the intermediate measurement after the
type work alone: 1677 / 738 / 1495 / 0, +4.)

Clustering the failure side by directory rather than by message -- the messages
are truncated in `-v` output and cluster badly -- put `type_declarations` at 79
files and `asymmetric_visibility` at 13. Both turned out to be one rule missing
in several positions.

### A scalar union type was silently not applied

`ParseDeclaredType` answers false for anything it cannot coerce, and every
caller reads that as "no type here". A union is uncoercible by that test, so
`public int|string $a` accepted **null, an array, anything at all** -- no
coercion, no refusal. The same for a union parameter and a union return.

The rule, measured across six unions and nine values:

1. A value whose type is already one of the alternatives is kept **unconverted**:
   `int|float` given `1.0` stays `float(1)`, where the preference order would
   have made it `int(1)`.
2. A **numeric string** prefers its own numeric type when the union offers it:
   `int|float` given `"5.5"` is `float(5.5)`. Where it does not -- `bool|int`
   given `"5.5"` -- the ordinary order applies, and the precision deprecation
   with it.
3. Otherwise the first of **int, float, string, bool** that the union contains
   and that accepts the value wins. Read off the engine: `string|float` given
   `7` is `float(7)` so float outranks string; `bool|int` given `"x"` is
   `bool(true)` so bool is last.

The message renders the union in the engine's own canonical order --
`int|string` reports `of type string|int` -- and that came out right for free,
because the harvested declaration string is the engine's.

Two more in the same family:

- A **class-typed property** accepted any object. `declaredClassRejects` already
  existed for parameters and returns; `CoerceProperty` did not ask it. The same
  one-sided check, the same wording rule.
- A float that is **not an int64's worth of value** was wrapped rather than
  refused: `$d->i = 1e20` on `public int $i` stored
  `int(-9223372036854775808)`. The engine says `Cannot assign float to property
  D::$i of type int` for `1e20`, `-1e20`, `NAN` and `INF` alike. This is a
  refusal, not a lossy conversion, and it belongs in `coerceInt` where the
  argument and return paths get it too.

### `private(set)` refuses three operations, with three verbs

PHP 8.4's asymmetric visibility was checked on the direct write only. The engine
picks the verb by **how the property is reached**, not by what is done to it:

	$o->p = 1   $o->p++   $o->p += 1        Cannot modify
	unset($o->p)                            Cannot unset
	$o->a[] = 1   $o->a[$k] = 1   &$o->p    Cannot indirectly modify

The third is why this is a shared check rather than a line inside the setter:
reaching a place is a different operation from storing through it, and the IR
already keeps them apart -- `prop.ref` feeding `dim.append` or `bind_ref` is the
indirect form, `place.get`/`store` is the direct one. So the check goes at the
**consumers**, and the verb falls out of which consumer asked.
`CheckPropertyAsymmetric` is that rule, called from the setter, the unset
intrinsic and the generated unit's place-ref.

Not done, recorded in TODO: `++`/`--` on a typed **int** property that overflows
is `Cannot increment property C::$i of type int past its maximal value`, not the
assignment refusal the coercion now gives -- the increment needs to be an
operation over the place rather than get/step/store. And a reference bound to a
typed property carries the property's type in the engine
(`Cannot assign string to reference held by property T::$z of type int`);
`php.Ref.sources` exists and the interpreter registers sources, but the compiler
never does.

Fixtures: `typed_property_unions.php` (six unions x nine values, plus the same
rule through a parameter and a return, class-typed properties, and the
out-of-range floats) and `asymmetric_visibility_operations.php` (all three verbs
from outside, from the declaring class, and from a subclass for both `private`
and `protected`).

## 2026-09-11 -- a string offset's key follows four rules, and we had one

	1673 passed / 742 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   69.3%   (+10 / -10)

Baseline `y5b*` 1663 / 752 / 1495 / 0; this run `y5c*`, same corpus and command.
Passing-set diff: **+10, -0**.

The cluster was three files stuck on `Cannot access offset of type string on
string`. Probing every key kind against a string subject showed the engine using
**four different rules** for the same syntax, depending on what the offset is
being read *for*:

**The loud read** (`$s[$k]`) distinguishes three kinds of string key:

	$s["1"] $s[" 1"] $s["1 "] $s["-1"] $s["+1"]   silent, used
	$s["1x"] $s["0x1"] $s["1_0"]   Illegal string offset "1x", then the prefix
	$s["1.5"] $s["1e0"] $s["1.5x"] $s["x"] $s[""] $s[" "]   TypeError

A *float-shaped* string is refused outright where a float **value** is merely
cast with a warning, and a leading-integer string warns and is truncated where
`IsNumericString` would have called it not-numeric and thrown. We asked
`IsNumericString` alone, which is exactly the two cases the engine treats
specially -- and got both of them backwards.

**The silent read** `??` uses is not the loud one with diagnostics suppressed. A
string key that names no offset is *not set*: `$s["x"] ?? "d"` and
`$s["1.5"] ?? "d"` are both `"d"` with no TypeError, while `$s[[1]] ?? "d"`
still throws -- so the refusal survives for an array or an object key and
becomes a miss for a string one. And `$s["1x"] ?? "d"` **warns** and yields the
character: the diagnostic is not suppressed either.

**isset** is a fourth rule again. `isset($s["1x"])` is plain `false` where the
`??` on the same expression warns and answers `"e"`; `isset($s[1.5])` emits the
array key's `Implicit conversion from float 1.5 to int loses precision`
deprecation, not the read's `String offset cast occurred` warning; and an array
or object key is `false` rather than a throw. The generated `existsIn` read its
key with `key.Int()`, which answered 0 for every one of those, so
`isset("hello"[$obj])` was `true`.

So `??` and `isset` are not the same question asked twice, and the tree already
had the shape for that -- `isset` goes through `existsIn` while `??` goes through
`ReadDimSilent`. Both needed fixing, in different directions.

`stringOffset` now returns a *usable* bool alongside the index, which is what
lets the silent mode turn a string-key refusal into a miss without turning the
array-key one into a miss too. `StringOffsetIndex` is isset's rule, exported
because the generated unit needs it; it is excluded from the intrinsic
catalogue as a shared conversion rather than a second home for `isset`.

Fixture: `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/string_offset_keys.php`, 22 key shapes across
all four modes, expected output from the engine.

**Method note.** Three waves of the corpus ran to completion against *nothing*:
`php2gotest` has no `@file` argument form, so `-v @.../q00` named a missing path
and the tool printed `files 0` inside a full, well-formed summary block. The
per-chunk `files` check that the seg README already prescribes catches this in
one line -- it was run after the third wave instead of the first. Recorded there
and in TESTING.md.

## 2026-09-11 -- two rules about class constants, and one wrong fix in between

	1663 passed / 752 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.9%   (unchanged)

The same cross -- asking scope against member kind -- applied to **class
constants and static methods**. No corpus movement; two correctness fixes, and
the second only exists because the first was wrong in an interesting way.

**A private class constant is not inherited.** `static::PRIV` inside the
declaring class, with `static` resolving to a subclass, answered the parent's
value where the engine says `Undefined constant E::PRIV`. The lookup walked up
the hierarchy, found the private constant on the ancestor, and the visibility
check then passed because the *caller* was that ancestor. The name is not there
at all; it is not there-and-unreachable, and the difference is the message.

**Then the fix broke `static::PROT` in the same position.** A method of the
declaring class writing `static::PROT`, with `static` a subclass, is reading its
own constant through the child's name -- and the check asked only whether the
scope *extends* the named class. Protected reaches **both ways** along the
hierarchy, which the static-property check written last tick already knew and
this one did not. Two implementations of one rule, again, and the fixture caught
it in the same tick only because it was written to cover the whole cross.

Left recorded: `constant("self::X")` and `constant("static::X")` do not resolve
the scope keywords. `self::` needs only the lexical scope, which `scopedBuiltins`
can now carry; `static::` needs the late-static-bound class, which is the same
channel the closure item wants.

## 2026-09-11 -- 1663 passing: a static property had no visibility at all

	1661 passed / 754 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%
	1663 passed / 752 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.9%

Passing-set diff **+2 / -0**, found by applying the rule the previous tick
wrote: **vary the asking scope**.

The probe declares a private, a protected and a public member of each kind, then
reads every one of them from four places -- the declaring class, a subclass, an
unrelated class, and global scope -- and records what came back. That structure
is what surfaced it:

**`C::$prots` from outside answered the value.** Static properties were not
visibility-checked *at all*: `staticSlot` resolved the owner, found the slot, and
returned it. Instance properties have had the check since early on, so the gap
was invisible to anything that tested one kind and assumed the other.

The check needed the calling scope, which the four static accessors did not
carry. They take their arguments through the catalogue's `Args` shapes, and one
of those shapes is already `"scope"` -- the emitter supplies it -- so adding it
to `sprop.get`, `sprop.get.silent`, `sprop.set` and `sprop.ref` was a four-word
change plus the check itself. A declared argument vocabulary is worth having for
exactly this: the plumbing was already there and unused.

The message names the class **as the access wrote it** (`C::$prots`), not the
one that declared the property -- the same rule as the instance form, read back
rather than assumed.

Also found and left for later: `static::PC` inside the parent, where `static`
resolves to the child, is `Undefined constant C::PC` -- a private constant is
looked up on the late-static-bound class, which does not have it. php2go answers
the parent's value. Recorded in TODO.

## 2026-09-11 -- property_exists is scope-sensitive, and an uninitialised property is not an element

	1661 passed / 754 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%   (unchanged)

Two correctness fixes the corpus cannot see, and one near-miss that it could.

A wide probe over object introspection -- `var_dump` and `foreach` from outside,
from the child and from the base, plus `property_exists`, `method_exists` and
the array cast. Two answers were wrong:

**An uninitialised typed property is not an element of `(array)$o`.** It has a
slot and no value, and the cast copies values; php2go emitted it as `null`, so a
one-element object cast to two. `var_dump` shows it as `uninitialized`, which is
a different question answered by a different renderer -- and getting that right
is presumably what made this look right.

**`property_exists` is scope-sensitive**, which I got wrong twice in one tick.
First I had it answering from the object's property map, which says true for a
parent's private on a child instance. Fixing that to consult the class table
broke `bug50810`, and the engine explains why:

	outside, instance of the child   false
	outside, "Child"                 false
	outside, "Parent"                true
	inside the parent, $this a child TRUE
	inside a STATIC method of it     TRUE

So the private is visible when the **caller** is the declaring class. The
builtin needs the calling scope, which `callBuiltin` did not carry. It is the
only library name that does, so it gets a table of its own -- `scopedBuiltins`
-- rather than a scope threaded through all twenty-odd entries.

**The near-miss is the part worth keeping.** My first fix passed the probe I had
just written and lost a corpus file. The probe asked only from global scope; the
corpus asked from inside the class. Neither alone was enough, and the passing-set
diff is what caught it -- which is the argument for running the corpus on a
change that "obviously" only makes things more correct.

## 2026-09-11 -- 1661 passing: a static property's default was silently null

	1660 passed / 755 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%
	1661 passed / 754 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%

Passing-set diff **+1 / -0**, and again the count understates it.

Last tick found a *silently wrong* value hiding behind a "cannot render" label,
so this tick probed the same renderer wide: class constants, property defaults,
static-property defaults, default parameters, all against the engine.

**Every static property whose default named a constant was `null`.**
`public static $s = B * 2;` gave NULL where the instance property beside it gave
the right answer -- `initStatics` had a `Default != ""` arm and a fallback, and
no arm at all for `DefaultLiteral`, the deferred form the instance path has had
for a while. Nothing failed; the value was simply absent.

Adding the arm was not enough, and the reason is the more useful half.
`initStatics` runs **before** `initConstants`, so evaluating eagerly gave
`Undefined constant "B"` -- and eager is the wrong model anyway. Measured:

	class S { public static $s = B * 2; }  const B = 10;   works
	class T { public static $t = LATER; }  define(...)     works
	class U { public static $u = MISSING; }                Error at the ACCESS,
	                                                       program carries on

So a static's initializer is evaluated on **first use**, exactly as a class
constant's is, and for the same reason: it may name something not declared yet.
The slot is created at start-up and its value is not; `staticSlot` runs the
thunk once, on the first read, and returns whatever it raised to the *access*
rather than parking it.

Getting this from the engine rather than from the shape of the code is what
turned a one-line fix into a correct one. The eager version would have passed
the fixture I was about to write.

## 2026-09-11 -- 1660 passing: a constant expression owes the same diagnostic walk

	1659 passed / 756 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%
	1660 passed / 755 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%

Passing-set diff **+1 / -0**, and the value is in what the one file was hiding.

Last tick's finding -- a refusal standing in for a run-time Error -- suggested an
audit of the emitter's other refusals. Most survive it: `self`, `parent` and
`static` outside a class are **compile-time** fatals in the engine (it bails on
the file rather than raising), so declining those is right.

The census is now flat: no non-library entry above seven, and the largest,
`ZEND_FETCH_GLOBALS`, still sits behind library names its files also need.

So the tick went to `unrenderable operand <lit:N>` (5), and the first case
turned out not to be a rendering gap at all. `const T = array(1,2) - array(0);`
was rendering **and answering `int(0)`** where the engine says
`Unsupported operand types: array - array`.

**A constant expression runs the same operator and owes the same diagnostic
walk.** The ordinary path guards every arithmetic operator with
`AcceptsArithmetic` -- the left-to-right walk that stops at the first failure,
which is why `"" %% "2abc"` reports only the TypeError -- and `constOp` called
the value function straight. Six operators (`+ - * ** & | ^`) now go through
`constArith`, which runs the walk, parks the throw, and also parks whatever the
walk itself raised: a float losing precision deprecates *before* the operator
runs, and under a throwing handler that is the answer.

`Concat` is deliberately not in that set -- concatenation accepts anything a
string can be made from -- and `+` on two arrays is the union rather than an
arithmetic failure, which is why the walk has to ask the operator and not just
the operand types. Both are in the fixture.

A wrong value that no test caught is worse than a refusal that several do. The
gap list said "cannot render"; the actual behaviour was "renders, silently
wrong", and only one corpus file happened to look.

## 2026-09-11 -- 1659 passing: `$this` outside a method is the program's error, not ours

	1655 passed / 756 failed / 1499 unsupported / 0 errored   68.6%
	1659 passed / 756 failed / 1495 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%

Passing-set diff **+4 / -0**.

**A compile-time refusal standing in for a run-time Error.** Reading `$this`
where there is no object is `Error: Using $this when not in object context` --
catchable, and the program carries on. php2go declined to compile the body at
all, which turned a program PHP runs into one php2go could not. Emitting the
Error is both simpler and more faithful.

`isset($this)` is a **different opcode** -- `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_THIS` against
`ZEND_FETCH_THIS` -- and answers `false` in silence. The lowering had kept them
apart all along (`isset $this` against `this`), so only the read arm needed the
change; had they shared an instruction there would have been no way to give both
answers.

**And the preventive half of the tick.** Last entry noted the
compound-assignment arm had now been the odd one out three times. Rather than
wait for a fourth, the "an unused receiver is `$this`" rule became a helper,
`receiverOperand`, that both arms call. The comment on it says why it exists,
which is the part that stops it being re-inlined later:

> It is a helper rather than four copies because it has already been forgotten
> twice. A rule with more than one site keeps being applied at all but one of
> them.

That is worth doing at the moment a bug repeats rather than at the moment it
first appears: the second instance is what tells you the rule has sites, and the
third is late.

## 2026-09-11 -- an abandoned generator runs its finally

	1647 passed / 747 failed / 1516 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%   (unchanged)

No corpus movement -- no file's *only* gap was this -- and a real capability
landed, so it is worth the entry.

A wide probe over generators was clean but for one line: a `finally` in a
generator body did not run when the generator was abandoned. Completion ran it,
`throw()` out of it ran it, abandonment did not.

**The timing is ownership, and the engine says so in three different places:**

	foreach (g() as $v) { break; }     finally at the loop's end
	$h = g(); foreach ($h ...) break;  finally at `unset($h)`
	$k = g(); foreach ($k ...) break;  finally at end of script

Only the first is decidable without a refcount -- and it is decidable
*statically*: `iter.new`'s subject being an SSA value rather than a place is
exactly "no name reaches it", which is what a temporary is. So the lowering
emits `iter.free.owned` there, and that variant unwinds the generator before
freeing the cursor.

**The unwind travels as an exception no clause can match.** `g.Throw` with a Go
sentinel returned straight out of the compiled body -- `materialise` declines a
non-PHP error, and `onError` then returns rather than jumping to the handler,
skipping the very blocks the unwind exists to run. So the sentinel is
materialised as an object whose class is `generator@close`, a name no program
can declare: every `instanceof` test fails, `catch (Throwable)` included, and
the **unmatched-catch edge fixed two ticks ago** carries it out through the
finally. Two fixes composing was not planned and is the reason this one was
cheap.

Left open: the other two timings, which need the refcount the destruction family
has always needed. The shutdown case is closer than the `unset` one -- a
registry of live generators drained at program end -- but its ordering against
other destructors is the same open question.

The rest of the generator probe was right: `send`, `throw`, `getReturn`,
`yield from` over a generator and over an array, the delegated return value,
automatic keys and how an explicit integer moves the counter, and rewind
refusing only past the first yield. It is a fixture now.
