## 2026-09-11 -- 1646 passing: a finally that did not run

	1642 passed / 745 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%
	1646 passed / 747 failed / 1517 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%

Passing-set diff **+4 / -0**, `unsupported` down 6 and `failed` up 2 -- the same
six files, four of which now pass.

A wide probe over exceptions and `finally`, and the second line of it failed:

	try { throw new LogicException("x"); }
	catch (RuntimeException $e) { ... }
	finally { echo "finally\n"; }

The `finally` **did not run** when no clause matched. Everything else in the
probe was right -- finally overriding a return, nested finallys, `getPrevious`
chaining, multi-catch, a finally around an uncaught throw -- so this was one
edge, and a common one.

The lowering already intended it. `catchBodies` says, for the last unmatched
clause: *"`Region.Finally` is the exceptional copy, which already ends in
`rethrow`, so an unhandled exception runs the finally on its way out exactly as
the engine does"* -- and then looked the region up as `req.from.Region`. **A
catch handler is not in the region it protects**: that is what lets
`catch (E) { throw; }` escape rather than re-entering its own clause, so the
handler's region is the *enclosing* one, or -1. For a plain `try/catch/finally`
it is -1, the lookup found no finally, and the edge went to a bare `rethrow`.

The question to ask is not "which region is this block in" but **"which region
names this block as its catch"**, which is `regionCaughtBy`.

That exposed an ordering problem worth recording separately: `Regions[r].Finally`
is *rewritten* by `unwindPaths` to point at the exceptional copy, and
`catchBodies` runs before it. Reading the field at drain time gives a block id
that will not be emitted -- `jump to a block that is not emitted (bb6)`. So the
edge is **recorded and resolved after** the copies exist, which is the same
shape as the fetch and inline queues already in that pass.

## 2026-09-11 -- 1642 passing: the undecided send, third attempt

	1640 passed / 747 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%
	1642 passed / 745 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%

Passing-set diff **+3 / -1**. Two reverts, then this, and the difference is that
this time I **classified before changing**.

The classification is one command. Of the ten helpers that consume an argument
list, count the ones that read `args[i]` themselves rather than handing the
slice to a compiled body:

	callUser 0   invokeClosure 0   callMethodFrom 0   callStaticFrom 0
	callStaticCallable 0   callValue 0   callBuiltin 0
	callMethod 5   callStatic 5   callCtor 3

Three, not "however many the corpus happens to catch". Their thirteen reads are
all engine classes -- Generator's `throw`/`send`, Closure's `call`/`bind`,
Throwable's constructor, and (found by the diff, in `callStatic` but outside the
Closure arm) a backed enum's `from`/`tryFrom`. None declares a by-reference
parameter, so each takes `php.UnboxArgs` at the top of its arm.

With that done, `ZEND_SEND_VAR_EX` becomes `preferref` and a by-reference
parameter reached through a variable finally writes back. The two earlier
attempts cost 17 files and then 3; this one gains 3 and loses 1.

**The loss is a divergence I can state exactly, which is why it is acceptable.**
`f($undef)` warns and leaves `$undef` undefined when `f` takes by value, and is
**silent and defines it** when `f` takes by reference. The engine knows which
because it settles `_EX` at the send, after `INIT` has resolved the callee;
php2go builds its argument list before it has one, so a single send cannot
produce both. `php.RefArg` boxes and therefore defines, so we match the by-ref
case and lose the by-value warning. `named_params/undef_var` is the only corpus
file that sees it, and it is the right trade against a whole class of silently
discarded writes.

## 2026-09-11 -- the receiving ends, enumerated by failing at them

	1640 passed / 747 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%   (unchanged)

Second attempt at `SEND_VAR_EX`, reverted again, and this time the tick bought a
table and a list rather than only a lesson.

Last tick said the prerequisite was by-reference arginfo for the builtin
surface. **I asked the engine for it** rather than recalling it -- walking
`get_defined_functions()["internal"]` through Reflection and recording every
parameter with `isPassedByReference()`. 57 functions, and the table is now
`runtime/php/byrefargs.go`. It covers names php2go does not implement yet on
purpose: a name outside the library surface is refused before the table is
consulted, and having the answer already right is what stops the day `sort`
lands from being the day by-value arguments start aliasing.

Not one of the 29 builtins php2go implements takes a by-reference parameter, and
neither does any of the 20 class-introspection names. So `callBuiltin` can unbox
unconditionally today -- and does, through the table, so it keeps being right
when that stops being true.

**Then the same shape appeared a third time.** With the builtin end fixed,
`new Exception($t)` came back with an empty message: `callCtor`'s Throwable arm
reads `args[0].String()` directly, and a box stringifies to "". Then a fourth:
Closure's and Generator's methods read `args[i]` the same way.

That is the real finding. The receiving ends are not "user functions and
builtins" -- they are **every place that consumes an argument list**, and the
compiled unit has ten:

	callUser  invokeClosure  callMethod  callMethodFrom  callStatic
	callStaticFrom  callStaticCallable  callValue  callBuiltin  callCtor

Some route to a compiled `recv` and are already right; some read `args[i]`
themselves and are not. I have been finding them one corpus failure at a time,
which is exactly what the note I wrote last tick told me not to do. So: reverted
to baseline, and the next attempt starts by classifying all ten before changing
the send.

Kept: `php.Unbox`, `php.UnboxBuiltinArgs`, `php.UnboxArgs`, the engine's by-ref
table, and `callBuiltin`'s unboxing. All correct on their own, all inert until
the send changes.

## 2026-09-11 -- a reverted tick: SEND_VAR_EX is undecided at BOTH ends

	1640 passed / 747 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%   (unchanged)

Attempted, measured at **-11**, and reverted. The finding is worth more than the
attempt, and this is the second reverted tick this session -- both for the same
reason: a change that is right about the engine and wrong about who else is
listening.

`ZEND_SEND_VAR_EX` means *the callee's arginfo decides at run time*, and
`sendMode` mapped it to `byval` beside plain `SEND_VAR`. That is why a
by-reference parameter reached through a variable silently discarded its writes.
Mapping it to `preferref` and passing the caller's storage fixed exactly that --
`add_optional_by_ref_arg`, `closure_014`, `first_class_callable_refs` and three
more -- and broke **17**.

The reason is one sentence: **every consumer has to unbox, and only a user
function's `recv` does.** The engine emits `SEND_VAR_EX` far more widely than
"a closure with `&$x`" -- `$this->m($x)` and a plain `get_class($a)` both get it,
because neither callee is resolved at compile time -- so the box reached
`callBuiltin`, which hands its arguments straight to the library surface. A
reference arrived where a value was wanted, and `get_class`, `sort` and their
neighbours failed.

Two things survive:

- `php.Unbox` and its use in `recv`: a **by-value parameter takes the value out
  of the box**, and only when a box actually arrives, so the ordinary send pays
  nothing. That is correct on its own and is the receiving half of the eventual
  fix.
- The measurement of what the real fix needs: **by-reference arginfo for the
  builtin surface inside the compiled unit**, so the undecided send can be
  settled at the receiving end for both kinds of callee. The harvest already has
  it (`Manifest.builtins` carries by-ref flags); the emitted unit does not.

There was also a cost the golden IR showed plainly and I nearly waved past: an
argument passed as storage **stops the place being promoted**. `call.method
$this, "decorate"(preferref $who)` keeps `$who` alive where `byval %0` did not.
Correct, and worth knowing before choosing to pass storage everywhere.

## 2026-09-11 -- 1640 passing: a recursive closure, and a static one

	1638 passed / 749 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.6%
	1640 passed / 747 failed / 1523 unsupported / 0 errored   68.7%

Passing-set diff **+3 / -1**. A wide probe over closures again, and three bugs.

**A recursive closure did not work at all.** `$f = function () use (&$f) {...}`
lowered to `bind_lexical %0, $f, use=ref` and then `slot.set $f, %0`, and the
store **replaced the box** the bind had just put in the slot -- so the body's
`$f` was undef. The cause is one line in `placeRepresentation`: the only value
ever stored into `$f` is a closure, so the place narrowed to `*obj`, and a
narrowed place is written as a frame slot rather than through `write_var`.

The narrowing was reading the stores and nothing else. A place a closure
captures **by reference** holds a box whatever the stores look like -- the fact
is about the slot having storage something else holds, not about what goes in
it -- so those places are collected first and kept at `zval`.

**A static closure had `$this`.** `static function () {}` and an ordinary
closure compile to the same `DECLARE_LAMBDA_FUNCTION`; the flag is on the
closure body, and `Static` was harvested but stopped at `internal/ir` -- the
third flag this session to be plumbed the last inch (`ReturnsRef`, `Static`).

The receiver is dropped in `newClosure`, where the record carrying the flag is
already in hand, rather than at the instruction that would have to look the body
up by key. That mattered: two closures written on the same source line share one
key, so the instruction cannot tell them apart and the record can.

**`php.Obj(nil)` was an object.** Nilling the receiver was not enough --
`isset($this)` reads `php.Obj(this)`, and a KindObject value wrapping a nil
pointer is neither undef nor null, so isset said true. There is no PHP value
that is "an object that is not there"; `Obj(nil)` is `Null()` now.

`bindTo` with an instance on a static closure is `Warning: Cannot bind an
instance to a static closure` and answers **null** rather than a new Closure --
and binding only a *scope* to one is still allowed, so the refusal asks about
the receiver rather than about being static.

**The loss is two bugs cancelling, again.** `closure_049` has a static closure
inside a method returning `static::class`, and it passed because `$this` was
wrongly bound -- late static binding rode on the receiver that should not have
been there. A static closure keeps the *called* class while dropping `$this`,
and the compiled closure body has no channel for it: the body signature carries
`this`, `bound`, `clScope`, and LSB is read off `this.ClassName`. Recorded.

Left open from the probe: a closure with a **by-reference parameter** called
through a variable (`$mut = function (&$x) {...}; $mut($s);`) does not write
back. The engine emits `SEND_VAR_EX`, which means "the callee's arginfo decides
at run time", and the lowering maps it to `byval` alongside plain `SEND_VAR`.

The lowering treated `FE_FETCH_R` and `FE_FETCH_RW` as one opcode and
`FE_RESET_R`/`FE_RESET_RW` likewise, so a by-reference loop iterated a snapshot
and assigned copies into the loop variable.

Four things had to be right, and the engine settled each:

- **The cursor is live, not a snapshot.** `foreach ($a as &$v)` sees an element
  the body appends and skips one it unsets, because the engine holds a bucket
  position. A by-value loop iterates a copy and sees neither. `Array.LiveNext`
  already existed for this; `php.Iter` gained a `live` mode that uses it.
- **The loop variable binds to the element's box**, so `iter.current.ref`
  answers `RefAt(key)` and the fetch is a `bind_ref` rather than a `local.set`.
- **One mark, one drop.** I marked the box `Shared` in the intrinsic *and* in
  the bind, so every element the loop had visited kept `var_dump`'s `&`.
  Rebinding a name has to drop the old binding -- which is also what
  `$r = &$a; $r = &$b;` needs -- and the mark belongs at the bind alone.
- **The array fast paths still have to ask which walk this is.** The specializer
  proved "the subject is an array" and picked `IteratorNextArray`, which steps
  the snapshot index. A live cursor satisfies that proof and ignores that index,
  so the loop **hung**. A specialization is a claim about the subject; it is not
  a claim that there is only one way to walk it.

Two more answers came out of writing the fixture, both of which contradicted
what I had written in its comments:

	foreach (gen() as &$v)       Exception: You can only iterate a generator
	                             by-reference if it declared that it yields
	                             by-reference
	foreach ($aggregate as &$v)  runs, by value, silently

So a generator refuses (an **Exception**, not an Error) and a Traversable does
not. `Generator.ByRef` is threaded from the `ReturnsRef` plumbed in two ticks
ago for `&get` hooks -- the third feature that flag has now paid for.

**A plain object by reference is now `unsupported`.** `foreach ($o as &$v)`
binds to the property slots and changes the object; `foreachProps` builds a
detached array, so the writes would land there and vanish. A loop that appears
to work and quietly discards its writes is exactly what the honesty rule is
about, so it says so instead. That is the `unsupported` rise of 7.

because it is not "we don't support ticks": `register_tick_function` is not in

`unrenderable operand <lit:N>` was 9 sole-gap files. A deferred initializer --

evaluated on first use, and `constNode` answered for a third of what can appear

  need wrapping the value-returning operators do not.
- **`>` and `>=` are their own AST kinds.** The parser has no greater-than
  opcode -- it emits the smaller-than form with the operands swapped -- and the
  AST keeps the *source* order, so rendering means swapping them back. This was

  see why the kinds exist.

  Printer` must build no Printer, and two rendered Go expressions would build it
  before the operator saw either -- the same reason `conditional` already took
  closures.
- **`/`, `%`, `<<`, `>>` can refuse.** They answer `(Value, bool)` and the false
  arm is a throw: `1 / 0` in a default parameter is a `DivisionByZeroError`
  **when the call happens**. The old comment said diagnostics were "deliberately
  absent: it would have to run at start-up" -- but a deferred initializer does
  not run at start-up, that is the whole point of deferring it. A correct
  observation attached to the wrong conclusion.

backing store, so the object grew a field named after the property that the
class never declared -- the "plausible answer" failure again, and the doc
comment on `ref` had said as much for a while.

**`ReturnsRef` now reaches `lower.Function`.** It was harvested all along
(`internal/zend/zend.go`) and stopped at `internal/ir`. `&get` and
`function &f()` are the same engine flag, so one line of plumbing unlocked the
whole distinction.

The rule, probed for all three storage shapes (`$o->p[] = 1`, `$r = &$o->p`, a
by-reference argument), turned out to have four parts and I found them one at a
time by re-running the family after each:

1. **The read runs first, then the refusal.** `$a->p[] = 1` prints the get
   hook's output *and then* raises. Going through the ordinary `propGet` rather
   than calling `h.get` directly is what makes the neighbouring answers come out
   for free: a *virtual* property with only a `set` hook is
   `Property C::$p is write-only`, and a *backed* one with only a `set` hook has
   an implicit get that reads the stored value and then refuses like any other.
2. **`&get` hands back the box its body named**; anything else is
   `Indirect modification of C::$p is not allowed`.
3. **Binding *to* a hooked property is refused whatever the hooks are** --
   `Cannot assign by reference to overloaded object`, `&get` included, because a
   reference would let a write reach the store without the set hook running. It
   reads first as well.
4. **An object needs no storage.** `$o->hooked["k"] = 1` where the hook returns
   an ArrayAccess is `offsetSet` on that object, and `$o->hooked->p = 1` is a
   write through the handle. Neither modifies the property, so neither is an
   indirect modification. A throwaway box carries the handle to the consumer;
   writes that would land *in* the box go nowhere, which is what the engine does
   with its temporary.

**Every hook rule has to step aside inside the hook.** `set { $this->p = &$value; }`
is a legitimate rebinding of the raw store, and refusing it turned two working
oss-fuzz regression tests into fatals. The read path had that guard already; I
added the write paths without it and the corpus caught it as `-3`. It is now a
named predicate, `insideHook`, so the next rule cannot forget.

**A by-product: `unset` of a local never dropped the program's `&` binding.**
`php.Unshare` exists and the interpreter calls it at its unset points; the
emitter did not, so a reference the program had already unset still printed `&`
in `var_dump`. One line, and it is the same asymmetry the `__unset` gap was --
a mechanism `runtime/interp` uses and `internal/gogen` never learned about.

Still open in this family: `__get`/`__set` reached as storage wants a **Notice**

uses the returned value, and `&__get` hands back a reference. Two files, plus
one for the ArrayAccess wording (`overloaded element of C`). And two
`interface_get_*_virtual` files need a reference bound in a callee to be
unbound when that frame exits -- `unset` is now right, scope exit is not.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1574 passing: the NUL namespace, `__unset`, and where a stack is recorded

	1558 passed / 800 failed / 1552 unsupported / 0 errored   66.1%
	1574 passed / 784 failed / 1552 unsupported / 0 errored   66.8%

Passing-set diff **+16 / -0**, `unsupported` unchanged. Three fixes, and the
largest movement came from the one I was not aiming at.

**A property name beginning with NUL is the engine's private namespace.** The
`bug52484*` cluster (3 files) wanted `Cannot access property starting with
"\0"`. Probed, the rule is narrower than the message sounds:

	$p->{"\0"}      Error         -- read, write and unset alike
	isset($p->{"\0"})  false      -- silent; the one access that does not raise
	$p->{"a\0b"}    ordinary      -- only the FIRST byte counts
	$p->{""}        ordinary      -- an empty name is fine

And the refusal comes **after** the magic method *for that operation*: a class
with only `__get` answers a NUL read and still refuses a NUL write, because it
is `__set` that is missing. So the check sits at each point where a name would
otherwise reach the property table, not at the entry.

**It must be asked of the source name, not of the slot.** I first asked it of
`propertySlot`'s result, which is the mangled `\0Class\0name` key for a
shadowed private property -- so two `typed_properties_*` files that legitimately
touch one began failing. The corpus caught it as a `-2` in the passing-set diff.
The rule is about what the *program wrote*; the mangling is the engine's own
storage and is not a name any program can utter. Both halves now go in the
fixture.

**`__unset` was not in `hasMagic`.** The table was built from `__get`, `__set`,
`__call`, `__callStatic`, `__isset` -- so `magic(ctx, o, "__unset", ...)`
answered `handled: false` for a class that has one, and `unset($o->absent)`
silently did nothing where PHP runs the hook. The unset path had no magic
dispatch at all; it now follows the same rule the other three do, verified
against the engine: the hook runs for a name that is absent *or* invisible from
the calling scope, and a present visible property -- declared or dynamic -- is
unset directly.

**The stack is recorded where the error is raised, not where it is caught.**
This is the change that moved most of the sixteen. `materialise` builds the
exception object at the handler, by which point `ctx` names a later line and the
frames a magic method or a hook pushed have been popped -- so an error raised by
`runtime/php` inside `__get` reported `#0 {main}` and the *caller's* line:

	engine   #0 php2go-eval(4): A->__get('\x00')   line 4
	php2go   #0 {main}                             line 12

`e.onError()` now attaches at the instruction that produced the error.
`AttachStack` declines an error that already carries a position, so the
innermost site wins and every outer frame re-attaching is free. A `throw` in PHP
source never needed this -- it builds the object itself and the constructor
captures the stack -- which is why the gap only showed on **raised** failures.
The eleven files this fixed had nothing to do with NUL properties: `bug29015`,
`bug48248`, `objects_029/030`, `match/007` and the rest were all wrong about a
trace line or a `getLine()`.

The lesson is the one this tick keeps repeating in different clothes: **a
mechanism that runs at the wrong moment gives a plausible answer.** `#0 {main}`
is a real stack trace, just not this one's.

	22  ZEND_ASSIGN_REF   VAR:11, VAR:13

`bindLocal` and `bindPlace`, and in `bindPlace` it fires only after the bind
*succeeds* -- the place is resolved lazily there, so the refusal surfaces from
`BindDim` rather than from a prior instruction.

Only a `make_ref` result can reach a bind unboxed -- a local source goes through
`php.RefArg` and a place source through `refBox`, both of which always box -- so
the notice cannot be lost by moving it.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1555 passing: two refusals at the edge of a legal write

	1547 passed / 811 failed / 1552 unsupported / 0 errored   65.6%
	1555 passed / 803 failed / 1552 unsupported / 0 errored   65.9%

Passing-set diff **+8 / -0**, and `unsupported` did not move -- this tick fixed
what already-graded files were wrong about rather than admitting new ones, which
is the decision rule the previous entry wrote down after the autoloading tick
returned 25 new `failed` for 5 new `passed`.

Both fixes came out of clustering the `failed` reasons and taking the two
coherent groups: `Cannot indirectly modify readonly property Foo::$value` (10
files) and `Cannot add element to the array as the next element is already
occupied` (5).

**Indirect readonly modification is a different rule from the direct write, not
a special case of it.** The direct write permits exactly one assignment, from
inside the declaring class, to an uninitialised property. Reaching the property
as *storage* -- `$o->arr[] = 1`, `$o->arr[0] = 1`, `$r =& $o->arr`, passing it to
a by-reference parameter -- has **no exceptions at all**. Probed:

	ctor-uninit:    Cannot indirectly modify readonly property A::$v
	ctor-init:      Cannot indirectly modify readonly property A::$v
	inside:         Cannot indirectly modify readonly property A::$v
	outside-uninit: Cannot indirectly modify readonly property B::$w

Every state, every scope. Had I reasoned from the direct-write rule I would have
written an initialisation exemption that the engine does not have. Visibility is
asked **first** -- a private readonly property reached from outside says `Cannot
access private property A::$v` -- and the object a readonly property *holds* is
not itself readonly, so `$h->inner->p = 1` is an ordinary write.

The check belongs on the **place**, not on the property write: `place.ref` and
`place.refBox` are the two functions that hand out somewhere to write through,
and every one of the four spellings above goes through one of them. One
predicate at that choke point covers the family; the alternative was four
call-site checks and no reason to believe the fourth was the last.

**A saturated array has no next key.** `$a = [PHP_INT_MAX => "m"]; $a[] = "next"`
raises rather than wrapping, and the element is not added -- `count($a)` stays
1. `php.Array.CanAppend` already answered the question and `constArray` already
asked it; the runtime `writeDim` append arm did not. This is the shape of gap
worth looking for: a check that exists, is correct, and is asked on one of two
paths.

**Three of the eight files gained are `Zend/tests/enum/`.** An enum case's
properties are readonly, so `no-write-properties-through-references`,
`no-pass-properties-by-ref` and `no-return-properties-by-ref` were answered by a
change that never mentions enums. A rule stated where the engine states it
covers cases the failure list did not show.

**Method note, and it cost a full corpus pass.** `php2gotest -n 8` is *"stop
after this many files"*, not a parallelism setting. Twelve chunks each reported
`files 8` and the completeness check passed, because a chunk that stops early
still writes a summary line -- the existing per-chunk check only catches a chunk
that writes *none*. The tally read `files 96` and I caught it there, but only
because the total is checked against 4,986. Second method note: `-v` prints only
**non-passing** files, so a passing set has to be built as the complement of the
chunk's input list, not by grepping for `passed`. Both are now in TESTING.md.

Passing-set diff **+5 / -0**; 30 files left `unsupported`, 5 passed and 25
became `failed`. `spl_autoload_register` was 46 sole-gap files.

**A compiled program has no files to load**, so the only way an autoloader can
make a class exist here is `class_alias`. Everything else about autoloading is
the same, and it is what the tests are about: which callbacks run, in what
order, and that the chain stops as soon as the class exists. All four rules were
measured:

	two loaders, unknown name        A then B, both run
	a loader that aliases            only A runs -- the chain stops
	class_exists($n, false)          neither runs
	a loader asking about its own
	  name                           does NOT re-run the chain

That last one is not a nicety: without the guard it is infinite recursion rather
than a wrong answer.

**An autoloader's failure travels.** The first version parked the error and
answered "not found", which turned a php2go gap -- `eval` is how a test's
autoloader usually defines a class -- into `Class "X" not found`. A wrong answer
standing in for an honest refusal is the one thing the buckets exist to prevent,
so `autoload` returns the error and every caller propagates it.

**`new` of an undeclared class is now a run-time question, but only in a program
that registers an autoloader.** Ungated, `new ReflectionClass` would become
`Class not found` instead of the named gap it is -- a wrong answer replacing a
refusal, the same trade in the other direction.

**On the ratio.** Two consecutive library ticks have moved the rate down 1.9
points while adding 25 passes, and 25-for-5 here is the worst trade recorded.
That is worth stating rather than hiding behind "failed rising is normal":

- The 25 are not newly broken. `bug37138` registers an autoloader purely to
  observe whether `call_user_func(['self','e'])` triggers one; it now fails on
  `call_user_func` with `'self'`, which is its **real** blocker and was
  invisible while `spl_autoload_register` masked it.
- The rate is the newly graded population, not a regression: the passing set has
  not lost a file in twenty ticks.
- But the *label* was more useful for some of them. A `failed` reading
  `want object(A)#2 got ""` says less than `unsupported: spl_autoload_register`
  did. The information improves only where the new blocker is named.

The library surface is where the census head now is, and this is what opening it
looks like. Worth watching whether the next library tick keeps the same ratio;
if it does, the ordering should change -- fix what the newly graded files fail
*on* before unblocking more of them.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1542 passing: the cycle collector this program does not have

	1522 passed / 732 failed / 1656 unsupported / 0 errored   67.5%
	1542 passed / 786 failed / 1582 unsupported / 0 errored   66.2%

Passing-set diff **+20 / -0**, and **74** files left `unsupported` -- 20 passed
and 54 became `failed`. The rate falls 1.3 points, which is the largest single
drop this project has recorded, and it is the expected shape: the newly graded
population is almost entirely destruction-dependent, so it grades against the
gap php2go has always had.

The census head is now the library surface. `gc_collect_cycles` alone was **57**
sole-gap files, `register_shutdown_function` 16.

**`gc_collect_cycles()` returns 0, and that is truthful rather than a
placeholder.** php2go does not refcount, so there are no cycles for it to
collect, and 0 is what PHP returns when there are none. What it does *not* do is
force the destructors PHP would run while collecting -- and that is the
destruction gap, reported on its own and not hidden here. The distinction
matters because the rule is about a gap masquerading as behaviour: this reports
a real count of a real thing (zero collections by a collector that does not
exist), while the destructors are absent for a reason stated elsewhere.

Checked the gained set rather than trusting it: none of the 20 expects
destructor output. They expect `DONE`, `ok`, `End` -- crash and leak tests that
need the program to survive -- and `bug70805` expects `int(0)`, which is what
PHP prints too. `gc_001` tests only the *setting*, which is now tracked honestly:
`gc_enable`/`gc_disable` move a flag that starts on, because that is all
`gc_enabled` reports and it says nothing about a collector.

**Shutdown functions are ordinary and were simply missing.** A callback with its
own arguments, run after the body in registration order, and three things
measured rather than assumed: they run on `exit`, they run **after** an uncaught
exception's fatal block, and an `exit` inside one stops the remaining ones.

**Two Go initialization cycles in one tick**, and the second was a consequence
of the first's fix. `function_exists` reading `classBuiltins` from inside its
own literal was the first; making `exit` run the shutdown list closed the loop
`classBuiltins -> phpExit -> runShutdown -> callValue -> classBuiltins`. The
table is now filled at start-up like `userFuncs` and `propHooks`, which is the
third table to hit that wall -- a generated table whose entries can call back
into the program cannot be a package-scope literal.

method pair and one registered from inside another function, plus the gc
setting. Local fixtures 154/154.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1522 passing: function_exists, and a tick that knew it was small

	1521 passed / 730 failed / 1659 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%
	1522 passed / 732 failed / 1656 unsupported / 0 errored   67.5%

Passing-set diff **+1 / -0** -- `function_exists_basic`. The previous tick left
`function_exists` named in TODO as the companion to conditional declarations,
and it was always going to be about one file: the sole-gap ranking never had it
above 1. Taken because it was cheap and named, not because it was next by size.

**It cannot come from a compile-time table**, which is the whole reason it
belongs to the generated program rather than to the library. The same source is
false before its branch runs and true after:

	if (false) { function never() {} }   function_exists("never")   false
	if (true)  { function later() {} }   function_exists("later")   true, after the branch

`userFuncs` holds both kinds -- filled at start-up for the unconditional ones
and by `declare_function` for the rest -- so it is the one table to ask.

**The engine's list is the last word**, and it is wider than what this program
can call. Measured: `function_exists("strlen")` is true and `strlen` is compiled
to an *opcode*, so it is in no library table at all; `function_exists("array_map")`
is true and calling it is a gap php2go reports. PHP says both exist, and
existing is the question being asked -- answering "no" because we cannot call it
would be a wrong answer about PHP rather than an honest report about php2go.

One Go-shaped detail: the first version asked `classBuiltins[name]` from inside
`classBuiltins`'s own initializer, which is an initialization cycle. The names
are now emitted twice -- once as functions and once as plain data -- because a
table cannot read itself while it is being built.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1521 passing: a function declaration is an instruction

	1517 passed / 728 failed / 1665 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%
	1521 passed / 730 failed / 1659 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%

Passing-set diff **+4 / -0**; 6 files out of `unsupported`. `declare_function`
was 7 sole-gap files.

`function f() {}` inside an `if` is a **declaration instruction**, not a
definition: the engine emits `ZEND_DECLARE_FUNCTION` where the source put it,
and the function does not exist until that runs. Two consequences the emitter
had neither of.

**The body is not in the function list.** The harvest keeps a nested op_array
among the *closures* -- that is where any nested body goes -- so the unit's
function list holds only the unconditional ones, and `e.defined` said the name
was undefined. A call to it was reported as `Call to undefined function` **at
emit time**, which is the program's error attributed to the wrong party: it is
the *engine's* answer only if the declaration never runs.

**Whether it has been declared is a run-time question.** Each conditional
function gets a wrapper under the name an unconditional one would have, so
every call site is unchanged, and the wrapper carries the one thing a direct
call cannot:

	func php_later(ctx *php.Ctx, args []php.Value) (php.Value, error) {
		if !declaredFuncs["later"] { return php.Value{}, php.ThrowUndefinedFunction("later") }
		return cl_later(ctx, nil, nil, "", args)
	}

`declare_function` sets the flag and registers the name in `userFuncs`, so a
`$f = "later"; $f(...)` finds it too.

The wrapper's call had its arguments in the wrong order first -- a closure body
takes `(ctx, this, bound, clScope, args)` and I wrote the receiver first, which
Go caught as `cannot use "" as map[string]*php.Value`. The `errored` bucket, and
a build failure is the cheapest of its three kinds.

Fixture `conditional_functions.php`: a call before the declaration, a branch
that never declares, a declaration inside a function body that only exists once
that function has run, the name reached through a variable, and a conditional
function reading a global. Local fixtures 153/153.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1517 passing: a variable name is an arbitrary byte string

	1511 passed / 727 failed / 1672 unsupported / 0 errored   67.5%
	1517 passed / 728 failed / 1665 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%

Passing-set diff **+6 / -0**; 7 files out of `unsupported`.
`variable name that is not an identifier` was 8 sole-gap files, and the refusal
had been in place long enough to have its own regression test.

`${"b\nb\n d"}` is a legal PHP variable, and the emitter could already *mangle*
one -- `place()` hex-escapes anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_]`. What it could not
do was **find** one: the IR spelled the name raw, so a newline, a space or a
quote landed in the middle of an operand and no scanner could find its end
again. The place scanner's regex is `\$[A-Za-z0-9_]+` for that reason, and a
name outside it was therefore never declared -- `undefined: p_u0000` at Go build
time, which is `errored`, so the refusal was the right call at the time.

**The fix is in the spelling, not the scanner.** A name that is not an
identifier is now written `${"..."}` with the quoting Go's `%q` gives, so the
operand has an unambiguous end whatever bytes the name contains. `PlaceOperand`
writes it and `PlaceName` reads it back, sitting together for the same reason
`LiteralText` and `ParseArrayLiteral` do -- a renderer and a scanner that
disagree about what the text says is a defect this project has had twice.

One ordering detail decides whether it works: **the quoted form is matched
before string literals are blanked.** `PlaceNames` hides a `$` inside a literal
so that `echo "$x"` names no variable; running that first would erase the name
this form exists to carry.

The refusal's regression test is now the opposite test. It used to assert that
such a program is refused; it asserts that the mangled place is **declared as
well as used**, because checking only that the name appears would pass on
exactly the build failure it exists to prevent.

The gained files are the three `flexible-heredoc-complex-test`s -- which is
where PHP's own suite keeps its arbitrary-byte-string names -- plus
`named_params/basic` and two others that had one such variable among ordinary
code.

Fixture `odd_variable_names.php`: newlines, a leading space, an embedded quote,
an embedded `$`, the empty name, a digit, an undefined read whose warning must
quote the **real** name rather than the operand's spelling, the name in an
argument list as well as an operand, and a computed `$$n` naming the same slot.
Local fixtures 152/152.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1505 passing: destructuring by reference

	1502 passed / 718 failed / 1690 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%
	1505 passed / 727 failed / 1678 unsupported / 0 errored   67.4%

Passing-set diff **+3 / -0**; 12 files out of `unsupported`, nine of them into
`failed`. `ZEND_FETCH_LIST_W` (12 sole-gap files) is `[&$u, &$v] = $src` --
list destructuring **by reference**.

The opcode itself is a dimension fetch for write like any other, and joining it
to the `FETCH_DIM_W` family was one line. What it needed was the two things
underneath.

**`make_ref` of a local is a variable, not an expression.** The opcode wears two
hats and only one of them was reading the operand as a variable: over a *place*
it opened the box, and over anything else it went through `makeRefValue`, which
reads the **value**. A local read as a value has no box behind it, so the notice
`Only variables should be assigned by reference` fired, the binding degraded to
a copy, and writing `$u` changed nothing. A local is as much a variable as a
place is.

**A dimension write through a reference *value*.** `[&$u, &$v] = $src` fetches
each element for write through `make_ref $src`, so the container arrives as a
zval whose box is the storage to open -- neither a named local nor a place,
which were the only two shapes `ptr` accepted. `refSlot` opens it, and reports
rather than guessing when the value holds no box: writing to a copy would be a
change nothing can observe, which is the worst kind of wrong answer.

Two gaps found while writing the fixture, both left in and written down:

- **A nested list with an inner reference shows an `&` the engine does not.**
  `[$outer, [&$inner, $plain]] = $nested` fetches the outer element for write,
  which boxes it, and PHP drops that box again on the `ZEND_FREE` that ends the
  assignment. This compiler treats FREE as a no-op -- "the IR has no slot to
  free" -- so the box outlives the statement and `var_dump` prints `&array(2)`.
- **`foreach ($src as &$each)` over an array whose elements are already boxed**
  does not write through them.

Both are reference *bookkeeping* rather than reference semantics, and both are
now reachable where they were behind a refusal before. That is most of the nine
files that moved from `unsupported` into `failed`.

Fixture `list_by_reference.php`, with the two excluded shapes named in comments
rather than quietly dropped. Local fixtures 150/150.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1502 passing: which finally bodies a block is inside

	1499 passed / 714 failed / 1697 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%
	1502 passed / 718 failed / 1690 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%

Passing-set diff **+3 / -0**. A small number for the tick that finally got the
`finally` machinery right; the refusal counts say more than the pass count does:

	terminator <pending finally>         10 -> 0
	handler inside an inlined finally     6 -> 3
	timeouts introduced                        0

The previous tick wrote two correct fixes, watched them turn two refusals into
**hangs**, and reverted rather than ship a guard that refused four working
programs. This one builds the fact that makes them safe, and the fact is
smaller than any of the three guards was.

**`Block.InFinallyOf`: which finally *bodies* a block's oplines sit inside.**
Not the same as `Region`, which says which `try` protects them. An exception
raised inside a finally is handled by none of the finallys enclosing it -- a
finally does not catch what it throws, and neither does one it is nested inside
-- and that is a different set from the region chain.

It is **positional**: region `r` is inside finally `f` exactly when
`finallyRange(f)` contains `r`'s first opline. So a copy gets the same answer as
the body it came from, nothing has to be threaded through the inlining, and
`Block.OfRegion` -- added two ticks ago and threaded from the inline request --
is subsumed and gone. `handlerFor` takes the set and skips all of it.

With routing correct, the two reverted fixes went back in unchanged:

- **The accumulators must outlive `inlineFinally`'s restore.** `*l = saved` put
  back the work queues along with the per-opline cursor, discarding everything
  the copy had just queued.
- **The handler passes must reach a fixed point.** `catchBodies` and
  `fetchBodies` run before `unwindPaths`, so a `foreach` or a `catch` inside a
  finally queued its request after the pass that would drain it had run. Each
  pass now consumes its queue and the three loop until all are empty.

And one more that only became correct once the first three were:

- **An unwind copy has no normal continuation.** A jump leaving the copy is the
  FAST_RET's continuation arriving through a nested finally, and on the
  exceptional path there is nothing to continue to. PHP forbids `break`,
  `continue` and `goto` out of a finally, so a jump leaving the copy can only be
  that. Applied on its own last tick it produced the hang; applied on correct
  routing it is what stops `try { throw } finally { try {} finally {} }` from
  running both finallys and then carrying on past the try.

What is left is honest: three files still refuse with `handler inside an
inlined finally` -- a `catch` written inside a finally, whose region's `Catch`
still names the original block the inlining left dead -- and the nested-finally
tests that used to time out now **fail** with wrong output rather than hanging.
Both are in TODO with what they need.

Fixture `finally_nesting.php`: a loop inside a finally on the normal exit and on
the exceptional one, a finally that returns with a loop in it, and a nested
finally whose inner body also loops. Local fixtures 149/149.

## 2026-09-10 -- a tick that landed nothing, and the design it produced

	1499 passed / 714 failed / 1697 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%   (unchanged)

**Nothing shipped.** Two real fixes were written, measured, and reverted,
because together they turned two refusals into two *hangs* and no guard I could
write refused the hanging shape without also refusing four working programs.
Recording it because the next attempt should start from what this found rather
than from the census.

The target was the nested-`finally` cluster: `ZEND_FAST_CALL: FAST_CALL with no
finally range` (9 sole-gap files) and `terminator <pending finally>` (7).

**Two defects, both real, both reverted.**

*The accumulators do not survive the restore.* `inlineFinally` ends with
`*l = saved`, which puts back the per-opline cursor -- the block being filled,
the todo list, the slot map -- and also puts back the **work queues**,
discarding everything the copy just queued. A finally containing its own `try`
left `<pending finally>` in the copy's terminator because the request that would
have resolved it was thrown away.

*The passes do not reach a fixed point.* `catchBodies` and `fetchBodies` run
**before** `unwindPaths`, so a `foreach` or a `catch` inside a finally queues its
request after the pass that would drain it has already run. Each pass has to
consume its queue and the three have to loop until all are empty.

With both applied, `terminator <pending>` went to zero and a `foreach` inside a
`finally` compiled. And two files that had been refusals became **timeouts**:

	try { throw } finally { try { return 42; } finally { throw } }

Copy A's rethrow routes to copy B and B's to A. That is the routing hole the
previous tick already named -- `handler inside an inlined finally` and the
`OfRegion` work are the same missing fact -- and resolving the pending
terminators is what made it reachable.

**Three guards were tried and each was wrong**, which is the part worth keeping:

1. *An unwind copy has no normal continuation* -- rewrite a jump leaving the
   copy as `rethrow`. Correct in principle; it turned the wrong answer into the
   hang, because the rethrow then entered the cycle.
2. *The handler chain cycles.* Catches both hanging files and refuses **four
   working ones**: a graph cycle is not an execution cycle, and
   `try { throw } finally { try { throw } finally { return 42; } }` cycles in the
   graph and returns 42 without going round, because the inner finally returns.
3. *A finally throws into another finally.* Narrower, still two false positives.

A false refusal costs coverage and a false pass costs a hang, so neither
direction is safe to guess at. Reverted to the last measured state rather than
shipping a fix that hangs or a guard that refuses working programs.

**The fix the next attempt should build.** The missing fact is *which finally
bodies a block sits inside*, and it is **computable from opline positions
alone**: region `r` is inside finally `f` exactly when `finallyRange(f)` contains
`r`'s first opline. That is static, needs no provenance threading, and answers
every case this cluster has produced --

- `handlerFor` skips every enclosing finally, not just `Block.OfRegion`'s one,
  so a rethrow cannot re-enter a finally it is already running;
- a `catch` inside a finally can have its region's `Catch` remapped to the copy,
  which is what `handler inside an inlined finally` needs;
- `Block.OfRegion` becomes derivable rather than threaded, since a copy's blocks
  keep their original opline positions.

Compute it in `linkRegions`, store it per region, and the three guards above
stop being necessary at all.

`parent::$x::get()` inside a property hook is an INIT for an ordinary call, so
the pending-call machinery already had it. What it needed was reading the
opline: op1 is the property name, and **op2 is the hook kind** -- an unused
operand holding 0 for `get` and 1 for `set`.

An unused operand's value is not otherwise meaningful, so that is not something
to read off a header. Harvested one class with both hooks and compared the two
lines; they differ in exactly that field. This is the third opcode in this
project where an *unused* operand carries the whole distinction -- `$this` in
the FETCH_OBJ family, `__construct` in INIT_STATIC_METHOD_CALL, and now the
hook kind.

**It walks the parent chain, not the immediate parent.** A hook two levels up
answers when the level between declares none, which is the same rule method
dispatch follows and worth pinning in the fixture rather than assuming.

**Where the chain has no hook the property is a plain slot**, and the call is
the raw backing-store access. Measured with a hook-less parent and a hooked
child, which is exactly what `bug005` is -- `class B { protected mixed $x; }`
under a child that writes `parent::$x::set(1)`.

The fixture needed one correction from the engine, and it is a gap rather than
a mistake: **a hooked redeclaration drops the parent's default**, so

	class Plain  { public mixed $y = "plain"; }
	class Hooked extends Plain { public mixed $y { get { ... } } }

leaves `$y` uninitialised, and reading it is `Typed property Hooked::$y must not
be accessed before initialization` -- which php2go does not model. Restating the
default in the child is what the fixture does, with the reason written down
beside it.
