## 2026-09-10 -- 1488 passing: switch has three comparison opcodes, not one

	1471 passed / 703 failed / 1736 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%
	1488 passed / 705 failed / 1717 unsupported / 0 errored   67.9%

Passing-set diff **+17 / -0**; 19 files out of `unsupported`. `case` (8 sole-gap
files) and `case_strict` (7), and then the jump tables behind them.

`switch` already worked, which is what made the head confusing: a switch over a
**named variable** compiles to `ZEND_IS_EQUAL`, which has been an intrinsic all
along. A switch over a **temporary** -- `$s[0]`, `strlen($x)` -- compiles to
`ZEND_CASE` instead, and `match` over one to `ZEND_CASE_STRICT`.

The reason for the separate opcodes is **operand lifetime, not operation**: the
comparison must not free op1, because the next case needs the same subject. That
is nothing the IR models, and nothing that changes what the comparison does, so
they are the same two intrinsics `is_equal` and `is_identical` already name --
two lines in `intrinsicFor`.

**Then the fixture found a third form.** A switch whose cases are all ints, or
all strings, gets a jump table: `ZEND_SWITCH_LONG` / `ZEND_SWITCH_STRING`, the
same shape as `ZEND_MATCH`. They lower through the same path, and the reason
that is correct despite `switch` comparing with `==` and `match` with `===` is
worth stating:

	The table is a fast path, not the statement.

It is consulted only when the subject is exactly that type, and anything else
falls to `extended_value` -- which is where the sequential `ZEND_CASE` chain
begins. So identity is right *inside* the table and the loose comparison still
happens, just further along. `switch (1.0) { case 1: }` misses the int table,
reaches the chain, and matches there; `number(1.0)`, `number("2")` and
`number(true)` in the fixture pin all three.

That also means the `match` work from the previous tick paid for this one: the
terminator, the block-leader rule that reads the jump targets out of a literal,
and the identity comparison all carried over unchanged.

Fixture `switch_statement.php`: a temporary subject evaluated once, `0` against
`"0"`, all-string and all-int tables, subjects of the wrong type reaching the
chain, fallthrough, a `default` that is not last, and a switch that matches
nothing. Local fixtures 147/147.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1471 passing: match, and a jump table that is not an array

	1455 passed / 698 failed / 1757 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%
	1471 passed / 703 failed / 1736 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%

Passing-set diff **+16 / -0**, every one of them `match/*`. 21 files out of
`unsupported`: `ZEND_MATCH` and `ZEND_MATCH_ERROR`, the third and fifth
sole-gap heads.

The design question was whether the engine's jump table could be used at all.
`ZEND_MATCH`'s op2 is a literal mapping each arm's value to the opline it starts
at, and op2 literals reach the IR as array text. **A table read back as an
array would be wrong**, and a probe said so before a line was written:

	match ($x) { 1 => "int1", "1" => "str1" }

keeps `1` as an **int** key and `"1"` as a **string** key in the same table,
where any PHP array literal folds the second into the first. So the table is not
an array; it only looks like one.

What makes it safe is that `ParseArrayLiteral` is not PHP either -- it reads the
*text*, so a bare `1` is an int key and a quoted `"1"` is a string key, with no
coercion anywhere. The renderer and the parser have been one contract since they
were written, and this is the first consumer to need the property they were
built with rather than the values they carry.

The arms then render as a chain of `php.StrictEqual` in order, which is what
`match` means; the jump table is the engine's optimisation over exactly that,
and reproducing the optimisation would have put the array rules back in.

**The first version matched every subject to arm one**, and the cause was one
level below the terminator: `blockLeaders` did not know `ZEND_MATCH` branches.
`ZEND_MATCH_ERROR` was already in the list of block-enders and `ZEND_MATCH` was
not, so the whole `match` stayed in one block, the terminator was overwritten by
the first arm's fallthrough, and every subject fell into it. Every arm is a
target, and the targets are in the table -- so `blockLeaders` reads the literal
too.

`UnhandledMatchError` names its subject by **value** for a scalar and by *type*
for anything else, and the value spelling is `var_export`'s rather than
`var_dump`'s. Measured, because the two differ exactly where it matters:

	5        Unhandled match case 5
	0.0      Unhandled match case 0.0        -- var_dump says float(0)
	1e100    Unhandled match case 1.0E+100
	'a'b'    Unhandled match case 'a'b'      -- quoted, and NOT escaped
	null     Unhandled match case NULL
	[1]      Unhandled match case of type array

Fixture `match_expression.php`: `1` against `"1"`, `true` and `null` as arms,
all six UnhandledMatchError shapes, arms with side effects that must run only
when taken, and `match (true)`. Local fixtures 146/146.

One note on the gate: `TestDNSQueriesMatchEngine` in `internal/bundlebuild`
failed once with `Warning: DNS Query failed` and passed on re-run. It resolves
`localhost` against the real resolver, so it is environment-dependent rather
than anything this tick touched -- checked rather than assumed, by re-running it
alone.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1455 passing: which finally a copy *is*

	1454 passed / 698 failed / 1758 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%
	1455 passed / 698 failed / 1757 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%

Passing-set diff **+1 / -0** -- `try/bug70228_2`, the file the last tick refused
to keep `errored` at 0. A one-file tick by the count, and it closes a class of
infinite loop rather than a case of one.

The refusal was right and the fix is one field. `Block.Handler` says a block is
part of an inlined `finally`, and the emitter used it to route an exception
**outward from the block's region**. Two different questions were being answered
with one:

	an exception raised in a finally is not handled by that same finally
	an exception raised in a `try` written inside a finally IS handled by it

`Region` is the innermost try the block's *oplines* sit in, which is the right
answer for the second. What the copy also needs is to know **which finally it
is**, and nothing recorded that -- so `Regions[blk.Region].Parent` walked from
the inner try straight past the thing that should have caught it and back to the
copy's own entry.

`Block.OfRegion` records it, set from the inline request that already carried
it. `handlerFor` takes a region to skip, and skips **only** that one:

	try { throw } finally { try { throw } finally { return 42; } }

now returns 42, where before it ran for ever.

Worth stating as a rule, because the same shape has now appeared three times in
the finally machinery: **a copy needs its provenance, not just its position.**
`Handler` and `Unwind` are both provenance marks added for exactly this reason,
and `OfRegion` is the third. Position -- which region an opline sits in -- can
never answer a question about the copy, because every copy of a body shares it.

The body-level refusal stays as a backstop, now stated over any block rather
than a finally copy: **a block that is its own handler** is an infinite loop
whatever produced it. It fires on nothing in the corpus.

Still refused nearby, and the analysis is in TODO: `handler inside an inlined
finally` (6 files) is a `try/catch` written **inside** a finally. `unwindPaths`
rewrites `Regions[r].Finally` to point at the copy and does not rewrite `Catch`,
so the region still names the original -- which the inlining left dead. The
copies each need their own region entries, because a finally is inlined once per
exit and they cannot share one table.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1454 passing: a finally that leaves, and a static that cannot be folded

	1434 passed / 689 failed / 1787 unsupported / 0 errored   67.5%
	1454 passed / 698 failed / 1758 unsupported / 0 errored   67.6%

Passing-set diff **+20 / -0**; 29 files out of `unsupported`. Two opcodes, the
top two sole-gap heads at 25 and 18.

**`ZEND_DISCARD_EXCEPTION`** is the head of a `finally` body that leaves by
another route -- `return`, `break`, `continue`. Whatever was in flight is
abandoned, because the finally is taking over:

	function f() { try { throw new Exception("x"); } finally { return 1; } }

returns 1 and throws nothing. The engine keeps the in-flight exception in the
FAST_CALL's temporary and this drops it; here the finally is **inlined**, so the
unwind copy is the one carrying it and clearing `pendingExc` is the whole
instruction. On the normal copy there is nothing to clear.

**`ZEND_BIND_INIT_STATIC_OR_JMP`** is `static $o = new stdClass;` -- an
initializer the compiler could not fold, so the value is computed on **first
entry** and the slot consulted on every later one. op2 is where to jump when the
static already holds a value; falling through runs the initializer, which a
`BIND_STATIC` *carrying op2* then stores. That second form is the same opcode
the constant case uses, with a value in op2 instead of nothing -- the fifth time
this project has met one opcode asking two questions.

One thing needed saying about the slot: `declareStatics` only made one for a
static the table marks as having a default, and the table does **not** mark a
computed one -- the value is in the body, not in the table. So the body says
instead: the names `static.bound` mentions are exactly the computed statics.

**Then `errored` went to 1, as a *timeout*.** Not a build failure this time --
an emitted program that loops for ever, on:

	try { throw } finally { try { throw } finally { return 42; } }

`Block.Handler` exists precisely for this, and its comment already describes the
symptom: *"routing a `throw` to `handlerFor` sent it back into the finally it
was raised in, and the generated program looped for ever"*. The emitter applies
the mark. What it gets wrong is **which** region to go outward from: the outer
finally's inlined copy sits, by opline position, inside the *inner* try's
region, so `Regions[blk.Region].Parent` walks to a handler that is the copy
itself.

Refused rather than half-routed -- sending it one level further out is a guess
about which finally is which, and a guess there is a silently wrong catch. A
block that is its own handler is now a body-level refusal, so the shape is
`unsupported` instead of a hang. The real fix wants the region the finally
*belongs to* rather than the one its copy sits in, and that is in TODO.

Also: **`-keep` now writes the source on a timeout**, not only on a wrong
answer. A program that does not terminate is the hardest output to look at and
was the one case that produced none.

Two fixture attempts were wrong before the engine agreed. `break` out of a
`finally` is a **fatal compile error** in PHP, not a discard -- and it bails the
engine with no message at all, which is what `noreference` looks like.

Fixture `finally_discard_and_computed_static.php`. Local fixtures 145/145.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1434 passing: three small gaps that shared a shape

	1410 passed / 669 failed / 1831 unsupported / 0 errored   67.8%
	1434 passed / 689 failed / 1787 unsupported / 0 errored   67.5%

Passing-set diff **+24 / -0**; 44 files out of `unsupported`. Four gaps, none
big enough for a tick of its own, picked by the **sole-gap** ranking the last
tick added:

	ZEND_INIT_PARENT_PROPERTY_HOOK_CALL  15    local.get of a non-local        14
	ZEND_FETCH_LIST_W                    12    ZEND_FETCH_GLOBALS              11
	call.static with a dynamic method    10    ZEND_UNSET_VAR                   9

**`parent::__construct()` had no method name.** `call.static parent()` -- one
operand where the emitter wanted two. The compiler resolves a constructor call
at compile time and leaves a *cache address* in op2 rather than a name, so
`l.operand` answered "". Measured over all four spellings, which is what makes
the rule safe to state:

	parent::__construct()   UNUSED:514  UNUSED:1933922424
	self::__construct()     UNUSED:513  UNUSED:1933922464
	A::__construct()        CONST:0     UNUSED:1933922504
	static::__construct()   UNUSED:515  UNUSED:1933922544

The addresses differ between runs, so it is the *unusedness* that carries the
meaning and nothing else does. An unused op2 on INIT_STATIC_METHOD_CALL is
`__construct`.

**`C::$m()` named its method with a value**, and the emitter quoted the operand
text as a Go string literal. It renders through `e.operand(...).String()` now,
and a **named argument** in such a call is refused rather than bound to a guess,
since there is no signature to look up.

**`unset($$n)` and `unset($GLOBALS["g"])`** are `ZEND_UNSET_VAR`, the same
name-in-op1-plus-scope-bit shape as the fetch family and ISSET_ISEMPTY_VAR --
the third opcode in that family, and the third time the rule has been needed.
`unset($x)` is ZEND_UNSET_CV and never comes here.

The slot is **emptied and left in the map** rather than removed: the map holds
the address of a Go variable, and dropping the entry would leave that variable
holding its old value for a plain `$x` read. An undef is what `unset` leaves
anyway -- reading it warns again, which is the difference from null.

**`local.get` of a place.** `$a[0] =& f()` binds through a `dim.ref` and then
reads back what the bind put there; the operand is a place, not a slot. It is
the place's own read, which is what runs its diagnostics.

One thing this exposed rather than fixed: `$a[0] =& returnsVal()` now emits and
is missing `Notice: Only variables should be assigned by reference`. It moved
from `unsupported` to a `failed` naming exactly what is absent, which is the
trade the count shows -- `failed` up 20 while `unsupported` fell 44.

Fixture `dynamic_names_and_parent_ctor.php`. Two attempts at it were wrong
before the engine agreed: `self::__construct()` inside a child constructor is
**infinite recursion**, not a call to the parent, and it exhausted the engine's
memory limit rather than failing cleanly. Local fixtures 144/144.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1410 passing: exit is a function, and it ends the process

	1397 passed / 667 failed / 1846 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%
	1410 passed / 669 failed / 1831 unsupported / 0 errored   67.8%

Passing-set diff **+13 / -0**; 15 files out of `unsupported`, including
`exit_finally_1/2` and `throw/exit_in_finally`, which are the tests that pin the
one design decision here.

Chose the target by measuring **how many files a gap blocks *alone*** rather
than how often it appears, which is a different ranking:

	library function exit                     appears 29   only gap 17
	call.static with a dynamic method                 17            10
	ZEND_FETCH_LIST_W                                 12             0
	ZEND_INIT_PARENT_PROPERTY_HOOK_CALL               25             0

The last two are worth doing and will not move the count at all, because every
file that needs them needs something else too. That distinction is now the
first thing to check before picking a head.

**`exit` ends the process rather than unwinding**, and the reason is `finally`:

	function f() { try { exit("bye\n"); } finally { echo "no\n"; } }

prints `bye` and nothing else. Our finally is *inlined at every exit path*,
including the error path, so propagating a sentinel error would run every
inlined copy on the way out. Ending the process is both simpler and what PHP
observably does. Destructors do run in PHP and this compiler does not run them
at normal termination either -- the same gap, not a new one.

**Since 8.4 `exit` really is a function**, so the argument goes through ordinary
coercion and a bad one is a **catchable** TypeError that leaves the program
running. Measured, because none of it follows from "it takes an int or a
string":

	exit("7")          prints 7                    -- a STRING is the message
	exit(true)         status, nothing printed     -- an INT arm
	exit(null)         Deprecated: ... of type string|int is deprecated
	exit(1.5)          Deprecated: Implicit conversion ... loses precision
	exit(new S)        prints [S]                  -- __toString takes the string arm
	exit(new stdClass) TypeError: exit(): Argument #1 ($status) must be of type string|int, stdClass given
	die([1])           the same TypeError, naming exit() -- and the program carries on

`CoerceInternalArgument` does not parse a union: it passed `string|int` straight
through, so the first version lost both the deprecation and the TypeError. The
arm selection is written out here instead, and union coercion is now a TODO of
its own rather than a thing half-done.

**Two collisions the new feature exposed.**

`exit(3)` was graded `unsupported`. Exit code 3 is how a generated program
reports a capability gap, and a PHP program can pick its own status -- so the
signal and the program's own answer were the same byte. The harness now requires
the code **and** the stderr marker `php2go: unsupported:`, which only the
generated program writes. A private channel that a program can forge is not a
channel.

`errored` went to 1: `globals[...] = &p_x_t11` where the slot holds an `int`.
The globals table takes `*php.Value`, and a compiler temporary -- a loop
counter, a string builder -- is not a global at all. That registration never had
a type test; `exit` working simply let a file reach the emitter that has one.
The locals map added last tick had the test, so the two now agree. `errored` is
back to 0, and it is the bucket that caught it.

Fixture `exit_and_die.php`. Local fixtures 143/143.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1397 passing: one opcode, two symbol tables

	1381 passed / 677 failed / 1852 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%
	1397 passed / 667 failed / 1846 unsupported / 0 errored   67.7%

Passing-set diff **+16 / -0**, and `failed` fell by **10** -- three of the four
changes here are wrong answers removed, not features added. The rate moved for
the first time in several ticks.

Went in for `ZEND_ADD_ARRAY_UNPACK` (10 files) and found two live wrong answers
next to it.

**`[...$a]` in an array literal** was not lowered at all. Measured rather than
assumed, because the rules are not the ones a merge would give:

	[...[PHP_INT_MAX => "m"], ...[1]]   [0 => "m", 1 => 1]
	[...["x" => 1], "x" => 2]           ["x" => 2]
	[...gen()]                          drains the generator, keys and all
	[...$int]        Error:     Only arrays and Traversables can be unpacked, int given
	[...$stdClass]   TypeError: Only arrays and Traversables can be unpacked, stdClass given

Integer keys **renumber** and string keys keep their name, so the saturation
question an ordinary append has does not arise. The two refusals are different
*classes*, which is the kind of thing only the engine tells you.

**`$GLOBALS["g"]` inside a function read the local `$g`.** The FETCH family is
one opcode for two questions and only `extended_value` separates them. Read
back by harvesting both shapes in one function:

	@$u              ZEND_FETCH_R CONST UNUSED TMP  4     local
	$$n              ZEND_FETCH_R CV    UNUSED TMP  4     local
	$GLOBALS["g"]    ZEND_FETCH_R CONST UNUSED TMP  2     global
	$GLOBALS["h"]=1  ZEND_FETCH_W CONST UNUSED VAR  2     global

The globals map built for `global $g` is already the file body's slots by
address, so a global fetch reaches exactly what `global` reaches. One attribute
on the instruction, two cases in the emitter.

**`isset($$n)` and `isset($GLOBALS["g"])` were always true.** Both put the
*name* in op1, and both were answered by asking whether that string is set. The
opcode is what separates them from `isset($x)` -- `ISSET_ISEMPTY_CV` takes a
slot, `ISSET_ISEMPTY_VAR` takes a name -- and the operand spelling cannot,
because the name arrives as a CV for `$$n` and as a literal for `$GLOBALS[...]`.
My first attempt branched on the spelling and got `$$n` exactly backwards.

**Then mem2reg ate a store.** Making a *global* dynvar no longer opaque to
promotion -- correctly, since it names another frame's table -- exposed this:

	%2:place = dynvar.ref "g", mode=W, scope=global
	call.intrinsic "write_var"(%2, 2)     <- gone after promotion

`promotable` recorded the target of every store, and the target here is an
**SSA place value**, not a named slot. `%2` then had stores and no reads, so the
promotion dropped the store and substituted nothing: the write vanished from the
emitted body. One line -- only a `$`-prefixed name is a place -- and it is a
latent bug that was simply unreachable before, because every other write through
a place value goes through `store` rather than `write_var`.

Two rules worth keeping from this:

- **A refusal that gates an optimisation is load-bearing.** `frameIsOpaque`
  refusing promotion for `dynvar.*` was hiding the mem2reg bug, not preventing
  it. Narrowing a conservative guard is how you find what it was covering.
- **Where two questions share an opcode, the operand cannot answer.** Twice in
  one tick -- the fetch scope and the isset form -- the distinguishing fact was
  in `extended_value` or in the opcode name, and both times the shape of the
  operand looked like it would do and did not.

Fixture `globals_and_unpack.php`. Local fixtures 142/142.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1381 passing: a variable variable needs the names at run time

	1364 passed / 669 failed / 1877 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%
	1381 passed / 677 failed / 1852 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%

Passing-set diff **+17 / -0**; 25 files out of `unsupported`. `dynvar.get` and
`dynvar.ref` with a **computed** name -- `$$n`, `${$x}` -- were the largest
compiler-side head that is not Reflection, a Fiber or the library surface.

The literal-named half already worked: `@$r` compiles to a fetch by name rather
than to a CV, and that name is an ordinary local. What was refused is the half
that gives the family its name.

**The map is a second view, not a second store.** A body that names a variable
at run time now builds `map[string]*php.Value` at entry, one entry per slot,
holding the **address** of the Go variable. So `$$n = 2` writes through the map
and `$b` reads the Go variable and they cannot disagree -- there is one slot
with two ways in. A name no slot answers to is created in the map alone, which
is what `$$n` can do that nothing else can.

`bindGlobal` already worked this way for `global $g`, and at the file level the
two are the same thing: **for `{main}` the map *is* `globals`**, because the
file body's variables are the globals and `$$n` at top level has to reach the
slot `global $n` reaches.

Three things had to be right, and the fixture found the first:

- **The test for which slots go in the map is the *Go* type, not the IR type.**
  Keyed on `ptypes[name] == "zval"`, a slot nothing writes *directly* was
  skipped -- and `$b`, written only through `$$n = 2`, is exactly that. The map
  then created a slot of its own and `var_dump($b)` printed the undefined Go
  variable beside it. One name, two slots, which is the failure this design
  exists to prevent.
- **Reading must not create.** `dynvarGet` looks the name up and reads a zero
  value when it is absent, rather than going through `dynvarSlot`; otherwise
  `@$$missing` would bring `$missing`'s target into existence and the second
  read would be silent where PHP warns again.
- **A place holding an iterator or a string builder is not a variable.** Those
  are the compiler's own bookkeeping and no name can reach them, so the Go-type
  test excludes them for the same reason it includes `$b`.

Refused, and named rather than left to look like the general case: a computed
dynvar in a **resumable** body. The map is rebuilt at every entry from the
frame's fields, so a name it created rather than found would not survive a
`yield` -- a variable that silently disappears, which is a wrong answer and not
a missing feature.

Still open in the same area: `extract`, `compact` and `get_defined_vars` are
library functions and refused; a variable whose name is not a Go identifier --
`${"\0"}` -- is still refused by name, though the map is now the mechanism that
could hold one.

Fixture `variable_variables.php`. Local fixtures 141/141.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1364 passing: instanceof never matched an interface

	1363 passed / 670 failed / 1877 unsupported / 0 errored   67.0%
	1364 passed / 669 failed / 1877 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%

Passing-set diff **+1 / -0**, and the one file is `anon/002`. A near-flat tick
for a defect that was neither small nor rare, so the number is the least
interesting thing here.

Started by checking what the previous tick's TODO entry asked: whether class
constants, statics and interfaces have the same unlinked-entry problem the
property table did, for a class declared at run time. They do not -- constants
and statics resolve through tables the parent chain is walked over at emit
time, and methods through the run-time dispatcher. The probe answered that in
one file.

What it also showed was `Eager instanceof I` returning **false**, and `Eager` is
linked at compile time. So the run-time-declaration question was a red herring
and the real finding was underneath it:

	interface A {}
	interface B extends A {}
	class C implements B {}
	$c instanceof B     false, want true
	$c instanceof A     false, want true

**`instanceOf` walked only `parentOf`.** The declared hierarchy is not a chain:
a class has one parent but any number of interfaces, and each of those may
extend any number more. A `for c = parentOf[c]` loop can express the first and
none of the rest, so every interface test answered false -- and `catch
(SomeInterface $e)` never caught. The interface table was sitting in the same
generated file the whole time, emitted for **class-constant lookup only**.

Now a work list over `parentOf[c]` plus `interfacesOf[c]`, with one change to
the throwable arm: it used to `return php.ThrowableIsA(c, class)`, ending the
walk. A no from the engine's hierarchy is not a no overall -- an interface this
program declared may still be on the list -- so it now only short-circuits on a
yes.

**Why the corpus barely moved.** 38 corpus files use `instanceof` at all, and
15 of those are still `unsupported` for other reasons. Of the rest, most test
`instanceof` against a *class*, which already worked. The fix is a wrong answer
removed rather than a feature added, and its value is in what it stops
producing.

That is worth stating as a measurement rule of its own: **a correctness fix can
be broad and still move nothing**, because the corpus reaches a defect only
through files that clear every other gap first. Reading `+1` as "small fix"
would be the wrong conclusion, and reading it as "no fix" would be worse.

Fixture `instanceof_interfaces.php`: a diamond of interfaces, a class
implementing one at each level of a three-deep chain, a `catch` naming an
interface, and one reached only through a run-time-declared class. Local
fixtures 140/140.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1363 passing: one rule, two sites, and the second never learned it

	1360 passed / 667 failed / 1883 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%
	1363 passed / 670 failed / 1877 unsupported / 0 errored   67.0%

Passing-set diff **+3 / -0**; 6 files out of `unsupported`. Small by count, and
both defects are wrong-answer bugs rather than missing features.

**`++self::$n` lost its class.** `intrinsic sprop.ref wants a class argument the
IR does not carry`, 13 files. The incdec lowering handles the object and static
forms together, and for a static property the operands are the other way round:
op1 is the property **name** and op2 the **class**, which arrives as a
fetch-class code rather than an operand. `l.operand` answers `""` for one *and
reports success*, so the place was built with an empty class.

The neighbouring `ASSIGN_*_OP` path already carries a comment about exactly
this:

	// For a static property op2 is the **class**, and it arrives as a
	// fetch-class code rather than an operand -- `l.operand` returns ""
	// for it, which silently produced `sprop.ref "count", ,`.

One rule, two sites, and the second was written without it. The lesson is not
about fetch-class codes: **an accessor that answers "" and true for an operand
that is not there** will keep producing this, because the caller's `if !ok`
never fires. Every reader of `l.operand` on an op2 that may be UNUSED is a
candidate.

**A class declared at run time inherited nothing.** Fixing the first bug turned
`bug39721` from `unsupported` into a wrong answer, which is how the second
surfaced:

	Deprecated: Creation of dynamic property test2_child::$instance is deprecated

The harvest flattens a child's property table -- an inherited property listed
with its declaring class -- for a class the engine linked at **compile** time.
`if (is_object($foo)) { class test2_child extends test2 {} }` is a
DECLARE_CLASS, linked when it runs, so the entry is unlinked and the flattening
never happened. Writing an inherited property was then a *dynamic* one.

`inheritAncestorPrivates` already walked the chain for the one thing the
flattening deliberately omits -- an ancestor's private, a real slot the child
cannot name. Widening it to everything the child's table lacks answers both,
and it is now `inheritAncestorProps`. Two things had to be right, and the
fixture found both:

**A private is one slot per declaring class; protected and public share one
slot however many classes redeclare it.** Keying every slot by declaring class
made `class Sharer extends Base` with its own `$shared` and `$open` carry
Base's copies as well -- five properties dumped for a three-property object.

**Slot order is strict declaration order along the chain**, and prepending the
ancestors' entries as a block only looks right when the private happens to be
declared first. `private_slots.php` has exactly that shape, which is why the
old code passed it; a `Base` declaring `public $open` before `private $hidden`
does not. So the table is now **rebuilt from the chain** rather than patched:
each ancestor contributes what it declared, in its own order, and a class that
redeclares a shared property takes the ancestor's position with its own value.

Fixture `runtime_declared_class.php`: eager and lazy subclasses of one Base
dumped side by side, a redeclaring subclass, and the three static-property
incdec forms. Local fixtures 139/139.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1360 passing: three coercion rules behind one opcode

	1354 passed / 663 failed / 1893 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%
	1360 passed / 667 failed / 1883 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%

Passing-set diff **+6 / -0**; 10 files out of `unsupported`. A small tick by
count, and three of the four changes are general rules rather than anything
about the opcode that exposed them.

`emit: strlen` sat at 11 files and `emit: get_type` at 5. Neither is a library
function: **the compiler specializes a handful of calls into their own
opcodes**, so they never reach the library table and need an implementation on
this side of it. `count`, `bool` and `type_check` were already intrinsics;
`strlen` and `gettype` had no catalogue entry at all.

`gettype` is a table, with one thing worth pinning: it answers in the **old
vocabulary** -- `integer`, `double`, `boolean`, `NULL` -- where every diagnostic
in `runtime/php` says `int`, `float`, `bool`, `null`. Two vocabularies, and
`get_debug_type` is the function that gives the other.

`strlen` is where the work was. It is **not** a length with rules of its own:

	strlen("abc")      int(3)
	strlen(123)        int(3)
	strlen(new S)      int(5)     -- S::__toString
	strlen([1])        TypeError: strlen(): Argument #1 ($string) must be of type string, array given
	strlen(null)       Deprecated: strlen(): Passing null to parameter #1 ($string) of type string is deprecated
	                   int(0)

Every row is `CoerceInternalArgument` to `string`. So the intrinsic calls the
coercion rather than reimplementing it -- and then three rows of it did not
work, none of them specific to `strlen`:

**Null to a non-nullable scalar parameter of an internal function deprecates,
it does not throw.** The allowance comes from the ZPP macros that coerce, so it
stops at `bool|int|float|string` -- `object`, `array` and a class type refuse
null outright, and `strict_types=1` removes the difference. The interpreter had
this rule; `CoerceInternalArgument`, whose whole reason to exist is being the
internal-callee coercion, did not.

**And ZPP writes the type's zero into the parameter**, so the callee never sees
the null. `coerce` refuses null for a non-nullable type -- correctly, for a
userland callee -- so it cannot be reused for the value. Measured, including a
union:

	strlen(null)              int(0)      -- ""
	str_repeat("ab", null)    string(0)   -- 0
	round(null)               float(0)    -- int|float takes the float arm

**An object with `__toString` satisfies a `string` parameter in weak mode**, and
`coerceString` had no object arm at all. That is not a `strlen` bug: it made
every user function fail too --

	class S { function __toString() { return "hello"; } }
	function u(string $x) { var_dump($x); }
	u(new S);

was `must be of type string, S given` where PHP prints `string(5) "hello"`. An
object *without* one still falls through to the TypeError naming the class,
which is what the engine does, and a `__toString` that **throws** is that throw
rather than a coercion failure.

That last one is why the gained files are what they are: `concat_002`,
`heredoc_015/016` and `nowdoc_016` have nothing to do with `strlen`.

`coerce` is reached only from the exported `Coerce*` functions and the
interpreter calls none of them, so this is compiler-side despite living in the
shared package -- checked rather than assumed.

Fixture `compiled_opcodes_strlen_gettype.php`. Local fixtures 138/138.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1354 passing: a constant array is not a composite literal

	1335 passed / 666 failed / 1909 unsupported / 0 errored   66.7%
	1354 passed / 663 failed / 1893 unsupported / 0 errored   67.1%

Passing-set diff **+19 / -0**; 16 out of `unsupported` and 3 that were `failed`.
The whole `ns_077_*` family and most of `bug43344_*`.

`unrenderable operand <lit:0>` was 23 files, and all of them were a constant
array in a deferred initializer -- `function f($a = array(bar => 0))`.

**A helper that was referenced and never emitted.** `constexpr.go` rendered
`constArray(ctx, []php.Value{...})` for an `array` node, and no such function
was ever printed into the generated program. It had never fired, because it
read the children as *values* and they are `element` nodes -- so the refusal
that hid it was also what kept it from being an `errored`. Two defects
cancelling out is not a state to leave alone: the first one to be fixed would
have turned the second into a build failure.

What an element actually carries, and why none of it fits a Go composite
literal:

- **A key is separate from its presence.** `[null => 1]` has a key and it is
  null; `[1]` has none. One `hasKey` field, and the AST holds value-then-key
  while evaluation goes key-first -- `[UNKNOWN_KEY => UNKNOWN_VALUE]` reports
  the key.
- **Appending can fail.** When the largest integer key is taken there is no
  next one, and the engine says `Cannot add element to the array as the next
  element is already occupied` rather than wrapping.
- **A spread renumbers integer keys and keeps string ones**, and a constant
  expression is evaluated before there is anything to iterate, so unlike the
  runtime opcode it takes arrays only.

So the entries are a slice of `constEntry` and the array is built in a loop.

**An undefined constant in an initializer throws, and the old comment said
otherwise.** `mustConstant` returned null, reasoning that "the engine leaves
such a constant undefined rather than inventing a value". That is what the
engine does at *compile* time. What the program sees is:

	function f($a = unknown) { return $a; }
	f()    Error: Undefined constant "unknown"
	f(1)   int(1)

-- it throws, and only when the initializer runs. The unqualified-inside-a-
namespace fallback to the global name comes with it, and the refusal names the
**namespaced** form, which is what the engine reports even though it looked in
two places.

**Then the position and the trace were both wrong, and for the same reason.**
`ns_077_1` still differed by one trace line and a line number:

	want  Undefined constant "unknown" in FILE:3      #0 FILE(7): foo\foo()   #1 {main}
	got   Undefined constant "unknown" in FILE:8      #0 {main}

Line 8 is the *call*; line 3 is where the default is written. A constant
expression is evaluated with the reported position moved to its declaration --
the harvest carries that line on the `Expr` node -- so the initializer now
renders inside a `constAt` that sets the location and restores it.

The missing frame is more general than constant expressions. `php.Raise` takes
no ctx and records no stack; that is invisible until a failure is raised
**inside a call whose frame the unwind drops** before anyone materialises it. A
deferred initializer runs in the callee, so the frame was gone by the time the
error became an object. `php.AttachStack(ctx, err)` fills in position and trace
on an error that recorded none, and every `ParkError` site in the emitted
program goes through it or through `RaiseAt`. An error that already knows where
it was keeps what it has: the first site to know is the right one.

Left in this family: `constBinary` still omits every operator that can
diagnose, so `PHP_EOL === "\n"` in a default is refused and `self::A - self::B`
on arrays prints nothing where PHP raises `Unsupported operand types`. The
runtime (non-constant) array literal does not check saturation either --
`[PHP_INT_MAX => 42, new stdClass]` builds a two-element array where PHP
refuses.

Fixture `const_array_initializers.php`. Local fixtures 137/137.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1335 passing: a census head that named the wrong thing

	1306 passed / 644 failed / 1960 unsupported / 0 errored   67.0%
	1335 passed / 666 failed / 1909 unsupported / 0 errored   66.7%

Passing-set diff **+29 / -0**; 51 files left `unsupported`, 29 of them passing
and 22 now honestly `failed`. Almost all of the gain is `generators/`.

The census head read:

	80  emit: unrenderable operand

with nothing after it. Eighty files, and the reason ended mid-sentence -- the
refusal names the operand, and the operand was **empty**. Naming the operand
said nothing at all, so the first change was to the measuring instrument: an
empty operand now reports `empty operand to <opcode>`. `operand()` has no error
return, so the opcode is parked on the emitter as each instruction starts.

That turned one uninformative head into two real ones, and 79 of the 80 were
the same thing:

	39  empty operand to frame.set_state
	 1  empty operand to get_class

**`frame.set_state` was a red herring, and instructively so.** It renders its
operand directly and never calls `operand()`. What it was, was the last
*instruction* of a block whose **terminator** could not render -- `e.op` is set
per instruction and a terminator comes after the last one. The CPS pass appends
`frame.set_state` just before rewriting a terminator, so it sat in front of
every one of them.

The terminator was `ret.yield` with nothing to yield: **`yield;`**. The opline's
op1 is `IS_UNUSED` and the lowering carries no operand for it rather than a
null, so the absence had to be read where the terminator renders. Asked the
engine rather than assuming:

	function g() { $a = yield; yield; yield 5; }
	  key 0, current NULL      -- next automatic key, NULL value
	  key 1, current NULL
	  key 2, current int(5)

So a bare yield is `yield null` in every observable respect, and the automatic
key keeps counting. One case in the terminator renderer.

`get_class()` with **no argument** was the other one, and it is not the
receiver's class: measured, a `foo2 extends foo` calling an inherited `bar()`
that does `get_class()` reports `foo`. It is the class the call was *compiled*
in -- `e.scope` -- with a deprecation since 8.3, and an `Error` outside a class.

	Deprecated: Calling get_class() without arguments is deprecated
	string(3) "foo"
	Error: get_class() without arguments must be called from within a class

The lesson is about the census rather than about generators. **A refusal that
quotes a value has to say what to do when the value is empty**, or it hides the
largest cluster in the tail behind a reason nobody can read. This one had been
sitting at the head of the list for weeks.

Fixture `bare_yield.php`: a bare yield's key and value, one reached as a
half-built call's argument (`new Foo(yield)`, which is what makes the frame have
to survive the suspension), and the three `get_class()` shapes. Local fixtures
136/136.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1306 passing: a deferred initializer had no way out of the IR

	1271 passed / 628 failed / 2011 unsupported / 0 errored   66.9%
	1306 passed / 644 failed / 1960 unsupported / 0 errored   67.0%

Passing-set diff **+35 / -0**. 51 files left `unsupported`: 35 passed and 16 are
now honestly `failed`. The whole `prop_const_expr` family moved, and with it
`ns_034/050/052/057/058`, `class_constants_002`, `constant_expressions_arrays`
and the enum-as-constant tests.

`const A_name = A::Case->name;` refused with `unrenderable operand <lit>`. The
refusal was right and the cause was two levels up.

**A literal that is not a value.** `LiteralText` renders an opline literal as
IR operand text, and for the one kind that is a *tree* -- `KIND_EXPR`, an
initializer the compiler could not fold because it names something that may not
exist yet -- it answered `<lit>`. Not a spelling: a shrug. Every consumer then
had a hole with nothing behind it, and `internal/gogen/constexpr.go` -- which
already renders such a tree for a class constant and a property default -- had
no way to get at one from an instruction.

So the operand now indexes it: `Function.Literals` carries the harvested
literal and the operand spells `<lit:N>`. The `<...>` stays, because nothing
should mistake it for a value; the index is the part that was missing. One
lowering hook (`constText`), one emitter case, and `declare_const` -- which is
where these actually appear -- renders through the evaluator that was already
there.

**Then the evaluator turned out to handle 6 node kinds where the interpreter
handles 18.** Ported the ones the corpus asks for: `prop`/`nullsafe_prop`,
`dim`, `new`, `conditional`, `coalesce`, `negate`/`identity`. Four things had to
be got right, and three of them are about *what does not run*:

**The short circuit is a value.** `?->` on null skips the rest of the chain,
and "the rest of the chain" includes the expression naming the next property:
`(null)?->{new Printer}` never builds the Printer. The interpreter carries that
on a flag (`unit.constShortCircuit`); an emitter rendering an expression has
nowhere to put a flag, so it travels as an **undef** -- distinct from null,
which is what the chain answers when it ends. `constEnd` turns one back into
null at the end of a chain, and a chain node in a container position renders
unwrapped so the undef can travel. Nothing else in a constant expression
produces an undef, so this cannot hide one.

**A thunk, not an argument.** For the same reason, the property name and the
array index are `func() php.Value` rather than values: rendering them as Go
arguments evaluates them before `constProp` can decline to. That is the
difference between printing `Printer` and not.

**The branches of a conditional are not both taken.** `new Printer ? 1 : 0`
builds one Printer, and a Go expression with both arms inline builds it either
way, so the arms are a closure. That is also what makes `a ?: b` -- the middle
left out of the AST -- answer with the condition itself.

**A failure stops the chain.** First version parked the error and returned
null, and `lhs_class_not_found` then reported `Warning: Attempt to read
property "prop" on null` where PHP reports `Class "A" not found` -- the second
diagnostic, from reading a property on the null the failed `new` left behind.
PHP reports only the first. So a parked error answers with the same undef `?->`
uses, and the rest of the chain declines to speak.

Two smaller corrections found the same way, by running the family rather than
by reading the code:

- The property **name is converted before the container is judged**:
  `(new A)->{new B}` reports the object that cannot be a name, not the container
  that cannot be read. It goes through `php.ToString`, which can throw.
- A `dim` on an object is refused **before the index is evaluated**. An enum
  case may implement ArrayAccess, but a constant expression cannot call a
  method, so the engine refuses outright -- and it refuses first, so an
  undefined constant in the index is never reported.

Still refused, and each for a reason rather than for want of a case:
`enum case value <lit>` needs the backing-type check deferred too, because
`enumValueFault` reads the value's *text* to decide `int` against `string`;
`static_initalizer` is `ZEND_BIND_INIT_STATIC_OR_JMP`, a lowering gap.
`constBinary` still omits every operator that can diagnose, which is why
`self::BAR - self::BAR` on arrays prints nothing where PHP raises
`Unsupported operand types`.

Fixture `deferred_const_expressions.php`. Local fixtures 135/135.
## 2026-09-10 -- 1271 passing: named arguments bind at the call site

	1267 passed / 628 failed / 2015 unsupported / 0 errored   66.9%
	1271 passed / 628 failed / 2011 unsupported / 0 errored   66.9%

Passing-set diff **+4 / -0** -- `cannot_pass_by_ref`, `ctor_extra_named_args`,
`duplicate_param`, `required_param_after_optional_named_args`. The rate is flat
because four files moved out of `unsupported` and all four passed; the count is
what moved.

`f(b: 2, a: 1)` was refused with `named argument`, the last of the call
conventions this emitter did not have.

**Where the binding belongs.** The engine sends a named argument *under its
name* and lets the callee's RECV opcodes claim it. The emitted call protocol is
a positional `[]php.Value`, so either the names travel to run time -- a second
channel beside `args`, on every emitted function -- or the binding happens at
the call site. The call site is possible only if reordering the sends is
unobservable, and it is: the lowering computes every argument into an SSA value
*before* the call node, so `f(b: g(), a: h())` has already run `g()` then `h()`
by the time the send list is read. Reordering the list reorders nothing.

That leaves one thing the call site must know that the engine does not need to:
**who the callee is**. So the emitter now indexes every body the program
declares (`collectCallees`), keyed `fn:<name>` and `<class>::<method>`, with the
method table **flattened down the parent chain** -- the harvest does not
flatten it, so `new Child(x: 1)` reaching an inherited constructor would
otherwise find no signature at all.

Four call sites can name their callee, and each is refused where it cannot:

| site | how the callee is found |
| --- | --- |
| `call.fn` | the literal name |
| `call.static` | the class operand, plus `self`/`static` |
| `call.ctor` | the class `new` made the object from, recorded by `new` |
| `call.method` | only when **every** declaration of the name agrees |

The method rule is the one worth stating. A method call's callee is a run-time
fact -- the receiver's class decides it, and an override may spell its
parameters differently, so binding by one declaration would be a guess.
Agreement across all of them makes it not a guess: whichever declaration the
receiver reaches, the name lands in the same position. A program with `__call`
anywhere is excluded, because a trampoline can answer for a name no class
declares.

**A skipped parameter is an undef, not a null.** `f(a: 1, c: 3)` leaves a hole
where `$b` would be, and the slice has to carry it: everything after the hole is
still positional. `php.Value{}` is that hole -- the zero Value is `KindUndef`,
which is exactly "not passed" -- and `recv` reads it back with
`!args[N].IsUndef()`. That is what makes the default apply.

**Required is by position, not by default.** `function f($a = 1, $b)`
deprecates at compile time and then treats `$a` as required too, so `f(b: 2)`
reports `ArgumentCountError: f(): Argument #1 ($a) not passed` -- the default is
compiled into the body and never applied. `RequiredParams` already carried that
(it is `zend_op_array.required_num_args`), so `recv` checks the *position*
against it rather than looking for a default.

The check fires **only on a hole**, not on a short slice. Too few positional
arguments still bind null, which is a different diagnostic --
`Too few arguments to function f(), 0 passed in FILE on line L and exactly 2
expected` -- and a wider change than this one. It stays in TODO.md.

**Asked the engine for all four messages** rather than reading them off the
opcode handlers, and two were not what a guess would give:

	f(zz: 5)      Error: Unknown named parameter $zz          -- names no function
	f(1, a: 2)    Error: Named parameter $a overwrites previous argument
	f(e: 42)      Error: test(): Argument #2 ($e) could not be passed by reference
	f(a:1, d:'d') ArgumentCountError: t3(): Argument #2 ($b) not passed

The first names no callee where every other argument diagnostic in
`diagnostics.go` is prefixed with one, and the second is the same message for a
name colliding with a *positional* argument as for one colliding with another
name.

**All three failures are Errors the program can catch**, so none of them is a
refusal. They are emitted as a prelude that throws, leaving the call itself
inside the `else` it opens -- unreached, but still rendered. That last part bit:
the first version returned the *original* item list alongside the throw, and
`1 as "b"` is not a Go expression, so a file that should have thrown a catchable
Error failed to build instead. `stripNames` drops the names on that path.

Four refusals replace the one, each naming what is missing rather than the
feature:

- `named argument to an unknown callee` (6 files at the head) -- a closure, a
  first-class callable, `__invoke`, and **every library function**: a builtin's
  parameter names live in the harvested arginfo and never reach
  `internal/gogen`. Plumbing `Manifest.builtins` through covers the library half
  in one step.
- `named argument with unpacking` -- which positions are free is a run-time fact
  about the unpacked array.
- `named argument to a variadic` -- an unclaimed name reaches the variadic under
  a **string key**, which a positional slice cannot carry.
- `named by-reference argument to an unnamed callee` -- several classes agreed
  on a signature without agreeing on a name, and the message quotes the class.

Fixture `named_arguments.php` covers reordering, a hole taking its default, a
method, a static method, a constructor, and all four diagnostics. Local
fixtures 134/134.

Passing-set diff **+20 / -0**; 44 files left `unsupported`. Two census entries

**`$obj->$name`** -- a computed property name -- was refused because the `lit`

### The fourth `undefined: p_this`, and the fix the first three should have been

Fixing that produced `undefined: p_this` -- for the **fourth** time in a week.
Each earlier one was fixed at its site by reaching for `objOperand`; this time I
went looking and found two more waiting (`$this instanceof X`, `$this::class`).

`$this` can appear in **any** value position, so the renderer is where it
belongs. `operand` and `rawOperand` handle it now, and the per-site list is
gone. That immediately surfaced the case none of the sites had: `isset($this)`
in a **static** method, where there is no receiver parameter at all and PHP
answers false -- so it renders as undef rather than as a name that does not
exist.

Three fixes, one cause, and the cause was that a rule lived in the callers.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1233 passing: the gate refused what the answer already knew

Nothing was missing from the *implementation*. The emitted `instanceOf` already
walks into the engine's hierarchy and hands off to `php.ThrowableIsA`, which
answers about the `Throwable` interface. What refused it was the **gate** in
front: `e.defined` is seeded from `ThrowableClasses()`, which iterates
`throwableParents` -- a map of class to parent, so the interface is not in it.

Two questions wearing one list. A consumer asking what it may **instantiate**
wants the classes; one asking what `instanceof` can **test** wants the interface
too. `ThrowableNames` and `IsThrowableName` are the second question, and the
comment on each says which is which -- `IsThrowableClass` deliberately still
answers no to the interface, because a class is what *it* is asked about.

Worth noticing how this hid: the refusal message named the class, which reads
like "this class is not implemented", and the implementation was there the whole

## 2026-09-10 -- 1222 passing: the casts, and the only place a mangled name shows

	1194 passed / 556 failed / 2160 unsupported / 0 errored   68.2%
	1222 passed / 573 failed / 2115 unsupported / 0 errored   68.1%

Passing-set diff **+28 / -0**, the largest tick since the Closure surface; 45
files left `unsupported`. `(int)`, `(float)`, `(array)`, `(object)` and
`(unset)` all reached the emitter as opcodes it refused by name -- the
specialize table said so in a comment: *"The other casts have no implementation
yet and stay opcodes."*

Most of the value semantics were already in `Value.Int` and `Value.Float`,
including the ones nobody would guess -- `(int)"1.0E+121"` saturates where
`(int)1.0E+121` is 0, and `(float)"-0"` keeps the sign. What was missing was the
**object** rule, which is a warning and not an Error:

	(int)$obj    Object of class C could not be converted to int, then int(1)
	(string)$obj Error, because __toString is a thing an object can have

### `(array)` is where a mangled name becomes visible

	var_dump((array)new C)   ->   ["a"], ["\0*\0b"], ["\0C\0c"]

The storage keeps the plain name -- only a *shadowed* private is mangled there
-- so the cast has to mangle on the way out, `*` for protected and the
declaring class for private. This is the one construct that shows those names
to a program, which is why the fixture pins all three visibilities rather than
the public one that would have passed either way.

`(object)` splits the way `clone` does: `runtime/php` builds the property table
and the generated unit numbers the handle.

### Two tables that had to be told

The catalogue test refused the new functions until they had entries, and
`TestIntrinsicForNamesRealOpcodes` then refused three of the *names*: the cast
opcodes are built as `"to."+target` from `ZEND_CAST`'s extended_value, so a
scan for literals cannot see them and they have to be declared unary. Both
tests earned their keep -- between them they would have caught a cast wired to
nothing, and a name that matched nothing.

### A fixture that had to avoid an unrelated gap

`var_dump((object)...)` differs on the **handle number**, which is the
object-lifetime gap and not this work. The fixture dumps `(array)(object)...`
instead and says why, rather than leaving a case that fails for a reason it does
not test.

## 2026-09-10 -- 1194 passing: readonly is asymmetric visibility, and is not it

	1180 passed / 543 failed / 2187 unsupported / 0 errored   68.5%
	1194 passed / 556 failed / 2160 unsupported / 0 errored   68.2%

Passing-set diff **+14 / -0**; 27 files left `unsupported`. PHP 8.4's
`public private(set) int $x`, refused at class level in 29 files.

The read half is the first modifier and the write half is the `(set)` one, with
its own message naming the modifier and the calling scope:

	$o->a = 5   ->   Cannot modify private(set) property C::$a from global scope

### The trap the old refusal was already half-aware of

`cmd/php2gotest` refused `pr.GetSetVisibility() != "" && !pr.GetReadonly()` --
the `!Readonly` was there because **the engine reports `protected(set)` for
every readonly property**. Readonly *is* modelled as asymmetric visibility, and
that is why its diagnostic reads `Cannot modify protected(set) readonly
property`.

So carrying the harvested field through unfiltered would have refused a
readonly property's first write with the wrong message, before the readonly
rules ever ran -- two rules for one write, and the loud one wrong. The filter
moved from the refusal into `setVisibilityOf`, and the fixture pins both: an
explicit asymmetry refuses **any** outside write, readonly refuses the
**second** write from anywhere.

The two are close enough that the check order matters as much as the messages,
and both are written down where the code makes the choice.

## 2026-09-09 -- 1171 passing: `f(...)` is a call node nobody performs

	1163 passed / 525 failed / 2222 unsupported / 0 errored   68.9%
	1171 passed / 531 failed / 2208 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%

syntax, 34 files.

The lowering's own comment calls `ZEND_CALLABLE_CONVERT` *"the neatest proof
that the three-phase stream describes a call node rather than executing one"* --
it pops a pending call and never performs it. The emitter's job is to turn that
node into the callable it is equivalent to, and then **every shape goes through
`callValue`**, which already knows all of them:

	plain(...)     ->  "plain"          a function name
	$o->m(...)     ->  [$o, "m"]        an instance callable
	C::s(...)      ->  ["C", "s"]       a static one
	count(...)     ->  "count"          a builtin, same as the first

No second dispatcher, because the receiver-versus-class-name question is one
`callValue` already asks. A namespaced `f(...)` picks between its two names at
**emit** time, since the program's own function table is known then.

	go build: undefined: p_this

`$this->m(...)` names the method's own receiver, which is a **parameter** and
not a local slot. `e.operand` renders locals; `e.objOperand` exists precisely
for this and I did not reach for it. That is the fourth `undefined: p_this`-shaped
slip in this file's history and the second today caught only by the corpus --
the local fixtures all used a variable receiver, because that is what reads
naturally when writing an example.

`first_class_callables.php` now has the `$this` form.

`var_dump` of a first-class callable shows `function` as `C::m`, `this` for the
instance form, and a **`parameter` list taken from the target's declaration**.
The first two are set; the parameter list is not, so a test that dumps one
differs visibly and grades `failed`. That is a wrong answer rather than a gap,
and it is the honest trade for having the calls work -- recorded here rather
than discovered later.

## 2026-09-09 -- 1154 passing: `static $x` and `use ($x)` share a table, and a comment lied

	1139 passed / 501 failed / 2270 unsupported / 0 errored   69.5%
	1154 passed / 512 failed / 2244 unsupported / 0 errored   69.3%

Passing-set diff **+15 / -0**; 26 files left `unsupported`. `static $x = 5`
inside a function; 31 files.

The scope question first, because it decides the storage. Measured:

	counter()          1, 2, 3            persists across calls
	$a->m(), $b->m()   11, 12             shared by every INSTANCE
	(new D)->m()       14                 and by a subclass inheriting it

**Per function definition**, then -- not per object and not per class -- and one
emitted Go body is exactly one definition, so a package-level pair per (body,
name) is the right shape. Initialized on first entry, bound by reference so an
assignment to the local is the static's.

### The comment I trusted was wrong

`ir.proto` said of the initializer field:

> Absent for a closure's `use` variable, whose value comes from the enclosing
> scope rather than an initializer.

So I keyed on it, and `use ($cap)` bound to a fresh static holding null. The
engine keeps captures and statics in **one table** and sets the field for both.
Comment corrected in place, with what it actually does.

`ZEND_BIND_STATIC`'s `extended_value` does separate them -- captures measured
**2, 4, 5, 36, 37** against statics **1, 33, 65, 97** -- and I wrote those
numbers into the proto rather than the rule they suggest. Two disjoint sets over
nine samples is a pattern, not a specification, and "bit 2 means capture" is
precisely the kind of inference this project has been wrong about before.

What the generated program uses instead is **exact by construction**: a closure
already has a capture map that `bind_lexical` fills, so a name in it is a
capture and a name not in it is a static. No bit theory, and it degrades
correctly for a closure that has both.

## 2026-09-09 -- 1119 passing: the file body's variables *are* the globals

	1112 passed / 475 failed / 2323 unsupported / 0 errored   70.1%
	1119 passed / 482 failed / 2309 unsupported / 0 errored   69.9%

Passing-set diff **+7 / -0**; 14 files left `unsupported`. `global $g` had no
emitter case; 68 files.

The design question was where a global lives. The emitted program keeps every
local as a Go variable, so a function has no way to name one of `{main}`'s --
and PHP's globals are exactly `{main}`'s variables, not a separate namespace.
So `{main}` now **registers its slots by address** in a `globals` map at the top
of its body, before any of it runs, and `global $g` binds the function's local
to that slot by reference.

By address, and by reference: both halves are what the engine does, and the
probe shows each of them separately.

	global $g; $g = 2;        the global is 2 afterwards      -- by reference
	global $g; unset($g);     the global keeps its old value  -- the binding drops, not the global
	$g = 5 after that unset   writes a LOCAL $g

The last line is the one that would have been wrong under any design that
treated `global` as an alias for a lookup rather than a binding.

A name `{main}` never mentions has no slot to register, so `bindGlobal`
allocates one on demand -- `function f() { global $n; $n = 7; }` creates the
global, and whatever reads it later has to find that same one.

the tests that do it failed rather than lying. A program that binds and moves on

`ZEND_MAKE_REF` reads like "wrap an expression so it can be bound". I wrote it

`$a[0][] =& $a[0]` wraps a *write fetch*. There the source **is** a variable,

jobs, one opcode; the operand's type is what tells them apart.

`$q =& notRef()` emits the notice with **no MAKE_REF at all** -- the engine

`$e = ($d = &$c)` lowered to a `local.get` typed `*ref`, which reads plausibly:

`$e` kept the value it was given. Typing it `*ref` made the assignment that
consumed it an alias PHP does not have -- and it was that type, not the missing
case, that made the emitter refuse with `place of type *ref` rather than
`local.get`. A wrong type in the IR reported itself as a missing feature two
passes downstream.

records the probe rather than the conclusion, because the conclusion looks
obviously wrong from the opcode's point of view.

The obvious spelling for "read the local back" is the read intrinsic, which
**warns** about an undefined variable. The slot was written one instruction
ago, so every chained assignment would have carried a warning PHP does not

## 2026-09-09 -- 1011 passing: the same place, and the opposite decision about the box

	1002 passed / 365 failed / 2543 unsupported / 0 errored   73.3%
	1011 passed / 379 failed / 2520 unsupported / 0 errored   72.7%

23 files left `unsupported`; 9 pass, 14 fail, passing-set diff **+9 / -0**. Same
shape as the previous tick and the same reading: the rate falls because newly
graded files join the denominator, and nothing that worked stopped working.

`$r = &$a["k"]` and `$s = &$o->p` were `bind_ref to a non-local` -- **186 files
in the census**, the largest of the family the nested-write tick opened up.

### One mechanism, two opposite requirements

Both operations need the same thing from a place: the box behind its storage.
Then they want the exact opposite of each other.

	$a["x"]["y"] = 1    open the box, write through it, take it out again
	$r = &$a["k"]       open the box and leave it: it IS the reference

So `DimTarget` split into `DimRef`, which hands back the box and a release func,
and a thin `DimTarget` that takes the slot inside and lets the caller run the
release. Neither function decides; the caller does, by running the func or not.
Writing one function with a `keep bool` would have been the same mistake the
catalogue notes about `ReadDim`/`ReadDimSilent`: a boolean that changes what the
operation *means*.

### Two ways to get the box wrong

**Boxing the box.** `place.ref` hands back `ref.Slot()` -- the storage *inside*
the box -- and passing that to `BindRef` boxes it a second time. The array
element would hold box A, `$r` would hold box B, and a write through either
would be invisible to the other. `bindTo` passes a value that already holds the
box, which is the one input for which `BindRef` reuses rather than creates.

**Marking it wrong.** With the binding correct, `var_dump($a)` still printed
`int(2)` where PHP prints `&int(2)`. `AddBinding` is diagnostic accounting;
`Shared` is the marker -- and the distinction exists because php2go boxes slots
for its own reasons, and those must *not* print an `&`. It is spelled out in
`bindLexical` a few hundred lines above, from the last time someone needed it.

`php.ReadDim` cannot call a method: `runtime/php` has no dispatch. The

**With no hop installed the behaviour is unchanged**, not "throws now". That is
deliberate: the interpreter answers for indexed objects itself and never

Writing a realistic accessor was blocked three times over: `$o === null` is

## 2026-09-09 -- 983 / 359: a closure's scope is not fixed when it is written

	969 passed / 373 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   72.2%
	983 passed / 359 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   73.2%

Set diff **+14 / -0**, the largest tick of the day. `Closure::bind`, `bindTo`,
`call`, `__invoke` and `fromCallable` were all `Call to undefined method
Closure::x()`.

### How the cluster was found

The 373 sorted by *what we print* rather than what is expected: 128 begin
`got ""`, which -- by the same leading-blank rule as `want ""` -- means **we**
emit a diagnostic where PHP prints a value. Running four of them through the
emitted program showed three different fatals and one real difference, and two
of the three were `Call to undefined method Closure::...`. Grepping the 373 for
the Closure surface found 22.

Reading the first-difference *text* would not have found this: those tests fail
at `int(0)` or `foo`, which clusters with nothing.

### The scope had to become a run-time value

The obvious cut -- rebind `$this` and keep the emitted scope -- is refuted by
one line of the engine:

	$f->bindTo(new A, A::class)   int(7)      reads A's private
	$f->bindTo(new A)            "none"      same receiver, cannot

The scope argument *is* the feature. So `e.scope`, a literal baked in at emit
time everywhere else, becomes a **parameter** inside a closure body:
`scopeRef()` renders either. A generator closure carries it in its frame, since
its body runs long after the call that bound it.

`self` and `parent` stay lexical, which is a real difference from the engine and
is written down rather than half-done: following them means resolving a class
name only known at run time.

### A fatal the new feature exposed

`$this->p ?? "none"` on an inaccessible property came out a fatal. The silent
read modes were checking `ThrowInaccessibleProperty` **before** the `silent`
branch, so `isset($a->priv)` and `$a->priv ?? "d"` threw where PHP answers false
and "d". A pre-existing bug that nothing had reached, because reading an
inaccessible property through `??` is exactly what a not-quite-bound closure
does. `silent_inaccessible_read.php` pins it on its own, away from closures.

### Shared boxes on rebind

`bindTo` gives a new Closure over the same body with the capture boxes
**shared**, not copied, so `use (&$x)` still writes through to the same
variable. `closure_bindTo_preserves_used_variables` is the test that says so,
and it is in the +14.

	965 passed / 377 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   71.9%
	969 passed / 373 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   72.2%

Closure, and `[$object, "method"]` -- and not the two static ones:

the function table, so it failed as `Call to undefined function
TestClass::method()`; both now go through the static dispatcher, which is what
makes yesterday's non-static and abstract refusals reachable from a callable.

`indirect_call_from_constant` and `bug63468` came along with the two the cluster
named -- the usual sign that a missing *shape* was costing more than the tests
that mention it.

### The one that did not fall, and what it turned out to be about

`dynamic_call_non_static` expects `Non-static method Foo::bar() cannot be called
statically` for `['Foo','bar']` where `Foo` has **no `bar` at all** -- only a
`__call`. I read that as a rule about callables and was about to write it that
way. The probe says otherwise:

	global scope, ["A","bar"]     ->  Call to undefined method A::bar()
	global scope, "A::bar"        ->  Call to undefined method A::bar()
	inside B,     ["B","bar"]     ->  Non-static method B::bar() cannot be called statically
	inside C, literal C::bar()    ->  runs __call

The discriminator is not the callable form at all -- it is whether the caller
has a **compatible `$this`**. With one, the `__call` trampoline is found as a
non-static method and the static-style call refuses it; without one it is never
considered. Our callable path carries no receiver, so the case stays open and is
recorded rather than guessed at. Had I encoded "callable" as the rule it would
have passed this test and been wrong about the other three lines.

### A deliberate gap, stated

`callStaticCallable` passes the class as its own scope, so **visibility is not
checked** on this path. PHP checks it, from the scope that built the callable,
and nothing here carries one. Guessing a scope would refuse programs the engine
runs; passing the class keeps exactly the behaviour that was already there. The
comment on the function says so, and TODO carries it.

I read it as *"the read found nothing, and a static of that name exists"* and

	$d->s = 4;      Notice ... D::$s as non static   +  Creation of dynamic property
	var_dump($d->s) Notice ... D::$s as non static      int(4)
	var_dump($d->s) Notice ... D::$s as non static      int(4)

So it is a notice **in front of** the ordinary path rather than a branch in it,
which is why it also does not change what the read answers. Four rules, and
three of them are the kind that only a probe gives you:

- it names the **instance's** class -- `$this->b` on a `D extends B` says

- visibility is irrelevant: a `private static` in a parent draws it from a

- silent reads -- `isset`, `??` -- say nothing;
- `__get` suppresses it entirely.

which we emitted nowhere. Its `--INI--` sets `error_reporting=4095`, which drops

silent and re-writing a declared one that was `unset` is not a creation at all.

inherited; an engine class without the flag -- `Exception` -- deprecates like
any user class. A class with `__set` never reaches the code at all, which is why
it needs no rule of its own.

Adding a diagnostic that fires on every dynamic property write anywhere in the
corpus produced **zero** regressions, which is its own measurement: the absence
was uniform.

### An abstract method is reachable, and calling one has its own Error

`cmd/php2gotest` skipped abstract methods with the note *"nothing to call, since
a class with one cannot be instantiated"*. That is true of instantiation and
false of the call: `C::foo()` on an abstract class, `parent::inst()` from a
subclass that overrode it, and -- the case nothing would have suggested --
`Foo::bar()` on an **interface declaring `__callStatic` abstract**, which makes
every name it would have trampolined an abstract call under *that* name.

So the name is now carried without a body, resolved up the parent chain **and
across the interfaces**, and dropped wherever a concrete body answers.

### The two refusals quote opposite spellings

	T::METH()  on `abstract static function Meth`  ->  Cannot call abstract method T::Meth()
	$x->CAMEL()  on `private function Camel`       ->  Call to private method X::CAMEL()

The abstract one quotes the **declaration**; the visibility one quotes the
**call site**. Two refusals about the same call, one asked of the engine three
hours after the other, and neither is derivable from the other. `methodOwnerOf`
now carries the declared spelling for exactly this.

### Non-static beats `__callStatic`

`Foo::bar()` on an instance method is legal only when the current `$this` is an
instance of the class the call named -- `parent::m()`, or `Foo::bar()` from a
`Kid extends Foo`. From an unrelated scope, or none, it is
`Non-static method Foo::Bar() cannot be called statically`.

The ordering is the load-bearing half: a class with both an instance `m()` and a
`__callStatic` **refuses** `C::m()` rather than trampolining. Putting the check
after the fallback would have passed the three tests that have no `__callStatic`
and silently kept `bug48533` wrong; it passed because the check went first.

Both refusals are raised before the frame is pushed, since PHP reports them at
the call site with nothing entered -- the rule from this morning, applied
without having to rediscover it.

## 2026-09-09 -- 957 / 385: a stack frame names the class that wrote the body

	955 passed / 387 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   71.2%
	957 passed / 385 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   71.3%

Set diff **+2 / -0**. The two defects the `RaiseAt` fix exposed an hour ago, both
in emitted frame pushes.

### The declaring class, for the fifth subsystem today

One `php2eval` probe answered every form at once, and the answer is uniform:

	(new C)->go() -> parent::who()   #1 A->who()        declaring class, arrow
	(new C)->who()                   #1 A->who()        declaring class
	C::st()                          #1 A::st()         declaring class
	new F (ctor declared in E)       #1 E->__construct()
	(new G)->nope() with __call      #1 G->__call('nope', Array)

`hasMethod` -- which already switched over exactly the right table -- became
`methodOwnerOf(class, name) (owner string, static, ok bool)`, and `hasMethod`
now calls it. One table, no duplication, and the three frame pushes read the
owner from it.

The `static` result is load-bearing and was the second thing I got wrong:
`parent::who()` is static *syntax* reaching an instance method with `$this`
still bound, and the engine renders it `A->who()`. So the separator follows the
**method's own modifier**, not the call's spelling.

### A magic call gets one frame, not two

`$g->nope()` on a class with `__call` shows only `G->__call('nope', Array)`. We
pushed a frame for `nope` first and then another inside `__call`. The fix is
ordering: decide `__call` **before** pushing anything, which means asking
`methodOwnerOf` up front -- and then asking `throwableMethod` too, so a
Throwable subclass that also declares `__call` still gets a real `getMessage()`.
That guard is the one thing here no test demanded; it is the case the
restructure would silently have broken.

### The constructor frame belongs in one arm, not the function

`callCtor` pushes a frame now, but only in the **user-class** arm. The engine
exception arm below it captures a new throwable's trace from the same stack, and
PHP captures that trace at `new`, *before* entering the constructor. A frame
pushed for the whole function would have put `__construct` into every
exception's own trace -- a wrong answer manufactured by fixing a different one.
`stack_frame_naming.php` pins that case alongside the five above.

## 2026-09-09 -- 955 / 387: private methods were callable from anywhere

	949 passed / 393 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   70.7%

Compiled code enforced **no method visibility at all**: `$a->privateMethod()`
from global scope ran the body. Found by clustering the 37 failures whose first
difference is `want "" got ...` -- an empty expected line is the blank PHP
prints before a diagnostic, so that cluster is *"we omitted a diagnostic"*, and
six of its members were this one gap.

`internal/lower` now carries `OpArray.visibility` onto `Function`, `internal/gogen`
emits a `methodVisibility` table beside the dispatch table it is built from, and
`callMethodFrom` / `callStaticFrom` take the calling scope.

### Four rules, all measured, none of them guessable

	$b->p()   on B extends A     ->  Call to private method A::p()      declaring class
	$x->CAMEL()                  ->  ... method X::CAMEL()              call-site spelling
	A::sp() private static       ->  Call to private method A::sp()     no mention of static
	private + __call             ->  routes to __call, no Error

The spelling one is the sharpest: the message quotes **how the call site wrote
the name**, not how the declaration did. So the emitter had to stop lowercasing
at the call site and lowercase only for the lookups.

The `__call` rule is what keeps this from being a regression machine: an
unreachable method falls through to `__call` exactly as an undefined one does,
and checking visibility without it turns working programs into Errors.

### Protected is measured against the prototype, not the override

The first corpus run was **945 / 397** -- seven regressions for three fixes. Two
causes, and both are the same mistake: I checked the class that holds the *body*.

`grandparent_prototype.phpt` is the shape, and its own comment names the bug it
was written for: `B` and `D` both extend `A`, `A` declares `protected test()`,
`D` overrides it, and `B::test2()` may call `$d->test()`. Owner `D` is no
relation to `B`; **prototype** `A` is. So the table carries three strings --
the class the message names, the modifier, and the class the check is measured
against -- and only the first two coincide.

	tbl[n] = [3]string{owner, visibility, proto}

A gap in the chain does not stop the walk up: the engine copies an inherited
method into every subclass's table, so a class redeclaring two levels down still
has the top one as its prototype.

### `use T { m as public; }` is the composing class's word, not the trait's

The other four regressions. A trait alias that changes visibility was carried in
the IR and never applied -- invisible while nothing checked visibility, and four
tests started refusing programs the engine runs the moment something did.

It cannot be written onto the method: the body is the trait's, shared with every
class that composes it, and two classes may compose one method at different
visibilities. So `Class.ComposedVisibility` records it per composing class. Three
parts, each with a test that needed it:

- `A::foo as public` -- no new name, modifier on the method (`bug55137`);
- `A::bar as public baz` -- modifier on the **alias**, not the method
  (`semi_reserved_006`);
- a trait composing a trait passes the modifier onward, so `T2 { use T1 { aa as
  public; } }` publishes `aa` to everything using T2 (`bug76700`).

### A refusal several frames deep must capture its own stack

`access_modifiers_010` got the message right and the trace wrong: `#0 {main}`
where PHP has two frames. `Raise` records no stack, and the unwind pops the
frames before anything materialises the throwable -- the same shape as the
generator-position bug earlier today. `RaiseAt` fixes it.

It moved no test, because that trace is still wrong for two *other* reasons the
fix made visible: a method frame renders `c->test()` where PHP writes
`a->test()` -- **the declaring class again, in a fourth subsystem** -- and
`callCtor` pushes no frame at all. Both in TODO.

Probed rather than designed, and three things were not what I would have built:

	F::cases()     ok                <- exempt
