at once. The case values are literals, so the fault is computed at **emit time**
and only the raising is deferred; "throws every time" then comes free, because
there is nothing to cache.

Two rules in the engine's order: a case whose value is not of the backing type
is a `TypeError`, and a value already taken is an `Error` naming **both** cases

backwards.

## 2026-09-09 -- 940 / 402: a private property is one slot per declaring class

	935 passed / 407 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   69.7%
	940 passed / 402 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   70.0%

Twelve chunks, `t[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
88 / 88, gate green. Diffed against the run **before** the change, not the
intermediate one -- that one contained my own regression, and diffing against it
would have listed `bug33171` under "now passing", folding a bug I introduced
into the credit column. Five fixed, nothing broken.

### The defect

	class Base            { private $hello = 'base'; }
	class Sub extends Base { private $hello = 'sub'; }

Two slots, each labelled with the class that wrote it. php2go keyed
`Object.Props` by name alone, so the child's declaration overwrote the parent's
and the object showed one property where PHP shows two. Anything reading an
inherited private by name was answering about the wrong slot -- a **wrong
value**, not a missing diagnostic.

### Five rules, and I had four of them wrong at some point

1. **A private is keyed by its declaring class** when the name has more than one
   declarer. `php.MangleProperty` and `Object.Shadowed` already existed for
   engine exception properties; only the compiler was not producing them.
2. **The ancestor chain has to be walked.** A child's `properties_info` lists
   its inherited *public and protected* properties and **not** an ancestor's
   private, which it cannot see by name. The slot exists on the instance all
   the same. `runtime/interp` walks the chain for exactly this reason.
3. **Only what each ancestor declared.** Its table also lists what *it*
   inherited, and copying those duplicates a grandparent's slot on the way up.
4. **Slot order is declaration order along the chain**, root first --
   `Base::$hello, Base::$shared, Base::$open, Middle::$hello, Leaf::$hello`.
   My first version prepended the inherited privates as a block, which put
   `Middle::$hello` ahead of `Base::$shared`. A two-class fixture passes that;
   the three-level one caught it.
5. **Access resolves the slot from the calling scope.** With storage fixed and
   lookup not, `var_dump` was byte-exact and every method reading `$this->hello`
   warned `Undefined property`. **The object looked perfect and behaved
   wrongly** -- storage and lookup are two agreements, and checking the dump
   alone would have called it done.

### The wrong turn, and the tell I ignored

I read `ReflectionClass::getProperties()` returning one entry as evidence that
the engine's table was missing the parent's private. It is not -- Reflection
*filters* what the child cannot see. Both facts are true and I read one as
evidence about the other.

The tell was in front of me: **the interpreter gets this right using the same
harvest.** That alone proves the data is there and the consumer is at fault. I
spent a probe on the harvest before checking how `runtime/interp` consumes it,
which is the reverse of the order that has worked all session.

### The regression the total concealed

The corpus moved 935 -> 939, four better, no reason to look further. The set
diff said **five fixed and one broken**: `foreach ($this as $k => $v)` over an
object with a shadowed private yielded the storage key, `\0B\0c`, where PHP
yields `c`.

One key was doing two jobs. Visibility needs the **storage** spelling, because
that is what carries the declaring class; the loop needs the **plain** one.
Both are correct answers to different questions, and the bug was letting one
stand in for the other.

Swept the other leak surfaces afterwards. `get_object_vars`, `(array)` casts,
`property_exists` and `isset($this->p)` are all **already `unsupported`** for
unrelated reasons, so none can leak today -- and each will need the same
unmangling when implemented. "No other leaks" and "no other *reachable* leaks"
are different claims and only the second is true.

## 2026-09-09 -- the `close the gap` loop, end to end

	820 passed / 521 failed / 2583 unsupported / 0 errored   61.1%   Milestone 3
	940 passed / 402 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   70.0%   now

**120 corrected wrong answers**, `errored` 0 throughout, and `unsupported`
essentially flat -- 2583 -> 2568, with every movement diffed and named. The two
files that moved between buckets both did so honestly: `func_get_args.phpt`
left `unsupported` because the construct became supported, and `bug72107.phpt`
entered and later left it as a gap was surfaced and then closed.

### What the defects had in common

Four shapes accounted for most of the session.

**A renderer and its parser disagreeing.** `fmt.Sprint(9.0)` is `"9"`, and every
reader of IR operand text tries `ParseInt` first -- so every integral float
literal in the compiler track was an int. `LiteralText`'s own comments describe
this defect twice, in the arms either side of the float one.

**A throwable's position read after the frame it belongs to is gone.** Four
places: argument coercion, return coercion, the generator driver, the
`#[\Deprecated]` constructor. php2go separates *detecting* a failure from
*constructing* the exception, and the construction always happens further out.
The rule is that position and stack are fixed **at the raise**.

**A scan keyed on a spelling where the question is about a role.** The
trait-alias map key, `enumCases` where the question was "is this an enum",
`c??.txt` matching `cur.txt` in a tally glob. The seg README warned about the
last one using the example it was first met in, and did not fire when the same
defect arrived wearing a different filename.

**An answer reported at a layer that can never hold it.**
`unsupported: library function func_get_args` -- it is a frame question and
`runtime/php` has no frame. Refusing honestly is not enough if the refusal
points somewhere the answer will never be.

### What worked

**Ask the engine.** `ZEND_BIND_LEXICAL`'s `extended_value` is a bitmask, not a
flag: `use ($n, &$m)` gives `$m` 33, not 1. `== 1` was right for a lone
`use (&$x)` and silently made every later by-reference capture a copy. Four
printed integers settled what a plausible reading had backwards.

**Read the other track first.** `runtime/interp` had already settled typed class
constants, closure debug info, capture ordering and the private-slot rules --
including, each time, the detail I would have got wrong.

**Enumerate the family in the fixture.** Four separate bugs were caught only
because a fixture covered a case the motivating failure did not need: the
closure named from `srcFile`, the two frame functions with different messages,
the empty deprecation message, the three-level property chain.

**Diff the sets, not the totals.** A broad change with small net movement hides
regressions. `+5/-1` and `+4/-0` are the same number.

**Run the local corpus after every emitter change.** `go build ./...` passing
says nothing about the emitted program building; a renamed parameter left 85
generated programs failing with `undefined: v` while php2go itself compiled
clean.

### What is left, and why it is not tick-sized

	~10 handle-numbering + ~7 destructor-ordering failures

Both need one fact: **when does an object die.** `Unit.freeHandles` already
models handle reuse; it lacks the death point. That is the plan's D3 -- escape
analysis and static destruction -- and it is the largest coherent thing left in
the corpus, as the original attestation predicted.

Recorded and not started: per-declaring-class privates are done, but
`get_object_vars`, `(array)` casts and `property_exists` will each need the
unmangling when implemented; `call_user_func('func_get_args')` needs an escape
hatch whose probe table is in TODO -- three mechanisms, not one.

## 2026-09-09 -- 935 / 407: a generator's frame carries the driver's line

	934 passed / 408 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   69.6%
	935 passed / 407 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   69.7%

Twelve chunks, `r[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
87 / 87, gate green.

### The defect

A generator's **own frame is on the stack while its body runs**, and we never
pushed it. Every throw out of a generator traced one frame short:

	engine   #0 php2go-eval(7): gen()      <- 7 is the foreach that drove it
	         #1 {main}
	ours     #0 {main}

The subtlety is *which* position the frame carries: not a line inside the body,
but the line that **drove** the generator. So it is pushed around the body entry
in `Generator.step` with the driver's location, and the body then moves the
location itself as it executes. Pushing it with the body's own position would
have looked entirely plausible and been wrong in every trace.

It coexists with the `Generator->getReturn()` frame from two entries ago:
`getReturn` does not step the body, so it gets no spurious `gen()` beneath it.

### The set diff was the result, not the total

`Generator.step` is on the path of **every** generator advance in compiled code.
A net +1 is equally consistent with "one fixed" and "three fixed, two silently
broken", and the totals cannot tell those apart:

	comm -23  now passing:    generators/generator_throwing_in_foreach.phpt
	comm -13  newly failing:  (none)

**When a change is broad and the movement is small, the aggregate is the least
informative view of it.** Two `comm` invocations over the failing sets carry
what the totals do not, and cost one command. Same reasoning as naming the file
that moved in and out of `unsupported` in the two entries before this.

### Not compared, deliberately

`generators/*.phpt` plus subdirectories is 30 passed / 17 failed over 159 files
after the change. I have **no prior for that glob** -- the earlier "15 failures"
was `Zend/tests/generators` alone, from the corpus run's directory clustering.
Quoting one against the other would be two denominators presented as one
measurement, which is the `c??.txt` matching `cur.txt` mistake in a different
costume.

Remaining generator failures are mostly `yield from` delegation, which is the
standing TODO item and a different problem.

## 2026-09-08 -- 934 / 408: func_get_args is not a library function

	933 passed / 408 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   69.6%
	934 passed / 408 failed / 2568 unsupported / 0 errored   69.6%

Twelve chunks, `p[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
87 / 87, gate green.

**`unsupported` fell**, and the diff names the file: `func_get_args.phpt` left it
and passed. That is coverage genuinely added, not a corrected wrong answer, and
the running claim shrinks for this run accordingly. Both directions have now
been checked by name this session -- `bug72107` in and back out, `func_get_args`
out -- at one `comm` each.

### The wrong layer, named in the refusal

`func_get_args()` and `func_num_args()` were reported as
`unsupported: library function func_get_args`. They are **not library
functions**: the engine gives each its own opcode because the answer is a
property of the **frame** -- what this call was passed -- and `runtime/php` has
no frame to ask. The refusal pointed at a layer that can never hold the answer.

As intrinsics they need a new argument shape, `frameargs`, rendering the emitted
function's own `args` slice, exactly as `obj` renders `this`. Both are facts
about the frame being emitted rather than operands the IR carries.

They report what was **passed**, not what was declared: `f($a, $b = 2)` called
`f(1)` gives `[1]`, and the default never appears. That falls out of the
argument slice being the passed arguments -- and would have been easy to get
wrong by reconstructing from parameters.

### Two names, two sentences

	func_get_args() cannot be called from the global scope
	func_num_args() must be called from a function context

Not derivable from each other, and I had written the first for both. **The
fixture caught it because it exercises both names, not the one being debugged**
-- the third time today that habit has paid, after the closure name built from
`srcFile` and the empty deprecation message.

The rule: when a fix covers a *family*, the fixture enumerates the family.
Verifying against the case that motivated the change proves the change compiles,
not that the rule is right.

At global scope the engine emits an ordinary **call** rather than the opcode, so
that case arrives at the emitter's `call.fn` path -- which is why it was
mislabelled rather than merely unimplemented.

### The dynamic spelling: three mechanisms, not one

`call_user_func("func_get_args")` was raised as needing an escape hatch. Probing
before designing one was worth it -- a single name lookup would have been wrong
twice over. Measured inside `f(1, 2)`:

	call_user_func / call_user_func_array   [1, 2]   reaches through to the
	                                                CALLER's frame
	$c = "func_get_args"; $c()              Fatal: Cannot call ... dynamically
	array_map("func_get_args", [1])         ArgumentCountError -- it IS called,
	                                        as an ordinary internal function

Recorded in TODO with the table. **An intrinsic keyed on an opcode is
unreachable by name, and every PHP function has a name** -- which applies to
every future frame intrinsic, not just these two.

## 2026-09-08 -- 933 / 407: compiled code never collected a thrown handler

	925 passed / 416 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   69.0%
	933 passed / 407 failed / 2570 unsupported / 0 errored   69.6%

Twelve chunks, `m[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
86 / 86, gate green.

### The defect

`set_error_handler` may **throw**. A diagnostic is raised from places that
cannot unwind -- deep inside the value model -- so `Ctx.raise` parks the
exception in `pendingError` and expects the consumer to pick it up.
`runtime/interp` calls `TakePendingError` at every opcode boundary. **The
generated unit called it nowhere.** Every diagnostic in compiled code swallowed
the handler's exception:

	set_error_handler(fn($no, $str) => throw new ErrorException($str, 0, $no));
	echo $undefinedVariable;   // engine: caught.  ours: nothing
	echo $a['missing'];        // engine: caught.  ours: nothing
	$x = 1 + 'abc';            // engine: caught.  ours: nothing

Three deprecation tests were where it surfaced. It is a whole PHP mechanism
absent from the compiler track.

### The framing was the fix

I first filed this as "deprecations do not propagate the handler's exception"
and nearly fixed it at the deprecation site alone. Rewriting the TODO entry as
**"compiled code never collects a parked handler exception"** pointed at the
catalogue's effect column instead of at the diagnostic sites, and `canDiagnose`
became a lookup -- does this variant declare `Warns` or `Deprecates`? -- rather
than an audit of every emission path. Twenty lines.

Anything uncatalogued is treated as *able* to diagnose: a redundant check is a
nil comparison, a missing one is a swallowed exception. The check routes through
`onError`, so the throw reaches an enclosing `catch` like any other.

**I also reversed my own deferral.** The previous entry parked this as "wants its
own measured step". That was right about the measurement and wrong about the
delay -- I had deferred *before* probing the breadth, and the probe took a
minute. "Its own measured step" meant the corpus run, not another tick.

### `unsupported` moved for the first time in twelve runs

	2569 -> 2570

One file, `bug72107.phpt`, from `failed` to
`unsupported: library function func_get_args`. Collecting the parked exception
stopped the program running *past* a gap it had been reaching through, so a
plausible wrong answer became a declared refusal -- the direction
QUALITY_GATE asks for.

Worth the two lines to say so. A run where the headline improves and a secondary
counter drifts is exactly where a real refusal gets misread as a regression, or
a regression gets rounded away as noise. `comm -13` over the two runs'
`unsupported` sets turns "2569 -> 2570" from a question into a fact, and costs
one command.

## 2026-09-08 -- 925 / 416: the dividend from a reframing

	923 passed / 418 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%
	925 passed / 416 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   69.0%

Twelve chunks, `k[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
85 / 85, gate green. `attributes/deprecated` **11 -> 13 passed**.
`unsupported` unmoved for the twelfth measurement running.

### A deferred argument cost five lines

	#[\Deprecated(DEPRECATION_MESSAGE)]
	function test() {}
	define('DEPRECATION_MESSAGE', 'from constant');   // after the function

There is no text form for that: the constant may be defined after the function,
so the engine keeps the tree and evaluates it where the deprecation fires. The
harvest already carries the literal, `ConstExpr` already renders one, and the
result is a `php.Value` exactly like the literal case -- **so the coercion path
underneath needed no change at all.**

That is the previous entry's reframing paying off. Once `message` and `since`
are `?string` *arguments* flowing through the ordinary coercion, a new **source**
for those values is just a different expression feeding the same pipe. Under the
old model -- strings spliced into a notice -- a constant expression would have
needed its own rendering, its own emptiness rule and its own type check, and
would probably have got at least one of them wrong.

**The general form is worth keeping: when the next case in a family costs five
lines, the previous change was structural; when it needs another special case,
the abstraction is still at the wrong level.**

### Still open in the cluster

- An error handler that **throws** out of a deprecation
  (`throwing_error_handler_002/003`, `deprecated_handler_002`): 3 tests, and we
  print nothing at all, so it is a control-flow question rather than a message
  one.
- `functions/001` wants a closure's own `{closure:FILE:LINE}` in the notice.

## 2026-09-08 -- 923 / 418: an attribute argument is an argument

	920 passed / 421 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   68.6%
	923 passed / 418 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   68.8%

Twelve chunks, `j[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
85 / 85, gate green. `attributes/deprecated` **7 -> 11 passed**, 16 -> 13
failed. `unsupported` unmoved for the eleventh measurement running.

### The reframing that did the work

`#[\Deprecated]`'s `message` and `since` are not string *fields*, they are
`?string` **constructor arguments**. The harvest read them with
`GetStringValue()`, which is "" for every non-string, so `#[\Deprecated(1234)]`
silently lost its reason.

Once they are arguments, the existing coercion path answers everything:

	weak     #[\Deprecated(1234)]  ->  "is deprecated, 1234"
	strict   #[\Deprecated(1234)]  ->  TypeError: Deprecated::__construct():
	                                    Argument #1 ($message) must be of type
	                                    ?string, int given

They travel as IR operand text now and the unit coerces both at run time, in
declaration order -- message is #1, since is #2.

### Three engine facts, each of which I would have got wrong

- **An internal callee's argument TypeError has no call site.** PHP appends
  `, called in FILE on line LINE` for a userland callee and never for an
  internal one -- `strlen()` and a user function side by side settle it.
  `CoerceInternalArgument` is the same rule without the suffix, and it applies
  to every builtin argument error, not just this attribute.
- **The attribute is evaluated during call setup**, so its trace has *no frame
  for the function carrying it*:

	#0 t.php(8): Deprecated->__construct(1234)
	#1 {main}

  We emit the notice from the top of the callee's body, where its frame already
  exists, so the generated code lifts that frame for the duration. Matching the
  engine meant modelling **when in the call protocol** the attribute runs, not
  just what it prints.
- **An empty value is an absent one.** `#[\Deprecated("")]` prints plain
  `is deprecated`, no trailing comma -- and the test has to be on the *coerced*
  value, since `#[\Deprecated(null)]` arrives as null either way.

### Two self-inflicted breaks, both caught by running the local corpus

I regressed two passing tests with the empty-message case, then broke **every**
generated program with a dangling parameter reference:

	errored  anon_and_temporaries.php   go build: undefined: v
	...
	files 85   passed 0   errored 85

`go build ./...` on php2go stayed green throughout: the emitter compiles, and
the error is in the Go it *writes*. **That is the failure mode specific to
writing a compiler, and the local differential corpus is the only check that
closes the loop** -- which is why it belongs after every emitter change rather
than only before a claim.

The total break was the good case. 85 files failing identically is unmissable;
a rename that touched only some paths would have produced a handful of
confusing failures mixed in with real ones.

The underlying mistake was treating `message` as a value and `since` as a
string. Splicing `since` in as raw operand text printed
`is deprecated since "1.0"`, quotes included. **The asymmetry was the bug**;
both are the same kind of thing and now take the same path.

## 2026-09-08 -- 920 / 421: literal types, and a bool named wrong everywhere

	915 passed / 426 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   68.2%
	920 passed / 421 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   68.6%

Twelve chunks, `h[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
84 / 84. `unsupported` unmoved for the tenth measurement running.

### The zero-byte sweep, and a correction to the last entry

The previous entry framed "a sentinel with nobody to map it" as a **category**
and implied more of it was hiding. 63 of the 426 failures produce no output at
all; running the first 20 emitted programs gave **one** translation hole
(`assign_obj_ref_return`: `attempt to assign property "ref" on undef`) and 19
clean exits, which are the genuine article -- PHP raises a fatal, we do nothing.

So the category is real and small. Recording that now is cheaper than letting
the earlier write-up send a future session mining a seam that yields one bug per
twenty files. The triage recipe is in TESTING.md and is worth keeping; the
expectation of volume is not.

### PHP 8.2 literal types

`null`, `true` and `false` admit **exactly one value** and coerce nothing:

	public false $f;  $o->f = true;   TypeError: Cannot assign true to ... of type false
	public null $n;   $o->n = 1;      TypeError: Cannot assign int to ... of type null

`ParseDeclaredType` did not know them, so nothing was checked. They are
verify-only for the same reason `array` and `object` are -- and the trap is that
reading them as a flavour of `bool` is wrong in the **silent** direction: a
`bool` declaration turns `1` into `true`, a `false` declaration refuses it.

### A bool is named by value in every type-error shape

	Cannot assign true to property C::$i of type int
	g(): Argument #1 ($x) must be of type int, true given
	h(): Return value must be of type int, true returned

All three say `true`/`false` where our `TypeName` said `bool`. `ValueName`
already existed for exactly this and the coercion path was not using it. Six
call sites; it corrects **every** type error with a bool operand, well beyond
the cluster that surfaced it. Each shape was probed separately rather than
generalised from one, because they are three renderings in the engine and
agreeing was not a given.

### A `= null` default makes a parameter implicitly nullable

`function f(false $v = null)` accepts and returns `null`. The fact lives in the
declaration's **default**, not in the type, so any consumer reading only the
type string gets it wrong -- the emitter has both and adds the `?` there. PHP
8.4 deprecates the spelling while still accepting the value, and that
deprecation was already emitting correctly.

This exposed an ordering bug in the literal-type change above: literal types are
answered *ahead* of `coerce`'s null guard -- necessary, since that guard refuses
null for a non-nullable scalar and would refuse a declared type of `null` -- and
the new branch skipped the nullability check the old path performed. `?false`
given `null` was refused. **A reordering that fixes one case can silently drop a
check the old path did.**

Still open: `array|bool` given `0` must coerce to `false`. That is the
scalar-union item already in TODO, not a loose end here.

## 2026-09-08 -- 915 / 426: a sentinel with nobody to map it

	911 passed / 430 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   67.9%
	915 passed / 426 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   68.2%

Twelve chunks, `g[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
83 / 83. `unsupported` unmoved for the ninth measurement running.

### `$o++` printed nothing at all

`runtime/php` owns the `++`/`--` table and reports "cannot step this" as a
**sentinel**, because `Cannot increment Foo` names a class and that package has
no class table. Its own comment says the layer above maps it. The interpreter
does, in three lines. **The emitter never did**, so the sentinel escaped the
generated program as a Go error: `php2go: php: cannot increment`, exit 255, no
PHP output.

The bucket makes this worth naming. It graded `failed` with **zero bytes**,
which reads exactly like a missing feature -- and every one of those tests
compiled fine and needed four lines of translation. **A sentinel with no mapping
layer is a gap that looks like a gap and is not one.**

`Zend/tests/in-de-crement` 6 -> 2 failures.

### The sweep, which came back mostly clean

Seventeen sentinels in `runtime/php`. `ThrowableFor` maps every one from
`frame.go` -- generators and fibers -- and only incdec's two were unmapped, for
a real reason: `Cannot increment Foo` needs the **value** to name the class, and
`ThrowableFor` only sees the error. So the caller is the right home for those,
and both consumers now do the same three lines. Category closed rather than one
instance fixed.

### The generator sentinels had the other half of the bug

They produced the right message and the wrong trace:

	want   #0 g.php(4): Generator->getReturn()
	got    #0 {main}

Pushing a frame around the driver dispatch was not enough. The sentinels are
plain Go errors carrying **no stack**, and `materialise` reads the stack when it
builds the object -- after the frame is popped. `generatorRaise` converts the
sentinel to a raised error inside the frame.

This is the fourth place today the same rule has applied: **a throwable's
position is fixed at the raise.** Argument coercion, return coercion, `RaiseAt`
itself, and now the driver. The common structure is that php2go separates
*detecting* a failure from *constructing* the exception, and the construction
always happens further out, after frames have unwound.

Two guards, both load-bearing: an error that already carries a stack -- a body's
own `throw` -- keeps its own position rather than being re-dated; and an error
`ThrowableFor` does not recognise passes through untouched, because dressing a
gap as a PHP exception is the masquerade the quality gate forbids.

### The catalogue test refused a plausible optimisation

	Increment has both Local and runtime/php variants; an operation has one home

I had made only the *wide* variants `Local`, leaving `increment.int` and
`increment.numeric` bound straight to `php.Increment` -- they are `Pure` and
cannot reach the sentinel, so why pay for the wrapper. The cost was one
`errors.Is` against a nil error; the rule protects against the thing that put
this table in `runtime/php` in the first place, which is two homes drifting
apart. All four variants now route through the unit's `stepIncrement`.

Prose could not have caught that. `INTRINSICS.md` described the wrong layer for
a year without anything noticing, which is why the catalogue is a **table**.

Found while writing the fixture: `$g->throw(1)` raised `Error: ... must be of
type Throwable` where the engine raises `TypeError: ... must be of type
Throwable, int given`. An ordinary argument type failure wearing the driver's
clothes, and it should read like every other one.

## 2026-09-08 -- 911 / 430, and a bitmask read as a flag

	905 passed / 436 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   67.5%
	911 passed / 430 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   67.9%

Twelve chunks, `e[01][0-9].txt`, files listed, `files 4986`. Local corpus
81 / 81. `unsupported` unmoved for the eighth measurement running.

### `use (&$x)` after the first capture was a copy

Chasing a missing `&` in `var_dump` output reached the lowering's
by-reference test, `op.GetExtendedValue() == 1`. Printing the raw values rather
than reasoning about the field:

	use ($n, &$m)    $n -> 0     $m -> 33   (32|1)
	use (&$m, $n)    $m -> 1     $n -> 32

**It is a bitmask.** Bit 0 is by-reference; the engine also sets bit 5 on every
capture after the first. So `== 1` was right for a lone `use (&$x)` -- which is
how nearly every example is written -- and wrong the moment anything preceded
it. A by-reference capture in second position became a **copy**: writes through
it went nowhere, silently, in ordinary code.

This is `AGENTS.md`'s founding rule paying for itself. Nothing in the code looks
wrong, the single-capture case passes, and the failure is a corrupted value
rather than a diagnostic. Four printed integers settled what a plausible reading
had backwards.

`use_by_ref.php` was then checked **against the absent fix**: reverting to
`== 1` makes it fail on `int(4)` vs `int(3)`. A fixture written after a fix
passes either way until you do that, which is what QUALITY_GATE's "identify how
it would fail if the claimed behaviour were absent" asks for.

### var_dump's `&` is `Shared`, not `AddBinding`

`bindLexical` called `r.AddBinding()`, which is diagnostic accounting for
`debug_zval_dump`. The marker `var_dump` prints comes from `Shared`, and the
two are deliberately separate because php2go boxes slots for its own reasons --
descending into a property to write through it -- which must **not** print one.

### A closure is named after its enclosing scope

	top level          {closure:the-file.php:4}
	inside a method    {closure:Host::make():34}

I had been building the name from `srcFile` unconditionally, which matches the
engine exactly at top level and is wrong for every closure inside a function.
The harvest already has the right shape; what it gets wrong is only the *path*,
carrying the absolute one the engine was handed at compile time where
`var_dump` prints the path the program refers to itself by. One substitution
keeps both shapes -- and this closes the `{closure:FILE:LINE}` absolute-versus-
reported-path item that has been open in TODO.

**A fix verified on one example can encode the example rather than the rule.**
The `srcFile` version passed its own probe; the method case in the fixture is
what caught it.

### Closure and Generator debug info

`var_dump` of a Closure shows a table the engine builds, and its layout depends
on how the closure was made: a literal shows `name`/`file`/`line`, a
first-class callable shows `function`, and `static`, `this` and `parameter`
appear only when non-empty. `runtime/interp/closure.go` had already settled all
of it, including the detail I would have got wrong -- **capture order comes
from the static-variable table**, because the captured map does not keep it.
Iterating the map passes a one-capture test and shuffles every other.

Two facts had to be plumbed onto `lower.Function`: `LineStart`, and
`RequiredParams` -- the second because `<required>` versus `<optional>` is the
only place that distinction is observable, and it is not derivable from the
parameter list the IR already carried.

Still open in the cluster: `closure.from_call` (a first-class callable,
`f(...)`) has no emission at all, so those tests remain `unsupported` rather
than wrong.

both after the pop collapses them into an answer that still looks

The lesson recorded this morning was about *when* state is read. The half it
missed: a fix of that shape is a property of **every raise site on the path**,

## 2026-09-08 -- 895 / 446, and a tally that read double

	893 passed / 448 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   66.6%
	895 passed / 446 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   66.7%

`Zend/tests/property_hooks` **11 -> 9 failures**, local corpus 78 / 78,

### Both hook rules came from a probe, and both would have been guessed wrong

**`isset` runs the get hook.** Not a slot check -- the engine printed the hook's
own `echo` once per `isset`, which is what settles it:

	$b->p = 42;  var_dump(isset($b->p));   // GET \n bool(true)
	             var_dump(empty($b->p));   // GET \n bool(false)

So a **write-only** property has to refuse under `isset` exactly as it does
under a read. Answering `false` there is the honesty rule broken at expression
level: `false` is a legitimate-looking answer to `isset`, so nothing downstream
could tell it from a real one.

**`unset` on a hooked property is refused unconditionally.** I expected a
carve-out for the property's own hook, since reads and writes have one -- that
is what `magicInFlight` is for -- so I asked:

	public $p { get { unset($this->p); return 1; } }
	// Error: Cannot unset hooked property T::$p

No carve-out. `unset.phpt` pins the other half with a `__unset` that prints
"Never reached": the refusal comes **before** the magic method, not instead of
finding one. A *backed* hooked property refuses too, so the rule keys on
"hooked at all" rather than on virtuality -- unlike the read-only and write-only
rules two lines above it, which key on `virtual`. Three neighbouring rules, two
different keys, and only the engine says which is which.

like the method path's would refuse a program the engine accepts.

Composing them made `constant_001` fail *later* rather than pass, at a derived

the harvest:

	// has to go sideways as well as up.

It is not flattened. `class Derived extends Base {}` had no entry in

session. The comment was load-bearing and wrong, which is why reading the code
confirmed it and only a fixture printing `Derived::OWN` contradicted it.

`Marker::TAG` and `new Marker()` both silently worked. A trait has to be in the
table so composition can *find* it, which is exactly why reaching it directly
has to be refused. `Cannot instantiate trait T` is a third sentence beside the
abstract and enum forms rather than one with a substitution -- visible only by
asking the engine for each.

### Every `C::K` in a deferred initializer evaluated to NULL

`x.GetName()` and `x.GetMember()`. The harvest **never fills those** for a
`ZEND_AST_CLASS_CONST`; it fills `Children` -- child 0 the class, child 1 the
member -- which is what `runtime/interp/constexpr.go` reads and why the
interpreter was right about this all along. Every deferred initializer naming a
class constant emitted:

	mustClassConst(ctx, "", "", "A")

**This is the second bug this session whose output was valid Go.** The first was
`fmt.Sprint(9.0)` rendering `9`, which every reader of IR operand text parses as
an int. Neither errors, neither reaches the `unsupported` bucket, neither
declares a gap -- the failure arrives as a plausible *value*. That is the exact
thing QUALITY_GATE.md forbids, reached without any refusal path being involved,
so the honesty rule needs a second clause: **an emitter that cannot see a field
is missing has no refusal to make.** The defence is not a bucket, it is having
two implementations of the same question and one oracle between them.

`parent::` in a constant's class position needed adding while here; only `self`
and `static` were resolved.

### Typed class constants: a rule I did not have to re-derive

The check is **not** the one a parameter or a property gets, and the interpreter
had already probed it -- `runtime/interp/types.go`, `checkConstantType`:

> nothing is coerced -- not a numeric string to int, not an object with
> `__toString` to string, and the object's `__toString` is not even called --
> except the one widening the language always allows, int to float.

So `php.CheckClassConstantType` is `WidenDefault` plus a *verification*, never
the weak path. Reaching for `coerce` by analogy with properties would have
stringified an object where PHP raises.

The verification is deliberately **one-sided**, on `declaredClassRejects`'s
precedent: it refuses only when every alternative of the DNF type is provably
unsatisfied, and reads anything undecidable -- `iterable`, `callable`, a class
the unit does not declare -- as satisfied. A check that had nothing before it can
afford to miss a TypeError; it cannot afford to invent one.

It runs **before** the value is cached, so a refused constant refuses again
rather than answering with the value it just rejected. `type_error2` reads twice
and wants the message twice, which is what pins that ordering.

Two facts found while building the fixture, both of which shaped it:

- `const S CLS = 'literal'` is a **compile-time** fatal, not a runtime
  TypeError. The engine checks whatever it can fold, so only a *deferred* value
  reaches the read-time check at all.
- `constant("C::K")` does not route through `classConst`, so it sees neither the
  type check nor the deprecation. Recorded in TODO.

## 2026-09-08 -- 875 / 466: the enum cluster was mostly not about enums

	868 passed / 473 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   64.7%
	875 passed / 466 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   65.2%

Twelve foreground chunks, `files 4986` checked first. `Zend/tests/enum` went
**34 / 20 -> 39 / 13**; `readonly_props` held at 5 / 6, which is the check that
matters here, since two of the four changes are on paths every program takes.

Four rules came out of the cluster and only one is enum-specific.

### `from`/`tryFrom` bind before they search

We matched with `LooseEqual` against the raw argument. The engine binds the
argument to the **backing type** first and searches on the coerced value, and
both halves are observable:

	Suit::from(42)   // string-backed: ValueError, and it names "42" -- the
	                 // coerced value, quoted
	Foo::from('H')   // int-backed: TypeError from the *binding*; the search
	                 // never runs

Once the value is known to be of the backing type, loose equality is wrong as
well: it matches across exactly the types the coercion has just ruled out. So
the search is `StrictEqual` and the refusal is `php.ThrowInvalidBackingValue`,
which quotes a string and nothing else.

### Three rules that are not about `from`

- **`name` and `value` are readonly.** The machinery was already there; the
  declarations simply did not set the flag.
- **An enum refuses dynamic properties**, as an `Error` -- not 8.2's
  deprecation, which is what an ordinary class gets. A *pure* enum reaches this
  for `value` too, since it declares no such slot.
- **`unset` on a readonly property**, which is not enum-specific at all.

### The unset rule, probed rather than assumed

	unset($c->x)   initialised          -> Cannot unset readonly property C::$x
	unset($d->y)   uninitialised, outside -> Cannot unset protected(set) readonly
	                                        property D::$y from global scope
	unset($this->y) uninitialised, inside -> allowed

The same two-rule split as writing, with one word changed -- and the third row
is the one assumption would have got wrong: a constructor **may** `unset` its
own uninitialised readonly property, which is how a class makes one lazily
initialisable. `CheckPropertyUnset` mirrors `CheckPropertyWrite`, and the two
message pairs share a body rather than being copied, because they differ only in
the verb.

### The keying, again

These rules key on `Class.IsEnum` from the harvest, **not** on a non-empty case
list. `enum Foo {}` is legal and has no cases, and `no-new.phpt` is exactly that
-- keyed on `enumCases` it would have stayed broken. Same defect shape as the
trait-alias map key: a scan keyed on a spelling where the question is about a
role.

`cmd/php2gotest/testdata/enum_rules.php` runs all four rules, including the
empty enum and the dynamic `new $c()` path, which needed the same refusal in
`newDynamic` and found that `enumClasses` had to be keyed lowercase to be
reachable from it.

## 2026-09-08 -- 868 / 473: a float literal that read back as an int

	860 passed / 481 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   64.1%
	868 passed / 473 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored   64.7%

Same corpus and command throughout: twelve foreground chunks of
`php2gotest -php2eval <built binary> -v -root . $(cat q<NN>)`, tallied with the
file-count check first -- `files 4986`, so no chunk dropped out. `unsupported`
is unchanged again; all eight are corrected wrong answers.

Two fixes, and the second was found while chasing the first.

### The raise position is fixed at the raise

`return_types` reported argument and return `TypeError`s at the **call site**
where the engine reports them at the function's closing brace, with the call
site in the trace's first frame in both.

The cause was an interaction between two of my own changes, each right alone:
`PopCall` restoring the caller's location, so a diagnostic after a call names
the right line; and `RaiseAt` capturing the stack at the raise. The *position*
was still read when the error was materialised -- which is after `PopCall` has
restored the caller's location -- so the throwable recorded where it was caught.
`php.Error` now carries `File`/`Line` set in `RaiseAt`, read back by
`RaisedAt`, and generated `materialise` restores the location around building
the object.

The rule, which is the engine's: **a throwable's position is fixed at the
raise.** Anything read later is a different question. Two individually correct
changes to *where* and *when* state is read can still disagree with each other.

### A renderer and its parser disagreeing, for the third time

`internal/lower/cfg.go` rendered a float literal with `fmt.Sprint`, so `9.0`
became the text `9`. Every scanner of IR operand text -- the emitter's
`operand`, `Specialize`'s type facts -- tries `ParseInt` before `ParseFloat`, so
that text came back an **int**. `var_dump(9.0)` printed `int(9)`.

`LiteralText`'s own comments already name this defect shape twice, in the
adjacent `KIND_BOOL` and `KIND_ARRAY` arms ("rendering both as `bool` made
`$t = true` and `$f = false` the same instruction"). The float arm was the third
instance sitting between two write-ups of it. `FloatText` now appends `.0` when
the shortest round-trip spelling has no `.`, `e` or `E`, and `+Inf`/`NaN` keep
their `%v` names because the emitter translates those by name.

The test asserts in the **reader's** terms rather than on the spelling: not that
the text is `"9.0"`, but that `strconv.ParseInt` refuses it. Pinning the
spelling would pass against any renderer that happened to match and would say
nothing about the property that matters.

### Declared types widen an initializer, at four sites

Found first, and the reason the float bug surfaced at all: `function f(float
$arg = 0)` must bind `float(0)`, and `public float $x = 2` must store
`float(2)`.

This is **not** weak-mode coercion, and treating it as such would be wrong in
both directions. It applies under `strict_types=1` too, and it is the *only*
conversion allowed -- `public float $x = "2"` is a compile error in the engine,
not a coerced `2.0`, so reaching for the general coercion path would accept a
program PHP rejects.

The membership rule was read back from the engine rather than assumed:

| declaration | `= 2` stores |
|---|---|
| `float`, `?float`, `float\|bool`, `float\|string` | `float(2)` |
| `int\|float`, `mixed` | `int(2)` |

So the question is not "is the type float" but **"does it accept float and not
int"** -- and `float|string` widening is the row that rules out any
weak-coercion-order reading of it. `php.WidenDefault` holds the rule; the
emitter applies it at all four declaration sites (parameter, property, static
property, class constant) so they cannot drift apart.

The class-constant site is what exposed the float bug. The engine folds a typed
class constant into the opline as the double it has already widened to, so
`const float F = 9` never reached `WidenDefault` at all -- it arrived as a
literal, and was un-widened on the way through the IR's text. The fix at the
declaration site was invisible until the rendering was fixed underneath it.

## 2026-09-08 -- one-sided property hooks, and a rule that was too broad

A hooked property with only one accessor refuses the other direction:
`Property C::$p is read-only` / `is write-only`. My first version applied that
whenever the opposite hook was nil, and it **regressed the suite 45 -> 43**.

The rule is narrower, and the narrower half is the common one:

	virtual  (no backing store)   set-only is write-only, get-only is read-only
	backed   (hook touches $this->prop)   the implicit accessor still works

`public $p { set { $this->prop = $value; } }` is readable from outside -- the
implicit get returns the stored value. `Prop.Virtual` already recorded the
distinction; the emitted `hookPair` simply was not carrying it.

	property_hooks   45 -> 48 passed,  14 -> 11 failed

**My probe passed the broken version.** It used only virtual properties, so it
tested exactly the half that made the wrong rule look right. The suite caught
it. `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/hook_one_sided.php` now carries both shapes, and
the backed case is the one that fails if the rule widens again.
