## 2026-09-08 -- a reference is written through, not copied out and back

`writeDim`'s reference path was copy-out, mutate, copy-back:

	inner := r.Get()
	writeDim(ctx, &inner, key, v, appending)
	r.Set(inner)

Asked whether that branch could simply go away, the answer is no, and the reason
is the interesting part: for an array the copy is cheap because the `*Array` is
shared either way, so the branch *looks* like ceremony -- but the **write-back
is load-bearing**. `$r = &$u; $r[0] = 1;` autovivifies an array into the copy,
and only `r.Set` puts it where `$u` can see it.

So it became a pointer instead. `Ref.Slot()` exposes the storage a reference
shares -- collapsing ref-to-ref as `Get` does -- and `writeDim` retargets its
slot to it and falls through. The copy in, the recursive call and the copy back
all go, and autovivification now works *because the pointer is the shared
storage*, not because someone remembered the write-back. A required write-back
is exactly what a later refactor drops, and its absence is invisible until
something autovivifies through a reference.

Hoisting the unboxing into the **emitter** was the other half of the question,
and it buys nothing today: whether a local holds a reference is a run-time
property, so the emitter would emit the same check one frame out. It would pay
inside a loop -- `$a[$i] = ...` re-resolves the box every iteration -- but that
needs a proof that nothing rebinds `$a` in the loop, which is D3's escape
analysis rather than a local change.

**Chunks q00-q01 are byte-identical before and after** (172 passed / 123 failed
/ 534 unsupported / 0 errored over 981 files), which is what a pure refactor
owes. Behaviour spot-checked against the engine for autovivification through a
reference, aliased array writes, a string-offset write through a reference, and
a by-reference parameter.

## 2026-09-08 -- `#[\Deprecated]`, and three defects it dragged out

Chosen by clustering the 521 failures by **shape** rather than by expected text:
387 of them die early (101 print nothing, 286 stop partway), which is 71% of the
gap in one shape. Sampling the silent ones found the biggest identifiable
feature: `#[\Deprecated]`, 30 of 31 tests failing or refusing, **none passing**.

The IR already carried `deprecated` and `deprecated_message` on op_arrays and on
class constants. Nothing downstream read them. Functions, methods, constants and
enum cases now emit the diagnostic, with the wording taken from the engine --
the reason follows the whole phrase (`Function g() is deprecated, use g2()`) and
an enum case says `Enum case` where a constant says `Constant`. That suite is
0 -> 7 passed.

Three defects fell out, each larger than the feature:

**The location was not restored when a call returned.** The emitter writes one
`SetLocation` per source *line*, so with `f(); g();` on one line, `g()`'s
diagnostic inherited whatever line `f`'s body last set -- it reported a position
inside a function that had already returned. `PopCall` now restores the call
site, which the frame already recorded. This is general: any diagnostic raised
after a call on the same line was wrong.

**We raised `E_DEPRECATED` where the attribute requires `E_USER_DEPRECATED`.**
8192 against 16384, and an error handler is handed the number, so the two are
distinguishable from PHP and the wrong one is a wrong answer rather than a
nuance. `Ctx.UserDeprecated` already existed; the call site used the wrong one.

**`e.scope` leaks between emissions.** The property-hook emitter sets it and
restores it only on the *error* path, so a plain function emitted afterwards
announced itself as `Method C::f()`. Caught by the new fixture rather than the
corpus. Fixed by stating the invariant where it belongs -- `e.function` clears
the scope, because a plain function has none -- rather than inferring the answer
from the function's name, which was my first attempt and got methods wrong in
the other direction.

**Measured on the first quarter of the corpus** (chunks q00-q02, 1,485 files, the
same command and files both times):

	before   234 passed / 191 failed / 854 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    240 passed / 185 failed / 854 unsupported / 0 errored

`unsupported` unchanged: six corrected wrong answers, no coverage shuffling.

## 2026-09-08 -- Milestone 3 reached: 820 passed, 61.1% gap-free, 0 errored

Same corpus and command as the baseline, 4,986 files:

	at M3's writing   307 passed / 252 failed / 3351 unsupported / 0 errored
	now               820 passed / 521 failed / 2569 unsupported / 0 errored
	gap-free rate     56.3%  ->  61.1%   (492 -> 1,341 gradable)

The rate and the counts have to be read together: the gap-free denominator
nearly **tripled** as capabilities landed, so the rate rising at all means
correctness kept pace with coverage instead of trailing it. That is the whole
point of criterion 3.

The last two gaps closed this session were `static::class` and the chained
uncaught block; both are written up in their own entries above.

**What criterion 1 does and does not claim.** The uncaught *reporting* is
byte-exact -- simple, chained, empty-message, raised-inside-a-function, root
cause first as `Uncaught` and each wrapper as `Next`. 82 failures still mention
an uncaught block, and every one sampled is a throwable **the engine raises and
we do not**: an argument-type `TypeError` on an internal constructor, a throwing
destructor. That is a missing diagnostic, not a broken format, and saying so is
the difference between a milestone and a claim.

**Measuring it took three attempts and the reason is worth keeping.** Three
whole-corpus background runs were killed mid-flight. Not the corpus and not the
changes: **a background task does not survive the end of the turn that started
it**, and under `/loop` the turn ends the moment `ScheduleWakeup` returns. The
box at load ~26 with 207 users made each run slow enough to still be unfinished
by then. Runs started earlier in the session, outside the loop, had completed
fine -- which is exactly why the pattern took three tries to see.

The fix was foreground twelfths. Two things had to be right for the sum to mean
anything, and one of them nearly was not: the segment list has to be `*.phpt`
**and** `*.php` (4,986 files, matching what the runner reports) because `*.phpt`
alone is 4,966 -- summing those would have been a different denominator from the
baseline, which is the comparison QUALITY_GATE.md forbids. The twelve chunks sum
to exactly 4,986, which is the check that they covered the corpus once each.

## 2026-09-08 -- traits: +40, the largest single move of the session

`use T;` brought in **nothing**. The engine resolves traits at compile time by
copying their members into the class; the IR keeps the link instead
(`Class.Traits`), and every table downstream walks the *parent* chain only. So
every trait method was `Call to undefined method`, and trait properties and
statics did not exist either.

`gogen.flattenTraits` does what the engine does, at the start of `Emit`.
Flattening rather than teaching each table about traits is both smaller and more
faithful: a copied method is compiled **once per using class, with that class as
its scope**, which is what makes `self::` inside a trait mean the using class.
Pointing several classes at one compiled body would get that wrong in a way no
lookup could fix.

Two rules fall out of copying only what the class does not already declare: the
class's own member wins, and a trait's beats an inherited one. Both are pinned.

**The using class becomes the declarer.** Keeping the trait as `Prop.Class` made
`declaresStatic` point every using class at the trait's single slot, so two
classes using one trait *shared* a static property PHP gives each of them
separately -- `$a->get()` answered `"in-B"`. Caught by writing the probe for it
rather than by the corpus.

	before   770 passed / 558 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    810 passed / 517 failed / 2583 unsupported / 0 errored

**An `errored` appeared on the way and is gone.** Two traits defining one name
were both copied, and the generated map literal had a duplicate key, which does
not compile -- `semi_reserved_006.phpt`, where `TraitA::catch insteadof TraitB`
resolves exactly that. `insteadof` is applied now, and a conflict that survives
it is **refused** rather than emitted.

**Aliases are carried and deliberately not applied.** `use T { m as n; }` under
the obvious implementation -- copy the function under the second name -- put a
second entry in a map literal that already had one, and reintroduced the same
uncompilable output. It is reverted, and the field says so at its declaration: an
alias needs its own emitted method, not another key. Better a recorded gap than
an `errored`.

## 2026-09-08 -- an object standing where a class name goes

Found by clustering the failing programs' **fatals** rather than their output
diffs, which is the more useful cut when the diff is "got nothing": several said
`Call to undefined method class@anonymous::...` and one
`Access to undeclared static property ::$foo` -- an empty class name, which is a
strong tell.

`fetch_class` on a runtime value emitted `php.String(v.String())`. For a string
that is the class name and works; for an **object** it is the empty string, and
PHP accepts an instance wherever a class name goes:

	$o::K        $o::$foo        $o::m()

All three named nothing. The anonymous-class tests failed for this reason and
not for anything to do with anonymous classes -- `new class` works, and the only
way to reach one's statics is through the variable holding the instance, which
is exactly the broken path.

`php.ClassNameOf` answers the class for an object and the string otherwise, and
`fetch_class` uses it.

	before   768 passed / 560 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    770 passed / 558 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored

Local corpus 64 -> 65. The fixture runs all three member kinds through an
instance, a string variable **and** the literal class name, because the string
form already worked -- the two look alike and only one of them was tested, which
is how this survived.

## 2026-09-07 -- an object used as an array offset is refused, not converted

Picked by clustering the 564 failures rather than by guessing. The clusters are
shallow -- a long tail of distinct causes, no single family worth a batch -- so
this is one concrete defect from the sample.

`ArrayKey`'s default arm is `StringKey(v.String())`, which is right for every
scalar: null becomes `""`, true becomes `1`, a numeric string becomes an int,
all silently. It is wrong for an object or an array, which PHP refuses:

	$a[$o]         TypeError: Cannot access offset of type stdClass on array
	$a[$o] = 1     TypeError: Cannot access offset of type stdClass on array
	isset($a[$o])  TypeError: Cannot access offset of type stdClass in isset or empty
	unset($a[$o])  TypeError: Cannot unset offset of type stdClass on array

Three wordings, because the message names what the offset was being used *for*.
A Closure used as a key had been quietly becoming some string.

**The engine autovivifies and then throws.** `$undef[$o] = 1` leaves `$undef`
**set** -- `isset($undef)` is `true` afterwards. I put the check before the
autovivification, which is the order that reads as obviously right and is wrong;
the differential case caught it on the line that asserts `isset($undef)`. The
check now sits after `*slot = Arr(NewArray())`.

	before   764 passed / 564 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    766 passed / 562 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored

Local corpus 63 -> 64. The new case also pins the *other* half of the claim --
that null, bool, float and numeric-string keys stay silent -- because a refusal
that fires too widely would pass every test that only checks the refusals.

`isset`, `empty` and `unset` followed. Each needed a signature to change before
it could refuse anything: the generated `existsIn` answered a `php.Value` and
`place.unset` answered nothing, so neither had anywhere to put an error. Both
return one now, and `isset($a[$o])` is a statement rather than an expression --
a refusal has to have somewhere to go.

	after isset/unset  768 passed / 560 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored

## 2026-09-07 -- exception chaining when a `finally` throws over one in flight

The engine's rule, asked for rather than reasoned about:

	try { throw new Exception("Bar", 0, $foo); }
	finally { throw new Exception("Dummy"); }     // Dummy -> Bar -> Foo

The finally's exception wins and the interrupted one becomes its **ancestor**,
attached at the **end** of the chain rather than the head -- a finally throwing
`new Exception("Fin", 0, $c)` over an in-flight `InFlight` gives
`Fin -> C -> InFlight`. Nested finallys compose: `C2 -> B -> A`.

`php.ChainInFlight` does the link, and the lowering marks which copy of an
inlined finally runs with an exception in flight (`Block.Unwind`), because the
same body is inlined at every normal exit too and there `pendingExc` holds
nothing this throw has any business chaining.

**The cycle guard has to look both ways, and mine did not.** The engine's own
test is `try { throw new Exception("Bar2", 0, $b); } finally { throw $b; }`,
which catches `$b` alone -- no link, because one would be circular. I checked
whether the interrupted exception was already an ancestor of the thrown one, and
that is the *other* direction: here the **thrown** exception is an ancestor of
the interrupted one. Case 1 passed and this one spun for ever.

It was caught in seconds rather than wedging the run, by the per-file timeout
added an hour earlier: `errored -- timed out after 10s`. That is the first time
that guard has paid for itself, and it paid on the very next change.

**Corpus: 764 / 564 / 2582 / 0, unchanged.** Nothing moved, and the reason is
worth recording rather than glossing: `exception_009.phpt`, the test this came
from, is `noreference` -- the *engine* bails on it -- and its neighbours are
blocked on `Exception::__toString` rendering a stack trace under EXPECTF. The
behaviour is verified against the engine directly and covered by
`cmd/php2gotest/testdata/exception_chaining.php`, which is where the evidence
lives. Local corpus 62 -> 63.

## 2026-09-07 -- the harness can report a hang

A hang was the one failure mode `php2gotest` could not report. With no bound on
a child process, one looping generated program left a whole run wedged and
printed no summary at all -- an hour of wall clock, still in the `b`s. Nothing
in the output said so; the tell was `pgrep` showing a `/tmp/php2gotest-*/prog`
still alive.

Every child is now bounded by `-timeout` (30s default), the compiled program and
the `php2eval` oracle alike, and an overrun grades as **`errored`** -- the bucket
that is meant to stay empty, so a hang is loud. Not `failed`, because there is no
output to compare and a program that does not terminate is not a wrong answer;
not `unsupported`, because it is not a gap the compiler declared.

**Verified against the case that motivated it**, which is the strongest form
available: reverting the `Block.Handler` mark reproduces the real loop, and
`try { throw } finally { throw }` then reports `timed out after 10s` in eleven
seconds rather than never returning. With the mark, it passes.

**Corpus, same command and corpus: 764 / 564 / 2582 / 0, unchanged** -- and the
number that matters here is `errored` staying **0**, which says the 30s bound
falsely accuses nothing. A timeout that graded working programs as errors would
be worse than no timeout at all.

A run with a different `-timeout` is a different measurement, and TESTING.md says
to quote the flag beside the number.

## 2026-09-07 -- `try { throw ... } catch` never worked, and `echo $e` said the wrong thing

Chasing `Exception::__toString` -- which several "delegation" failures actually
wanted -- turned up a much larger defect underneath it.

**`Exception::__toString` is the engine's, not a method the program declares.**
`hasMethod` said no, so `echo $e` reported that the object could not be
converted to a string, which is what PHP says for a class that is **not** a
Throwable: the diagnostic was wrong twice over. `php.ThrowableString` already
rendered it, engine-checked and unit-tested; the hook just never asked. A user
`__toString` still wins, including on a class extending Exception.

**Then the probe would not catch.** `try { throw new Exception(...); } catch
(Exception $e)` came out as an uncaught fatal. The `throw` terminator returned
unconditionally instead of routing to the enclosing handler -- the thing
`onError` does for every failing call. So an exception raised by a *called*
function was caught correctly and one thrown in the `try` itself was not, which
is exactly why the gap survived: every test that caught an exception caught one
the runtime raised. `rethrow` had the same shape, so a `finally` inside another
`try` left the function instead of handing the exception outward.

**Routing `throw` outward then hung the corpus.** `try { throw } finally
{ throw }`: the throw inside the finally routed to `handlerFor`, which is that
same finally, and the goto is a loop. The corpus ran for an hour and was still
in the `b`s -- the tell was a generated `prog` still running with no per-file
timeout to stop it.

**The first fix for that was a guess and it broke two passing files.** I asked
"is this block reachable from the handler's entry?" -- but a finally's
continuation rejoins the normal path, so the try body is reachable from the
handler too, and two ordinary programs stopped reaching their `catch`. The
lowering **knows** the answer: `inlineFinally` allocates the copies, so it marks
them `Block.Handler`, and an exception raised in a handler body goes to the
enclosing region. Exact, one line at the point of construction, where guessing
from the shape of the CFG could not be.

**Corpus, same command and corpus:**

	before   748 passed / 580 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    764 passed / 564 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored

`unsupported` unchanged, so all 16 are corrected wrong answers. Local corpus
62/62.

Still wrong and now visible: exception **chaining**. `try { throw new
Exception("Bar", 0, $e); } finally { throw $e; }` renders the wrong exception's
string, because which throwable wins when a finally throws over an in-flight one
is its own rule.

## 2026-09-07 -- three delegation defects, and one of them was hidden by another

Working the 17 `yield from` failures that became visible when the construct
started compiling. Three fixed, and the third only after the second exposed it.

**"No hop installed" and "not Traversable" were the same answer.** `ctx.traverse`
returns a bare false for both, so `yield from new stdClass` -- the *program*
being wrong, which PHP throws for -- was reported as a missing capability and
printed nothing. Now that a resolver exists the two are different questions, and
`hasTraversableResolver` separates them: absent hop is a gap, a negative answer
is `ErrNotDelegatable`.

**`Generator::throw()` was simply not in the generated dispatcher.** current,
key, next, valid, rewind, getReturn and send were; throw was not, so every
`$gen->throw()` died as `Call to undefined method`.

**A delegate is copied, not read through.** Two generators can delegate to the
same one, and it can be advanced directly besides:

	$g1 = one();  $g2 = via($g1);
	$g2->current();   // int(1)
	$g1->next();      // $g1 is spent
	$g2->current();   // int(1) still -- what $g2 took when it took it

We read through the delegate, so the shared case answered NULL. `snapDelegate`
copies at the two points the delegate is established and advanced.

**That change broke the test the previous one had just fixed**, which is how the
fourth defect surfaced. Reading through had been masking it: throwing into a
generator that delegates to another forwards the exception to the inner one, and
when the inner does not handle it, the engine continues it **into the delegating
generator's body** at the `yield from`, where a try/catch around the delegation
may catch it. We handed it straight back to the caller, leaving the outer
generator neither finished nor resumed -- so it went on answering its stale
element, which read-through had been papering over by consulting the finished
delegate instead.

	before   744 passed / 584 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    748 passed / 580 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored

`unsupported` unchanged: these are correctness, not coverage. Zend/tests/generators
alone went 25 -> 28 passed. Local corpus 61/61.

**Not every "delegation" failure is one.** `basic_yield_from_exception_handling`
and its neighbours fail on `print "$e"` -- the built-in `Exception::__toString`,
with file, line and a stack trace -- which has nothing to do with `yield from`.
Clustering by the directory a test lives in is not clustering by cause.

## 2026-09-07 -- `yield from` compiles: one line, and 30 bodies stopped refusing

The whole delegation protocol was already built. `runtime/php` had `NewDelegate`
over arrays, generators and Traversables, the `Delegated` outcome, the driver
that pumps a delegate and resumes with its return value; `internal/lower` had
emitted `ret.yield_from` all along. `internal/gogen` had no terminator case for
it, so **every** `yield from` refused to compile. The fix is one case, handing
the source over as `php.Outcome{Kind: php.Delegated}`.

Worth noting how this was found: it was the loose end recorded when `foreach`
over an object landed -- "`yield from $obj` reaches `ctx.traverse` through
`resumable.go` and was not part of this change". The guess in that note was
wrong. The traverse path was fine; the construct did not compile at all.

**Corpus, same command and corpus:**

	before   731 passed / 567 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    744 passed / 584 failed / 2582 unsupported / 0 errored

**Read those together.** 30 bodies stopped refusing: 13 now pass and 17 now fail
on something further in. Checked rather than assumed -- all 17 carried
`emit: terminator ret.yield_from` in the previous run, and no file newly became
unsupported. `failed` rising as `unsupported` falls is the documented shape of
closing a gap, and the numbers account for each other exactly.

The 17 are a real and now-visible list, not noise: exception propagation through
a delegation, `getReturn()` and `send()` into a delegate, `finally` ordering
inside a delegated generator, and throwing into `yield from` over an array.
Recorded in TODO by name.

Local differential corpus 60 -> 61 files. The new case covers what the protocol
actually promises: a delegate's keys are **its own** (two delegated arrays repeat
0,1 rather than continuing a count), and the value of the expression is the
delegate's `return`, not its last element.

## 2026-09-07 -- foreach over an object works, and the step was in the wrong place

Three separate things, found in that order.

**Nobody installed the hop.** `runtime/php` declares `ResolveTraversable` and
documents it carefully -- iterating a PHP object means calling PHP methods, which
needs a class table that package does not have -- and **no consumer had ever
installed one**. The interpreter has its own iteration, so the resolver existed
for the compiled path alone and was never wired up. `internal/gogen` now emits a
`methodTraversable` over `callMethod`, resolves `IteratorAggregate` by calling
`getIterator()` and recursing, and installs it beside `SetSubclassOf`.

**The step was in the wrong place, and had been all along.** With the methods
running, the output was byte-for-byte the right length and in the wrong order:
`next()` came before the body. The lowering put `iter.next` in the *fetch*
block, which is invisible for an array -- the element is already out of a
snapshot -- and plainly wrong for a Traversable, whose `next()` is user code that
prints. The engine's order, from an Iterator whose methods echo, is

	rewind, valid, current, key, [body], next, valid, ...

so the step belongs on the **back edges**. `fetchBodies` now emits a step block
and redirects every edge into the loop header except the loop's own entry, which
`fetchRequest.reset` names. `continue` is a back edge and steps; `break` leaves
by the exit and does not -- which the old shape got wrong too, advancing an
iterator the engine leaves alone.

The runtime design was already right and said so: "next is always immediately
followed by valid, so Next may do both, which is what lets Iter.Valid stay a
pure read". That only holds if the step is where the engine puts it.

**A plain object iterates the properties visible from the calling scope**, which
is exactly why `runtime/php` refused it -- it has neither a scope nor a class
table. The generated unit has both, so `iter.new` became a local intrinsic that
snapshots the visible properties and iterates that array, and everything else
goes to the shared constructor. Checked from inside and outside the class and on
`stdClass`.

That tripped a catalogue invariant worth keeping: **an operation has one home**.
`iter.new` was Local while `iter.new.array` was not, and the test named it. Both
are Local now, with `php.NewIterator` and `php.NewArrayIterator` recorded in
`notIntrinsic` as the value-level halves the unit calls -- the test asks you to
decide which they are rather than letting a family straddle two homes.

**Corpus, same command and corpus:**

	before   722 passed / 576 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    731 passed / 567 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored

Local differential corpus 60/60. The new case grades the call **sequence**, not
just the values: every method announces itself, so a step in the wrong place
shows up as a reordered line rather than as nothing at all.

## 2026-09-06 -- array.* and iter.* become type aware, and a keyed foreach was wrong

Two kinds of type-awareness, and a wrong answer found on the way that matters
more than either.

**A third lattice axis, for a fact PHP's types cannot hold.** `foreach` over an
array and over a Traversable produce the *same PHP type* -- an object holding a
cursor -- with completely different effect contracts: stepping an array indexes
a snapshot, while `Iterator::current()`, `key()` and `next()` are method calls
that print, throw and re-enter. Nothing at run time separates them either; both
cursors are objects of the same unspellable internal class. So `php.Type` gained
`Backing`, recording what the compiler proved about the **subject**.
`iter.current.array`, `iter.key.array` and `iter.next.array` require it and each
drops the `*Ctx` and the error return -- three fewer error branches per
iteration. It is set only where the subject's mask is *exactly* array.

**A parameter type, not just a container shape.** `array.set`'s only diagnostic
is `ArrayKey`'s float-precision deprecation, so an int or string key -- numeric
strings included, which become int keys silently -- makes the operation pure.
`array.set.key` is the first variant selected on what a parameter *is* rather
than on the container's shape.

**A test that could not fail, and the inference gap under it.** The soundness
half was `overMaybeArray(?array $a)`, asserting a `?array` does not narrow. It
passed against a deliberately loosened guard, because `declaredParamType` did
not parse `?T` at all: the subject was *unknown*, and unknown narrows nothing by
accident. **Unknown and "known to be wider" look identical from outside and are
not the same fact.** Teaching the inference nullable types made the case real,
and the mutation then failed as it should.

**The wrong answer: every keyed `foreach` inside a function lost its key.**
`foreach ($a as $k => $v)` printed an empty `$k` in the default pipeline. A
foreach binds the key through a compiler temporary -- `write_var($__t4, <key>)`
then `write_var($k, $__t4)` -- and mem2reg promoted the temporary, dropping its
store while the second instruction still named it. `$k` was bound to a slot
nothing wrote.

The renamer's `resolve` follows substitutions from *removed reads*; a place
mentioned directly in a value position was never a read, so nothing looked it up
in `cur`, which is where the walk carries a promoted place's current value. One
lookup fixes it.

Why it survived: `foreach.php`'s fixture bound a key it never **used**, so the
dead `iter.key` looked correct, and no differential case in the corpus used a
keyed foreach over an array inside a function. The regression test asserts that
**no promoted temporary is still named after promotion** rather than checking
the key's value, because the stale name is a perfectly well-formed operand and a
value check would pass against it.

**Measurements, same command and corpus.**

	corpus        722 / 576 / 2612 / 0   -- unchanged
	specialized   681 of 2461 (27.7%)  ->  1222 of 3673 (33.3%)
	local corpus  59 -> 60 files, all passing

The corpus did not move: the keyed-foreach fix reaches no Zend case that gets
that far, and the narrowing emits different Go for the same behaviour. The
numerator is the honest figure for the second line -- 681 to 1222 calls now
reach a narrower implementation -- and the denominator grew because four more
intrinsics gained a second variant.

Not fixed, and now recorded: **`foreach` over an object does not compile at
all** -- the runtime answers "foreach over an unsupported source" at run time,
which grades as `failed` with empty output rather than as `unsupported`. That is
why the Traversable half of the narrowing claim is pinned by a unit test on the
selected variants instead of by a differential case.

## 2026-09-06 -- sprop.ref converts; the static-property family is all calls

The last `sprop` opcode. `dim.ref` and `prop.ref` had been intrinsics for a
while, so this was the odd one out in a family whose other members had all been
converted.

It differs from the other place builders in one way that earns it its own
contract: **it can fail.** `dimPlace` and `propPlace` are total -- they defer
every check to the write -- but an undeclared static property is an Error, and
the slot lookup is where that surfaces. So `sprop.ref` alone among place
builders takes the `*Ctx`, returns an error, and declares `Effects: Throws`.

`internal/gogen` now has **no `sprop` opcode case at all**, and `mode=` is gone
from the last instruction that carried it. What still holds a place is the
compound assignment -- `self::$count += $by` is a `sprop.ref`, a `place.get`, an
`add` and a `store` -- which is a genuine read-then-write and the documented
remaining role of places.

**Corpus, same command and corpus: 722 / 576 / 2612 / 0, unchanged.** Right for
a refactor; local corpus 59/59.

**A scripted edit silently discarded two earlier edits to the same file, and
nothing failed.** The script asserted before each replacement but wrote
`specialize.go` once at the end, so when the third match missed -- on
`"sprop.set":  true,`, where gofmt aligns one map's values with two spaces and
another's with one -- the two correct, already-applied edits went with it. The
symptom was an intrinsic that stayed an opcode while the build and the whole
test suite passed. One edit, one assertion, one write; and compare whole lines
rather than substrings whose interior whitespace gofmt owns. Written up in
QUALITY_GATE.md.

## 2026-09-06 -- the last five operators become intrinsics; the emitter is all translation

`is_smaller`, `is_smaller_or_equal`, `is_not_equal`, `is_not_identical` and
`bool_xor` had no catalogue entry and went through `internal/gogen`'s own
`comparison()` helper, which composed `!php.LooseEqual(a, b)` and
`php.Compare(a, b) < 0` from an operator table of its own. That table is deleted.
**Every operation the emitter handles is now a translation of a name to a Go
function, deciding nothing.**

The hazard was not tidiness. A second operator table beside the catalogue is the
exact shape that drifted before: `pureBinary` spelled the bitwise operators the
catalogue's way rather than the engine's and had no entry for `div`, `mod`, `sl`
or `sr`, so seven compound operators did not compile at all. `comparison()` was
the same construct with the same failure available to it.

`is_equal` and `is_identical` were already intrinsics while their negations were
not -- a **half-converted family**, which is the asymmetry that keeps biting
here.

Contracts follow their bases: `!==` is `Pure` because identity never calls user
code, `xor` is `Pure` because boolean coercion emits nothing, and `!=`, `<`, `<=`
inherit `Compare`'s `Warns | ReEnters`. The engine has no `greater` opcode --
`>` is `is_smaller` with the operands swapped -- so four PHP operators come out
of two intrinsics.

**Corpus, same command and corpus: 722 / 576 / 2612 / 0, unchanged.** Right for
a refactor that emits the same Go by a different route.

**The new differential case uses parameters, not literals.** `comparisons.php`
compares `$a` against `$b` across ints, numeric strings, arrays, null and float,
because `arith_contracts.php` tested only constants for two weeks: Zend folded
every one of them, the file passed, and `$a & $b` did not compile at all. A
comparison between literals proves nothing about the operator. Local corpus
58 -> 59 files, all passing.

## 2026-09-06 -- the static-property family becomes calls, and an isset bug falls out

`sprop.get` was the last read still an opcode, and converting it turned up a
**wrong answer** that had nothing to do with the conversion.

`isset(C::$z)` on a declared-null static property answered `true`; PHP says
`false`. The lowering handled every `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_*` alike, so the static
form emitted `isset "z", "C"` -- **the same opcode and arity as a dimension's
`isset <container>, <key>`, meaning something else entirely**. The emitter did
the only thing it could with that: `existsIn(ctx, "z", "C", scope)`, reading the
property name as a container and the class as a key, and answering from a string
offset. One spelling, two operations, and the wrong bucket -- a wrong answer
rather than an honest `unsupported`.

It is fixed by lowering the static form through the silent read, which is what
that intrinsic is for. The engine settled both halves of the pair:

	C::$nope          Error: Access to undeclared static property C::$nope
	C::$nope ?? "d"   "d"          -- no Error at all
	isset(C::$null)   false        -- set-and-not-null

So `ReadStaticProp` (`Effects: Throws`) and `ReadStaticPropSilent`
(`Effects: Pure`) are a pair like the dim and prop reads, and `mode=` is now
gone from the IR entirely -- `sprop.get` was its last carrier.

**`Ctx` and `Effects` are independent axes**, and `sprop.get.silent` is the first
variant to show it: it takes the `*Ctx` only because the slot lookup it calls is
spelled that way, while emitting nothing and raising nothing. The catalogue's
`Ctx` doc had claimed the ones without a ctx "are exactly the pure ones".

`prop.get` needed no work -- it became an intrinsic earlier the same day, with
`prop.get.silent` beside it.

**Corpus, same command and corpus:**

	before   722 passed / 576 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    722 passed / 576 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored

Unchanged, which is right for the conversion half -- it is a refactor. Worth
saying plainly about the other half: **no Zend case moved on the isset fix**, so
that wrong answer is covered only by the local differential case added with it.
A corpus that does not move is not evidence the bug was imaginary; it is
evidence the corpus did not reach it.

**Two process notes.** A `python3 -c` edit to `nonOperatorIntrinsics` silently
did nothing, because gofmt had realigned the map and the matched string now had
two spaces; the surrounding assertion passed because *other* replacements in the
same script had succeeded. Assert per replacement, not per script.

And the first `sprop.get.silent` did not compile: the catalogue said `Ctx: false`
while the emitted helper took a ctx. That surfaced instantly because the probe
exercised the silent path -- the previous variant in this family had been
committed unexercised and passed everything.

## 2026-09-06 -- a mode is a different intrinsic: the silent reads and the writes

Two families carried a *mode* beside the instruction rather than in it. Both are
now separate intrinsics, and the IR no longer has a `mode=` attribute at all.

**The access mode.** `mode=R/W/RW/IS/UNSET/FUNC_ARG` rode on `Inst.Attrs`. Most
values had already chosen the callee at lowering -- a `W` on a dimension becomes
`dim.ref`, never `dim.get` -- so only `IS` was still read, by three sites in two
packages. A `silent bool` parameter could not tell the truth about it, because
**the two modes return different values**: `$s[9]` is `""` with a warning and
`$s[9] ?? "d"` is `"d"`, since out-of-range is *not set* under IS. One signature
had to declare `Effects: Warns` for a form that does not warn.

So `ReadDim`/`ReadDimSilent`, `PropGet`/`PropGetSilent` and `CopyValue`/
`CopyValueSilent` are pairs with their own effect contracts, chosen once in
`IntrinsicCalls` and then **dropped from the instruction** -- a spent fact left
in the IR is how it came to be scanned for three times. `ExplicitReads` and the
emitter now read a declared `Variant.SilentReads` instead of the attribute.

Asked rather than assumed: a float key still deprecates under `??`
(`$a[1.5] ?? "d"` emits the precision-loss Deprecated), so the silent variants
keep their `*Ctx` and are **not** `Pure`. Reading `ArrayKey` would have suggested
otherwise. While there, `ReadDim`'s effects gained the `Deprecates` bit they had
always been missing.

**The write mode.** `$a[$k] = $v` was a place-producing fetch plus a `store`, and
`store` dispatched on the place's *shape at run time* -- `p.direct`, then
`p.slot != nil`, then `p.recv` -- to recover which kind of write it was. The
lowering knew, having just emitted `dim.ref` rather than `prop.ref`. Writes are
now `op(container, key, value)`:

	dim.set(c, k, v)     dim.append(c, v)     prop.set(o, n, v)

`WriteDim` had **no variants at all** before this: writes had never entered the
intrinsic layer, so nothing about a write was described anywhere. `appending
bool` was the same defect as `silent`, and `AppendDim` is its own intrinsic. The
place producer keeps its role under a name that says so, `dim.append.ref`.

Places survive where a place is genuinely the thing: the intermediate fetch in
`$a["x"]["y"] = 1`, by-reference binds, `unset`, and a compound assignment's read
half.

`sprop.set(name, class, value)` followed, so **no assignment lowers to a `store`
any more**. The class operand is a reference rather than a value, so it needed
its own argument shape; `self`/`parent`/`static` resolve against the emitting
scope, and an undeclared static property is the only effect left -- no `__set`,
no hook, nothing to autovivify.

Its first version was **unexercised**, which is the defect this session keeps
finding. `static_props.php` writes only `self::$count += $by`, and a compound
assignment still fetches a place because it reads before it writes -- so the new
intrinsic compiled, passed, and never ran. Plain writes are now in that
differential case and in `write.php`'s golden, with a test pinning that the
assignment is one call and no `store` or `sprop.ref` survives it.

**Corpus, same command and corpus:**

	baseline        717 passed / 581 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored
	after the modes 720 passed / 578 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored
	after sprop.set 722 passed / 576 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored

Local differential corpus 58/58 throughout.

**One `errored` appeared and was fixed before it could be reported as progress.**
`prop.set` on a place receiver -- `$this->son->dad = $this` -- emitted Go that
did not compile, where the same case had been a declared `unsupported` before.
The cause is worth keeping: the refusal was written as
`if v.PlaceGap != "" && vtypes[a] == "place"`, so it fired only for a variant
that had *declared* a gap. A new variant that forgot one failed **open**, in the
mechanism whose entire job is failing closed. The check is now unconditional and
the declaration supplies only the message.

## 2026-09-06 -- specialization becomes generic-aware; the covariance gets a user

`Type.Subsumes` had been covariant since the lattice landed, but **no variant
declared a container-shaped `When`**, so the match was live and unexercised --
a declared capability nothing performed, which is the defect shape this project
keeps finding. Three variants now select on the shape alone:

	iter.new.array(array<K,V>)          NewArrayIterator   pure, no ctx, no error
	dim.get.array(array<K,V>, scalar)   ReadDimArray       warns, cannot throw
	count.array(array<K,V>)             CountArray         pure, no ctx, no error

**None narrows a representation** -- all three still take and return
`php.Value`. What the shape buys is the *effect* half of the signature: an
array has no `rewind()` to run (so no user code, so no `*Ctx` and no error
return), no `Countable::count()` to call, and no non-container offset to throw
on. The parameters `K` and `V` are unconstrained, which is why they fire so
widely: a declared `array` parameter is enough.

**Corpus, same command and corpus as the 2026-09-0x baseline:**

	before   717 passed / 581 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored
	after    717 passed / 581 failed / 2612 unsupported / 0 errored

Unchanged, which is the whole claim -- a specialization that moved a count
would be a specialization that changed behaviour. Local differential corpus
58/58.

**The census rate fell while the thing it measures grew**, and the two numbers
are not the same measurement:

	before   266 of  835  (31.7%)
	after    681 of 2461  (27.7%)

Adding a second variant to an intrinsic moves *every* one of its call sites
into the specializable denominator, so `dim.get`, `count` and `iter.new`
entered a denominator they were previously excluded from. The numerator is the
honest figure: 266 -> 681 calls reach a narrower implementation. Same trap as
reading `failed` without `unsupported`.

**Three BUILD files were stale, and one test had never run.** `bazel build
//...` was the check that caught it: `runtime/php` was missing `catalogue.go`,
`coerce.go`, `constants.go` and `intrinsics.go`; `internal/lower` was missing
`mem2reg.go`, `reads.go` and `specialize.go`; `internal/gogen` was missing every
file but one. `go build ./...` compiles by directory and never noticed.

The sharp end is `catalogue_test.go`: absent from `php_test`'s `srcs`, it ran
under `go test` and **not at all** under Bazel, and adding it surfaced three
failures immediately -- it reads the runtime's own sources, which the sandbox
does not stage. They are now declared as `data`, with `gogen.go` reached through
an `exports_files`. A test that runs in one harness and silently does not exist
in the other is the same shape as a gap masquerading as working behaviour, and
`go test` passing is not evidence about Bazel.

A first attempt regenerated *every* `srcs` in the tree from its directory, which
churned two other tracks' files and broke `surfacegen_test` -- that rule lists
`main.go` on purpose, because the test is `package main` with no library to
embed. Reverted to the three packages that were actually wrong. `gogen_test`
needed `embed` rather than `deps` for the same reason: `unrenderable_test.go` is
`package gogen`.

**A test asserted a proxy again.** `TestMixedElementsDoNotNarrow` counted *all*
specializations over an `array<int|string>` and demanded zero. That stopped
meaning what it said the moment `iter.new.array` began firing -- correctly,
since iterating an `array<int|string>` with the array iterator is right whatever
the elements are. The property it meant is that **`+` does not narrow**, because
the walk owes a diagnostic on the string; it now asserts that. Counting a total
where the question is about one operation is the same "keyed on a spelling where
the question is about a role" defect, in a test rather than in a pass.

Both directions are pinned and mutation-checked:
`TestContainerShapeSelectsTheNarrowerEffectContract` requires a declared `array`
to select the narrow variants and a `?array` -- null reaches it, and both
operations throw on null -- not to. Widening `count.array`'s `When` to
`Of(MaskAny)` fails the second half; treating an unknown element as bottom
rather than top fails `TestUnknownElementsAreTheTop`.

## 2026-09-02 -- debug ownership closes the declared 534-function surface

Factored `debug_zval_dump()` from the final `main` / `ext/standard` surface
unit. The generated ledger now reports **272 native + 262 userland = 534/534
(100%)** available functions, with **0 pending** and **15 unavailable** in the
linked build. “Available” remains the precise denominator: the unavailable
names are compile-time/platform absences reported by the linked engine, not
callable functions hidden to improve the percentage.

### The minimum new state is diagnostic provenance, not a Zend heap

The ordinary runtime still uses Go values and eager array copies. Recreating
Zend's allocator or exposing made-up heap addresses was unnecessary. The
public output needs three facts the runtime can own honestly: whether a string
or empty array came from a compiled literal, how many durable PHP storage slots
share an explicit reference, and the identity/type already carried by objects
and resources. `Value` and `Array` now retain literal provenance; the first
array content mutation clears the empty-array marker. `Ref` keeps diagnostic
binding count separate from the broader `shared` marker, because the latter
also includes php2go's eager-copy holders and previously inflated visible
counts.

Reference creation starts with its original storage slot. A successful durable
`&` assignment adds one diagnostic binding, and unset/rebind paths remove one
through the established release operation. Array-literal references and the
compiled `BindRef`/lexical-capture paths record the same event. Expression
temporaries and eager array copies deliberately do not become public PHP
bindings. This was load-bearing: an initial attempt to encode counts by
changing `ASSIGN_REF` value flow broke existing global, array, cycle, WeakMap
and ArrayObject differentials and was reverted; the side-band counter leaves
execution semantics unchanged.

`runtime/php` owns the renderer beside `var_dump`, including scalars, raw byte
strings, packed/non-packed arrays, reference wrappers, objects, resources and
recursion guards. The interpreter installs the same class-table property hook
as `var_dump`; generated programs already install that hook on their context.
The output uses php2go's real logical ownership boundary for ordinary dynamic
values (one nested owner, plus the top-level call owner) rather than claiming
Zend COW bookkeeping that the eager model does not retain. Consequently an
unmodified constant array shared through several Zend CVs can show a different
aggregate refcount even though its shape and values match; that known
diagnostic-model difference is not disguised as allocator parity.

### The engine differential exercises ownership transitions

The generated-bundle case matches the linked engine byte for byte for null,
booleans, integers and floats; interned and dynamic strings; interned literal
and request-created empty arrays; a dynamically built packed array; an object
with an interned property; a stream resource's type/count shape; and the null
return. Its reference sequence covers one array binding, two bindings, one
after element unset, one after the original variable is unset, plus the
`[&$value]` literal form. Those transitions produce exact `2 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1`
reference counts rather than a fixed placeholder.

### Verification

- rebuilt linked `php2eval` probes settled scalar, string, empty-array,
  constant-array, mutation, reference, object and resource output
- `TestDebugZvalDumpTracksLiteralAndReferenceFacts`: green
- `TestDebugZvalDumpNativeMatchesEngine`: green, byte-exact apart from the
  intentionally identity-independent resource assertion inside the PHP case
- the existing 1,096-case interpreter differential remains green at its prior
  1,079 matched / 6 honestly unsupported result
- `go generate ./internal/userland` and surface `-check`: green;
  272 native, 262 userland, 0 pending, 15 unavailable
- `GATE_TEST_COUNT=2 hack/gate.sh` with the documented CGO environment: green

## 2026-09-02 -- phpinfo is a report composite, not a new introspection primitive

Factored `phpinfo()` from the remaining `main` / `ext/standard` surface.
Coverage is now **271 native + 262 userland = 533/534 (99.8%)** available
functions, with **1 pending** and **15 unavailable** in the linked build. The
only remaining name is `debug_zval_dump`.

### Every flag gets a full page, even flag zero

The linked embed SAPI renders HTML rather than the CLI text form. Every call
starts the complete XHTML/style/title/body frame and closes it, including
`phpinfo(0)`; that zero-section report is 1,805 bytes and now matches byte for
byte by reusing `credits_html_head_impl()`. The public flag is narrowed to 32
bits, so `INFO_ALL` and `-1` select the same seven sections, and the function
always returns true.

The seven bits are independent and retain php-src's order: general,
configuration, modules, environment, PHP variables, credits and license.
`INFO_CONFIGURATION` prints the Configuration heading and a standalone Core
INI table only when `INFO_MODULES` is absent. With modules selected, their
section-owned INI tables carry the configuration instead. Credits reuse the
already byte-covered renderer without its full-page bit; the license is a
fixed linked-build block.

### Existing state already owned every dynamic input

No new native leaf was needed. General/module rows use the finite linked build
facts and the live wrapper, transport and filter registries. INI tables come
from `ini_get_all`, preserving harvested order, nullable “no value” cells,
request-local changes, On/Off rendering and highlight color spans. Environment
rows use the existing process environment snapshot. PHP-variable rows read the
live request superglobals, include embed-SAPI environment exposure and escape
names and scalar values with the same HTML rules as credits.

The bundle differential changes `highlight.comment`, adds an environment value
containing HTML metacharacters and mutates `$_GET`, then checks section
selection and escaped live values against the linked engine. It also covers
the exact empty report, the complete known-bit combination, scalar coercions,
invalid types and arity.

## 2026-09-02 -- user stream wrappers are a registry plus buffered callback resources

Factored `stream_register_wrapper`, `stream_wrapper_register`,
`stream_wrapper_restore` and `stream_wrapper_unregister` from the remaining
`main` / `ext/standard` surface. Coverage is now **271 native + 261 userland =
532/534 (99.6%)** available functions, with **2 pending** and **15 unavailable**
in the linked build. The two remaining names are `phpinfo` and
`debug_zval_dump`.

### Registry behavior is request-local and spelling-sensitive

Linked probes established that the active list starts as `php`, `file`,
`glob`, `data`, `http`, `ftp`; a registration appends its exact spelling and
lookup is case-sensitive. Protocols admit ASCII alphanumerics plus `+`, `-`
and `.`, including the empty string, while diagnostics stop at an embedded NUL.
An unknown class raises the public argument-2 `TypeError`. Duplicate
registration, repeated unregister and restore of a never-global wrapper warn;
restoring an unchanged global wrapper emits a notice and succeeds.

Unregistering a built-in removes its list entry. A user class can then occupy
that spelling, and `stream_wrapper_restore()` replaces it with the original
wrapper at the current list tail rather than its startup position. The
registry lives on the freshly loaded `Unit`; `bundle.App.Run` constructs a new
loader, interpreter and unit for every request, so mutations cannot leak while
App-owned persistent sockets retain their separate intended lifetime.

### A registered wrapper needs the streams layer, not only four booleans

`runtime/interp/streamwrappers.go` now instantiates the registered class,
injects its stream context before running the constructor, and invokes driven
methods with normal PHP frames. `fopen` selects the exact active scheme and a
user resource supplies `stream_open`, `stream_read`, `stream_write`,
`stream_eof`, `stream_seek`, `stream_tell`, `stream_flush`, `stream_stat`,
`stream_close`, locking, truncation and option callbacks. Metadata exposes the
actual wrapper object with the linked eleven-field `user-space` shape.

The engine probe exposed a load-bearing buffer boundary: `fread($handle, 2)`
calls `stream_read(8192)`, advances logical position by two and keeps four
unread bytes. EOF remains false until that buffer drains. A relative seek is
therefore normalized from logical position to an absolute `SEEK_SET` callback,
then `stream_tell` confirms the new position. `ftell` itself reads cached
logical position and does not call the wrapper. Unbounded
`stream_get_contents` asks `stream_stat` for a size hint before reading, and
write position must update the same logical cursor. The implementation models
those facts explicitly rather than treating callbacks as direct `io.Reader`
methods.

Registered directory resources use the same constructor/context lifecycle and
dispatch `dir_opendir`, `dir_readdir`, `dir_rewinddir` and `dir_closedir` for
`opendir`, `dir` and `scandir`. Public directory contexts are now forwarded to
the native gateway instead of being validated and discarded.

- fresh linked probes covered protocol grammar, aliases, exact diagnostics,
  class validation, built-in replacement/restore ordering and callback events
- `TestUserStreamWrapperLifecycleAndIOMatchesEngine` differentially covers
  registry mutation, stream buffering/metadata/stat/I/O and directory callback
  lifecycle against the linked engine
- adjacent stream registry, operation, directory and `Directory` object
  differentials remain green
- `go generate ./internal/userland` records 271 native, 261 userland, 2 pending
  and 15 unavailable
- affected-package tests for `runtime/interp`, `internal/userland` and
  `internal/bundlebuild`: green
- `GATE_TEST_COUNT=2 hack/gate.sh` with the documented CGO environment: green

## 2026-09-02 -- realpath cache is native virtual-cwd state, not an empty facade

Factored `realpath_cache_get()` and `realpath_cache_size()` from the remaining
`main` / `ext/standard` surface and connected `clearstatcache(true, ...)` to
their invalidation path. Coverage is now **267 native + 261 userland = 528/534
(98.9%)** available functions, with **6 pending** and **15 unavailable** in the
linked build.

### The cache record itself is public behavior

A fixed empty array and zero size would have made both names callable while
lying as soon as any path was resolved. Linked probes instead established the
observable virtual-cwd record: each entry costs a 48-byte bucket plus the path
and terminating NUL, and also the resolved path plus its NUL when the strings
differ. The key uses Zend's 64-bit multiply-then-XOR path hash; keys above
`PHP_INT_MAX` are exposed as float. `realpath_cache_get()` iterates 1,024 hash
buckets in order and collision chains newest-first, while each value preserves
the `key`, `is_dir`, `realpath`, `expires` field order.

Path spelling is equally observable. Ordinary components create prefix
records, repeated separators and prior `.` / `..` segments remain in later
keys, but a prefix ending at `.` or `..` is not stored. Resolving a symlink also
stores the canonical target chain. Repeating a cached lookup does not grow the
size. `clearstatcache(false)` leaves it alone; the true form with no filename
clears all records, while a supplied filename removes only that exact spelled
key. The read-only `realpath_cache_size=4096K` and
`realpath_cache_ttl=120` settings come from the harvested INI registry.

### Native resolution remains the capability boundary

`runtime/libc` now owns a copied, errno-preserving `realpath(3)` result and an
explicit unavailable stub. `runtime/interp/realpath.go` builds the cache around
that result; it does not use `filepath.EvalSymlinks` or a PHP path substitute.
The public `realpath()` dispatch now shares the same leg, including empty input
resolving the current directory, false for a missing path and the exact NUL
`ValueError`. Non-CGO/Windows builds keep native resolution an honest
unsupported capability.

### Verification

- `go test ./runtime/libc -run TestRealPath -count=1`
- `go test ./runtime/interp -run TestRealpathCacheTracksSymlinkTargets -count=1`
- `go test ./internal/bundlebuild -run TestWrapperAndRealpathCacheStateUserlandMatchesEngine -count=1`
- `go run ./internal/userland/cmd/surfacegen -root . -check`
- `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./runtime/interp`
- `GATE_TEST_COUNT=2 hack/gate.sh` with the documented CGO environment: green

## 2026-09-02 -- source rendering needs lexical classes, not a parser

Factored `highlight_file()`, `highlight_string()`, `php_strip_whitespace()` and
the `show_source()` alias from the remaining `main` / `ext/standard` surface.
Coverage is now **265 native + 261 userland = 526/534 (98.5%)** available
functions, with **8 pending** and **15 unavailable** in the linked build.

### The smallest faithful boundary is one shared lexer

The linked build does not register the tokenizer extension, and generated
bundles do not link Zend. Calling `token_get_all()` or retaining an engine in
the runtime was therefore not an available implementation boundary. Engine
probes showed that the public family also does not need a parser: Zend's
highlighter reduces tokens to inline HTML, comments, value-bearing/default
tokens, keywords/punctuation, strings and whitespace. The stripper uses the
same stream, discarding comments and collapsing whitespace, with a special
newline rule after heredoc terminators.

`runtime/interp/source_render.go` implements those bounded lexical classes over
the original bytes. It covers PHP/open and close tags, HTML, line/doc/block
comments, names, variables, all numeric literal families, punctuation and
reserved words, single/double/backtick strings, interpolation, attributes,
heredoc and nowdoc. Highlighting escapes only `<`, `>`, `&` and tabs, preserves
the previous span color across whitespace, and reads all five colors from the
existing mutable INI state. Malformed quoted input is rendered to EOF just as
the linked scanner does; tokenization diagnostics are suppressed by the public
function.

Both file functions reuse `readFile`, so a checksum-validated `/app` asset is
rendered without a host copy. Missing-file and NUL-path diagnostics, the
`show_source` called name, return-versus-output modes, and the alias result are
covered separately. No parser, generated lexer table, native library or new
filesystem abstraction was introduced.

## 2026-09-02 -- getimagesize covers the complete linked image dispatch

Factored `getimagesize()` and `getimagesizefromstring()` from the remaining
`main` / `ext/standard` surface. Coverage is now **261 native + 261 userland =
522/534 (97.8%)** available functions, with **12 pending** and **15
unavailable** in the linked build.

### The linked engine corrected the compressed-SWF premise

One generated probe supplied minimal valid bytes for every dispatch branch and
recorded the exact result and optional metadata. GIF, JPEG, PNG, uncompressed
SWF, PSD, BMP, both TIFF byte orders, raw JPC, boxed JP2, IFF, WBMP, XBM, ICO,
all three WebP dimension layouts and AVIF are byte parsers. JPEG alone copies
the first occurrence of each APP marker into the second argument. AVIF requires
more than an `ftyp` brand and a loose `ispe` search: its primary item must be
joined through `pitm` and `ipma` to the indexed `ispe` plus `pixi` or `av1C`
properties.
The differential also covers `dimg` tile inheritance: a primary item may own
only dimensions while a referenced tile supplies depth and channel count.

The earlier audit said compressed SWF needed decompression. A fresh engine
probe disproved that for this linked build: `CWS` is identified, but the image
handler was compiled without a static zlib extension. The observable contract
is therefore its specific notice followed by false. Implementing Go zlib here
would have claimed behavior the oracle does not have. This is another instance
of the project rule that build-time php-src conditions must be settled by the
linked engine rather than by source inspection alone.

Short reads also matter. Inputs shorter than the detector's current threshold
raise `Error reading from <input>!`; a sufficiently long unknown payload simply
returns false. The optional output is reset to an empty array before opening or
parsing, except that a NUL in the path raises its `ValueError` before touching
that argument. Missing files warn and return false.

### One parser serves strings, embedded assets and host files

`runtime/interp/image.go` owns the bounded byte grammars and constructs the
public mixed-key result. The path form crosses the existing `readFile`
boundary, so checksum-validated loader bytes win before host fallback and no
second filesystem abstraction was introduced. The parser bounds every box,
chunk, directory entry and variable-length field before reading it. The AVIF
path handles 32- and 64-bit boxes, full-box headers, primary-item associations,
pixel properties and codec configuration without an image decoder or a new
dependency.

The full-format differential uses deterministic engine-validated hex fixtures,
including JPEG APP output, tiled AVIF, malformed input, missing/NUL paths and
the unavailable compressed-SWF branch. A separate integration runs `getimagesize()` against a loader-only
`/app/assets/pixel.gif`, proving that a bundled asset need not exist on the host
filesystem.
