I have been comparing compiled numbers against remembered ones on a tree three
sessions are writing, so every diff has silently carried whatever landed in
between. The complete rule is three measurements and no judgements: **bound the
reach before, compare against the run immediately before, enumerate your symbols
if it still moves.**

Worth stating what their acceptance result actually established, because it is
stronger than "no change": with a reach of 135 tests -- 27x the `array_reduce`
move, which could touch exactly one -- an **unchanged** number is evidence
rather than the absence of it. That is what the reach bound buys.

### Numbers

Compared against the run immediately before, on the same tree:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| immediately before | 215 | 154 | 3,541 | 0 |
| **now** | **216** | **158** | **3,536** | **0** |

Compiled corpus 16/16 with `callbacks.php` and `error_handler.php`.

## 2026-09-01 -- assert the rendered artefact, not the properties you remembered

Two defects in the Throwable boundary, one each side, and both were found by a
*rendered* comparison rather than by checking the parts anyone had thought of.

### Theirs: seven properties, and my case would not have caught it

`InitThrowable` set the engine-defined properties as **plain public** ones. The
engine does not: `var_dump(new Exception("x"))` prints seven with visibility
labels and mangled keys, and they had six, in the wrong order, with no
visibility, missing `string` entirely. 444 corpus files construct an Exception.

Their own diagnosis is the durable part: **the test asserted the property names
and their order, and passed while order, visibility and mangling were all
wrong.** Replaced by rendering through `php.VarDump` and comparing with the
engine byte for byte -- one assertion that pins all three.

**My `exceptions.php` would not have caught it either.** It throws and catches
and never *dumps* an exception, so all seven could have been wrong and every
case I own would still have passed. `exception_dump.php` closes that.

And the private ones belong to the **root**, not the declaring class:
`class MyEx extends RuntimeException` still dumps `["trace":"Exception":private]`.
Declaring-class is the natural guess and prints the wrong label.

### Mine, found by the new case on its first run

**Fourteen properties instead of seven.** The harvest *flattens* the property
table, so `MyEx` arrives carrying all seven inherited engine properties; my
constructor declared them as plain public slots and `InitThrowable` then added
the mangled ones. Skipped now -- a property whose declaring class is an engine
throwable belongs to `runtime/php`. Same you-allocate-I-fill split already
agreed for the object, applied one level down.

That the case found it on its first run, without my having predicted the failure
mode, is the argument for the case rather than for my carefulness.

### Case folding, and why only half of it folds

The IR carries `new "exception"` because Zend lowercases a class-name literal.
`php.CanonicalThrowableClass` now folds on lookup -- and *display* deliberately
does not, which is the sharper half: `get_class(new EXCEPTION("x"))` is
`"Exception"`, the **declared** spelling rather than the written one. Folding
`DisplayName` too would have printed `object(exception)`, which reads as
cosmetic and is a wrong answer.

### The general form

**Assert the rendered artefact, not the properties you remembered to check.**
That is what the compiled corpus does by construction -- no expected output is
written down, the engine supplies it at grading time -- and it is why a case
added to guard *their* defect immediately found *mine*.

### One confound removed rather than solved

The first version of `exception_dump.php` dumped the exceptions as temporaries
and failed on `#1` versus `#2`: **PHP reuses the handle of a dead temporary** and
this emitter numbers monotonically. They are held in variables now, because the
case is for property shape. That is a confound removed from a test, not a gap
closed, and the gap is still open.

Corpus unchanged at 215 / 154 / 3,541 / 0 -- correctness rather than coverage,
which is the expected shape for both fixes. Compiled corpus 14/14.

## 2026-09-01 -- exceptions run: passed 204 -> 215, and errored back to 0

The runtime session landed `runtime/php/throwable.go`, which was the thing I had
said would be worth the most, and it was.

### Their hierarchy, verified by an independent consumer

Five cases through generated Go, byte-identical to the engine, including the two
facts they said they would have got wrong from memory and never noticed:

- **`TypeError` takes the `Error` branch, not `Exception`.** The two roots are
  disjoint.
- **`ParseError` takes the `CompileError` branch, not `Error`.** They asked the
  engine by `ReflectionClass` rather than writing it from memory; from memory it
  would have been `Error`, `catch (Error $e)` would still have caught it, and
  the mistake would never have shown.

Plus a user class extending `RuntimeException` caught by `catch (Exception $e)`,
so the type test spans the program's hierarchy and the engine's in one walk.
That is their work confirmed from the other side rather than agreed with.

`php.Throw`/`php.AsThrown` replace the wrapper I had invented, for the reason
they gave: a `catch` must test the class **and** bind the object, so both halves
must agree what an exception is. Their deliberate omission is respected -- **I
allocate and number, they fill** -- so there is exactly one source of handles.

### A case-sensitivity gap across the boundary

The IR carries `new "exception"`, lower-case, because PHP class names are
case-insensitive and Zend lowercases the literal. `php.IsThrowableClass`
matches the canonical spelling, so it answered false and my emitter silently
took the user-class path and called a constructor helper that does not exist.

Worked around here rather than by editing their file -- `ThrowableClasses()`
gives the list, so lower-case → canonical is built once and normalised before
asking. Flagged to them because every consumer will hit it.

### `errored` went 0 -> 6, and the structural fix is worth more than the causes

Six generated programs failed to build when exceptions landed. Rather than chase
six causes I added a guard that cannot be wrong: **no emitted `goto` may name a
block that was not emitted.** It converts a dangling label from a build failure
into a named refusal automatically, including for causes nobody has predicted --
and it caught two of the six on its own.

The other four were specific and worth recording:

- **A catch handler can be `Dead`.** When the clause sits inside a `finally`,
  IR-DESIGN.md inlines the finally at each exit and marks the original a
  template, so the region still names the template while the live handlers are
  in the copies -- and *which* copy depends on the path that raised. Refused.
- `$this` outside a method.
- The case-sensitivity above.
- A handler reachable only along an exception edge, which `Reachable` does not
  model, so the emit set has to be **closed over the handlers** rather than
  taken from the CFG.

### And I made the edit-not-applied mistake in the same round I agreed about it

The runtime session had just reported mutating `ParseError` to extend `Error`,
seeing the test report OK, and nearly concluding their test was weak -- the
substitution had silently not matched because `gofmt` had realigned the map.
Their rule: **a mutation check must prove the mutation applied.**

Mine, the same hour: a `python` edit whose `assert` on the anchor *failed*, and
I read the test results anyway as though the change had landed -- so a round was
spent concluding a fix did not work when it had never been applied. Theirs was
worse in kind, a no-op that reads as a pass; mine was louder and I ignored the
noise. Every structural edit now prints a checksum before and after.

### Numbers

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before exceptions | 204 | 103 | 3,603 | 0 |
| exceptions, six broken | 213 | 155 | 3,536 | 6 |
| **after the fixes** | **215** | **154** | **3,541** | **0** |

Compiled corpus 13/13 with `exceptions.php` added, which pins the disjoint-roots
and `ParseError` facts so they cannot silently regress.

## 2026-09-01 -- array literals, and the fifth lossy-IR defect was the dangerous one

### `<array>` discarded the entries the harvest kept

The operand renderer wrote `<array>` for every constant array literal, so every
array-shaped body was unrenderable **for any consumer**, not only the emitter --
the fourth instance of the same category, and 438 files by population.

Now rendered the way PHP spells it, `[0 => 1, 1 => 2]`, so the IR stays readable
by hand, with `lower.ParseArrayLiteral` **adjacent to the renderer** and
`TestArrayLiteralRoundTrips` failing if they drift. That adjacency is the
`${"10"}` lesson applied before being bitten rather than after: a scanner and a
renderer that disagree about what the text says has been a defect here twice.

It also unblocked `__debugInfo`, which had been emitted and unexercisable
because the only way to write such a method is to return an array literal.
`[7]=>` unquoted from the hook against `["p":protected]` from real properties --
so the `described` flag round-trips, and the runtime session's check that the
flag is *observable* was what made it worth putting in the contract.

### `ZEND_CATCH` dropped the class it accepts

The fifth instance, and the most dangerous: op1 carries the accepted class and
the lowering never read it, so **every clause bound unconditionally**. The first
handler ran for any exception and `catch (ValueError $a)` caught a TypeError,
with nothing in the IR distinguishing two clauses.

Both halves settled against the engine rather than reasoned about:

- A non-matching clause **does not bind its variable** -- after
  `catch (ValueError $a)` fails to catch a TypeError, `isset($a)` is false -- so
  the test has to precede the assignment.
- A subclass matches a parent clause, so the test is `instanceof` over the
  hierarchy rather than a name comparison.

The chain encoding came from the engine's own output rather than the flag bits:
with three clauses `op2` points at the next catch except the last, where it
points at **itself**; `extended_value & 1` agrees independently, and two
convergent signals is why the rule is trusted. The caught exception became a
**place**, which is the IR's own rule for a value crossing a block --
`php2lower -verify` refused the first version and was right to.

### The emitter side is complete and cannot be run

`thrown` as a Go error, region-aware routing so a PHP exception reaches its
handler while a Go-level failure keeps propagating, `instanceof` over the
declared hierarchy, `rethrow` through the finally copy. **None of it has ever
executed**: PHP refuses to throw anything that does not implement Throwable, and
neither Throwable nor Exception exists in `runtime/php`, so every catch refuses
with `instanceof undeclared class Exception`. Honest, and worth saying rather
than claiming exceptions work -- the same shape `__debugInfo` was in until array
literals landed. Throwable in `runtime/php` is the blocker, and it is 706 files.

### And I broke ten call sites with a regex

Routing every fallible site to the new error handler was done with a pattern
substitution over `fmt.Sprintf` calls. It rewrote the format strings correctly
and put the new argument **first** in all ten, where its `%s` sits in the middle.

`go vet` caught **four** -- the ones whose argument *count* also changed. The
other six had the right count and the wrong order, which vet cannot see because
every argument is a string; the compiled corpus caught those by going
12/12 -> 4/12. Both layers earned their keep, in order, and neither alone was
enough.

A substitution that edits both a format string and its arguments is not a
substitution, it is a refactor. In TESTING.md.

### Numbers

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 181 | 68 | 3,661 | 0 |
| after array literals | 199 | 73 | 3,637 | 0 |
| **after the catch fix** | **204** | **103** | **3,603** | **0** |

`failed` rising as `unsupported` falls is the expected direction -- 34 files got
far enough to disagree. Checked that they are honest: missing `Fatal error:
Uncaught` text, and `php2go: uncaught exception` where a thrown error reaches
top level. No silently-wrong cases like the property hooks. Compiled corpus
12/12.

### Two methods adopted from the runtime session

**Enumerate every path from your code into the thing that moved.** Their
acceptance rule -- "the corpus must not move at all" -- is unusable on a
three-writer tree, and applying it literally would have reverted correct work.
The usable form is *must not move because of me*, which needs a reachability
bound: only one corpus file uses `array_reduce`, so the change could move at
most one test and four moved. Then `grep` for every exported symbol of theirs in
the package that moved -- zero uses -- which closes the question **without
identifying the cause**, something a shared tree often makes impossible. Run on
myself: none of `gogen.Emit`, `lower.Lower`, `lower.Resumable`,
`lower.ParseArrayLiteral`, `lower.LiteralText` or `lower.Analyze` appears
anywhere under `runtime/`.

**The third writer is Codex**, confirmed by the user, so both of our denials
were right and neither of us should have been asked to answer for
`internal/userland`.

## 2026-08-30 -- the builtin surface, and 17 files that were passing by luck

The runtime session landed a shared builtin surface with `var_dump` as the first
instance -- `php.LookupBuiltin`, `php.BuiltinNames`, and one hook,
`ctx.SetObjectProperties`. Wired it in on this side.

**The manifest is an input, not a discovery.** `Program.Builtins` is supplied by
the caller from `php.BuiltinNames()`, so a call site lowers to a builtin call at
*emit* time and a name that is not there stays a refusal by name. Declared, not
discovered, again.

The hook needs a class table and the generated program has one, so
`objectProperties` is emitted next to the dispatcher: it answers with the
object's own properties, or calls `__debugInfo` where the class defines it.
Property **visibility** is now carried into `php.Declaration`, because
`var_dump` annotates with it -- `["prot":protected]`, `["priv":"P":private]` --
so it is output rather than bookkeeping.

`var_dump` of scalars and of an object with public, protected and private
properties matches the engine byte for byte. **The `__debugInfo` path is emitted
but not exercised**: the only way to write such a method is to return an array
literal, and `<array>` is still unrenderable. Worth stating rather than claiming
the hook works.

### Four defects, and the important one was not a build failure

| | what it was |
|---|---|
| named argument | `byval 1 as "b"` emitted verbatim -- `1 as "b"` in a Go argument list |
| nested write | `$a->b->c = 1` puts a *place* in receiver position |
| `${"10"}` | the place **scanner** required a leading letter and the **renderer** did not, so `$10` was spelled and never declared |
| **property hooks** | **emitted as a plain field, silently bypassing get and set** |

The first three were build failures, which are loud. The fourth compiled and ran
and produced wrong answers, and it is the one that mattered: reading a hooked
property runs a get hook, and emitting it as a slot skips that.

**So `passed` went 197 -> 180, and the drop is the honest part.** 17 files were
passing while emitting code that bypassed property hooks -- they matched by luck,
because the hook happened not to change the output on those inputs. A refusal is
now recorded instead.

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| before the builtin surface | 144 | 55 | 3,711 | 0 |
| after wiring, before the fixes | 197 | 108 | 3,602 | 3 |
| **after the fixes** | **180** | **69** | 3,661 | **0** |

The middle row is the flattering one and it is wrong in both directions at once.

### The dependency-path rule, used in anger

The gate was RED across this measurement: `runtime/interp/userland.go` was
literally half-written (`unexpected EOF`), plus two unformatted files in
`runtime/interp` and `runtime/bundle`. Established rather than assumed that it
could not reach the result -- `go list -deps ./runtime/php` contains no
`runtime/interp`, `runtime/php` builds and vets clean, and `errored` was 0 for
the whole run, so every generated program compiled. Reported valid with the
evidence, which is the rule the runtime session drew after I voided a
measurement for the opposite reason.

### Their sequencing rule, which is the durable part

They nearly picked `var_dump` as the first builtin for the wrong reason -- it is
the biggest number -- and it turned out right for a different one: it is the only
builtin so far that needs a re-entry hook, so it **settles the hook shape**. That
only held because the hook count came out at one; had it been five, a pure
builtin should have gone first. **Pick the first instance by what it settles, not
by what it counts, and read the hard case before committing to it as the
exemplar.**

## 2026-08-30 -- inheritance and abstract methods: passed 86 -> 144

Two changes, both cheap, and the larger one was a bookkeeping gap rather than a
capability gap.

**Abstract methods no longer poison a class.** The harness refused any class with
an abstract or static method. An abstract method has no body: there is nothing
to emit and nothing to call, since a class holding one cannot be instantiated.
Skipping it costs one line. Only `static` still refuses.

**Single inheritance**, after asking the harvest what it actually provides rather
than assuming a shape:

| | flattened by the harvest? |
|---|---|
| property table | **yes** -- a child lists inherited properties, with `declaring_class` recorded |
| method table | **no** -- a child lists only its own methods |

So properties emit directly and the *method* chain has to be resolved. Resolved
at **emit** time rather than walked at run time: the set is static, and a
dispatch table that already lists inherited methods needs no chain at all. A
parent that is not declared in the same file is refused by name, as is `new` of
an abstract class -- PHP raises "Cannot instantiate abstract class", a fatal this
emitter cannot produce, and emitting a construction that succeeds where the
engine stops would be the gap-as-behaviour the project forbids.

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files, gate green before and after
(observed in separate commands from the ones that wrote this):

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored | noreference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 86 | 46 | 3,778 | 0 | 1,076 |
| **after** | **144** | 55 | 3,711 | **0** | 1,076 |

Over the 3,910 gradable: 3.7% / 1.4% / 94.9% / 0. Compiled corpus 8/8 with
`inheritance.php` added.

### The three-instance diagnosis, which is the runtime session's

They named their own failure mode more precisely than I would have, across three
cases in one day: evidence correct, **connective tissue invented and unmarked**,
and each time the invented step is exactly the one that makes the finding
interesting -- *yours* rather than merely not-mine, *both ends* rather than just
before, *new today* rather than always true.

Their misparse is worth keeping because it is checkable and I checked it: a
`go.sum` diagnostic reads
`sub/sub.go:3:8: missing go.sum entry for module providing package .../proto (imported by probe/sub)`.
The **file** and the `(imported by ...)` **package** are different fields of one
compound message; reading them as a dependency edge invents a link that is not
there. Then `go list -deps` showed 27 protobuf packages -- true, and consistent
with both the wrong story and the right one, so the confirming measurement did
not discriminate.

The predictive part: check **the clause that makes the finding worth sending**,
not the observation. That is a sharper target than "be careful", and it composes
with the structural fix on this side -- assertion and observation separated by
structure rather than intent.

## 2026-08-30 -- objects land: passed 53 -> 86, and a measurement declared void

Ended the tooling stretch and went at the product, on the runtime session's
observation that the last several rounds had made the numbers more trustworthy
without making them better.

**Objects.** Classes, declared properties with defaults, constructors, methods,
run-time dispatch, property read and write. Verified their bucket read before
taking it, and it was understated: classes 2,112 and everything else 1,204, but
`*obj` values and places are another 380 and *those are also objects* -- roughly
**75%** of the unsupported bucket rather than half.

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files, gate green before and after:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored | noreference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 53 | 30 | 3,827 | 0 | 1,076 |
| **after** | **86** | 46 | 3,778 | **0** | 1,076 |

Two design points. **There is no Go type per PHP class**: properties are
dynamic -- added, unset, iterated in declaration order -- so an object is a
`php.Object` with an ordered property map and the class name is *data*. Dispatch
switches on it at run time, because an interface-typed variable can hold any
implementor; `InferReceivers` can narrow a site later and correctness does not
depend on it. And the emitter **widens** the IR's narrowed representation types
-- `*obj`, `*arr`, `*str` all carry as `php.Value` -- because narrowing is a
later phase whose whole point is that this one is correct without it. Refused by
name: inheritance, static properties, static and abstract methods.

### A measurement declared void, and the rule that made it cheap

The first re-measurement read 68 / 39 / 3,778 / **25**. It was taken against a
tree that did not build, and **all 25 `errored` were one line of a half-written
`runtime/php/iter.go`** -- a generated program links against `runtime/php`, so
Go was rejecting *someone else's* runtime, not my emitted code. Reported as void
rather than sent.

That is the two-populations problem in a fourth system: `errored` conflated *our
generated code is bad* with *the runtime it links against is bad*, and again the
misleading reading needed no explanation -- 3 to 25 reads as a compiler
regression and I would have gone looking in `internal/gogen`. A build error
whose file is not the generated `main.go` is now `noreference`.

Two sequencing rules came out of it, one from each side: **announce a
shared-API change before making it** (theirs -- an incomplete warning beats a
complete one that arrives after the other session has measured), and **do not
start a 25-minute measurement without checking the gate first** (mine).

### The fifth instance, and the first one in a person

The same break was attributed to me on four pieces of sound evidence, none of
which identifies an author -- they establish *not mine*, *recent*, *new* and
*self-consistent*. There are **three** writers on this tree. Their own summary is
the one worth keeping: *eliminating yourself from a set of two does not identify
the other member unless you have checked that the set has two members.*

They rate it above the four tool instances combined, and I agree with the
reason: those were buckets in software, this was a bucket in someone's head with
no code to blame -- so the tools inherit the conflation from **the specifying
step**, which is where the missing case actually gets dropped. In TESTING.md.

I only got the mirror image right earlier because I *knew* I had not written
`runtime/bundle`; when they were asked to accept `finally.ir` they knew the same
about `internal/lower`. Ownership from knowledge beats ownership from
elimination, and the timestamp method -- interleaved mtimes distinguish
concurrent from sequential, which a diff cannot -- is what settled it.

### Iterators, under new signatures

`Iter.Current` and `Iter.Key` now take `ctx` and return an error, because a
Traversable's `current()` and `key()` are PHP methods and can throw. Three
engine-derived properties are recorded **as obligations at the emission sites**:
current before key (the order is the caller's, `Iter` cannot enforce it, and it
is observable); key only where the IR has it (`foreach ($it as $v)` never calls
`key()`); and `Valid` stays pure -- where **the reason moved even though the code
did not**, since purity held only for arrays and generators and stops holding
the moment user code is behind the iterator. That last is exactly the kind of
fact that survives as still-true-for-the-old-reason and then quietly stops being
true.

## 2026-08-30 -- the forward fix created the backward bug

`GATE_REPEAT_TESTS=1` found a real non-idempotent differential case on its first
use, in `runtime/interp`: `-count=1` passes, `-count=2` fails on a clean tree.
Reported by the compiler side rather than touched, which was right -- the case is
mine, and so is the comment that caused it.

### The mechanism is better than "process state"

The case already carried a comment about the coupling **and a fix for it**:

```php
// The engine's ini table outlives one case, so the setting is put back:
// a later case that starts a fiber would otherwise find no stack for it.
ini_set("fiber.stack_size", "1M");
```

A previous session recognised the coupling in the *forward* direction and
handled it. **That restore is exactly what makes the case inherit from its own
previous run.** `ini_set` answers the *previous* value, the case prints it, and
after one run the previous value is the `1M` the restore left rather than the
empty string it starts life with:

```
run 1   '4096' set=''   get='4096'
run 2   '4096' set='1M' get='4096'
```

So the forward fix created the backward bug, and it survived because **it looks
like cleanup**.

The rule, now in TESTING.md, and sharper than what was there:

> Restore what you found, or seed what you read. Restoring to a third value
> chosen to suit whatever runs next does not remove a coupling -- it turns a
> forward one into a backward one.

Fixed by seeding `ini_set("fiber.stack_size", "")` before the loop, so the value
the case *reads* is set by the case, keeping the `1M` restore for the forward
direction, each comment now saying which direction it serves.

**Verified at `-count=3`, not `-count=2`.** Two runs only show that the second
equals the first, which a coincidence also satisfies; three shows a fixed point.
`GATE_REPEAT_TESTS=1 hack/gate.sh` is green. One case out of 1,077 -- worth
stating as a measurement rather than an absence.

### Their near-miss is the best-caught instance of the probe rule

Their first `-count=2` wiring put it on the **first pass only**. The pass-then-fail
probe then reported `GATE FLAKY`, which looked like success -- the blind
direction detected -- and the tell was that the verdict *text* said "failed then
passed" while the probe did the reverse. The exit code alone would have confirmed
it.

The result agreed with what they were hoping for, and the only thing separating
*it works* from *the two passes ran different commands and are not comparable*
was reading what the tool **said** rather than whether it was happy.

And that defect is the harness's own, one level in: two observations meant to be
compared, produced differently. It now has instances in the differential harness
(the `<?php` line shift, the `php2go-eval` filename, the relative path against an
absolute diagnostic), in the gate, and in my reproduction across space rather
than time. **When two observations are meant to be compared, any difference in
how they were produced invalidates the comparison.**

Default gate green, opt-in gate green. Corpus 53 / 30 / 3827 / 0 / 1076, the 6
cases 6/6, interpreted 4,362 / 195 / 154 / 2.

## 2026-08-30 -- the flake detector is one-directional, and the blind side is the flattering one

`GATE FLAKY` (exit 3) landed on the compiler side, with an input-set hash over
every `*.go` and `testdata/` file, pruning `third_party`, `.agents-workspace` and
`.git`. Those exclusions pre-empt the objection worth raising -- generated output
churning the hash and producing a false `UNSTABLE` -- by the same *output is not
source* reasoning as the gofmt exclusion.

Verified here. The three-way split is clean: the gate moved (script sha), the
source moved (input sha, still `UNSTABLE`, now naming which), or nothing moved
and the verdict flipped, which is `FLAKY` and a defect rather than noise.

### The gap: it only re-runs on failure

So a check that **fails then passes** is `FLAKY`, correctly -- and a check that
**passes then fails** is never looked at. Constructed rather than inferred: a
test that passes on its first run and fails on every run after gives

```
GATE GREEN, exit 0
```

Put in `runtime/php` to keep a failing test out of their half, mirroring their
putting theirs in `internal/gogen`. Removed in the same command.

### Which is the session's pattern, for the last time

The conflation that survives is the one that makes the number look better:

| | what it hid |
| --- | --- |
| `php2gotest`'s `unsupported` | *the oracle could not ask* |
| `GATE UNSTABLE` | *the check is nondeterministic* |
| `GATE FLAKY` | nondeterminism that happens to pass first |

Each time the missing case is the one nobody is motivated to look for. Their
sentence for it is better than the individual findings, because it predicts where
to look rather than only recording where we have looked: **these are the
conflations that make the number look better and cost nothing to believe.**

### Not a demand to double-run

Two smaller things instead, and the first is free:

- `GATE GREEN` means *passed once*, not *passes reliably*, and `FLAKY` existing
  may now suggest flakiness is covered when it is covered one way round. The risk
  is over-trusting `GREEN` **because** the gate got more sophisticated. In
  TESTING.md next to the verdict table.
- **Of the four checks, only `test` can be nondeterministic.** `gofmt`, `build`
  and `vet` are pure functions of the input set. So closing the asymmetry costs
  one extra *test* run -- `go test -count=2` -- not a doubling of everything.
  Their call on the wall-clock.

Gate green and stable. Corpus 53 / 30 / 3827 / 0 / 1076, the 6 cases 6/6,
interpreted 4,362 / 195 / 154 / 2.

## 2026-08-30 -- GATE UNSTABLE calls a flaky check "not a result"

The compiler side encoded the shared-tree rule rather than documenting it:
`hack/gate.sh` re-runs on failure and reports three verdicts -- `GREEN` (0),
`RED` (1, failed *and reproduced*), `UNSTABLE` (2, did not reproduce). It also
checksums itself, so `UNSTABLE` now distinguishes "the gate script changed
mid-run" from "shared tree", which fixes the exact ambiguity that nearly made me
report their working fix as broken.

Verified here: exit 0 / GREEN, exit 1 / `RED: gofmt (gate 4cae80f146ab)`, script
sha identical before and after the sequence.

### The finding: UNSTABLE conflates two populations

The branch has exactly two cases -- script changed, or "shared tree". So a
**genuinely nondeterministic check** falls into the second and is reported as
something to disregard.

Constructed rather than inferred. A test dropped into `runtime/php` that fails on
its first run and passes on its second:

```
GATE UNSTABLE: test did not reproduce -- shared tree (gate 4cae80f146ab); not a result
```

The tree was not the cause. The check was flaky -- a real defect -- and the
verdict said to dismiss it.

Same bucket problem as `php2gotest`'s `unsupported`, one level in: *we cannot
compile it* vs *the oracle could not ask* there, *the tree moved* vs *the check is
nondeterministic* here. Both mix a gap with a non-result, and in both the
non-result reading is the flattering one.

Not hypothetical here: TESTING.md already records that differential cases can
depend on the engine **process** state -- the `gc_collect_cycles` coupling, where
trimming one case changed another's answer. A check whose verdict depends on what
ran before it is precisely what produces a spurious `UNSTABLE`.

**The split is available by the move already made one level out.** The script
checksums *itself*; checksum the **input set** to separate what remains. Source
byte-identical across both runs and the verdict flipped means nothing external
changed, so the check is nondeterministic. Reported rather than implemented --
their file, and they are in it.

### Their better version of my corollary

I had it as *knowing the failure mode does not protect you*. Theirs is sharper,
and they earned it: checking the new exit code they had just written, they used
`hack/gate.sh 2>&1 | tail -2; echo "exit=$?"` -- which reads **`tail`'s** status.
The pipeline-swallows-exit-status bug, inside the verification of its own fix,
one command after writing it up.

> Species (2) is not a bug you fix once in the code. It is the shape of the
> convenient shell command, so it recurs in the **checking** as readily as in the
> thing checked.

Which is where nobody looks, because the checking is the part you trust.

Gate green, tree clean, `4cae80f146ab`. Corpus 53 / 30 / 3827 / 0 / 1076, the 6
cases 6/6, interpreted 4,362 / 195 / 154 / 2.

The compiler side fixed the cwd hole -- `hack/gate.sh` now anchors to the repo

## 2026-08-30 -- the gate had the same hole one level in, and the input was the working directory

Both sessions wrote the unconditional-banner bug independently, both after
writing up the failure mode. The compiler side replaced the hand-typed gate with
`hack/gate.sh`, whose verdict is computed from the accumulated status of every
check, mutation-checked in four directions.

### Verified it, then went looking for a hole

Sixth direction, not in their list: **a build failure.** Solid -- a package that
does not compile gives `GATE RED: build vet test`, both scoped and tree-wide.
That was the direction the old `&&` chain handled by accident, so it was the one
most worth confirming survived the rewrite.

Then the hole. **`gofmt -l .` is cwd-relative**, so the gofmt check silently
narrows to whatever subtree the script is invoked from:

```
with an unformatted runtime/php/zz_probe.go in the tree:
  from the repo root   -> unformatted: runtime/php/zz_probe.go
                          GATE RED: gofmt
  from internal/       -> GATE GREEN            (file still unformatted)
```

**Species (3) again, and the recursion is the point.** The script exists because
of the banner bug and was mutation-checked four ways -- all four, presumably,
from the repo root, which is the normal case and therefore the case anyone tests.
The input-set question one more time: not *does it fail when I break the code*
but *does it run on the input where the code is hard* -- and here the input is
the **working directory**, which does not look like an input at all.

The fix already exists in the same directory: `hack/cgoenv.sh` opens with
`root=$(CDPATH='' cd -- "$(dirname -- "$0")/.." && pwd -P)`. Sibling script, same
problem, already solved. Reported rather than edited -- they had just written the
file and we have both seen transients from concurrent edits on this tree.

Secondary and fail-safe: the `^third_party/` and `^\.agents-workspace/`
exclusions are anchored, so from a subdirectory they would not match either --
producing false *positives*, which is the harmless direction.

### Their three experiments are the sharper finding

Proving their own gate bug took three probes, and the first two would each have
supported a confident wrong conclusion:

| probe | said | actually |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | GATE RED, so the gate works | the probe was under `.agents-workspace/` and `./...` skips dot-directories -- the tool never saw it |
| 2 | GATE RED, so the gate works | right answer, wrong reason: `go test` re-runs a subset of vet and `printf` is in it |
| 3 | GATE GREEN with two findings on screen | `copylocks` is outside that subset -- the real hole, much narrower than "the gate is broken" |

Only the third separated *sound* from *broken, but not for the reason you think*.

Recorded in TESTING.md as its own rule, because it generalises past gates: **a
probe that agrees with you may be agreeing for a reason you have not checked, and
the danger is worst when it agrees, because agreement ends the investigation.** A
disagreeing probe gets interrogated; a confirming one gets believed.

They also took the reproducibility-displaces-disclosure ordering into the

## 2026-08-30 -- record the policy, not the root; and a guard that only bit on the happy path

Two corrections, one each way, and both are about the same thing: having the
requirement right and the mechanism wrong.

### They were right about recording, and the reason is bigger than theirs

I said: record the chosen compilation root in the artifact, so a reader can
interpret the paths. They implemented `sourceRootPolicy` instead -- the *policy*,
not the root -- on the ground that recording the root would re-disclose the
build-machine path and undo the change. They asked whether I meant it literally.

I did, and I was wrong, and **the stronger reason is one they did not give.**
Disclosure is the secondary purpose. The primary one is reproducibility: an
artifact that records the absolute root makes two checkouts of one project in
different directories produce **different artifacts**, which is exactly what
`-trimpath` exists to prevent. Go does not record the original directory
anywhere -- it *erases* it. Recording it would have satisfied the letter of the
path rewriting while defeating its main goal.

So the adjustment does not solve a different problem than the one posed; it
solves that problem better than it was posed. Symmetric with their own
correction the round before -- they had the root default right and the mechanism
wrong (walk-up discovery), I had the interpretability requirement right and the
mechanism wrong (record the root).

Offered, not insisted: policy alone is fully interpretable when it is
entry-file-directory, because the reader infers the entry sits at the root. It is
thinner under an explicit `-root`, where "explicit" says a root was chosen but
not which. Recording the **root-relative path of the entry file** would close
that at zero disclosure cost, since it is already relative.

### Their hole completes a family

Following the design through their own code found a leak they had already
shipped: the trimming fell back to the **absolute** path whenever `filepath.Rel`
produced a `../` prefix -- so a file above the root re-leaked the build layout,
reintroducing precisely what the change removed.

`TestNoBuildMachinePathReachesTheArtifact` was real, and mutation-checked, and
missed it -- because it only ever exercised a file *inside* the root, and the
fallback only fires *outside* it.

That is a third species, and TESTING.md now has all three:

| | how it failed |
| --- | --- |
| a comment asserting a property | `UNRENDERABLE` was valid Go under a comment saying it was not |
| a check that cannot distinguish the failure | `capture-pane \| grep` matched unsent text like sent text |
| **a guard that bites, but only on the happy path** | the leak test never ran on a file above the root |

The third survives the usual check. Mutation testing asks *does it fail when I
break the code*; it does not ask *does it run on the input where the code is
hard*. The second question is about the **input set**, not the assertion.

And the way it was found matters: by following a design through, not by testing.
The `../` case read as an aesthetic detail when I raised it, and it turned out to
be the only input that exercised the fallback at all.

Verified their fix rather than taking it: `-root internal` forces `../` on every
case and is 6/6; `-root /` is 6/6. `gogen.DefaultRoot` is the entry file's
directory, and they took stability-under-adding-files as the deciding argument
over longest-common-prefix rather than the `../` aesthetics, which is the right
reason.

The through-line table is now a rule in IR-DESIGN.md with two consequences added
by them: **declared beats discovered even where discovery would usually be
right**, and **where nothing is declared, prefer the deterministic function that
is stable under adding inputs**.

### And I wrote the same bug while documenting it

The gate command used to check the above was:

```sh
go test ./... 2>&1 | grep -v "^ok" | head -3; echo "gate clean"
```

The `echo` is unconditional, and it printed `gate clean` alongside a package
that failed to build -- species (2) from the table, written *after* the table,
by the person who wrote it, in the session about that failure mode.

Which supplies the corollary the taxonomy needed: **knowing the failure mode does
not protect you from it**, because the broken shape is the convenient shape. Grep
for problems, print a banner, and the banner is not connected to the grep.
Vigilance is not the defence -- vigilance is what just failed. The defence is to
make the success message a function of the check. Fixed, re-run, and it is a real
pass.

Corpus unchanged: 53 / 30 / 3827 / 0 / 1076. Gate green -- and now the word means

## 2026-08-30 -- declared, not discovered: the third instance, and it names the session's shape

The compiler side implemented the `-trimpath` answer: `php2gotest -root`, both
arms reporting root-relative paths, `gogen.TrimBuildPath` rewriting the captured
diagnostic, zero absolute build paths in emitted source,
`TestNoBuildMachinePathReachesTheArtifact` guarding it and mutation-checked.

Verified here, including the claim that made the choice free in the first place.
Ran the corpus with `-root` at four different places, one of them *above* the
repository:

| `-root` | |
| --- | --- |
| `.` | 6/6 |
| `cmd` | 6/6 |
| `cmd/php2gotest/testdata` | 6/6 |
| `/home/moriyoshi` | 6/6 |

Grading is independent of the root. Both of us had said the tension was not
real; neither of us had run it.

### The open item: the instinct is right, the mechanism is not

They filed: when `php2go build` exists it must default `-root` to the module or
project root rather than the working directory. Right about the problem.
Judgement rather than measurement on the mechanism, and the correction is the one
Go actually made:

**`-trimpath` does not discover a root. It uses the module path declared in
`go.mod`.** That is exactly why two checkouts of one module in different
directories produce identical binaries -- the identifier is declared *in the
source*, not derived from where the source sits.

A discovery heuristic -- walk up for `.git`, or `composer.json` -- reintroduces
the problem it was meant to solve, because the artifact then depends on
filesystem context outside the compiled source: whether a `.git` is present, how
deep the checkout is, whether the build ran from a subdirectory.

PHP has no reliable declared identifier, so the root has to be a deterministic
function of the *input set* instead. Two candidates:

- **Longest common directory prefix of the compiled inputs.** Deterministic, no
  filesystem probing, cwd-independent. Flaw: adding one file outside the current
  tree shifts every reported path, so a build is reproducible only against a
  fixed input set.
- **The entry file's directory**, with `../` for anything above it. Also
  deterministic and cwd-independent, and *stable under adding files*. The `../`
  is honest rather than a defect.

Recommended the second, with `-root` as an explicit override, and -- the part
that matters most -- **the chosen root recorded in the artifact.** Without it the
paths are relative to something the reader cannot recover.

### The through-line

Third time this session the answer has been the same, and it is worth naming
because the three look unrelated:

| question | rejected | accepted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| which functions must not be called directly | infer at each call site | `.suspends_to_caller` **declared on the function** |
| which operand positions warn on undef | let the emitter judge | `mode=IS` **declared on the operand** |
| what a diagnostic's path is relative to | discover from the filesystem | the compilation root **declared and recorded** |

Each rejected alternative is a rule someone has to apply correctly every time.
Each accepted one moves the fact to where a consumer reads it. The compiler
side's gate-versus-rule finding is the same shape from the enforcement end: do
not ask people to remember, arrange for the machine to already know.

Corpus agreed and matching: 53 / 30 / 3827 / 0 / 1076, and the 6 cases 6/6.
Interpreted corpus unchanged.

## 2026-08-30 -- the build machine's directory layout is a string constant in the artifact

The compiler side moved the compiled corpus 45 -> 53 passed, 38 -> 30 failed, by
reading `Unit.compile_diagnostic` -- a field the harvester had been populating
all along, whose own comment said the text is program output. Eight failures
closed by reading something already there. Their corpus is 6/6 on this tree.

### Their caveat, verified and one step worse

They flagged: a compiled artifact replays the compile-time diagnostics for the
path it was *built* from, not the path it runs from, and PHP never faces the
question because it compiles where it runs.

Two things checked here rather than taken.

**The engine always canonicalises.** Compiling one file three ways -- relative,
absolute, and with a `..` in the middle -- gives the identical absolute path in
the diagnostic every time:

```
given ".agents-workspace/tmp/rt-pathprobe/ct.php"
  diagnostic: "Warning: ... in /home/moriyoshi/src/php2go/.agents-workspace/tmp/rt-pathprobe/ct.php on line 4"
```

It does not echo what it was handed, so normalising the oracle's input is not
sufficient on its own; both arms have to be normalised to the same thing, which
is what their fix does.

**And the path is a string constant in the binary.** `internal/gogen` emits
`const compileDiagnostic = %q` and replays it with `ctx.Write`. So this is not
only a question about which path is truthful -- **the artifact tells whoever runs
it where on someone else's disk the source lived.** That is disclosure, not just
noise.

### Which Go has already answered

`-trimpath` exists because Go embeds absolute build paths for panics and
`runtime.Caller`, and shipping them is both noise and directory-structure
disclosure. Its answer is to rewrite to a module-relative path.

The same answer fits here, and for a reason beyond precedent. Ask what the
filename in a diagnostic is *for*: so a developer can open the file. Then:

- the **build path** is useless to whoever runs the artifact, because that
  directory does not exist on their machine;
- the **binary's own runtime path** is a lie -- the diagnostic names a line in a
  PHP file and the binary is not that file;
- the path **relative to the compilation root** is the only one that stays
  meaningful, naming the source file within the project, which is actionable by
  anyone holding the source.

**And the apparent tension with grading is not real.** Byte-exact grading against
an engine that emits absolute paths looks like it forces the artifact to embed
them. It does not, because the harness controls *both* arms: it already rewrites
both to absolute, and could equally rewrite both to compilation-root-relative
with grading unaffected. The shipping decision is not constrained by the grading
decision -- the harness is currently winning by default rather than by anyone
choosing.

### My own guard was the comment-shaped kind

They flagged, as process rather than technique, that `tmux send-keys "$msg"`
followed by `send-keys Enter` races the receiving TUI's paste handling, and that
when it loses the text sits unsent while the sender reports success.

Worse on my side: my verification was `capture-pane | grep -c "$text"`, and **text
sitting in the input box appears in `capture-pane` just as happily as text that
was submitted.** The check would have passed in exactly the case it existed to
detect. It did fail once -- a send came back with `paste again to expand` -- and I
caught it by eye and treated it as one bad send rather than as a fact about the
channel.

Adopted their check: verify the probe is *gone from the input box*, and
separately that it reached the history; retry three times; fail loudly. In
TESTING.md generalised as: for any guard, ask what it prints when the thing goes
wrong -- if that is the same as when it goes right, it is a comment.

Which puts my grep and their `UNRENDERABLE` comment in one family, and mine is
the more embarrassing of the two because it *looked* like a check.

### The third instance of one harness hazard

Their find, and it is now a rule in TESTING.md: **when the two arms disagree,
suspect they were given different inputs before suspecting the compiler.** Three
for three, and all three looked exactly like compiler bugs -- the `<?php` line
shift, the `php2go-eval` filename, and now a relative path against a
compile-time diagnostic that carries an absolute one.

Gate green; interpreted corpus unchanged.

## 2026-08-29 -- the undef-warning mapping is exact except for `??`, and that hole is in the lowering

The compiler side closed the filename gate (`Engine.EvalAs`, additive) and
started emitting diagnostics: `.line` renders as `ctx.SetLocation`, and program
variables read through a generated `readLocal` that warns on undef. The stated
reason for the mapping being exact:

> a PHP local starts UNSET, a Go var starts as the zero `php.Value`, and the zero
> Value is `KindUndef` distinct from `Null` -- so "still undef at the read" is
> precisely "PHP would warn here"

The premise checks out: `Undef()` is `Value{}`, `KindUndef` is the zero `Kind`,
and it is distinct from `KindNull`. The conclusion is nearly right, and where it
is not, the defect is upstream of the emitter.

### Which undef reads actually warn

Asked the engine rather than reasoned about:

| | warns |
| --- | --- |
| read of a never-assigned local | **yes** |
| `unset($b)` then read | **yes** -- so unset must reset the Go var to zero, not to Null |
| `$e++`, `$f .= "x"` on undef | **yes** |
| `$c[] = 1`, `$d['k'] = 1` on undef | no -- auto-vivification |
| `$q ?? 5` | no |
| `isset($i)`, `empty($j)` | no |
| `@$z` | no |
| `static $n; $n++;` | no -- `static` initialises to NULL |

### All but one are already distinguished in the IR

The lowering carries the fetch mode where it matters, which is better than I
expected:

```
$w[] = 1;      ->  %0:place = dim.append $w, mode=W
$x['k'] = 1;   ->  %1:place = dim.ref $x, "k", mode=W
isset($i);     ->  %4:bool = isset $i
unset($b);     ->  unset $b
@$z;           ->  silence_begin / dynvar.get "z", mode=R / silence_end
static $n;     ->  bind_static $n
```

Every non-warning context has its own opcode or an explicit `mode=`. An emitter
that routes only *ordinary reads* through `readLocal` gets all of these right.

### `??` is the exception, and it is a lowering defect

```
$c = $q ?? 5;

  %2:zval = copy $q          <- an ordinary read. no mode, no marker.
  local.set $__t10, %2
  br.null %2, bb1, bb2
```

Harvested rather than inferred, the engine's own op_array for that line is **one
opcode**:

```
0  ZEND_COALESCE   CV:1  UNUSED  ->  TMP:2
1  ZEND_QM_ASSIGN  CONST:0       ->  TMP:2
2  ZEND_ASSIGN     CV:0  TMP:2
```

`ZEND_COALESCE` *is* the non-warning read -- suppression is intrinsic to the
opcode, not a separate fetch. The lowering splits it into a read plus a branch,
and the read it produces is indistinguishable from `echo $q`. So `readLocal` will
warn on `$q ?? 5` where PHP does not.

This is the third instance of one category, and the sharpest, because **the
vocabulary already exists**: `mode=R` / `mode=W` ride on the dim and dynvar
operations and the coalesce read carries no mode at all. Not an oversight about
whether to track fetch modes -- an inconsistency in applying the tracking that is
already there.

The other two: `true` and `false` both rendered as the operand text `bool`; and
`.suspends_to_caller`'s criterion not covering delegation. All three are
structurally perfect and semantically lossy, and `-verify` cannot see any of
them, which is the TESTING.md point restated -- *only a second consumer checks
meaning*.

It will fail loudly rather than silently (an extra Warning line breaks the diff),
but it will look like an emitter bug and it is not one.

### And the mirror hole: reads a `readLocal` never sees

The opposite direction, found by asking which *other* opcodes read a place
without producing a value first:

```
$e++;         ->  pre_inc $e
$f .= "x";    ->  assign_op $f, "x", op=concat
$g += 1;      ->  assign_op $g, 1, op=add
echo $h;      ->  echo $h
```

`pre_inc` and `assign_op` take the place **directly**. There is no `copy` or
`local.get` for a generated `readLocal` to intercept -- and the engine warns on
all three (`Undefined variable $g`, `$h`, `$i`, checked). So an emitter that
warns only inside `readLocal` **misses** these.

Both holes come from the same wrong assumption: that "reads a local" is a thing
the emitter can recognise by which helper it routes through. It is not. Some
opcodes consume a place without any intervening read, and one opcode (`copy`
from a coalesce) looks like a read and is not one. The reliable form of the
question is per opcode -- *does this operand position warn on undef* -- and the
IR is where the answer belongs, since it is the engine's answer and not the
emitter's.

### Their own correction is worth recording as a pattern

They found a silent hole: an unrenderable operand emitted
`/* UNRENDERABLE: x */ php.Undef()` under a comment asserting that this was
invalid Go and would fail the build. It is valid Go -- a block comment followed
by an expression -- so programs built and ran with holes in them. Every pass
reported before the fix could in principle have been a program running with an
undef where a value belonged and matching anyway; they are re-measuring and
expect the number to go **down**.

The failure mode is the one this exchange keeps producing: **a conclusion whose
stated reason was never checked.** Its new form is that the unchecked assertion
lived in a source comment. A comment claiming a safety property is a test that
was never written, and it reads as documentation.

The runtime session fixed the non-idempotent case and the mechanism is better
than "process state". The case **already carried a comment about the coupling**

back for later cases -- and ended with `ini_set("fiber.stack_size", "1M")`.

returns the *previous* value, so on a second run the opening call answered `1M`
where the first answered empty. A previous session had seen the coupling, handled
the direction it was looking at, and created the other one.

**Restoring to a convenient value rather than the original does not remove a
coupling; it turns a forward coupling into a backward one** -- and restoring to a
third value chosen to suit downstream cases is the worst of the three options,
because it looks like cleanup. The rule: *restore what you found, or seed what
you read.* Their fix seeds the value the case reads and keeps the `1M` restore
for the forward direction, with each comment saying which direction it serves.

since 2 only shows run 2 matching run 1 rather than a fixed point. The gate's
repeat is now a **count** rather than a boolean (`GATE_TEST_COUNT=3`) so that
check is reachable from it. Across 1,077 differential cases this was the only

The runtime session closed the loop on the gate work by asking which direction

caught and **pass-then-fail is never looked at**. Constructed, not inferred: a
test that passes on its first run and fails on every run after gives
`GATE GREEN`, exit 0.

Their reading of the pattern is the one to keep, and it is now four instances:
`unsupported` hiding "the oracle could not ask"; `UNSTABLE` hiding "the check is
nondeterministic"; and now `FLAKY` detecting nondeterminism only when it
inconveniences you. **Each time the missing case is the one nobody is motivated
to look for** -- and having a `FLAKY` verdict at all makes it worse, by
suggesting flakiness is handled when it is handled in one direction.

Their observation that made the fix cheap: **of the four checks only `test` can
be nondeterministic.** gofmt, build and vet are pure functions of the input set,
so the asymmetry needs closing for exactly one check. `go test -count=2` buys it
without doubling the other three.

Measured rather than guessed before choosing a default: cached gate 2s, uncached
tests 18s, `-count=2` 34s -- because `-count` disables the test cache. So it is
opt-in via `GATE_REPEAT_TESTS=1`, and `GATE GREEN` now says in its own output
that the tests ran once.

### And the first attempt at it was wrong in a way I nearly shipped

With the opt-in wired to the *first* pass only, the pass-then-fail probe reported
`GATE FLAKY`. That looked like success -- the blind direction was now detected --
except the verdict text said "failed then passed" and the probe did the reverse.
The two passes had run **different commands**, so the two observations were not
comparable at all.

Fixed so both passes use the same flags, and the honest verdict appears:
pass-then-fail with the opt-in is `GATE RED`, because it *does* reproduce; the
test is simply broken rather than flaky. Noticing required reading the verdict
text against the probe rather than the exit code, which is the probe rule again
-- **a result that agrees with what you were hoping for ends the investigation.**

## 2026-08-30 -- UNSTABLE conflated two populations, and the flattering one was winning

The runtime session found that my `GATE UNSTABLE` had exactly two cases --
script changed, or "shared tree" -- so **a genuinely flaky test landed in the
second and was reported as noise to be dismissed**. Constructed rather than
inferred: a test that fails on its first run and passes on its second produced
`GATE UNSTABLE: test did not reproduce -- shared tree; not a result`. The tree
was not the cause. The check was nondeterministic, which is a real defect, and
the gate told the reader to disregard it.

**Same bucket problem as `php2gotest`'s `unsupported`, one level in.** Then it
was "we cannot compile it" versus "the oracle could not ask"; now it is "the tree
moved under me" versus "the check is nondeterministic". Both mix a gap with a
non-result, and **in both cases the non-result reading is the flattering one.**
Not hypothetical either -- TESTING.md already records differential cases whose
answer depends on engine *process* state, which is precisely a check whose
verdict depends on what ran before it.

Their fix is my own script-checksum move one level out, which is why I took it
whole: checksumming the script separates "the gate moved" from everything else,
so checksum the **input set** to split what is left. Every `*.go` and
`testdata/` file, hashed before each pass. Source identical and the verdict
flipped means nothing external changed and the check itself is at fault.

Four verdicts now, and they were all constructed rather than assumed:

| | exit | how it was produced |
|---|---|---|
| `GATE GREEN` | 0 | clean tree |
| `GATE RED` | 1 | a persistent unformatted file |
| `GATE UNSTABLE` | 2 | a file deleted one second into the run; separately, a copy of the script appended to mid-run |
| `GATE FLAKY` | 3 | a test keyed on a marker file, failing once then passing |

`UNSTABLE` also now names *which* thing moved rather than assuming the tree.

They took my corollary about hitting the pipeline bug inside verifying its own
fix, and their restatement is worth keeping: the checking is where nobody is
looking, **because that is the part you trust**.

Their near-miss exposed a real defect in my message rather than in the logic:

```

```

A RED verdict carries the checksum too, so two observations can be told apart.
Verified by constructing it -- appending to a copy of the running script one
second in -- rather than assuming the branch works.

So it needs the sibling of a rule the corpus already has. For a shared *box*:

and re-take it.* For a shared *tree*: **a single `GATE RED` is not a result.**

### And the entry-file refinement, with their correction to my reasoning

`sourceEntry` is recorded alongside `sourceRootPolicy`, so an artifact built
under an explicit `-root` pins what its paths hang off rather than only saying
that *some* root was chosen. Zero disclosure: it is already relative.

They also gave the better reason for recording the policy rather than the root,
and it displaces mine. I argued disclosure. The larger reason is
**reproducibility**: recording the absolute root would make two checkouts of one
project in different directories produce different artifacts, which is exactly
what `-trimpath` exists to prevent. Go does not record the original directory
anywhere -- it erases it. Corrected in `internal/gogen`.

## 2026-08-30 -- declared, not discovered; and my disclosure guard covered only the happy path

The runtime session ran the compiled corpus with `-root` at five places
including `/` and above the repo -- **6/6 every time** (checked here too), so
grading really is independent of the root and the shipping decision is
unconstrained. Both of us had said that; neither had run it.

### The open item was the right instinct with the wrong mechanism

I had filed "default `-root` to the module or project root". Their correction:
**`-trimpath` does not discover a root**, it uses the path *declared* in
`go.mod` -- which is exactly why two checkouts of one module in different
directories produce identical binaries. A discovery heuristic (walk up for
`.git`, for `composer.json`) reintroduces the problem the root exists to solve,
because the artifact then depends on filesystem context *outside* the compiled
source: whether a marker happens to be present, how deep the checkout is,
whether someone built from a subdirectory.

PHP has no dependable declared identifier, so the root has to be a deterministic
function of the **input set**. Of their two candidates I took theirs: the entry
file's directory, with `../` for anything above it -- deterministic,
cwd-independent, and **stable under adding files**, which the longest-common-
prefix alternative is not. `-root` stays an explicit override, and the artifact
now records the *policy* (`sourceRootPolicy`) rather than the root itself,
because the root is a build-machine path and emitting it would undo the point.
Without that, paths are relative to something the reader cannot recover.

### My guard covered the happy path, which is the comment-shaped kind one level in

Following their `../` argument through my own code found a hole I had shipped in
the previous round. The trimming fell back to the **absolute path** whenever
`filepath.Rel` produced a `..` prefix -- so a file above the root leaked the
build layout, reintroducing exactly what the change existed to prevent.
`TestNoBuildMachinePathReachesTheArtifact` did not catch it because it only ever
exercised a file *inside* the root.

Fixed by keeping the `../`, which is honest: it says the project is shaped that
way. `TestAFileAboveTheRootIsReportedRelativelyNotAbsolutely` covers it and
bites. Verified end to end as well -- grading with `-root internal`, which forces
`../cmd/...` paths on every case, is still 6/6.

### The through-line, which is theirs and is the best generalisation of the session

Three unrelated questions settled the same way: `.suspends_to_caller` on the
function rather than inferred per call site; `mode=IS` on the operand rather
than judged by the emitter; the compilation root declared rather than discovered.
**Each rejected alternative is a rule someone has to apply correctly every time,
and each accepted one moves the fact to where a consumer reads it.** Written up
in [IR-DESIGN.md](./IR-DESIGN.md) with the two non-obvious consequences --
declared beats discovered even where discovery would usually be right, and where
nothing is declared, prefer the deterministic function that is stable under
adding inputs.

Its enforcement-side twin is the gate-versus-rule point: declaring removes the
judgement, gating the output removes the chance to forget it.

Corpus unchanged: 53 / 30 / 3,827 / 0 / 1,076.

## 2026-08-30 -- the build machine's directory layout was shipping in the artifact

The runtime session checked my compile-time-path caveat instead of taking it,
and made it sharper in a way I had missed: it is not only a question about which
path is *truthful*, it is **disclosure**. `internal/gogen` emitted the captured
diagnostic as `const compileDiagnostic = %q`, so the build machine's absolute
directory layout became a string constant in the shipped binary, telling whoever
runs the artifact where on someone else's disk the source lived.

Two things verified here rather than taken:

- **The engine always canonicalises.** Compiling the same file as
  `cmd/.../x.php`, as an absolute path, and as `cmd/php2gotest/../php2gotest/.../x.php`
  produced the *identical* absolute path in all three diagnostics. It does not
  echo what it was handed -- so the earlier harness fix worked by making both
  arms agree on one absolute path, not because the engine reflects the input.
- **The tension with byte-exact grading is not real.** It looks like grading
  forces the artifact to embed absolute paths. It does not, because the harness
  controls *both* arms: it can rewrite the engine's output the same way it
  rewrites the emitted program. Grading was unaffected -- the compiled corpus
  stayed 6/6 across the change. The absolute path was winning by default rather
  than by anyone choosing it.

Their argument for what to use instead is the one to keep, and it is not merely
precedent from Go's `-trimpath`: **ask what the filename in a diagnostic is
for.** It is so someone can open the file. The build directory does not exist on
the machine running the artifact; the binary's own path is a lie, since the
diagnostic names a line in a PHP file and the binary is not that file. The path
relative to the compilation root is the only one that stays actionable for
anyone holding the source.

So `php2gotest` gains `-root`, both arms report compilation-root-relative paths,
and `gogen.TrimBuildPath` rewrites the captured diagnostic.
`TestNoBuildMachinePathReachesTheArtifact` guards it and bites: neutering the
rewrite fails it. Emitted programs now contain zero absolute build paths.

I moved to a helper that verifies the text is *gone from the input box*.

The runtime session then reported that their own check had the same defect and

distinguish the failure it existed to catch**, since unsent text in the input box
appears in `capture-pane` exactly like submitted text. It had failed at least
once and been recovered by eye. Both sides now use the send-then-confirm-absent
form.

Worth recording because the channel is the one both sessions use to correct each
other, and because it is the session's own recurring lesson arriving in the
tooling: a guard nobody has watched fail is a comment.

## 2026-08-29 -- the compiler already had the compile-time diagnostics and was throwing them away

Biggest single movement of the session, from data already in hand.

Some of PHP's diagnostics are emitted when it **compiles**, not when it runs:
`continue` targeting a switch warns four times in
`continue_targeting_switch_warning.phpt` even though the function containing
them is never called. A script compiles at startup, so those land before the
program's first statement.

An AOT compiler performs that compile at build time -- and php2go is unusually
placed here, because **the engine prints the text while we harvest**. What I
did not expect is that `internal/zend` has captured it all along:
`php2go_compile_file` takes a `zend_string **diagnostic`, `OpArray.Diagnostic`
carries it, and it is already in the proto as `Unit.compile_diagnostic`. The
comment on that field says outright *"That text is the program's output too."*
The emitter simply never read it.

Wiring it into the prologue -- `ctx.Write(compileDiagnostic)` before the file
body runs -- moved the corpus:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored | noreference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before | 45 | 38 | 3,827 | 0 | 1,076 |
| **after** | **53** | **30** | 3,827 | 0 | 1,076 |

Eight failures closed by reading a field that was already populated. Over the
3,910 gradable files: 1.4% / 0.8% / 97.9% / 0.

### The path had to be spelled the same way in both arms

The first attempt failed on `cmd/php2gotest/testdata/compile_time_warning.php`
and passed on the identical file at `/tmp/cts.php`, which is the sort of
difference worth chasing rather than shrugging at. **Zend resolves a path when
it compiles**, so a diagnostic captured at compile time carries the *absolute*
path, while the oracle reports whatever name it was handed. A relative path on
the command line made every compile-time diagnostic differ in its filename
alone. The harness now resolves to absolute before either arm sees it.

That is the same hazard as the earlier `php2go-eval` filename problem and the
`<?php` line-shift, and it is now three for three: **whenever the two arms
disagree, suspect that they were given different inputs before suspecting the
compiler.** All three looked exactly like compiler bugs.

### A note on what this does *not* claim

The generated program replays the text the engine produced **for the path it was
compiled from**. That is truthful -- it is where the code came from -- but it
means a compiled artifact's compile-time diagnostics name the build machine's
path, not the run machine's. PHP has no equivalent question because it compiles
where it runs. Not a problem for grading, and worth knowing before anyone ships
an artifact.

The runtime session put `Increment`/`Decrement` in `runtime/php` --
**moved, not copied**. The value logic came out of `(*Interp).increment`, which
reached into the interpreter for exactly one thing (the TypeError on an array or

sentinel so the *throw* stays above `runtime/php`. Copying would have been safer
for their corpus and wrong for everything else: two implementations of one table
diverge on whichever consumer is exercised less. Their acceptance test was the
interpreted corpus unchanged, and it was: 4,362 / 195 / 154 / 2, compile-error 0.

All four of `pre_inc`, `pre_dec`, `post_inc`, `post_dec` are now emitted.

### The table verified rather than taken

They sent the table with the emission; I ran it against the engine instead of
emitting against the description, and it holds in every particular. It is
genuinely asymmetric:

| | |
|---|---|
| `null++` | `1`, **silently** |
| `null--` | no-op, *warns* |
| `true++` / `false--` | no-ops, warn, both directions |
| `"5"++` | `int(6)`, not a string |
| `"z"++` / `"Az"++` / `"a9"++` / `"zz"++` | `aa` / `Ba` / `b0` / `aaa` |
| `""++` | `"1"`, "Increment on non-alphanumeric string is deprecated" |
| `""--` | `int(-1)`, **different wording**: "Decrement on empty string is deprecated as non-numeric" |
| `"a-b"++` | `"a-c"` -- deprecated *and then incremented anyway* |

All byte-identical from generated Go.

`reportedStep` is preserved by construction: `Increment` is called and the place
is assigned only on success, so a handler that turns a deprecation into a throw
drops the pending value and the variable keeps what it had. The comment at that
call site says why, so nobody inlines a fast path and loses it.

remembered; a gate is not optional.

`cmd/php2gotest/testdata`, five cases, all passing: a whole program with calls
