## 2026-08-29 -- diagnosed the failing bucket; two more lossy-IR defects, and a rule made enforceable

Classified the 39 remaining `failed` rather than guessing at them, and the
diagnosis turned up more than a worklist.

| | count | |
|---|---|---|
| want `Fatal error: Uncaught ...` | 24 | 12 TypeError, 10 Error, 2 ArgumentCountError |
| want `Deprecated:` | 6 | mostly the `#[\Deprecated]` attribute |
| engine died before any output; we ran on | 6 | e.g. `errmsg_022` |
| want `Warning:` | 3 | several are **compile-time** |

**Uncaught-error reporting is the single biggest lever** and needs exceptions,
which need objects: nothing smaller unlocks those 24.

**Some diagnostics are emitted at compile time.**
`continue_targeting_switch_warning.phpt` never calls the function it defines and
still expects four warnings. For an AOT compiler those belong in the generated
program's prologue -- and php2go is unusually placed to produce them, because
**the engine emits them while we harvest and we currently throw them away.**
Not implemented; the mechanism is the interesting part.

### Two more defects of the same kind, one from each side

- **`??` lost its no-warn property** (found by the runtime session, and sent
  before I could mistake it for an emitter bug). The engine compiles `$q ?? 5`
  to a single `ZEND_COALESCE` where suppression is *intrinsic to the opcode*;
  the lowering split it into an unmarked `copy` plus a branch and discarded
  that, leaving a read indistinguishable from `echo $q`. Verified both halves
  against the engine before touching anything: `$q ?? 5` prints 5 silently,
  `echo $r` warns, and the op_array is one `ZEND_COALESCE`. Now
  `copy $q, mode=IS`, and `br.null` is emitted too -- where the engine settled
  that "null" means **null-ish**, since an undefined name also takes the
  right-hand branch. Four cases byte-identical end to end.
- **`.params` dropped `arg.GetByRef()`** (found by the emitter, via
  `errmsg_022`), so `f($v)` and `f(&$v)` lowered identically. A consumer could
  not tell a by-value call from one binding the caller's place, and the emitter
  compiled `function f(&$v) { $v = 5; }` by value, silently dropping every
  write-back. Now `0 &$var ""`, read by `lower.ParamIsByRef`, and the emitter
  refuses. Receiver inference held at 67.4% after teaching it to strip the `&`.

That is **three instances of one category** now, with `<array>` still open: the
harvest had the answer and the operand renderer discarded it, and none of them
is findable by `php2lower -verify`.

### The mirror hole, and why I did not build the table

The runtime session then found the opposite defect: `$e++` and `$f .= "x"`
consume a place with **no intervening read at all**, so an emitter that warns
only inside its read helper emits too *few* diagnostics -- a failure that reads
as an unimplemented feature rather than a mapping bug. Their conclusion was that
"reads a local" cannot be recognised by which helper the emitter routes through,
and that the answer belongs in the IR per opcode and per operand position.

I agree with the diagnosis and took a different remedy, deliberately: **writing
that table is the judgement, just relocated.** A per-opcode/per-position table
nobody diffs against the engine is the same untested-prose failure in another
file. So the rule is enforced over the *output* instead --
`TestEveryPlaceReadIsCheckedUnlessMarkedSilent` scans emitted Go and fails if
any place is read outside the check, exempting only instructions marked
`mode=IS` and compiler temporaries the program cannot name.

Two things settled it. First, the hole was **latent, not live**: `pre_inc` and
`assign_op` were both *refused*, so nothing was mis-emitting -- which is exactly
why raising it early was worth something. Second, the remedy was then tested by
using it: I implemented `assign_op` next, and it was **correct on the first
attempt** -- `$f .= "x"` on an undefined `$f` emits the warning, then `x|`, then
`42|`, byte-identical. I did not have to remember the rule.

`pre_inc` stays refused: `++` has no implementation in `runtime/php` (it lives
in `runtime/interp`, which this session stays out of).

### The golden I regenerated and did not author -- except I did

`go test -update` for the coalesce change also rewrote `finally.ir` and
`foreach.ir`. I recorded these as stale against the *other session's* in-flight
lowering change and asked them to confirm the diff.

**Both halves of that were wrong, and the correction is more interesting than
the mistake.** The runtime session has never edited `internal/lower` at all --
their work this whole exchange is `runtime/php` plus docs -- so there was no
in-flight change of theirs for the goldens to be stale against. **Both files are
mine**, already modified in the working tree when this session started:
`foreach.ir` is my FE_FETCH header/fetch split, and `finally.ir` is my finally
work. I asked the wrong session to accept authorship of my own changes, and
declining to accept it is what surfaced the rest.

They checked the content anyway and both are correct, including two things I had
not looked at:

- The dropped catch arm was **spurious**. `finally.php` has no catch at all --
  both bodies are try/finally -- and the old header said `catch -> bb0`, aiming
  the catch arm at the function *entry*, where `recv` and parameter binding
  live. Dropping it is a fix.
- The `.line` attribution changed, **and the old one was a real bug**. It
  attached the finally body's position *before* the position of the `return`
  expression preceding it. The engine settles it:
  `try { if ($early) { return $undef_in_return; } } finally { echo "finally ran\n"; }`
  prints the undefined-variable warning at the return's line and *then*
  `finally ran`. Verified here rather than taken on report.

That defect was invisible until the emitter began rendering `.line` as
`ctx.SetLocation` and diagnostic positions started being graded byte-exact --
**a latent defect in the IR stays invisible until a consumer needs the part that
is wrong**, which is the same shape as the `true`/`false` and `??` findings.

The uncomfortable part is mine to keep. **`-update` regenerated a golden nobody
had reviewed and it happened to be right.** Asking was the correct instinct and
the answer merely went the favourable way. A golden regenerated from the
implementation is the implementation asserting its own correctness -- the
project's rule about hand-written expected output, one level up. So the
behaviour now has a test whose expected value came from the engine,
`TestAReturnExpressionIsAttributedBeforeTheFinallyBody`, with the probe in its
comment; the golden goes back to pinning format only. Written up in TESTING.md.

The runtime session withdrew the per-opcode/per-position table in favour of
enforcing the read rule over the emitted output, and is taking
`Increment`/`Decrement` -- moving the value logic out of `(*Interp).increment`
into `runtime/php` with `interp` delegating, rather than leaving two
implementations of one semantics.

### Numbers

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files: **passed 43, failed 38,
unsupported 3,829, errored 0, noreference 1,076.** Over the 3,910 gradable:
1.1% / 1.0% / 97.9% / 0.

The runtime session re-ran the interpreted corpus and confirmed `EvalAs` moved
nothing: 4,362 / 195 / 154 / 2, compile-error 0, identical to before.

## 2026-08-29 -- diagnostics start landing, and my emitter had a silent hole

Started on the top open item -- the emitter emits no diagnostics, which is the
whole `failed` bucket -- and found a worse bug on the way.

### The filename gate is closed

Diagnostics could not be graded at all while the oracle said `php2go-eval` and a
compiled program said its own path. `php2go_eval` now takes the reported name,
`Engine.EvalAs(code, name)` exposes it, and `Eval` delegates with the historical
default so nothing else moves. `php2eval -as` and `php2gotest` pass the real
path, and both arms now name the same file.

### Diagnostics

Two pieces, both small once the gate was open:

- **`.line` directives become `ctx.SetLocation`.** The emitter was dropping
  them. A diagnostic names the position it was raised at and that position is
  graded byte for byte, so dropping them left the position at whatever it last
  happened to be.
- **Program variables are read through a generated `readLocal` that warns on
  undef.** The mapping is exact rather than approximate, and it was checked
  rather than assumed: a PHP local starts *unset*, a Go var starts as the zero
  `php.Value`, and the zero Value is `KindUndef`, distinct from Null. So "still
  undef at the read" is precisely "PHP would warn here". Compiler temporaries
  are excluded -- written before read by construction, and the program cannot
  name them, so warning about one would invent a diagnostic the engine never
  emits.

Also ported the iterator opcodes into `internal/gogen` (they existed only in the
throwaway) and typed **places** by the join of their writes, which `foreach`
forces: `$__iterN` holds a `*php.Iter`, deliberately not a `php.Value`.

### The silent hole, which matters more than the number

An operand the emitter could not render was emitted as
`/* UNRENDERABLE: x */ php.Undef()`, under a comment I wrote claiming it was
*deliberately invalid Go so the build fails loudly rather than the program
running with a hole in it*.

It is perfectly valid Go. The program built and ran with exactly that hole.
`$a = [1, 2, 3]` left `$a` unset and the `foreach` over it died on null -- a
constant array literal prints as `<array>` and the operand text carries nothing
else, so that is the case that hit it. Now a hard refusal, tested.

This is the project's recurring failure with a new surface: **a conclusion
survived and its stated reason was never checked** -- except the reason was a
claim about Go, written as a comment, in the file whose job is to be correct
about Go. Its confident presence made it *less* likely anyone would test it.
Written into QUALITY_GATE.md as a rule: a refusal is a returned error, never a
rendered placeholder; and a comment claiming downstream rejection owes a test
that downstream rejects it.

### The numbers

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored | noreference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before this entry | 40 | 40 | 3,831 | 0 | 1,075 |
| diagnostics + filename | 42 | 38 | 3,830 | 0 | 1,076 |
| after the silent-hole fix | **42** | **39** | **3,829** | **0** | **1,076** |

I said before re-measuring that I expected the silent-hole fix to move the
number **down**, because a program running with an `undef` where a value belonged
could have matched by luck. **It did not**: `passed` held at 42 and the other
movement is one file. So there is no evidence the hole was manufacturing passes
-- which is worth stating precisely because I predicted otherwise, and a
prediction that fails quietly is how a flattering number survives.

**33 of the 39 remaining failures still want a diagnostic**, now mostly
`Deprecated:` from attributes and `Fatal error: Uncaught ...`, neither of which
the emitter can produce. Uncaught-error reporting is the next lever and is worth
more than any opcode: 29% of the corpus expects a `Fatal error` or `Parse error`
line.

with generated Go graded against the engine over 4,986 files.

### The numbers, same corpus and command throughout

`php2gotest` over `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored | noreference |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| first run | 35 | 43 | 4,903 | 5 | — |
| after the `true`/`false` fix | 37 | 41 | 4,903 | 5 | — |
| after the emitter fixes | 40 | 40 | 4,906 | **0** | — |
| after splitting the oracle out | 40 | 40 | 3,831 | 0 | **1,075** |

Over the **3,911 files the oracle could actually grade**: passed 40 (1.0%),
failed 40 (1.0%), unsupported 3,831 (98.0%), errored 0.

`internal/lower` is unmoved by all of it: CakePHP 6,730 / 6,782 = 99.2%,
`Zend/tests` 10,475 / 10,782 = 97.2%, no invariant violations, 418 suspending
bodies rewritten.

### Findings worth carrying

**1. Two consumers of one IR are a differential oracle for the IR itself.**
The strongest result of the session, and it is the runtime side's formulation
built on both halves. Mine: *an emitter is a checker for IR properties no IR
invariant asserts* -- Go's unused-label rule found the dead block that
`php2lower -verify` was structurally incapable of caring about. Theirs:
*a verifier checks shape; only a second consumer checks meaning* -- `true` and
`false` both rendered as the operand `bool`, so `$t = true` and `$f = false`
were the same instruction, and nothing could catch it because there was nothing
to compare against until something had to produce a value.

Tally for the session: **defects found by running generated code, 5. By
reviewing the IR, 0.**

**2. A measurement can hide most of itself, and the direction is predictable.**
36 of 40 failures want a diagnostic the emitter never produces -- the plan's
risk #2. But **1,438 of 4,966 corpus files (29%) expect a `Fatal error` or
`Parse error` and 1,853 (37%) expect some diagnostic**, counted independently
on both sides and converging within six files. The tests the oracle cannot ask
about are disproportionately the diagnostic tests, so a low `failed` count is
not evidence that diagnostics are a small problem. `030.phpt` --
`catch (Exception $this)`, a *fatal compile-error test* -- scored as a php2go
gap while `php2phpt` passes it. Hence the `noreference` bucket: **1,075 files
were never put to the compiler at all.**

**3. Body counts flatter an emitter; instruction counts do not.** The census
said 440 of 6,256 CakePHP bodies (7.0%) would emit and **831 of 149,404
instructions (0.6%)** -- mean emittable body 1.9 instructions against 23.9. I
nearly reported 13.5% before noticing 474 "successes" were abstract and
interface methods, which Zend gives a `recv` per parameter and a `ret null`, so
they lower cleanly and render fine. Excluded by asking the harvest
(`OpArray.abstract`), not by a size threshold -- a three-parameter abstract
method has four instructions, so any threshold that excludes it also excludes
real one-line functions. Same trap as counting bodies lowered rather than
lowered correctly.

**4. There is no cheap subset.** 83 distinct gaps; greedy by instructions
unlocked, 13 gaps buys 10%, and past 25 no single remaining gap unlocks a body
by itself. The order is not the frequency order -- `store` is 4th by bodies
blocked and 9th by instructions unlocked, because it rarely blocks alone. This
is what changed the plan: the harness and the emitter are one task, and a
harness pointed at a toy emitter measures nothing.

**5. An oracle that grades a different input than the compiler sees is worse
than no oracle.** `bug36037.phpt` wanted `1` and `6`, the compiler produced `2`
and `7`, and it reads as a compiler bug until you look: `php2eval` strips
`<?php\n` and shifts every line up by one. Both arms must see identical source.
Still unfixed and now the blocking issue for the diagnostics work: the engine
reports the filename `php2go-eval` and a compiled program reports its own path,
so **any test whose expected output contains a filename cannot pass regardless
of correctness.**

**6. Refuse in the compiler, not in the driver.** The terminal-state defect --
`counter(3)` returning 3 and then 4 -- was invisible because both drivers
guarded it, which made correctness a property of every driver rather than of the
emitted code. Fixing it in `Resumable` deleted the obligation instead of
documenting it. The same instinct made a catch handler a refusal rather than
straight-line code that would run when nothing was thrown.

### Corrections made to my own claims

- The generated-frame handoff said all 95 fiber bodies are refused. **Stale
  against my own later work**, which the runtime side caught: `Resumable`
  rewrites them and records `.suspends_to_caller`.
- I called the dead block "harmless, cosmetic, not worth a special case". It
  broke the build within a day.
- The greedy worklist's cumulative column ran past 100% by re-counting bodies
  unlocked in earlier rounds.
- I said the harvest discarded which boolean a literal was. It does not; the
  operand renderer did.

### Still open, in the order that matters

1. The emitter produces **no diagnostics and does not halt on a fatal**. That is
   the entire `failed` bucket and, per finding 2, more of the corpus than the
   bucket shows.
2. The oracle's filename problem, which blocks grading any of that.
3. A generator that **threw** still leaves a continuation state behind; the
   runtime side verified it (`re-entry gave yielded value=10`). The return path
   is fixed, the throw path is not.
4. Constant array literals are unrenderable from the IR text -- `<array>`
   carries nothing, though the harvest keeps the entries. Audit the other
   literal kinds for the same loss.

## 2026-08-29 -- ran the first generated frame; Iter landed, and yield-from was snapshotting wrong

The compiler side emitted a generator end to end -- PHP, harvest, lower,
`Resumable`, emit, `go build`, run -- with no hand transcription. Ran it here
rather than taking the result: builds clean on this tree, and `cmp` against
`php2eval -engine` is **32 bytes identical**.

That closes the condition set two rounds ago. The protocol is exercised rather
than unfalsified -- for `zval` slots, on two hand-picked bodies out of 418, which
is what it is worth and no more.

### The generated body has no terminal state

Pushing on it rather than confirming it. The emitted `switch` dispatches on
`f.State()`, and a body that returns never sets a state for "done": after
`counter(3)` returns 3, `f.State()` is still 2 -- the last continuation -- and
another `Step` resumes the loop and returns **4**.

```
driver says finished, return 3
state after Returned: 2
re-entry gave returned value=4 err=<nil>
```

Nothing hits it today because both drivers guard: `Generator` on `finished`,
`Fiber` on `FiberTerminated`. But that is a *driver-side* guarantee the generated
code depends on with nothing enforcing it, so a third driver would get it wrong
silently. Written into the `Resumable` doc as the one obligation on a driver, with
the alternative noted: the emitter could give every body a terminal state that
answers Returned idempotently, which is cheap and would retire the paragraph.

### `Iter` landed, and it is a snapshot

`runtime/php/iter.go`. The `*iter` slot type, and the thing that matters about it
is what it is *not*: not a `Value`, not boxable, not storable in an array. That
is the property the IR's separate slot type exists to express and the argument
that forced a generated struct per function.

The semantics were settled by asking the engine, and the obvious implementation
is wrong:

```php
$b = ['x'=>1,'y'=>2,'z'=>3];
foreach ($b as $k => $v) { if ($k=='x') { $b['z'] = 30; } echo "$k=$v,"; }
// x=1,y=2,z=3,     -- not z=30
```

Snapshotting the **keys** gets appends and unsets right and still reports 30 for
`z`. `foreach` iterates a copy, so both keys and values are taken at reset.
A generator is the opposite -- not snapshotted at all, since it has no elements
until asked -- so the two sources share an interface and nothing else.

`Valid` is pure and may not fetch or advance, which is the property that makes
the correct `FE_FETCH` emission possible: the loop header only asks, the body
block fetches. That is the ordering whose reversal dropped the last iteration of
every `foreach` in the corpus.

### The same bug was already in `yield from`, unobserved

Building `Iter` found it. `arrayDelegate` snapshotted keys and read values
*through* the array, which is exactly the wrong half. Reachable as soon as
compiled code shares an `*Array` across a delegation boundary. The engine
settles it, and by reference too:

```php
$b = [1,2,3];  function h(&$r) { yield from $r; }
$it = h($b);  $it->current();   // 1
$b[1] = 77;   $it->next();  $it->current();   // 2, not 77
```

Fixed, and the test was mutation-checked rather than assumed: restoring the live
read makes `TestYieldFromAnArrayHoldsASnapshot` fail with *second element is 77,
want 2*.

Worth noting how it was found. Not by review, and not by a test of `yield from`
-- by implementing a *different* feature whose semantics turned out to be the
same question. The probe written for `foreach` answered a question about
delegation that nobody had asked.

### What is still not executed

`*iter` slots still have never run inside a generated frame: both emitted shapes
are `while` loops, chosen to dodge the missing `Iter`. That gap is now closed
from this side, so a `foreach` generator is emittable and the `FE_FETCH`
ordering property gets its first execution instead of its first structural check.

Gate green, BUILD.bazel updated. `runtime/interp` untouched: `Zend/tests` 4,362
/ 195 / 154 / 2.

`internal/gogen` emits a whole PHP file as a self-contained Go program: the

First corpus number, `Zend/tests`, 4,986 files:

| | passed | failed | unsupported | errored |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| first run | 35 (0.7%) | 43 | 4,903 | 5 |
| after the bool fix | 37 | 41 | 4,903 | 5 |
| **final** | **40 (0.8%)** | **40 (0.8%)** | **4,906 (98.4%)** | **0** |

`passed` means a generated Go program's stdout was byte-identical to the
engine's. Low, and the buckets are what matter: **`errored` is zero**, so no
known gap is hiding inside a build failure any more.

**All 40 remaining failures are one cause.** 36 want a `Warning`, `Deprecated`
or `Fatal error` the emitter never produces; the other 4 want *empty* output
because the engine died before printing anything and the generated program
happily ran on. That is the plan's risk #2 -- "diagnostics are observable per
instruction, in order" -- arriving as a measurement rather than a worry.

### Four defects, three of them mine, one in the harness

- **Library calls emitted as user functions.** `undefined: php_var_dump`: a
  known gap landing in `errored` and reading as a compiler bug. Library calls
  are now refused by name. This is the `unsupported`/`errored` distinction
  earning its keep on the first run.
- **A label whose only predecessors are edges nothing emits.** `cfg.Preds` was
  the wrong question: it counts exception edges (which walk the region parent
  chain) and edges from unreachable blocks. The set of labels needed is the set
  of `goto` targets in the lines *actually emitted*, so it has to be computed
  after rendering rather than predicted before it.
- **A catch handler cannot be emitted, so it is refused.** Its block is reached
  only along an exception edge and carries the caught value as a *block
  parameter*; rendering it gave `undefined: v0`. Papering that over would have
  been worse -- the handler would run as straight-line code with nothing thrown.
  Also fixed properly: `valuesOf` collected instruction results only, so block
  parameters were declared nowhere.
- **`INF`/`NAN` printed as `+Inf`/`NaN`**, which are not Go literals.

### The harness graded two different inputs, and I nearly believed it

`bug36037.phpt` wanted `1` and `6`; the compiler produced `2` and `7`. It looks
exactly like a compiler bug and is not. The oracle **evaluates a string** and
the compiler **compiles a file**: `php2eval` strips `<?php\n`, which shifts every
line up by one, so `__LINE__` disagreed by construction. `sameLines` now removes
the tag and keeps the line it occupied -- it cannot merely be blanked, because
text before an opening tag is *output*. The test passes now.

**Still unfixed and written into TESTING.md**: the engine reports the filename
`php2go-eval` and a compiled program reports its own path, so **any test whose
expected output contains a filename cannot pass regardless of correctness**.
That does not bite yet only because the emitter produces no diagnostics at all,
and it will bite the moment it does. A `failed` count from this harness must not
be quoted as a semantics-bug count without checking that.

`true` and `false` both lowered to the operand `bool`, so **`$t = true` and
`$f = false` were the same instruction** -- indistinguishable to every consumer.
The harvest never lost it (`IS_TRUE` arrives as `Int: 1`); the operand renderer
discarded it. Fixed and mutation-checked; it moved 2 files from `failed` to
`passed` on its own.

Nothing in `php2lower -verify` could have caught this. The IR was *structurally
perfect and semantically lossy*, and "bool" reads as a type annotation rather
than a discarded value when the IR is only ever looked at. It took writing a
consumer that had to produce a value.

Tally worth keeping: **defects found by running generated code, 4 (plus 1 in the
grading harness); by reviewing the IR, 0.**

## 2026-08-29 -- foreach emitted, a finished body stays finished, and there is no cheap subset

Three things, all downstream of the runtime session running the generated frame
rather than reading it.

**A finished body did not stay finished.** They stepped `counter` again after it
returned and got 4. `frame.set_state` records where to *resume*, so the last
thing a body recorded was its final continuation; re-entry resumed the loop. Both
their drivers guard it -- `finished`, `FiberTerminated` -- which is precisely
what made it invisible: correctness was a property of every driver rather than
of the emitted code, so a third driver gets it wrong silently.

Fixed on this side, which is where it belongs. `Resumable` gives every body a
terminal state: each `ret` parks its value in `$__ret`, records the terminal
state, and returns; the terminal block is `ret $__ret` and nothing else. Re-entry
is idempotent instead of guarded. Probed directly, bypassing the drivers:
`state after Returned` 2 -> 3, re-entry `value=4` -> `value=3`, and 3 again.
`TestAFinishedBodyStaysFinished` covers three fixtures and fails when only the
`frame.set_state terminal` is dropped -- their exact defect, not a cruder one.

`Function.Terminal` names the state, because **three checks assumed every state
after 0 is a continuation** and all three flagged the terminal state as one that
fails to read a resumed value -- including `php2lower -verify`. Corpus after
fixing them: no violations either side, 418 suspending bodies unchanged, slots
587 -> 1005 and 66 -> 78, exactly one `$__ret` per frame.

**foreach is emitted.** `runtime/php/iter.go` landed and the blocker went with
it. The header emits `Valid()` alone, which their purity guarantee is what makes
legal; the fetch block does `Current`/`Key`/`Next`. `doubled` -- foreach with a
yield in the body -- is byte-identical to `php2eval -engine`: `0 => 10`,
`1 => 12`, `2 => 14`, `return 3`. **Three elements, not two**, so the FE_FETCH
ordering defect is now checked by execution and not only structurally. `*iter`
frame slots have run. Three shapes go end to end: `counter`, `join2`, `doubled`.

**The emitter census says there is no cheap subset.** Before building the
third-arm harness I asked what it would measure. Over CakePHP's 6,256
non-abstract bodies, calling the emitter's own switch so the census cannot drift
from it:

| | |
|---|---|
| bodies the emitter could render | 440 (7.0%) |
| **instructions** it could render | **831 / 149,404 (0.6%)** |
| mean size, emittable vs all | 1.9 vs 23.9 instructions |
| distinct gaps | 83 |

The body count is the misleading one. I nearly reported 13.5% before noticing
that **474 of the "successes" were abstract and interface methods** -- Zend emits
a `recv` per parameter and a `ret null`, so they lower cleanly and the emitter
renders them, and a body-count metric scores that as working. Excluded by asking
the harvest (`OpArray.abstract`), not by an instruction-count threshold: a
three-parameter abstract method has four instructions, so any threshold small
enough to exclude it also excludes real one-line functions. Same shape as
counting bodies lowered rather than lowered correctly.

Greedy by instructions unlocked: 13 gaps closed buys 10%, and past 25 no single
remaining gap unlocks a body by itself. The order is not the frequency order --
`store` is 4th by bodies blocked and 9th by instructions unlocked, because it
rarely blocks alone. **So the harness and the emitter are one task**: a harness
pointed at `genemit` would measure roughly nothing, and an emitter worth
measuring is essentially the whole intrinsic set Phase C0 estimates at ~90.

Two corrections to my own previous entry's write-up. The generated-frame handoff
said "all 95 fiber bodies are still refused" -- **stale against my own later
work**, which they caught: `Resumable` rewrites them and records
`.suspends_to_caller` (`cps.go:55-59`). The true, narrower claim is that no fiber
body has been emitted or run. And the greedy worklist's cumulative column ran
past 100% on first run, because a body unlocked in one round was re-counted in
every later one.

Running tally worth keeping: **defects found by running generated code, 2; by
reviewing the IR, 0.** Neither the dead label nor the terminal state is
expressible as an IR invariant, which is why `php2lower -verify` caught neither.

The runtime-side reply and final emitter census are recorded in the next
journal entries.

The frame protocol had been designed, handed off, implemented on the runtime

| body | generated | engine |
|---|---|---|
| `counter` (`yield $i * 10`, `return $i`) | `0 => 0` / `1 => 10` / `2 => 20` / `return 3` | identical, `cmp`, 32 bytes |
| `join2` (`$s = $s . "x"` across yields) | `x` / `xx` / `xxx` / `return xxx` | identical |

Two bodies is thin evidence about the compiler and adequate evidence about the
protocol: a wrong state number, a slot that failed to survive a suspension, a

The category is worth keeping: **an emitter checks IR properties that no IR
invariant asserts.** Everything `php2lower -verify` tests was chosen by someone
who suspected it. Go's compiler tests a different set, chosen by nobody, and it

What this is not, stated so the two numbers above are not read past: not an

## 2026-08-29 -- rule 2's third hole, and a corpus that is not one program

The runtime session found two more ways the `.suspends_to_caller` emitter rule is
insufficient, both settled against the engine rather than reasoned about. Both
hold, and their `yield from` census reproduces here exactly: 112 sites, 38 named
call (33.9%), 26 a place (23.2%), 20 constructor (17.9%), 10 literal, 8 dynamic,
6 array literal, 4 other.

### (A) Enumerating driver methods by spelling is wrong

`current()`, `valid()`, `key()` and `rewind()` all prime the body, and
`foreach ($gen as $v)` does too -- spelled `FE_RESET_R`/`FE_FETCH_R`, with no
method name to match on at all. A rule naming "next, send, resume" misses both.
The rule has to be structural: *any* operation that can advance a generator.

### (B) The marker does not survive `yield from`

`gh15108-004`'s `gen2` is unmarked -- it contains no literal `Fiber::suspend`,
only `ret.yield_from $gen` -- yet `$b->next()` on it is exactly the call the
suspension escapes through. Rule 2 keys on *an object whose body is marked*, and
gen2's body is not.

So the marker must be **transitive over `yield from`**, and
`CallGraph.PropagateMarks` now carries it up every delegation chain it can
resolve.

**It fires zero times on `Zend/tests`, and saying so is the point.** The
resolvable case is the 33.9% named-call bucket; `gh15108-004`'s own delegate is a
*place*, in the 23.2% bucket, which needs to know which generator a value holds.
That is a value question, not a type one -- the same `call_user_func` lever
identified from the other direction two entries ago, reached again from a
completely different problem. The mechanism is right and the corpus does not
exercise it; that is a null result, not a win.

### A corpus is not necessarily one program

Adding the hierarchy walk sent the process to **119 GB resident** and an OOM
kill. Not the retained functions -- an unbounded loop in `Descendants`.

`Zend/tests` has hundreds of *independent* files, each declaring its own
`class A extends B`. A parent map keyed by name alone merges them, so `a` extends
`b` from one file and `b` extends `a` from another, and walking the children
appends for ever. Bounded with a visited set: 119 GB became **91 MB**.

The deeper point is a caveat on every whole-corpus number taken over
`Zend/tests`: it is not one program, and merging its declarations by name
produces relationships no program has. Over CakePHP, which *is* one program, the
graph means what it says. Worth remembering before the two are compared again --
this is the third distinct way those corpora have turned out not to be
comparable.

### Also mine, and mine to have avoided

Retaining every lowered `Function` until the World was complete is what made the
memory question live at all. Declarations need only the harvest, so they get a
pass of their own now and pass two discards each function after inferring on it.

### Where the emitter is

Not started this turn. Rule 2 is what stops an emitter generating a call that
loses a suspension, so fixing it is a prerequisite rather than a detour -- but it
consumed the turn, and I would rather say that than hand over a rushed version of
the milestone both sides agreed should falsify the protocol properly.

## 2026-08-29 -- receiver inference: 67.4% from declarations, and the lever is now spent

`internal/lower/types.go`. It types the one thing the call graph said was worth
typing: the receiver of a `call.method`.

### Measured the shapes before building anything

The census that decided the design, over CakePHP's 9,071 method call sites:

| receiver | share | what it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `$this` | **43.9%** | nothing — the enclosing class |
| a local variable | 18.8% | dataflow |
| a parameter with a declared class type | 15.3% | the signature |
| a property read | 10.7% | the declared property type |
| a call result | 9.4% | the callee's declared return type |
| `new "C"` | 0.6% | one instruction |

`$this` alone is 44%, and **59.9% needs no dataflow at all**. So the first pass
reads declarations only and does no dataflow whatever.

(The first version of that census reported 78.7%, because the string "local"
matched both "a **local** variable — needs dataflow" and my test for the cheap
cases. Corrected before it was used for anything.)

### Result

**6,133 of 9,101 method call sites — 67.4% — now carry `recv="C"`.** Annotated
onto the instruction rather than kept in a side table, so it is visible in the
printed IR, diffable, and readable by any consumer without re-derivation.

Narrowing to the *declared* class alone would be unsound, since a subclass may
override, so a narrowed edge covers the class and its descendants. That is the
class hierarchy doing the work, not the declaration.

### What it bought, and what it did not

| CakePHP | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| call-graph edges | 41,027 | **21,150** |
| maybe-suspending, methods only | 1,973 (29.3%) | **1,131 (16.8%)** |
| maybe-suspending, sound | 2,777 (41.3%) | **2,275 (33.8%)** |
| receiver's class costs | 29.1% | **16.6%** |
| opaque calls cost | 11.9% | **17.0%** |

Half the graph's edges were the method-name approximation, and they are gone.
But **the two costs have swapped**: opaque calls are now the larger imprecision,
so the lever this session identified is substantially spent, and the next one is
a different problem — values flowing into `call_user_func`, not types.

67.4% also undershoots the census's ~80%, which predicted property and return
types would add 20 points over the 59.9% base. They added about 7.5. Declared
property and return types are rarer, or resolve to non-class types, more often
than the site counts suggested — worth knowing before anyone budgets the next
increment off a site census.

### And it completes a rule I had stated incompletely

The runtime session found it, and I verified it: **26 of the 95 bodies carrying
`.suspends_to_caller` in `Zend/tests` are also generators** — bodies that both
yield and suspend. My emitter rule, *never emit a direct call to a marked
function*, never fires for those, because nothing calls them directly: calling
one makes a Generator. The suspension escapes through `$b->next()` instead, an
ordinary method call the marker does not mark.

So the rule has a second part: never emit a *driver* call on an object whose body
is marked. And that part needs the receiver's class — which is what this pass
supplies. The two pieces of work met without being aimed at each other.

## 2026-08-29 -- rule 2 has two more closures, and the same defect was one level up

The compiler side verified the `.suspends_to_caller` finding and split the
emitter rule in two: (1) no direct call to a marked function, (2) no driver call
-- `next`, `send`, `resume` -- on an object whose body is marked. Receiver
inference landed to make part 2 computable: 6,133 of 9,101 CakePHP method call
sites (67.4%) now carry `recv=C`, edges 41,027 -> 21,150, maybe-suspending
ceiling 41.3% -> 33.8%, and the lever is spent -- opaque calls now cost 17.0%
against the receiver's 16.6%.

Rule 2 is still not sufficient, in two ways, and the second one is the shape of
the test that motivated the rule.

### Every entry point primes, and one of them is not a method name

Settled with `php2eval -engine`, not reasoned about:

```php
function g1() { Fiber::suspend('from current'); yield 'never'; }
$f = new Fiber(function () { $g = g1(); var_dump($g->current()); });
$f->start();   // string(12) "from current" -- the fiber is suspended
```

`current()` suspends. So do `valid()`, `key()` and `rewind()`: all of them
prime. And `foreach ($gen as $v)` does too -- a driver call spelled as
`FE_RESET_R`/`FE_FETCH_R`, with no method name to match on. A rule enumerating
`next, send, resume` by spelling misses both.

### The marker does not survive `yield from`

`gh15108-004`'s own `gen2` is **unmarked**:

```
func gen2 -> zval {
  .frame [ $gen: zval, $__t1: zval ]      <- no .suspends_to_caller
bb1:
  frame.set_state 2
  ret.yield_from $gen                     <- a place, not a callee
```

It contains no literal `Fiber::suspend()`, so nothing marks it -- and yet
`$b->next()` on it is exactly the call the suspension escapes through in the
test. Confirmed against the engine with the names shortened:

```php
function inner() { yield 1; Fiber::suspend('escaped'); }
function outer($g) { yield from $g; var_dump("not executed"); }
// $b->next() inside a fiber: string(7) "escaped", isSuspended() true
```

The delegate is a **parameter**, so which generator it is is a value and not a
type. Receiver inference does not reach it; this is the `call_user_func` problem
wearing a different hat, which is the same next-lever the compiler side just
identified from the other direction.

Census of the operand of all 112 `ret.yield_from` sites in `Zend/tests` -- the
definition is always in the same block, so the no-cross-block-values invariant
makes this a one-pass count rather than an analysis:

| delegate operand | sites | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a named function call | 38 | 33.9% |
| a place (`$var`) | 26 | **23.2%** |
| a constructor | 20 | 17.9% |
| a literal | 10 | 8.9% |
| a dynamic call | 8 | 7.1% |
| an array literal | 6 | 5.4% |
| other | 4 | 3.6% |

Two thirds could propagate the marker with no dataflow at all. The 23.2% is the
motivating test's shape.

### The same defect, one level out

Finding it cost me a bug. `Generator.resume` did

```go
if err := g.delegate.Advance(ctx, sent); err != nil {
    g.abort()
```

which is the mistake I had just fixed *inside* `step`, repeated at the
delegation boundary: a suspension arriving from a delegate is not the delegate
failing, and aborting discards the entire `yield from` chain. Now it sets
`stuck` and propagates, so both generators stay parked -- which is what the
engine does.

`TestASuspensionTravelsUpAYieldFromChain` covers it, and the assertion was
mutation-checked rather than assumed: stubbing the branch to `if false && ...`
makes it fail with *the outer generator was aborted*, so the test is load-bearing
and not decoration.

### The pattern, twice now

Both findings this session came from the same move: take the claim stated as a
general rule and ask the corpus whether it holds. "A generator never carries the
marker" had 26 counterexamples; "a driver call on a marked object" misses the
case the rule was written for. Neither needed cleverness -- one `grep -c` and
one census over output already on disk -- and neither would have surfaced from
reading the rule, because the rule is locally reasonable both times. The check
is the whole of the method.

Gate green. `runtime/interp` untouched: `Zend/tests` stays 4,362 / 195 / 154 / 2.

## 2026-08-29 -- the fiber driver comes back, and the marker misses 26 of its own cases

The compiler side split the fiber question in two and only the second half was
ever hard: **always rewrite the suspending function, defer only the decision
about its caller**. The callee's CPS form is the common prefix of uniform, dual
entry, selective and keep-goroutines alike, so building it commits to none of
them. `Resumable` no longer refuses fibers; it rewrites them and records
`.suspends_to_caller` on the function instead.

Checked rather than taken, `php2lower` over `third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `.resumable` functions | 418 |
| carrying `.suspends_to_caller` | 95 |
| `ret.suspend` sites | 103 |
| `ret.generator` sites | 349 |
| `-cps -verify` | no violations |

### The driver is restored, and the reason it was removed is the reason it is back

`php.Fiber` went because nothing could produce `Outcome{Suspended}`: exported
API with no producer advertises a capability that does not exist. That premise
is now false at 103 sites, so the same rule that removed it puts it back. It is
in `runtime/php/resumable.go`, and it is executed against `App\inside`
transcribed by hand from `php2lower -cps -print`. **That is the first time
`ret.suspend` has run.**

Two things fell out of the IR rather than having to be arranged. A fiber body
has **no `ret.generator`**, so its `recv` opcodes sit in state 0 and the
arguments bind on the first `Step` — which is exactly what `start(...$args)`
is, where a generator binds at the call. And `ret.suspend` carries a value and
no key, which is the whole of its difference from `ret.yield` at the driver
level.

The error surface was settled by running the cases, not by reading the source:
`getReturn()` has **three** distinct refusals for a fiber — `The fiber has not
been started`, `has not returned`, `threw an exception` — where a generator has
one message for all of them. So three sentinels, not one, and the asymmetry with
`ErrGeneratorNotReturned` is deliberate.

### The finding: `.suspends_to_caller` does not describe one of its own cases

The stated criterion is "only where a suspension can escape to a PHP caller —
a generator never carries the marker, because calling one returns a Generator
object and the suspension happens inside the driver."

**26 of the 95 marked bodies are generators.** `Zend/tests/gh15108-004.phpt`:

```php
function gen1() {
    yield 'foo';
    Fiber::suspend();
    var_dump("not executed");
}
```

The code is right — the marker is set per suspension point, so a body that both
yields and suspends gets it. The *criterion* is what is incomplete, and so is the
emitter rule that follows from it. **Never emit a direct call to a function
carrying `.suspends_to_caller`** never fires for these 26: nothing calls `gen1`
directly, because calling it makes a Generator object. The suspension escapes
through `$b->next()` instead — an ordinary method call, on a call site the
marker does not mark. The set of call sites a suspension can escape through is
not the set of direct calls to marked functions; it is closed over *driver*
calls too.

### A defect on my side, found by the same fact

`Generator.step` sent `Suspended` to its `default:` arm, which called `abort()`
and returned `ErrProtocol`. Both halves wrong. `ErrProtocol` means the emitter
and `frame.go` disagree, and here they do not — the IR is right and so is the
emitter; what is missing is a resumable form for the PHP frame that called
`$g->next()`. And `abort()` destroys state the engine keeps: it leaves such a
generator *parked* at the suspension, to continue when the fiber resumes.

Now `ErrSuspendAcrossDriver`, with the generator left unfinished and a `stuck`
flag so a second `next()` reports the same gap. Without the flag it would
re-enter the continuation with a stale resumed value and look like it worked,
which is the gap-masquerading-as-behaviour QUALITY_GATE.md forbids.

### What this cost me to believe

Every claim in the message I was sent was true. The one I had to check anyway
was the one stated as a general rule — "a generator never carries the marker" —
and it is the one that turned out to have 26 counterexamples sitting in the
corpus the message itself quoted. The pattern from last session's TESTING.md
entry holds up: the claim that fails is the one carrying no check. Here the
check cost one `grep -c` against output I had already generated.

Gate green; `runtime/interp` untouched, so `Zend/tests` stays at 4,362 / 195 /
154 / 2.

## 2026-08-29 -- the call graph, and the number the fiber argument needed all along

`internal/lower/callgraph.go`, run by `php2lower -callgraph`. It exists to
settle by measurement a question that had been argued three times: if a function
suspends, how far does *might be on the stack when it does* spread?

### The answer, and the two corpora disagree completely

| | CakePHP | `Zend/tests` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| functions / edges | 6,730 / 41,027 | 7,222 / 97,085 |
| suspending | 12 | 165 |
| with an opaque call site | 700 (10.4%) | 370 (5.1%) |
| **floor** — directly named callees only | 12 (**0.2%**) | 325 (4.5%) |
| + every method of a matching name | 1,973 (**29.3%**) | 439 (6.1%) |
| + opaque calls treated soundly | 2,777 (**41.3%**) | 1,132 (15.7%) |
| **the receiver's class costs** | **29.1%** | 1.6% |
| **opaque calls cost** | 11.9% | 9.6% |
| blast radius, median / p90 | 4 / 1,964 | 0 / 3 |

**In the real application the receiver's class is worth 2.4× what opaque calls
are.** Type inference is the dominant lever, which is the same conclusion the
call-site census reached from the other end and is now confirmed on the graph
itself. In `Zend/tests` it inverts — opaque calls cost 6× the receiver — because
that corpus barely uses objects. A framework and a language test suite are not
the same shape of program and should stop being quoted as if they were.

The other half matters as much: **the ceiling is 41.3%, not 100%.** Even with
today's imprecision, three fifths of CakePHP could stay direct. Selective CPS is
not the dead end the earlier argument made it — and with the receiver's class
supplied, the true figure lies somewhere between 0.2% and 29.3%.

### What this does not say

The 12 suspending bodies in CakePHP are **generators**, and a generator's
suspension does not propagate to its caller. So this measures the *shape* of
propagation — the blast radius if something suspended in a way that escaped —
rather than a requirement CakePHP actually has. It is a proxy, and a good one,
but it is not "CakePHP needs 41% of itself compiled CPS".

### A wrong number caught by an implausible one

The first run reported `edges via a method name alone: 100.0%`, meaning not one
directly named callee resolved. That is not a plausible property of a real
codebase, and it was a bug: the IR renders literals with `%q`, so a namespaced
name arrives as `Cake\\Foo` with its backslash doubled, while definitions carry
`Cake\Foo`. Every namespaced name missed its own definition — and CakePHP is
namespaced throughout, so *all* of them did.

Fixed with `strconv.Unquote`, which recovered 702 direct edges and moved the
headline from 26.2%/37.1% to 29.3%/41.3%. The tell was a percentage that was too
round to be true; the guard is now a test asserting a namespaced callee resolves
to its own definition.

### Where it leaves the fiber question

Nothing is decided, and the decision now has a number to rest on instead of an
argument. The next thing that would move it is type inference supplying receiver
classes, which Phase D wants anyway — this is not fiber-specific work, which is
the best property it has.

## 2026-08-29 -- the refusal was in the wrong place: emit the callee, defer the caller

Proposed decomposition: always emit the suspending function as CPS, and defer
the decision about whether its *caller* is CPS too. It is better than what I had,
and it exposes that my refusal was aimed at the wrong half of the problem.

### Why it is the right cut

The callee's CPS form is the **common prefix of every option** on the table --
uniform CPS, dual entry points, selective CPS, or keeping goroutines for fibers.
All four need it. Building it therefore commits to none of them, which is exactly
what a deferred decision should cost.

And the caller question has a precise criterion rather than being a vague
"later": it arises only where **a suspension can escape to a PHP caller**. For a
generator it provably cannot -- calling one returns a Generator object and the
suspension happens inside the driver, which is CPS-aware. That is why generators
already worked end to end, and it is the same fact the runtime session had
noticed from the other side when they observed that `ret.generator` is what makes
the first return safe.

### What changed

`Resumable` no longer refuses fibers. It rewrites them and records
`.suspends_to_caller` on the function instead -- the open question made explicit
in the IR rather than resolved by declining to lower.

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` suspending bodies rewritten | 323 / 418 | **418 / 418** |
| of which fibers | 0 (95 refused) | **95** |
| invariant violations after the rewrite | none | **none** |
| CakePHP coverage | 6,730 / 6,782 | unchanged |

**The 95 fiber bodies were always rewritable.** They satisfy every structural
invariant the generators do. Refusing them said "this cannot be done" when the
truth was "this can be done and something else is undecided", which is the same
class of over-statement as the two before it.

### The emitter rule that falls out

*Never emit a direct call to a function carrying `.suspends_to_caller`.* A driver
may call one, being CPS-aware; a compiled PHP call site may not, until the caller
decision is made. That is a checkable rule at the point where it matters, rather
than a restriction baked into an earlier pass where it removed information.

Worth noting the consequence for the runtime side: something now *does* produce a
fiber state machine, which was their stated reason for removing the Fiber driver.
A fiber whose suspension sits directly in its entry callable has the driver as
its only caller and is therefore runnable today; one that suspends deeper is not.

## 2026-08-29 -- there is a static set after all, and the blocker is receiver types

Asked what changes if we could infer types correctly and identify which
functions may resume. Answering it honestly costs a sixth correction, mine.

### "There is no static set to compute" was over-stated

I had sharpened the fiber argument to: whether a frame lies inside a fiber's span
is a property of the *activation*, so there is no static set. True about
activations, wrong about sets. **The set exists**: it is the transitive callers
of `Fiber::suspend()`, it is closed under "caller of", and an over-approximation
is sound, because compiling a function CPS that never suspends costs speed rather
than correctness.

So selective CPS is well defined. The true statement is narrower and duller: it
is only *worth* anything if the set is much smaller than everything.

### Which makes it measurable, so I measured it

Every call site in both corpora, classified by how resolvable its callee is:

| | CakePHP | `Zend/tests` |
|---|---|---|
| statically resolvable to a named callee | 53.2% | 73.6% |
| `call.method`, name known / **receiver class not** | **44.8%** | 21.6% |
| `call.dynamic`, callee genuinely a value | **1.0%** | 3.3% |

**The unresolvable bulk is not hostile dynamism.** It is method calls where the
name is known and the receiver's class is not — precisely what type inference
supplies, and precisely the gap already recorded against method specialization in
`TYPE-INFERENCE.md`. The genuinely opaque category is *one percent* of CakePHP's
call sites.

That does not produce a sound call graph on its own. But soundness does not have
to come from the analysis: at an unresolvable site, take the CPS path
conservatively. At 1% of sites that is cheap, and it is a wholly different
proposition from uniform CPS taxing every call.

### The question that actually decides it, unanswered

Propagation. A function is maybe-suspending if it suspends, calls a
maybe-suspending function, **or contains an unresolvable call** — so one
`call_user_func` infects every caller above it. Whether 1% of sites infects 5% of
functions or 95% of them is the number the fiber decision should rest on, and
nothing measures it today: it needs a cross-file call graph keyed by function and
by class-plus-method, which does not exist.

Worth saying plainly that this reopens a decision I had recorded as deferred on
good evidence. The evidence for deferring is unchanged — 0 fibers in CakePHP. What
changed is that the *reason it looked permanent* has gone: it is not that no
useful set exists, it is that we have not built the analysis that would size it.

Sixth correction, and the third in a row where the conclusion held and the reason
did not. This one at least failed in the safe direction — I had talked myself
into a stronger impossibility than the facts supported, which is the same
mistake as the call-graph claim two rounds ago and should probably have been
caught by its own precedent.

## 2026-08-29 -- the discriminator does not have to be static, and I endorsed an argument that assumed it did

Two corrections and a measurement, and the fifth instance of the pattern this
handoff has been generating.

### Why uniformity is forced, stated properly

I had it as "selective CPS needs the transitive closure of functions that can be
on the stack at a suspension, and dynamic dispatch makes that closure
unsound." True, and weaker than the real reason:

> **There is no static set to compute.** Whether a frame lies inside a fiber's

> on the fiber stack in one call and not in another.

That is why, if each function gets one compiled form, it has to be the CPS one.

The runtime session ranked dual entry points last on the grounds that something
must choose which entry a call site uses, and the honest form of that choice is
"can this callee reach a suspension" — the call graph in a different coat. I
called it the sharpest thing in the exchange.

**It assumes the discriminator is static, and it need not be.** Whether we are
inside a fiber is exactly the kind of thing a dynamic flag answers:

- the fiber entry sets it
- every call site branches on it
- inside a fiber, everything runs CPS, so suspension works at any depth
- outside one, everything runs direct, at full speed

No call graph anywhere. Real costs instead: about 2× code size, because both
versions must exist everywhere precisely *because* the flag is dynamic; one
well-predicted branch per call; and the flag has to survive every boundary. That
is a genuine option, and the only one that keeps a fast path.

It shares the native-frame limit with the others — `usort` calling a suspending
comparator has a Go frame in the middle either way.

It does not move the deferral — 0 fibers in CakePHP against 95 in a language

## 2026-08-29 -- the goroutine fiber is a concurrency primitive doing control flow, measured

Runtime track. The compiler side corrected its own framing again: option 3 was
recorded as a *decision* and it is a **deferral with a known workaround**. I
checked the claim it rests on against `runtime/interp/fiber.go` rather than
taking the endorsement, and then put a number on it, because "two scheduler
handoffs per transfer" is the sort of cost that should be measured before it is
quoted.

### The rendezvous claim is correct

`held.toFiber = make(chan resumption)` and `held.fromFip = make(chan suspension)`
are both **unbuffered**, and `switchTo` is

```go
held.toFiber <- message
out := <-held.fromFip
```

so the resumer blocks the instant it hands over, and the fiber side mirrors it.
Strict rendezvous, exactly one of the two runnable. The goroutine is not there
for concurrency -- there is none in a fiber -- it is there to **own a native
stack that can be parked**.

That is forced rather than sloppy, and the reason is worth stating because it
turns the option list into a dichotomy: Go has no stack switching, so suspending
a computation with native frames means either parking a stack, which only a
goroutine can own, or having no native frames, which is CPS. There is no third
mechanism without cgo, and cgo is out because the artifact must stand alone.
**CPS is therefore the answer rather than an alternative to one.**

### What a transfer costs

`BenchmarkTransferRendezvous` / `BenchmarkTransferStateMachine`, bare mechanism
on both sides, `-benchmem -count 5`:

| mechanism | ns per transfer | allocs |
|---|---|---|
| unbuffered channel round trip (two handoffs) | 331-351 | 0 |
| one state-machine entry through `Resumable` | 2.14-2.16 | 0 |

About **160x**, and the rendezvous figure is a *floor*: the real `switchTo` also
swaps the interpreter's frames, call stack and scope across the handover.

Two things this number is not. It is not "fibers are 160x slower than generators
in php2go" -- the interpreter's per-opline cost dwarfs both sides. And the state
machine is measured through the `Resumable` interface deliberately, because a
concrete receiver lets the compiler inline the whole step and flatters the
mechanism by a factor the real thing never sees.

### Nothing changed, and that is the right outcome

`php.Fiber` stays out of `runtime/php` -- nothing produces a fiber state machine,
so exported API for one would still advertise a capability that does not exist.
`fiber.go` stays in the interpreter, as the only thing that can run a fiber
today. What changed is the label: TODO.md now says this postpones the
"runtime should not be suspension-aware" instruction for fibers rather than
satisfying it, and carries the measured per-transfer cost instead of a
qualitative claim about scheduler handoffs.

## 2026-08-29 -- a goroutine is the wrong shape for a fiber; the deferral stands, the framing does not

I recorded "keep goroutines for fibers" as a decision. It is a **deferral with a
known workaround**, and calling it a decision hid a real piece of debt.

A fiber and its resumer are never concurrent. `runtime/interp/fiber.go` is a
strict rendezvous over two unbuffered channels:

```go
// resume:   held.toFiber <- message            ; out := <-held.fromFip
// suspend:  held.fromFip <- suspension{value}  ; message := <-held.toFiber
```

Each side blocks the instant it hands over, so exactly one of the two runs at
any moment. **The goroutine is not there for concurrency.** It is there to own a
native stack that can be parked, and we pay two scheduler handoffs per transfer
for a construct with no parallelism in it. A concurrency primitive standing in
for a control-flow one.

### The choice is forced, which is the useful part

Go has no stack switching. Suspending a computation that has native frames means
either **parking a stack** — and only a goroutine owns a parkable one — or
**having no native frames**, which is CPS. There is no third mechanism, and no
amount of cleverness produces one without cgo, which the standalone-artifact
goal rules out.

So the dichotomy is real: goroutine or CPS. That makes CPS the answer rather
than an alternative, and makes the present mechanism a placeholder.

### What actually changes

Not the decision — the evidence for deferring is unchanged: 0 fibers in
CakePHP's 12 suspending bodies against 95 in a language test suite. What changes
is that it is now recorded as *deferring the work*, not as endorsing the
mechanism, and two consequences are written down rather than implied:

- **It does not satisfy the original instruction.** "The runtime shouldn't be
  suspension-aware" is postponed for fibers, not met. `php.Fiber` living in the
  runtime is the visible form of that.
- **The cost is per transfer, not per fiber.** Two scheduler handoffs on every
  suspend and every resume, which is the thing to quote if a workload ever makes
  this hot.

Third correction in two rounds where a conclusion of mine was right and its
stated basis was not. Here the conclusion was even reached for a defensible
reason — the corpus evidence — but I let "chosen" stand for "we are not doing
the right thing yet", which is the kind of wording that stops a question being
re-asked.

stated reason gets carried to the next case it appears to cover. Written up in

## 2026-08-29 -- fibers keep goroutines, on evidence; and a third narrower-than-stated reason

The runtime session answered the fiber question and caught the same class of
mistake a third time.

### The decision: option 3, and for the right reason

Keep fibers on goroutines. **Not because uniform CPS is too slow** -- that would
be the corrected-away answer wearing a new label -- but because the corpus says
fibers are a test-suite phenomenon rather than a workload one:

| corpus | suspending bodies | fibers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CakePHP `src/` | 12 | **0** — all 12 rewrote |
| `Zend/tests` | 418 | 95 (23%) |

Zero fibers in the one real application corpus we measure, and 23% in a language
test suite, which is exactly where every fiber edge case would be exercised.
Uniform CPS taxes 100% of calls in every compiled program to serve a construct
that appears **0 times in real code**. Wrong trade at this evidence level, and it
flips the moment a workload shows fibers hot -- which is what the correction
bought: a costed option waiting rather than a closed door.

### Dual entry points is the impossible option in disguise

Their sharpest point, and it goes in `TODO.md` so nobody re-derives it as the
obvious middle path. Something has to choose which entry a call site uses, and
the honest form of that choice is *"can this callee reach a suspension"* -- which
is the call graph again in a different coat. It looks like a compromise and is
the impossible option with extra code size. Ranked last, not middle.

### A continuation *can* be a join point

I wrote that a suspension terminates its block, so the continuation is a fresh
leader and any join lands in a later block. **False**, and they asked me to check
rather than take it, so I read the CFG instead of the printed IR:

```
state 2 = bb4  preds=[10]     resumed=%2 used=true
state 3 = bb6  preds=[4 10]   resumed=%8 used=false
```

`bb6` is state 3's dispatch target *and* the false arm of `br $reply, bb5, bb6`.
A fresh leader can still have other in-edges. It is a counterexample to the
reason and not to the assertion -- bb6 does not use its resumed value.

So the property is the narrow one, and it is **checked, not proven**: verified
over 335 rewritten bodies and guarded permanently by `php2lower -cps`, rather
than derived from block structure. The comment now says so.

**Three times now** a conclusion of mine has been right for a reason narrower
than I stated: the call-graph claim, and this twice over. The pattern is
specific -- reaching for a structural argument that sounds inevitable instead of
checking the structure. The guard against it is not more care, it is that these
are all *checkable*, and the checks now exist.

### Nothing else outstanding

They promoted the effect-once argument above the value-is-stale one in their doc
comment, which is the right ordering: consume-once is what makes the re-read safe
in general, and the value being unused is a narrower observation that happens to
hold.

Next milestone unchanged and agreed on both sides: an emitter. Their drivers have

## 2026-08-29 -- correction: CPS for fibers is a cost decision, not an impossibility

I wrote that fibers cannot get the CPS treatment because "only a whole-program
rewrite would be sound, and that needs a call graph PHP's dynamic dispatch
denies." **The two halves of that sentence contradict each other**, and I
propagated the framing from the runtime session's report without examining it.

- A **selective** rewrite -- transform only the functions that can reach a
  suspension -- does need a call graph, and that is exactly why it cannot be
  done over dynamic dispatch. This is the pass that exists, and refusing fibers
  in it remains correct.
- A **uniform** rewrite needs no call graph *at all*, because it never asks the
  question. If every function takes a continuation then every call is already a
  suspension point and there is no native stack left to lose. It is sound.

What uniform CPS costs is the Go stack everywhere: a heap frame per call, a
dispatch per entry. That is close to what the interpreter already does with
frames, and it is most of what compiling was supposed to buy — a real trade-off,
and one worth stating as a trade-off rather than hiding behind "unsound".

Three options, recorded in `TODO.md` rather than decided here: uniform CPS; dual
entry points per function, keeping a direct fast path at roughly double the code
size; or keeping goroutines for fibers, which is what happens today and which
keeps the runtime suspension-aware for exactly one construct.

**The one genuine hard limit is narrower than the claim I made.** Suspending
across a *native* frame -- `Fiber::suspend()` inside a `usort` comparator -- has
an engine frame between the suspension and the fiber, and no PHP-level rewrite
reifies that. PHP's own fibers switch real stacks, which is precisely how they
avoid the question. The affected set is enumerable, being the builtins that call
user callbacks, so it bounds the claim instead of defeating it.

No code changed: the selective pass still refuses fibers, for the reason that
actually applies to it. The comment in `cps.go`, `TODO.md` and the reply to the
runtime session are corrected, and the wrong version is kept visible in each
because the mistake is more instructive than the conclusion -- "needs an
analysis that does not exist" is a much easier thing to believe than it should
be, and I believed it without checking whether the analysis was needed.

## 2026-08-29 -- three defects back from the runtime session, all real

The frame handoff came back with three defects, recorded with the compiler-side
answer in the surrounding journal entries. All
three were real and all three are fixed. The first is the one that matters.

### foreach dropped its last iteration, and coverage could never have caught it

```
2: FE_RESET_R  -> exit 8
3: FE_FETCH_R  EXT=8      <- the loop header: tests, THEN fetches and advances
4-6: body
7: JMP -> 3               <- the back edge targets the FETCH, not past it
```

`FE_FETCH` is the loop header and tests *before* it fetches. I emitted
`current; local.set; next; br iter.valid`, which asks whether there is a
**further** element before running the body for this one. `[1,2,3]` ran the body
twice; `[5]` not at all. Every `foreach` in both corpora, and the committed
golden agreed with it.

The fix is a block split: the test terminates the block and the fetch moves into
a block of its own, reached only once the test has passed.

**Why it survived is worth more than the fix.** Coverage counts *bodies
lowered*, not bodies lowered correctly, so 99.2% was as true after the bug as
before it. Nothing I had built could see it: not the coverage number, not the
bail histogram, not the golden — the golden encoded the wrong answer. It took
someone executing the IR.

That is now a test rather than a lesson. `TestForeachTestsBeforeItFetches`
asserts the structural signature -- **the block that tests the iterator must not
touch it** -- and restoring the old order fails it by name.

### The resumed value was only read where a block parameter existed

`frame.resumed` is not there to produce a value: it is where a thrown-in
exception surfaces, so `Generator::throw()` can be caught by the generator's own
`try`. `yield $x;` written as a statement had no parameter and so no read, and
the exception was lost silently. Every continuation reads it now.

### CPS is unsound for fibers, and the call is: generators only

Not a bug -- a design question, correctly refused rather than patched.

`yield` is confined to the generator's body by a language rule, so rewriting
that body reifies all of its suspension points with no call graph at all.
`Fiber::suspend()` suspends the current fiber from **any depth**, so `a()`
calling `b()` which suspends leaves a's frame on the Go stack with nothing to
reify. Rewriting only the lexically enclosing function looks transformed and is
not.

Doing it properly needs every function that can transitively reach a suspension,
which needs a sound call graph, which PHP's dynamic dispatch denies. So:
**generators lose their goroutines, fibers keep them.** `Resumable` refuses
fibers cleanly, with no partial rewrite.

**95 of the 418 suspending bodies in `Zend/tests` are fibers** -- 23%, not a
corner. It stayed hidden because the fixture put `Fiber::suspend` in the entry
function, which is the one shape where the lexical rewrite happens to be enough.

The intrinsic stays: making the suspension point visible is right whether or not
this pass can rewrite it.

### Result

Coverage unchanged by all three -- CakePHP **6,730 / 6,782 = 99.2%**,
`Zend/tests` **10,475 / 10,782 = 97.2%**, no invariant violations -- which is
exactly the point the foreach bug made about coverage. Suspending bodies
rewritten: CakePHP 12/12, `Zend/tests` 323/418 with 95 refused as fibers.

Two tests on their side deliberately assert the old wrong answers as labelled
reproductions; they have been asked to retire them now that both are fixed.

## 2026-08-29 -- frames for resumable functions, and the first execution of the CPS path

Runtime track, from the compiler side's [FRAME-HANDOFF.md](./FRAME-HANDOFF.md).
The full runtime-side reply has been consolidated into this entry.

Landed: `runtime/php/frame.go` (`FrameState`, `Outcome`, `Resumable`, the
refusal sentinels), `runtime/php/resumable.go` (the `Generator` and `Fiber`
drivers, `Delegate` for `yield from`), `runtime/php/frame_test.go`. Nothing in
`runtime/interp` was touched and the corpus counts did not move -- the handoff's
boundary is that compiled code gets frames and the interpreter keeps its
goroutines.

### The representation is a generated struct, and the choice was forced

Not preferred -- forced, twice over. A slot's declared type is authoritative and
`$__iterN: *iter` must not be boxed, so a uniform `[]Value` cannot hold an
iterator without inventing a `Value` kind to box it in. And "every declared slot
must outlive the frame" becomes *structural* when a slot is a field: there is no
operation that clears one, so the emitter promises nothing.

Benchmarked anyway, because the handoff asked for a measurement rather than an
assumption: struct 834-1014 ns/op, 240 B, **1 alloc**; slice 900-1026 ns/op,
272 B, **2 allocs**. The time difference is inside the noise and I am not
claiming it. The allocation difference is real and is the second indirection.

### Three defects, which is the point of running something that never ran

The handoff said to expect the IR to be wrong and to say so rather than work
around it. It was wrong in three places, and the first one is not about
resumability at all.

**`foreach` drops its last iteration.** The engine's harvested op_array has
`FE_FETCH_R ... EXT=8`, and `FE_FETCH` tests for exhaustion *before* it fetches.
`lower.go` emits `iter.current; local.set; iter.next; br iter.valid` -- it asks
*after* consuming. `[1,2,3]` iterates as `[1 2]`; `[5]` runs the body not at all.
It is in the committed golden `foreach.ir` too, so every `foreach` in both
corpora is affected. The 99.2% CakePHP figure is a coverage number and this does
not change it, which is exactly why the defect survived: **coverage counts
bodies lowered, not bodies lowered correctly.**

**`Generator::throw()` has nowhere to surface.** A thrown-in exception has to be
raised inside the function, at the suspension point, or the generator's own
`try` around the `yield` cannot catch it. Making `frame.resumed` fallible is the
whole mechanism and needs no new opcode -- but the CPS pass emits `frame.resumed`
only where the continuation had a block parameter, so a `yield` whose value is
discarded (`counter`'s bb6) has no read at all and the exception is lost.

**CPS is unsound for fibers in general.** `yield` is lexically confined to the
generator body by a language rule; `Fiber::suspend()` is not. `function a() {
b(); }` calling a `b()` that suspends leaves `a` unrewritten with an ordinary Go
stack frame that cannot be reified. The testdata puts the suspend directly in the
entry function, which is why it had not shown up. The compiled backend can drop
goroutines for generators and not for fibers -- and separately, a direct call to
a rewritten function hands an `Outcome{Suspended}` to a caller expecting a
value, with nothing at the call site marking the callee as resumable.

### The trap: an assertion that encodes a bug on purpose

Two tests assert the *wrong* answer, labelled as reproductions rather than
specifications, so that fixing the compiler makes them fail and they get retired
instead of quietly diverging. That is only defensible because each says so in
its own doc comment and names the correct answer; a bare `want := []string{...}`
would have looked like agreement.

## 2026-08-29 -- frame implementation handed to the runtime session

The compiler half of the resumable path is done: the CPS rewrite, the frame
contents, the slot types and the one narrowing that would be a correctness bug.

What the brief pins down, because these are the parts that are easy to get
wrong from the outside:

- **Every declared slot must outlive the frame.** Freeing one after its last
  read moves a generator's `__destruct`, which is graded byte-exact. Only the
  slots marked `Compiler` are narrowable, and nothing narrows them yet.
- **The declared type is authoritative** — it is the join of every write, so a
  slot written both `*obj` and int is a `zval`, and `$__iterN: *iter` must not be
  boxed.
- **The representation is theirs to choose**, with the measured sizes to choose
  from: 1.4 slots per frame on `Zend/tests`, 5.5 on CakePHP, largest 18.

And the boundary, stated so it does not have to be rediscovered: **this does not
remove the interpreter's goroutine fibers.** `runtime/interp` executes op_arrays,
not this IR, so it keeps its own mechanism and its `php2phpt` counts must not
move.

The thing most worth their scepticism, and it was said explicitly: **none of the
resumable path has ever executed.** It is verified structurally — invariants,
mutation checks, corpus counts — and theirs will be the first code to run any of
