## 2026-08-29 — why the variance family does not fall to one change

Interpreter track. Net zero tests: two changes tried, measured, and reverted.
The finding is the point.

### What the six variance tests want

`class B extends A { function m(): C {} }` followed by `class C extends B` is
`Fatal error: Could not check compatibility between B::m(): C and A::m(): B,
because class C is not available` -- because when B is bound, C has not been
compiled yet. php2go prints nothing.

The machinery is all there: `signatureCompatible` returns *undecidable* with the
missing name, and `verifySignatures` turns that into exactly this message. What
never happens is the "not available" part.

### The two things in the way

**1. `resolveTypeClass` falls back to the harvest.** When a class is not
declared yet it autoloads, and if that fails it hands back the harvested
declaration anyway -- deliberately, so that reflection and closure types do not
refuse a class the program plainly owns. For a *variance* check that fallback is
wrong: it makes every check decidable.

Giving the variance path its own resolver without the fallback cost **16 tests**
and took `errored` from 3 to 15. Many classes the engine does have are not
"available" by php2go's reckoning -- internal parents especially -- so checks
that were decidable started inventing fatals.

**2. Early-bound classes are never linked at all.** A class whose parent is
known when the file compiles has no `DECLARE_CLASS` opline, and php2go runs its
link checks nowhere. Adding a pass over them at `RunUnit`, in declaration order,
also took `errored` to 15.

Both reverted. The tree is exactly as it was; a clean run reads 4215 either way.

### What it would take

The two are one problem: the engine's ordering is *compile-time* ordering, and
php2go's is run-time ordering. A faithful model needs the harvest to record
which classes the compiler bound and in what order, so a link can be given the
class table as it stood at that moment. That is a harvest change plus a link
scheduler, not a patch to a resolver -- and until it exists, the "not available"
half of the variance checks cannot be right.

Recorded in TODO rather than attempted piecemeal again.

### Result

| | round 267 | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4215 | 4215 |
| failed | 341 | 341 |
| unsupported | 154 | 154 |

`php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, `compile-error 0` on both.

## 2026-08-29 -- Phase C lands: internal/lower, and three bugs a coverage number cannot see

Compiler track. The lowering prototype moves out of the gitignored workspace and
into the tree as `internal/lower`, with `cmd/php2lower` as its corpus driver.

### The port is faithful, and that was the test

A 2,071-line `main.go` became a package: the per-opline closures (`operand`,
`define`, `keep`, `emit`, `bailOn`) became methods on a `lowering` struct, and
the opcode switch became one method rather than a body nested four levels deep.
That is the kind of refactor that quietly changes behaviour, so the check was
the corpus, not the diff:

| | prototype | `internal/lower` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` op_arrays / lowered | 10,780 / 10,331 (95.8%) | **identical** |
| CakePHP op_arrays / lowered | 6,782 / 5,030 (74.2%) | **identical** |
| oplines in the lowered bodies | 63,338 | identical |
| IR instructions | 56,608 | identical |
| bail histogram | 556/456/352/167/97/62/... | identical |

Byte-identical on every figure including the histogram, which is a stronger
statement than a passing test suite: a port that changed which bodies lower
would move at least one of those numbers.

### Golden files found three bugs the coverage number never would

Coverage says a body lowered. It says nothing about whether what came out is
right. Committing the rendered assembly as golden files -- which IR-ASSEMBLY.md
justifies anyway, since the format exists to be read and diffed -- surfaced three
defects immediately, all inherited from the prototype:

- **`$a[] = v` rendered as `dim.ref $rows, , mode=W`** -- an empty operand the
  grammar has no term for. An append addresses the next free slot, which is not
  a value any expression can name, so it is a place *kind* of its own. The plan
  already listed `Append` alongside `Local | Dim | Prop | StaticProp`; the
  prototype just did not implement it. Now `dim.append $rows, mode=W`.
- **`verify_return` on a CV computed the coercion and dropped it.** The check
  *widens* -- `function f(): int { return 1.0; }` -- and the RETURN that follows
  reads the variable, not the check's result. So the function returned the value
  it had just been asked to coerce. The prototype handled the TMP/VAR and CONST
  cases and its comment even explains why both matter; CV was the third case
  nobody looked for.
- **`foreach ($a as $k => $v)` wrote its key to a variable that does not
  exist.** The value goes to a CV but the key goes to a *temporary*, and the
  code assumed both were CVs. `cvName` fell through to its `v%d` fallback and
  produced `local.set $v6` -- a name invented from a slot number -- while the
  next block read `$__t6`, which nothing had written. Wrong in both directions
  at once, in the most ordinary loop in PHP, at 95.8% coverage.

That last one is the argument for goldens in one line. All three are now pinned
by tests that assert the specific claim rather than the whole file.

### Also fixed while landing

- The driver counted `.line` directives as IR instructions, which put the
  instruction-to-opline ratio above 100%. `Inst.Directive()` now marks them and
  the count excludes them -- and includes terminators, which the prototype
  counted and the first port did not.
- Consecutive `.line` directives with nothing between them are collapsed. They
  appear whenever an opline ends its block before emitting anything, which is
  every `return` inside a `try`.

### Where the remaining 4.2% and 25.8% are

Unchanged, and worth restating because it is a short list rather than a tail:
CakePHP is stopped almost entirely by six short-circuit opcodes --
`JMP_FRAMELESS` (556), `JMPZ_EX` (456), `COALESCE` (352), `JMPNZ_EX` (167),
`ASSERT_CHECK` (97), `JMP_SET` (62) -- 1,690 body-stops against 1,752 bodies
that did not lower.

### Gate

`gofmt`, `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...` clean; `internal/...` and `cmd/...`
tests pass. **`runtime/interp` has one failing differential case, which is not
mine**: it and `interp.go` were modified at 23:53, forty minutes after my last
touch of any shared file, and the case is about `unset()` on a shadowed private
property -- interpreter semantics, nothing the harvester or the lowering can
reach. Reported rather than folded into a green summary.

## 2026-08-28 — where the NUL falls in a printf

Interpreter track. One test, and a rule that will be needed again.

An anonymous class's real name is `class@anonymous\0<file>:<line>$<hash>`. Every
diagnostic naming one is a printf over C strings, so the name is cut at the NUL
-- but **each interpolated argument is cut separately, not the finished
message**. That single fact explains three different-looking outputs:

| built as | result |
|---|---|
| argument error: `"%s(): Argument #%d..."` with `func_name` = `"Class::method"` | `class@anonymous(): Argument #1 ...` -- the method is *inside* the cut string and goes with it |
| return error: `"%s%s%s(): Return value..."` with class, `"::"`, method separate | `class@anonymous::test(): Return value ...` -- only the class is cut |
| a type: each class name resolved separately | `class@anonymous\|string` -- the union survives |

php2go had `DisplayName` cutting names at call sites, which got the *type* case
wrong (it printed the whole mangled name, NUL and all, because the type string
never went through it) and the *argument* case wrong in the other direction
(cutting the class before appending `::method`, so the method survived).

The first fix -- cutting the finished message -- made the argument case right
and the return case wrong, which is what sent me to
`zend_argument_error_variadic` and `zend_verify_type_error_common` to see how
each message is actually assembled. `resolve_class_name` in zend_compile.c even
says why the type case cuts per name: *"to avoid larger parts of the type being
omitted by printing code later"*.

(`type_declarations/union_types/anonymous_class`)

| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4214 | **4215** |
| failed | 342 | 341 |
| unsupported | 154 | 154 |
| pass rate | 89.4% | **89.5%** |

## 2026-08-28 — a by-reference argument is converted in place, and an include is a frame

Interpreter track. Three tests.

### The conversion a by-reference parameter makes is kept

`function to_int(int &$x)` called with a float `1.0` leaves the *caller's*
variable as `int(1)`. php2go checked the type and threw the conversion away --
the comment there said the binding has to stay the slot, which is true, but the
engine writes the converted value *through* the slot before the body runs.

Everything that follows from a normal weak conversion follows here too: `"5"`
becomes `int(5)`, `1.5` becomes `int(1)` with
`Implicit conversion from float 1.5 to int loses precision`, and `"x"` is a
TypeError that leaves the variable alone. (`type_declarations/scalar_weak_reference`)

### An include is a stack frame

`#1 /path/caller.php(6): require('/path/inc')` sits between the frame that threw
and `{main}`. php2go ran the included body without pushing anything, so every
trace crossing an include was one frame short. The frame is named for the form
that was written -- `require`, `require_once`, `include`, `include_once` -- and
carries the resolved path as its argument.

That was the whole difference in two tests whose *message* already matched:
`weak_include_strict` and `explicit_weak_include_strict` are about
`declare(strict_types=1)` surviving an include, which php2go had right.

## 2026-08-28 — unset takes the slot away for writing too

Interpreter track. Two tests.

### A write after unset() reaches __set

Yesterday's fix made a cleared typed property *read* as the declaration's -- the
uninitialized error rather than "undefined property" -- when there is no
`__get`. The write side is the mirror image: unset() took the slot away, so the
next write is to a property that is not there and `__set` answers.

php2go had that rule already, but only inside the branch that handles a
*visibility* refusal. A public typed property never reaches it, so
`unset($t->foo); $t->foo = 43;` wrote the slot back. The distinction that has to
survive is between cleared and merely uninitialized: a declared property that
was never written still has its slot and is written directly.
(`type_declarations/typed_properties_magic_set`)

### A readonly property has no reference to give, whichever walk asks

`foreach ($o as &$v)` refuses on a readonly property, and php2go had that for
the ordinary property walk. The test asks through an `ArrayIterator($this)`
returned by `getIterator`, which takes the engine-iterator path -- the walk goes
through Go methods and the slots come from the array behind it. That path bound
the reference without asking.
(`type_declarations/typed_properties_115`)

## 2026-08-28 — growing an array in a property that cannot hold one

Interpreter track. One test, three places the same refusal has to be made, and
two wordings.

`$o->p[] = 1` where `$p` is declared `?string` and holds nothing has to grow an
array inside it, which the declaration forbids:
`TypeError: Cannot auto-initialize an array inside property Foo::$p of type
?string`. A property already holding a string takes the ordinary
`[] operator not supported for strings` instead, so the refusal only applies
when the slot is null or uninitialized.

Which forms refuse, probed one at a time:

| write | outcome |
|---|---|
| `$o->p[] = 1`, `$o->p["k"] = 1` | refused |
| `Foo::$s[] = 1` on a static | refused, same wording |
| `$ref = &$o->p;` then `$ref[] = 1` | refused at the **use**, with `inside a reference held by property ...` |
| `$ref = &$o->p;` alone | allowed -- taking the slot is not writing through it |
| `unset($o->p[0])` | allowed, and does nothing |
| `$o->p[0] .= "x"` | not refused; it reads first and warns `Undefined array key 0` |

Two things this needed that were not obvious:

- **The reference wording is different**, and it is what tells the two paths
  apart: php2go models a static property's slot as a reference too, so the
  ref-source check alone would have reported the static case in the wrong
  words. The static fetch checks first, in the property's name.
- **Taking a reference and writing through one are the same opcode.**
  `ZEND_FETCH_OBJ_W` is followed by `ASSIGN_REF` in one case and `ASSIGN_DIM`
  in the other, and only the look-ahead tells them apart -- which is why the
  first version refused `$ref = &$a->p` and failed the test further along than
  it started.

(`type_declarations/typed_properties_083`)

## 2026-08-28 — an unset slot is still the declaration's, and defaults are checked strictly

Interpreter track. Two tests, both about typed properties.

### unset() on a declared typed property

The slot survives holding nothing, and php2go knew that -- `Clear` keeps it and
`var_dump` still lists `uninitialized(?int)`. What the read path did was turn a
cleared slot into "absent" unconditionally, so `__get` could answer. With no
`__get` there is nothing to answer, and the engine reports the uninitialized
error rather than `Undefined property`. `uninitializedTyped` already had the
`hasMagic` condition; the fetch path did not.
(`type_declarations/typed_properties_047`)

### A deferred default is checked on every instantiation, strictly

`class B { public string $foo = FOO; }` where FOO is 5 is
`TypeError: Cannot assign int to property B::$foo of type string` -- once per
`new B`, not once per class, which is what places the check at instantiation
rather than at `updateClassConstants`.

The check is **strict whatever the file declared**, which had to be probed:

| default | weak-mode file | why |
|---|---|---|
| `public float $f = FIVE;` | `float(5)` | int widens to float, which strict allows |
| `public int $n = NUMSTR;` | TypeError | a numeric string does not coerce, which only strict refuses |

Only a *deferred* default can fail: a literal one that does not match is refused
when the file compiles. The widening also has to be kept -- the stored default
becomes `float(5)`, not `int(5)`. (`type_declarations/typed_properties_058`)

## 2026-08-28 — a keyword nothing can satisfy, and __toString is a coercion

Interpreter track. Three tests, following on from yesterday's `self`/`static`
resolution.

### An unresolvable `static` refuses everything

With the three check sites resolving the keywords against the frame, a keyword
still arriving at `matchesType` is one no class scope could name -- an unbound
closure declared `: static`. The engine refuses every value there and keeps the
word in the message: `{closure:...}(): Return value must be of type static,
stdClass returned`. php2go accepted any object, which was the right caution
before the sites resolved and the wrong answer after.
(`type_declarations/static_type_return`)

### `__toString` does not satisfy `string` in strict mode

The comment at that branch said the opposite -- "in strict mode as well:
__toString is a conversion the language treats as part of the type rather than
as a coercion" -- and it is wrong. Probed all three sites under
`declare(strict_types=1)`:

| site | strict | weak |
|---|---|---|
| argument | `f(): Argument #1 ($x) must be of type string, S given` | converts |
| return | `g(): Return value must be of type string, S returned` | converts |
| property | `Cannot assign S to property H::$p of type string` | converts |

An internal function's argument behaves the same way -- `strlen(new S)` is a
TypeError in strict mode. (`type_declarations/union_types/type_checking_strict`)

### json_encode had no flags at all

`JSON_PRESERVE_ZERO_FRACTION` is what makes `json_encode(42.0)` write `42.0`
rather than `42`; the corpus uses it and `JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR` and nothing else.
The fraction is written *into* the number the encoder already produced --
`1.0e+20`, not a re-formatting -- and `JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR` turns the `false`
into `JsonException: Inf and NaN cannot be JSON encoded`.
(`type_declarations/scalar_strict_64bit`)

## 2026-08-28 — `self` and `static` in a declared type name classes

Interpreter track. Three tests.

### The gap

`matchesType` had a case for `static`, `self` and `parent` that accepted **any
object**, with a comment saying which class they name depends on the frame and
the check does not have one. So `function t($x): static { return $x; }` never
refused anything, and neither did `function m(self $x)`.

The frame is available at all three sites; only the resolution was missing.
`frameType` substitutes the three keywords the same way `classNameFrom` does for
an operand -- `self` is the class whose body is running, `static` the class the
call was made on, `parent` the first's parent -- and each site applies it before
checking.

Where the *diagnostic* shows the resolved name differs, and had to be probed:

| site | message |
|---|---|
| return type | resolved: `SC::u(): Return value must be of type SD, SC returned` |
| parameter | resolved: `PB2::m(): Argument #1 ($x) must be of type PB2, stdClass given` |
| property | **not** resolved: `Cannot assign stdClass to property PC2::$p of type PA2\|self` |

A property's `self` is the class that *declared* it, not the instance's, which
is why the property site builds a frame for the declaring class rather than
using the running one.

## 2026-08-28 — a foreach that follows its array, and why it was reverted

Interpreter track. Net zero tests. Two findings worth more than the tests would
have been.

### The change, and why it looked right

A by-reference foreach is bound to the *variable* (2026-08-28, earlier entry).
Two tests want more than the type check that landed then: reassigning the
variable to a **different array** inside the body is followed, and the walk
starts over in the new one.

- `array_splice_empty_ht_iter_removal`: `$m = array_splice($m, 0)` inside
  `foreach ($m as &$r)` yields 4 twice.
- `$h = [1,2,3]; foreach ($h as &$v) { $h = [9,8,7]; }` yields 1 then 9 forever
  -- probed; the position does not carry over, because the engine's iterator was
  registered on the old hash and the one it gets for the new array starts at the
  beginning.

Implemented, both passed, and six by-reference shapes matched the engine.

### Why it had to go back

`gh11171` -- which *passed* before -- became an infinite loop:

```php
$all = ['test'];
foreach ($all as &$item) { $all += [$item]; }
```

`+=` on an array is a union, and the engine can perform it **in place**: the
hash is not replaced, so the iterator carries on and the loop ends after one
turn. php2go's union allocates a new array, so "the variable holds a different
array" was true every turn and the walk restarted forever.

The distinction the engine draws is whether the *hash* was replaced, not whether
the variable was assigned. php2go cannot draw it: its array operations allocate
freely, and making them not do so is a copy-on-write question, not a foreach
one. Reverted rather than landed -- a passing test turning into a hang is worse
than two failing tests staying failed.

Recorded in TODO with the shape that distinguishes them.

### The corpus number is only trustworthy when the machine is quiet

Five consecutive runs of the *same binary* gave 4200, 4195, 4181, 4145 and 4191
passed. The tell is in the same line: `compile-error` was 0, 7, 23, 60 and 12.
The machine is shared -- load average 26 on 20 cores while this was running --
and the engine's compiles fail under contention, which the harness reports
honestly as compile errors and which drags `passed` down with them.

**A measurement with `compile-error > 0` is noise and must be re-taken.** Every
figure in this journal should be read that way; round 259's `4199 passed,
1 compile-error` was one such, and the same tree reads 4200 on a clean run.

### Result

| | round 259 (as measured) | now, clean run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4199 (1 compile-error) | **4200** |
| failed | 356 | 356 |
| unsupported | 154 | 154 |
| pass rate | 89.1% | **89.1%** |

The tree is unchanged: what this round added was reverted in full, and the
difference in the table is the flakiness above rather than any work.

## 2026-08-28 -- the harvester's use-after-free: a class name outlives its class

Compiler track. `TODO.md` said a harvester that corrupts memory is worse than a
gap; this was one, and it had been there the whole time.

### The symptom

Compiling CakePHP's `src/` in one process died at file 216 of 771,
deterministically, with `SIGSEGV` inside `php2go_compile_file`. Running the same
files per directory -- 24 short engine lifetimes -- never crashed and covered
every op_array, which said the fault was accumulated state rather than any one
input.

Reducing it produced a two-file reproducer, `Core/Exception/CakeException.php`
then `Database/Exception/DatabaseException.php`. Neither file crashes alone, and
**every synthetic pair of the same shape compiled quietly** -- a parent
extending a builtin, a child redeclaring a typed property, namespaces and `use`
aliases. Four rounds of bisection produced nothing, because there was nothing
about the source to find.

### The cause

A backtrace ended it in one step:

```
zend_hash_find_known_hash  <-  zend_can_early_bind  <-  zend_try_early_bind
                           <-  zend_compile_class_decl
```

`zend_try_early_bind` had been handed a `parent_ce` whose `ce_flags` read
`0x61737265` -- ASCII `"esra"`. It was the exact pointer harvested from file 1,
freed and reallocated as string data. `zend_can_early_bind` iterates
`parent_ce->function_table`, so the garbage key reached `zend_hash_find_known_hash`
and it dereferenced it.

An interned class name carries a `map_ptr` slot holding the last class entry
looked up under it, and `zend_lookup_class_ex` answers from that slot **before**
it consults the class table. `php2go_forget_classes` removed and destroyed the
class but never cleared the slot, so the next file naming that class was handed
freed memory. The reset path did clear it -- for `ce->name`, under
`ZSTR_HAS_CE_CACHE` -- but by then `php2go_forget_classes` had already run and
the class was gone from the table, so the loop saw no user classes at all:
instrumenting it printed 308 classes over the two-file run, every one internal.

Two details decide where the fix goes:

- **The slot is keyed on the string used at the *use* site**, not on `ce->name`
  (`zend_lookup_class_ex` sets it from whatever name it was called with). So
  clearing `ce->name` alone misses any spelling in a different case. Every slot
  lives on an interned string, so `CG(interned_strings)` is the complete set.
- **The slot is filled by inheritance linking.** A class with no parent takes
  the `zend_hash_add_ptr` branch in `zend_compile_class_decl`, which never
  touches the cache. That is why the first synthetic reproducers were quiet, and
  why `CakeException extends RuntimeException` mattered.

`php2go_drop_user_ce_caches` now walks the interned strings and clears every
slot holding a user class, and both cleanup paths call it before they delete
anything. Clearing is always safe: the slot is a cache, and a miss falls back to
the table.

### Testing a use-after-free

The tempting observable -- whether the child was early-bound -- **does not
discriminate**, and asserting on it would have shipped a test that passes either
way. Verified directly: with the fix disabled, the child still emits
`ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS`, because early binding against a stale parent can fail on
its own terms and produce the same opline. What the engine does with freed
memory depends on what has been allocated over it, which is exactly why the two
files crash inside a corpus run and compile quietly on their own.

So the test asserts the pointer instead: `DanglingClassNameCaches` counts cache
slots holding an entry the class table no longer has, comparing pointers and
never dereferencing them, so it stays safe to call when the invariant is broken.
It reports 1 with the fix disabled and 0 with it enabled.

### Result

Measured by A/B against the same binary, the cleanup gated on an environment
variable, so only the fix differs:

| | stale cache | fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CakePHP `src/`, 771 files, one process | SIGSEGV at file 216 | **completes** |
| `Zend/tests` op_arrays | 10,776 | 10,780 |
| `Zend/tests` passed | 4199 | **4200** |
| failed / unsupported | 356 / 154 | 356 / 154 |
| pass rate | 89.1% | 89.1% |

Both corpus figures reproduced twice, alternating, same command. **The fix is
worth one test on `Zend/tests`** -- and that one test is the clearest statement
of the bug in the tree:

`return_types/inheritance005.phpt` declares `class Foo` and `class Bar extends
Foo` *in the same file*, and under the stale cache it stops compiling. An
earlier test in the corpus had declared its own `Foo` and left it owning the
cache slot; because a **parentless declaration never writes the cache** -- it
takes the `zend_hash_add_ptr` branch, not the linking one -- this file's own
`Foo` could not displace it. So `Bar` was linked against a dead class belonging
to another test. The slot is written only by inheritance linking and read by
every lookup, and that asymmetry is the whole bug.

A first pass reported +42 op_arrays and attributed them to the fix. **Wrong**:
A/B says +4, and the other 38 came from the other session's harvester changes
landing between the two measurements. Two sessions editing one file is not a
before-and-after.

### `compile-error` is load-sensitive, and it moves `passed` without moving the rate

Worth recording because it nearly produced a fabricated result. Identical runs of
the identical binary on this shared box returned **0, 1, 3, 10, 12, 18, 45 and 71
`compile-error`** as the machine's load average moved around 25. `attempted`
excludes that bucket, so `passed` tracked it -- 4140 to 4200 -- while
**`pass rate` stayed at 89.1% in every single run**.

Read naively, one pairing of those runs says the fix costs 59 tests and another
says it gains 5. Both are noise. The rate, `failed` and `unsupported` were stable
throughout and are what the comparison should quote; `passed` on its own is not
safe to quote from a loaded machine.

## 2026-08-28 — an alias carries the requirement, and a shebang belongs to the SAPI

Interpreter track. Two tests, one of them a harness fidelity fix rather than an
interpreter one.

### An alias of an abstract trait method is a second requirement

`use T { T::doStuff as doOtherStuff; }` where `T::doStuff` is abstract requires
**both** names. php2go's abstract walk iterated the trait's own methods, so
`doStuff` was checked and satisfied while `doOtherStuff` was never asked about.
The diagnostic names it on the composing class -- `Bar::doOtherStuff` -- as it
does for any trait requirement. (`bug69084`)

### A `#!` first line is skipped for the primary script only

`CG(skip_shebang)` is a compiler global that every SAPI sets before compiling
the file the request starts from; `zend_compile_file` itself never sets it. An
*included* file with the same first line echoes it as inline HTML.

php2go's harvester compiled everything through one path with the flag off, so
the shebang came through as output. Splitting it -- `CompileMainUnit` for the
script the request starts from, `CompileUnit` for an include -- is the same
distinction the SAPI makes, and php2phpt now compiles the test's own file the
way run-tests.php's CLI would. (`bug48930`)

This is a harness fidelity fix, in the same family as the three already in
[phpt-harness-fidelity](./LTM/phpt-harness-fidelity.md): the interpreter was
right and the thing feeding it was not.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4197 | **4199** |
| failed | 358 | 356 |
| unsupported | 154 | 154 |
| pass rate | 89.1% | **89.1%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: `bug69084` and `bug48930` fixed, nothing broken. Differential cases
952 -> 953.

## 2026-08-28 — a constructor is its own root

Interpreter track.

### Why a sibling can reach a protected method but not a protected constructor

`class B extends A` calling `$c->m()` on a `class C extends A` works when both
declare `protected m` -- the protected check runs against the class that *first*
declared the method, which is A. php2go had that right.

The same pair of constructors is refused:
`Call to protected C::__construct() from scope B`. The engine uses the same
`zend_get_function_root_class`, and the difference is upstream of it: a
constructor has **no prototype**, because overriding one is not overriding
anything. With no prototype the root is the declaring class, so C's own
declaration is what the check sees -- and B is not a subclass of C.

The tell is that removing C's redeclaration makes the same call legal: the
constructor found is then A's, and A is B's parent. Probed both ways.
(`bug37632`)

### unserialize into a virtual property

A virtual property has no storage, so a value serialized for one has nowhere to
go. The engine warns
`unserialize(): Cannot unserialize value for virtual property T::$v` and then
fails the whole unserialize at the offset the *value* starts at -- not the key,
and not the object. A hooked property that is backed unserializes normally.

`property_hooks/unserialize` still fails, but only on object handle numbering
now: php2go's handles run one behind the engine's from the failed unserialize
onwards. That is the known family.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4196 | **4197** |
| failed | 359 | 358 |
| unsupported | 154 | 154 |
| pass rate | 89.0% | **89.1%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: `bug37632` fixed, nothing broken. Differential cases 951 -> 952.

### An oracle limit worth recording

A warning raised from inside a *builtin* during the oracle's `eval` is prefixed
`PHP Request Startup: ` by the engine -- `Warning: PHP Request Startup:
Cannot unserialize value for virtual property ...`. The same program in a file
has no such prefix, which is what the corpus expects. So a differential case
cannot cover a builtin's warning text; the corpus test is the only oracle for
those.

## 2026-08-28 — a method name is a string, and nothing else

Interpreter track.

### The refusal

`$obj->$name()` and `C::$name()` take a string. Not a number, not null, not an
array, not an object with `__toString` -- all six are
`Error: Method name must be a string`. php2go ran the operand through
`.String()`, so `F::$one()` reached `__callStatic` with `"1"` and
`$o->$null()` reached `__call` with `""`.

### The ordering is not the same on both sides

Probed, because the two forms disagree:

| call | what is reported |
|---|---|
| `$null->$one()` | the *name*: `Method name must be a string` |
| `$null->$str()` | the *receiver*: `Call to a member function m() on null` |
| `Missing::$one()` | the *class*: `Class "Missing" not found` |

So the object form checks the name first and the static form checks the class
first. The first version of the fix put both checks in the same place and got
the static one wrong -- `Missing::$one()` blamed the name.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4192 | **4196** |
| failed | 361 | 359 |
| unsupported | 156 | 154 |
| pass rate | 89.0% | **89.0%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: `call_static_004` and `objects_025` fixed; two more came out of
`unsupported`, which is what a program that used to reach an unmodelled path
with a nonsense method name does once the name is refused first. Nothing broken.
Differential cases 950 -> 951.

### Not taken

`set_value_parameter_type_variance_004` again. The engine autoloads both sides
of a variance check; php2go stops at the first unresolved name, and the comment
at that spot records a *probe* saying the engine does the same for method
signatures. Both cannot be true of the same code path, so this needs its own
probing rather than a change made on one test's evidence.

## 2026-08-28 — the rest of the property-hook link checks

Interpreter track. The four that were left; the family is now done, and the
pass rate crosses 89%.

### A hook is a declaration like any other

`B::$prop::set(Y $prop): void must be compatible with A::$prop::set(X $prop):
void` is `signatureCompatible` with a different name in front of it. The hook
op_arrays are harvested as `$prop::get` and `$prop::set`, so
`renderSignatureIn(class, class, hook)` already prints
`B::$prop::set(Y $prop): void` -- and the `& ` a by-reference get earns, which is
what `& I::$prop::get()` is. Both tests passed on the first run.
(`set_value_parameter_type_variance_007`, `get_by_ref_implemented_by_val`)

### A property with no set hook still has a set type

Writing it goes straight to the storage, so what it accepts is its declared
type. An abstract declaration that named a wider set type is asking for
something the storage cannot take:
`Set type of C::$prop must be supertype of string|int (as in interface I)`.
The engine's guard is narrow -- the *parent* has to be abstract and have a set
hook, and the child must have none. (`gh15140`)

### readonly carries an implicit protected(set)

Which is what puts an ordinary-looking `public readonly int $prop` in front of
the asymmetric-visibility check and earns
`Set access level of C::$prop must be omitted (as in class I)`. Two details:
the message says "as in class" whatever the ancestor really is, and " or weaker"
is appended only when the ancestor had a set level of its own.

The first version broke `interface_get_only_readonly`, and the engine's
condition says why: the check is skipped when the ancestor is a *virtual*
property with hooks and no set hook. A get-only property is never written, so it
says nothing about who may write the one redeclaring it.
(`interface_get_set_readonly`)

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4188 | **4192** |
| failed | 365 | 361 |
| unsupported | 156 | 156 |
| pass rate | 88.9% | **89.0%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: the four named tests fixed, nothing broken. Differential cases
949 -> 950. property_hooks is 179/198.

The differential case added here is the *negative* one: link-time fatals cannot
be asked of the oracle, so what it pins down is the set of shapes the new checks
must **not** refuse -- a widened set parameter, a widened set access level, and
an interface property implemented by a plain one.

## 2026-08-28 — what decides whether type specialization pays, measured three ways

Compiler track. Phase D1 built over the prototype lowering, then measured
against two corpora and one controlled experiment. Nothing in `runtime/` was
touched. Detail in `.agents-workspace/tmp/TYPE-INFERENCE.md`; the durable part
is folded into [LTM/lowering-and-corpus-shape](./LTM/lowering-and-corpus-shape.md).

### The metric everyone reaches for is the wrong one

"What fraction of definitions have a type" does not decide anything — most
definitions are calls, fetches and constructions no specialization covers. The
question Phase D4 needs is **how often a specialization can fire**: of the IR's
instructions, how many are sites a table entry covers, and of those, how many
have both operands typed.

On `Zend/tests` that is 3,028 sites of 95,491 instructions — **3.2%** — which
alone caps the whole typed path at a few percent of the IR whatever the
inference does.

### Three limits, and the ranking is the finding

| limit | effect | fixable by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **the source declares no types** | 40% → 100% on identical code | nothing local |
| the corpus does no arithmetic | 3.5× firing rate | a benchmark corpus |
| the inference ignores available facts | 29.8% → 36.6% | the manifest and call graph |

**`Zend/tests` does essentially no arithmetic.** `ZEND_ADD`, `SUB`, `MUL`, `DIV`,
`MOD`, `POW` and `IS_SMALLER` do not appear in its top 45 opcodes — `DIV` occurs
14 times in 130,187 oplines, `POW` twice, `SPACESHIP` once. It tests semantics
and error wording, not throughput.

Re-run against `Zend/bench.php` and `Zend/micro_bench.php`, both vendored in the
submodule: specializable sites go from 3.2% of the IR to **12.5%**, and the
firing rate from 1.05% to **3.7%**. So the corpus is worth about 3.5×.

But the *hit rate on those sites* barely moved, 33.1% → 29.8%, and chasing that
found the limit that dominates both others:

> **Zero of the 30 functions in `Zend/bench.php` declare a parameter type.**

Isolated on one function body, changing only the signature:

```php
function work($n)            // 5 specializable sites, 2 typed —  40%
function work(int $n): int   // 5 specializable sites, 5 typed — 100%
```

**The typed path's payoff is a property of the PHP being compiled, not of the
compiler.** No local analysis recovers a parameter type that was never written;
only whole-program call-site inference would.

### Final numbers, after fixing the inference

The pass now reads the harvested builtin return types, the engine constant
table and user function return types, and models increments through places —
the sources A1 had counted and this one had ignored.

| | `Zend/tests` | benchmark |
| --- | --- | --- |
| definitions typed | **58.4%** (was 33.1%) | 36.1% (was 30.5%) |
| specializable sites with both operands typed | **43.0%** (was 33.1%) | 36.6% (was 29.8%) |

Note the inversion: **`Zend/tests` now types better than the benchmark.** It is
modern PHP written against a typed engine; `bench.php` is 2001-era and untyped.
The corpus with almost no arithmetic types better than the one written to do
arithmetic.

### The verdict I am not giving

**Neither vendored corpus is the one that matters.** `Zend/tests` has the types
and no arithmetic; `bench.php` has the arithmetic and no types. Arithmetic-heavy
code *with* declared types — the only configuration in which the typed path is
clearly worth building — is unmeasured, because none is vendored. Extrapolating
from either would be guessing.

What can be said: the payoff tracks the input's typing discipline, and
**representation narrowing is unaffected either way.** It needs only "which kind
of thing", not the exact scalar type, and applies to every value rather than
only to specializable sites — 21.6% of definitions have a known handle kind, each
a 72-byte `zval` that could be an 8-byte pointer. The design's split between the
two turns out to be the split between *pays regardless* and *depends on the
input*.

### A soundness caveat on these numbers

`pre_inc`/`post_inc` propagate the operand's type through a place, so `$i` stays
`int` however many times it is incremented. That is usually right and wrong
exactly where it matters, since **integer overflow promotes to float** — so the
loop-counter sites that dominate a benchmark are **over-counted**. A real
specialization needs range tracking or must keep the check, and every `int`
arithmetic figure above should be read as an upper bound.

## 2026-08-28 — two of the property-hook link checks

Interpreter track. Two of the six link-time refusals property hooks want.

### A set hook's parameter is contravariant

The hook is handed the property's value, so its parameter has to *accept* the
property type -- `zend_verify_property_hook_variance` is a covariant check with
the property type on the narrow side. Three rules, and the middle one is the
one that would be missed: no parameter type declared is always fine, a declared
one on an **untyped** property is refused outright, and otherwise the property
type must be a subtype of the parameter type.
(`property_hooks/set_value_parameter_type_variance_003`)

### Two hooked properties cannot be composed

`checkTraitProperties` already compared a trait's property against the class's
and refused an incompatible pair. A *hooked* one is refused before that
comparison is even reached: the engine has no rule for choosing between two
bodies, and says so at length -- `Conflict resolution between hooked properties
is currently not supported`. Even two identical declarations are refused.
(`property_hooks/traits_conflict`)

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4186 | **4188** |
| failed | 367 | 365 |
| unsupported | 156 | 156 |
| pass rate | 88.8% | **88.9%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: the two named tests fixed, nothing broken. Differential cases
948 -> 949. property_hooks is 176/198.

### Two things the probing turned up

- `public int $b { set($v) {...} }` -- a set hook with an **untyped** parameter
  on a **typed** property -- is a compile error, not a runtime one. So is a
  backed hook that writes `$this->b` from inside its own set hook. Both bail the
  oracle, which is how they were found; the legal shapes had to be narrowed to
  a supertype, a union containing the property type, and an untyped parameter on
  an untyped property.
- `set_value_parameter_type_variance_004` is the same check with both class
  names unresolvable. The engine autoloads *both* before deciding; php2go's
  `typeAccepts` stops at the first and reports the answer as unknown, so only
  one autoload happens and the fatal never comes. Left alone: making the check
  resolve both sides changes a function every variance check goes through.

## 2026-08-28 — staticness, and what unserialize is allowed to create

Interpreter track. Three tests from the link-time and serialization gaps.

### Making an inherited method static, or not

`do_inheritance_check_on_method` settles staticness *before* it looks at the
signature, and the message names three different classes: the prototype's own,
the method, and the class the overriding declaration belongs to -- which for a
trait being bound is the trait, not the class using it. `bug78776` is the case
that shows it: `Cannot make non static method A::createApp() static in class C`
where C is the trait.

`inter_007` is the same rule reached differently -- interface `a extends d, w`
where d and w each declare the name, neither of them being `a` -- and php2go's
check runs over the *declaring* class's own methods, so it has no candidate
there. Left alone rather than widened on one example.
(`traits/abstract_method_5`, `bug78776`)

### unserialize writes properties like anything else

`O:1:"C":1:{s:1:"x";b:1;}` into a readonly class is
`Cannot create dynamic property C::$x`. php2go's unserialize wrote straight into
the property table, so every refusal and deprecation the write path makes was
skipped. Probed the whole set rather than the one case:

| class | what happens |
|---|---|
| readonly, or any with NO_DYNAMIC_PROPERTIES | `Error: Cannot create dynamic property C::$x` |
| ordinary | `Deprecated: Creation of dynamic property C::$y is deprecated` |
| `#[AllowDynamicProperties]` | nothing |
| property is declared | nothing |
| enum | `Error: Cannot instantiate enum E` -- before any property is read |

The enum one was worth probing: php2go's first version refused it at the
property, with the property's wording, which is the right answer to the wrong
question. `instantiable()` already had the right refusal.
(`readonly_classes/readonly_class_unserialize_error`)

## 2026-08-28 — three small refusals, and one family confirmed out of reach

Interpreter track.

### A step whose diagnostic was thrown does not happen

`$s = ""; $s++` with an error handler that throws on E_DEPRECATED leaves `$s`
as `""`. php2go reported the deprecation and then wrote `"1"`: the engine reports
first and checks for an exception afterwards, so the value it was about to store
is dropped. `reportedStep` makes that the rule for every incdec diagnostic.
(`in-de-crement/incdec_strings_exception`)

### `instanceof self` is a class reference, not a name

`ZEND_INSTANCEOF` with an unused op2 carries the same fetch-class encoding
`ZEND_FETCH_CLASS` does. php2go read op2 as a string, got "", and answered
false; it now goes through `classNameFrom`, which resolves `self`, `parent` and
`static` -- and refuses each of them outside a class in the engine's words.
(`self_instanceof_outside_class`)

### An enum is checked against Traversable too

`verifyInheritance` returned early for an enum, which skipped the
"Traversable only as part of Iterator or IteratorAggregate" check along with the
UnitEnum/BackedEnum one it was there for. `gh7792_5` says the engine applies the
first to enums and names it `Enum Foo ...`. The early return moved to just
before the check it was written for.

Left alone deliberately: whether the engine also refuses an *enum* claiming both
Iterator and IteratorAggregate. No corpus test says, and a link-time fatal
cannot be asked of the oracle, so that case keeps today's behaviour rather than
a guess.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4180 | **4183** |
| failed | 373 | 370 |
| unsupported | 156 | 156 |
| pass rate | 88.7% | **88.8%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: the three named tests fixed, nothing broken. Differential cases
945 -> 947.

### bug71604_2 is refcount timing, not finally

Worth writing down because it does not look like it. `gen()->rewind()` where the
generator throws inside nested `finally`s and yields in the innermost one:

- The generator *does* suspend at the yield, holding the exception. Kept in a
  variable it stays suspended and `current()` answers -- probed both ways.
- In the test nothing holds it, so the engine destroys it at the end of the
  statement, which force-closes it, which resumes the finally and rethrows --
  from inside `rewind()`, which is what the expected stack trace shows.

php2go has no refcount, so the generator survives to shutdown and the exception
is lost. The other three tests in that shape (`try/bug71604_3`,
`try/try_finally_023`, `generators/basic_yield_from_exception_handling`) look
the same. Nothing to do here until objects die when their last holder does.

## 2026-08-28 — the reflectors print themselves

Interpreter track. The round set aside for `Reflection*::__toString`, which four
tests want and which is one shared format rather than one method per class.

### What it is

ext/reflection's `_class_string` and the four helpers under it. Written out
rather than probed into existence: the format is exact in ways guessing would
not find, and reading a *formatter* is not the same as reasoning about operand
encodings.

The details that would have cost a round each to discover:

- `@@ file 11-17` for a class but `@@ file 8 - 8` for a method. Spaces on one
  and not the other.
- Every section prints its braces even when empty, and each is preceded by a
  blank line -- but `Static methods` and `Methods` put the newline *before* each
  entry rather than after, so an empty one needs one written explicitly.
- The `Parameters` block appears whenever the declaration has an arg_info table,
  which it has as soon as there is a parameter **or a return type**: a
  `function f(): void {}` prints `Parameters [0]` and a `function g() {}` prints
  nothing at all.
- An ancestor's *private* members are in the tables but excluded from both the
  listing and the count.
- Method annotations are three separate questions: `inherits X` when the body
  came from elsewhere, `overwrites X` when this class replaced a visible one,
  `prototype X` for the interface or abstract declaration it answers -- and they
  can both appear (`<user, overwrites Base, prototype Base>`).
- A default is rendered by `format_default_value`, not by the declaration
  renderer used in signature diagnostics: `'x'` in full rather than cut at ten
  bytes, and an array expanded to `[1, 'k' => 2]`.
- A user parameter's default is not on the parameter at all. It lives in the
  `RECV_INIT` opline, which is where `get_default_from_recv` reads it; the
  harvest's `ArgInfo.default_value` is only ever set for internal declarations.

`Class.line_end` had to be harvested -- only this needs it -- which is why the
IR golden fixture moved.

### One thing that was not formatting

`use T { test as __construct; }` makes `getMethod("__construct")` answer with
T::test's body under the name `__construct`, with `, ctor`. The reflector kept
only the op_array, so it printed `method test`. It now records the name it was
reached by, which is also what `->name` reports.

The dump prints the file it was written in, and the harness normalises only

## 2026-08-28 — laziness dropped, and what it leaves behind

Interpreter track. Two lazy-object tests, both about the moment an object stops
being lazy.

### markLazyObjectAsInitialized

Three things wrong in six lines: it returned null where the engine returns the
object, it refused to mark a *proxy*, and it left the properties blank.

The last one is the interesting one. php2go models a lazy ghost by blanking its
slots (`stripState`), so dropping the laziness left an object with nothing in
it. The engine's ghost has the class defaults all along -- laziness defers the
*initializer*, not the state -- so marking it initialized shows
`a => 1, b => "x", c => uninitialized(int)`. The declared defaults are applied
now for whatever has no value.

A proxy is marked the same way: there is no real instance behind an
un-initialized one, so it becomes an ordinary object of the class it stood in
for.

### Nothing to defer means nothing to keep

`resetAsLazyGhost` on a class that declares no properties hands back an
*ordinary* object -- there is nothing to defer -- and an ordinary object of such
a class has no properties at all. A dynamic property set beforehand does not
survive. php2go kept a blanked slot for it.

Probed the neighbouring case rather than generalising: an object that *does*
have declared properties keeps its dynamic ones across the reset (they are
counted by var_dump but not listed while lazy, and gone once the initializer
runs). So the drop belongs specifically to the "nothing to defer" branch, not to
`stripState`, and the first version of the fix -- which put it there -- was
wrong in a way no corpus test would have caught.

`traits/bugs/gh13177`. It is four tests for a large, exacting text format whose
every line has to be right; worth doing, but as its own round.

## 2026-08-28 — an `as` clause belongs to the pair, not to the body

Interpreter track. Two tests, both about what a trait alias changes and who has
to know.

### Reflection answered for the body, not for the composition

`use T { m as final; pub as private; }` changes the method as the composing
class holds it, leaving the trait's own declaration alone.
`ReflectionMethod::isFinal` read `fn.GetFinal()` and `isPublic` and its two
siblings read `fn.GetVisibility()` -- the trait's, in both cases.
`effectiveVisibility` already existed for the call path; `effectiveFinal` is its
twin, and reflection now goes through both. (`traits/gh12854`)

### An alias in a trait travels into whoever uses that trait

`trait T2 { use T1 { aa as public; } }` and `class B { use T2; }` gives B a
*public* `aa`. Both helpers looked only at the composing class's own aliases, so
the clause was invisible one level down and `B::aa()` was refused as protected.
They share `aliasFor` now, which follows the trait graph. (`traits/bug76700`)

### Private and final says nothing, and the engine says so

`Private methods cannot be final as they are never overridden by other classes`
has two sites: the compiler's, for a declaration that writes both, which the
harvest already carries as a compile diagnostic; and trait binding's, for an
alias that *makes* an already-private method final. Only the second was missing.

The engine's condition is narrower than it looks
(`zend_traits_check_private_final_inheritance`): it warns only when the alias is
what added `final`, so `final1 as private` -- already final, newly private --
earns nothing, and `__construct` is exempt under the name the class *composes*
it as, not the name the trait wrote.

## 2026-08-28 — a comparison that finds itself

Interpreter track. Went looking at the private-property mangling family, scoped
it, decided it does not fit in one round, and wrote the design down instead.
Then took the recursion-in-comparison family, which does.

### Comparing a structure that contains itself

`$a = [&$a]; $a === [[]]` is `Error: Nesting level too deep - recursive
dependency?`, not `false`. php2go had a depth bound (`maxCompareDepth`) that
answered `false` silently -- the comment already said it was a gap.

The engine's mechanism is not a bound at all: `zend_hash_compare` and
`zend_std_compare_objects` *protect* the container they are about to walk and
raise the moment the walk enters a protected one. Two things follow that a depth
bound gets wrong:

- **The protection runs before the size check.** Comparing a recursive array
  with one of a different length is still a cycle, not a "no". Getting this
  order wrong left `[[]] === $a` answering false.
- **The same container on both sides is not a cycle.** `$a === $a` and
  `[$x, $x] === [$y, $y]` are settled by the identity check before the guard
  ever runs.

The engine protects only the *left* container, and says why: the right one may
be reachable from the left, so protecting both would report a cycle where there
is none. php2go records both, because it has no VM specialisation deciding
which operand ends up on the left -- `$a === [[]]` and `[[]] === $a` both raise
in the engine, and only one of them has the recursive array on the left. The
identity check makes recording both safe.

`LooseEqualChecked` / `StrictEqualChecked` return the recursion answer
alongside; the plain `LooseEqual` / `StrictEqual` keep their pure signature for
the many callers -- `in_array`, sorting -- that have nowhere to throw.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4169 | **4172** |
| failed | 384 | 381 |
| unsupported | 156 | 156 |
| pass rate | 88.5% | **88.5%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: `bug63882`, `recursive_array_comparison` and `gh18572` fixed, nothing
broken. Differential cases 940 -> 941.

### A differential case can perturb the cycle collector

The new case creates two self-referencing objects and a self-referencing array.
That made a `gc_collect_cycles()` case *later in the list* report 4 where it had
reported 0: the collector is shared across cases, and it counts whatever earlier
cases left cyclic. Moving the case did not help -- there are several such cases,
before and after. The fix is for the case to leave nothing cyclic behind
(`$rec[0] = 1; $o1->p = null; $o2->p = null;`), which is now a rule worth
following for any case that builds a cycle on purpose.

## 2026-08-28 — what a refused reference must not reach, and a default that runs

Interpreter track. Grouped the remaining failures by the *shape* of the first
differing expected line rather than by how few lines differ, which turned up
families the other lens had scattered. Three tests from two of them.

### A refused by-reference argument must not reach the original

`array_splice(X::getArr(), 1, 1)` earns
`Only variables should be passed by reference` -- php2go already had that -- and
then must leave `X::$arr` alone. It did not: php2go hands arrays over by
pointer, so the builtin spliced the very array the getter returned. The engine
gets the detachment from copy-on-write; here it has to be made explicitly, at
the send that emitted the notice. (`bug33257`, `bug35393`)

`function test(string $foo = new Foo() . '')` prints "0", "1", "2" across three
calls. php2go printed "" three times: the constant-expression evaluator's binary

one that does not run `__toString`. It renders its operands now, like the
interpreter's own concat -- and a class without `__toString` is an Error there
too. (`function_default_argument_cache`)

## 2026-08-28 — three tests that printed nothing

Interpreter track. The ranking's "GOT is empty" rows turned out to be three
unrelated gaps rather than one crash, and each was small.

### `global $x` creates the global

Binding a name no global has yet *creates* it, holding null. Reading it
afterwards is reading a variable that exists, so there is no
`Undefined variable` warning -- `array_key_exists` says true and only `isset()`
can still tell the difference. php2go's `RefAt` left the new slot undefined,
which is the state that warns. (`bug43851`)

### A variable named by an expression is a string conversion

`global ${new stdClass}` has to say
`Object of class stdClass could not be converted to string`. The
variable-variable fetch was reading the operand with `.String()`, which does not
run `__toString` and cannot fail; it goes through `in.toString` like every other
place a value is used as a string. `$$objectWithToString` works for the same
reason. (`global_to_string_exception`)

### getIterator() has to hand back something walkable

An array is not: the engine refuses it in the same words as a plain object --
`Objects returned by C::getIterator() must be traversable or implement interface
Iterator` -- and php2go had a branch that accepted one and iterated it.

`zend_user_it_get_new_iterator` also refuses the aggregate *itself*
(`Z_OBJ(iterator) == Z_OBJ_P(object)` with a user `get_iterator`), which the
first version of the fix missed: `return $this` passed the Traversable test and
recursed until the Go stack ran out. A different aggregate is fine and is
unwrapped again. (`bug26229`)

## 2026-08-28 — a string subject is a class name, and readonly guards a value

Interpreter track. Two fixes, four tests.

### is_a/is_subclass_of autoload the subject

Accepting a class *name* means resolving it the way any run-time class name is
resolved, autoloaders included. php2go used `findClass`, which deliberately has
no side effects. Probed, and the asymmetry is the point:

| call | autoloads |
|---|---|
| `is_a("Y1", "Y2")` | nothing -- is_a's `$allow_string` defaults false, so a string subject is simply not a class |
| `is_a("Y3", "Y4", true)` | `Y3` |
| `is_subclass_of("NOPE", "P")` | `NOPE` -- its `$allow_string` defaults true |
| `is_subclass_of("C", "Z")` where C exists | nothing, not even `Z` |

The class being tested *against* is never autoloaded: if it is not declared,
nothing can be an instance of it. (`is_a`)

### Readonly refuses unset only once there is a value

`unset($this->p)` on an *uninitialized* readonly property is allowed from a
scope that could have written it -- nothing is being taken back, and the slot
returns to having no value, so a later write still counts as the first one.
php2go refused outright. The scope half was already right, and is what produces
`Cannot unset protected(set) readonly property Test::$prop from global scope`
for the same property from outside. (`readonly_props/variation`,
`readonly_props/unset`, `readonly_props/magic_get_set`)

### Two families looked at and left alone

- **An error handler that mutates what the failing opcode is working on.**
  `$a['b'] += 1` with a handler that sets `$a['b'] = 2` ends as `2`, not `3` and
  not `1`: the compound assignment's own write does not land. `bug70662`,
  `falsetoarray_002` and `dynamic_prop_deprecation_002` are all this shape.
  Recorded rather than guessed at -- the answer is about what the engine holds
  across the handler call, and getting it wrong is a wrong answer everywhere.
- **A by-reference `__get` reached through a lazy proxy.** `gh21478` wants
  `Warning: Undefined property` where php2go creates the property. Reduced to
  its parts the engine *does* create it, so the difference is in the proxy plus
  the recursion guard, not in the by-reference fetch.

Also a repeat of yesterday's lesson: `unset((new C)->p)` is an E_COMPILE_ERROR
("Cannot use temporary expression in write context"), so a differential case
cannot be written that way. It bailed the engine and took the neighbouring case
down with it, exactly as recorded.

## 2026-08-28 — an absent offset, a check made too late, and a reference that was copied

Interpreter track. Three from the ranking; six tests, three of them found by the
third fix rather than aimed at.

### A string offset that is not there is *absent*

`$s[5] ?? "default"` gave `""`. The quiet (`FETCH_DIM_IS`) read of an
out-of-range offset was returning the same empty string the loud read warns and
gives, and `??` has nothing to reject there. It is `null`: isset() already said
false, and the two have to agree. (`bug69889`)

### Readonly is settled before the value is converted

`$this->readonlyString = new S()` ran `S::__toString` and *then* refused the
write. The engine's `zend_std_write_property` settles readonly before
`zend_verify_property_type`, so the conversion never happens.

The check could not simply be moved: `checkPropertyWrite` runs after the hook
branch and spends the `__clone` reinitialization permission. The early check is
a separate, non-consuming one -- it steps aside when a reinitialization is
pending, which is the case where the conversion *does* run.
(`readonly_props/readonly_assign_no_sideeffect`)

### A by-reference return sent as an argument

`takes_ref(returns_ref())` wrote to a copy. `$r = &returns_ref()` worked, so the
reference was there; what dropped it was the *send*. A call result goes out
through `ZEND_SEND_VAR_NO_REF`, which php2go handled nowhere: the by-reference
branch listed `_FUNC_ARG`, `SEND_USER` and `SEND_VAR_EX` only.

`ZVAL_COPY_VALUE(arg, varptr)` is all the engine does there -- the zval travels
as it stands, `IS_REFERENCE` included. The first version of the fix routed the
NO_REF forms through the *whole* by-reference branch, which also makes a
reference out of a plain variable, and that silenced
`Only variables should be passed by reference` for a value result. Passing a
reference on and manufacturing one are different things, and this opcode only
does the first. (`nullsafe_operator/027`, `bug39944`, `bug72038`, `bug73663`)

The nullsafe test turned out to have nothing to do with nullsafe: the same
program without `?->` failed identically.

## 2026-08-28 — a temporary has nowhere to write, and a loop follows its variable

Interpreter track. Three unrelated things from the "how few lines differ"
ranking; six tests.

### Cannot use temporary expression in write context (4 tests)

`ZEND_FETCH_DIM_FUNC_ARG` and `ZEND_FETCH_OBJ_FUNC_ARG` decide at run time
whether the argument is going by reference. When it is and op1 is `IS_CONST` or
`IS_TMP_VAR` there is nothing to write back into, and the engine throws. php2go
was falling through to the write fetch and silently succeeding.

The compiler refuses the same thing when it can see it, as an
**E_COMPILE_ERROR** -- which is why the corpus tests declare the by-reference
callee *after* the caller, and why the differential case has to as well: a
compile error bails the shared engine process, and it took the anonymous-class
case down with it before the case was rewritten.

### #[Attribute] validates its argument before its flags

`#[Attribute("foo")]` is the constructor's own parameter check, not a flags
check: `Attribute::__construct(): Argument #1 ($flags) must be of type int,
string given`. Only an *integer* with unknown bits set -- or a negative one --
is `Invalid attribute flags specified`. Probed all six shapes; the check is
strict, so a numeric string is refused too, and the thrown class is `Error`
rather than `TypeError`.

### A by-reference foreach follows the variable

`foreach ($a as &$v)` is bound to `$a`, not to the array `$a` held: the engine
makes the variable a reference and reads it again each turn. Probed:

| in the body | what happens |
|---|---|
| `$a = null` / `$a = "s"` | `Warning: foreach() argument must be of type array\|object, %s given`, loop ends |
| `unset($a)` | nothing -- the reference outlives the name |
| `$a = [9, 8]` | the loop follows it, and the engine runs out of memory |
| by-value loop, any of these | nothing; it iterates a copy |

php2go now records the compiled variable a by-reference reset came from and
re-reads it before each fetch. Undef -- the unset case -- is deliberately not a
warning.

## 2026-08-28 — the parameter list an engine function has, and the default it wrote

Interpreter track, continuing from named arguments. Four tests, and two gaps
that were reported honestly rather than answered wrongly.

### A callee whose parameters were never asked for

`calleeParameters` had no answer for three shapes, so a name given to any of
them was `unsupported: named arguments to X`:

- **A method the engine supplies.** The harvest records its signature
  (`EngineMethod.args`), which is all a name needs; nothing was reading it.
- **A class that declares no constructor.** That is an *empty* parameter list,
  not a missing one -- `new stdClass(x: 1)` and `new Plain(x: 1)` are both
  `Unknown named parameter $x`, which is what the engine says.
- **The trampoline for `parent::$p::set()`** where the parent wrote no hook. It
  has the arity of the hook it replaces and its parameter is `$value`; a hook
  the parent *did* write names its own (`gh20270` checks both, one against
  `$custom`).

### An internal parameter's default is text, and was never harvested

`str_pad("foo", 6, pad_type: STR_PAD_LEFT)` left a hole at `$pad_string`, and a
hole reaches an engine function as null -- there is no RECV_INIT to fall back
on. The default is on the arg_info as source text (`' '`), which
`convertBuiltin` was not reading at all, though `convertEngineMethods` was.

`internalDefault` parses the forms the stubs use: the three keywords, `[]`, a
quoted literal, a number, a constant name, and `A | B | C` for a flags
parameter. Anything else is a gap, not a guess.

The same field settles a diagnostic that reads like a riddle without it: an
*optional* parameter with no default text is one the engine refuses to invent,
and says so -- `array_keys(): Argument #2 ($filter_value) must be passed
explicitly, because the default value is not known`.

### array_keys ignored its filter

Found by `missing_param`, which passes `filter_value:` explicitly. The
implementation returned every key whatever the second and third arguments said.
