promoting to `9.2233720368548E+18` rather than wrapping, `"10" + 5` giving 15,
`0 < "abc"` true, `"0" == null` false, assignment copying — and, more
importantly, **all three rows of `INTRINSICS.md`'s diagnostic ordering table**:
`2.5 % ""` deprecating then throwing, `2.5 % "2abc"` deprecating then warning,
`"" % "2abc"` throwing *only*, with no warning for the operand the walk never
reached.

Two design claims are now code rather than prose. `.line` directives become
`ctx.SetLocation(file, line)` calls — the argument that a source line is
semantics, not debug information, is that dropping them makes every message
report the wrong line. And the diagnostic half is emitted before the value half:
`php.AcceptsArithmetic(ctx, php.OpMod, a, b)` then `php.Mod(a, b)`, which is the
split `runtime/php` was written with (`ops.go:19-20` — the value functions never
raise "because the caller has the Ctx needed to raise it"). The compiler is that
caller.

User calls work too, and need no library: `INIT`/`SEND`×N/`DO` becomes one Go
call expression. Recursion, mutual recursion across a forward reference,
by-value argument copying, and `fact(21)` overflowing int64 to float
mid-recursion all match.

**The artefact is standalone, confirmed rather than assumed:** it builds with
`CGO_ENABLED=0` and `ldd` reports "not a dynamic executable". No engine, no
libc. `runtime/php` being pure Go is what makes that possible.

### The wall, and what it costs to defer Phase B

Pushing the emitter into arrays found the boundary of `runtime/php`, and it is
sharper than expected:

> `runtime/php` is the **data structure** — `Array.Get`/`Set`/`Append`, the
> operators. `runtime/interp` is the **semantics** — what a dimension *access*
> means. An emitter outside `interp` can build a PHP array and cannot read one
> faithfully.

Reproducing `arrayKey` and `dimensionRead` in the emitted file cost **47 of 117
lines — 40% of it** — and they were silently wrong. Twenty-two cases passed.
Then one more:

```php
$n = 1; $a = [$n, $n + 1, $n + 2]; echo $a[1.5];
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| engine | `Deprecated: Implicit conversion from float 1.5 to int loses precision`, then `2` |
| emitted Go | `Warning: Undefined array key "1.5"` |

Wrong diagnostic **and** wrong value: the copied `arrayKey` had no float case, so
`1.5` became the string key `"1.5"` instead of the integer `1`. That is
`QUALITY_GATE.md`'s "gap masquerading as working behaviour" arriving *by itself*,
without anyone choosing the trade — which is the argument for the extraction
rather than for working around it. The case is kept in
`.agents-workspace/tmp/divergent/` rather than deleted or patched over.

A requirements list for `runtime/rt`, derived from what the emitter actually
needed and could not get, is in
`.agents-workspace/tmp/RUNTIME-RT-REQUIREMENTS.md`. The one to note: the
uncaught-fatal text is graded byte-for-byte by the corpus and now exists in two
copies — `throw.go` and a hand-written emitter helper.

### The lowering measurement, finished

92.3% → **95.9%** (10,293 of 10,738 op_arrays), and **every remaining bail names
an unimplemented opcode**. No entry above 36 bodies (0.34%).

| step | bodies |
| --- | --- |
| cross-block values promoted to places | 94.0% |
| `finally` inlined at each exit | 95.1% |
| dropped assignment and coercion results | **95.9%** |

**Cross-block values needed no block arguments.** The design already says a value
outliving its block is a *place* — the rule that keeps CVs and the `foreach`
iterator as places. Applying it to temporaries is a pre-pass that finds slots
read in a block that did not define them and mirrors each definition into a
named local: no liveness analysis, no edge rewriting. Block arguments remain the
design where they are the natural shape, for a `yield` resumption and a caught
exception.

**`finally` inlining fits a linear lowering better than block duplication.**
Hitting `FAST_CALL` splices the finally body's oplines into the front of the work
queue; `FAST_RET` disappears because the continuation is already next; the body's
own blocks are never emitted standalone. Verified on a two-exit function.

### A wrong conclusion of mine, and what caused it

An earlier pass recorded 62 "cross-block" bails as unexplained and guessed the
instrumentation was at fault. **The instrumentation was right; the guess was
wrong.** What made it unreadable was comparing the lowerer's view against a
second tool's dump of a *differently extracted* file. Printing the lowerer's own
leaders, its own `crossBlock` set and its own opline list — rather than a second
opinion — resolved it at once.

They were not cross-block bails at all. Two bugs of the same shape: **a result
slot ignored because the writeback was assumed to go elsewhere.**

- **Compound assignment is an expression.** `ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_OP` and its siblings
  carry a result slot, because `$x = ($y .= "a")` yields the assigned value.
  Emitting them as statements dropped it.
- **`VERIFY_RETURN_TYPE` on a CONST writes to the *result* slot.** A TMP/VAR
  operand is verified in place; a CONST one cannot be, so the engine puts the
  coerced value there instead.

The second is `INTRINSICS.md`'s "verify_return transforms, it does not assert"
met in the wild — `function f(): int { return 1.0; }` widens, and treating the
check as an assertion is exactly what drops the value. The catalogue predicted a
bug in code written against it.

Lesson worth keeping: **when two tools disagree about the same input, instrument
the one that is failing rather than trusting the other.** The second opinion was
reading a different file.

## 2026-08-28 — a name forwarded, and a name rewritten

Interpreter track. Four tests, taken from the "how few lines differ" ranking.

### call_user_func drops named arguments

`call_user_func(["T", "m"], b: 0)` ran `m` with `$b` at its default. The name
had nowhere to go: `applyNamedArguments` resolves against the *callee's*
parameters, and the callee there is `call_user_func`, whose `...$args` swallows
any name into `pending.extraNamed` -- which only a frame reads, and a builtin
builds no frame. The engine resolves such a name against what is being called
(`call_user_func("f", zzz: 0)` says `Unknown named parameter $zzz`, naming f's
parameters, and `call_user_func(callback: "f")` names call_user_func's own), so
the leftovers are now handed to `callValueNamed`.

They travel in a field of their own rather than in `pending`, because nothing
else would ever clear them: every other builtin drops them at the same
boundary, which is where a frame would have consumed them.

`forward_static_call` is *not* the same -- probed: it answers
`ArgumentCountError: forward_static_call() does not accept unknown named
parameters`. That is still unimplemented.

Following `named_params/call_user_func` through, three more callees had no
parameter list: `$closure->__invoke(...)`, `Closure::call($newThis, ...)` --
where a name resolves against the closure one position along, `newThis` being
Closure::call's own -- and the reflectors' `invoke`. Their `*Args` forms take a
string key as a parameter name exactly as `call_user_func_array` does, which
`namedFromArray` + `resolveArgumentNames` now do.

### An unhandled match names an enum case

`smart_str_append_zval` writes `Class::Case` for an enum and refuses everything
else, which is why every other object is `of type X`.

### Eval'd code, continued

`constants/dir-constant-eval` wanted `__DIR__` inside eval to be the directory
of the *file that ran the eval*. Two things were wrong with yesterday's rename:
the directory is not derivable from the eval's name (that name is a sentence,
not a path), so it has to be passed in; and `__DIR__ . "\n"` is folded into one
literal, so exact-match rewriting missed it. Substring replacement is safe here
-- the harvester's temporary path is unique per compile.

That widened rewrite then broke an anonymous class: `class@anonymous<file>:<line>$<hash>`
embeds the filename, and rewriting the literal the declaring opline carries but
not the class's own name left the declaration unable to find its class -- which
the runtime reported honestly as `unsupported: anonymous class declaration`
rather than as a wrong answer. Both sides move together now.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4139 | **4143** |
| failed | 412 | 408 |
| unsupported | 158 | 158 |
| pass rate | 87.8% | **87.9%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set: `constants/dir-constant-eval`, `match/unmatched_enum`,
`named_params/call_user_func`, `named_params/runtime_cache_init` fixed, nothing
broken. Differential cases 918 -> 923.

### On reading the counts

Mid-round the totals were 4142/408/**159** -- one test had moved from `failed`
to `unsupported`, and the four names leaving the failing set no longer accounted
for the passes. Guessing which change did it was wrong twice (the forwarding,
then staleness in `pending.extraNamed`). What settled it was disabling one
change at a time and re-running the corpus: with both off the counts returned
to 4139/412/158 exactly, which named the eval rename and led to the anonymous
class above. A set difference alone would not have shown it -- the test never
entered the failing set.

## 2026-08-28 — where a trait's method lives, and what eval'd code is called

Interpreter track. Took the five remaining `Declaration of X must be compatible
with Y` tests as one family. Each turned out to be a different missing fact, and
all five now pass.

### What was wrong

**A trait's method is invisible as a prototype.** php2go keeps a trait's methods
with the trait rather than flattening them into the composing class, so that
`self::` inside one names the using class. `prototypeMethod` consulted only
`class.methods`, so a subclass overriding a method its parent got from a trait
was checked against nothing -- and in `bug62358` the message named the
*interface* further down the source list instead of the parent. `prototypeMethod`
now follows the composition (`composedTraitMethod`), which is the only place the
flattening has to be simulated.

**The declaration printer resolves `self`.** `zend_get_function_declaration`
takes a scope separately from the function, and `zend_type_to_string_resolved`
substitutes that scope for `self` and its parent for `parent` -- `static` stays
`static`, since it is a promise about the called class rather than a name. For a
trait the two part company: the `T::` prefix is the method's own scope, the types
resolve against the class that composed it, which is `fixup_trait_scope` in the
engine and `selfScope` here. `abstract_method_10` wanted
`T::method(C $x): C` where php2go printed `self`.

**An abstract trait method is checked against what was inherited.** The engine
looks the name up in the class's function table, which already holds the
parent's entry, so `gh14009_002` reports `P::common()` -- a method neither the
class nor the trait wrote. `overridingMethods` now offers that inherited method
as a candidate, restricted (`against`) to the trait that requires it, since it
was already checked against its own ancestry when its own class linked.

**`as final` was harvested as a visibility change.** The alias modifiers were
mapped through `visibility()` whenever they were non-zero, so `T::foo as final`
silently made the method public and `final` was dropped entirely. The flag now
travels (`TraitAlias.final`, field 5) and only a PPP bit decides visibility --
which is a fix in its own right, and one the differential oracle can see:
a protected method aliased final stays protected.

**Eval'd code was named after the temporary.** The harvester compiles a temp
file, so every op_array in the result -- and the `__FILE__` literal the compiler
folded in -- carried `/tmp/...`. The engine names it `<site>(<line>) : eval()'d
code`. `renameCompiled` now rewrites the filename of every op_array, class and
closure, plus any string literal equal to the old name, which is what `__FILE__`
is by the time it reaches the IR.

### Result

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| passed | 4134 | **4139** |
| failed | 417 | 412 |
| unsupported | 158 | 158 |
| pass rate | 87.7% | **87.8%** |

`php2phpt -diff 1300 third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`, 4712 attempted both times.
Diff-set comparison: the five named tests fixed, nothing broken.

Differential cases 912 -> 918. Two of the new ones failed when first written and
were real bugs, not bad expectations:

- the tentative-return deprecation named the *trait* (`ItT::getIterator`) where
  the engine names the composing class, because `noteTentativeReturn` used
  `candidate.owner` instead of the `reported` class `verifySignatures` had
  already worked out;
- `__FILE__` inside eval was still the temporary, because the compiler folds it
  into a literal rather than reading the filename field at run time.

### What the oracle still cannot be asked

Nothing in this family could be tested differentially -- a class-link failure is
an E_ERROR and an E_ERROR bails out of the shared engine process, even inside
`eval`. The five were worked from the corpus's expected output, and the
differential cases added alongside cover only the parts that do *not* fatal: a
compatible override of a composed method, the visibility of an `as final` alias,
the eval filename, and the deprecation above. `ReflectionClass::getFileName` is
not implemented, so the eval-named class could not be checked that way.

## 2026-08-28 — an IR designed against measurements, and a lowering that reached 92.3%

Compiler track. Three new documents — [INTRINSICS.md](./INTRINSICS.md),
[IR-DESIGN.md](./IR-DESIGN.md), [IR-ASSEMBLY.md](./IR-ASSEMBLY.md) — and a
prototype lowering in `.agents-workspace/tmp/lower/` that exercises all of the
design. Interpreter work is a separate track and no corpus metric here is a
claim about it.

### Result

Prototype lowering over `Zend/tests`, counted in **bodies**, because one
unhandled opline bails a whole function:

| after | of 10,738 op_arrays |
| --- | --- |
| calls un-flattened | 46.5% |
| `OP_DATA`, arrays, ropes, `foreach`, catch | 59.4% |
| declarations | 69.6% |
| write paths, resolution, `incdec`, eval-as-refusal | 80.7% |
| references, compound assignment, silence, `isset` | 89.4% |
| generators | **92.3%** |

### Coverage counted in oplines is a lie

194 distinct opcodes occur. The top 40 are 87.7% of *oplines* and **59.3% of
bodies**; reaching 88% of bodies takes 100 opcodes. So Phase C is "most of the
opcode set", not "the head of the distribution". The tail is cheap per item —
39 opcodes occur fewer than 20 times each — but you need all of it.

The call protocol alone is **43.9% of all oplines** (`INIT_*` 13.9%, `DO_*`
17.5%, `SEND_*` 12.6%) describing ~18,060 calls, which is why un-flattening it
was the first thing built and why the IR comes out around a fifth smaller than
the opline stream.

### The design, and what decided each part

- **Register, not stack.** The input is already three-address, and its one
  stack-like structure — the call protocol — is what the un-flattening pass
  exists to remove. We emit Go source, so neither compactness nor register
  allocation argues for a stack.
- **Not sea-of-nodes**, despite that being what PHP's own JIT uses. Of the
  intrinsic rows, **44 declare an effect against 16 pure**. A sea-of-nodes IR
  buys freedom for pure nodes and discards the total order the other three
  quarters *are defined by* — and `php2phpt` grades byte-exact stdout.
- **Region-based exceptions, not `invoke`.** Same 44: if every throwing
  instruction were a terminator there would be one instruction per block.
- **`finally` inlined at each exit, not a subroutine.** Measured cost: 907
  oplines, **0.70% of the corpus**; 68% of finallys have one exit and 86% are
  ≤5 oplines. It also makes every CFG fully static, and `finally`'s hard cases
  fall out — its own `return` replacing the try's is just a `ret` in that copy,
  swallowing an in-flight exception is the exceptional copy ending in `ret`.
  Go's `defer` can express neither.
- **Values that cross blocks start as places**, and mem2reg promotes later. This
  began as "CVs stay as places" — the CV/TMP split maps exactly onto LLVM's
  alloca/register split — and the `foreach` iterator then forced the same rule,
  being defined by `FE_RESET`, read by `FE_FETCH` and ended by `FE_FREE` in
  three different blocks. The interpreter keeps it in a side map for the same
  reason.

### Zero irreducible control flow, and the detector was validated first

**0 of 10,738.** A measurement that reports zero is worthless until shown able
to report non-zero, so: PHP's `goto` cannot jump into a loop, but two labels can
form a cycle entered at both ends, and the engine accepts and runs such a
function. The tool reports it irreducible.

The first run had to exclude the 147 op_arrays containing `finally`, because
`FAST_RET` is an indirect jump — the same imprecision `zend_cfg.c` accepts.
Inlining removes `FAST_RET` entirely, so the re-run covers all 10,738 and the
answer is unchanged.

Two thirds of op_arrays are a **single basic block** and 92.5% are four or
fewer, so the emitter should special-case the straight-line function.

### Three claims in the intrinsic catalogue were wrong until probed

Written from the source, then checked against the engine one by one:

- **`instanceof` does not autoload.** Neither operand form triggers a registered
  autoloader, and nor does a type check against an unknown class — a name that
  is not loaded cannot be an ancestor of one that is. `new`, `::CONST`,
  `::$static` and `::m()` all do; a global constant never does.
- **`isset` is not effect-free.** `isset($a[[]])` throws
  `TypeError: Cannot access offset of type array in isset or empty`.
- **`true` and `false` differ under autovivification.** `$a["x"]=1` on `false`
  deprecates and converts; on `true` it is a fatal `Error`. So a `Dim` write over
  an operand merely known to be `bool` cannot be specialized.

Also pinned: `finally` can replace the try's return *and* swallow an exception;
`yield from [1,2]; yield 3;` produces keys `0,1,0` because delegation does not
renumber; array unpack takes the later value and renumbers integer keys where
`+` does the opposite; copying an array preserves a `&` element as the same box.

### Four engine facts the harvest had to be asked for

- **`sprintf("%d", $x)` is constant-folded into `(string)(int)$x`** — two
  `ZEND_CAST`s and no call. Read as an opcode-numbering bug at first; checked
  `ZEND_CAST` is 51 and `ZEND_FRAMELESS_ICALL_2` is 206 in both the harvest and
  `zend_vm_opcodes.h` before concluding the folding is real.
- **`ZEND_CAST`'s target type is in `extended_value`.** Lowering it without that
  emits an instruction that does not say which cast it is; `(string)7` and
  `(array)7` are otherwise indistinguishable.
- **`DECLARE_*`'s `op2` is typed `IS_UNUSED` and indexes `OpArray.closures`** —
  which therefore holds conditionally declared *named* functions too, despite
  the name. Verified: two closures plus one such function give indices 0, 1, 2
  against exactly those three entries.
- **A declaration's operand is a lowercased lookup key.** `class MixedCase {}`
  gives `literals[1] = "mixedcase"` alongside
  `literals[2] = "\x00mixedcase/path:2$0"`, a mangled key **starting with a NUL
  byte**. Concrete evidence for the outstanding `Literal.string_value` → `bytes`
  change, not a hypothetical.

And a generator's parameter check fires **at call time, before the generator
object exists** — so `GENERATOR_CREATE` is a split point between an eager
prologue and a resumable body, not a function flag.

### A measurement of mine that was wrong, and why

The prototype does per-block SSA only. At 59.4% coverage that blocked **60
bodies (0.6%)**, and I concluded block arguments were not on the critical path.
At 92.3% the same limitation blocks **246 (2.3%)** and is the largest remaining
category — bodies that stopped early on a missing opcode had never got far
enough to need a cross-block value.

General caution: **a coverage-limited measurement understates every limitation
it has not yet reached.** The corrected reading is that cross-block values are
the next structural piece after `finally`, not something to defer.

### Touched in shared files, and why

Two edits in `runtime/interp`, made before it became clear the other session was
working there; nothing since:

- ~19 differential cases for the intrinsic contracts. All pass (863/863).
- **A real bug they found**: the `ASSIGN_DIM` string branch excluded the empty
  string via `container.String() != ""`, a PHP 7.0 leftover, so `$s = "";
  $s[0] = "a"` threw `Cannot use string offset as an array` where the engine
  yields `"a"`. The guard is gone. **Corpus effect unmeasured** — the grading run
  collided with a concurrent one, and two `php2phpt` runs write the same `.php`
  beside the same `.phpt`.

### Filed, not fixed

- `cmd/php2harvest` does not print `extended_value` at all
  (`cmd/php2harvest/main.go:161`), so its listing is misleading rather than
  incomplete: two `ZEND_CAST` rows print identically and mean different things.
  Also hidden are `FE_FETCH`'s loop-exit target, `CATCH`'s `ZEND_LAST_CATCH`
  flag, `SEND`'s argument number and `SWITCH`/`MATCH`'s default.
- `cmd/php2eval` does not normalise the source filename between its two arms, so
  any case whose output names a file diverges by construction.
  `differential_test.go` already normalises this.
- Thirteen `IteratorIterator` subclasses instantiate without being modelled;
  `AppendIterator` throws an error the program did not earn and
  `InfiniteIterator` silently iterates once.

## 2026-08-28 — a final constant, and what the oracle cannot be asked about linking

**4133 -> 4134 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.7%); failed 418 -> 417,
unsupported 158 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `traits/constant_014`; broke
nothing.

php2go refused a `final` constant overridden through an *interface* and not one
overridden through the *parent chain*:

```php
class Composing { final public const C = 123; }
class Derived extends Composing { public const C = 456; }
// Fatal error: Derived::C cannot override final constant Composing::C
```

Telling "the class's own constants" from "what it inherited" is the flattened
table again -- the check reads `declaring_class` rather than assuming the table
it came from.

### The oracle cannot be asked about a link-time fatal

Trying to probe this first produced `zend: evaluation bailed out`: a class-link
failure is an E_ERROR, and an E_ERROR bails out of the shared engine process --
even inside `eval`, so wrapping it does not help. So the twelve remaining
link-time tests have to be worked from their expected output rather than from a
probe, which is slower and needs more care. Recorded with the other shapes the
oracle cannot be asked.

The rest of that family is not this cheap. Five want method signature variance
with the declaration rendered back (`Declaration of C::m(int $x): int must be
compatible with T::m(C $x): C`), and the others want trait, enum and interface
composition rules -- each a separate check.

## 2026-08-28 — a function's name, split

**4131 -> 4133 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.7%); failed 419 -> 418,
unsupported 159 -> 158, so one of the two gained tests came out of the gap
bucket. Diff-set: fixed `closure_068`; `closure_067` moved from `unsupported`
to passing. Differential cases 911 -> 912.

`ReflectionFunction::getNamespaceName()` and `inNamespace()` were unimplemented,
and `getShortName()` split on the last `\` -- which is right for a function and
wrong for a closure, whose compiled name is `{closure:WHERE:LINE}` and whose
WHERE may itself be a namespaced method:

```
{closure:Foo\Bar::baz():6}
   getShortName()      the whole thing
   getNamespaceName()  ""
   inNamespace()       false
```

A closure is in no namespace whatever its name contains.

`new ReflectionFunction(foo(...))` also failed outright. A first-class callable
of a plain *function* is represented by the name rather than by a body -- there
is no op_array to wrap -- so the constructor fell through to reflecting a
closure that had none. It looks the name up instead.

### On the buckets

Adding `getNamespaceName` moved `closure_067` from `unsupported` to `failed`
before the closure rule was right, and the diff-set reported that as BROKE. It
was not: the test had never passed, and what changed was which honest bucket it
sat in. Reading the two counts together is what tells them apart -- `failed`
rose by one while `unsupported` fell by one.

## 2026-08-28 — an unset chain removes nothing it does not find

**4128 -> 4131 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.6% -> 87.7%); failed 422 -> 419,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed
`asymmetric_visibility/variation_nested`, `readonly_props/variation_nested` and
`bug78644`; broke nothing. Differential cases 910 -> 911.

Three rules, found one after another because each fix exposed the next.

### A read-modify-write *descent* reads first too

`$o->prop->prop += 1` on an uninitialized `private(set)` property reports
`Typed property Test::$prop must not be accessed before initialization`, not the
visibility. The direct forms were fixed two rounds ago; `ZEND_FETCH_OBJ_RW` is
the same rule one level down.

### An unset chain through a non-object stops there

```php
$null = null;   unset($null->a->b);      // nothing happens
unset($undefined->a[0]);                 // Warning: Undefined variable, then nothing
```

php2go raised `Attempt to assign property "a" on null`. `ZEND_FETCH_OBJ_UNSET`
is not a write fetch: it does not create what it walks through, and what it
cannot find it simply does not remove.

That was already a bug, and the previous round's short-circuit -- skipping the
visibility check when unsetting into an uninitialized property -- turned it into
a visible one, because the skip hands the rest of the chain a value that is not
an object.

### And it reads the container it walks through

`unset($undefined->a[0])` warns about the undefined variable; `unset($undefined->a)`
does not. The first is a `FETCH_OBJ_UNSET` chain, which reads; the second is a
single `ZEND_UNSET_OBJ`, which does not. php2go had the fetch quiet along with
the write forms.

## 2026-08-28 — two things a callable cannot supply

**4126 -> 4128 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.6%); failed 424 -> 422,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug77877` and `exception_004`;
broke nothing. Differential cases 908 -> 910.

### Only a Throwable can be thrown

`throw new Foo` where Foo implements nothing is
`Error: Cannot throw objects that do not implement Throwable`. php2go checked
that the operand was an *object* -- "Can only throw objects" for anything else,
which is the engine's wording for that case -- and then threw whatever it was.

### A static method never has a $this

```php
class F { public static function s() { var_dump($this); } }
array_map([new F, 's'], [1]);      // Using $this when not in object context
call_user_func([new F, 's']);      // same
(new F)->s();                      // same
```

php2go got the last two right and the first two wrong: reaching a static method
through `[$object, 'method']` bound the object as `$this`. The object in that
pair supplies only the *class*, and the method resolution already knew the
method was static -- it just was not consulted before binding.

## 2026-08-28 — sweeping for the flattened-table pattern

**4125 -> 4126 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.5% -> 87.6%); failed 425 -> 424,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `enum/value-property-type`; broke
nothing. Differential cases 907 -> 908.

Having named the pattern in LTM last round, this round went looking for the rest
of it rather than waiting: one probe asked the engine about fourteen
inheritance-sensitive behaviours on a `class Sub extends Base` -- a typed
default, a readonly reassignment, a hook, a constant, a static, protected
access, a protected call, and seven reflection accessors.

**Two disagreed, both the same pattern:**

```php
(new ReflectionProperty('Sub', 'typed'))->getDeclaringClass()->getName();      // Base
(new ReflectionClassConstant('Sub', 'KIND'))->getDeclaringClass()->getName();  // Base
```

php2go answered `Sub` for both -- the class the lookup went through.
`ReflectionMethod` was already right, which is why neither had shown up before.

The sweep also turned up two unrelated gaps: `ReflectionClass::getDefaultProperties`
is unimplemented, and `(string) $type` on a `ReflectionNamedType` raised
"could not be converted to string". The second is fixed: `toString` knew how to
reach a Throwable's engine-supplied `__toString` and nothing else's, so any
engine class declaring one now goes through the same dispatcher. The string form
keeps the `?` a nullable type was written with; `getName()` does not.

Only one corpus test moved. The sweep's value is in what it did *not* find --
eleven of fourteen behaviours already agreed -- and in fixing two more instances
of a pattern that has cost four bugs so far.

## 2026-08-28 — a flattened table, for the third time

**4123 -> 4125 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.5%); failed 427 -> 425,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug30451` and
`get_class_vars_003`; broke nothing. Differential cases 906 -> 907.

A static property's storage belongs to the class that declared it -- php2go
already keyed it that way -- but its *initializer* does too, and that half was
missing:

```php
class B { public static $aa = 4; }
class C extends B {}
get_class_vars('C');   // ["aa" => 4]
```

Zend flattens inherited statics into the subclass's table without their
defaults. Asking `C` for `$aa` found C's copy, saw no default, and built the
shared storage holding **null** -- which then answered for `B::$aa` too, since
they are one slot. The first read of the subclass's name silently emptied the
parent's static.

This is the third time this session the same shape has cost a bug: a flattened
table says where a thing was *found*, never where it was *written*.

- Property visibility compared against the class whose table held it.
- A class constant's `self::` resolved against the class it was read through.
- Now a static property's default taken from the inheriting copy.

Two of the three were fixed by harvesting `declaring_class`; this one had it
already and simply was not following it back to the declaration.

## 2026-08-28 — what does not produce a lazy object's state

**4120 -> 4123 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.4% -> 87.5%); failed 430 -> 427,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). `lazy_objects` alone: 178 -> 184 of 223. Diff-set:
fixed `lazy_objects/fetch_hook_virtual_may_not_initialize`,
`isset_hooked_may_not_initialize` and `use_case_002`; broke nothing.
Differential cases 905 -> 906.

Grouping the failures by the shape of the *interpreter's* output rather than the
engine's turned up four tests all printing `string(11) "initializer"` where the
engine printed nothing -- php2go was producing the state where the engine does
not. Two causes.

### A virtual hooked property has nothing to produce

Its value comes from the hook, not from a slot, so reaching it initializes
nothing. Whatever the hook body touches produces the state itself if it needs
to. `resolveLazy` already had a list of things that do not trigger -- a skipped
property, a magic accessor for a name the class does not declare -- and this
belongs on it.

### Calling a method does not produce it either

```php
$e = $r->newLazyGhost(...);
(new ReflectionProperty(User::class, 'id'))->setRawValueWithoutLazyInitialization($e, 123);
$e->getId();     // 123, no initializer
$e->getName();   // initializer runs
```

The method is resolved on the object's own class; the state is produced by
whatever the *body* touches, and `getId()` touches only a property the
initializer was told to skip. php2go resolved the lazy object at
`ZEND_INIT_METHOD_CALL`, which produced the state before the body could decide.
The resolution was doing nothing else by then -- an earlier round had already
stopped it replacing a proxy with its instance -- so the whole step went.

```
object(MyArrayObject)#2 (1) { ["storage":"ArrayObject":private]=> ... }
```

either -- a subclass the program wrote inherits the label from the engine class
above it -- so the walk stops at the first builtin ancestor.

Three `try/` tests want an exception thrown inside a `finally` to become the

inside the finally, php2go lets it escape. The object is still held by the

open, and that is a timing question rather than a wording one. Left for a round

## 2026-08-28 — a class in the table but not yet linked

**4110 -> 4114 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.2% -> 87.3%); failed 440 -> 436,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug30922`,
`type_declarations/variance/unlinked_parent_1`, `_2` and `use_unlinked_class`;
broke nothing. Differential cases 902 -> 903.

A class is in the class table from the moment its declaration starts, and not
*linked* until its parent, interfaces and traits have been found. Three things
can happen in between, because resolving a dependency can run an autoloader:

```php
spl_autoload_register(function ($c) { class X extends B {} });
class B extends A {}          // Class "B" not found
```

php2go had no third state -- a class was either in the table or not -- and
php2go's harvest puts every class of the file in the table up front, so `B` was
found and `X` linked against a class that does not exist yet.

A `linking` set, held for the duration of `resolveDependencies`, gives the third
state. What consults it took three passes and the corpus found each miss:

- **Linking against it** is refused: `Class "B" not found`.
- **Autoloading it** must not happen. The first version let the refusal fall
  through to the autoloader, which re-entered and redeclared everything it
  declares -- `Cannot redeclare class X`, and
  `type_declarations/variance/infinite_recursion` said so.
- **Reflecting on it** is refused too: `new ReflectionClass(A::class)` from
  inside the autoloader A's own declaration triggered is
  `ReflectionException: Class "A" does not exist`.

The first two are the same statement from opposite sides -- the name *is* in the
table, so there is nothing to autoload, and it is *not* linked, so there is
nothing to extend.

## 2026-08-28 — what happens first when a write also reads

**4108 -> 4110 passed** of 4712 attempted (87.2%); failed 442 -> 440,
unsupported 159 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `asymmetric_visibility/variation`
and `enum/print_r`; broke nothing. Differential cases 900 -> 902.

### print_r says what an object is

`Suit Enum:string`, `Pure Enum`, `stdClass Object`. php2go said "Object" for
everything.

### A compound assignment reads before it writes

```php
class C { public private(set) int $p; }
$o->p++;      Typed property C::$p must not be accessed before initialization
$o->p .= "x"; Typed property C::$p must not be accessed before initialization
$o->p = 5;    Cannot modify private(set) property C::$p from global scope
```

The first two read the property to combine with it, so an uninitialized typed
property is reported before the write is judged at all; the plain assignment
reads nothing and reports the visibility. php2go ran the write check first in
both compound paths.

### Unset is the operation that does nothing

`unset($o->p[$k])` where `$o->p` is a *declared but uninitialized* property does
exactly nothing -- there is no element to remove, so who may modify the property
never comes up, and a `private(set)` one is not refused. A write descent
(`$o->p[] = 1`) still is, because it would create the property.

The first version of this skipped the check whenever the property held nothing,
and an existing differential case caught it: `unset($e->n["k"])` on a property
the class never declared *does* create it as null, with the dynamic-property
deprecation. "Uninitialized" and "not there at all" are different states and
this is one of the places that can tell.


scope* rather than where it was written. Two of the three tests fixed.

`Call to a member function bar() on false`, not "on bool". Same for
`Attempt to read property "p" on false`, `Attempt to assign property`, and

## 2026-08-28 — a constructor nobody may call, and a return value still being written

**4094 -> 4099 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.9% -> 87.0%); failed 455 -> 450,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `gh14456`, `gh18736`,
`lazy_objects/typed_properties_004`, `oss_fuzz_438780145` and
`return_types/return_reference_separation`; broke nothing. Differential cases
891 -> 893.

### An unreachable constructor refuses before the object exists

`new PrivateUser()` from outside the class is
`Error: Call to private PrivateUser::__construct() from global scope`, and
**no destructor runs** -- there is no object yet. php2go built the object, found
nothing to complain about, and later destructed it. Reflection's
`newInstance` had this check; `ZEND_NEW` did not.

The contrast is what makes it worth a case: a constructor that *throws* did make
the object, and its destructor does not run either -- but for the other reason,
that the object never finished being constructed.

### A by-reference return is checked on the box, not on a copy

```php
function &test(): int { $x = 0; try { return $x; } finally { $x = 'test'; } }
$x = &test();   // TypeError: Return value must be of type int, string returned
```

The compiler emits `VERIFY_RETURN_TYPE` **twice** for this -- once before the
`FAST_CALL` into the finally and once after -- and the second one is the one
that matters. php2go ran both, but its first one wrote the converted value into
the *slot*, replacing the reference with a plain int. From then on there was
nothing left to see the finally's assignment, so the second check passed and the
caller got the stale value.

Converting *through* the box when the function returns by reference fixes both
halves: the check sees what the finally left, and a by-reference return whose
type is fine hands back a slot that is still live. Two of the five tests fixed
are about the second half rather than the first.

## 2026-08-28 — the order the two operands of `$a[$k] = $v` are taken in

**4080 -> 4082 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.6%); failed 469 -> 467,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug79599` and `bug79927`; broke
nothing. Differential cases 884 -> 886.

### rewind() is the start, and only the start

A generator sitting on its first yielded value may be rewound; one that has been
*resumed* past it may not, and says
`Cannot rewind a generator that was already run`. `current()` does not count --
it starts the generator, which is what rewind does anyway -- and neither does
reaching the first yield through an empty `yield from`:

```php
(function () { yield from []; yield 4; })()   // ->current(); ->rewind() is fine
(function () { yield 1; yield 2; })()         // ->next();    ->rewind() throws
```

php2go's `start` calls `advance`, so the flag has to be cleared again after the
first one -- the start is not a resume even though it goes through the same
code.

### Three operands, one order, and two tests that disagree about it

`$a[$k] = $v` reads its container, then its index, then the value. php2go read
the value first, so `$a[$c] = $b` with both undefined reported `$b` before `$c`.
Reordering that fixed `bug79599` and broke two tests -- `bug79784` and
`objects_034` -- which pin down something more interesting:

```php
set_error_handler(function () { $GLOBALS['a'] = null; });
$a[$c] = 'x';     // $a is NULL afterwards, not an array
```

The handler runs while the *index* is being read and replaces `$a`. The
assignment still goes ahead, and yet `$a` keeps the handler's null. So the
container the write lands in was taken before the index was read -- and for an
undefined variable that means the empty array was **grown out of the slot
first**, then detached by the handler's assignment, and the write went into the
detached array.

php2go grew the array after reading the index, from whatever the slot held by
then. Growing it up front, and keeping the value rather than re-reading the
slot, is what makes all three agree. The two "regressions" were the useful part
of the round: the operand order alone would have looked right.

`$x .= $y` went through `arith`, a pure function with no context, so an object

`exception_from_toString` reach line 59; a gap two thirds of the way down a

  the caller's `$this` and runs. php2go already had `forwardThis` for exactly
  this, with a comment describing the asymmetry -- but it returns early when
  `$this` is already set, and the first version set it. Leaving `$this` for
  `forwardThis` to supply is what makes both forms right, and it broke
  `bug45186_2` until it did.

`is_callable` follows the call's choice: from inside an instance of the class a
class-name callable forwards to `__call`, so it answers true there and false
outside, whatever `__callStatic` says.

## 2026-08-28 — a hooked property names the class the program was holding

**4073 -> 4076 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.4% -> 86.5%); failed 475 -> 472,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). `property_hooks` alone: 168 -> 171 of 198.
Diff-set: fixed `property_hooks/magic_interaction`, `override_add_get` and
`set`; broke nothing. Differential cases 881 -> 882.

### A set hook with no get and no storage is write-only

php2go answered `null`. There is nothing to read -- the property is virtual, so
there is no backing store, and there is no get hook to ask -- and the engine
refuses:

```php
class A { public $p { set { ... } } }        (new A)->p        // Error: Property A::$p is write-only
class B { public $p { set { $this->p = $value; } } }   // backed: reads its storage
```

`isset()` is refused the same way. var_dump leaves such a property out
entirely, which php2go already did.

### Which class these name

`read-only`, `write-only` and `Cannot unset hooked property` all name the class
of the **object the program was holding**, not the class that declared the
hooks. All three named the declaring class in php2go. A subclass that merely
inherits the hooks is what the message says.

### What is still missing

Six of the remaining `property_hooks` failures want a *link-time* fatal error --
a hook signature incompatible with an interface's, a set type that is not a
supertype, two traits defining the same hooked property. `zend.Class` has had a
`LinkError` field since the harvester was written and nothing has ever set it;
these are the tests that would use it. They are six separate rules, so either
php2go implements each check or the harvester learns to capture what the engine
says when it refuses to link a class.

## 2026-08-28 — a fiber nobody can resume, and a stack too small to run in

**4069 -> 4073 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.4%); failed 479 -> 475,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). `fibers` alone: 62 -> 71 of 91 across the last two
rounds. Diff-set: fixed `fibers/gh10249`, `negative_stack_size`,
`suspend-in-force-close-fiber-catching-exception` and
`throw-during-fiber-destruct`; broke nothing. Differential cases 879 -> 881.

### The same fix the generators needed

`forceClose` wrote the fatal-error text for anything a closing fiber threw, so
a `try` around the point that abandoned the fiber never saw it -- exactly the
shape fixed for generators two rounds ago, in the same collector. Split into
`forceCloseFor`, which hands the error back, and `forceClose`, which prints it
because at request shutdown there is nobody left to catch it. Worth noting that
the generator fix did not generalise on its own: the two live side by side in
`collect` and only one of them was reading its result.

### fiber.stack_size

Two tests, and the rules are all observable:

```
ini_set("fiber.stack_size", "-1")   Warning: must be a positive number, returns false, unchanged
ini_set("fiber.stack_size", "0")    accepted
ini_set("fiber.stack_size", "4096") accepted
$fiber->start()                     Exception: Fiber stack size is too small,
                                    it needs to be at least 8192 bytes
```

The size is a byte quantity, so `1M` is a valid setting. Two pages is the floor.
The subtlety is that *unset* and *set to the empty string* both read back as
`""` and behave differently: unset means the platform's default and a fiber
runs, while an explicit `""` is zero and no fiber can start. So the runtime has
to keep whether the setting was assigned, not just what it holds.

### A note on the differential harness

The engine's ini table outlives a single case, so a case that calls `ini_set`
changes the world for every case after it -- the first version of the
stack_size case left the engine unable to start any fiber, and the *next* case
failed. It puts the setting back at the end now. This belongs with the other
shared-engine-state hazards already recorded (classes and autoloaders survive
the reset too).

## 2026-08-28 — error_reporting belongs to the fiber

**4066 -> 4069 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.3% -> 86.4%); failed 482 -> 479,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `fibers/error-reporting`,
`silence-operator-inside-fiber` and `silence-operator-outside-fiber`; broke
nothing. Differential cases 877 -> 879.

Moved to `fibers`. The three tests that ranked closest turned out to be one
feature and one unrelated bug underneath it.

### trigger_error raises at E_USER_*, and is filtered there

`error_reporting(E_ALL & ~E_USER_NOTICE)` did not hide a `trigger_error(...,
E_USER_NOTICE)`, because php2go routed it through `ctx.Notice` -- E_NOTICE,
which was still enabled. The E_USER_* levels print under the engine levels'
labels but filter on their own bits, and an error handler is told the E_USER_*
code. php2go already had that distinction for E_USER_DEPRECATED; the other two
were missing.

### A fiber keeps its own level

Probed rather than reasoned about, because the interaction with `@` is not
obvious:

```
error_reporting(E_ALL);
@$f->start();          in-start: 30719   -- the @ does not cross
                       out1:     30719
inside: error_reporting(E_ERROR)
                       out2:     30719   -- and the change does not come back
                       in-resume2: 1     -- but the fiber remembers it
```

So each fiber has its own level. It inherits one at its **first start**, from
the level in force *with any `@` disregarded* -- `error_reporting(E_ERROR)`
before the start is inherited, an `@` around the start is not. From then on the
two sides keep their own.

That "with any `@` disregarded" is the awkward part: php2go models `@` the way
the engine does, as the mask itself dropped to the fatal-only levels, so there
is no flag to consult. `Ctx` now tracks the depth of open `@` expressions and
the level the outermost of them replaced, which is enough to answer the
question without changing what `@` does.

## 2026-08-28 — a generator nobody can resume

**4063 -> 4066 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.2% -> 86.3%); failed 485 -> 482,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `generators/bug74954`,
`errors/yield_in_force_closed_finally_error` and `yield_from_force_closed`;
broke nothing. Differential cases 875 -> 877.

Same directory, next rank. These three share the state left behind when a
suspended generator is abandoned.

### A force-closed generator's finally may not suspend

php2go already unwound an abandoned generator so its finally blocks run. What it
did not do was refuse the yields inside them -- and there is nobody left to
resume what such a yield suspends. Two messages, one per form:

```
yield        Cannot yield from finally in a force-closed generator
yield from   Cannot use "yield from" in a force-closed generator
```

The first reads oddly until you notice it means "yield, from a finally" rather
than "yield from, in a finally".

### And what it throws belongs to where the program lost it

The collector was writing the fatal-error text itself for anything a closing
generator threw, so a `try { ... unset($gen); } catch (Error $e)` around the
abandonment never saw it. The destructor path in the same collector already got
this right -- it chains what escapes onto `thrown` and hands it back to the
release point -- so the generator loop now does the same. `chainOnto` gives the
"Next Exception" behaviour for free when more than one escapes.

### An aborted delegate has no return value to hand on

Two generators can `yield from` the same source. When the source throws, the
first delegator sees the exception; the second finds the source finished and
asks for its return value, and the engine refuses with
`ClosedGeneratorException: Generator yielded from aborted, no return value
available`. The `failed` flag added in the previous entry is exactly what
distinguishes this from an ordinary finish, which is a reasonable sign it was
the right thing to record.

### What is still missing

`yield_from_multi_tree_exception` wants the same refusal five delegation levels
deep, with the stack trace naming each level; php2go stops after the first
fifteen yields. The trace shape rather than the refusal is what is missing.

## 2026-08-28 — a generator that threw has not returned

**4059 -> 4063 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.1% -> 86.2%); failed 489 -> 485,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `generators/clone`,
`get_return_and_finally`, `get_return_errors` and `throw_not_an_exception`;
broke nothing. Differential cases 873 -> 875.

Moved to `generators`, ranked within the directory as before.

### Finished is not the same as returned

`getReturn()` refuses with `Cannot get return value of a generator that hasn't
returned` -- and a body that ended by *throwing* is one of those. php2go had a
single `finished` flag and handed out the (null) return value once it was set,
whichever way the body ended. A separate `failed` marks the throwing exits, and
the refusal covers both.

### Generator::throw() takes a Throwable

php2go checked for an *object*, which let `throw(new stdClass)` through -- and
what came out the other side was a fatal error announcing an uncaught stdClass,
which is not a thing PHP can produce.

### What refuses to be cloned is the engine's answer, not a list

`clone` on a Generator, a Fiber or a WeakReference is
`Trying to clone an uncloneable object of class X` -- the same words an enum
case gets. ArrayObject, Closure and WeakMap clone perfectly well, so the set is
not "the interesting internal classes"; it is exactly those whose
`default_object_handlers->clone_obj` is null. Harvested as `Class.no_clone`
(proto field 34) rather than written out here, for the same reason
`custom_create` was in the previous entry: a list of class names in the runtime
is a guess that ages, and the engine already knows.

## 2026-08-28 — a proxy is not the thing it forwards to

**4055 -> 4059 passed** of 4712 attempted (86.1%); failed 493 -> 489,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). `lazy_objects` alone: 174 -> 178 of 223. Diff-set:
fixed `clone_preverves_object_class`, `init_preserves_proxy_class`,
`init_sets_prop_default_values` and `invalid_options`; broke nothing.
Differential cases 871 -> 873.

Second pass over `lazy_objects`, ranked within the directory again.

### A method call on a proxy stays on the proxy

```php
class A { public string $s; }
class B extends A { public function foo() { ... } }
$o = (new ReflectionClass(B::class))->newLazyProxy(fn () => new A);
$o->foo();      // B::foo, with $this === $o
```

php2go resolved the lazy object to the instance before the call, so it looked
for `foo` on `A` and did not find it. The proxy is what the program holds: its
*class* is the one the method resolves against, its identity is what `$this`
binds to and what `spl_object_id` answers, and only its **property** reads
forward to the instance. Probed, not inferred -- `$this->s` inside `B::foo`
reads the instance's value while `spl_object_id($this)` is the proxy's.

### While the initializer runs, nothing is labelled lazy

`var_dump($obj)` inside the initializer prints `object(C)#3` with no prefix, for
a ghost and a proxy alike -- the object is not waiting for an initializer, it is
*in* one. A proxy gets its label back once the initializer has returned, and
shows the `["instance"]` slot from then on.

### The options mask takes exactly two bits

`-1` is not "everything": anything outside the two known bits is
`contains invalid flags`. SKIP_DESTRUCTOR only means something where there is
state to destroy, so `newLazyGhost` and `newLazyProxy` refuse it specifically --
`does not accept ReflectionClass::SKIP_DESTRUCTOR` -- while the reset forms take
it. The argument number differs between the two families (#2 and #3), and the
message carries it.

## 2026-08-28 — making an object lazy again

**4047 -> 4055 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.9% -> 86.1%); failed 501 -> 493,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). `lazy_objects` alone: 166 -> 174 of 223. Diff-set:
fixed six `reset_as_lazy_*`, `rfc/rfc_example_009`, `support_no_internal_classes`
and `support_no_internal_sub_classes`; broke nothing. Differential cases
869 -> 871.

Switched lens from "fewest differing lines" to the largest remaining directory.
`lazy_objects` was 54 failures with no obvious cluster, but ranking *within* it
put the `resetAsLazy*` family at the top, and that family shared one cause:
php2go's implementation stripped the object's state and did nothing else.

### resetAsLazyGhost/Proxy has three checks and a destructor

- The object must be an instance of the reflected class -- a subclass will do --
  and the refusal names the declared type:
  `Argument #1 ($object) must be of type A, C given`.
- An object already *waiting* for an initializer has nothing to throw away:
  `ReflectionException: Object is already lazy`. An already-*initialized* lazy
  object, ghost or proxy, may be reset.
- Throwing an object's state away is what its destructor is for, so it runs --
  between the call and its return, which is what `reset_as_lazy_calls_destructor`
  pins down. `ReflectionClass::SKIP_DESTRUCTOR` says not to. The object lives
  on afterwards, so php2go also has to *forget* that it destructed it, or the
  real destruction later would be skipped.

### What refuses to be made lazy is not "internal"

`stdClass` can be made lazy; `Exception` and `ArrayObject` cannot, and neither
can a user class extending them. Internal-ness is not the test -- stdClass is
internal too. What the engine actually looks at is `ce->create_object`: a class
with its own object-creation handler carries engine state that a lazy object
cannot stand in for, and the handler is inherited.

So it is harvested (`Class.custom_create`, proto field 33) rather than guessed
from a list of class names. The message still says "internal", and which class
it names depends on where the handler came from:

```
Cannot make instance of internal class lazy: Exception is internal
Cannot make instance of internal class lazy: E1 inherits internal class Exception
```

### What is still missing

`reset_as_lazy_readonly`: resetting a `final class C extends B` leaves B's
readonly `$a` alone, so the initializer's `__construct` gets
`Cannot modify readonly property B::$a`, while resetting a plain `B` resets it.
The rule that separates the two is not obvious from the test and was not probed.

## 2026-08-28 — a sign, a spelling, and what the offset was for

**4044 -> 4047 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.8% -> 85.9%); failed 504 -> 501,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug70089`, `bug70804` and
`bug73954`; broke nothing. Differential cases 867 -> 869.

Third round on the same ranking. The pool of two-line differences is thinning
and what is left in it is mostly destructor ordering and GC counts.

### (float)"-0" keeps its sign

`-0` reads as an *integer* -- there is no fractional part and no exponent -- so
php2go returned `float64(0)`, which is positive zero. The engine converts a
string to a float through the C library, which keeps the sign: `(float)"-0"` is
`-0.0`, while `(float)0` is `0.0`. The only thing left to tell them apart once
the digits have been read is the minus sign in the text, so that is what the
conversion looks at.

### NAN, not NaN

A backtrace argument goes through `strconv.FormatFloat`, which spells these
Go's way. `takes_int(NaN)` should be `takes_int(NAN)`, and the infinities are
`INF` and `-INF` rather than `+Inf` and `-Inf`. php2go already had this right
for `var_export` and for a string cast; the trace renderer had its own path.

### A string offset is refused by what was about to be done with it

```php
$s = "ab";
$s[0][0] = 1;   // Cannot use string offset as an array
$s[0][] = 1;    // [] operator not supported for strings
$s[0]++;        // Cannot increment/decrement string offsets
$s[0] += 1;     // Cannot use assign-op operators with string offsets
unset($s[0][0]) // Cannot unset string offsets
&$s[0]          // Cannot create references to/from string offsets
```

The fetch that fails is the same one in every case; the wording comes from the
*next* opline. php2go already read the append, the reference and the unset off
the opline's own flags; the increment is not on the fetch at all -- it is a
separate `ZEND_PRE_INC` on the result -- so it takes a look-ahead, the same
shape as `returnsCallResult`.

## 2026-08-28 — four wordings and results, from the same ranking

**4037 -> 4044 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.7% -> 85.8%); failed 511 -> 504,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `arrow_functions/006`, `bug44827`,
`bug44899`, `bug53432`, `function_arguments/variadic_argument_type_error`,
`variadic/typehint_error` and `variadic/typehint_suppressed_error`; broke
nothing. Differential cases 863 -> 867.

Same lens as the previous round -- the failures ranked by how few lines actually
differ. Four fixes, one of which was worth four tests.

### A variadic parameter is not named in the argument TypeError

```
function v(int $a, ?int ...$rest) {}   v(): Argument #2 must be of type ?int, string given
function n(int $a, ?int $b) {}         n(): Argument #2 ($b) must be of type ?int, string given
```

The position belongs to the *argument*, and past the last declared parameter
there is no parameter it corresponds to -- `$rest` would name the whole tail.
Worth four corpus tests, which is unusual for a wording fix and a reminder that
the cheap-looking ones are worth checking against the whole corpus rather than
the test that surfaced them.

### define() will not make a class constant

`define('foo::bar', 1)` and `define('::', 1)` are both
`ValueError: define(): Argument #1 ($constant_name) cannot be a class constant`.
The separator anywhere in the name is enough; nothing looks at either side.

### A refused string-offset write answers null

`$s = ""; $s[-1] = "a";` warns `Illegal string offset -1` and does not write.
php2go had the warning and the untouched string right, and still handed back
`"a"` as the value of the assignment expression. Nothing was assigned, so the
expression is null.

### empty() has nothing to read without __get

```php
class M { public function __isset($n): bool { return true; } }
empty((new M)->anything);   // true
```

__isset says the property is set; empty() then needs its *value*, and only
__get can supply one. php2go treated "__isset said true" as "not empty", which
is right only when there is a __get to ask. A class that says a property is set
and then cannot say what it holds is empty either way.

## 2026-08-28 — a constant remembers where it was written

**4033 -> 4037 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.6% -> 85.7%); failed 515 -> 511,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug46665`, `bug62763`,
`bug69676_2` and `bug69676_3`; broke nothing. Differential cases 862 -> 863.

Ranked the 515 failures by how many lines actually differ (difflib over the
expectation, with EXPECTF lines that match normalised away). Most are two-line
differences with nothing in common; these three were the tractable ones.

### `self::` in a class constant means the class that wrote it

```php
class Foo { const A = 'Foo::A'; const B = self::A . ' and ' . self::C; const C = 'Foo::C'; }
class Bar extends Foo { const A = 'Bar::A'; const C = 'Bar::C'; }
var_dump(Bar::B);   // "Foo::A and Foo::C"
```

php2go gave `Foo::A and Bar::C`, and the asymmetry is the clue: `self::A` was
folded by the compiler (A was already declared when B was compiled) and came
through as a literal, while `self::C` was left as an AST for later. php2go
evaluated that AST with the class the *walk* found the constant in -- Bar, since
Zend flattens inherited constants into every subclass's table.

The engine records the answer on the constant itself, so the harvester now takes
`zend_class_constant.ce` as `declaring_class` (proto field 15, matching what
`Property` already carries), and the initializer is evaluated with that class as
its scope. This is the same shape as the property-visibility bug two entries
ago: **a flattened table says where a thing was found, never where it was
written**, and anything that needs the latter has to ask the engine for it.

### A leading separator is not part of a class name

`new '\\Foo\\Bar\\Baz'` calls the autoloader with `Foo\Bar\Baz`. php2go
passed the name through unchanged, so an autoloader that maps names to paths
built the wrong path. The class *table* already trimmed it -- `findClass` has
done so all along -- but the autoload call did not.

The not-found message keeps the leading separator: `Class "\Foo\Bar\Baz" not
found` names what was written.

### exit() in a shutdown function ends the sequence

The remaining shutdown functions do not run, though destructors still do.

This one cannot be asked of the differential oracle at all: the engine runs
shutdown functions when the *process* ends, long after the harness has compared
the two outputs, so the engine side is always empty. Recorded in TODO with the
other shapes the oracle cannot be asked; `bug62763` is the corpus test that
covers it.

## 2026-08-28 — an object's properties are walked live

**4029 -> 4033 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.5% -> 85.6%); failed 519 -> 515,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `bug41929`, `foreach_010`,
`property_hooks/foreach_002` and `property_hooks/gh16185`; broke nothing.
Differential cases 859 -> 862.

Found by asking a different question of the corpus: which tests differ from the
engine on **exactly one line**? Only five did, and four of them were these.

### foreach over an object reaches what the body adds

An array is iterated from a snapshot -- a by-value loop sees none of what the
body does to it -- but an object's property table is walked live, by value as
much as by reference:

```php
foreach ($o as $k => $v) { if ($k === "a") { $o->b = 2; } }   // reaches b
foreach ($arr as $k => $v) { if ($k === "a") { $arr["b"] = 2; } }  // does not
```

php2go flattens an object's visible properties into an array at `FE_RESET` and
walks that. Rather than replace the flattening, the walk now *extends*: when the
snapshot runs out, `extendObjectWalk` looks for properties the object has grown
since, judged from the scope the loop started in. A hook that creates a property
in its `set` body -- `gh16185` -- is reached the same way.

### A private property belongs to the class that declared it

`propVisible` compared a private property's visibility against the class whose
table it was found in. Zend flattens inherited properties into the subclass's
table, so `class D extends C {}` lists C's private `$priv` with
`declaring_class = C`, and iterating `$this` from inside `C::doLoop()` on a `D`
found `current.Name == "D"` and hid it. The declaring class decides.

### A property name has to be one a property access can find again

The regression this round threw up, and the more interesting bug of the three.
`(object) [1, 2, 3]` built its properties with a *raw* string key
(`php.Key{Str: "0"}`), while every property access looks up
`php.StringKey("0")` -- which canonicalises to the **integer** key 0. So the
properties were there, `var_dump` showed them, and `$o->{"0"}` said
"Undefined property". `$r = &$o->$p` then created a second property alongside
the first, which the new live walk dutifully handed out on a second pass.

The cast now keys its properties the way a property access keys its lookups.
Two representations of one name, only one of which anything could find, is the
kind of thing a snapshot walk hides and a live walk exposes.

### What is still missing

`get_object_vars($o)` and `(array) $o` drop the `&` from a property that shares
a box; the engine keeps it. Noted in TODO -- it is a display question about
references surviving a conversion, not about the walk.

## 2026-08-28 — three small rules the engine words its own way

**4024 -> 4029 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.4% -> 85.5%); failed 524 -> 519,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed
`class_name_as_scalar_error_005/006/007`, `assign_ref_error_var_handling` and
`array_merge_recursive_next_key_overflow`; broke nothing. Differential cases
856 -> 859.

Picked from the root directory, whose 277 failures cluster badly -- the largest
"cluster" is 16 tests that share nothing but the shape `int(N)`. These three
were the coherent groups left in it.

### `X::class` is a *use*, everything else is an *access*

```
self::class    Cannot use "self" in the global scope
self::FOO      Cannot access "self" when no class scope is active
self::m()      Cannot access "self" when no class scope is active
new self       Cannot access "self" when no class scope is active
self::$p       Cannot access "self" when no class scope is active
static::m()    Cannot access "static" when no class scope is active
parent::m()    Cannot access "parent" when no class scope is active
```

Only `ZEND_FETCH_CLASS_NAME` -- which is what `X::class` compiles to -- gets the
first wording. Worth noting that this is only reachable at all from the global
scope: inside a function the compiler rejects `self::class` outright, which is
why the message says "global scope" rather than naming the frame.

### An append needs somewhere to go before a reference to it can be taken

`$arr[] = &$var` on an array whose next integer key is `PHP_INT_MAX + 1` is an
Error, and it comes from the `FETCH_DIM_W` that opens the write path -- before
the `ASSIGN_REF` has said anything, which is what the test is checking (the
"Only variables should be assigned by reference" notice must not appear).

### array_merge_recursive merges into the entry it already has

php2go rebuilt a duplicate string key's entry from scratch, appending both
sides. The engine merges the incoming value *into* the existing one, so the
destination keeps its keys and its next free index:

```php
array_merge_recursive(["a" => [5 => "x"]], ["a" => ["y"]]);
// engine: ["a" => [5 => "x", 6 => "y"]]      php2go was: ["a" => [0 => "x", 1 => "y"]]
array_merge_recursive(["a" => ["k" => 1]], ["a" => ["k" => 2]]);
// engine: ["a" => ["k" => [1, 2]]]           php2go was: ["a" => ["k" => 2]]
```

The recursion is what the overflow test needs: `["" => [PHP_INT_MAX => null]]`
merged with `["" => [null]]` appends into an array whose next index is taken.
The key-preserving merge was the real bug; the overflow was only how it showed.

### What is still missing

The root directory is now 272 failures with no group larger than the GC tests
(`gc_016`, `gc_017`, `gc_048`, `gc_053`, `bug70805*`), which want a cycle
collector php2go does not have and should be recorded as such rather than
chased.
