```
$t->$opaque = 1;     // Error: Object of class stdClass could not be converted to string
var_dump($t->$list); // Warning: Array to string conversion, then Undefined property: T::$Array
$t->$five = 9;       // Deprecated: Creation of dynamic property T::$5
```

`propertyName` now does this at all eleven property opcodes -- read, write,
compound, incdec, isset, unset, both by-reference fetches and the func-arg
fetch. It is a helper rather than a `.String()` because `__toString` can throw,
and each site has its own error path.

### __get answers for a declared type on the write path too

`magicReadType` already held `__get` to an unset typed property's declaration
on the read path. The write-mode fetch -- `$r = &$o->val` -- did not, so
`&__get` returning a string box stood in for `int $val` unchallenged. It now
runs the same check, and because a `&__get` hands back the box itself, the
coerced value is written *into* the box: the engine's `int(42)` where the
accessor returned a string `"42"`, source property and all.

### A by-reference return out of a temporary is not a hold being released

A frame's teardown unshares every slot, so that a reference whose only other
name was a local stops being marked. A `&__get` returning `$this->prop` broke
on this: the property's box passed through a *temporary*, and the frame ending
unshared a hold nothing had taken -- the property lost its `&`.

Two narrower rules, both wrong, came first. Exempting every temporary broke
`[&$o->i]`, where the temporary's unshare happens to cancel the array element's
share. Exempting the returned box unconditionally broke `bug75573`, where the
accessor really does bind a local (`$retval = &$this->_stdObject->$p; return
$retval;`) and the frame ending really does release it. The rule that holds is
the operand's kind: a **temporary** carried out by reference was never a
binding, a **CV** was.

### What is still missing

The remaining `type_declarations` failures are no longer a family: variance,
`iterable` display, static trait properties. `lazy_objects` (56) and the root
directory (275) are the largest remaining pools, both scattered.

## 2026-08-28 — rebinding a property leaves the box it held

**4017 -> 4018 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.3%); failed 531 -> 530,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `typed_properties_076`; broke
nothing. Differential cases 853 -> 854. A small move for three corrections that
were each wrong on their own.

Continuing the previous entry's remainder. `typed_properties_076` walks twenty
pairs of typed properties, binding each pair both ways round, and it caught two
bookkeeping errors and one ordering error.

### The share count has to fall when a property lets go

`$t->int = &$t->nint; $t->nint = &$t->nstring;` leaves `int` holding its box
alone, and the engine stops printing `&` for it. php2go dropped the *type*
source from the old box but never the share, so `int` stayed marked. `unset()`
had the same hole, fixed in the previous round; this is the rebinding half.

### Detach before attaching, not after

`ASSIGN_OBJ_REF` recorded the property's type on the new box *before* dropping
it from the old one. For `$t->nstring = &$t->nint` where `nstring` already holds
that very box, the two steps cancelled: the source was added and immediately
taken away, and the box was left answering for one property instead of two. The
detach now happens first, before the binding is even checked.

### A rebound property goes to the end of the sources

Which two properties the conflicting-coercion error names, and in what order,
follows the box's source list:

```php
$t->nint = &$t->nstring;                       // ... property $nstring ... and property $nint
$t->nint = &$t->nstring; $t->nstring = &$t->nint;  // ... property $nint ... and property $nstring
```

Rebinding a property to the box it already holds moves it to the end. Doing the
detach first gets this for free -- which is a good sign that the engine does the
same thing rather than keeping a separate order.

### What is still missing

`typed_properties_073` and `_074` want a `&__get()` that returns a reference to
stand in for an unset typed property. `typed_properties_093` wants an object
used as a property name: **php2go never calls `__toString` on a property name**,
on any path -- `$o->$name` with an object reads and writes a dynamic property
called `""`. That is a general gap rather than a typed-property one, and it
wants a helper at every property opcode, since `__toString` can throw.

## 2026-08-28 — references held by typed properties

**4009 -> 4017 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.1% -> 85.3%); failed 539 -> 531,
unsupported 160 (unchanged). Diff-set: fixed `typed_properties_068`, `_078`,
`_079`, `_097`, `_107`, `union_types/incdec_prop`, `union_types/prop_ref_assign`
and `lazy_objects/typed_properties_002`; broke nothing. Differential cases
849 -> 853.

The machinery for this (`php.RefSource`, `verifyRefWrite`, `notePropertyType`)
was already in place; what was missing were the rules around it, each settled by
a probe.

### An overflow through a referenced property is a reference step

`++$o->p` on `public int $p` at `PHP_INT_MAX` says `Cannot increment property
C::$p of type int past its maximal value` -- unless the program has bound a
reference to it, when it says `Cannot increment a reference held by property
C::$p ...`. A plain *assignment* to the same name keeps the property wording
either way; only the overflow changes.

The signal is `Ref.IsShared()`, not "the slot holds a box": php2go boxes every
typed property's slot to carry its type, so `RefHeld != nil` is true for all of
them. `shared` counts the bindings an explicit `&` made, which is the question
being asked.

### Binding a reference between two typed properties

Three outcomes, and which one applies is decided by whether the value could be
coerced, not by whether it fits:

```php
class F { public int $i = 0; public string $s = "x"; public float $f = 1.5; }
$a->i = &$a->s;   // "x": int cannot take it at all
// Cannot assign string to property F::$i of type int
$b->s = "5"; $b->i = &$b->s;   // coercible, but $s is holding the box
// Reference with value of type string held by property F::$s of type string
//   is not compatible with property F::$i of type int
$d->i = &$loose;  // an untyped box: plain wording again
// Cannot assign string to property F::$i of type int
```

The float case shows the engine really does attempt the conversion: binding
`int $i` to `float $f = 1.5` prints the precision-loss deprecation *and then*
refuses. "Fits outright" has to mean the value as it stands -- strict mode still
widens an int to a float, and that widening is a conversion like any other here.

### One box cannot hold two different values

`verifyRefWrite` chained its conversions, handing each property the answer the
one before it gave. The engine asks every property about the value that was
*written*, and refuses when two of them would make different things of it:

```php
class Both { public int|string $x; public float|string $y; }
$t->x = &$r; $t->y = &$r; $r = 42;
// Cannot assign int to reference held by property Both::$x of type string|int
//   and property Both::$y of type string|float, as this would result in an
//   inconsistent type conversion
```

### unset() detaches, it does not empty

`Object.Clear` wrote `undef` through the slot, which for a property sharing a
box emptied the box every other name could see. unset() detaches: the property
drops out of the reference's sources, the share count falls, and the slot is
rebound rather than written through (`Array.Rebind`).

### A rebound static box takes only its own type

`ZEND_ASSIGN_STATIC_PROP_REF` copied *every* source off the box it was replacing
onto the new one, so after `A::$a = &A::$it; A::$a = &$x;` the box behind `$x`
answered for `A::$it` as well. Only the property being rebound travels
(`noteStaticPropType`, the static form of `notePropertyType`). The same opcode's
plain sibling now also applies the box's sources when the program has bound a
reference to the property -- instance properties already did.

### What is still missing

`typed_properties_073`, `_074`, `_076` and `_093` are in the same area and did
not move. `_074` wants var_dump's `&` on a property sharing a box, which is the
same share-count question from a different side.

## 2026-08-28 — a by-reference foreach over hooked properties, and array_walk over an object

**4006 -> 4009 passed** of 4712 attempted (85.0% -> 85.1%); failed 542 -> 539,
unsupported 160 (unchanged), corpus wall clock ~89s. Diff-set against the
previous run: fixed `property_hooks/foreach_val_to_ref`,
`property_hooks/gh18268`, `indexing_001`; broke nothing. Differential cases
846 -> 849.

### A `&get` hook hands back a box; a plain `get` has none

Continuing the previous round's remainder. `foreach ($object as &$v)` over a
property with a hook has nothing of its own to alias -- the property's storage
is not what the loop should reach. The engine's rule, asked of it directly:

- `&get` returns the box it wants aliased, so the loop variable binds *that*
  and a write through the loop reaches whatever the hook returned.
- a by-value `get` computes a value and there is no box behind it, so the
  engine refuses with `Cannot create reference to property C::$p`, naming the
  **declaring** class. The hook is not run at all: the refusal comes first.

`iterator` grew a `byRef` flag (set from `ZEND_FE_RESET_RW`) so `iterNext` can
tell the two apart at the property's turn, which is where the deferred hook
runs.

### A private property's hook belongs to the scope that declared it

`lazyVisibleProps` walked the *object's* class, so iterating `$this` inside a
class that declares `private $p { get => 'A'; }` found a subclass's public
`$p { get => 'B'; }` instead. Same rule already fixed for plain properties
(`ownPrivateProperty`), now applied to the hook lookup: a private property of
the reading scope is a different property from a subclass's of the same name,
hooks included.

### array_walk takes an object

`array_walk()` refused anything but an array. The engine accepts an object and
walks its **raw property table** -- probed, not assumed:

```
class C { public $a = 1; protected $b = 2; private $c = 3; ... }
in a=1 / in  * b=2 / in  C c=3       <- from inside C
out a=1 / out  * b=2 / out  C c=3    <- from outside, the same three
```

There is no visibility filtering and no scope check; mangled names are handed
to the callback as they are stored, and writes through the by-reference
parameter reach the property. php2go now walks `Object.Props` directly. The
`TypeError` for a non-array, non-object still says `must be of type array` --
the engine did not widen the message when it widened the type.

### What is still missing

`property_hooks/foreach` needs two private properties of the same name to have
separate storage (the access rule is right, the storage is not) -- its last two
lines are a private `$shadowed` of the declaring class hidden by a dynamic
property of the same name. `property_hooks/foreach_002` needs the object's
property table to be walked *live*, so a property added inside the loop body is
reached; php2go snapshots the key list at `FE_RESET`.

## 2026-08-28 — the op_array is a flattened AST, measured

Compiler-track work, not interpreter work: Phase A of an exploration into
emitting Go. **No tracked file was changed**, so no corpus metric moved. Tools
and full write-ups are in `.agents-workspace/tmp/` (`PHASE-A-SUMMARY.md`,
`A1-findings.md`, `A2-A3-findings.md`, `A4-library-manifest.md`).

### Result

Measured over `Zend/tests`: 4966 `.phpt`, of which 4020 harvest, 716 do not
compile, 229 carry a skip condition, 1 has no `--FILE--`. That yields 10,738
op_arrays and 130,187 oplines.

| question | answer |
| --- | --- |
| temporaries read exactly once | **90.6%** |
| op_arrays free of contagious constructs | **93.8%** |
| definitions with a known handle kind | **27.3%** |
| definitions with an exact scalar type | **22.2%** |
| global functions implemented / provided | **305 / 690** |

### A temporary is an AST edge, not a value

Of 29,267 `IS_TMP_VAR`/`IS_VAR` definitions, **90.6% are read exactly once**;
3.3% twice, 0.6% three or more, 5.6% never (largely comparisons fused into the
following branch). A value stream spreads out. This is a tree serialised into a
reused slot space, which is what an un-flattening pass would have to recover.

Counting this needs the per-opcode jump flags from `zend_get_opcode_flags`:
twenty opcodes carry a branch target in an operand, and `ZEND_FE_FETCH_R`/`_RW`
carry theirs in `extended_value`. A target and a slot are both small integers,
so guessing invents edges out of branches.

"Producers whose consumer-opcode set has cardinality 1" -- the obvious
formulation -- is **the wrong metric**. Aggregated over a corpus it is diluted
to nothing: `ZEND_DO_FCALL` has 4,120 definitions and 54 distinct consumers,
because a call result can legitimately feed anything. It reports 2.6% of
definitions. Where it does bite it picks out exactly the multi-opline node
groups: `ZEND_ROPE_INIT` (1 consumer), `ROPE_ADD` (2), `FE_RESET_R` (2),
`FAST_CALL` (2), `FETCH_LIST_R` (4) -- interpolation, `foreach`, `try/finally`,
`list()`.

### Most type information is a property of the opcode, not of dataflow

A deliberately weak pass -- forward walk, no phi, no call graph -- types 49.5% of
temporaries. **81% of what it typed came from the opcode alone**: a comparison
yields a bool, `new` yields an object, `.` yields a string. Only 19% came from
constants, declared return types, casts and copies combined.

Known *handle kind* (27.3%) beats exact *scalar type* (22.2%), and `object`
alone is 21.0% of all definitions. Both are lower bounds: arithmetic results,
user function returns, property types and class-constant types are all left
unread.

### The contagious constructs are rarer than they feel

93.8% of op_arrays contain none of `$$x`, `extract`/`compact`/
`get_defined_vars`, `func_get_args`, `eval`/`include`, or a by-reference local.
The largest blocker is by-reference locals at 2.4%; `eval`/`include` is 1.8%.
Caveat both ways: `Zend/tests` over-represents corner cases, and a dynamically
named `$f = 'extract'; $f()` is not detected.

### Three defects found while measuring

- **`cmd/php2eval` does not normalise the source filename between its arms.**
  The engine side evaluates a string named `php2go-eval`; the interpreter side
  writes a temp file. Any case whose output names a file -- a stack trace, an
  uncaught exception, `__FILE__` -- diverges by construction. This made a
  class-instantiation sweep report 28 spurious mismatches.
- **`AppendIterator` is instantiable but not modelled.** It passes the gate at
  `interp.go:3960` only because it is `instanceof IteratorIterator`; a
  well-formed use throws `TypeError: ... must be of type Traversable, null
  given` where the engine prints `12`. Twelve other `IteratorIterator`
  subclasses are admitted the same way. A gap presenting itself as a PHP error.
- **`new ReflectionClass()` raises the wrong error** -- `ReflectionException:
  Class "" does not exist` where the engine raises `ArgumentCountError`.

### The library surface, and why the class half is not a list

`runtime/interp` answers **305** distinct global function names of the **690**
this build provides; every one of the 305 is a real engine function. Reading
only dispatcher switches and map literals finds 155 -- half. Registration has
five shapes, and the one that is easiest to miss is `jsonBuiltin`'s
`if name != "json_encode"`.

**77 of 154 engine classes pass the instantiation gate**, but the gate is a
predicate over the harvested hierarchy, not a name list: four of its terms admit
any subclass of a seed. It has to be recomputed per program, since a user class
extending `ArrayObject` is admitted too.

### Two traps in the measurement tools, recorded because they look like findings

- **`engine.Reset()` between tests is mandatory** when one engine serves the
  corpus (`cmd/php2phpt/main.go:143`). Without it the second test to declare a
  given class name fails to compile: 1258 "does not compile" instead of 716, a
  third of the corpus in a bucket reading as "these tests are unusual".
- **Every `INIT_*` opcode pushes a pending call, and so does `ZEND_NEW`** -- a
  constructor is invoked through the same three-phase protocol. Pushing only for
  `ZEND_INIT_FCALL` left the stack misaligned and handed one call's declared
  return type to another call's result. The symptom was `null` at 14.4% of
  definitions; 0.1% once fixed.

### Not done

The two dynamic counters -- how often a `Value.Copy` source is dead afterwards,
and what fraction of objects ever escape -- need instrumentation inside
`runtime/php` and `runtime/interp`, where the interpreter track is working.
Deferred rather than taken. The escape rate is the number that says whether
compiled code could carry refcounts only on what escapes, and get destructor
timing right for the rest.

## 2026-08-28 — a get hook runs at its turn

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 4006 | 4006 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 85.0% | 85.0% |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 542 | 542 |
| differential cases | 845 | 846 |

**No test moved.** The behaviour is right where it was wrong, and the tests that
cover it need one more piece before they pass. Recorded as such rather than
dressed up.

### The ordering was wrong and is now right

`foreach ($object as $name => $value)` over a class with property hooks: php2go
flattened the whole property table first, running **every** get hook, and only
then ran the loop body. The engine runs each hook at the turn its property comes
up, so a hook that prints interleaves with the body:

```
get first
body first = hooked-1
get second
body second = hooked-2
```

php2go printed both `get` lines before either `body` line. The walk now carries
the hooks it has not run yet and reaches each at its own step. A differential
case pins it.

### What is still missing

`property_hooks/foreach` and its three siblings need one more thing: a `&get`
hook hands back the box it wants aliased, and a by-reference loop binds *that*.
php2go's `hookedRead` produces a value, so writing through the loop variable
reaches a copy and the backing property keeps its old contents. Everything up to
that line in the test now matches.

That is the honest state: two of the three visible differences in these tests are
fixed, the third is not, and nothing passes yet.

## 2026-08-28 — the harness was mangling its own expectations

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 4004 | 4006 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 85.0% | 85.0% |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 544 | 542 |
| differential cases | 845 | 845 |

**This is a measurement fix, not an interpreter fix.** Two tests were passing
all along and being reported as failures. No behaviour changed.

### `string(oneByte)` is not one byte

The open question from the previous entry is answered. `expectFToRegexp` builds
the pattern a byte at a time:

```go
out.WriteString(regexp.QuoteMeta(string(format[i])))
```

`format[i]` is a `byte`; `string(aByte)` converts it as a **rune**, so `0xF0`
becomes U+00F0 and is written as two bytes. Every byte of a multi-byte character
turns into something else, and a pattern written from text containing one no
longer matches that text.

`in-de-crement/incdec_strings` has an elephant in it.

### Why it took so long to see

Every diagnostic I reached for agreed the outputs were identical: the printed
diff, a line-by-line comparison, even a hand-rolled EXPECTF translation -- which
reproduced the same bug, because I wrote it the same way. The thing that broke
the tie was calling the harness's **own** `Matches` on the printed output from a
throwaway program: `matches=false` against text that visibly matched. From there
the byte dump showed the two lines were byte-identical, which left only the
pattern.

The lesson worth keeping: when a comparison disagrees with every reimplementation
of it, suspect the comparison, and call the real one rather than writing a third.

A regression test in `internal/phpt` now pins it: an expectation containing an
emoji must match itself, and must not match a *different* emoji.

## 2026-08-28 — a box handed out by name belongs to the name

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 4003 | 4004 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 85.0% | 85.0% |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 545 | 544 |
| differential cases | 844 | 845 |

Diff-set: one fixed, nothing broken.

### `global $$name` is not `global $name`

Written out, `global $x` compiles to `ZEND_BIND_GLOBAL` and php2go handled it.
With a *computed* name -- `global $$which`, `global ${sf("a")}` -- the compiler
emits something else entirely: two fetches by name, one flagged global, and an
`ASSIGN_REF` between them.

php2go executed all three faithfully and still bound nothing, because the
rebinding stopped at the temporary. A write fetch by name hands out the box that
belongs to *that name*; rebinding the temporary the box arrived in has to reach
the name, exactly as rebinding an array element's temporary has to reach the
array. php2go already had that machinery -- `writeTarget` -- for elements and
properties, and the by-name fetch had never registered one.

`global ${"a"}` works either way, because the compiler folds a constant name back
to `BIND_GLOBAL`. That is what made the difference visible only through the
variable-variable and side-effecting forms.

### Left open

`in-de-crement/incdec_strings` and its two siblings fail with no line that
differs: applying the harness's own EXPECTF translation to the printed
expectation and the printed output matches, and the lengths agree. Something in
the comparison or in a byte the diff does not show is at fault. Recorded rather
than guessed at.

## 2026-08-28 — the deprecated interface still has to work

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 4000 | 4003 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.9% | **85.0%** |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 548 | 545 |
| differential cases | 843 | 844 |

Diff-set: three fixed, nothing broken.

### `Serializable` writes its own payload

php2go serialized a `Serializable` object with the ordinary `O:` form, ignoring
its `serialize()` entirely, and refused to read a `C:` at all. The form is
`C:<len>:"<Class>":<len(payload)>:{<payload>}`, the payload is whatever the
method returned, and reading one builds the object **without its constructor**
and hands it the bytes through `unserialize()`.

Two details from the probe rather than from the shape of the code:

- `__serialize` **wins** when a class has both, and the result is written with
  `O:`. The `C:` branch therefore has to sit after it.
- A `serialize()` that answers null writes `N;` -- a plain null, not an empty
  payload.

### An enum cannot implement it at all

`Enum Foo cannot implement the Serializable interface` is a fatal, and it reaches
an enum that implements it *indirectly* through an interface that extends it.
php2go printed the deprecation the interface earns and then carried on. The
refusal belongs after that deprecation, which is the order the test pins down.

## 2026-08-28 — `[&$x]` creates $x, and a subclass can reach an engine constructor

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3994 | **4000** |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.8% | **84.9%** |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 554 | 548 |
| differential cases | 842 | 843 |

Diff-set: six fixed, nothing broken. Four of the six were not aimed at.

### Binding does not read

`[&$x]` stores the variable's *slot*, so an `$x` that does not exist yet is
created -- silently, the way `$y = &$x` creates one. php2go read the operand
first and reported *Undefined variable*, which the engine never does. Four of
this round's six fixes came from that one line.

### A subclass can reach an engine constructor

`class foo extends ArrayObject { function __construct($a) { parent::__construct($a); } }`
-- php2go refused with *Cannot call constructor*, because an engine class has no
harvested body to resolve. Two halves were needed: the static-call path falls
through to the Go implementation the way it already did for `parent::rewind()`,
and `ArrayObject::__construct` now *fills the storage*, which is what it is for.

A subclass that declares its own constructor is instantiated without a store --
the engine class's constructor is what makes one -- so the store is built when
`parent::__construct` reaches it rather than at instantiation.

### A shape the differential cannot be asked

That last case **segfaults the engine** inside the differential harness, which
evaluates hundreds of snippets into one process with a reset between each. From
a file it is fine: `indirect_method_call_005` covers it and passes. Added to the
list of things the oracle cannot be asked, alongside fatal errors, closure names
and autoloader registration.

## 2026-08-28 — an empty method name is a name

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3992 | 3994 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.7% | **84.8%** |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 556 | 554 |
| differential cases | 841 | 842 |

Diff-set: two fixed, nothing broken.

### The empty string as a sentinel

`$class::$method()` where `$method` is `""` reaches `__callStatic` with an empty
name -- which is legal. php2go used `forwardTo != ""` as the test for "this call
forwards to an accessor", so the empty name looked like "not forwarding": the
arguments went through positionally instead of being packed into the array the
accessor expects, and the call failed with *Too few arguments to
a::__callStatic(), 1 passed*.

A `pendingCall` now says whether it is forwarding rather than inferring it from
a name that may be empty. Four sites set it.

### And a method name stops at the first NUL

The rest of the same test uses `$method = "\0"` and expects the accessor to
receive `""`. Asked directly, the engine truncates at the first NUL in every
shape:

| named | received |
| --- | --- |
| `"\0"` | `""` |
| `"\0after"` | `""` |
| `"before\0after"` | `"before"` |

Both the static and the instance form, and `__call` sees the truncated name --
which is the only way to observe it.

## 2026-08-28 — two private properties, one name

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3991 | 3992 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.7% | 84.7% |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 557 | 556 |
| differential cases | 840 | 841 |

Diff-set: one fixed, nothing broken.

### The scope decides which property a name means

`class A { private $prop; }` and `class B extends A { private $prop; }` declare
**two different properties**. Inside `A`, `$this->prop` is A's -- even on an
instance of B, and even though B's declaration is the one a flat lookup by name
finds first. php2go looked the name up in the object's flattened table, found
B's, and refused the access from A as private-to-B.

The rule is small: if the reading scope declares a private property of that name
itself, that declaration is the one the name means.

### What is fixed and what is not

The **access** rule is now right, and `typed_properties_090` -- which takes a
reference to the shadowed property, unsets it and writes through the reference
-- passes.

The **storage** is not. php2go keeps one slot per property *name* on an object,
so A's and B's `$prop` share it: give them different values and both classes see
the last write, where the engine keeps two. A faithful fix means mangling the
key by declaring class, as the engine does. Recorded in the TODO with a repro
rather than papered over -- and the differential case added here pins down only
the access rule, which is what actually changed.

## 2026-08-28 — a closure's static table is not only its captures

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3988 | 3991 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.6% | **84.7%** |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 560 | 557 |
| differential cases | 839 | 840 |

Diff-set: three fixed, nothing broken.

### Three things wrong in one rendering

`var_dump` of a closure shows a `static` entry. php2go built it from the `use`
captures alone, and got all three of the following wrong:

- A `static $x` **declared inside** the closure belongs there too, and shows as
  `NULL` until the closure has actually run. php2go omitted it entirely.
- A by-reference capture keeps its `&` marker. php2go dereferenced on the way
  into the display array and lost it.
- After the closure runs, the static's value is the one in the op_array's table,
  which php2go was not consulting from the display path at all.

### And a static whose initializer threw is not initialized

`static $var = LATER;` where `LATER` does not exist yet: the first call throws.
php2go's `syncStatics` records every registered static on the way out -- which it
should, since that covers a suspension and a throw alike -- and so recorded the
*empty* slot. The static then counted as initialized and every later call
skipped the initializer, leaving it null forever even after the constant was
defined.

An empty slot is the one shape that cannot mean "initialized to something": the
initializer is the only thing that fills it, so if it is still empty the
initializer did not finish. Skipping those is enough, and
`static_variables_throwing_initializer` was waiting for exactly that.

## 2026-08-28 — `static $x` displaces what the name held

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3986 | 3988 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.6% | 84.6% |
| unsupported | 160 | 160 |
| failed | 562 | 560 |
| differential cases | 838 | 839 |

Diff-set: two fixed, nothing broken.

### A release point the opcode loop was missing

`$held = new Noisy(); static $held;` -- the second statement rebinds the name to
the static's box, so the object the local held loses its last holder *there*. Its
destructor runs at that point, inside whatever `try` is open, and a throw from it
is catchable.

php2go rebound the slot and left the object for the collector, which runs it at
shutdown where nothing can catch it: the test saw an uncaught fatal after the
`try` had already printed its "after".

php2go has the machinery -- `releaseCheck` at a release point, used by the temp
paths -- and `ZEND_BIND_STATIC` simply was not one of them. Two tests, and both
are about the *timing* rather than the destructor itself.

This is the destruction-timing family the TODO has measured at ~47 tests. It is
not one mechanism: each release point the loop is missing is its own small fix,
and this round found one by following a two-test cluster rather than by
attacking the family head-on.

## 2026-08-28 — a trait cannot know which class it will join

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3982 | 3986 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.5% | **84.6%** |
| unsupported | 162 | 160 |
| failed | 564 | 562 |
| differential cases | 837 | 838 |

Diff-set: two fixed and two out of `unsupported`, nothing broken.

### Unfolded because it cannot be folded

`#[Attr(self::class)]` on a method of a *class* is folded by the compiler and
arrives as a literal. On a method of a **trait** it cannot be: the answer belongs
to whichever class composes the trait, so it arrives as an AST node and is
resolved when the attribute is read.

php2go handled neither of the two shapes that reach it:

- `ZEND_AST_CONSTANT_CLASS` -- what `__CLASS__` compiles to -- was not in the
  harvester's node list at all, so it became `unsupported` and the argument came
  out null.
- `ZEND_AST_CLASS_NAME` for `self::class` arrives with **no children**: the
  keyword is in the node's attribute, in the same `ZEND_FETCH_CLASS_*` encoding
  the opcodes use. php2go's evaluator only knew the form with a child and
  reported the class name as unresolvable.

The giveaway was that `self::FOO` in the same attribute worked while
`self::class` did not -- so the scope was right and only the node shape was
wrong.

### The engine says "use" here and "access" there

`self::class` in a constant expression with no class scope is *Cannot **use**
"self" when no class scope is active*; the opcode path's is *Cannot **access**
...*. Both are the engine's own wording, and the first attempt used the one
php2go already had.

## 2026-08-28 — three kinds of quiet

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3980 | 3982 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.5% | 84.5% |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 566 | 564 |
| differential cases | 836 | 837 |

Diff-set: two fixed, nothing broken.

### `isset()` and `??` are not equally quiet

php2go had one `quiet` flag on `stringOffset` standing for "asked without
raising", and used it for both `isset($s[$i])` and `$s[$i] ?? x`. Probed, they
differ:

| written | reports |
| --- | --- |
| `$s[3.14]` read, or write | *String offset cast occurred* |
| `isset($s[3.14])`, `empty($s[3.14])` | *Implicit conversion from float ... loses precision* |
| `$s[3.14] ?? null` | **nothing** |

So the flag had to split in two: whether it raises, and whether it reports.
`dimensionRead` is only reached by the coalescing form, so it never reports.

### And the number is spelled twice over

The precision-loss message spells the float the way **var_dump** does, at full
precision -- `3.141592653589793`, not the `3.1415926535898` an `echo` gives.
php2go's *array*-key path already knew this, with a comment explaining it; the
string-offset path, written separately, used the ordinary string conversion.

### A resource is not an offset a string has

`empty($str[$handle])` is `true`: the offset is unusable, not offset 3. php2go
cast the handle to its id and found a character there. Only the quiet forms are
changed -- a read and a write still cast it, which is what the "String offset
cast occurred" warning has always been about.

## 2026-08-28 — static syntax still needs an instance

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3977 | 3980 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.4% | **84.5%** |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 569 | 566 |
| differential cases | 835 | 836 |

Diff-set: three fixed, nothing broken. Two of the three were not aimed at.

### The last place the rule was missing

Three rounds ago a *callable* naming an instance method statically learned to
refuse. The **opcode** path -- `C::m()` written out -- had never learned it, and
ran the body with no `$this` at all. Since a method that does not touch `$this`
then succeeds, the failure was silent: `bug48533` printed `int(2)` where the
engine raises.

php2go already computed exactly the right condition: it works out whether the
`$this` in scope is compatible and drops it when not. All that was missing was
refusing when the answer is "none" and the method is not static.

The full shape, probed:

| written | with $this in scope | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `self::m()`, `C::m()`, `$obj::m()` inside a method of C | yes | runs, `$this` kept |
| `parent::m()` inside a method | yes | runs |
| the same from a **static** method of C | no | Error |
| the same from another class, or at top level | no | Error |
| `$obj::privateOrProtected()` | -- | **__callStatic**, not an Error |

That last row is why the refusal has to sit *after* the accessibility check: an
inaccessible method is answered by the forwarder and never reaches it.

## 2026-08-28 — which constants are deprecated is the build's answer

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3976 | 3977 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.4% | 84.4% |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 570 | 569 |
| differential cases | 834 | 835 |

Diff-set: one fixed, nothing broken. This is the item the previous entry
recorded rather than doing.

### Harvested, not named

`E_STRICT` is deprecated in 8.4, and the tempting fix is to write that name into
the runtime. The manifest already carries every engine constant the build
registers, so it carries this too: `zend_constant` has `ZEND_ACC_DEPRECATED` in
its flags, and one shim reads it. Nothing here decides which constants are
deprecated -- if a future build deprecates another, php2go reports it without
being told.

### Used, not merely named

Probed: `defined("E_STRICT")` says **nothing**, while `constant("E_STRICT")` and
the bare `E_STRICT` both report. php2go already had a `silentDeprecation` counter
for exactly this, wrapped around `defined()` in the builtin table -- but
`defined()` has its **own opcode**, `ZEND_DEFINED`, which the compiler emits
instead, and that path had no guard. The builtin-table version was dead code for
this shape.

## 2026-08-28 — the dynamic spelling of `::class`

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3975 | 3976 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.4% | 84.4% |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 571 | 570 |
| differential cases | 833 | 834 |

Diff-set: one fixed, nothing broken.

### Written out it is folded; named at run time it is not

`Foo::class` never reaches the interpreter -- the compiler folds it -- so
php2go had no answer for `Foo::{$name}` where `$name` happens to be `"class"`,
and reported an undefined constant. It is the class's own name, in the
*declared* spelling: `Bar::{$n}` is `"Bar"`, and `$object::{$n}` is the object's
class.

Probed: the match is **exact**. `Foo::{'CLASS'}` is `Undefined constant
Foo::CLASS`, even though the written keyword is case-insensitive. That is the
kind of asymmetry worth a case rather than an assumption.

### Recorded, not done

`e_strict-deprecated` wants `Deprecated: Constant E_STRICT is deprecated`. The
manifest carries engine constants as name and value only, with no deprecation
flag -- `ZEND_ACC_DEPRECATED` on the `zend_constant` is there to harvest, and
that is the honest way to do it rather than naming E_STRICT in the runtime.

## 2026-08-28 — a private property of an ancestor is not the same property

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3973 | 3975 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.3% | **84.4%** |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 573 | 571 |
| differential cases | 832 | 833 |

Diff-set: two fixed, nothing broken.

### The declared type travels with visibility

`class a extends Exception { public function __construct() { $this->string = null; } }`
-- `Exception::$string` is `private string`, so from the subclass's body that
name is **not** the declared property at all: the write makes one alongside it,
and the ancestor's type does not apply. php2go's `verifyPropertyWrite` read the
object's flattened declaration table, which keeps inherited private entries, and
refused with `Cannot assign null to property Exception::$string of type string`.

`propertyAccess` already had this rule for *access* -- it answers `accessHidden`
for an ancestor's private property, with a comment saying why. The type check was
a second path that had never learned it.

### A constructor that writes its own line keeps it

`ZEND_THROW` fills in the throw site "only when it is not already set", and
php2go read "not set" as *absent or zero*. bug64821 writes `$this->line = 0`
deliberately and expects `Uncaught a in %s:0`. Zero is a value like any other;
only an object whose position was never recorded gets the throw site.

## 2026-08-28 — what a short-circuit yields depends on what it was part of

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3969 | 3973 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.2% | **84.3%** |
| unsupported | 161 | 162 |
| failed | 578 | 573 |
| differential cases | 830 | 832 |

Diff-set: five fixed. One test moved from `failed` to `unsupported` -- a
silently-wrong attribute instantiation became an honest gap, which is the
direction that counts.

### `?->` yields three different things

php2go's `ZEND_JMP_NULL` always stored null and skipped the chain. The engine
stores what the surrounding construct needs:

| written | short-circuit yields | reports the subject? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `isset($x?->y)` | `false` | no |
| `empty($x?->y)` | `true` | no |
| `$x?->y` | `null` | **yes** |
| `$x?->y ?? $d` | `null` | no |

The flavour is in the opcode's `extended_value`, but it can be read off the
oplines instead, which is what php2go does: the opcode being jumped over says
which construct this is -- `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_PROP_OBJ`, a plain `FETCH_OBJ_R`,
or the quiet `FETCH_OBJ_IS` behind `??`. No numbering assumed.

The correction the corpus forced: it is the **last** opcode being jumped over,
not the next one. `isset($x?->y->z)` jumps over two links, and only the final
one says what the chain was for; reading the first gave "expression" and
answered null where a bool was wanted.

### An engine class has a constructor even without a body

`#[Attribute]` is written on `Attribute` itself, so `newInstance()` on it
constructs an `Attribute`. php2go looked for a harvested `__construct`, found
none -- an engine class has no op_array -- and handed back the object
unconstructed, leaving its typed `$flags` with no value at all. It now falls
through to the same builtin constructor `new Attribute(...)` uses.

Where that constructor is one this runtime does not model, the object would be
silently wrong rather than merely empty, so an attribute with arguments reports
the gap instead. That is the test that moved into `unsupported`.

## 2026-08-28 — a Closure is one object, and only itself

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3966 | 3969 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.2% | 84.2% |
| unsupported | 161 | 161 |
| failed | 581 | 578 |
| differential cases | 829 | 830 |

Diff-set: three fixed, nothing broken.

### Cloning a Closure

`copyState` copied the property table and, for a `SensitiveParameterValue`, the
value behind it -- but nothing else an engine class keeps outside the table. A
cloned Closure therefore came out with no body at all: `Object of type Closure
is not callable`.

The copy is shallow, and that is right: a `use (&$x)` capture stays **shared**,
so both copies see a later write. What must differ is identity.

### Only itself

Which led to the second half. Two distinct Closures are **never** `==`, however
alike -- not even a clone and what it was cloned from. php2go compared them the
way it compares any object, by class and properties, and a Closure's property
table is empty, so every pair was equal.

Probed alongside: `Generator`, `ArrayObject` and `WeakMap` all compare by
properties in the ordinary way. Closure is the only one with its own rule.

### A first-class callable from a Closure *is* that Closure

`$c(...)` and `$c->__invoke(...)` hand back the very object, which `===` can
see; `Closure::fromCallable($c)` already did. A first-class callable made from a
*method* makes a new Closure each time, so `$o->m(...) === $o->m(...)` is false
-- the identity rule is about the source already being a Closure, not about
first-class callables in general.

## 2026-08-28 — a temporary is not a name, and a reset is not a fetch

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3965 | 3966 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 84.1% | **84.2%** |
| unsupported | 161 | 161 |
| failed | 582 | 581 |
| differential cases | 827 | 829 |

Diff-set: one fixed, nothing broken. A round of two mechanisms, one of which
moves no test at all -- and is still worth having.

### The aliasing bug from the last entry: a result slot is not a name

`storeResult` went through `f.store`, which **writes through** a reference the
slot already holds. That is right for a CV -- `$a = 1` where `$a` was bound with
`=&` has to reach the shared box -- and wrong for a VAR or TMP, which are
temporaries the engine frees before reusing.

The consequence was the repro recorded last round: a loop whose single call site
first ran a by-reference function returning `$shared`, then one returning a
literal, wrote the literal *into* `$shared`. Two different oplines never showed
it, which is why the static spelling was correct and only the dynamic one was
not.

**No corpus test moved.** It is in the differential now, and the TODO entry is
closed.

### The foreach protocol has two halves

`bug49269` has an Iterator whose `key(): mixed` returns nothing -- a TypeError if
it is ever called -- iterated by `foreach (... as $item)` with no key variable.
The engine never calls `key()`, so it never raises.

php2go called it twice over: once because the *reset* pulled a whole element to
find out whether the iterator was empty, and once because the fetch always asked
for a key. The engine's reset is `rewind()` then `valid()` and nothing else;
`current()` and `key()` belong to the fetch, and `key()` only when the loop has
somewhere to put one.

Two corrections the diff-set forced, both instructive:

- The reset can only be that cheap for a **user Iterator**. An aggregate that
  produced a generator or an array cannot say whether it is empty without being
  pulled, so that path still pulls -- and now hands the element to the first
  fetch instead of dropping it.
- A **by-reference** loop needs the key even when the program does not: php2go
  finds the slot to bind *by* the key. Skipping it bound a property named `""`.

## 2026-08-28 — a value has no slot to lend

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3955 | 3965 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.9% | **84.1%** |
| unsupported | 161 | 161 |
| failed | 592 | 582 |
| differential cases | 825 | 827 |

Diff-set: ten fixed, nothing broken -- after seven regressions on the way, all
from one over-broad first cut.

### Passing a value where a slot is wanted

`function f(&$x)` called as `f(1)`, `f($a + 1)` or through a variable: php2go
ran the body against a copy. The engine refuses at the *send*, before the body
runs -- `f(): Argument #1 ($x) could not be passed by reference` -- and the
refusal was missing entirely. Ten tests, most of them not on the list this round
started from.

The first cut refused whenever the by-reference table said so, and broke seven
tests, every one of them about `extract()`. That is the lesson: an **engine**
function's by-reference parameter may be *prefer*-reference -- `extract()`'s is
-- which takes a temporary happily, and the flat by-reference table php2go
harvests cannot tell the two apart. So the refusal applies only where a body the
program wrote is in hand, and engine functions keep their old behaviour until
the harvest carries the send mode.

### Returning a value by reference

The companion notice, *Only variable references should be returned by
reference*, was firing for a literal and a temporary but not for a **by-value
call's result**, which the engine also notices.

Getting the condition right took three attempts, and the failures are the
interesting part. "The slot holds no reference" is wrong -- a fetched array
element or property may have been flattened by an intervening return-type check,
and `bug70117` is exactly that shape. "Ask `slotRef`" is wrong the other way --
it boxes anything. What works is to ask **whether the operand was written by the
call immediately before**: only then does an unboxed slot mean the callee
returned by value.

### Left recorded, not fixed

A by-reference return still aliases where it should copy, but only through a
*dynamic* call:

```php
function &viaCall() { return viaVariable(); }   // returns $shared by reference
function &viaLiteral() { return 42; }
foreach (["viaCall", "viaLiteral"] as $f) { $r = $f(); }
var_dump($shared);   // engine: 1   php2go: 42
```

The static spelling of the same thing is correct, so it is the dynamic call
path reusing a slot. It is in the TODO with this repro; the differential case
added this round orders around it deliberately rather than hiding it.

## 2026-08-28 — keys that are not keys, and a generator that gets the last word

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3946 | 3955 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.7% | **83.9%** |
| unsupported | 162 | 161 |
| failed | 600 | 592 |
| differential cases | 822 | 825 |

Diff-set: eight fixed, nothing broken. Three of the eight were not aimed at --
they fell out of the key-type rule.

### Unpacking takes keys as they are

Four rounds ago `iterNext` stopped converting a foreach key to a `php.Key`, and
the array-building callers took over the conversion. That was right for
`iterator_to_array`, and **wrong** for unpacking: `[...$generator]` and
`f(...$generator)` do not convert at all. Only an int or a string is a key
there, and anything else is

    Keys must be of type int|string during array unpacking
    Keys must be of type int|string during argument unpacking

php2go had been landing a null key on `""` and a float on its truncated int,
with the truncation's own deprecation for company.

### An abandoned generator runs its finally, and it wins

`gh11028_3` broke on the way in, and the reason is worth the entry. Refusing the
key abandons the generator mid-`yield`, which runs its `finally` -- and a
`finally` that throws **replaces the error that abandoned it**. The engine
reports the exception from the finally block, not the key error.

php2go had `closeGenerator` for this, but it writes a fatal directly, on the
reasoning that "the program that abandoned the generator is not on the stack any
more". Here it *is*: the unpack is still running. Splitting out
`closeGeneratorFor`, which hands the error back instead, let the caller carry it.

### Two more from the same list

A **class reference** must be a string or an object. `$undefined::method()` is
`Class name must be a valid object or a string`, refused before the name is
looked up and before the method-name operand is read at all -- php2go converted
to `""` and reported a class named "" not found, having warned about both
variables on the way.

A **constant** array literal has the same next-key limit a runtime one has:
`[PHP_INT_MAX => 42, "appended"]` as a parameter default is refused. The unpack
form of this was fixed four rounds ago; the plain appended element was not.

## 2026-08-28 — an accessor that cannot be entered is not an accessor

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3941 | 3946 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.6% | 83.7% |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 605 | 600 |
| differential cases | 819 | 822 |

Diff-set: five fixed, nothing broken. One of the five --
`property_access_errors_for_guarded_properties` -- is literally named after the
mechanism and was not aimed at.

### The guard changes the answer, not just the call

php2go asked `hasMagic(object, __set)` to decide whether a refused write should
go to the accessor. That is the wrong question. `__set` answers for a property
the caller may not reach **only while it can be entered**; inside `__set`
already, `$this->$name = $value` reaches the *declared* property and the refusal
stands.

php2go was instead growing a **dynamic property beside the one it had just
refused** -- so `bug38461` printed a deprecation and carried on where the engine
raises `Cannot access private property ExtOperation::$x`. The fix is one word in
three places: `magicAvailable`, which already accounts for the in-flight guard,
instead of `hasMagic`. The read path had the same bug with `__get`.

Worth keeping: a **protected** property declared by the ancestor is reachable
from that ancestor's `__set` body, so the same write there succeeds. Only the
private one is refused, and the probe had to cover both to see that the rule is
ordinary visibility rather than "inside an accessor nothing is writable".

### A refused static property names the reference, not the declaration

`self::$x` inside B where A declared it private: the engine says **`B::$x`**.
`parent::$x` and an explicit `A::$x` say `A::$x`. So the class named is the one
the *reference* resolves to, which php2go already had in hand as `className` and
was throwing away in favour of the declaring class.

### A default value can raise before its body runs

`function test($y = new Foo > '')` where `Foo::__toString()` returns nothing:
the comparison renders the object, and `__toString`'s implicit `string` return
type is enforced there. php2go's runtime comparison already did this; the
constant-expression evaluator compared without rendering, so the default was
computed silently and the failure surfaced later as an unrelated arity error
from the body.

## 2026-08-28 — call_user_func lends what a direct call refuses

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3935 | 3941 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.5% | 83.6% |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 611 | 605 |
| differential cases | 817 | 819 |

Diff-set: six fixed, nothing broken -- after three regressions on the way that
the diff-set named immediately and that turned out to be the interesting part.

### An instance method reached through a class name

`"C::m"` and `["C","m"]` where `m` is not static: php2go called it with no
`$this` and it quietly worked. The engine refuses -- *Non-static method C::m()
cannot be called statically*. Since the callable still **resolves**, the refusal
is carried on the pending call and raised where the call would have happened,
rather than becoming "not callable".

Landing that broke three tests, and each one taught a distinction the first
implementation had flattened. The final rule is four-way, and every branch was
probed:

| how it is reached | is_callable | the call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `["C","m"]` from outside any class | **false** | Error |
| `["C","m"]` from inside a method of C | **true** | **Error** |
| `["C","parent::m"]`, `"parent::m"`, `"self::m"` | true | **runs, with $this** |
| `call_user_func(["C","m"])` from a method | true | **runs, with $this** |

Two things worth keeping. First, `is_callable` and the call **disagree** on the
second row: inside the class the callable is callable and calling it still
fails. Second, `call_user_func` genuinely lends its caller's instance where a
direct `$c()` will not -- probed side by side in the same method, which is the
only way to see it, since the compiler folds `call_user_func` into a direct call
and marks it with `ZEND_INIT_USER_CALL`. That marker is where the lending
belongs; the argument-carrying `SEND_USER` is too late, because a zero-argument
call never emits one.

### Two small ones

`UnhandledMatchError` names its subject the way the language writes a *literal*:
`true`, not the `1` a string cast gives; `1.0` keeps its point; an array is
named by type the way an object is.

Rendering a `TypeError` or `ArgumentCountError` -- `(string) $e`, or the
uncaught report -- completes a message ending in `, called in FILE on line N`
with ` and defined`, so it reads *"... called in A on line 3 and defined in
B:7"*. `getMessage()` never shows it. The rule is exact-class, not instanceof: a
subclass of TypeError does not get it.

## 2026-08-28 — two stacks that were not stacks, and a diagnostic nobody forwarded

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3927 | 3935 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.3% | **83.5%** |
| unsupported | 162 | 162 |
| failed | 619 | 611 |
| differential cases | 816 | 817 |

Diff-set: eight fixed, nothing broken. Two of the eight were not aimed at.

### `set_error_handler(null)` pushes

php2go treated null as "remove the handler" and cleared the whole stack, with a
comment saying so. The engine pushes it: it installs *no handler, for now*, and
`restore_error_handler()` brings back whatever was underneath. A six-step probe
settles it -- install A, install B, install null, restore twice, and the engine
is back on A, which clearing could never reach.

`set_exception_handler` was worse: not a stack at all, one slot, and
`restore_exception_handler()` cleared it. Same shape, same fix.

### A compile-time diagnostic from eval belongs to the running program

`bug65322` and `errmsg_045` both hang on `eval('class A { private function
__invoke() { } }')` reporting *The magic method A::__invoke() must have public
visibility*. php2go already produced that text for a class in the **main** file
-- the harvest captures what the compiler printed and `ctx.Write`s it before the
body runs -- but `include` and `eval` threw their copy away.

Writing it as text would not have been enough. Both tests install an error
handler *before* the eval and check that the handler receives it, with `$file`
reported as `%s(%d) : eval()'d code` rather than as the temporary the compiler
was handed. So the captured text is parsed back into level, message and line,
and re-raised through the context at the eval's own name -- the same rewrite
`compileFailure` already did for the fatal case.

That fixed two more nobody was aiming at: `bug69388` and `bug69388_2` want *The
use statement with non-compound name 'Exception' has no effect*, which is the
same kind of report from an `include`.

### What the clustering says now

Re-running the wildcard-aware clusterer over the 611: still no mechanism above
eighteen, and the top two clusters (`int(N)` against a different `int(N)`, and
`int(N)` against nothing) are the refcount and destruction-timing families that
have been measured before as under a tenth of what remains. The productive
lens is still the small, sharply-worded families -- this round's three were two
tests each.

## 2026-08-28 — a foreach key is a value, not an array key

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3925 | 3927 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.3% | 83.3% |
| unsupported | 163 | 162 |
| failed | 620 | 619 |
| differential cases | 814 | 816 |

Diff-set: `iterator_key_by_ref` fixed, nothing broken. `weakrefs/weakmap_iteration`
went straight from `unsupported` to passing, so it does not appear in the
diff-set at all.

### The conversion was in the wrong place

`iterNext` returned a `php.Key`, so every foreach key went through `arrayKey`
before the loop ever saw it. That is wrong twice over, and the engine says so
plainly when asked:

```
foreach (new Keys([null, 1.5, true, false, "s", 3, [1,2], new stdClass]) as $k => $v)
```

hands back **exactly those values** -- null stays null, 1.5 stays a float, an
array stays an array -- with no diagnostic. php2go turned them into `""`, `1`
(with a spurious *Implicit conversion from float 1.5* deprecation), `1`, `0`,
and `"Array"`.

The conversion belongs to whoever is **building an array**, which is also where
its diagnostics belong: `iterator_to_array($it, true)` reports the float, and
the `foreach` that produced the same key does not.

So `iterNext` now returns a `php.Value`, and the three callers that need a key
convert for themselves -- `iterator_to_array`, argument unpacking, and array
unpacking. The `foreach` opcode keeps the raw value for the key destination and
converts only inside the by-reference branches, which are reached only when the
walk is over an array or an object's properties and the key really is one.

This was the two-test TODO item written up yesterday, and it is the same root
cause the WeakMap note named.

### A WeakMap can be iterated now

With object keys expressible, a WeakMap is walked directly rather than through
`getIterator`. `foreach`, `iterator_to_array` and the by-reference form all work;
an explicit `->getIterator()` is still a gap, because what the engine hands back
is an `InternalIterator` and the class name is observable.

One detail the corpus settled. After `foreach ($map as $k => &$v)`, var_dump
shows `&` on **every** entry the loop visited -- not just the last, the way an
array does. An array element's box flattens once the loop variable moves on; a
WeakMap's does not, because the map goes on holding it. `refAt` marks the box
shared when it makes it, which is what `php.Shared` is documented to mean: the
box exists because the program wrote `&`.

tests. `lazy_objects` is the biggest directory at 55, but clustered it is 56

  stdClass as array`, the same as a read.

  array offset on <type>` for every scalar kind and had simply left

  overloaded element of A has no effect` before refusing the unset. The write

`class B extends ArrayObject {}` got no store: `var_dump` showed no `storage`,
and a `foreach` over a subclass of ArrayIterator reported `Iterator::rewind on
<subclass>` as a gap. This was the standing "three allow-lists should be one
predicate" TODO in its third instance; `isArrayBackedClass` now walks ancestry
the way `isFilterIteratorClass` and `isEmptyIteratorClass` already did.

- **A method the subclass writes wins over the store.** `offsetCall` consulted
  the store first, so `class B extends ArrayObject { public function
  offsetSet(...) }` never ran B's body. Resolving a harvested body first and
  falling back to the store is the same ordering the iterator path needed two
  rounds ago -- the third place this rule has come up.
- **Extending one does not earn the Serializable notice.** `hasSerializePair`
  looked only for harvested bodies, and ArrayIterator's `__serialize` /
  `__unserialize` are C functions with no op_array. It now also asks the engine
  method table, which is what `method_exists` has always done.

`iterator_key_by_ref` was `Iterator::rewind on Test`; with a store it runs, and

a reference to an undefined variable, so the key really is null -- and
`iterator.iterNext` hands back a `php.Key`, which cannot hold one. That is the
same limitation already recorded against WeakMap's object keys, and it now has a
