## 2026-08-28 — a class constant's type is not a parameter's type

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3911 | 3917 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 83.0% | 83.1% |
| unsupported | 166 | 166 |
| failed | 631 | 625 |
| differential cases | 809 | 812 |

Diff-set: six fixed, nothing broken. All six were the tests the previous round
scoped in the TODO.

### Nothing coerces into a typed class constant

php2go was running a class constant's declared type through `checkType`, the
same check a parameter gets, in weak mode. Probed shape by shape, the engine
coerces **nothing** here:

| written | engine |
| --- | --- |
| `const string S = <object with __toString>` | TypeError, and `__toString` is **not called** |
| `const int A = 1.0` | TypeError |
| `const int A = "5"` | TypeError |
| `const int\|string A = 1.5` | TypeError |
| `const float F = 1` | `float(1)` |

The one exception is int to float, the widening the language always allows.
`typed_class_constants_type_error9` is built around the object case and checks
that the side effect in `__toString` never prints, which is what made the
difference visible.

`static` as a constant type means the class the constant was declared in, and
nothing else -- an enum case of a *different* enum is refused.

### A redeclared constant's type is covariant, and undecidable means no

Two link-time fatals php2go did not check at all. Probed in all four directions:
a redeclaration may **narrow** the type (`?B1` to `?B2` where B2 extends B1,
`int|string` to `int`) and may **add** one where the overridden constant had
none, but may not widen it and may not drop it -- declaring nothing counts as
`mixed`.

The part worth remembering is what happens when a class named in either type is
missing. A method's variance check *defers*: the engine has obligation machinery
for that, and php2go models it, reporting `Could not check compatibility ...
because class X is not available`. **Constants have no such machinery.** A class
that stays missing after the autoload attempt makes the types *incompatible*,
not the question undecidable -- which is exactly what
`typed_class_constants_type_error10` is, since it names `B1` and `B2` and never
declares either. The first implementation skipped when the answer was unknown
and the test stayed failing.

The autoload still happens, narrower side first, and an autoloader that prints
can see it.

### A default the compiler could not fold is an argument

`function int_val(int $a = STRING_VAL)` -- php2go filled the default and let the
body run, so the failure surfaced as a *return* TypeError. A comment at
`ZEND_RECV_INIT` said "a default is not type-checked -- the compiler already
accepted it", which is true only of a *folded* default. One naming a constant
has no value until the call and is checked then, like any argument, in the
caller's mode: `int_val(): Argument #1 ($a) must be of type int, string given,
called in ...`.

## 2026-08-28 — a constant expression is ordinary code, and was not being treated as such

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3901 | 3911 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.8% | **83.0%** |
| unsupported | 167 | 166 |
| failed | 640 | 631 |
| differential cases | 806 | 809 |

Diff-set: ten fixed, nothing broken.

### The pattern behind all of it

Every one of these was php2go treating a failure inside a constant expression as
*unresolvable* -- a gap -- where the engine treats it as an ordinary error the
program can catch. The evaluator kept returning `ok = false` and discarding the
reason.

- **Subscripting an object**: `const X = SomeEnum::Case[0]` is `Cannot use [] on
  objects in constant expression`. Probed: the refusal happens **before the
  index is evaluated**, so an undefined constant in the index is never reported.
- **An object as an offset**: `[1,2][Marker::One]` and `[Marker::One => 3]` are
  both `TypeError: Cannot access offset of type Marker on array` -- the same
  words a runtime subscript earns, and `dimensionRead` already produced them.
  The const path was throwing the error away and calling the constant a gap.
- **Refused operands**: `const T = [1,2] - [0]` is `Unsupported operand types:
  array - array`. `checkOperands` already existed; the const path never called
  it. The same call is what reports `A non-numeric value encountered`, so wiring
  it fixed a warning nobody was looking for.
- **A property named by an object**: `(new A)->{new B}` reports `Object of class
  B could not be converted to string`, and reports it **before** judging whether
  the container is an enum -- php2go was refusing the container first.

Two operand-order details the differential caught: unary minus compiles as
`-1 * value`, in that order, which shows in the message (`int * string`, not
`string * int`).

### `?->` short-circuits the chain, not the step

`prop_const_expr/basic_nullsafe` wanted seven shapes. The rule is that a `?->`
on null skips **everything further along the same chain**: a following property,
a following subscript, and the expression that *names* a property -- so
`(null)?->{new Printer}` never builds the Printer. The chain ends at the
enclosing operator, which is why `(null)?->test + (new Printer ? 1 : 0)` still
builds one and answers 1.

php2go had modelled it per-step, so `(null)?->test->test` warned about the
second `->test` and `(null)?->test['test']` warned about the subscript. It now
carries a flag that only the chain nodes propagate; every other node ends the
chain, which is exactly what the engine does by passing a null pointer down.

### Still open in this area

The typed-class-constant checks (four tests) and the pair where a *parameter*
default of the wrong constant type should be an argument `TypeError` rather than
a return one. Recorded in the TODO with the shapes.

## 2026-08-28 — a constant expression is evaluated somewhere else

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3893 | 3901 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.6% | 82.8% |
| unsupported | 167 | 167 |
| failed | 648 | 640 |
| differential cases | 804 | 806 |

Diff-set: eight fixed, nothing broken. All eight came out of `failed`.

### Reaching a static property uses the class

`class R { public static $s = [1][5]; } R::$s` was a silent NULL. Two separate
misses: `staticPropRef` read the declaration through `literalValue`, which
cannot evaluate an expression at all, and nothing called
`updateClassConstants` on a static-property access -- it was wired only to
`new`.

The engine's timing, probed: touching **any** static property of a class --
reading, writing, or `isset()` -- resolves **every** deferred initializer that
class has, constants first and property defaults after, in declaration order,
before the access itself happens. So reading `$b` reports what `$a`'s default
and the class's constants report. Four tests.

### The `[constant expression]` frame and the position are one mechanism

Yesterday's entry recorded the frame as "not a real frame" -- synthesised at
backtrace time from a filename/line override. The other half of that override is
that a diagnostic raised inside a constant expression is reported against the
**declaration**, not the read. php2go had the frame and not the position, which
made the two disagree; they now come from one place, `enterConstExpression`.

That needed the AST's line, which the harvest was not carrying: `Expr` gained a
`line` from `zend_ast_get_lineno`, and the class already carried its filename.
The frame is pushed only when the two positions actually differ, which is what
the engine's condition amounts to.

Two refinements the corpus insisted on, each worth a test:

- The override is re-applied at **every class-constant reference inside** a
  constant expression, using that reference's own line. `gh7771_2` declares
  `public const BAR =` / `self::BAZ` / `+ NonExistent::CLASS_CONSTANT` across
  three lines and expects the *third*. Setting the position once per initializer
  gives the first.
- It has to be applied **before the class is resolved**, not just around the
  constant fetch -- `Class "NonExistent" not found` is raised by the resolution.
  The first attempt put it after, and gh7771_2 stayed exactly one line off.

`Undefined constant self::B` also names the class **as written** rather than as
it resolves, the same rule the self-referencing message follows.

### A note on stale binaries, again

Two of these looked unfixed after the change because `php2phpt` had not been
rebuilt -- only `php2eval` had. The same trap as the earlier revert. Rebuild
*both* before believing a per-test result.

## 2026-08-28 — frames the engine pushes, and where a constant cycle is noticed

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3885 | 3893 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.4% | 82.6% |
| unsupported | 172 | 167 |
| failed | 651 | 648 |
| differential cases | 800 | 804 |

Diff-set: nothing broken across the round.

### The missing-frame lens, taken further

The previous round found that a `foreach` never pushed a backtrace frame for the
Iterator methods it drove. A six-shape probe -- `__toString`, `__get`,
ArrayAccess, `usort`, `array_map`, `Countable::count` -- showed the same hole in
three more places: **`__toString`**, **the ArrayAccess offsets**, and
**`Countable::count`**. `__get` already had one, so the pattern was "whatever
`magic.go` reaches for has a frame, whatever anything else reaches for does
not". They now share one helper, `invokeDriven`.

Two details the probe settled that guessing would have got wrong:

- The frame is named for the class that **declared** the body, not the object's.
  An inherited `__toString` reports the parent. The iterator helper written the
  round before had used the object's class and happened to agree only because
  the test's method was declared on the anonymous class itself.
- `usort` calls its comparator with the operands in the other order from
  php2go's (`cmp(3,1)` against `cmp(1,3)`) -- the engine's `zend_sort` is a
  hybrid whose exact call sequence php2go does not reproduce. **Measured: no
  failing test in the corpus calls `usort`, `uasort` or `uksort` at all**, so
  porting `zend_sort` would buy nothing today. Recorded rather than done.

### `...` in a constant expression

Three `array_unpack` tests were blocked on AST node kind 258, which is
`ZEND_AST_UNPACK`: the parser puts it *in place of* an element rather than
inside one, so the array evaluator sees it among the elements. Unpacking in a
constant expression differs from the runtime opcode in one way -- there is
nothing to iterate yet, so a Traversable is refused outright with *Only arrays
can be unpacked in constant expression*. The runtime opcode was also missing the
refusal when the largest integer key is already taken; it has it now, in both
the array and the Traversable branch.

### Where the engine notices a self-referencing constant

`Cannot declare self-referencing constant self::B` looks like it should name the
fetch that closes the cycle. It does not, and thirteen probed shapes were needed
to see why. For `class D { const A = self::B; const B = self::A; }`, reading
`D::A` reports **`self::B`**, not `self::A`.

The rule: **the fetch the program makes does not count as visiting the
constant.** Only fetches made *from inside a constant expression* mark, so the
cycle is caught one lap later than expected, and the message names the fetch as
it is written -- `self::B`, `Z3::B`, `Ot2::V` -- rather than what it resolves to.
Every one of the thirteen shapes falls out of that, including the ones where the
entry point is outside the cycle.

One further ordering matters: the mark goes on **after** the class is resolved.
`gh10709` autoloads a class from inside the fetch of the very constant being
evaluated, and marking first calls that legitimate re-entry a cycle. It broke on
the first attempt and the diff-set named it.

### The `[constant expression]` frame is not a frame

The two remaining self-reference tests wanted a `[constant expression]()` line
in the trace. php2go had one for property defaults with a comment recording that
*a class constant does not get one* -- and an existing differential case proving
it. Both are true. The discriminator is not which kind of declaration it is:

> An initializer that is a **single bare constant fetch** is evaluated with no
> frame and is reported against the *use* site. The same fetch with anything
> around it -- `FOO + 0`, `[FOO => 1]` -- is reported against the *declaration*
> and adds one frame.

That holds for class constants, static property defaults and instance property
defaults alike; the earlier note had read the difference off two shapes that
differed in both respects at once. php2go's property-default path had been
pushing the frame unconditionally, which no case had caught.

The frame is also not a real one in the engine: it is synthesised at backtrace
time from a filename/line override, which is why it always appears at index 0
and why the whole evaluation contributes exactly one however many constants it
reaches through.

### Left undone, deliberately

php2go still reports these errors against the **use** site where the engine
reports the declaration -- the other half of the same override. Every corpus
test that covers it matches with `%d`, so it is invisible there. And a static
property default whose initializer is an expression is never evaluated at all:
`class R { public static $s = [1][5]; } R::$s` is a silent NULL where the engine
warns. Both are in the TODO.

## 2026-08-27 — the wrapping iterators, and a frame the loop never pushed

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3879 | 3885 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.3% | 82.4% |
| unsupported | 178 | 172 |
| differential cases | 797 | 800 |

Diff-set against the previous round: the failing set is **identical**. All six
tests came straight out of `unsupported`, none broke.

### IteratorIterator is CallbackFilterIterator with nothing filtering

The machinery added in iteration 144 for `CallbackFilterIterator` already asked
the inner iterator every question and moved it until `accept()` agreed. A plain
`IteratorIterator` is that with no callback: `accept()` is always true, so
`skipRejected` stops on the first element. The class predicate had to grow up
at the same time -- it was matching the class *name*, and `CallbackFilterIterator`
descends from `IteratorIterator`, so "which of the two is it" is a question
about ancestry, not spelling.

Three things the engine does that reading the class list would not have
suggested, each settled by a probe:

- Its constructor takes a **Traversable**, not an Iterator -- a generator or an
  `IteratorAggregate` is accepted. An aggregate is unwrapped **once**, at
  construction: `getIterator()` runs there, and `getInnerIterator()` hands back
  the same object every time afterwards.
- A method the wrapper does not have is **passed through** to what it wraps.
  That is why `method_exists($it, 'offsetGet')` on an `IteratorIterator` over an
  `ArrayIterator` is `true` (bug76901) and why calling it reaches the array.
  It is not special-cased to SPL: a user Iterator's own `foo()` is reachable
  through the wrapper too.
- `EmptyIterator` holds nothing at all. It is never valid, `rewind()` and
  `next()` are silent, and `current()`/`key()` are a `BadMethodCallException`
  rather than null -- there is nothing to be on.

`parent::rewind()` from a subclass of one of these was a separate gap: the
static-call path had no fallback to the Go implementation the instance-call path
has had all along. It does now, when there is a receiver below the named class.

### The frame a foreach never pushed

`generators/gh8289` stopped being unsupported and started *failing*, one line
short: the backtrace was missing the `IteratorIterator@anonymous->key()` frame.
That turned out to be nothing to do with the new classes. The engine makes every
Iterator method it drives from a `foreach` an ordinary call with an ordinary
frame, and php2go had been calling them straight through `invoke` with no
`PushCall` at all -- so *any* exception thrown from a user `current()`, `key()`
or `valid()` reached the catch with that frame missing. A three-line probe on a
plain user Iterator showed it, with no wrapper in sight.

The fix has a second half worth remembering. The loop asks several of these in a
row -- `current()` then `key()` -- and each call leaves `ctx.Location()` pointing
inside the method that just ran. The ordinary call path takes the call site from
the *opcode* rather than from the context, so it never noticed. Here the frame
has to be pushed from a Go helper, so the location is saved before the call and
put back after it; without that, `key()`'s frame was attributed to the last line
of `current()`.

### Still not there

`bug60138` needs `RecursiveIteratorIterator`, and `return_types/006` and
`iterator_key_by_ref` still report `Iterator::rewind on <subclass>` -- the
standing gap where a subclass of an engine array store is instantiated without
one. Those are three different shapes of the same missing piece and stay
`unsupported`.

## 2026-08-27 — forwarding a static call, and an asymmetry in the engine

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3877 | 3879 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.3% | 82.3% |
| unsupported | 181 | 178 |
| differential cases | 796 | 797 |

Diff-set: 2 straight out of `unsupported` into passing, 1 into `failed`, 0
broken.

### Three more from the blocker list

- `ZEND_UNSET_STATIC_PROP`. A static property belongs to the class, so unset()
  has nothing to take away: `Attempt to unset static property C::$p`, and the
  property keeps its value.
- `forward_static_call` and `forward_static_call_array`. These are
  `call_user_func` with the late static binding kept -- `static::` inside the
  callee still means what the *calling* method's did -- which is the whole
  reason they exist, and php2go already had `forwardCalled` for the same idea in
  callable strings.
- `getcwd`, which is the process's and has no per-request notion to model.

### The asymmetry

`forward_static_call("strtoupper", "ab")` at top level throws
`Cannot call forward_static_call() when no class scope is active`.
`forward_static_call_array("strtoupper", ["ab"])` in the same place **does not**
-- it just calls, and returns "AB".

I had implemented the check for both, reasoning that neither has a binding to
forward. The differential caught it in the first run: the engine emitted one
refusal where php2go emitted two. There is no principle behind the difference;
the array form simply lacks the check in the engine's source. This is the rule
the project is built on doing its job -- a plausible symmetry, written down as
code, and refuted by asking.

### Next

The blocker list still has small entries: `json_last_error_msg` (php2go's json
tracks no error state, so this needs one first), `get_loaded_extensions` and
`get_defined_constants` (which would report the *engine's* capabilities, and
should probably not), `microtime`, and the SPL instantiations.

*blocker* list still has a long cheap tail that the failing list does not. Six
gaps in one round, each a few lines, all settled by one probe:

- `xor` had no handler. It has an opcode rather than the jumps `&&` and `||`
  compile to, precisely because it evaluates both sides.
- Unpacking a non-Traversable was an honest gap; it is a `TypeError` in a call
  and a plain `Error` in an array literal, with identical wording. The engine
  classes them differently in the two places.
- `array_key_exists` on a non-array, through its specialised opcode, carries the
  same argument diagnostic the call does.
- A compound assignment through an index on a scalar is
  `Cannot use a scalar value as an array` -- except on a *string*, which has a
  refusal of its own: `Cannot use assign-op operators with string offsets`. A
  string offset can be assigned but not read-modify-written.
- `error_get_last` and `error_clear_last`. The first records *whatever*
  error_reporting said and whatever `@` suppressed -- it answers about what
  happened, not about what was printed -- so the record has to be taken before
  the reporting filter rather than from the printed list.

### And a unit test earning its keep

`TestUnsupportedOpcodeIsReported` broke: it walks the opcodes until it finds an
unimplemented one and insists the gap is *named after an opcode*. Closing the
compound-index gap let it fall through to a report reading
`compound assignment using ZEND_NOP` -- which names an opcode, but not first, so
the gap list would not have sorted it with its siblings. Renamed to
`ZEND_NOP as a compound assignment`.

That test exists to keep the gap reports legible as gaps get closed, and it did
exactly that.

### Next

Seven tests moved from `unsupported` to `failed` and two are close:
`operator_unsupported_types` now differs at line 1022 of its output, and
`offsets/invalid_container_offset_behaviour` reaches its own "Failures:"
summary. Both are self-checking tests worth reading properly.

## 2026-08-27 — an undefined variable passed as an argument is null

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3874 | 3876 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.2% | **82.3%** |
| differential cases | 793 | 794 |

Diff-set: 2 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~87s.

### Two warnings where PHP gives one

`func1($undefined)` warns once, at the read, and the parameter receives *null*.
php2go passed the undefined value through, so reading the parameter inside the
callee warned a second time -- naming the parameter, which the program never
wrote.

The fix is at the SEND opcodes rather than at RECV, because the two Undefs are
not the same thing and only the sender knows which is which: a value that was
*read* and turned out undefined is null, while an undefined slot in the argument
list is a hole the caller never filled, and a hole has to stay a hole for
`Argument #N ($x) not passed` and for the arity check to keep working.
`passedValue` names that distinction in one place.

### And an append that named no offset

`$o[] += 5` on an ArrayAccess calls `offsetGet(null)` then `offsetSet(null, …)`.
php2go's compound-assignment path fetched op2 unconditionally, and for an append
op2 is unused -- so the accessor was called with no argument at all and its
`$offset` parameter was undefined. That is the third place this round has found
where an append has to pass null explicitly; the other two were the write-fetch
path and `offsetSet` itself.

### Note on the survey

The re-cluster that opened this round found nothing above three tests, and four
of the seven groups at three are the refcount/destruction families. The two
fixed here came from the one group that was not. The failing set is now genuinely
long-tailed: 643 tests, no mechanism above three.

## 2026-08-27 — a class that failed to link was never declared

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3872 | 3874 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.2% | 82.2% |
| differential cases | 792 | 793 |

Diff-set: 2 fixed, 0 broken -- and neither is the test that motivated the round.

### Aiming at one thing and hitting another

The target was `type_declarations/variance/loading_exception1`, which wants
`During inheritance of B with variance dependencies`. It fails much earlier
than that: the test declares `class B extends A {}` twice in a loop, expecting
both to fail gracefully, and php2go refused the second with
`Cannot redeclare class B`.

Two bugs behind it, and the second is the interesting one:

- A class whose dependencies could not be obtained stays declared in php2go.
  PHP unlinks it, which is the whole reason the retry is legal.
- `bindDeclaration` treated "the harvest saw this name twice" as proof that one
  of them was bound at compile time. It is not: *both* can be conditional, each
  with its own `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` opline, and then neither is taken until an
  opline runs. Counting the declare oplines and subtracting gives what the
  compiler actually bound -- a `deferredClasses` scan already existed and only
  needed to count rather than flag.

`bug49908` and `bug78926` were failing on that second bug and were not on any
list.

### What it still does not do

`loading_exception1` and `2` now get as far as the two graceful failures and
then print a third instead of the fatal. The third attempt is a fatal in PHP
because by then something else holds a *variance obligation* on B, so it can no
longer be unlinked. php2go has no deferred-obligation machinery at all, and
inventing a rule that guesses when a class "cannot be unlinked" would be
scaffolding rather than semantics. Left alone.

## 2026-08-27 — the narrower side is always looked up

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3869 | 3872 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.1% | **82.2%** |
| differential cases | 791 | 792 |

Diff-set: 3 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~86s.

### The rule

A variance check resolves the *narrower* side's class names whatever the wider
side names. `object` accepts any class -- but the engine still looks the class
up, and that lookup can autoload, and an autoloader can print or throw. php2go
answered "any class satisfies object" without asking for the class at all.

The rule was settled by probing rather than reading, with a printing autoloader
and six parent/child pairs:

| parent | child | loads? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `object` | `K` | yes |
| `?object` | `K` | yes |
| `mixed` | `K` | no |
| `K` | `K` | no |
| `iterable` | `array` | no |
| `K` (param) | `object` (param) | yes -- `K` is the narrower side here |

The last row is the one that makes the rule legible: for a *parameter* the child
widens, so the parent's type is the narrower side, and it is the parent's name
that gets loaded. It is not "the child is resolved" -- it is "the narrower is".

`mixed` and an identical pair short-circuit before any lookup, which is why
neither reports a missing class. Both of those were already right.

### Two neighbours came with it

`intersection_types/variance/invalid4` and `variance/enum_forward_compat` were
failing for the same reason and were not on the list -- a reminder that a
correctly-scoped rule tends to pay more than the test that motivated it.

### The differential case had to be trimmed

Half the interesting shapes -- an unresolvable name under `object`, a scalar
under `object` -- are *fatal* errors, and the oracle cannot be asked about
those. The case keeps the shapes that link, which still pins that `mixed` and an
identical pair need no class. The failing shapes are covered by the corpus.

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3867 | 3869 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.1% | 82.1% |

Diff-set: 2 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~85s.

### The intended fix, and the one that mattered

The intended one was the third `During inheritance` context: an autoload
triggered *by* a variance check, reported as `During inheritance of B, while
autoloading Y`. `resolveTypeClass` already captured the failure into
`unit.linkAbort` for `verifySignatures` to hand on; it just had to remember
which class it was loading.

The one that actually paid was underneath it. `in.autoload` dispatched the
registered callback without pushing a stack frame, so an autoloader appeared in
no backtrace at all -- `#0 {main}` where PHP has `#0 file(line):
{closure}('Y')`. Pushing the frame, with the call site being wherever the
program asked for the class, fixed the variance test *and*
`generators/bug65161`, which had been failing on exactly that missing frame and
has nothing to do with inheritance.

Worth the note: a missing stack frame is invisible until something prints a
trace, so it hides in whatever feature happens to print one first.

- `exception_during_variance_autoload_2` still fails. Its autoloader is reached
  while checking `Y` against `object`, and php2go's `typeAccepts` answers
  "object accepts any class name" without resolving the name at all. PHP loads
  it. Changing that would make the variance check autoload in more places than
  this one test, so it wants its own round.
- No differential case: registering an autoloader in one interferes with the
  harness's engine reset between cases -- `spl_autoload_unregister` then fails
  on a name from the previous case. Another entry for the list of things the
  oracle cannot be asked (after fatal errors and closure names containing file
  paths).

## 2026-08-27 — a type the engine means to enforce eventually

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3865 | 3867 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.0% | **82.1%** |
| differential cases | 790 | 791 |

Diff-set: 2 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~87s.

### The notice

A *tentative* return type -- what the engine put on `ArrayAccess`, `Countable`
and their kin when it added types to the interfaces it ships -- is not enforced.
A class that does not match one is deprecated:

```
Return type of C::offsetGet($o) should either be compatible with
ArrayAccess::offsetGet(mixed $offset): mixed, or the #[\ReturnTypeWillChange]
attribute should be used to temporarily suppress the notice
```

and it can say it knows by putting that attribute on the method. Matching
exactly says nothing. The parameters are enforced whatever the return type does,
which is why last round's work had to come first.

Everything it needed existed by the end of last round: the harvested tentative
flag, `renderSignature`, the attribute list on methods, and `linkFatal` for the
case where a handler turns the deprecation into an exception. This round was
mostly wiring, which is what a well-scoped predecessor buys.

The one thing worth stating: the notice is reported at the *offending method's*
line, not at the class declaration, so the location has to be moved for the
duration of the call and put back -- the same shape as the accessor diagnostics
in `magic.go` and the ArrayAccess offset notice.

### `record_errors_001` came along too

Not obviously related, and not investigated -- it is a test about which
diagnostics a run records, and one more of them now exists.

## 2026-08-27 — an engine method now has a signature

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3862 | 3865 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 82.0% | 82.0% |

Diff-set: 3 fixed, 0 broken. No differential case -- the behaviour is a fatal
error, so the engine bails out and the oracle has nothing to compare.

### The harvest

`zend.EngineMethod` carried name, visibility, static and abstract. It now
carries the parameter list, the return type, the required count and the variadic
flag, harvested through the same shims the internal *functions* already used --
an engine method is a `zend_internal_function`, so `arg_info` is read exactly
the same way.

`verifySignatures` reaches them through a new `Unit.prototypeMethod`, which
synthesises an `OpArray` on demand and caches it on the class. Deliberately not
in `class.methods`: that table is what decides whether a method has a body to
run, and putting shapes with no body in it would change dispatch.

Two details the corpus insisted on:

- An internal declaration keeps its parameter defaults **on the arg_info**, as
  source text, where a user function keeps them in a `RECV_INIT` opline. Without
  that, `DateTimeInterface::diff(..., bool $absolute = false)` rendered as
  `= <default>`.
- `ArrayAccess`'s return types are **tentative**. A mismatch against one is a
  deprecation the engine has not started enforcing, and
  `#[\ReturnTypeWillChange]` silences even that -- so php2go must not refuse
  it. The first attempt dropped the type from the prototype entirely, which was
  wrong in the other direction: the diagnostic about the *parameters* still
  prints it. The flag has to travel and be consulted only at the comparison.

That one was caught by php2go's own differential suite, which contains an
`ArrayAccess` implementation with `#[\ReturnTypeWillChange]` on `offsetGet` --
a case written two rounds ago for something else entirely.

### And one the new check exposed

An enum declaring `from()` earns `Cannot redeclare Foo::from()`, not an
incompatible-override fatal: those three names are the engine's, and writing one
is a redeclaration. `verifyEnum` says so, but it runs after `verifySignatures`,
which could now see `BackedEnum::from`'s prototype and got there first.

## 2026-08-27 — which class a trait method's diagnostic names

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3861 | 3862 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.9% | **82.0%** |

Diff-set: 1 fixed, 0 broken. No differential case: the behaviour is a fatal
error, which makes the engine bail out and leaves the oracle nothing to compare.

### It depends on what the prototype is

`Declaration of X::m() must be compatible with Y::m()` for a method a class
composed from a trait names *the trait* in one case and *the class* in the
other, and which one is not arbitrary:

- against a **parent class**: the trait, because the check happens while the
  method is being bound, when it is still the trait's;
- against an **interface**: the class, because that check happens afterwards,
  when the method belongs to whoever composed it.

php2go named the trait in both. Changing it to name the class in both fixed
`traits/bug60153` and broke six others -- `inheritance003`, `trait_error`,
`bug70957`, `bug81192` and two `abstract-methods` -- which is what said the rule
had two halves rather than one. Selecting on the prototype's kind at the report
site fixes all seven.

Worth noting how cheap that was to discover: the first version was written,
measured, and the diff-set named the six counter-examples in one run. Reading
`zend_inheritance.c` for the answer would have taken longer and been less
certain.

### And a blocker found on the way

`argument_restriction_005` and
`parameter_default_values/internal_declaration_error_false` want the same check
against an *engine* interface -- `class Sub implements ArrayAccess { public
function offsetSet(): void {} }`. php2go cannot make it: `zend.EngineMethod`
carries name, visibility, static and abstract, and no parameters at all. There
is nothing to compare against.

The fix is the same shape as the `ArgInfo` attributes work: the cgo shims for
internal function signatures (`php2go_builtin_arg_name` and friends) apply to an
internal *method* too, since it is a `zend_internal_function`. Then
`verifySignatures` needs a prototype lookup that can synthesise an `OpArray`
from one -- deliberately *not* by putting them in `class.methods`, which would
change what `resolveMethod` reports a PHP body for.

## 2026-08-27 — an exception raised while a class is being linked

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3860 | 3861 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.9% | 81.9% |

Diff-set: 1 fixed, 0 broken. A thin round; most of it went on sizing the
declaration-check family, which turned out to be smaller and more fragmented
than the TODO had it.

### The declaration-check family is 22, not 60

Sweeping the diff dump for a `Fatal error:` about a *declaration* that php2go
does not produce: 22 tests, in groups of 6, 6, 4, 2 and four singletons. The
TODO carried "~60" from an old measurement. Corrected.

### An exception does not escape a link

`zend_exception_uncaught_error` is a shape worth knowing: when an exception is
raised while a class is being linked -- a deprecation a user error handler
turned into a throw, an autoloader that failed, a variance check that could not
resolve -- the engine does **not** let it out. It catches it, renders it inside
a fatal of its own that names what was being linked, and stops:

```
Fatal error: During inheritance of C, while implementing Serializable: Uncaught Exception: ... in %s:%d
Stack trace:
#0 %s(%d): handler(...)
#1 {main} in %s on line %d
```

The tell is the last line. An uncaught exception ends with `  thrown in <file>
on line N`; this ends with the trace's own `{main}` followed by `in <file> on
line N`, because it is an ordinary `E_ERROR` whose *message* happens to contain
a rendered exception. `linkFatal` builds exactly that.

Four prefixes exist in the engine, each raised where its own context is known:
`During inheritance of %s`, `..., while implementing Serializable`,
`..., while autoloading %s`, and `... with variance dependencies`. Only the
Serializable one is wired up; the others need the check that can throw to know
what it was doing, which is per-site work rather than a wrapper.

### Not every fix can have a differential case

The natural case for this -- a handler that throws on the Serializable
deprecation -- makes the *engine* bail out, and the oracle has nothing to
compare. The `.phpt` corpus covers it instead. Worth remembering before writing
a case for anything that ends in a fatal error.

### Next

`deprecation_to_exception_during_inheritance` needs the tentative-return-type
deprecation (`#[\ReturnTypeWillChange]`), which php2go does not implement at
all -- it needs the engine's tentative return types for internal methods.

## 2026-08-27 — what the two call_user_func forms do with a reference

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3857 | 3860 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.9% | 81.9% |
| differential cases | 791 | 792 |

Diff-set: 3 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~84s.

### First, a measurement worth having

The tail is *not* dominated by the no-refcounts limitation. Tagging all 662
failures by what their output mentions: ~47 are destruction/refcount, 3 fibers,
100 involve an object handle in a dump -- and of those only **10 fail on the
handle number alone**. The remaining 512 are ordinary behaviour. Two earlier
rounds had started to assume the ceiling was near; it is not.

The 10 that are only handle numbers are still refcount-bound:
`object(Closure)#2` three times in a row is PHP reusing the slot of a temporary
that died, which needs the freeing to happen at the right moment, not just a
free list.

### `$closure->__invoke($x)` is the closure's own call

`argumentByRef` resolves the callee from `method`, `closure` or the function
table. A Closure reached through its `__invoke` method has none of those set --
the call carries `builtinMethod` and a `this` -- so every argument went by
value, and `function (&$n)` silently got a copy. Method names are
case-insensitive, so the corpus tests it as `__INVOKE`.

### The two call_user_func forms are not siblings

php2go treated them as one: `viaUserCall`, a warning per by-reference
parameter, and every reference in the argument list copied away. That is right
for `call_user_func`, whose own parameters are by value. It is wrong for
`call_user_func_array`, which hands the array's *elements* over as they are --
so an element that is already a reference stays one, and that is the only way a
by-reference parameter is reached this way at all.

Splitting them cost two follow-ups, both from rules the plain form already had
and the array form now needed:

- The warning has to know the harvested signature, not just PHP bodies:
  `str_replace`'s `$count` is as by-reference as any, and `bug79979` broke until
  `noteCallbackByRef` learned to ask `engineSignatures`.
- A function that refuses to be reached dynamically refuses *before* it looks at
  its arguments, so `extract` earns no argument warning on the way to
  `Cannot call extract() dynamically`. `dynamic_call_005` and `_007` broke on
  exactly that.

Both are cases where the older function had a guard and the new path did not --
the sort of thing that only shows up by running the corpus after each step.

### Next

`str_replace`'s `$count` out-parameter is not written at all, which the new
differential case had to step around. That is its own small gap.

## 2026-08-27 — which finally's exception a return discards

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3855 | 3857 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.8% | **81.9%** |
| differential cases | 790 | 791 |
| errored | 5 | 4 |

Diff-set: 1 fixed, 0 broken, plus one test out of `errored`. Corpus wall clock
~85s.

### The operand was being ignored

`ZEND_DISCARD_EXCEPTION` popped the top of php2go's unwinding stack. It has an
operand, and the operand says *which* finally's pending exception is being
abandoned -- which matters as soon as a `return` sits inside a finally nested in
another finally, because the compiler emits one discard per block being left,
innermost first.

The operand is the temporary that block's `ZEND_FAST_CALL` stored its return
address in, so the opline just before that address *is* the FAST_CALL, and its
target is the block's own start -- which is what the unwinding entry records.
No new state was needed; the association was already there to be read.

Without it, a return from an inner finally discarded the *outer* finally's
exception, so `try { throw 1 } finally { try { try {} finally { return 42 } }
finally { throw 2 } }` lost the chain: PHP reports 2 with 1 as its previous, and
php2go reported only 2.

### Isolating it was the cheap part

Five shapes of the same skeleton -- throw in the finally, return in the finally,
return then throw, a nested try that throws, a plain return -- and only the
third differed. Writing the matrix took less time than reading the handler
would have, and it became the differential case unchanged.

### What is left in try/

Seven, and six of them are the same known thing: php2go has no refcounts, so an
object dies at a collection or at shutdown rather than when its last holder goes
away. `catch (Exception)` with no variable, `$a = null` inside a loop body, a
destructor that throws while an exception is unwinding -- all of them are asking
when the destructor runs, not what the exception machinery does with it.
`bug71604_2` and `_3` are the exception left: nested finallys inside a
*generator*, where the unwind crosses the resume boundary.

## 2026-08-27 — the delegate was invisible to the collector

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3852 | 3855 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.7% | **81.8%** |
| differential cases | 789 | 790 |

Diff-set: 3 fixed, 0 broken. The same change that broke five tests last round
now breaks none, because the round was spent on the blocker rather than on the
feature.

### What the blocker was

`marker.frame` walks a frame's variables, its arguments, its pending calls and
its `f.iterators`. It did not walk `f.delegate` -- the source a `yield from` is
currently draining. A generator delegating to another holds the inner one
*there and nowhere else*, so the inner one was reported unreachable while the
program was in the middle of reading from it.

Instrumenting was the whole of the diagnosis: printing every generator's
reachability at each collection showed handle 4 -- the one `gen()` creates for
its own `yield from` -- as the only unreachable one, at a point where the test
had not finished with it.

Two things had to change together:

- The delegate is walked, through a `marker.iterator` helper the two call sites
  now share. (It also picks up `backing`/`backingOwner`, which the ArrayIterator
  work added a round ago and nothing was walking.)
- A generator needs a back-pointer to its own object. Reachability is decided
  about *objects*, and the walk previously marked `it.gen.frame` without ever
  marking the Generator the frame belongs to -- so even a walked delegate would
  not have counted.

### And a cycle the walk could not see

Marking the generator object closed a loop the frame walk had no guard for: a
generator delegating to itself (`yield_from_already_running` is that test)
recurses frame → delegate → object → frame. `marker.seen` guards objects and
`marker.arrays` guards arrays; frames had nothing, because until now no frame
could reach another. It cost a stack-overflow crash in the middle of a corpus
run to notice, which is a fair price for the reminder that adding an edge to a
graph walk means checking the walk still terminates.

### Then the feature landed unchanged

The generator force-close reverted last round went back in exactly as written --
no guards, no special cases -- and the five tests it broke then now pass, along
with the three it fixed. That is the argument for having reverted it: the guard
that would have made it "work" would still be there, hiding this.

### Next

`try/bug71604_2` and `_3`, `try_finally_017/019/020/022/023` and `catch_novar_2`
are still failing. They are about a *destructor* throwing while an exception is
already on its way out, which is a different mechanism from the one this round
built.

## 2026-08-27 — an abandoned generator's finally blocks: scoped, attempted, reverted

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3852 | 3852 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.7% | 81.7% |

Diff-set: empty in both directions. The change was written, measured at 3 fixed
and 5 broken, narrowed twice, and then reverted. What this round produced is a
scoped feature and a named blocker, not a number.

### The feature

`try/bug71604`, `generators/bug74606`, `finally/finally_ran_on_close`,
`run_on_dtor`, `yield_from_force_closed`, `exception_during_shutdown` and
`errors/yield_in_force_closed_finally_error` all want the same thing: a
generator abandoned part-way through is resumed one last time so its `finally`
blocks run. PHP does it when the Generator object is destroyed.

php2go has the exact machinery already, for fibers: `errFiberExit` is a sentinel
that `frame.raise` treats as "not an exception -- only the finally blocks on the
way out see it", and `forceClose` drives it. A generator sibling is about thirty
lines and fixes three of those tests immediately.

### The blocker

It also breaks five: `gh15108-005/006/007`, `gh19326` and
`generators/multiple_yield_from_on_same_generator`. In each, the collector
reports a generator unreachable that PHP still holds, and unwinding it runs code
PHP never runs -- `var_dump("not executed")` in the gh15108 tests says so by
name.

Two guards were tried and neither is the answer:

- Skip a generator whose frame is on `unit.frames`. It is not: the frame is
  suspended, which is the whole point.
- Skip a generator whose frame a fiber owns (`fiber.frames`). Also not: php2go
  runs a fiber on its own goroutine, so a generator suspended *inside* one has
  its frame on that goroutine's stack rather than in the fiber's list.

The marker does walk a generator's frame (`gc.go`, `case *generator`), so this
is not simply a missing edge. Something about a *delegating* chain --
`yield from` -- is being reported unreachable while still held;
`multiple_yield_from_on_same_generator` has no fibers in it at all and still
breaks, which rules out the fiber story being the whole of it.

### Why it was reverted rather than landed behind a guard

A guard crude enough to work -- "do not close generators if the program ever
made a fiber" -- would have netted +3. It would also have been a rule with no
counterpart in the engine, sitting in the collector where the next person to
read it would have no way to tell whether it was semantics or scaffolding. The
gap it papers over is in reachability, which is load-bearing for
`gc_collect_cycles()` too. Better to leave the tree at 3852 and the finding
written down.

### Next

Find out why an abandoned-looking generator in a `yield from` chain is reported
unreachable while the program still holds it. That is worth knowing whether or
not the force-close feature is built on top of it.

## 2026-08-27 — destructuring an ArrayAccess, and a slot that left its frame

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3842 | 3852 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.5% | **81.7%** |
| differential cases | 787 | 789 |

Diff-set: 10 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~90s. Both fixes reached
further than the tests that motivated them -- the list one alone took
`list_005`, `list_007` and the two `list_keyed_evaluation_order` tests, none of
which mention ArrayAccess in their titles.

### list() over an ArrayAccess

`FETCH_LIST_R` handed out null for anything that was not an array and
`FETCH_LIST_W` raised `Cannot use a scalar value as an array`. Both have to go
through `offsetGet`, and the by-reference form has the same two outcomes a
`&$o[$k]` fetch does: a class that declared `function &offsetGet` hands over a
slot, and anything else hands over a value, which the engine reports as
`Indirect modification of overloaded element` rather than refusing.

### A slot that left its frame

`function &gen(array &$a) { yield $a[0]; }` written back correctly but lost the
`&` on the element afterwards. The share counter was reaching zero, and the
arithmetic said it should not -- so the answer came from bisecting the count
rather than from reading the model: the *frame teardown* was the one taking it
away.

php2go unshares every slot when a frame ends, which is right for a local that
held a reference. It is wrong for a slot a by-reference yield handed *out*: that
box left the frame, so the frame ending is not it losing a holder. Two shapes of
fix were wrong before the right one:

- Marking the yield shared and letting the teardown undo it balances to zero,
  not one.
- Skipping temporaries in the teardown fixed this and broke an existing case,
  because temps do legitimately hold shares elsewhere.

What works is recording the specific boxes a by-reference yield handed out
(`frame.escaped`) and skipping exactly those. The general lesson is the same one
from the array-copy round: when an approximate count is wrong, find the
structural fact rather than adjusting the arithmetic.

The generator branch of `FE_FETCH_RW` was also missing the `Unshare` its array
siblings have, so a loop over two yields left both slots marked instead of the
last one. The differential case with two yields is what caught it.

### Next

`bug52193` and `dereference_011` are what remains of the old marker grouping:
`(array)` casting a Closure, and a chain of by-reference method returns.

## 2026-08-27 — an ArrayIterator over an object is that object's properties

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3840 | 3842 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.5% | 81.5% |
| differential cases | 786 | 787 |

Diff-set: 2 fixed (`type_declarations/typed_properties_113`, `_114`), 0 broken.
A thin round by count, but the grouping it settled was worth the check.

### The "reference marker" family was a symptom, not a cause

The TODO carried eleven tests grouped by *counting `&` lines in the expected
output against the produced ones*. Re-checking them against the copy rule that
landed last round -- as the TODO said to -- showed five distinct mechanisms, not
one. Only two shared a cause. Worth remembering: a grouping made from what the
output *looks like* is a starting point for a sweep, not a diagnosis, and it has
to be re-tested whenever the neighbourhood changes.

### The two that did share one

`new ArrayIterator($object)` does not copy: the store *is* that object's
property table. Writing through the iterator reaches the object, `count()`
reports the properties, and a by-reference `foreach` binds the property's own
slot. php2go's constructor only understood an array argument and produced an
empty store for an object -- so `count()` said 0 and the loop found nothing.

Two further pieces followed from it:

- A by-reference loop over an engine iterator had no slot to bind, because the
  walk goes through the store's Go methods and `it.array` is nil. The iterator
  now carries a `backing` array for exactly that: the walk is unchanged, and the
  binding path has somewhere to look.
- The slot is a *property's*, so the property's declared type travels with it.
  `public string $foo` bound this way turns `42` into `"42"` and refuses an
  array, which is what `_114` checks. `notePropertyType` already did this for
  the other by-reference-over-an-object path; the store had to remember which
  object its table came from so the new path could use it too.

### Next

The other three mechanisms from the old grouping, now separated:
`list(&$x) = $arrayAccess` with a `&offsetGet` (`list/list_reference_007`, a
fatal), a generator yielding an array offset by reference, and `(array)` casting
a Closure (`bug52193`).

## 2026-08-27 — a reference survives an array copy

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3835 | 3840 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.4% | **81.5%** |
| differential cases | 785 | 786 |

Diff-set: 5 fixed (`bug38469`, `bug71756`, `bug72508`, `foreach_reference`,
`gc_032`), 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~89s.

### The rule, and where php2go was on each side of it

`$b = $a` does not flatten a reference inside `$a`: PHP carries the slot across
when two or more names hold it, and flattens it when the copy would be the last
holder. php2go's `Array.clone` was carrying *every* reference across --
including the boxes the runtime makes for its own reasons -- and never counting
the copy as a holder. So it was wrong in both directions at once: it aliased
where PHP copies, and it stopped marking a reference the moment the name that
made it went away.

Both halves are now one condition, and the four tests that moved were all about
the first half: an unshared box being carried across made a copy alias its
source.

### Where a share counter that is not a refcount shows

Flattening on its own broke `bug69376`:

```php
function &test() { $var = array(); $var[] =& $var; return $var; }
$a = test(); $b = $a; $b[0] = 123;
```

PHP keeps that reference on the copy, because `$var[0]` and `$var` are the same
box and its refcount is 2. php2go's `shared` counter tracks bindings an explicit
`&` made and loses them when frames end, so by the time the copy happened it
read 0 and the flatten produced `*RECURSION*` instead.

The fix is not a special case for cycles: a reference pointing *into* the array
being copied is held by that array, so it has a holder whatever the counter
managed to track. `heldWithin` asks exactly that, using the `seen` map the clone
already carries for recursion. Worth remembering as a pattern -- when an
approximate count is the problem, look for a structural fact that settles the
same question.

### The same rule, in the functions that rebuild

`array_values()` and `array_reverse()` follow it too, which is what
`foreach_reference` was waiting for: an array a by-reference loop left a
reference in still has it after either. Both were reading through `Each`, which
dereferences, so the box was gone before they saw it. `Array.EachRaw` hands over
the bucket as it is and `php.CopyElement` states the rule once, so the next
function that needs it does not restate it.

### Next

Other rebuilders may want `CopyElement` as well -- `array_slice`, `array_merge`,
`array_filter`, `array_splice`'s replacement half. None is currently failing a
test for it, so the evidence for each should come from a test rather than from
symmetry.

## 2026-08-27 — clearing the cheap end of the blocker list

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3826 | 3835 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 81.2% | **81.4%** |
| differential cases | 783 | 785 |
| unsupported | 198 | 189 |

Diff-set: no change to the failing set at all -- all nine came straight out of
`unsupported` into passing. Corpus wall clock ~90s.

### Four gaps, none of them deep

Read off the blocker histogram, smallest first:

- **`ZEND_VERIFY_NEVER_TYPE`** (2). The compiler puts this opcode where control
  would fall off the end of a `never` function, so *arriving* at it is the
  error -- there is nothing to check. The message names what the declaration
  was: "never-returning method" when it is one.
- **`ZEND_SEND_ARRAY` with a non-array** (2). php2go raised an
  `UnsupportedError`; the VM handler has a diagnostic of its own, and it carries
  call_user_func_array's wording because that is the only call the opcode is
  ever compiled for.
- **`new \Deprecated(...)`** (3). The attribute is an ordinary object and a
  program may build one. Its two properties are readonly, and the harvest
  already records the flag -- but the constructor writes them through
  `object.Set`, which bypasses the check, so calling `__construct` a second time
  had to refuse explicitly. `property_readonly_003` is exactly that test, and it
  is why the first version of the change moved a test from `unsupported` to
  `failed` rather than to passing.
- **`CallbackFilterIterator`** (3, plus `iterator_to_array` over one).

### The filter iterator is not an array store

php2go's engine iterators are all array-backed: they hold a table and answer
from it. This one holds another *object* and answers every question by asking
it, which is a different shape and needed its own file. Two details are worth
recording:

- The filtering is expressed through `accept()` rather than by calling the
  callback directly, because the class is open: a subclass that overrides
  `accept()` and never touches the callback still filters. The differential case
  has such a subclass.
- Three dispatch points had to learn about it -- instantiation, the direct
  method call, and `iteratorMethod` for `foreach` -- and each was a separate
  allow-list. That these lists exist three times over is a smell; the next
  engine class added will have to touch all three again.

### Next

The blocker list's cheap end is now clear. What remains at the top is
`stream_wrapper_register` (12), the deliberately-unsupported pair, the PCRE pair
(9), `parse_ini_*` (7), `highlight_string` (4) and `register_tick_function` (3).
None of those is small.

## 2026-08-27 — one IR field, two features

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3811 | 3826 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.9% | **81.2%** |
| differential cases | 782 | 783 |
| unsupported | 201 | 198 |

Diff-set: 14 fixed, 0 broken; two tests moved from `unsupported` into `failed`.
Corpus wall clock ~88s. The largest single-round gain since the foreach cursor
work.

### The field

`message ArgInfo` carried name, type, by_ref and variadic. Adding the attribute
list unblocked both features that had been waiting on it, which is why this was
worth doing as one piece rather than two.

The harvest detail that matters: the engine does **not** keep a parameter's
attributes with the parameter. They are in the *function's* one list, told apart
by `zend_attribute.offset` -- 0 for the declaration itself, position plus one
for a parameter. So reading either kind means filtering, and php2go's existing
`convertAttributes` was reading the unfiltered list: a function's
`getAttributes()` was quietly including its parameters'. Fixing the filter was a
prerequisite, not a bonus.

### `#[\SensitiveParameter]`

The rule is that the call really passed the value -- the frame is what happened
-- and it is the *rendering* that must not show it. So the frame carries a mark
rather than a substitution, and the `SensitiveParameterValue` is built only when
a trace is actually taken. Building it eagerly would consume an object handle on
every such call even when nothing ever asks for a backtrace, and handle numbers
are observable.

That decision then forced the plumbing: `traceArray` takes the factory as a
parameter, because its two callers reach a live handle by different routes --
`debug_backtrace` had to move from the ctx-only builtins to `programBuiltin` to
get one, and `throwableMethod` had to be handed one for `getTrace`. The first
version passed `nil` there, and the corpus caught it immediately: the
`debug_backtrace()` array was masked and the exception's own `getTrace()` leaked
the value one line later. Two paths to the same rendering is exactly where a
half-applied rule hides.

A variadic parameter marks every argument that reached it, since they are all
the one declaration.

### ReflectionParameter, completed

`getAttributes()` now answers, and the constructor takes the callable spellings
PHP does -- a name, a `[class, method]` pair, a Closure -- so
`new ReflectionParameter(['A', '__construct'], 'b')` works. A promoted
constructor parameter carries its attribute on both the parameter and the
property, which `bug79897` checks in one test.

### Next

`attributes/013_class_scope` and `017_closure_scope` are now failing rather than
unsupported: both want `self::class` inside an attribute written in a *trait* to
resolve to the using class. That is an attribute-argument scope question, not a
parameter one.

## 2026-08-27 — a closure made from something is a handle on it

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3804 | 3811 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.7% | **80.9%** |
| differential cases | 780 | 782 |
| unsupported | 210 | 201 |

Diff-set: 1 fixed from the failing set, and nine tests left `unsupported` --
seven of them straight to passing. Three moved into `failed`, which is the
intended direction. Corpus wall clock ~91s.

### Switching lens paid

The diff dump had flattened to nothing above four tests. The blocker histogram
had `ReflectionFunction::getClosure` at four and `::getParameters` at three, and
both turned out to be small once looked at -- which is the argument for reading
the blocker list rather than the failure list when the tail goes flat.

### A fake closure cannot be moved

`ReflectionFunction::getClosure()` and `Closure::fromCallable()` make the same
thing: a *fake* closure, a handle on a function or method that already exists
rather than a closure written as one. php2go had the concept already; what it
did not have was that PHP refuses to move such a handle. `zend_valid_closure_binding`
gates on exactly that flag, and the rules are worth stating because they are not
symmetric:

- `call()` always names a scope, so it refuses every fake closure --
  `Cannot rebind scope of closure created from function`, or `from method` when
  the closure has one.
- `bindTo($obj)` alone names no scope, so it succeeds -- unless the closure is a
  *method's* handle and the object is not one the method is on, which is
  `Cannot bind method C::m() to object of class X`.
- Unbinding a method's handle is refused outright; unbinding an ordinary
  closure is only refused when the body uses `$this`.
- A static closure refuses an instance whatever it was made from, which is the
  missing warning `closure_041` had been waiting for.

`getClosure()` on a user function also has to share the function's static
variables with every other way of calling it -- `bug75474` checks precisely
that, and it falls out of wrapping the same op_array rather than copying it.

### ReflectionParameter, as far as ArgInfo goes

`getParameters()` now answers, with a reflector holding the harvested `ArgInfo`
and the position -- which the declaration itself does not carry. One ordering
detail: the parameter case has to come *before* the function case in the
reflector dispatch, since a parameter reflector carries the function it belongs
to as well.

What it deliberately does not answer is `getAttributes()` and the default value:
`ArgInfo` has neither, and inventing an empty attribute list would be a
plausible-looking lie. Those stay honest gaps.

### Next

The `ArgInfo` attributes field is now the clearest project. It unblocks
`ReflectionParameter::getAttributes` (`bug79897`, `ctor_promotion_attributes`,
`attributes/001_placement`, `013_class_scope`, `017_closure_scope`) and the
`#[SensitiveParameter]` family the TODO has carried for several rounds
(`gh20435`, `gh20435_2`, and ~12 more) -- one IR change serving two features.

## 2026-08-27 — writing through an overloaded offset, and three answers to one append

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3803 | 3804 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.7% | 80.7% |
| differential cases | 779 | 780 |

Diff-set: 1 fixed (`ArrayAccess_indirect_append`), 0 broken. A thin round: the
family looked like four tests and three of them turned out to be blocked on
something else.

### The notice php2go had for properties but not for offsets

`$o[$k][$j] = x` descends through offsetGet, which hands back a *value*, so the
write reaches a copy and PHP says `Indirect modification of overloaded element
of C has no effect`. The rule is the same one `overloadedWriteFetch` already
implements for properties: a reference is the class saying otherwise, an object
is one already, anything else earns the notice and is copied so the write really
does go nowhere.

Two details that only showed up by probing:

- offsetGet is a call, and a call moves the reported location. The notice
  belongs to the modification site, not to the accessor's body -- the same
  save-and-restore the property version does.
- An accessor that *threw* earns the notice too. The engine reports what the
  descent produced before it looks at whether anything was thrown, so the
  notice is printed and the exception then propagates.

### An append passes the accessor three different things

`$c[]` on an ArrayAccess is not one behaviour:

- A plain PHP class is called with **null**: the standard handler turns the
  missing dimension into one.
- An engine array store -- ArrayObject and its kin -- is **not called at all**.
  Its handler is given no dimension and has nothing to look up, which is why
  `$ao[][5] = 'v'` gives the notice and no `Undefined array key ""`, while
  `$ao->offsetGet(null)` written out *does* warn.
- A PHP class *extending* one of those keeps the engine's handler, which hands
  the override an **undefined** argument -- so it is called with no arguments,
  and a required parameter makes that `Argument #1 ($offset) not passed` (the
  hole's diagnostic, not "Too few arguments to function").

php2go now models all three. The third is unreachable today for a separate
reason: `class B extends ArrayObject` never gets the array store attached at
all, so `$b[0]` is an unsupported opcode. That is its own gap, recorded in the
TODO -- it blocks few tests, but it is why two of this round's four did not move.

### `[]` is refused before what it was for

`$r = &$text[]` on a string reports `[] operator not supported for strings`, not
`Cannot create references to/from string offsets`: an append names no offset at
all, and that is what PHP complains about first. php2go had the two arms of
`scalarIndexError` in the other order.

### Next

The blocker histogram is now the better lens than the diff dump.
`stream_wrapper_register` blocks 12 tests, `parse_ini_string` and
`parse_ini_file` together 7, `preg_match` and `preg_replace_callback` together
9. The INI pair is self-contained; the PCRE pair needs a regex dialect Go's
`regexp` does not have.

## 2026-08-27 — the small diagnostic families, and what "starts with an integer" means

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3797 | 3803 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.6% | **80.7%** |
| differential cases | 777 | 779 |

Diff-set: 6 fixed (`010`, `bug73792`, `get_parent_class_001`,
`iap_on_object_deprecated`, `numeric_strings/string_offset`, `offset_assign`),
0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~88s.

### The internal array pointer walks an object

`reset()`, `current()`, `key()`, `next()`, `end()`, `prev()` and `pos()` accept
an object and walk its property table, with a deprecation naming the function
twice -- once as the diagnostic's owner and once inside it:
`reset(): Calling reset() on an object is deprecated`. php2go answered false for
anything that was not an array.

### get_parent_class is declared wider than it accepts

`object|string|null` in the signature, and it rejects every string that does not
name a class -- *and* null, which is the default that same signature gives the
parameter. So the generic check against the harvested type reports the wrong
thing, and the function has to word the refusal itself:
`must be an object or a valid class name, %s given`. That is now a named
exception (`ownArgumentDiagnostics`) rather than a special case buried in the
loop, since the pattern will recur.

Calling it with no arguments at all is separately deprecated.

### "Starts with an integer" is whatever is_numeric_string read

`$str["7str"]` is offset 7 with `Warning: Illegal string offset "7str"`, and
php2go had that. What it had wrong was the boundary, which is not a hand-rolled
scan but the answer `is_numeric_string_ex` gives with errors allowed:

- Leading whitespace is allowed, so `"  7str"` warns rather than throwing.
- Trailing whitespace is not trailing data, so `"  7  "` is a clean offset.
- A prefix that turns out to be a *float* is no offset at all: `"7.5str"` reads
  as a double with trailing data, and a double is refused outright. `"7e2"` is
  a double; `"7e"` is the integer 7 with the trailing data `"e"`.
- An integer too large to fit is reported as a double, so it is refused too.

The differential case walks all of those boundaries, which is the only way to be
sure of a rule with this many corners.

### The offset is checked before the descent is refused

`$held["2bbb"][] = 1` and `$r = &$held["2ccc"]` both end in a fatal, and both
warn about the offset first: `zend_check_string_offset` runs before the refusal.
php2go threw the fatal straight from the write-fetch path. Unsetting is the one
form that checks quietly, which the handler's own `type != BP_VAR_UNSET` guard
says and the code now mirrors.

### A wording the differential cannot check

The IAP deprecation names the active internal function, and under `eval` there
is none -- the engine prints "PHP Request Startup" where a real file prints
`reset()`. So the differential case silences the deprecation and checks only
that the pointer walks the table; the `.phpt` corpus checks the wording. Worth
remembering: the oracle runs code through eval, and a diagnostic that names its
own frame will differ there for reasons that are not php2go's.

### Next

The missing-diagnostic sweep still lists
`Notice: Indirect modification of overloaded element` for an ArrayAccess offset
(4 tests) -- php2go has the property-level version but not the offset-level one
-- and `Warning: Resource ID#%d used as offset` (one test, six occurrences).

Four tests. `$o->x` where the class declares `static $x` is not redirected to
the static: the object grows a dynamic property of its own, the static keeps its
value, and PHP only says that what was written is not what the class declares.

Two conditions decide whether it says it, and both were found by probing rather
than by reading the handler:

- A subclass declaring an instance property of the same name wins, and there is
  nothing to complain about (`bug79862` is exactly this test).
- A class with the matching magic accessor says nothing: `__set` answers the
  write, so nothing falls through to a property of the instance's own.

It fires for a read, a write, a compound, an increment, an unset and a

that is `checkPropertyWrite`, `checkPropertyUnset`, the `FETCH_OBJ_R` handler

`ignorableIni` listed `error_reporting` as a setting "about how the *engine*

producing *correctly*.

carried one). The setting stays in `ignorableIni` so the tests still run rather
than becoming skips -- what changed is that it is honoured rather than ignored.

Worth remembering as a class of bug: a harness that disregards a test's
configuration turns correct behaviour into a failure, and the failure looks like
a runtime gap.

## 2026-08-27 — arity, callbacks that cannot hand over a slot, and names that survive into a frame

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3782 | 3791 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.3% | **80.5%** |
| differential cases | 771 | 776 |
| unsupported | 211 | 210 |

Diff-set: 9 fixed (`bug67856`, `bug72107`, `bug79979`,
`function_arguments/argument_count_incorrect_internal{,_strict}`,
`function_arguments/gh20435_2`, `named_params/backtrace`, and the two counted
from the intermediate run), 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~87s.

### The arity check was never written

An internal function reports the wrong number of arguments before it looks at
any of them, and the wording is mechanical -- `zend_wrong_parameters_count_error`
picks "exactly" when there is no choice, "at least" when too few arrived, "at
most" when too many did, names whichever bound was missed, and drops the plural
only when that number is one. `verifyBuiltinArity` is a transcription of it, on
top of the harvested `required_args` / `variadic` that were already there.

One guard matters: a call whose argument slots still contain `Undef` holes is a
named-argument call whose defaults have not been applied, and counting slots
there would report an arity the call does not have.

The check moved `array_multisort` from `unsupported` to `failed` -- the right
error with the wrong stack trace -- which is the intended direction and is what
led to the frame work below.

### An internal function has no slots to hand over

`function(&$a, &$b)` passed to `array_reduce` earns a warning per parameter per
call, because the call is assembled in C with no caller slots in it. php2go had
this machinery already (`noteUserCallByRef`) but applied it only to
`call_user_func`; every other Go-side dispatch went through `in.callValue`
silently. Generalising it needs one extra condition the `call_user_func` version
does not: skip the argument that *is* a reference, since `array_walk` genuinely
hands its callback the element.

The warning's location is the call the script made, not wherever the callee's
body left the reported line the previous time round the internal function's
loop -- so it is taken from the innermost script stack frame.

The same warning was missing for a *named* argument arriving through
`SEND_ARRAY`: `call_user_func_array("str_replace", [..., "count" => $x])` lands
on a by-reference parameter just as a positional argument would.

### A name survives into the stack frame

`test(1, 2, x: 3, y: 4)` renders as exactly that in a trace, and
`debug_backtrace()` reports `x` and `y` under string keys. php2go dropped the
names when it built the frame, so a variadic callee's extra named arguments
vanished from every backtrace.

`php.StackFrame` now carries `ArgNames` for the *trailing* extras only, which is
the whole of it: a named argument that found a parameter is rendered
positionally, because that is where it landed. `test(b: 1, a: 2, c: 3)` on
`test($a, ...$x)` prints `test(2, b: 1, c: 3)`. An empty name is a name --
`call_user_func_array($f, ["" => 1])` renders `: 1` -- which is why the model
needs "named" and "not named" to be distinguishable rather than testing for an
empty string.
