Left in the family: class-typed user parameters on the dispatch paths that skip
them (`bug43332_1`, `objects_022`), the `could not be passed by reference` fatal
a literal earns, and `named_params/missing_param`. `bug51827` wants an
`ArgumentCountError` raised at shutdown to report `[no active file]`.

## 2026-08-27 — the call site's file decides, and a folded opcode still owes the check

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3776 | 3782 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.1% | **80.3%** |
| differential cases | 768 | 771 |

Diff-set: 6 fixed (`call_user_func_array_array_slice_type{,_strict}`,
`call_user_func_by_ref`, `recv_init_ref_type`,
`type_declarations/internal_function_strict_mode`,
`unpack_iterator_by_ref_type_check`), 0 broken. Corpus wall clock ~88s.

### strict_types was never reaching an internal call

`verifyBuiltinArgs` passed `false` for strict, with a comment claiming the
corpus that depends on strict mode uses user functions. It does not:
`declare(strict_types=1); strlen(1)` is a TypeError, and php2go returned 1. The
rule is not "internal functions coerce"; it is "the file the *call* is written
in decides", and that is the same rule user functions already followed through
`unit.pending.strict`.

Three dispatch paths reach a builtin and each needed the flag: the FCALL
handler (from the op_array being executed, since the INIT opcode already stores
the same value), the frameless ICALL path, and the specialized opcodes
(`ZEND_STRLEN` and friends). The frameless path had also never set
`resultUnused`, which last round's `array_splice` work depends on.

Strict mode also removes the one place internal and user functions differed:
null for a non-nullable parameter earns a deprecation in weak mode and a
TypeError in strict.

### A by-reference parameter is bound, but its type is still checked

`verifyArgument` returned early for a by-reference parameter, reasoning that
replacing the binding with a coerced copy would break the write-through. True,
but the check is not the conversion: `function f(array &$r)` called as `f($x)`
with `$x = 1` throws, and calling it with a variable that does not exist yet
throws *for null* rather than quietly binding an empty slot. So the check runs
and its converted value is dropped.

### A folded opcode inherits the checks of what it folded

`call_user_func_array($f, array_slice($a, N, $len))` does not compile to two
calls. The compiler emits one `ZEND_SEND_ARRAY` with the length in op2 and the
offset in `extended_value`, and slices while it sends. php2go implemented the
opcode's plain form only, so the whole array went through and array_slice's
`?int` check on `$length` -- which the VM handler performs itself, in
array_slice's own wording -- never happened.

The general shape is worth keeping in mind: an opcode the compiler produced by
folding a call away owes every diagnostic that call would have made. Reading
`zend_vm_def.h` for the handler is what settled the semantics here -- the
`skip`/`len` clamping, and that the fold is only valid because array_slice runs
with `preserve_keys` false.

### Next

Still open in the same family: the internal `Warning: f(): Argument #N ($x)
must be passed by reference, value given` for a by-reference *internal*
parameter, the arity checks (`expects exactly N arguments`), and class-typed
user parameters on the dispatch paths that still skip them.

## 2026-08-27 — array_splice moves the iterator by walking, and a callable type is a lookup

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3770 | 3776 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 80.0% | **80.1%** |
| differential cases | 766 | 768 |

Diff-set: 6 fixed (`bug31720`, `bug70895`, `bug70898`, `exception_handler_004`,
`foreach_017`, `type_declarations/callable_001`), 0 broken. Corpus wall clock
unchanged at ~89s.

### array_splice does not shift a live position, it drags it

Last round gave a by-reference `foreach` a live cursor and taught `Prepend` and
`Renumber` to move it. `array_splice` was the obvious next holder, and the
obvious rule -- before the removed run keep your place, inside it land after it,
after it move by the length difference -- fits six of the eight shapes and is
wrong about the other two.

The differential caught it. `php_splice` does not compute a new position; it
walks the buckets rebuilding the array and carries the cursor along with the
element it is on, one element at a time. Two consequences fall out of the walk
rather than out of any rule:

- An insertion in front of a cursor drags it forward *again at every element
  after the insertion*, because the walk re-finds the same iterator at its new
  position each time. `foreach ($a as &$v) { ... array_splice($a, 0, 0, ["x"]); }`
  therefore jumps straight to the last element rather than repeating one.
- Whether the caller keeps the return value changes the iteration.
  `array_splice($a, 1, 2)` and `$r = array_splice($a, 1, 2)` count the removed
  elements into different variables, and the second ends the loop where the
  first continues it. This is not a subtlety of PHP semantics; it is what the
  two branches of the C function do.

So `Array.Splice` is a port of the walk, not an implementation of a rule, and
`Ctx.ResultUsed()` had to be plumbed (`unit.resultUnused`, set from the FCALL
opline's result type) so the builtin can tell the two branches apart. The
engine's `zend_hash_iterators_clamp_max` -- deleting the last bucket pulls every
position back to the new end -- is in there too; `array_splice($a, 0, count($a),
["x"])` needs it to land on the replacement.

Two smaller facts came out of the same port: the removed array receives the
*slot*, so an element the loop is holding arrives in it still marked `&`; and
the rebuilt array must carry buckets across rather than values, or the reference
the loop variable holds is quietly severed.

### A `callable` parameter is a lookup, not a shape check

`matchesType` accepted any string, array or object for `callable`, with a
comment saying the lookup belongs to the call. It does not: PHP resolves the
callable to check the type, and `f("no_such_function")` throws at the call site.
`callableReason` already knew how to say why something is not callable -- it
just returned "" for a plain function name without checking the name existed.

The wording differs by who is asking, which is why one predicate serves both:

- a user parameter typed `callable` gets the ordinary
  `must be of type callable, string given`;
- an internal function gets `must be a valid callback or null, function "x" not
  found or invalid function name`, and the `or null` is there only when the
  declared type admits null.

Since the check resolves the callable, it also reports the deprecated spellings
-- and the call resolves it again afterwards, so everything doubled. The
existing `quiet` flag threaded through `callableClassQuiet` /
`noteCompoundCallable` already models exactly this; `callableReasonQuiet` joins
it. A predicate that reports diagnostics is not a predicate.

The differential also turned up two neighbours: `["C", "m"]` for a non-static
`m` is refused *unless* the calling frame has a `$this` that is a `C`, which is
how `["C", "parent::m"]` works from inside a method; and `array_map(null, $one)`
returns the array, not a list of one-element tuples.

### Next

The internal-argument-type family is the largest one left (28 tests, from a
sweep of the diff dump): strict-mode checking for internal calls, the
`must be passed by reference, value given` warning, and user-function class-type
checks that some dispatch paths skip.

## 2026-08-27 — a by-reference foreach holds a position, not a list

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3759 | 3770 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 79.8% | **80.0%** |
| differential cases | 765 | 766 |

Diff-set: 11 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock unchanged at ~90s.

### The keys were snapshotted

php2go took `array.Keys()` at FE_RESET and stepped through them, skipping any
that had since been removed. That is right for a by-*value* loop, which iterates
a copy. A by-reference loop does not: PHP keeps a live position in the hash, so

    $a = ['foo'];
    foreach ($a as $k => &$v) { unset($a[$k]); $a[] = 'foo'; ... }

visits 0, 1, 2, … forever, and php2go visited only 0. `Array.LiveNext` walks
buckets from a position instead, and the loop uses it whenever the reset was
`ZEND_FE_RESET_RW`.

### And a position has to be moved when the array is rebuilt

That change alone hung `foreach_016`: `array_unshift` rebuilds the bucket list,
so a bucket index means nothing afterwards and the loop restarted from the
front. PHP registers its hash iterators *with the hash* and repositions them on
a rehash, and this now does the same -- narrowly, for the two operations that
rebuild:

    Prepend    every existing element shifts right by the number inserted
    Renumber   an element keeps its place among the *live* ones

Which is enough for the loop to end after the elements it started with. The
array is told about a live cursor at FE_RESET_RW and told to forget it at
FE_FREE.

### Finding it

The corpus run stopped terminating, which the ten-minute timeout reported as a
failure of the whole measurement rather than of a test. Bisecting the file list
by halves and then by twenties found `foreach_016` in about a minute; guessing
from the change would have taken longer and might have missed it.

### `#[\Deprecated(1234)]` constructs something

php2go read the attribute's arguments and rendered them, which is right for the
common case -- without `strict_types` an int or a float coerces, and
`#[\Deprecated(1234)]` really does report "deprecated, 1234". What it never did
was *refuse*: using what the attribute marks constructs a `Deprecated`, and its
`?string $message` is checked like any other parameter. Under `strict_types`
nothing but a string passes, and an array or an object never passes at all.

Making that reachable meant threading an error out of `deprecationSuffix`
through `noteDeprecatedCall*` to the nine places that report a deprecation. Two
of those are the call paths, which can raise; the rest cannot and do not need to.

Two details the tests pinned down. The frame is `Deprecated->__construct(...)`
and it points at the *call site* -- the engine constructs the attribute where
the marked symbol was used, not in an internal function. And the pending call
has already been popped by the time the deprecation is reported, so popping it
again is a panic, which is what the first attempt did.

### An enum case in a trace is written as the case

`Deprecated->__construct(Random\IntervalBoundary::ClosedOpen)`, not
`Object(Random\IntervalBoundary)`. That is a general rule and it fixed
`enum_in_stack_trace` as well, which had nothing to do with attributes.

`gc_status` (5 tests) reports a root-buffer threshold and a running flag from a
collector php2go does not have -- it walks on demand rather than buffering
roots. Most of the array would be invented. Together with `debug_zval_dump`
that is twelve tests reachable only by reporting numbers php2go cannot know.

## 2026-08-27 — exit flushes where it stands

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3754 | 3755 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 79.7% | 79.7% |
| differential cases | 764 | 764 |

Diff-set: 1 fixed, 0 broken. The last of the six output-buffering tests.

### Three things one test wanted

`exit/exit_string_with_buffer_output` needed all of these, and each is a rule on
its own:

*exit() flushes the buffers where it stands.* php2go drained them after the
shutdown functions, by which point the `try` around the exit is long gone. The
engine flushes at the exit, so a filter that throws there is catchable at the
exit site. `exit` and `die` moved out of the plain builtin map for it -- running
a filter needs the interpreter.

*A filter that throws writes the original.* Failing is not the same as producing
nothing: what the filter was handed goes out unchanged, exactly as returning
`false` would, and the throw travels on. That is true both when the buffer ends
and when a chunk overflows mid-write.

*`fwrite(STDOUT, ...)` is the request's output.* php2go wrote it to `os.Stdout`
directly, which is neither what the harness captures nor what a program means.
It goes through the context now -- but past the output buffers, because writing
to STDOUT is not `echo` and `ob_start` does not capture it.

### A gap left as a gap

`debug_zval_dump` is now the second-largest blocker at seven tests, and roughly
half of those wildcard the refcount it prints. Implementing it as var_dump plus
a plausible-looking `refcount(N)` would pass those and be a lie: php2go has no
refcounts and cannot have one to report. It stays unsupported.

## 2026-08-27 — an output buffer's filter

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3749 | 3754 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 79.6% | 79.7% |
| unsupported | 217 | 211 |
| differential cases | 764 | 764 |

Six tests left `unsupported`; five pass and one
(`exit/exit_string_with_buffer_output`) still fails. Diff-set: nothing
previously failing changed either way.

### ob_start with a callback

Probed rather than assumed, because the rules are not symmetric:

    ob_end_flush()      the filter's return replaces what is written out
    return false        the original buffer is written instead
    return null         an empty string -- null is cast, not treated as false
    ob_get_clean()      answers the *raw* buffer, and still runs the filter
    ob_get_flush()      writes the filtered text, returns the raw
    ob_end_clean()      runs the filter and throws the result away

The five functions that can involve a callback moved out of the plain builtin
map, which only gets a `*php.Ctx`, into the interpreter-aware path.

### A buffer nobody closed

php2go simply lost the contents: `ob_start(); echo "x";` with no matching end
printed nothing. The engine flushes every open buffer when the request ends,
innermost first and through its filter -- and a filter that throws there reaches
the exception handler, which is what `gh10695_6` checks.

### A chunk size is not a hint

`ob_start($cb, 10)` runs the callback *per chunk*, and a program can count the
calls -- which is exactly what the two tests that wanted it do. The check lives
in `Ctx.Write`, which cannot call a PHP callable, so the interpreter installs a
flusher the same way it installs the error handler. Two details it needs: the
filter's output belongs to the level *below* the buffer, and a write from inside
the filter must not re-enter the check.

### A limitation of the differential harness

An output-buffering case cannot be compared this way. What the engine leaves in
an unclosed buffer is written at shutdown, after php2eval has stopped capturing,
so the engine side comes back empty or out of order. The case written for this
round was removed for that reason; `Zend/tests` is what covers it.

## 2026-08-27 — a named argument occupies a slot

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3734 | 3738 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 79.2% | 79.3% |
| unsupported | 231 | 222 |
| differential cases | 759 | 761 |

Nine tests left `unsupported`: four now pass and **five now fail**. Reported
together because that is what the counts mean -- unblocking a gap moves a test
into `failed` until the behaviour behind it is right too. Diff-set against the
previous round: 0 previously-failing tests fixed, 0 broken.

### The composition walk was not needed anywhere else

Last round's `traitComposition` was worth checking against the other listings.
`class_uses`, `method_exists`, `property_exists`, `is_callable` and calling an
alias through a nested trait all already agree with the engine. Two reflection
methods -- `getMethods` and `getConstants` -- are unsupported rather than wrong.

### Three gaps closed

*`ZEND_ASSIGN_STATIC_PROP_OP`* had no handler at all: `C::$p += 1` was a gap.
Like the instance form it reads before it writes, so an uninitialized typed
static is an Error, and the result faces the declared type.

*String keys in an unpacked array* are named arguments -- `f(...['b' => 20])`.
php2go refused both spellings (`...$array` and `call_user_func_array`).

*A positional argument after a named one, within the same array*, is an Error,
and the two spellings word it differently: `Cannot use positional argument after
named argument during unpacking` for `...`, without the clause for
call_user_func_array.

### The part that was not obvious

A named argument does not sit *beside* the positional ones -- it **occupies its
parameter's slot**:

    f(...['b' => 20], ...[7])   // engine: a=1, b=20, c=7

The 7 does not become the first argument; it takes the slot after the one the
name filled. So an unpacked name is placed positionally, padding the slots
before it, rather than deferred to the named list. Two consequences had to be
handled: a name landing on a slot that already holds an argument is the
"overwrites previous argument" error, and the padding must *not* count as
filled -- `func1(...$args, a2: 'm2+')` needs the later name to take a padded
slot. That second one cost a passing test until `applyNamedArguments` learned to
read padding as free.

- `typed_properties_075`, `typed_properties_102`: the overflow message for an
  increment through a typed property says "a reference held by property" where
  the engine says "property".
- `bug79979`: output stops early.

### Result

### get_class_methods did not list aliases

`use T { m as n; }` adds the name `n`, and calling it worked -- the lookup has
always resolved aliases -- but `get_class_methods` never mentioned it. The alias
may also be declared on a *trait* the class composes rather than on the class
itself, so the whole composition has to be walked; `traitComposition` in
`class.go` is that walk, and it is the sort of thing other listings may want.

### The order took two tries and a second test to settle

A first version listed aliases before the trait's methods and fixed
`bug64239_1` while breaking `bug65579`; moving them after did the reverse. The
two tests disagree because they are different shapes:

    class A { use T { m as n; } }            n, then m
    trait C { use P { m as n; } function m() {} }
    class B { use C; }                        m, then n

So it is not "aliases first" or "aliases last". A holder's own methods come
first, then the aliases its own `use` clause introduced -- applied to the class
and to each trait alike. Both orders fall out of that.

Having two tests that disagreed was what made the rule findable. One alone would
have been satisfied by the wrong answer.

### A virtual property is not a class variable

`public $c { get => 42; }` has no backing store, so `get_class_vars` does not
list it. A *backed* hooked property is listed -- with its declared default, not
with what the get hook would answer, since there is no instance to run one on.

`$fn->call(new stdClass)` warns `Cannot bind closure to scope of internal class
stdClass` and answers null. php2go bound it and ran the body. The rule is about
the *scope*, not the instance: `call()` always sets the scope to the object's
class, and `Closure::bind($fn, $obj, Internal::class)` names one outright, but
`bindTo($obj)` with no second argument keeps the closure's own scope and is fine
whatever `$obj` is. `isBuiltinOnly` already knew which classes those are.

`call_user_func` hands its arguments over by value, so a callee that wanted a
slot gets a copy -- reported once per such parameter. php2go reported it for
`\call_user_func(...)` and not for `call_user_func(...)` written unqualified
inside a namespace, and the difference is entirely in the compiler:

    \call_user_func('f', $x)   INIT_FCALL + SEND_USER   -- folded to a direct call
    call_user_func('f', $x)    INIT_NS_FCALL_BY_NAME    -- a call to the builtin

php2go marked the folded form at `SEND_USER`, where the pending call *is* the
callee. In the unfolded form the pending call is `call_user_func` itself and the
callee is reached from Go, so the marking had to go there instead --
`callValueFor`, which every such builtin goes through.

A first attempt marked the pending call at INIT instead, which was wrong for the
same reason: that call is the builtin, not the callee, so nothing looked at its
parameters.

### Result

| metric | before | after |

| `Zend/tests` passing | 3722 | 3728 |

| handle-only failures | 25 → 15 | 15 → 11 |

### A receiver in a temporary is let go of by the call

`(new ReflectionClass(C))->getAttributes()[0]->newInstance()` gave the new
attribute object handle 3 where the engine gives it 1. The receiver of
`ZEND_INIT_METHOD_CALL` arrives in a temporary rather than through a SEND --
the same shape as the `INIT_USER_CALL` callee fixed last round -- so nothing
ever let go of it and its handle never reached the free list.

### The static key could not tell two methods apart

Chasing one of the remaining handle differences turned up something else
entirely. `staticKey` was file + function name + variable name, and that is not
unique:

    class Base { static function c() { static $n = 0; return ++$n; } }
    class Over extends Base { static function c() { static $n = 100; ... } }
    // both are "c" in one file -- php2go had them sharing $n

and a trait's method is *one* op_array composed into every class that uses it,
so `U1::c()` and `U2::c()` shared a counter where PHP gives each its own.

Both are the same missing piece, and the fix is one line: file the static under
the **declaring scope**. An inherited method's scope is the class that declared
it, so `Base::c()` and `Sub::c()` still share -- which is what PHP does. A
trait's method resolves with the *using* class as its scope, so each user gets
its own copy -- which is also what PHP does. The distinction php2go needed was
already sitting in `f.class`.

### Worth remembering

The override case was not on any list. It surfaced because the probe written for
the trait question happened to declare a second `c()` in the same file, and the
answer came back 45 where the engine said 1014. A probe that covers the
neighbouring shapes, not just the one being asked about, is worth the extra
three lines.

| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 78.7% | 79.0% |
| differential cases | 752 | 753 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 15 fixed, 0 broken. Corpus wall clock
unchanged at ~87s.

### 25 tests differed only in `#N`

Counting them was the first useful step: normalising `object(C)#N` on both sides
and re-comparing showed 25 failures whose *only* difference was an object
handle. That is the largest coherent group left, and the TODO item that has sat
open longest.

### Why a handle was never freed

`releaseTemp` decided whether dropping an argument was worth a walk, and said no
twice over: it ignored `VAR` slots -- and `ZEND_NEW` puts its result in one --
and for an object it asked `hasDestructorPending`. A `Point` with no destructor
was never worth collecting, so its handle never reached the free list, so the
next `new` got a fresh one. Both gates were about destructor timing; handle
reuse is observable without any destructor at all.

### Three things that had to be true at once

Lifting those gates broke seven tests, and each was the same shape: an object
that is legitimately live but that nothing the walk can see is holding.

*An engine class under construction.* `unit.building` protects an object between
ZEND_NEW and the end of its constructor -- but only when the class has a *user*
`__construct`. `new Fiber(...)` has a builtin one, so the fiber was collected
between its own construction and the assignment that stored it, and by the time
`unset($fiber)` came round php2go had already forgotten it existed.

*The object being constructed, at the release point after the constructor.* The
check held aside the call's return value, which for a constructor is null. What
needed holding is `ctorObject`.

*A call's arguments are dropped whether it succeeded or not.* `call_user_func(new
C)` where C is not callable still lets go of the C -- inside the `try` that is
open, which is where its destructor's throw has to land. php2go released it at
the next statement instead, one line too late. The callee of
`ZEND_INIT_USER_CALL` arrives in a temporary rather than through a SEND, so that
opcode's error path is the only place that can let go of it.

### Worth remembering

The instrumentation that settled it was three `println` calls in the collector
printing whether a fiber was reachable at each walk. The answer -- *one* walk,
before the fiber was ever started -- pointed straight at the constructor gap.
Reasoning about which root should have covered it produced four wrong theories
first.

### protected(set) has the same first-declaration rule

Last round's finding applies to asymmetric visibility unchanged: a sibling may
*write* what it inherited from the same parent, and redeclaring `protected(set)`
in a subclass does not narrow that. `checkSetVisibility` now asks
`protectedOwner` the same question `propertyAccess` does.

### readonly names the class that declared the property

    class A { public readonly int $v; ... }
    class B extends A {}
    (new B)->v = 2;   // Cannot modify readonly property A::$v

php2go named the instance's class. The message is about the declaration, not
about the object -- nothing regarding the instance is at fault -- and the engine
says so even when the property was promoted through a constructor.

### What the sweep did *not* find

`__get` reachability from a sibling scope needed nothing: a protected property
that is visible is read directly, and one that is not falls through to `__get`,
and php2go already had both. Reading a readonly property from anywhere was
already right too.

### Next: object handle reuse

`object_array_cast` and `static_variable_in_private_trait_method` both come down
to the engine handing a freed object's handle to the next `new` where php2go
does not. The obstacle is not the free list -- `unit.freeHandles` exists and
works -- but that no release point fires between two statements when the value
being dropped was only ever in a temporary. That is the ~20-test TODO item, and
it is the same "temporaries are not roots" boundary the last two rounds have
been working along.

### The temporary sweep the last round asked for came back clean

Six more shapes where an object lives only in a temporary -- `foreach ([new A,
new B] as $v)`, a method chain on `(new A)->m(new B)`, a concat of two objects
with `__toString`, an array union of two literals, two locals in flight, a
ternary -- all match. The array literal was the only one with a hole.

The one difference is a lag rather than a hole: in `(new D(11))->n > 0 ? new
D(12) : null` the engine releases D(11) before constructing D(12), php2go one
instruction later. That is the "answer reachability by walking when asked"
model, and nothing is destroyed early or kept past its container.

### Redeclaring a protected property does not narrow it

    abstract class P { protected $foo; }
    class C1 extends P { protected $foo = 1; }
    class C2 extends P {
        static function foo($c) { return $c->foo; }   // engine: fine on a C1
    }

php2go measured the access against `prop->DeclaringClass`, which for `C1::$foo`
is C1 -- and C2 is not a C1. The class that matters is the *first* one to
declare the name: redeclaring in a subclass does not start a new scope, which is
what lets one child of an abstract parent read the property off another child.

A private declaration in between *does* end the chain -- the child's protected
declaration is a different member as far as visibility goes -- so the walk stops
there rather than running to the top.

Static properties had the same gap and now share the helper. Protected *methods*
were already right, which is worth knowing: `effectiveVisibility` walks for them
and `propertyAccess` did not.

## 2026-08-26 — an array literal is only in a temporary

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3705 | 3705 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 78.6% | 78.6% |
| differential cases | 749 | 750 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 0 fixed, 0 broken. The fix is a correctness
one the corpus does not cover; the differential case added for it does.

### The elements were being destroyed while the literal was still being built

    $ar = [new A(1), new A(2), new A(3)];
    // php2go: ctor 1, ctor 2, dtor 1, ctor 3, dtor 2 ... and $ar held
    //         three objects whose destructors had already run

`marker.frame` deliberately excludes temporaries -- php2go does not clear them,
so every object a statement ever built would look reachable for the rest of the
frame's life. The comment listed what it believed was covered instead: the call
being assembled, the iterator being walked, the exception in flight. An array
literal is none of those. It lives *only* in a temporary between INIT_ARRAY and
whatever consumes it, and a constructor running for a later element is a release
point.

The frame now tracks the literals it is assembling, with the temporary each one
lives in, and an entry is dropped when an opcode **reads** that temporary --
which is exactly when the literal has gone somewhere that keeps it. That is
precise rather than approximate: no literal is retained past the statement that
consumed it.

### Two wrong versions before the right one

Both were caught by the corpus and the differential, and both are worth
recording because they are the obvious things to try:

*Clearing the literals at ZEND_ASSIGN, SEND and RETURN.* The SEND clear fires
for the *next element's constructor argument*, dropping the literal while its
elements are still only in it -- so nothing changed at all.

*Reading only the current opline.* A split opcode keeps its value half in the
following OP_DATA line, so `$map[$obj] = [$obj]` never consumed the literal and
four weakref tests broke: the frame kept `$obj` alive after `$obj = null`.

### And one thing the differential cannot assert

`$m[$k] = [$k]; $k = null; count($m)` answers 1 in the engine and 0 here,
because php2go answers reachability by walking when asked and the engine waits
for the cycle collector. The `weakrefs/gh10043-*` tests cover the shape properly
-- they call `gc_collect_cycles()` first -- so the differential case stops short
of it.

### Result

### The sweep the last round asked for came back clean

Twelve shapes where a diagnostic is raised mid-operation and a user error
handler throws -- an append reading a missing key, a string offset out of range,
a float array key, an array-to-string conversion, a property read on null, a
foreach over a scalar -- all match. The three sites patched last round were the
load-bearing ones.

### Every destructor runs; the last exception is the one that escapes

php2go already ran the remaining destructors after one threw, but kept the
*first* exception. The engine keeps the last and hangs the earlier ones off it
as causes, which is what it prints as "Next Exception":

    $ar = [new A(1), new A(2), new A(3)];   // each __destruct throws
    unset($ar);                             // engine: caught E3, then E2, E1

`chainOnto` in `gc.go` does the linking, with the same two guards `frame.raise`
uses: no link when the newer exception already has a cause, and none that would
close a loop.

### `[constant expression]` is a frame, but not for everything

A diagnostic raised inside a deferred initializer names `[constant expression]`
above the site that triggered it. The first attempt pushed that frame for every
unfolded literal and broke 25 tests. Probed, the rule is narrower:

    static property default     [constant expression]
    instance property default   [constant expression]
    class constant              no frame
    parameter default           the function's own frame

So the push belongs at the property-default site in `updateClassConstants`, not
in `constantLiteral` where every kind passes through.

### Two traps, one of them for the second time

A differential case must not print a closure's name: `{closure:FILE:LINE}`
embeds the path, and the harness does not normalise it. This is recorded two
entries above and I walked into it again -- use named functions in any case that
prints a trace.

And php2go releases the first element of `[new A(1), new A(2)]` while the
literal is still being built, so A(1)'s destructor runs inside A(2)'s
constructor. `exception_008` passes because it destroys at shutdown; the
in-literal timing is a separate gap, now in TODO.

## 2026-08-26 — the opcode that raised it does not finish

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3699 | 3702 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 78.5% | 78.6% |
| differential cases | 746 | 748 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 3 fixed, 0 broken.

### array_unique has a comparison mode, and php2go had one

`array_unique($a, SORT_REGULAR)` was ignoring the flag and comparing string
casts, so every object collapsed into one element -- an enum list of eight cases
came back with one. The three modes differ:

    SORT_STRING (the default)   compares string casts
    SORT_NUMERIC               compares as floats
    SORT_REGULAR               compares with ==

Only the regular mode needs the values compared against each other rather than
hashed: PHP's `==` is not an equivalence relation, so it cannot be reduced to a
key. Each kept value is compared against instead.

### A throw during a write means the write did not happen

php2go parks the exception a user error handler throws and picks it up at the
*next* opcode boundary -- "the opcode that raised it completes". That is the
right default for a diagnostic raised at the end of an operation, and wrong for
one raised in the middle of it:

    set_error_handler(fn() => throw new Exception());
    $test = [];
    $test[0] .= "xyz";      // engine: $test stays empty
                            // php2go: $test[0] === "xyz"

The read half of a compound assignment reports the missing key *before* the
write half runs, so the throw has to be picked up between them. Three sites now
do that: the two compound-assignment paths and the key computation in
ZEND_ASSIGN_DIM, which is where the float-precision deprecation is raised.

The differential case written for it caught the next thing straight away: for a
*property* the slot is made before the reports are handed out, so the object is
left holding `["missing"] => NULL` rather than nothing at all.

### `$GLOBALS["x"]` is not an array access

The compiler turns it into a fetch by name against the global symbol table,
which is why a missing name is `Undefined global variable $x` rather than
`Undefined array key "x"`. php2go had that for the plain read and not for the
read-modify-write form, which binds the slot -- and reads it first.

### Method order is observable, and `convertMethods` was sorting it away

`get_class_methods` and reflection report a class's methods in the order they
were declared. `convertMethods` in the harvester sorted them by name -- which
put `__construct` first in every class that has one, and `aa` before `zz`
everywhere. Removing that one line fixed four tests outright and two more in
passing.

The `sort.Slice` was presumably there for determinism. It was not needed: the
engine's function table is insertion-ordered and `php2go_collect_methods` walks
it in that order, so the output is stable without it. `convertEngineMethods`
keeps its sort -- the build's own method lists have no declaration order to
preserve.

Worth remembering: an edit meant for `convertMethods` landed in
`convertEngineMethods` first, and the symptom was "nothing changed". Two
adjacent functions ending in the same three lines.

Last round's `EndSilence` restored the saved mask only when the current one was
still exactly what `@` installed. The engine's test is
`E_HAS_ONLY_FATAL_ERRORS` -- whether anything but a fatal level is still
enabled. Probed:

    @f() where f calls error_reporting(0)              -> restored
    @f() where f calls error_reporting(E_ALL & ~E_NOTICE) -> not restored
    the same two with an exception on the way out      -> the same answers

Zero hides no less than the silence did, so it does not count as the script
having raised the level.

### get_class_methods answers for the calling scope

It listed everything the class had. From outside a class only the public
methods are named; from inside, whatever that scope can reach. The engine-method
branch already did this; the declared-method and trait branches did not.

## 2026-08-26 — three things the harvest could not have known

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |

| differential cases | 741 | 743 |

### `$o->p = &$v` is an expression

`ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF` never stored a result, so `var_dump($o->p = &$v)` printed
NULL and `$r = ($o->p = &$v)` warned about `$r` being undefined. What it answers
with is the property, read through the box it just bound -- and *after* the old
value's release, because the destructor that runs there can write through that
very box:

    $box->value = new Test;
    var_dump($box->value = &$tmp);   // NULL: the old Test's destructor
                                     // set $box->value = null through the box
    var_dump($box->value = &$tmp);   // object: nothing to destroy this time

### A generator body's frame is spelled like any other

`It->getIterator()` in a backtrace, not `getIterator()`. The generator push used
`op.GetName()`, which is the bare name; the declaring class has to be put back,
with `->` or `::` depending on whether a `$this` is in play.

### Stringable is added at link time, which is after the harvest

A class with `__toString` implements `Stringable` without saying so. The engine
adds the interface when it *links* the class -- and the harvest is taken before
that. For a method the class writes itself this is invisible, because the engine
had already linked that class by the time php2go asked. For one a **trait**
provides it is not: the trait is composed at link time too, so the interface is
missing from the harvested list.

This is the same shape as the trait properties and trait constants already
handled in `Unit.properties` and `Unit.constants`: what a class gets from a
trait cannot come from the harvest, and has to be recomputed. `instanceOf` and
`interfaceNames` both answer it now.

### Trap for the next session

The engine will not `eval` a script whose destructor writes to a global -- it
bails out during shutdown. A differential case for destructor timing has to be
reduced to the part that does not destruct, and the real behaviour left to the
`.phpt` corpus.

## 2026-08-26 — `@` is the mask, not a flag beside it

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3680 | 3685 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 78.1% | 78.2% |
| differential cases | 739 | 741 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 5 fixed, 0 broken.

### Suppression is a value the script can overwrite

php2go modelled `@` as a boolean beside `error_reporting`. The engine has no
such flag: `@` *sets* error_reporting to the levels nothing can hide, and
END_SILENCE puts the old value back only if the script did not set one of its
own meanwhile. That difference is observable:

    error_reporting(E_ALL & ~E_DEPRECATED);
    function f() { echo $a1; error_reporting(E_ALL); echo $a2; }
    @f();   // $a1 silent, $a2 *warns* -- the @ is over

The mask model needed one thing the flag did not: an exception escaping the
expression never reaches END_SILENCE, so the mask would stay at the silence
value forever. Five tests said so immediately. A frame now records the masks its
`@` operators opened, and a raise closes all of them -- which is safe because a
`catch` can never sit inside an `@` region of the same frame.

### Binding to something the program cannot name

Three related gaps, all about a box the engine makes over a function's by-value
result:

    $o->p = &f();     Notice: Only variables should be assigned by reference
    $c[0] = &f();     the same -- and php2go said nothing for either
    g(f());           Notice: Only variables should be passed by reference

And such a box has exactly one name once it is bound, so it is *not* one
var_dump marks: the engine prints `["p"]=> int(2)`, not `&int(2)`.

Two things worth keeping from getting that right. `ZEND_MAKE_REF` is the wrong
place for the notice -- list-destructuring by reference goes through it too, and
earns a different message. And `sharedRef(source)` marks the box as it builds
the value, so writing

    bound := sharedRef(source)
    if borrowed { bound = php.MakeRef(source) }

marks it anyway; the branch has to come first.

### prefer-ref is why the _EX form cannot be trusted

`ZEND_SEND_VAR_NO_REF` means the compiler knew the parameter is by reference:
the notice is unconditional. `_EX` means it could not tell, and that is exactly
where the engine's `ZEND_SEND_PREFER_REF` parameters live -- `extract()` takes
its array by reference and accepts a value without complaint. php2go's
`engineByRef` table records by-reference-ness and nothing else, so it cannot
tell the two apart. `userArgumentByRef` answers the `_EX` question only for
callees written in PHP, which never have prefer-ref.

An error handler's frame is *not* `[internal function]`. The engine calls it at
the place the diagnostic came from, and the frame names that place:

    array_map's callback   #0 [internal function]: boom(1)

entry point the error-handler bridge uses.

A differential case must not print a file path: the harness runs the engine and
the interpreter from different files and does not normalise them. That rules out
`getTraceAsString()`, and it also rules out any *closure* in the trace, since a
closure's name is `{closure:FILE:LINE}`. Walk `getTrace()` and print the fields
you mean, and give the probe named functions rather than closures.

## 2026-08-26 — unset descends without creating

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3667 | 3669 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 77.8% | 77.9% |
| differential cases | 734 | 737 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 2 fixed, 0 broken.

### `unset($x[0])` on something that is not a container

php2go did nothing at all unless the target was an object. The engine does
nothing either -- but it does not let every shape pass in silence. Probed:

    null, undefined   silent
    false             "Automatic conversion of false to array is deprecated"
                      (and nothing grows)
    true, int, float  Error: Cannot unset offset in a non-array variable
    string            Error: Cannot unset string offsets

### And the descent creates nothing

`unset($x[0][0])` on a null `$x` leaves it null. php2go took the descent through
the ordinary write fetch, which is BP_VAR_W's job -- it created `$x[0]` and then
unset an element of the array it had just invented, leaving `[0 => NULL]`
behind. `ZEND_FETCH_DIM_UNSET` now has its own handler: an existing element is
handed out as a box, and anything else is a detached null the UNSET_DIM that
follows finds nothing in.

The string case is decided by the *outer* index, which is worth writing down:

    unset($s["a"]["b"])   Cannot unset string offsets
    unset($s[0][0])       Cannot use string offset as an array

A legal offset picks out a byte and the complaint is that a byte is not an
array; an illegal one never gets that far, so what is reported is the unset.

### A throwing error handler makes a callback unresolvable

`call_user_func('self::y')` deprecates the spelling, and an error handler that
throws turns that into an exception mid-resolution. The engine still reports
`call_user_func(): Argument #1 ($callback) must be a valid callback, (null)` --
the empty reason it started with -- and hangs the handler's exception off it as
the cause. php2go let the exception escape directly. `throwChained` in
`throw.go` builds a throwable with a `previous`, and both places that validate a
callback consult `TakePendingError` before deciding.

### Two traps

The new `ZEND_FETCH_DIM_UNSET` case was first written directly above the
write-fetch group -- which the case above it reaches by `fallthrough`. Inserting
a case between a `fallthrough` and its target silently redirects it; three
differential cases caught it immediately, and the corpus showed five broken
tests. Put a new case *after* the group it is being split out of.

The direct `call_user_func('f')` form compiles to `ZEND_INIT_USER_CALL`, not to
the builtin path in `callback.go`. A fix applied only to `callValueFor` changes
nothing for the common spelling.

### Result

| differential cases | 730 | 734 |

### `(int)1.0E+30` is 5076964154930102272

php2go answered zero for every float outside int64, which was PHP 7's
behaviour. PHP 8 reduces the value modulo 2^64 and reads the result as signed --
`zend_dval_to_lval_slow`, which is what a C cast would have done where the cast
is defined:

    (int)1e30              5076964154930102272
    (int)-1e30            -5076964154930102272
    (int)(PHP_INT_MAX+1)  -9223372036854775808
    (int)NAN, (int)INF     0

The saturating conversion php2go already had is the right one for a float that
came from a *string*: `(int)"1.0E+121"` is PHP_INT_MAX while `(int)1.0E+121` is
not. The engine has both, and now so does this.

That conversion is also what decides whether an array key lost precision. The
test was `int64(v.Float()) != v.Float()`, and Go's cast is undefined out of
range, so it could not be the judge of its own correctness. Routing it through
`v.Int()` fixed the missing deprecation for `$a[PHP_INT_MAX+1]`.

One detail worth keeping: the number in that message is spelled the way
*var_dump* spells one. `9.2233720368548E+18` is what the value prints as;
`9.223372036854776E+18` is what the deprecation says.

### A get hook runs before the binding is refused

`$o->p = &$r` on a hooked property earns one of two errors, and php2go gave the
same one for both. Probed:

    &get or get present    the hook *runs*, then
                           "Cannot assign by reference to overloaded object"
    set only               "Indirect modification of C::$p is not allowed",
                           and nothing runs

### A __get already running does not answer for its own name

`$obj->x =& $this->_` from inside `A::__get` reached `deniedPropertyError` and
produced `Cannot access  property A::$x` -- with the tell-tale double space of
an empty visibility. `bindableProperty` asked `hasMagic`, which is true whether
or not the accessor is in flight. While `__get` is running for a name it does
not answer for that name: that is what the guard means, and a binding made from
inside it reaches the property table and creates the property. `magicAvailable`
already said so.

### A static's box always holds a value

`static $a = $a;` warned once per read, forever. The initializer read something
absent, php2go stored the *undefined* it got back, and every later read of the
name found an undefined box and warned again. The engine warns once: the
initializer yields null, and a static's box always holds a value.

## 2026-08-26 — unserialize says where, and it says why first

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3651 | 3658 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 77.5% | 77.6% |
| differential cases | 727 | 730 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 7 fixed, 0 broken.

### Three ways to fail, three offsets

php2go reported one offset for every malformed input: where the innermost value
that could not be read started. The engine distinguishes three cases, and the
`.phpt` corpus tests all of them. Probed:

    a:2:{i:0;i:1;        ran out of text     offset 13 of 13   (the end)
    a:1:{i:0;x:1;}       unreadable byte     offset  9 of 14   (the value's start)
    a:3:{i:0;i:1;}       count > braces      offset 13 of 14   ("Unexpected end of
                                                                serialized data")
    s:3:"abcd";          count is wrong      offset  8 of 11   (where the quote
                                                                should have been)
    i:1;junk             complete, then more offset  4 of  8   ("Extra data
                                                                starting at") -- and
                                                                the value stands

The reader now carries a `truncated` flag, set by the primitives that fail
because the input stopped rather than because it held something unreadable.
Reaching the closing brace early is a third thing again: it is not the end of
the text, so it gets its own message and blames the brace.

### The enum form says why before it says where

`E:<n>:"Class:Case";` had four unreported failures. Each has its own wording,
and *where* it is reported from splits them in two: a name the reader cannot
make sense of fails at the value's own start, while one it resolved and then
found no case for fails at the end of what it read.

    E:8:"Nope:Bar";       Class 'Nope' not found              offset 0
    E:14:"NotEnum:Bar";   Class 'NotEnum' is not an enum      offset 0
    E:7:"E1Foo";          Invalid enum name (missing colon)   offset 0
    E:4:"E1:K";           E1::K is not an enum case           offset 11 (the end)
    E:4:"E1:Z";           Undefined constant E1::Z            offset 11 (the end)

The last two are told apart by whether the name is a class constant at all.

### `self`, `parent` and `static` in a callable forward the binding

`call_user_func("parent::test")` from a method reached through a subclass
reports the *subclass* from `get_called_class()`; `call_user_func("A::test")`
reports A. php2go resolved the keyword to a class name and lost the binding.

The condition is not "it was a keyword" alone. A first attempt forwarded
unconditionally and broke `bug66719`, where `["B", "parent::who"]` is called
from an unrelated class C: the answer there is A, because C is not a B and there
is no binding of C's that A would accept. So: forward when the call site's
called scope is an instance of the class the callable resolved to. That fits
both, and naming a class outright never forwards even when it would be
compatible.

The same area had a deprecation firing once too often: `is_callable(['parent',
'm'])` in a class with no parent warned and then answered false. The engine says
nothing -- there is no callable there to call deprecated. The notice moved to
after the resolution succeeds.

### Trap for the next session

The engine's eval mode prefixes diagnostics with `PHP Request Startup:` where a
file gets the function's own name (`unserialize():`). A differential case that
prints `$msg` from an error handler will never match. Strip both prefixes in the
handler; the `.phpt` corpus is what checks the prefix itself.

## 2026-08-26 — the names in a type are enough to settle invariance

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3644 | 3651 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 77.3% | 77.5% |
| `type_declarations` passing (of 460) | 379 | 384 |
| differential cases | 724 | 727 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 7 fixed, 0 broken.

### An unresolvable class is not a reason to accept anything

`verifyPropertyTypes` compares a redeclared property's type against the
inherited one in both directions, and gave up -- accepting -- whenever either
direction could not be resolved. So `public X|B $prop` in the parent against
`public B $prop` in the child passed, because `X` is never declared:

    class A { public X|B $prop; }
    class B extends A { public B $prop; }
    // engine: Fatal error: Type of B::$prop must be X|B (as in class A)

The engine still refuses, and it is right to: two types naming different things
cannot be the same type whatever those things turn out to be. Invariance is the
one check where the *names* are enough. `sameTypeAtoms` compares the normalised
atom sets when resolution fails, which needed two spellings collapsed first --
probed, not assumed:

    iterable  ==  Traversable|array     accepted
    ?int      ==  int|null              accepted
    X|Y       ==  Y|X                   accepted (order is not part of a type)
    self      ==  the class it is in    accepted

### A rebound property takes its type off the old box

Last round the box a reference is bound to learned the property's declared type.
The other half was missing: when the property is rebound to a *different* box,
the old one stops being that property's storage and stops carrying its type.

    $x =& Test::$x;          // $x is now checked against int
    Test::$x =& Test2::$y;   // ... and now it is not
    $x = "foo";              // no error

`Ref.DropSource` does that, called from `rebindStaticProp` and from
`ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF`. The object side had to read the *raw* slot: `Object.Get`
dereferences, so the box was never in hand to drop anything from.

### A `callable` type hint resolves the callable

`Use of "self" in callables is deprecated` was already reported from
call_user_func, array_map, is_callable and Closure::fromCallable -- but not from
a `callable` parameter. Checking that type is not a shape test in the engine: it
*resolves* the callable, and resolving is what reports both this and the
`Callables of the form ["B", "self::foo"]` deprecation. `noteCallableForm` in
`types.go` does the resolution and throws the result away.

### `$a[] .= x` appends

The compound-assignment path took the key from op2 without checking whether
there was one, so an append got `arrayKey(undef)` -- the empty string -- plus a
warning about the key it had just invented. An append's element is new: no key
was missed, nothing is reported, and the read half sees null.

## 2026-08-26 — a reference to a typed property carries the type

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3635 | 3644 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 77.1% | 77.3% |
| `type_declarations` passing (of 460) | 373 | 379 |
| differential cases | 722 | 724 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 9 fixed, 0 broken.

### The type is on the box, and php2go was only putting it there sometimes

`$r = &$o->i` on `public int $i` makes `$r` a name for the property, so `$r =
"x"` is a TypeError. php2go had this for an instance property reached through a
write fetch and nowhere else. Three routes were missing it, and they are all the
same rule -- the box a typed property's slot holds records which property it
belongs to (`notePropertyType` in `types.go`, factored out of `elementRef`):

- **Static properties.** A static property's slot *is* the box, so the type can
  be attached once, where the storage is made (`staticPropRef`).
- **`foreach ($o as $k => &$v)`.** Iterating by reference binds the property's
  own box, so the loop variable is checked for as long as it holds it.
- **`[&$o->p]`.** The aliasing already worked; what was missing was the mark
  that says the program asked for the `&`, so var_dump printed no `&`.

### Two wordings, and which one belongs where

The engine has both "Cannot assign string to property F::$i of type int" and
"Cannot assign string to reference held by property F::$i of type int", and
php2go was using the second for both cases. They are not interchangeable:

- Making the binding -- `$o->i = &$x` -- is a **write to the property**, and the
  check runs before the box learns the type.
- Writing through an established binding -- `$x = "z"` afterwards -- is a write
  to the **reference the property holds**.

`ZEND_ASSIGN_STATIC_PROP_REF` did not check at all; it now runs
`verifyStaticPropertyWrite` and copies the property's sources onto the box that
takes over as the storage.

### A typed static property has the third state too

`public static int $s;` with no default holds *nothing*, not null. php2go seeded
null, so every read answered. Probed:

    isset(F::$s)   false, and no error
    empty(F::$s)   true
    F::$s          Error: Typed static property F::$s must not be accessed …
    F::$s++        the same -- the step reads first
    $r = &F::$s    Error: Cannot access uninitialized non-nullable property …

Two things worth keeping. The read error names it as a *static* property, which
the instance form does not. And the by-reference refusal is a different message
again, is shared with instance properties, and applies only when the type does
**not** take null -- `$r = &$o->n` on `?int $n` binds the box and leaves the
property holding NULL. That is `refuseUninitializedRef`, which asks the box
rather than the property: by the time a reference is being bound, the sources
recorded on it are what is known about where it came from.

Writing that case turned up one more: `$r = &$a; $r = &$b;` never dropped `$a`'s
share count, so var_dump kept marking `$a` as a reference after the only other
name for it had moved on. `ZEND_ASSIGN_REF` now unshares what the target let go
of, which is what the foreach path already did.

## 2026-08-26 — a read-modify-write reads first

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3615 | 3635 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.7% | 77.1% |
| `lazy_objects` passing (of 223) | 152 | 159 |
| differential cases | 719 | 722 |

Diff-set against the previous round: 20 fixed, 0 broken.

### `$o->n++` is a read and then a write, and php2go was only doing the write

`$o->n++`, `++$o->n` and `$o->n .= "x"` all read the property before they store
anything back. php2go went straight for the slot, which meant an uninitialized
typed property was stepped from null instead of being refused:

    class C { public int $c; }
    $o = new C;
    $o->c++;        // engine: Error, "must not be accessed before initialization"
                    // php2go: NULL, then 1

Probed, the rule is that being *declared* is what makes it an Error rather than
a magic call. `__get` is offered the name only once `unset()` has taken the
property away -- until then the property is there, it just holds nothing. That
is `uninitializedTyped` in `property.go`, called from both read-modify-write
paths.

The same reading turned up the rest of the read half. When the name does reach
`__get`, the accessor supplies the old value and `__set` -- or, failing that, a
real property created on the spot -- takes the new one; `magicCompound` in
`magic.go` does that for both paths. And when there is no accessor at all, the
read still warns and the write still creates:

    class I {}
    $i = new I;
    $i->x++;        // Deprecated: Creation of dynamic property I::$x
                    // Warning: Undefined property: I::$x
                    // NULL

### Every route that creates a property earns the deprecation

php2go emitted the 8.2 dynamic-property deprecation from the plain assignment
and nowhere else. The engine emits it wherever the property comes into
existence, so `$o->n[] = 1`, `$r = &$o->n` and `unset($o->n[$k])` all earn it
too -- the write-mode object fetch is the one place all three pass through. The
differential case written for it caught a second thing: the slot that fetch
makes holds *null*, not nothing, which is why `unset($o->n["k"])` leaves the
property behind as `NULL` rather than uninitialized.

### Lazy objects: nothing to defer, and where a proxy keeps its state

Two smaller ones in the same round.

A class that declares no properties has nothing to defer, so `newLazyGhost` on
it hands back an ordinary object: no initializer ever runs and `var_dump` prints
no label. `allSkipped` already answered this -- it returns true over an empty
property list -- it just was not being asked at construction. `resetAsLazyGhost`
needed the same.

And `(array)$obj` and `get_mangled_object_vars()` deliberately do not initialize
a lazy object, but an *initialized proxy* keeps its state in the instance behind
it, and that is what they must read. `lazyState` in `lazy.go` is the "resolve
only if already resolved" accessor; `mangledProps` uses it.

### Trap for the next session

Two differential cases had to be rewritten before the engine would evaluate
them. Class names collide across cases -- the harness shares one engine process,
so a second `class C` is a fatal redeclaration and shows up as `zend: evaluation
bailed out`. And `(new C)->d++` bails out too: a read-modify-write on a
temporary is not something the engine will compile. Name classes distinctly and
assign the object to a variable first.

## 2026-08-26 — a weak container answers when it is read

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3613 | 3615 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.7% | 76.7% |
| `failed` | 862 | 860 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `weakrefs` passing | 22 | 24 (of 33) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 2 fixed, 0 broken.

### Pruning when something looks

```php
$map = new WeakMap;
$map[new stdClass] = 1;   // the key dies immediately
var_dump($map);           // object(WeakMap)#1 (0) {}
```

php2go showed one entry. `pruneWeak` existed and was correct, but it only ran
during a collection, and a collection only happens at a release point -- and
there is none between those two lines.

The fix follows the model rather than working around it: php2go has no
refcounts, so it answers reachability by walking *when the question is asked*.
A weak container's contents are only observable through the container, so
reading one is exactly when the answer has to be right. `observeWeak` prunes at
that moment and destroys nothing -- the pruning is all the reader can see.

It fixed no test on its own. Two others in the same test still differ on object
handles, which is the gap from iteration 85.

### Refusing to grow, by every route

`weakmap_error_conditions` asks for the same refusal four ways, and php2go gave
it for one:

```php
$map->prop = 1;        // Cannot create dynamic property WeakMap::$prop
$map->prop[] = 1;      //   … a write descent creates it too
$r = &$map->prop;      //   … and so does a binding
unserialize('C:7:"WeakMap":0:{}');   // Unserialization of 'WeakMap' is not allowed
```

The last one is the Serializable `C:` form, which php2go does not reconstruct
at all -- but a class the engine refuses outright is refused here too, rather
than reported as a malformed byte at offset 0.

The binding needed its own wording: `bindableProperty` already said no, and the
error it fell through to was about *seeing* the name rather than creating it.

- `runtime/interp/gc.go` — `observeWeak`.
- `runtime/interp/weak.go`, `runtime/interp/builtins.go` — reading a WeakMap
  prunes it first.
- `runtime/interp/property.go` — `forbidsDynamic`; `bindableProperty` consults
  it.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — the write descent and the binding refuse.
- `runtime/interp/serialize.go` — the `C:` form.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case.

## 2026-08-26 — call_user_func has no slot to hand over

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3607 | 3609 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.5% | 76.6% |
| `failed` | 868 | 866 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 2 fixed, 0 broken.

### The rule

```php
function wants(&$a) { $a++; }
$i = 0;
call_user_func('wants', $i);
// Warning: wants(): Argument #1 ($a) must be passed by reference, value given
var_dump($i);   // int(0)
```

`call_user_func`'s own parameter is by value, so it has nothing to hand over.
The engine warns once per by-reference parameter and the call proceeds with a
copy -- and that holds even when the argument *is* a reference at the call site,
which the corpus states outright by making `$x =& $i` first and getting the same
answer.

php2go passed the reference through and the callee wrote to the caller's
variable.

### Where the flag lives

Not on the INIT. The compiler folds `call_user_func('f', $x)` into an ordinary
`ZEND_INIT_FCALL 'f'` and sends the arguments with **`ZEND_SEND_USER`** -- so it
is the send, not the call setup, that marks a call made this way. Reading the
opcode dump was the whole of that finding; the first attempt marked
`ZEND_INIT_USER_CALL` and left the common case untouched.

### And one ordering

The warning is about arguments, so it comes after the callee has been accepted.
`extract()` and its siblings refuse to be reached dynamically *before* looking
at their parameters, and warning first cost `dynamic_call_005`.

### Still open in this family

- `call_user_func_array` reaches the callee by a different route and is not
  marked, so `call_user_func_006`'s second call still passes the reference.
- `call_user_func_by_ref` wants the parameter's *type* checked after the
  warning: `test(): Argument #1 ($ref) must be of type Type, int given`.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/call.go` — `pendingCall.viaUserCall`.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `ZEND_SEND_USER` marks it, `argumentByRef`
  refuses, `noteUserCallByRef` reports, and reference arguments are copied.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case.

## 2026-08-26 — a mangled key, and an experiment that had to go back

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3606 | 3607 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.5% | 76.5% |
| `failed` | 869 | 868 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `errored` | 6 | 6 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 1 fixed, 0 broken.

One test for the round. The other half of it is an experiment that measured
badly and was reverted; both are written down, because the second is the more
useful of the two.

### The reverted experiment: releasing a loop's subject

```php
foreach ([new A(2)] as $b) { $b = null; }
echo "after loop\n";
// engine: the destructor runs before "after loop"; php2go: at shutdown
```

`ZEND_FE_FREE` clears the iterator and the temporary but ran no release check,
so what the loop was iterating over stayed alive. Adding one fixed the ordering
-- and turned **five** `try/finally` tests from wrong answers into *interpreter
errors*: `foreach fetch without a live iterator`. A destructor that throws at
that opline lands on a handler mapped for a pc still inside the loop the
opcode has just dismantled, and the next `FE_FETCH` finds nothing. Raising from
the following pc instead made no difference.

Five failures becoming five errors is worse than the ordering is better -- an
error is a gap, a failure is a wrong answer -- so it went back, with a note at
the opcode and in TODO. The right fix needs the iterator to survive an
exception raised while freeing it, which is a change to how the loop state is
held rather than to this opcode.

### The key that looks like a property name

```php
$o = (object) ["\0A\0b" => 42, "\0*\0c" => 24, "plain" => 1];
```

The engine stores a private property under `\0Owner\0name` and a protected one
under `\0*\0name`, and an (object) cast can put a key of that shape into an
ordinary stdClass. What each reader then does is not uniform, and the corpus
says so:

| reader | answer |
| --- | --- |
| `var_dump` | `["b":"A":private]`, `["c":protected]` |
| `foreach` | the plain names, and both are visible from anywhere |
| `get_object_vars`, `(array)` | the raw keys, mangling and all |
| `json_encode` | leaves them out |

php2go printed the raw bytes everywhere. It is worth noting what this is *not*:
php2go stores a real private property under its plain name, so none of this is
the mangling that iteration 104 left in TODO. This is only about a key that
happens to look like one.

- `runtime/php/object.go` — `UnmangleProperty`.
- `runtime/interp/builtins.go` — the two property labels.
- `runtime/interp/class.go`, `runtime/interp/hooks.go` — foreach unmangles,

- `runtime/interp/json.go` — such a key is not public.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — the note at `ZEND_FE_FREE`.

## 2026-08-26 — a flag the harvest was not carrying

### Result

| metric | before | after |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Refusing a property rather than deprecating one

```php
$c = function () {}; $c->a = 1;    // Error: Cannot create dynamic property Closure::$a
$a = new ArrayObject; $a->a = 1;   // Deprecated: … is deprecated
```

php2go deprecated both. The engine's answer is a class flag,
`ZEND_ACC_NO_DYNAMIC_PROPERTIES`, and the honest fix was to harvest it rather
than to write down which classes carry it -- Closure, Generator and WeakMap are
the ones this corpus reaches, and the list is the engine's to keep. A proto
field, a line in the harvester, and the existing enum refusal generalised to
"an enum, or a class the engine flagged".

### Looked at and left: two privates of the same name

`closure_038` and `closure_039` fail before they reach the closure at all:

```php
class A { private $x; function __construct($v) { $this->x = $v; } }
class B extends A { private $x; function __construct($v) { parent::__construct($v); … } }
```

`A::__construct` writing `$this->x` on a `B` is `Cannot access private property
B::$x` in php2go. The engine keeps two slots -- `\0A\0x` and `\0B\0x` -- and
php2go keeps one, mangling the name only for display. Seven tests want the two
slots (`bug60536_003`, `property_hooks/dump`, `return_types/inheritance009`,
`traits/property008`, `typed_properties_090` and the two closures), and giving
them one each means keying the property table by declaring class for every
private -- which every property path would have to learn. Recorded in TODO as a
model limitation rather than started at the end of a round.
