## 2026-08-26 — a Throwable's constructor has a signature

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3597 | 3602 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.3% | 76.4% |
| `failed` | 878 | 873 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 5 fixed, 0 broken.

### The family

The name-family lens moved on from traits: `exception_018` through `022` all
expect

```
TypeError: Exception::__construct(): Argument #1 ($message) must be of type
string, stdClass given
```

php2go's `throwableCtor` took `args[0].String()` and carried on, so
`throw new Exception(new stdClass)` produced an exception whose message was
whatever a string cast made of the object.

Two details the tests state and neither is the obvious one:

- **The class named is the one that *declares* the constructor**, not the one
  being instantiated. `class Hello extends Exception` reports `Exception::`,
  and `class MyArgErr extends ArgumentCountError` reports `Error::` -- three
  classes in the engine declare one, and `ErrorException` is the third because
  its signature differs.
- **The stack frame names it too**: `#0 …(4): Exception->__construct(Object(stdClass))`,
  not `Hello->__construct(...)`. That is the same rule as iteration 91's -- a
  frame names the declaring class -- reaching a builtin constructor, where
  `pendingCall.method` is nil and `traceName` had nothing to work from.

### A shape change

`builtinCtor` was `func(*php.Object, []php.Value)` -- a constructor that could
not refuse. It now returns an error, and the two that still cannot refuse go
through `noFailure`.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/throw.go` — `throwableCtor` checks; `throwableCtorScope`.
- `runtime/interp/call.go` — the `builtinCtor` shape.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — the scope is captured at setup and names the
  frame; `noFailure`.
- `runtime/interp/constexpr.go` — the constant-expression path propagates it.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case.

## 2026-08-26 — three more declaration rules, and a deprecation

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3593 | 3597 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.3% | 76.3% |
| `failed` | 882 | 878 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `traits` passing | 140 | 143 (of 165) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 4 fixed, 0 broken.

### Extending something that is not a class

`class A extends foo` where `foo` is a trait is
`Fatal error: Class A cannot extend trait foo`. php2go reported the *trait
composition* error instead, because `composeTraits` came first in `linkClass`
and `error_001` gives the class an incoherent `insteadof` as well. The engine
settles the parent during inheritance, before a trait is bound, so the check now
runs ahead of everything.

The first version also claimed `class Bar extends SomeEnum` -- and the engine
words that one as `Cannot extend final class Foo`. An enum *is* a class that
happens to be final, so it belongs to the finality check rather than this one.

### Overriding a final method

`class bar extends baz { use foo { test as public; } }` where `baz::test` is
final is `Cannot override final method baz::test()`. A trait's method counts:
composing it into a subclass is an override like any other.

`language019` needs the other half -- `T1::foo as final;`, where the *alias*
makes it final -- and the harvested `TraitAlias` carries class, method, alias
and visibility but no finality, so that one is still out of reach. One test.

### A trait's statics are not the trait's

```php
trait T { public static $foo; public static function foo() {} }
T::$foo = 42;   // Deprecated: Accessing static trait property T::$foo …
T::foo();       // Deprecated: Calling static trait method T::foo …
T::bar();       // … names T::bar, even though the trait has no bar
```

The storage belongs to each class that uses the trait, so naming the trait is
asking for a slot with no single answer. The method form fires on the name that
was *called*, before resolution -- which is what makes the `__callStatic` line
come out right.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/abstract.go` — `verifyParentKind`, `verifyFinalMethods`.
- `runtime/interp/signature.go` — both join `linkClass`, the first ahead of
  trait composition.
- `runtime/interp/class.go` — `noteTraitStaticAccess`.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — the three static-property sites and the static
  call site report it.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

## 2026-08-26 — a trait can use a trait, and an insteadof has to make sense

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3586 | 3593 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 76.1% | 76.3% |
| `failed` | 889 | 882 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `traits` passing | 133 | 140 (of 165) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 7 fixed, 0 broken.

### One level was not enough

```php
trait Hello { function sayHello() {} }
trait World { function sayWorld() {} }
trait HelloWorld { use Hello, World; }
class MyHelloWorld { use HelloWorld; }
```

`resolveMethod` walked a class's traits but not a trait's own, so
`MyHelloWorld::sayHello` was undefined. `traitMethod` now recurses, with a seen
set -- a `use` cycle is refused at declaration, but a lookup must not loop on one
regardless.

`bug63911` is the same shape with a twist: `class D { use B, C; }` where B and C
both use A. Both provide `a()`, and the engine allows it because it is the same
method. The collision check added last round does not see it -- it iterates each
trait's *own* declarations, and B and C declare none -- so this works by
omission rather than by a rule. Noted rather than claimed.

### Three things an `insteadof` must be

Each is its own diagnostic, and each is one test:

- **The method has to exist** on the trait that wins it:
  `A precedence rule was defined for A::bar but this method does not exist`.
- **The winner cannot also be excluded**: `T1::foo insteadof T1` is
  `Inconsistent insteadof definition. The method foo is to be used from T1, but
  T1 is also on the exclude list`.
- **A trait cannot be excluded twice for the same method**:
  `Failed to evaluate a trait precedence (test). Method of trait foo was defined
  to be excluded multiple times`.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/class.go` — `traitMethod`.
- `runtime/interp/traits.go` — the three `insteadof` checks.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

## 2026-08-26 — what a trait alias does to visibility

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3578 | 3586 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 75.9% | 76.1% |
| `failed` | 897 | 889 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `traits` passing | 127 | 133 (of 165) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 8 fixed, 0 broken.

### The visibility half of `as`

php2go handled `use T { m as n; }` -- the alias adds a name -- but ignored the
*other* thing `as` does:

```php
use HelloWorld { sayHello as protected; }      // changes m's visibility here
use A { A::bar as public baz; }                // gives the new name its own
```

Four tests, two in each direction: one where php2go left a method public that
should have been protected, one where it left it protected that should have been
public.

The visibility belongs to the **pair** -- the composing class and the name --
rather than to the op_array, which is the trait's and unchanged. So
`effectiveVisibility(declaring, method, name)`, consulted both by the
accessibility check and by the diagnostic that reports the refusal.

The name matters, and getting it wrong is instructive: with only the resolved
method's own name, `A::bar as public baz` looks like a visibility change to
`bar`. It is not -- `bar` stays private and `baz` is public. So the caller has to
say which name it reached the method by, which is why `methodAccessibleAs` takes
one.

### And a missing trait is not a missing class

`class C extends Missing {}` is a catchable `Error: Class "Missing" not found`.
`class C { use Missing; }` is a plain fatal: `Trait "Missing" not found`. php2go
treated all three dependency kinds alike.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/class.go` — `effectiveVisibility`, `methodAccessibleAs`.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go`, `runtime/interp/closure.go` — the call sites pass
  the name; two diagnostics report the effective visibility.
- `runtime/interp/signature.go` — a missing trait is a fatal.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case.

## 2026-08-26 — two traits cannot claim the same name

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3569 | 3578 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 75.7% | 75.9% |
| `failed` | 906 | 897 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `traits` passing | 118 | 127 (of 165) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 9 fixed, 0 broken.

### The composition check php2go was not making

`composeTraits` checked constants and properties but not methods, so a class
using two traits that both provide `m()` silently took the first. The engine
refuses:

```
Trait method c::test has not been applied as bar::test,
because of collision with foo::test
```

The message names three things and each is a different one: the *rejected*
method under its own name, the class and the **effective** name it would have
taken, and the trait that already holds it. `use Hello, World { world as hello; }`
reports `World::world has not been applied as MyClass::hello, because of
collision with Hello::hello` -- the original name on the left, the alias in the
middle.

So an alias belongs to its *source trait's* contribution and is processed with
it: Hello contributes `hello` and, through `hello as world`, also `world`; World
then collides on `world`. Processing aliases after all the traits would name the
two halves the other way round.

### And what resolves it

Three things, and the corpus supplied the third after the first version broke
five tests:

- `insteadof` takes one trait's version out of the running.
- The class declaring the method itself wins silently.
- **An abstract trait method is a requirement, not an implementation.**
  `trait TextArea { abstract function attributes(...); }` beside
  `trait HTMLAttributes { function attributes(...) {} }` is how `bug60717` is
  meant to work, and the first version called it a collision.

### Also

Four diagnostics named a class by its raw name rather than its display name,
which for an anonymous class is `class@anonymous` followed by a NUL and the file
and line it was declared at. `DisplayName` truncates at the NUL; these four were
not calling it.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/traits.go` — `checkTraitMethods`, `aliasSource`.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — four diagnostics use `DisplayName`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case covering the three
  resolutions.

## 2026-08-26 — a proxy and its instance are one object to an accessor

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3552 | 3569 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 75.4% | 75.7% |
| `failed` | 923 | 906 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `lazy_objects` passing | 135 | 152 (of 223) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 17 fixed, 0 broken.

### The lens, again

The test-name-family grouping picked the next entry: `lazy_objects/gh18038-*`,
nine tests named after one GitHub issue. They turned out to be two rules, and
fixing them took eight more tests with them.

### A guarded access inside an accessor is a real one

```php
$obj = $rc->newLazyProxy(fn() => new C);   // C has __set
$obj->prop = 1;
// C::__set          <- the accessor answers first, proxy still lazy
// init              <- $this->$name inside it is the *real* write
// int(2)
```

`resolveLazy` had the first half: a name the class does not declare is the
accessor's business and is asked before anything is produced. What it was
missing is that once that accessor is *running* for the name, the re-entry
guard sends `$this->$name` to the real property -- and reaching the state is
what produces it. The check is now `magicAvailable` rather than
`hasMagicNamed`: the accessor answers only while it *could* be entered.

### And then it ran twice

That alone made the accessor run again: `resolveLazy` hands back the instance,
which is a different object, so a different guard key. The engine does not --
a lazy proxy and the instance behind it are one object as far as a property
access is concerned. `php.Object.Guard` now lets a proxy lend its handle to its
instance, and every guard lookup goes through it.

### Left where it is

`gh18038-005` is `isset($obj->prop[''])`, where the engine asks `__isset` before
initializing and php2go asks `__get`. Mapping `ZEND_FETCH_OBJ_IS` to `__isset`
fixes that one and costs another, so the mapping stays as the `init_trigger_*`
tests pinned it. One test.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/lazy.go` — `magicAvailable` decides; the instance inherits
  the proxy's guard.
- `runtime/interp/magic.go` — `guardOf`.
- `runtime/php/object.go` — `Object.Guard`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case.

## 2026-08-26 — destructuring by reference

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3548 | 3552 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 75.3% | 75.4% |
| `failed` | 927 | 923 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |
| `list` passing | 5 | 9 (of 12) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 4 fixed, 0 broken.

### The lens

Last round's accident -- five failures sharing a name prefix -- made a lens.
Grouping the remaining 927 by test-name family: `typed_properties_*` 31,
`closure_*` 15, `exception_*` 11, `foreach_*` 9, `gh18038-*` 9,
`fibers/destructors_*` 8, `list_reference_*` 7. This round took the last of
those, where one feature clearly covers the whole group.

### Only the leaf becomes a reference

```php
$arr = [1, [2]];
list(&$a, list(&$b)) = $arr;
// $arr[1] is a plain array; only $arr[1][0] is a reference
```

`ZEND_FETCH_LIST_W` handed out a *share* of the element's box. For a leaf
target that is right -- but a nested list fetches the intermediate only to
descend into it, and the `&` printed there is one the engine does not. The
share belongs to the `ZEND_ASSIGN_REF` at the leaf, which already takes it.

### And a value with no home

```php
function byValue($x) { return $x; }
[&$v] = byValue($src);
// Notice: Attempting to set reference to non referenceable value
```

The notice looked like it belonged to `ZEND_MAKE_REF`, which is what sits over
the call's result -- and putting it there broke `bug69732`, where the same
`MAKE_REF VAR:<call result>` appears and the engine says nothing. Dumping both
opcode sequences settled it: what differs is that the list case then *reaches
through* that reference with `FETCH_LIST_W`. Making the reference is fine;
destructuring one is what is reported.

So `MAKE_REF` over a non-referenceable temporary now makes a box of its own --
holding a copy, so writes through it reach nothing, which is the engine's
semantics -- and records the fact; `FETCH_LIST_W` reads that and reports.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `ZEND_FETCH_LIST_W`, `ZEND_MAKE_REF`,
  `frame.borrowedRefs` with `noteBorrowed`/`borrowed`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — one case covering both halves.

### The lens

Listing the remaining `property_hooks` failures side by side, five of them share
a prefix in their names -- `parent_get_plain_*`, `parent_set_plain_*`,
`parent_superfluous_args` -- and a sixth, `default_value_inheritance`, was
failing with the same wrong message. All of them are
`parent::$prop::get()` naming a property the parent declares **without** that
hook, where the engine builds a trampoline straight to the storage.

php2go had the trampoline (`hookBackingAccess`) but it was a bare read and
write. Three things it was missing, each stated by a test:

- **It has the arity of the hook it stands in for**, and names itself the way
  that hook would: `A::$prop::get() expects exactly 0 arguments, 1 given`,
  `A::$prop::set() expects exactly 1 argument, 2 given` -- by the class that
  *declared* the property.
- **Reaching the storage is reaching the property.** A typed one never written
  is `Typed property C::$prop must not be accessed before initialization`, not
  a null that then fails the hook's return type. That last was the whole of
  `default_value_inheritance`'s wrong output.
- **The write form answers with what it wrote**, which is what
  `var_dump(parent::$prop::set($value))` prints. Probed, because "a set hook
  returns void" is the obvious guess and is wrong here.

A fourth thing was a plumbing slip on the way: the trampoline raises with
`Raise`, and the caller was not passing the result through `materialize`, so the
first three fixes turned five failures into five *errors* before turning them
into passes.

## 2026-08-26 — property hooks are part of what an object *is*

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3539 | 3542 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 75.1% | 75.2% |
| `failed` | 936 | 933 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 3 fixed, 0 broken. Three tests for the
round, but the behaviour behind them is wider than the count.

### Reading an object runs its hooks

```php
class H {
    public $plain = 'plain';
    public $virt  { get { return 'V'; } set { } }
    public $backed = 'b' { get { return strtoupper($this->backed); } set { … } }
}
foreach ($h as $k => $v) …   // plain, virt => V, backed => B
get_object_vars($h)          // the same three
(array) $h                   // plain, backed => 'b'  -- the raw table
```

php2go handed out `object.Props` in all three cases: virtual properties were
missing entirely and a backed one showed its storage rather than what its `get`
answers. `hookedVisibleProps` now runs the hooks for the two that observe state,
and the cast keeps the raw table. Inside the class it is the same -- probed,
because "the hook does not run on `$this`" would have been a reasonable guess
and is wrong; only the hook *currently running* is skipped, which `hooksFor`
already handles.

### Where a virtual property goes

The order is observable and php2go put virtual properties last. The harvester
sorts by `zend_property_info.offset`, which is the slot the engine assigned --
and a virtual property has no slot, so its offset is a sentinel. What places it
is the harvest order, which is `properties_info` in declaration order: a virtual
property now takes the offset of the last real property before it and sorts
immediately after that one.

### And a hooked property is not a slot

`$test->byVal =& $ref` on any hooked property is
`Error: Cannot assign by reference to overloaded object`. Probed all three
shapes because `&get` looked like the exception -- it is not. The binding would
replace the property rather than reach through it, so even a hook that hands out
a reference cannot take one.

### Left for later

`get_object_vars` and `foreach` disagree about one shape: a *backed* set-only
hooked property that is uninitialized (`public int $p { set => $value; }`)
appears as NULL in `get_object_vars` and is skipped by `foreach`. php2go skips it
in both. Noted in TODO rather than modelled on one example.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/hooks.go` — `hookedVisibleProps`, `hasHooks`.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — foreach and `ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF`.
- `runtime/interp/program.go` — `get_object_vars`.
- `internal/zend/zend.go` — virtual properties keep their declared place.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

The corpus is genuinely long-tail from here. Rounds will be thinner; the honest

### Two small rules

**A magic accessor can be abstract.** An interface may declare
`public static function __callStatic($m, $a);` with no body. php2go forwarded to
it and got null back; the engine has nothing to forward to and reports
`Cannot call abstract method Foo::bar()` -- naming the method that was *called*,
not the accessor that would have answered.

**`__COMPILER_HALT_OFFSET__` is not a name `define()` may claim.** It belongs to
`__halt_compiler()`, which defines it per file at compile time. Probed both
halves, because "already defined" reads like an ordinary collision and is not:

```php
var_dump(defined("__COMPILER_HALT_OFFSET__"));      // false
var_dump(define("__COMPILER_HALT_OFFSET__", 1));    // Warning; false
var_dump(defined("__COMPILER_HALT_OFFSET__"));      // still false
```

### Looked at and left

`Cannot make non static method X::y() static` -- three tests, and the wording
varies in a way the corpus alone does not settle: `bug78776` has no `in class`
clause, `inter_007` has `in class d` naming an interface that is neither the one
being linked nor the one that holds the prototype. Pinning that down needs more
probes than three tests justify today; noted rather than guessed at.

The signature checks php2go skips for *engine* interfaces (`ArrayAccess`,
`DateTimeInterface`) are two tests, and the whole
"must be compatible with" family is seven.

## 2026-08-26 — two declaration checks php2go was not making

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3526 | 3534 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 74.8% | 75.0% |
| `failed` | 949 | 941 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 8 fixed, 0 broken.

### Picking the lens

Clustering by first-differing line has gone flat -- `property_hooks` is 36
failures in 36 clusters, `traits` 41 in 41. So a narrower question: **which
`Fatal error:` does the corpus expect that php2go never prints at all?** That is
65 tests across 59 distinct messages -- mostly one-of-a-kind declaration checks,
but with a few small families in it.

### Naming the same interface twice

```php
enum Foo: int implements BackedEnum {}
interface c extends a, b { }          // b is a class_alias of a
```

Probed the boundary, because "duplicate interface" could mean several things:

| declaration | verdict |
| --- | --- |
| `implements I, I` | fatal |
| `implements I, K` where K is an alias of I | fatal |
| `implements I, J` where J extends I | fine |
| `extends P implements I` where P implements I | fine |
| an enum naming `UnitEnum` or `BackedEnum` | fatal |

So the rule is duplicates within the declaration's *own* list, resolved -- which
is why an alias counts and an inherited one does not.

The first version seeded the set with `UnitEnum`/`BackedEnum` for an enum, and
broke a hundred tests: the harvested interface list **already contains them**.
Dropping the seeding both fixes that and catches the explicit mention, since it
then appears twice. Six tests.

### Claiming a function name twice

`Cannot redeclare function test() (previously declared in %s:%d)` -- php2go
replaced the entry silently, both at `ZEND_DECLARE_FUNCTION` and when `merge`
folded an included file's declarations in. Two tests, and the second of them is
worth the note: `lazy_objects/gh20905` gets there by cloning a lazy proxy, whose
`__clone` calls a function that declares a nested one for the second time.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/abstract.go` — `verifyInterfaceList`.
- `runtime/interp/signature.go` — the check joins `linkClass`, after traits and
  before inheritance.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go`, `runtime/interp/include.go` — the redeclaration
  fatal; `merge` answers which name was claimed twice.

## 2026-08-26 — a reference assignment drops what was there, and $GLOBALS is the symbol table

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3517 | 3526 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 74.6% | 74.8% |
| `failed` | 958 | 949 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 9 fixed, 0 broken.

### `gh10168`

A whole directory named after one bug, and the shape is always the same:

```php
class Test { function __destruct() { $GLOBALS['a'] = null; } }
$a = new Test; $tmp = new Test;
var_dump($a = &$tmp);   // NULL
```

The rebinding drops what `$a` held; PHP runs that destructor **there**, and the
destructor writes through the very box the assignment has just made -- so the
expression answers null. php2go released the old value later, and answered the
object.

Three handlers needed it and one of them was doing something else entirely:
`ZEND_ASSIGN_STATIC_PROP_REF` wrote *through* the property's box instead of
rebinding it, so `Test::$test = &$tmp` never made them share. That one is now a
branch of its own, with `rebindStaticProp` beside `staticPropRef`.

Four of the twenty-five remain -- they turn on the second call through a cache
slot, and getting them right needs the refcount timing php2go does not have.

### `$GLOBALS` is the symbol table

```php
$x = "ok"; echo $x;
unset($GLOBALS["x"]);
echo $x;                // Warning: Undefined variable $x
```

`unset($GLOBALS[...])` compiles to the by-name `ZEND_UNSET_VAR`, which php2go
answered by dropping the entry -- leaving the top-level compiled variable, bound
to that slot since `runGlobal`, still holding the value.

The first fix emptied the box, which passed the three `unset_cv` tests and broke
`wrong_assign_to_variable`: emptying is not what PHP does. It **unbinds** the
name. Anything else sharing the box keeps what it held, which is exactly what
`var_dump($a =& returnsVal())` reports when the old `$a`'s destructor unsets the
name. `unbindGlobal` rebinds the top-level slot and drops the entry, and touches
nothing else.

The same rule covers an include: an included file's variables *are* the
caller's, so `unset($x)` in one removes the caller's name too. The frame now
records what a shared scope unset, and the caller applies it on the way out.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — the release at `ZEND_ASSIGN_REF` and
  `ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF`; the rebinding branch for `ZEND_ASSIGN_STATIC_PROP_REF`;
  `unbindGlobal`; `frame.sharedScope` and `frame.unsetNames`.
- `runtime/interp/class.go` — `rebindStaticProp`, `staticPropKey`.
- `runtime/interp/include.go` — `applyUnsets`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

## 2026-08-26 — which class a trace names, and when serializing wakes a lazy object

`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 20 fixed, 0 broken.

### A trace frame names the declaring class

`bug29674` differs from the engine on one line:

```
#0 ...(25): ChildClass->printVars()     php2go
#0 ...(25): BaseClass->printVars()      engine
```

Probed the shape rather than assuming "the declaring one" covered everything:

| the call | the frame |
| --- | --- |
| inherited method on a subclass | the parent that declares it |
| an override | the overriding class |
| a method reached through a trait | the class that *used* the trait |
| a static inherited by a subclass | the class that declares it |

So the frame is the resolved method's declaring scope, which `pendingCall`
already carried as `class` -- `traceName` was reading `name`, which is the class
the call site named. Nine tests.

### Serializing a lazy object

Four related rules, and getting one of them wrong is what showed the difference
between them:

- **Normally serialize() produces the state**, because it has to write it.
- **`__serialize` decides for itself what to write**, so the state is never
  wanted and the object stays lazy.
- **`__sleep` does not.** It answers with property *names*; the values behind
  them still have to exist. A first attempt exempted both and broke
  `serialize___sleep_initializes`, which says so directly.
- **`ReflectionClass::SKIP_INITIALIZATION_ON_SERIALIZE`** (8, alongside
  `SKIP_DESTRUCTOR` at 16) is the caller saying the same thing about an object
  rather than a class. php2go was ignoring the flags argument entirely.

And one more from the same corner: `__sleep` on a lazy *proxy* may touch the
object and so produce its state -- which lives in the instance, not the shell,
so that is what gets written from there on.

### Two smaller things

- `setRawValueWithoutLazyInitialization` skips the initializer, not the
  declaration: `new stdClass` into a `string $a` is still
  `Cannot assign stdClass to property C::$a of type string`.
- `__sleep` naming a declared property that holds nothing yet leaves it out
  *silently*. Only a name the class never declared earns
  `"y" returned as member variable from __sleep() but does not exist`. php2go
  warned for both, which is what the lazy tests tripped over.

## 2026-08-26 — how a compile failure is reported, and what a static is

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3482 | 3497 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 73.9% | 74.2% |
| `failed` | 993 | 978 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 15 fixed, 0 broken.

### Picking the lens

The message lens turned up a family that named itself: five failing diffs
contained the literal string `zend: ` -- php2go's own loader error text, leaking
into the program's output. Grepping the whole diff for it found **thirteen**
tests, all about how `eval` and `include` report a failure to compile.

php2go raised `ParseError` with the loader's raw text as the message:

```
Fatal error: Uncaught ParseError: zend: /tmp/php2phpt-evalNNN/eval.php:
Fatal error: Cannot use [] for reading in /tmp/php2phpt-evalNNN/eval.php on
line 1 in .../bug55007.php:4
```

Four rules, and the corpus states all of them:

- **A syntax error is a `ParseError`; anything else the compiler refuses is a
  `CompileError`** -- its parent, and equally catchable. `bug75218` catches
  `CompileError` for `final final`, `private protected`, `__HALT_COMPILER()` in
  a nested scope and a non-literal `declare(encoding=)`.
- **The message is the bare reason.** `bug75252` var_dumps
  `syntax error, unexpected identifier "FOO"` and nothing else -- no heading, no
  file, no line.
- **The position is inside the compiled code**, and the file is named after the
  site that ran it: `%s(%d) : eval()'d code`. For `include` it is the included
  file's own path.
- **Neither is displayed as an uncaught exception.** A ParseError prints
  `Parse error: <msg> in <file> on line <N>`, a CompileError prints
  `Fatal error: <msg> in <file> on line <N>`, and neither gets a class name, an
  "Uncaught", or a stack trace -- none of it was ever a call.

### A static is a box, not a value

Reading `errored` for once rather than `failed`, `bug74340` was recursing
forever where the engine stops after two calls. The smallest case:

```php
function f($n) {
    static $first = true;
    echo "f $n first=", var_export($first, true), "\n";
    if ($first) { $first = false; f($n + 1); f($n + 2); }
}
f(1);
// engine: true, false, false     php2go: forever
```

`ZEND_BIND_STATIC` copied the static's value into the compiled variable and
`syncStatics` wrote it back when the call ended -- so a call made from inside
the one that wrote it saw the old value. The comment on `syncStatics` even said
what it should have been: *"BIND_STATIC makes the compiled variable a reference
into that table"*. It does now: `setStatic` answers a box, the slot is bound to
it, and a write through the variable *is* the write to the static.

That cost `035`, which is a good statement of the remaining rule: at the top
level a `static $x` **is** the global `$x` -- `global $x` in a function reaches
it and `$GLOBALS` shows it -- so the globals entry has to be rebound to the same
box, the same way a top-level `$c =& $z` was two rounds ago.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/include.go` — `compileFailure`, `compileReport`.
- `runtime/interp/throw.go` — `compileErrorLabel`, the display branch.
- `runtime/interp/closure.go` — `setStatic` answers a box; `syncStatics` is
  down to the one case that still needs it.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `ZEND_BIND_STATIC` binds rather than stores;
  `bindGlobalStatic`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

## 2026-08-26 — a fatal that carried on, a NUL byte, and what a backtrace shows

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3472 | 3482 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 73.7% | 73.9% |
| `failed` | 1003 | 993 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 231 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 10 fixed, 0 broken.

### A fatal error that did not stop anything

`class_order_autoload_error3` prints one fatal in the engine and three in
php2go, in reverse nesting order. A variance check that needs a class the
program has not declared autoloads it; the autoloader declares it; linking
*that* class fails fatally -- and `resolveTypeClass` swallowed the error and
answered "class not available", so the outer check went on to report its own
inability on top of the failure below it.

`signatureCompatible` can only answer decidable or not, and neither is right
for "the request ended underneath me". The failure now travels on the unit as
`linkAbort`, cleared at the top of every `verifySignatures` so it only ever
answers for what happened below that call, and returned as-is when it is set.

### A property name starting with NUL

```php
$o = new stdClass; $p = "\0";
$o->$p = 1;      // Error: Cannot access property starting with "\0"
isset($o->$p);   // false, no error
$q = "a\0b"; $o->$q = 1;   // fine -- a NUL *inside* a name is how a mangled
                            // private property is spelled
```

Read, write and unset are errors; `isset` is not. The check belongs where the
property table is actually touched and not at the top of the handler, because
the magic accessors are asked first: `unset($a->$prop)` on a class with
`__unset` reports the failure *from inside that method*, on the recursive
attempt that magic re-entry sends to the real table.

### Two things a backtrace was not showing

Getting `bug52484`'s trace to match needed both:

- **A magic accessor is a frame.** `callMagic` invoked the method without
  pushing one, so an exception raised inside `__get` or `__unset` reported only
  `{main}`.
- **A trace escapes its string arguments.** Not-printable ASCII becomes `\xNN`
  in upper case, a backslash doubles, `\n`/`\r`/`\t`/`\f`/`\v` get their short
  spellings, and a quote is left alone even though the result is quoted. The
  15-byte cut happens *before* the escaping -- the engine counts the bytes it
  took, not the characters it printed.

And one the differential test found on its own: a call answered by `__call`
shows the *accessor's* frame, `C->__call('m', Array)`, not the name the caller
wrote with the arguments it wrote.

### A note on writing these tests

`"\xff"` in a differential case is folded by the compiler into a literal, and
an IR string field with an invalid UTF-8 byte will not marshal. Building the
byte at run time from a variable -- `$high = 255; chr($high)` -- keeps it out of
the literal table. `chr(255)` alone is not enough: the compiler folds that too.

## 2026-08-26 — three diagnostics and the compound callable behind one of them

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3465 | 3472 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 73.5% | 73.7% |
| `failed` | 1009 | 1003 |

`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 6 fixed, 0 broken; the seventh moved out of
`unsupported`.

### trigger_error's two missing levels

`E_USER_ERROR` was being reported as a warning and the script carried on. PHP 8.4
deprecates the level and still honours it: a `Deprecated:` line, then a
`Fatal error:` with the message, then the request stops -- shutdown functions and
all, like any other fatal. And a level that is none of the four user ones is a
`ValueError` naming all four, where php2go silently fell through to a notice.

### Serializable's deprecation is narrower than "implements it"

php2go emitted it for every declaration with `Serializable` in its
`implements` list, which is two notices where the engine prints one. Probed the
matrix:

| declaration | notice |
| --- | --- |
| `interface I extends Serializable` | no |
| `abstract class A implements Serializable` | no |
| `class C implements Serializable` | yes |
| `class G extends A` (inherits it) | yes |
| both `__serialize` and `__unserialize` | no |
| only one of the two | **yes** |
| `enum Foo implements Serializable` | yes -- and then the fatal |

So: anything not an interface and not abstract, that *is* a Serializable, and
does not supply both replacements. The enum row was found the honest way -- the
first version checked for `KIND_CLASS` and broke `enum/no-implement-serializable`,
which expects the notice immediately before the fatal that refuses the enum.

### The compound array callable

`callable_self_parent_static_deprecation` wanted
`Deprecated: Callables of the form ["B", "self::foo"] are deprecated` and
`is_callable(["B", "self::foo"]) === true`. php2go had the form in
`dynamicTarget` already, but `is_callable` did not use it -- it went through
`namedMethodCallable`, which knows nothing about `::` in the method half. Four
more things came out of probing the rest:

- **`self` and `parent` are relative to the class the callable named**, not to
  the calling scope, so `["B", "parent::s"]` works at global scope.
- **`static` is not.** It is late static binding, needs a calling scope, and at
  global scope earns `cannot access "static" when no class scope is active`.
- **Naming a scope the class is not in** -- `["A", "B::foo"]` -- is refused with
  `class A is not a subclass of B`, and *before* the deprecation: there is no
  callable there to call deprecated.
- **`$this` is forwarded.** A non-static method reached this way still runs on
  the caller's object when that object belongs to the method, which is why
  `call_user_func(["B", "parent::i"])` from inside a B reports B and not A.

That last one is what a first attempt got wrong in the other direction: setting
the *called scope* to the named class made `bug66719` report B where the engine
says A. The called scope really is the resolved one; it is `$this`, when there is
one, that carries the binding.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/scalars.go` — trigger_error's levels.
- `runtime/interp/abstract.go` — the Serializable scope, `hasSerializePair`.
- `runtime/interp/closure.go` — `scopedCallableClass` takes the context,
  `forwardThis`, the subclass check before the deprecation.
- `runtime/interp/program.go` — `is_callable` routes the compound form through
  `dynamicTarget`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — three cases.

### Picking the lens

Last round's grep-the-message trick generalised: for every failing diff, collect
the diagnostics (`Warning:`, `Notice:`, `Deprecated:`, `Fatal error:`) each side
produced, and report the ones that appear on only one. Two families came out of
the top of that list.

### The notice names the type on the *other* side

```php
$o = new stdClass;
var_dump($o < 2.5);
// Notice: Object of class stdClass could not be converted to float
```

php2go always said `int`. Six `compare_*_64bit` tests were failing on nothing
else. The conversion itself is unchanged -- an object beside a number is 1,
whatever the number is -- only the wording follows the operand.

### A by-reference binding needs a slot to bind

```php
class Test {
    private $x;
    public function &__get($name) { return $this->x; }
}
$test = new Test; $y = 5;
$test->x =& $y;   // Error: Cannot assign by reference to overloaded object
```

php2go bound into the property table regardless, quietly making a second,
shadowed property beside the overloaded one. Probed the whole matrix rather
than guessing which half of it mattered:

| the name is | `__get` | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| declared and visible | any | binds |
| an existing dynamic property | any | binds |
| private/protected from outside | present | `Cannot assign by reference to overloaded object` |
| undeclared | present | same error |
| private/protected from outside | absent | the ordinary visibility error |
| undeclared | absent | creates a dynamic property, deprecation and all |

Two details the probe settled that reading the message would not have:

- `__set` is not consulted at all. A class with only `__set` gets a plain
  dynamic property.
- A **by-value** `__get` produces `Notice: Indirect modification of overloaded
  property C::$z has no effect` before the error; a `&__get` produces no notice.
  That is exactly what `overloadedWriteFetch` already decides, so the handler
  calls it and then raises rather than repeating the rule.

While there, the binding now reports the dynamic-property deprecation it was
skipping when it did create one.

## 2026-08-26 — Throwable::__toString, and the chain it prints

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3439 | 3454 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 73.0% | 73.3% |
| `failed` | 1035 | 1020 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 15 fixed, 0 broken.

### Picking the lens

Grepping the GOT side of every failing diff for one error message found **24
tests blocked on `Object of class Exception could not be converted to string`**.
`throwableMethod` had a `__tostring` case, but it was a stub -- `ClassName ": "
message` -- and the `(string)` cast never reached it anyway: `toString` looks the
method up in the class table, and an engine class has nothing harvested for it.

### The format

```
RuntimeException: boom in file.php:1
Stack trace:
#0 file.php(2): inner()
#1 {main}

Next LogicException: wrap in file.php:2
Stack trace:
#0 {main}
```

The cause is printed *before* what it caused, each subsequent one prefixed with
`Next `. An exception with no message drops the colon rather than leaving a
dangling separator -- `MyEx in file.php:7`.

`fatalErrorText` was building the same thing by hand and did not know about the
chain at all, which is why `gh_21699` was missing its whole first half. Both now
come from `throwableString`; the uncaught report adds the `Fatal error: Uncaught`
prefix and the `thrown in` line, whose file and line are the *outermost*
exception's -- the one that actually escaped -- not the cause printed first.

### A chain is a list, not a graph

That cost `try_finally_recursive_previous`:

```php
$e = new Exception("M1");
try { throw new Exception("M2", 0, $e); } finally { throw $e; }
```

M2 already has M1 as its cause; the finally throws M1 over it, and php2go's
rethrow rule made M2 M1's cause in turn. The engine refuses a link that would
close a loop, and prints M1 alone. `chainsTo` now checks before linking.

### What is left of that family

Seven, and they are a different job: `ReflectionMethod`, `ReflectionProperty`
and friends have `__toString` exports of their own -- `Method [ <user, ctor>
final private method __construct ] { ... }` -- which php2go does not implement.

### Also this round

Two roots were missing from the walk and are now there: `spl_autoload_register`
and `set_error_handler` callbacks are held by the engine, not by the program, so
an autoloader closure survives the statement that registered it. It made no
difference to the count on its own, but it was found the honest way -- an
experiment that released *every* object temporary handed to a call fixed three
tests and broke fifteen, and six of the breakages were autoloader closures
losing handle #1. That experiment was reverted; the root fix was kept.

- `runtime/interp/gc.go` — autoloaders and error handlers as roots.

## 2026-08-26 — object handles come back, and the collector got four times cheaper

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3424 | 3439 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 72.7% | 73.0% |
| `failed` | 1050 | 1035 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |
| corpus wall clock | 2m03s | 28s |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 15 fixed, 0 broken.

### Picking the lens

The per-cluster view had gone flat, so the question became: how many tests fail
for *only one* reason? A script that matches EXPECT/EXPECTF line by line, with
the wildcards honoured, and asks whether every differing line is identical once
`#N` is normalised away, answered **37 tests differ only in object handles** —
the largest single cause in the corpus.

They are all the same shape:

```php
var_dump(new stdClass);   // engine #1
var_dump(new stdClass);   // engine #1 again
```

The engine's object store keeps freed slots on a free list and gives the most
recently freed one to the next `new`. php2go counted up forever.

### Handle reuse needs the collector to run always

Recycling a handle means knowing when an object died, which php2go answers by
walking. Until now the walk was gated on there being a destructor or a weak
container to observe -- so most programs never walked at all. Handles are
observable in *every* program, so the gate had to go.

Turning it on made the corpus take longer than ten minutes. Three fixes, and the
result is four times *faster* than before the change:

- `worthCollecting` scanned the object list at every release point. It is now a
  comparison of two lengths.
- The batching budget was a fixed 256 release points. It is now at least what
  the last walk cost, so the work spent walking is at worst proportional to the
  work the program did between two walks.
- That cost has to include the object list itself, not just what was marked.
  Cyclic garbage is never marked and is not freed at a release point either, so
  it stays on the list -- `gc_050` builds 100,000 cycles in a loop, and without
  counting the sweep the budget stayed at 256 while the list grew.

`object_gc_in_shutdown` makes a million objects in a loop; the list is now
compacted as objects are freed, so it stays flat instead of growing to a million
entries and a million-entry map beside it.

### Three things the walk could not see

Turning the collector on everywhere exposed roots that had been missing all
along. Each was invisible before only because nothing collected often enough to
notice.

**An object under construction.** Between `ZEND_NEW` and the end of the
constructor, the object lives in a temporary -- which is not a root -- and in a
pending call that `DO_FCALL` pops before the body even runs. The walk found it
unreachable, reclaimed its handle and dropped it from the list; its destructor
then never ran at any release point. `unit.building` now holds it for that
window. (The first attempt at this pointed the walk at the frame's live call
stack, which turned out to be a *different* latent bug -- `frame.calls` is only
written back when a generator suspends -- but the pending call is popped before
the constructor body runs, so it was not enough on its own.)

**A constant.** `define("Bar", new TestClass)` keeps an object for the whole
request and `ctx.Constants()` was not among the roots, so `bug37811` handed the
handle straight back out.

**A chain.** Freeing an object releases what it held, which may be the last
thing holding something else. PHP's refcount cascades down the whole chain at
once; php2go's single pass over the list freed the head and left the tail for
the next release point -- or for shutdown, if there was not one. The sweep is
now a worklist: freeing an object decrements the dead-holder count of everything
it held directly, and anything that reaches zero joins the queue.

That last one needed `deadReferences` fixed too. It walked *transitively* from
each dead object, so an edge got credited to whichever object the shared walk
happened to reach first -- and in `$e->o = $f; $f->o = $e; $g->o = $e;` freeing
`$g` cascaded through the whole `e`/`f` cycle and destroyed it. Both the count
and the decrement now use `edgesFrom`, which follows arrays but stops at the far
end of each object edge, because an edge belongs to the object it leaves.

### What is still not reused

`ctor_promotion_defaults` and friends still count up: `var_dump(new Point(...))`
drops its object at the end of the statement, and php2go has no release point
there. The passing-by-accident version of this round -- where the object was
reclaimed *during* its own constructor -- matched those tests, which is a
reminder that a matching number is not the same as a correct one.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/gc.go` — the budget, the worklist sweep, `edgesFrom`, the
  `shallow` marker mode, the new roots.
- `runtime/interp/cycles.go` — `handle`, `built`.
- `runtime/interp/call.go` — `freeHandles`, `building`, `lastWalk`.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `unit.handle()` at every creation site;
  `frame.callsRef`.
- `runtime/php/ctx.go` — `Constants`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

## 2026-08-25 — a global that is rebound by reference, and who outlives the symbol table

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3421 | 3424 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 72.6% | 72.7% |
| `failed` | 1053 | 1050 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 3 fixed, 0 broken.

Three tests is a thin round, but both changes are correctness fixes that were
visible well beyond the count they were found through.

### Chasing the rest of the gc family

Nineteen `gc_*` tests were still failing after the previous round. Five of them
under-counted — `int(0)` where the engine said 1 or 2 — and narrowing found the
smallest case is not about cycles at all:

```php
$c = []; $c[] =& $c; $z = 1; $c =& $z;
var_dump(gc_collect_cycles());   // 1 in the engine, 0 in php2go
```

The same program inside a function gave the right answer. What differs is that a
top-level compiled variable **is** the entry in the globals table —
`runGlobal` binds each slot to `ctx.Globals.RefAt(name)` — and `ZEND_ASSIGN_REF`
was rebinding only the slot. The globals entry kept the old box, which both kept
the cycle reachable and, much worse, was plainly wrong:

```php
$c = 5; $z = 1; $c =& $z;
var_dump($GLOBALS['c']);          // engine 1, php2go 5
function f() { global $c; var_dump($c); }
f();                              // engine 1, php2go 5
```

`unset` at global scope already had this (`ctx.Globals.Unset`); the reference
assignment did not.

One trap on the way: binding the globals entry with a second `sharedRef(source)`
raised `Ref.shared` twice for what is one name, so `$s = &$b[0]; unset($s);`
kept printing the `&` marker. The globals entry takes the box the slot took, not
another share of the source.

### Who outlives the symbol table

That fix cost `bug32322`, which was passing for a reason worth writing down: it
has two singletons, one in a static property and one in a function static, both
also named by globals. The engine destroys them in *creation* order; php2go was
destroying them in reverse declaration order, and only matched before because
the stale globals entry meant it never reached them there at all.

`runDestructors` tears the symbol table down in reverse insertion order and then
walks the object store. But a global is not the only thing that can hold an
object: one a static property or a function static still holds survives the
symbol table and dies with the store. So the teardown now skips an object that
is reachable from a root other than the globals — `storedMarker`, which is
`reachableMarker` without `ctx.Globals`.

### What is left in gc

The remaining ones need engine timing php2go does not have:

- `gc_028`, `gc_029`, `gc_016` count *after* destructors have run and broken the
  cycle, and what a refcount then frees is not attributed to the collector.
  php2go counts before, which is what every other probe agreed with.
- `gc_048`, `gc_049`, `gc_053` are about the automatic collector and its status.
- `gc_023`, `bug70805` depend on the root buffer filling mid-loop.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `ZEND_ASSIGN_REF` rebinds the globals entry.
- `runtime/interp/gc.go` — `storedMarker` split out of `reachableMarker`.
- `runtime/interp/call.go` — `runDestructors` leaves stored objects to the store.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — two cases.

## 2026-08-25 — what gc_collect_cycles() counts

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3404 | 3421 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 72.2% | 72.6% |
| `failed` | 1070 | 1053 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`. Wall clock unchanged at
about two minutes. Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300`: 18 fixed, 1 broken.

### Picking the lens

`lazy_objects` had gone fragmented (largest cluster: 3), so the lens moved to the
root of `Zend/tests`, 556 failures. The first clustering run produced a bogus
50-test cluster — normalising digits to `N` made numerically-different lines
look identical and they all fell through to a `<eof>` key. Dropping the digit
normalisation gave an honest picture, and the real family in it was **34 failing
`gc_*` tests**, the largest coherent group left in the corpus.

### The rule, probed rather than derived

php2go's collector answers "what can the program no longer reach". The engine's
`gc_collect_cycles()` answers something narrower, and the difference is the
whole family. Fifteen probes settled it:

| program | engine |
| --- | --- |
| `$a = new stdClass; $a = null;` | 0 |
| `$b->s = $b` | 1 |
| `$c->o = $d; $d->o = $c` | 2 |
| `$e->o = $f` (both dropped) | 0 |
| `$g[] =& $g` | 1 |
| `…cycle…; $c->extra = new stdClass` | 3 |
| `$g2->o = $e` pointing *into* a live-free cycle | not counted |
| `$i->arr = []; $i->arr[] = $i` | 2 |
| `$x->a = [1, 2, [3]]` hanging off a cycle | arrays not counted |

So: **the unreachable values on a cycle, plus everything unreachable that hangs
off one.** Garbage a refcount would already have taken is not counted at all,
which is why php2go's old "count what I destroyed" answer was wrong even for the
cases where it destroyed the right things.

Two details worth keeping:

- Arrays are values the collector frees, and count. An object's *property table*
  is not — it is not a separate array in the engine — so the graph runs from an
  object straight to what its properties hold, or `$b->s = $b` would count 2.
- The last row is the one divergence. The engine marks a compiler-folded array
  literal immutable and leaves it out of the collector entirely; php2go has no
  such mark, so it counts those. Recorded in `cycles.go` and in TODO.

### What it took

- `unit.objects`: every object, not just the destructible ones `unit.live`
  tracks. The automatic collection paths still consult `live` only, so their
  cost is unchanged — the complete list is read exclusively by
  `gc_collect_cycles()`.
- `unit.refHosts`: every array a reference has been bound into. A cycle made
  only of arrays needs a reference to exist at all, so these are the seeds for
  finding one without an object to start from. Arrays reachable from a dead
  object need no registry — the walk finds them.
- `cycles.go`: build the unreachable subgraph, find the nodes on a cycle with an
  iterative Tarjan, then count everything reachable from those.
- `unit.forget`: after a counting collection the unreachable values are gone in
  the engine's terms, so they leave both lists. Without this the counts were
  cumulative — every earlier corpse counted again — and the lists would have
  grown to every object the request ever made.

The count is taken *before* any destructor runs, since a destructor can make
more values unreachable and the engine likewise decides what it is freeing
before it starts.

### The one loss

`bug70805` builds 9,998 array cycles in a loop and expects `int(0)`: the
engine's root buffer fills, collection happens *during* the loop, and by the
explicit call there is nothing left. php2go has no automatic cycle collection,
so it now counts all 10,000. It was passing before only because the answer was
always 0. Reproducing it would mean reproducing the root-buffer timing, which
needs refcounts; left as a known gap rather than papered over.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/cycles.go` (new) — the counting rule and its evidence.
- `runtime/interp/gc.go` — `collectKind` gained a `counting` flag;
  `reachableObjects` became `reachableMarker` so the arrays survive the call.
- `runtime/interp/call.go` — `objects`, `refHosts`.
- object creation sites — wrapped in `unit.born`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — three cases covering the table above.

## 2026-08-25 — lazy objects: rollback, destructors, the proxy rule, and clone

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3386 | 3404 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.9% | 72.2% |
| `failed` | 1088 | 1070 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |
| `lazy_objects` passing | 110 | 122 (of 223) |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300` before and after: 18 fixed, 0 broken.

### Picking the lens

`lazy_objects` had become the largest failing directory (114 of 1088). Clustering
it by first-differing line — this time reading `--- EXPECTF ---` as well as
`--- EXPECT ---`, which the previous script silently skipped and which had been
hiding 81 of the 116 blocks — gave four families worth having.

### A failed ghost initializer is rolled back, not emptied

`resolveLazy` called `stripState` when the initializer threw. That is wrong in
two ways at once: a property given a value by
`setRawValueWithoutLazyInitialization` was never deferred and must survive, and
a dynamic property the initializer added must not. Both are the same fix — take
a snapshot of the property table before `restoreDefaults` and put it back — which
is what the engine does by swapping the table aside.

Five tests, and the visible symptom was as much the header count as the values:
`lazy ghost object(C)#N (1)` versus `(0)`, since the count is of properties that
hold something.

### A lazy object never runs its own destructor

Guard on `object.Lazy != nil`, in `destruct`, `destructAt`, and the collector's
`hasDestructorPending`. Three situations fall out of the one rule:

- An uninitialized ghost or proxy has no state to tear down, and its initializer
  is never run for the purpose.
- An initialized ghost has dropped `Lazy` by then, so it destructs normally.
- An initialized *proxy* keeps `Lazy` forever, and it is the instance behind it
  — a separate object — whose destructor runs. php2go had been running both.

### The proxy compatibility rule runs the other way round

php2go required the factory's instance to be the proxy's class or a subclass.
The engine requires the opposite, and more besides:

```
The real instance class A is not compatible with the proxy class WithStatic.
The proxy must be a instance of the same class as the real instance, or a
sub-class with no additional properties, and no overrides of the __destructor
or __clone methods.
```

(The article and the `__destructor` spelling are the engine's.) Probed the
boundary directly rather than reading it off the message:

| proxy class | verdict |
| --- | --- |
| same class as instance | ok |
| subclass adding only a method | ok |
| subclass adding a constant, or an interface | ok |
| subclass adding a property | rejected |
| subclass adding a **static** property | rejected |
| subclass declaring `__destruct` or `__clone` | rejected |
| subclass *inheriting* `__destruct` from the instance's class | ok |
| **parent** of the instance's class | rejected |

The first attempt at the property half rejected everything, because a harvested
class table lists inherited properties too; `declaring_class` is what separates
"added here" from "came from above".

### clone

Two bugs, both about the proxy shell versus the instance:

- `__clone` was invoked on the cloned *proxy*, which has no properties of its
  own, so `$this->v = clone $this->v` operated on nothing. It runs on the copied
  instance.
- A write descent — `$proxy->v->s = 'B'` — never initialized the object at all.
  `ZEND_FETCH_OBJ_W` and friends had no `resolveLazy`; reads had one, which is
  why the gap only showed on the write side.

Adding that raised a second question the corpus answered: which magic accessor
does a write descent consult? `gh20875_proxy_get_no_init` says `__get`, not
`__set` — `$x = &$proxy->x` on a class with `&__get` must not initialize —
because what a write descent wants is a slot to write *through*. It broke that
test on the first attempt and was fixed by mapping the write-fetch opcodes to
`__get` in `lazyProperty`.

### Files

- `runtime/interp/lazy.go` — `snapshot`/`takeSnapshot`/`restore`, rewritten
  `compatibleProxy` and its diagnostic.
- `runtime/interp/call.go`, `runtime/interp/gc.go` — the destructor guard.
- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `ZEND_CLONE` runs `__clone` on the instance; the
  write-fetch handler resolves laziness; `lazyProperty` maps the write fetches
  to `__get`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — five cases.

## 2026-08-25 — a declaration outlives the slot it was written on

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3380 | 3386 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.7% | 71.9% |
| `failed` | 1094 | 1088 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Diff-set comparison of `-diff 1300` before and after: 6 fixed, 0 broken.

### Picking the lens

`type_declarations` was the largest failing directory (90 failures, 353/460
passing). Clustering it by first-differing line gave 77 distinct shapes in 90
tests — too fragmented to attack as a whole — but one coherent family of four
stood out, differing only in whether a value read back as `int(N)` or
`string(N) "N"`. Both halves of it turned out to be the same idea: a property's
declared type outliving the slot it was written on.

### A reference bound to a typed property becomes typed

```php
class Test { public string $x = "x"; }
$test = new Test; $y = "y";
$test->x = &$y;
$z = 42; $y = $z;       // $y is string(2) "42"; $z stays int(42)
```

php2go already had the machinery. `php.RefSource` exists, `elementRef` adds one
for write descents, and its comment states the intent: *the constraint travels
with the box rather than with the property*. What was missing is that
`ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF` bound the incoming ref into the property slot without
adding the property's type as a source.

Two details the engine settled:

- The binding is itself a write to the property, so whatever is already in the
  box has to satisfy the declaration at bind time, not only later writes.
- Only a *declared, non-dynamic* property contributes a source. A dynamic
  property has no declaration to travel.

### `__get` for an unset typed property is held to that type

Unsetting a typed property does not remove its declaration, so the accessor
standing in for it is still bound by the type:

```php
class Test { public int $val; public function __get($n) { return "42"; } }
$test = new Test; unset($test->val);
var_dump($test->val);   // int(42), not string(2) "42"
```

The engine words the failure as a return-value problem rather than an
assignment, because no assignment took place:

```
Value of type string returned from U::__get() must be compatible with
unset property U::$w of type int
```

So this is `magicReadType` in `types.go` and not a reuse of
`verifyPropertyWrite`, which produces the `Cannot assign …` wording.

### The visibility caveat, found the honest way

The first version of that rule cost `typed_properties_100`, whose own title says
why: *"Property type not enforced for `__get` if the property is not visible"*.

```php
class Test { private int $prop; public function __get($n) { return "foobar"; } }
$test = new Test; var_dump($test->prop);   // string(6) "foobar"
```

Reaching `__get` because the caller *may not see* the property is a different
situation from reaching it because the property is unset. The declaration is not
part of what that scope was promised, so nothing is enforced. The handler
already computed the `verdict`; enforcement is now gated on `accessAllowed`, and
a probe confirmed the boundary cases — the same private property read from
inside the class *is* enforced, and a protected one read from a subclass never
reaches `__get` at all (it is an uninitialized-property `Error`).

### Files

- `runtime/interp/interp.go` — `ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF` adds the property's type as
  a `php.RefSource` and re-verifies the box; the `FETCH_OBJ_R` magic path calls
  `magicReadType` with the visibility verdict.
- `runtime/interp/types.go` — `magicReadType`.
- `runtime/interp/differential_test.go` — three cases: the binding, the typed
  `__get`, and the invisible-property exemption.

## 2026-08-25 — &__get hands back the slot

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3374 | 3380 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.6% | 71.7% |
| `failed` | 1100 | 1094 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### A magic accessor declared by reference

`$obj->box[0] = 1` where the class has `function &__get($n)` writes through to
the property. php2go was reporting `Indirect modification of overloaded property
has no effect` and then modifying a copy -- the notice was right about what
php2go did and wrong about what PHP does.

A `&__get` returns the slot itself. The reference travels out of
`overloadedWriteFetch` unchanged and the fetch *binds* it rather than storing a
copy, so the write lands in the object.

The by-value case turned out to be wrong in the other direction, and only a
probe caught it: php2go warned that the write would have no effect and then let
it through anyway, because it handed back the same `*php.Array` the property
held. It hands back a copy now, so the write really is lost.

`ArrayObject` also gained its `var_dump` shape while the same test was being
read: the elements live in an internal store, and the engine shows that store
as the private property it is, `["storage":"ArrayObject":private]`.

### The blanket temporary release does not work

Last entry's plan was to extend temporary release from the opcodes that take
ownership to *every* opcode that reads one, on the reasoning that Zend's
TMP_VAR is single-use. Measured: **3374 to 3090 passing, with 128 errored**.
Reverted.

So php2go reads a temporary across oplines somewhere its own handlers rely on,
and the single-use assumption is Zend's rather than this interpreter's. Whatever
`bug32596` and `bug43175` need, it is not that; finding it means knowing which
handlers re-read, and the blanket experiment does not say which.

## 2026-08-25 — a temporary is owned by whoever consumes it

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3373 | 3374 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.6% | 71.6% |
| `failed` | 1101 | 1100 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`. One test on the metric
and a correctness bug fixed that no test in the corpus catches.

### Scoping the thing that keeps coming up

php2go never frees a temporary: the slot keeps whatever the opcode left there
until the frame ends. That is why the collector cannot treat temporaries as
roots, why `f(new C())` did not destroy the C, and it was written up twice as
"the fix touches every opcode that reads one".

It does not have to be every opcode. Zend's TMP_VAR is single-use by
construction, and the places that matter are the ones that take *ownership*: a
`SEND_*` handing an argument to a call, and a frameless ICALL taking its
operands directly. Both clear the slot now, and when the call returns, whatever
those held may have no reader left -- which is where PHP's refcount would have
freed it. `ZEND_FREE` does the same: the compiler emits it exactly where a value
stops being needed.

A VAR is left alone. It can be read across many oplines -- a `foreach` iterates
one -- and the compiler emits `FREE`/`FE_FREE` for those.

### The bug the corpus did not catch

Collecting when a frame returns was freeing what the frame *returned*. Nothing
names it yet: the caller has not stored it, and a walk from the roots does not
find it. `$k = keep(new D(3))` printed the destructor before the assignment.

The value is now held aside for the length of that one collection --
`unit.keeping`, cleared straight afterwards. Nothing in `Zend/tests` failed
because of this; a nine-case probe did, and it is now a differential case.

### Two tests lost to the same fix

`bug32596` and `bug43175` were passing *because* of the bug: they build an
object, use it for one property read and drop it, and the destructor happened to
run at the right moment when returned values were being freed early.

They need the temporary released by the opcode that reads it -- `FETCH_OBJ_R`
here -- rather than only by the ones that take ownership. That is the next step
of the same work, and it is in TODO rather than being papered over by leaving a
correctness bug in place to keep two tests green.

## 2026-08-25 — three small ones, and a flag that is not there

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3370 | 3373 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.5% | 71.6% |
| `failed` | 1104 | 1101 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### A stack trace spells a function the way it was declared

php2go took the callee's name from the `INIT_FCALL` literal, which the compiler
stores lowercased, so `throwException()` appeared in a trace as
`throwexception()`. The declared name wins when the unit has one.

A destructor is also a frame of its own in a trace -- `#0 file(N):
Bar->__destruct()` -- attributed to wherever the program was when the object
stopped being reachable. `destructAt` pushes one now.

### `??` does not report what it is asking about

`A['undefined'] ?? 1` inside a *constant expression* was warning about the
undefined key. The whole point of the operator is that reading the left side
says nothing about it being absent. The left side is evaluated silenced, which
is exact here: the only diagnostics a constant expression's dim or property
fetch can raise are those undefined-ness reports.

### The fallback that has no flag to key off

An unqualified constant inside a namespace falls back to the global one.
`ZEND_FETCH_CONSTANT` can tell the two spellings apart from
`IS_CONSTANT_UNQUALIFIED_IN_NAMESPACE` on the opline, and php2go has always
honoured it. A *folded* constant expression -- a parameter default, a property
default -- has no such flag anywhere the harvest can see it: neither the AST
node's attribute nor the zval's `u2` slot carries it by the time the harvester
runs. Both were tried.

So php2go falls back for a folded constant whatever the spelling. That is right
for the unqualified case and wrong for a written-out qualified name that is
genuinely undefined and happens to share a short name with a global constant.
The comment at the call site says so, and it is in TODO -- rather than leaving
the fallback out and the common case broken, or leaving it in and pretending
it is exact.

### Recorded as out of reach for now

`frameless_throwing_destructor` wants `in_array(new Foo(), [new Bar()], true)`
to destroy the temporaries when the call returns. php2go never frees a
temporary -- the slot keeps whatever the opcode left there -- which is also why
the collector cannot treat temporaries as roots. Freeing them when consumed is
the fix and it is a change to every opcode that reads one.

## 2026-08-25 — where a destructor's exception goes

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3357 | 3370 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.2% | 71.5% |
| `failed` | 1117 | 1104 |
| `unsupported` | 232 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### A destructor was throwing into a wall

`destruct` ran a destructor and, if it threw, printed the exception as an
uncaught fatal. That is right at shutdown, where there is no program left to
catch anything. It is wrong everywhere else: since the collector started running
destructors at release points, a destructor throws *inside* whatever the program
was doing, and the try that is open there catches it.

`destructAt` returns the error instead, `collect` carries the first one out, and
the four release points -- `unset`, assignment over the last name, unsetting an
element, a frame returning -- raise it the way any other opcode error is raised.
`try_finally_012` and `_016` are the shape: a destructor throwing inside a
`finally` while another exception is already on its way out.

### The cycle collector's count, and what it is allowed to free

`gc_collect_cycles()` was reporting collections PHP does not report, because
php2go destroyed at the release point what PHP leaves for the cycle collector.
The distinction is refcount-shaped and looked out of reach, but it is not: after
the mark phase, an unreachable object that *another unreachable object still
holds* is one whose refcount has not reached zero. Those are left alone at a
release point and freed when `gc_collect_cycles()` asks; the rest are freed
immediately, which is what PHP's refcount would have done.

The counting walk is the marking walk with a different callback, so it costs
nothing when there is no garbage.

It is not exact. php2go only knows about objects that *have destructors*, so a
cycle made of ordinary objects that hold a destructible one is not recognised as
a cycle and is freed early. Recording that rather than pretending otherwise: the
differential case leaves the shape out.

### zend.enable_gc is now readable

`gc_enabled()` answered a hardcoded true and `ini_get`/`ini_set` answered false
for everything. There is now a small table of the settings php2go actually
models -- one so far -- with `ini_get` still answering false for anything
outside it, which is what PHP does for a setting that does not exist and is
honest for one php2go disregards.

`lazy_objects` ships fifteen tests named `init_trigger_*`, one per operation,

| produces the state | reports what is there |
| --- | --- |
| `foreach` | `(array)` cast |
| `get_object_vars` | `get_mangled_object_vars` |
| `json_encode` | `var_dump` |
| `serialize` | `debug_zval_dump` |
| `var_export` | |
| comparison | |

php2go had `(array)` and `get_mangled_object_vars` waking the object -- added
two days ago on the reasoning that "they read the properties, so the properties
have to exist". They do read the properties; they read the ones the object
*has*, which for an uninitialized lazy object is none, and the cast is
`array(0) {}`. `var_dump` was already right, and it is the same rule.

The other direction was missing: `var_export` and comparison are triggers and
were not. `var_export` is a plain builtin with no interpreter to call an
initializer with, so it is intercepted before the builtin runs -- and a proxy
has to export what it forwards to rather than the empty wrapper.

The probe covering all nine operations is now a differential case, because the
split is exactly the kind of thing that gets re-derived wrongly.

## 2026-08-25 — $a[k] = &$x did nothing

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3344 | 3355 |
| pass rate (of 4712 attempted) | 71.0% | 71.2% |
| `failed` | 1131 | 1119 |
| `unsupported` | 231 | 232 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The bug

`$a[0] = &$x` left `$a[0]` unchanged. So did `$a[] = &$x` and
`$a[0][0] = &$x`. Not an edge case -- the plain form, in every shape.

PHP compiles it as `FETCH_DIM_W` followed by `ASSIGN_REF`. The fetch hands back
a box for the element; the assignment is supposed to make the *element* share
the source's box. php2go's `ASSIGN_REF` wrote the temporary the fetch had
returned, which nothing reads afterwards -- so the element kept pointing at its
old box and the statement had no effect.

The temporary carries only the box, not where it came from, so `FETCH_DIM_W`
and `FETCH_OBJ_W` now record the container and key against the result slot and
`ASSIGN_REF` rebinds through that. The note is taken *after* the fetch, since an
append has no key until the element exists.

### Three things that only became reachable once it worked

A cycle made of arrays rather than objects was previously impossible to build,
so nothing had ever followed one:

- **`print_r` had no recursion guard.** `var_dump` did. PHP prints
  `Array\n *RECURSION*`, with the refusal on its own line indented by one space.
- **`serialize` recorded objects but not references.** PHP numbers references
  too and writes a repeated one as `R:<first position>;` -- which is what
  terminates `$a[] = &$a`, a cycle with no objects in it. Five shapes settled
  the numbering; the unserializer needed the matching `R:` and has to share one
  box between both ends.
- **`Array.Clone` deep-copied nested arrays** with nothing to stop it revisiting
  one. It now carries the arrays already being copied.

`var_dump` also had to learn not to put its `&` marker on a `*RECURSION*` line:
the marker belongs to a value it printed, and that is a refusal to print one.

### A package invariant, nearly broken

The first version of the comparison depth guard used package-level variables.
`ops.go` says in a comment that this package keeps no mutable state at package
scope, because a long-lived process serves many requests -- and `looseEqual`
already threads its depth as an argument for exactly that reason. The ordering
path now does the same and reuses the `maxCompareDepth` that was already there.

`bug63882` still fails: two objects that contain themselves compare as unequal
where PHP raises `Nesting level too deep - recursive dependency?`. Bounding the
walk stops the crash; reporting it the way the engine does is a separate piece
of work.

`bug63635` builds 87,000 objects that all have destructors. Walking the roots at
every release point is quadratic in that, and the corpus went from 19 seconds to
not finishing.

Below 512 live destructible objects php2go still walks at every release point,
which keeps destructor timing exact where a test is watching for it. Above that
the walks are batched one in 256 -- the same trade the engine makes with its own
root-buffer threshold, and for the same reason. The corpus runs in 86 seconds.
