**The rate went down and that is the point.** 103 tests that php2phpt had been

### php2phpt was skipping every test with an --INI-- section

257 of them. The section was recorded and then treated as "needs machinery we
do not have", which for most of these is not true: they set `memory_limit`,
`opcache.*`, `session.*`, `date.timezone` or `error_reporting` -- limits php2go
does not impose, subsystems it does not have, or settings about how the
*engine* reports rather than what a program observes.

`UnhonourableIni` now names the first setting that would change behaviour and
that php2go can neither apply nor disregard, and the test runs unless there is
one. Two of the judgements are worth writing down:

- **`zend.max_allowed_stack_size` is not ignorable.** A test that sets it is a
  test *about* running out of stack; running one without a limit runs out of
  Go's instead, which is a `fatal error: stack overflow` and not a test result.
- **`zend.enable_gc` is ignorable**, which looks wrong and is not. It switches
  off *cycle* collection; PHP still destroys by refcount. php2go has one
  collector and it is the only thing that destroys anything, so honouring the
  setting would switch off ordinary destruction too. Disregarding it keeps
  destructors running where PHP's refcount would have run them.

Enabling the INI tests immediately produced `fatal error: stack overflow`:
`bug64896` builds `$foo->foo = $foo` and serializes it, and php2go's serializer
had no notion of an object it had already written.

PHP numbers **every value** it writes, from one, and remembers the position it
first wrote each object at; a repeated object is `r:<position>;`. Keys are not
values and take no position -- which is the part a probe had to settle, since
seven shapes of nesting all agree with several wrong rules and only one right
one. The unserializer needed the same numbering, and an object has to register
itself *before* its properties are read or a self-reference inside them cannot
resolve.

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3277 | 3292 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 71.7% | 72.1% |
| `failed` | 1076 | 1061 |
| `unsupported` | 212 | 212 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### var_dump of a Generator

A Generator has no properties, and the engine describes it through a debug-info
handler like a Closure or a WeakMap: one entry, `function`, naming the body it
is running -- `Class::method`, `{closure:file:line}` or a bare function name.
php2go was printing `object(Generator)#N (0) {}`. Five tests.

### The harness was reading `%0` as two characters

`cast_to_array` expects `string(1) "%0"`, which looks like a contradiction until
you find `'%0' => '\x00'` in run-tests.php's specifier table: a `.phpt` file
cannot carry a NUL byte, so the harness spells one this way. Every test that
looks at a mangled private property name -- `\0Class\0prop` -- uses it, which is
why the mangling work landed earlier and the tests still failed. Ten tests.

Two other differences from run-tests.php came out of the same table:

- **`%f`** is written there with a lookahead, which RE2 does not have. The
  alternation `[+-]?(?:\d+(?:\.\d+)?|\.\d+)(?:[Ee][+-]?\d+)?` accepts the same
  language, and the old pattern rejected `-1.5e3`.
- **`%%` is not an escape.** run-tests quotes the pattern and then substitutes
  the specifiers it knows; a doubled percent stays doubled. php2go was
  collapsing it to one, which is *more lenient than the engine's own harness* --
  exactly the direction that lets a gap masquerade. No corpus test uses it, so
  the count did not move; the unit test that asserted the lenient behaviour now
  asserts the strict one.

### Release points, continued

`ZEND_UNSET_DIM` now runs a release check like the other three. It fixed nothing
on its own -- no corpus test drops its last reference through an array element
alone -- but it is the same event and leaving it out would be arbitrary.

## 2026-08-25 — asking the question the other way round

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3231 | 3277 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 70.7% | 71.7% |
| `failed` | 1122 | 1076 |
| `unsupported` | 212 | 212 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The premise that was wrong

"php2go has no refcounts, so destructor timing is out of reach" has been in this
journal, and in this loop's summaries, for weeks. It is half true and the half
that is true is not the important half.

php2go genuinely cannot know when the last reference goes away: a `php.Value`
holding an object is a Go pointer and Go copies one wherever it likes. But that
is only one way to answer the question. The other is to walk the roots and see
what is still reachable -- which is a *tracing collector*, needs no refcounts at
all, and answers exactly the two things a program can observe: a destructor
running, and a weak reference going empty.

`gc.go` is 240 lines. It marks from the globals, every executing frame, the
static properties and statics, the enum cases, the shutdown list and the
exception handler; it walks arrays, properties, closures' captures, generators'
suspended frames, fibers' saved frames and ArrayObject stores; and it
deliberately does **not** walk a WeakMap's keys or a WeakReference's target,
which is what finally makes those two classes weak.

### Temporaries are not roots

The first version collected nothing at all. `$x = new C(); $x = null;` still had
the object: `ZEND_NEW` had left it in a temporary and php2go never clears one,
so every object a statement had ever built stayed reachable for the life of the
frame.

Only the compiled variables are roots now. A temporary that legitimately holds
something *right now* is also held by the call being assembled, the iterator
being walked or the exception in flight -- all of which the walk covers -- so
excluding them is sound rather than merely convenient.

### Four release points, each measured

- **`gc_collect_cycles()`**, which had been returning a hardcoded zero: 27
  fixed, 1 broken. That includes all ten `generators/gh9750-*` and eight
  `weakrefs/gh10043-*`.
- **The fiber registry is not a root.** `unit.fibers` remembers every fiber for
  shutdown; treating that as a reference meant no fiber was ever unreachable.
  Marking a fiber only through its object: 14 more, 1 broken -- the whole
  `fibers/gh9735-*` group.
- **`unset()` and assignment over the last name**: 6 more. `unset` at global
  scope also had to remove the name from the globals table, which php2go was
  leaving behind -- a bug of its own, since `$GLOBALS` could still see it.
- **A frame returning**: 3 more.

Net across all four: 47 tests fixed, 2 broken.

### Cost

The whole `Zend/tests` corpus runs in 19 seconds. `worthCollecting` returns
false unless the program has an object with a destructor still to run or a weak
container, which is nearly every program, so nearly every program pays one
slice scan and nothing else.

### What is still wrong

`gc_collect_cycles()` reports one collection where PHP reports none: PHP had
already destroyed the object by refcount at the assignment, so its cycle
collector finds nothing to do. php2go's collection *is* the destruction, so it
counts it. The differential case leaves that pairing out.

## 2026-08-25 — comparing objects, and who resumed the generator

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3228 | 3231 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 70.7% | 70.7% |
| `failed` | 1125 | 1122 |
| `unsupported` | 212 | 212 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

A small round in tests won and a large one in fidelity: `php.Compare` had no
handling for objects at all, and a five-section probe that now matches the
engine exactly went from four failing sections to zero.

### An object is not comparable to much

`php.Compare` fell through to numeric comparison for every object, which made
`$o == $o2` false for two identical objects and `$a < $b` false for two that
differ. The rules, from the engine:

- **Two objects of the same class** compare property by property in declaration
  order, the way two arrays do -- count first, then pairwise.
- **Two of different classes** are *uncomparable*, and PHP expresses that by
  calling the object greater **whichever side it is on**. `$o < 1` and `$o > 1`
  are both false; `1 < $o` is true.
- **An object outranks an array**, which had to be checked before the existing
  array rule or the array won.
- **Beside a string**, an object with `__toString` is rendered and the two
  strings are compared. That was already right.
- **Beside a number**, it is *not* rendered even when it has `__toString`. It
  converts to `1` -- with `Notice: Object of class X could not be converted to
  int` -- so `$o == 1` is **true** and `$o <=> 1` is `0`. That is the one part
  no amount of reading would have suggested; the probe simply said so.

`ZEND_SPACESHIP` was skipping the conversion step entirely, so `<=>` and `<`
disagreed about the same pair of operands.

### Who resumed the generator decides what the trace says

A generator body has no call site of its own when the *engine* resumed it, and
PHP writes `[internal function]` for it. php2go already knew that for a
`Generator->` method and not for anything else, so `iterator_to_array($gen)`
attributed the body to the caller's line. The test is now "is the innermost
frame a user function?" rather than a name prefix.

### The clusters that are not reachable

Re-clustering the whole corpus by first differing line put three groups at the
top that are all one cause: `generators/gh9750-*` (10), `fibers/gh9735-*` (8)
and `try/try_finally_023..027` (5) all turn on a destructor running the moment
a value becomes unreachable. `try_finally_023` is the clearest: `unset($v)`
inside a `foreach` body, and the exception the destructor throws has to arrive
before the `return` completes.

### What the failed attempt actually said

Yesterday's measurement -- print `&` whenever a slot holds a `php.Ref`, 13
fixed and 22 broken -- was read as "this needs refcounting". Re-reading the 22
says something narrower: every one of them was a box php2go had made *for
itself*, to write through a property or a variable. The marker is not about
whether a slot is a reference in php2go's representation; it is about whether
the **program** asked for one.

`php.Ref` therefore carries a `shared` count, raised only where an explicit `&`
in the source binds a name: `ZEND_ASSIGN_REF`, `ZEND_ASSIGN_OBJ_REF`,
`ZEND_BIND_GLOBAL`, `ZEND_BIND_LEXICAL`, `ZEND_FETCH_LIST_W`, a by-reference

-- go through `php.MakeRef` and stay invisible.

### Three places a name goes away

Marking alone was 14 fixed, 8 broken: the marker outlived the second name. The
three places a program-made binding disappears, each measured on its own:

- **a frame ending** (`execFrame`'s defer walks its slots): took it to
  11 fixed / 2 broken;
- **`unset($ref)`**: 12 / 0;
- **a by-reference `foreach` moving to the next element**, which drops the loop
  variable's previous binding: 15 / 1.

Marking `foreach` *without* that last one was a net loss -- every element of an
array walked by reference inside a function kept a marker. The two changes only
make sense together, which is why the intermediate measurement is worth having.

### What is left, and it really is refcounting

`bug80037` is the one remaining over-marking, and it names the limit exactly: a
local **array** whose element holds the reference dies with its frame, and
nothing walks a dying local's array to say so. Doing that properly is
refcounting; counting bindings by hand covers the shapes a program writes and
stops there.

`foreach_reference.phpt` is the other side -- it wants a marker php2go does not
produce -- and is left alone rather than chased with a rule that would cost more
elsewhere.

### Result

| metric | before | after |

`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The bitwise operators work on bytes when both operands are strings

`"abc" & "def"` is a three-byte string. Neither operand is read as a number at
all -- and `"12" & "34"` is `"10"`, not `4`, so this is not a fallback for
non-numeric strings either. The three operators disagree about unequal lengths,
and a probe settled which is which: AND and XOR stop at the shorter operand,
since a missing byte is zero and zero wins for both; OR keeps the longer one's
tail, since zero loses. `~` follows the same rule on a string.

`AcceptsArithmetic` already let two strings through for these operators, so all
that was missing was the operation itself. `~` also gained the two diagnostics
it was skipping: the precision-loss deprecation for a float and
`Cannot perform bitwise not on array`.

### A private property's key carries its declaring class

`(array)$obj` and `get_mangled_object_vars` prefix a private property with its
declaring class and a protected one with a star, both between NUL bytes. That is
not decoration: it is how two classes in a hierarchy each keep a private
property of the same name. An uninitialized typed property is not in the array
at all.

### A literal with a byte above 0x7f cannot travel through the IR

Writing the differential case for the above failed with
`string field contains invalid UTF-8` -- from `MarshalUnit`, not from the
engine. `Literal.string` is a protobuf `string` field, which must be valid
UTF-8, and `~"abc"` is *constant-folded by the compiler* into a literal whose
bytes are 0x9e 0x9d 0x9c. The case now routes its operands through variables so
nothing folds. The underlying limit is real and is recorded in TODO.

### The & reference marker: measured, and reverted

`var_dump` prints `&` before a value whose slot holds a reference *shared by
more than one name*. php2go never prints it, and 57 corpus tests expect it --
the largest single family left.

Printing it whenever the slot holds a reference was tried and measured:
**13 tests fixed, 22 broken**, a net loss of nine. The failures say why. php2go
boxes a slot into a `php.Ref` far more eagerly than PHP marks one as a
reference, because boxing is how it implements writing through a path:
`elementRef` boxes a property while descending into it for a write, `slotRef`
boxes on any write fetch. Those boxes are internal and PHP would show nothing
for them -- the broken tests are `property_hooks/get_by_ref_*`,
`arg_unpack/by_ref*`, `objects_031`/`032` and seven `typed_properties_*`.

So the marker needs one of two things php2go does not have: holder counting, or
a way to tell a reference the *program* asked for from a box the runtime made
for itself. Recorded rather than left as a plausible-looking half-fix.

## 2026-08-25 — laziness is per property

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3162 | 3203 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 69.2% | 70.1% |
| `failed` | 1137 | 1143 |
| `unsupported` | 266 | 219 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`lazy_objects` 56 -> 97 of 223.

### The model was wrong in a way the first tests could not show

Yesterday's lazy objects were lazy as a whole: the object had state or it did
not. `ReflectionProperty::skipLazyInitialization` and
`setRawValueWithoutLazyInitialization` do not fit that at all -- they give *one*
property a value, and touching that property afterwards no longer initializes
anything. `fetch_skipped_prop_does_not_initialize` shows the consequence
plainly: skip every declared property and the object stops being lazy without
the initializer ever running, and `var_dump` drops the `lazy ghost ` prefix.

So `Lazy` grew a `Skipped` set, `resolveLazy` takes the property name, and the
nine property opcodes pass it through from op2. `skipProperty` writes the
declared default (or the caller's value) and clears the laziness once nothing is
left deferred.

### A ghost initializer starts from the declared defaults

An untyped property a ghost's initializer never assigns comes out **null**, not
uninitialized -- the engine installs the class's declared defaults into the
object before calling the initializer, and only the laziness had been hiding
them. An initializer that throws puts the object back to being lazy, so a later
access calls it again. Both fall out of doing the restore explicitly at the top
of `resolveLazy` and stripping again on failure.

### A magic accessor is asked before anything is initialized

`$proxy->undeclared = 1` calls `__set` on the *proxy*, before the factory runs.
The rule is about the property: a name the class does not declare is not
something the object can be deferring, so if the class supplies the matching
accessor it gets the call. `lazyProperty` therefore reports which accessor the
opcode would use -- `__get`, `__set`, `__isset`, `__unset` -- alongside the name.

What happens *after* that is not yet right. In the engine, `$this->$name = $v*2`
inside `__set` initializes the proxy and the value then does not come back out
of a later read: `var_dump($proxy->prop)` calls `__get`. php2go answers with the
value that was written. That is the `gh18038-*` family, about ten tests, and the
probe that found it is recorded rather than guessed at.

### Also landed

`serialize`, `json_encode`, `get_object_vars` and the `(array)` cast all read an
object's properties, so all four now produce a lazy one's state first.

## 2026-08-25 — lazy objects, and closing the fibers nobody resumed

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3096 | 3162 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 67.8% | 69.2% |
| `failed` | 1033 | 1137 |
| `unsupported` | 436 | 266 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`lazy_objects` 0 -> 56 of 223, `fibers` 37 -> 40 of 83. `failed` rose by 104
because 170 tests stopped being blocked and can now be wrong.

### Fiber force-close: an unwind no catch may see

PHP unwinds a suspended fiber that will never be resumed. Its `finally` blocks
run; no `catch` clause is offered the unwind, and suspending again during it is
`FiberError: Cannot suspend in a force-closed fiber`.

`frame.raise` only understood exceptions -- anything that was not a `*thrown`
propagated without running anything. It now recognises a sentinel `errFiberExit`
and looks for a handler with `finallyTarget`, which is `catchTarget` with the
catch clauses removed. `unwind` grew a `bail error` beside its `object`, and
`ZEND_FAST_RET` resumes whichever of the two the finally was entered for.

The mechanism is exactly right and the *timing* is not: PHP closes the fiber
when the Fiber object is destroyed, which in these tests is an explicit
`unset($fiber)` halfway through the script. php2go has no refcounts, so it
closes at the end of the request -- the same timing its destructors have. Three
tests differ only in where `done` appears relative to the finally output.

### Lazy objects: a class and a handle, with the state deferred

PHP 8.4 lets Reflection make an object whose properties do not exist yet. There
are two kinds and the difference is not cosmetic:

- a **ghost** is initialized in place -- the initializer receives the object,
  usually calls its constructor, and afterwards nothing about it is lazy;
- a **proxy** stays a wrapper -- the initializer *returns* an instance, and
  every property access forwards to it from then on.

That shows: `var_dump` of an initialized ghost is a plain object, while an
initialized proxy still prints as `lazy proxy object(C)#N (1) { ["instance"]=>
... }`. Uninitialized, both print with a `lazy ghost `/`lazy proxy ` prefix, a
count of zero, and their typed properties as `uninitialized(T)`.

The whole feature is "everything that can observe state has to ask for it
first". `resolveLazy` initializes on demand and answers with the object property
access should *actually* use, so a caller that has asked can go on working with
ordinary property operations. It is wired into the nine property opcodes, plus
`ZEND_CLONE` and `ZEND_FE_RESET_*` -- and `var_dump` deliberately does not ask,
because showing the lazy state is the point.

### Two things the corpus corrected

- **Declaration order survives.** The first version removed a lazy object's
  properties outright; the constructor then re-added them in *assignment* order,
  so `var_dump` listed `b` before `a`. Every declared property keeps its slot
  and merely holds nothing; the dump filters out the untyped ones, which PHP
  does not list because there is no type to name.
- **`clone` was losing every declaration.** It copied `Props` and nothing else,
  so a clone's typed property was no longer typed -- `uninitialized()` with an
  empty type gave it away. That was a pre-existing bug that only a lazy object
  made visible. `copyState` now carries `Declared`, `Dynamic` and `Cleared`, and
  cloning a proxy produces a proxy wrapping a clone of the instance.

`ReflectionClass::isLazyObject` does not exist; the probe asked for it and the
engine answered `Call to undefined method`, which is how it came out of the
implementation again.

### What is left

`ReflectionProperty::setRawValueWithoutLazyInitialization` (31) and
`skipLazyInitialization` (19) are the next block. Both are *per-property*:
they mark one property so that touching it does not initialize the object.
php2go's laziness is per-object, so this needs the property name at the point
`resolveLazy` is called -- which the opcodes have and the current insertion
points throw away.

## 2026-08-25 — a fiber is a goroutine

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3037 | 3096 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 66.5% | 67.8% |
| `failed` | 986 | 1033 |
| `unsupported` | 542 | 436 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`fibers` 0 -> 37 of 83, and `unsupported` fell by the whole 106-test `Fiber`
block. `failed` rose by 47 because those tests now run and can be wrong.

### Why this was written off and should not have been

`Fiber` was on the "structurally out of reach" list beside lazy objects and
refcounting, on the reasoning that a generator can be modelled by saving a
program counter and a fiber cannot -- `Fiber::suspend()` may be called from
anywhere in the call stack the fiber started, ten frames deep in code that knows
nothing about fibers, and the whole stack has to stop where it is.

That is true, and it is also exactly what a goroutine is. A fiber is a goroutine
whose control transfer is a send on an unbuffered channel: the resumer blocks
while the fiber runs and the fiber blocks while anything else does, so precisely
one of them is ever running. There is no concurrency to reason about, only a
handoff. The whole mechanism is under 250 lines.

### The state that has to move with control

The interpreter keeps per-request state that belongs to whichever side is
running: `unit.frames`, the `Ctx` call stack, and the executing and called
scopes. The first attempt *swapped* them -- install the fiber's, take them back
afterwards -- and every backtrace test failed, because PHP's trace does not stop
at the fiber boundary:

```
#12 file(24): suspend_fiber(0)
#13 [internal function]: {closure:file:23}()
#14 file(30): Fiber->resume('test')
#15 {main}
```

So the fiber's frames **stack on top of** the resumer's rather than replacing
them, with a synthetic `[internal function]` frame for the callable in between:
the engine and not the script made that call, so it has no file or line.
`switchTo` appends on the way in and splits at the resumer's length on the way
out, which keeps a backtrace taken while the fiber is *suspended* from seeing
its frames.

Since only one goroutine runs at a time and the handoff is a channel, the
channel operations supply the happens-before that makes all of this safe.

### What the corpus found

- `Cannot suspend outside of **a** fiber`, not "of fiber".
- `FiberError` may be caught but not constructed:
  `The "FiberError" class is reserved for internal use and cannot be manually
  instantiated`.
- An argument `TypeError` leaves off its `, called in %s on line %d` clause when
  the caller is internal. That was a pre-existing bug that only a fiber's entry
  frame exposed -- php2go was printing `called in [internal function] on line 0`.

### Still out of reach, and why

`destructors_*` (11), `gh9735-*` (8) and the `gc-cycle-*` pair turn on a
suspended fiber being *collected* -- refcounting and cycle detection, the same
family as before.

The next group that is reachable is force-close: PHP unwinds a suspended fiber
that is never resumed, running its `finally` blocks but letting no `catch` see
it. That is `invocable-class`, `unfinished-fiber-with-*` and
`suspend-in-force-close-*`, about seven tests, and it needs an unwind that runs
finally without being catchable -- which `frame.raise` does not currently have.

### Also landed

`Notice: Only variable references should be yielded by reference`, which fires
for `yield` of a constant or a temporary inside a `function &gen()`. The other
three members of that family -- assign, return, pass -- were already right.

## 2026-08-25 — the link-time checks the engine makes and php2go did not

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3014 | 3037 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 66.0% | 66.5% |
| `failed` | 1009 | 986 |
| `unsupported` | 542 | 542 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`enum` 103 -> 113 of 131.

### The lens: tests whose diff is one replaced line

`-diff` over the whole corpus, then a `difflib` pass keeping only the failures
whose expected and actual output differ by exactly **one** replaced line. 193 of
986, and clustering the (expected, actual) pairs made the families obvious. The
biggest was two dozen tests where the expected line is a link-time `Fatal error`
and php2go printed the program's ordinary output instead -- a check the engine
makes when a class is linked and php2go did not make at all.

### Ambiguous inherited constants: the rule is not "two interfaces"

`Class C inherits both A::C and B::C, which is ambiguous` fires when a name is
already in the table from a declaring class that is neither the interface now
supplying it nor the class being linked. Three shapes in the corpus pin that
down and no two of them agree with a simpler rule:

- two interfaces both declaring it (`final_const8`, `errmsg_025`),
- an interface **extending** two that do (`final_const12`),
- a **parent class** and an interface (`final_const11`) -- so it is not about
  interfaces at all,

and the case that must stay legal is the class declaring it itself, which is
what PHP 8.1 allowed. `final_const5` shows the order: a final constant is
refused with `C::X cannot override final constant I::X` before ambiguity is
considered.

### An enum's engine-supplied properties are in the harvest

`Enum X cannot include properties` looked like two lines of code and dropped the
`enum` directory from 103 passing to 34. Every enum has `name`, and a backed one
has `value` -- the engine adds them and the harvest carries them like any other
property, so the check refused every enum in the corpus. Neither name can come
from source (both are reserved), so skipping exactly those two is not a
heuristic.

The same section now consults trait-contributed methods, since a trait's members
are flattened into the enum: `enum Bar { use Foo; }` where `Foo` declares
`__construct` is `Enum Bar cannot include magic method __construct`.

`BackedEnum` can be checked and `UnitEnum` still cannot. The engine adds
`UnitEnum` to every enum, so finding it says nothing; it adds `BackedEnum` only
to a backed one, so finding it on an enum with no backing type means the source
asked for it.

### Also landed

- `new` on an interface, trait, enum or abstract class was refused only through
  Reflection. `ZEND_NEW` now calls the same `instantiable` check.
- `Access level to X::y() must be public (as in class Z)` for a method or a
  constant that narrows what an ancestor declared, with the engine's
  " or weaker" suffix for anything below public.
- A name in an `implements` list that is not an interface.
- `Cannot redeclare class stdClass` -- a name the engine already owns, which has
  no earlier declaration site to name.
- `Class X must implement interface Traversable as part of either Iterator or
  IteratorAggregate`, which the engine reports with no location at all:
  `in Unknown on line 0`, because it is settled after the file has compiled.
  That needed a `fatalUnknown` beside the existing `fatal`.

### What the differential case can cover here

Almost nothing of the above: a link-time fatal bails the engine out before
`php2eval` can capture any output, so the negative cases are `.phpt` material.
The differential case is the other side -- every legal shape a too-eager check
would refuse, which is what caught the enum-properties mistake and is the only
guard against the next one.

## 2026-08-25 — #[\Override] and #[\Deprecated], and what links a class

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 3001 | 3014 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 65.7% | 66.0% |
| `failed` | 1022 | 1009 |
| `unsupported` | 542 | 542 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`attributes` 60 -> 73 of 94.

### #[\Override]: four rules, all of them from a test

The check is simple to state -- a method carrying the attribute must override
something -- and every interesting part is in what counts as "something".
Implementing the obvious version broke two passing tests; the corpus then
supplied the four rules:

- **A concrete trait method does not count.** A class that redeclares one
  *replaces* it rather than overriding it, so `#[\Override]` on the class's copy
  is an error. A trait's **abstract** method is a prototype and does count.
- **A private ancestor method does not count**, because it is not inherited at
  all. A protected one does.
- **A concrete parent constructor does not count.** The engine gives a
  prototype to an abstract constructor and to nothing else, so
  `#[\Override] __construct` needs an abstract parent -- `gh12189_4` fails
  where `gh12189_5` passes on exactly that difference.
- **An engine class's methods count**, which needs the builtin method table
  rather than the harvested op_arrays -- `class Foo implements IteratorAggregate`
  with `#[\Override] getIterator()` is legal.

The diagnostic names the class doing the *using*, not the trait that wrote the
method: `Foo::t() has #[\Override] attribute, but no matching parent method
exists`.

### Anonymous classes were never being linked

`ZEND_DECLARE_ANON_CLASS` called `resolveDependencies` and stopped. Everything
else a declaration does -- composing traits, verifying inheritance, signatures,
property types, enum shape, abstract methods -- was skipped for anonymous
classes entirely. The chain is now `linkClass`, called from both opcodes, which
is what makes `#[\Override]` on one an error and closes a gap nothing had
noticed.

### An abstract method can be satisfied by an ancestor's trait

`concreteMethod` walked `abstractSources`, which holds the class's *own* traits
but not its ancestors'. A parent that got its implementation from a trait of its
own therefore looked as though it had none, and a later abstract trait method in
the subclass was reported unimplemented. `gh12189_6` is that shape exactly.

### #[\Deprecated] is reported wherever a call happens

`noteDeprecatedCall` was wired into `ZEND_DO_FCALL` and nowhere else, so four
kinds of call reported nothing:

- a **closure**, which PHP 8.4 names `{closure:file:line}`;
- a call that landed on **`__call`/`__callStatic`**, reported against the name
  the program wrote rather than the accessor that received it;
- a **destructor**;
- anything `dispatch` performs outside the main loop -- a callback given to
  `array_map`, or a handler the engine itself calls. The exception handler runs
  after the body, where there is no line to attribute the call to, and the
  engine says `Unknown on line 0`.

### Two recursion guards, and they are not the same guard

`defined('C::K')` was reporting the deprecation. It asks whether the constant
exists, not for its value, so it does not report -- a plain counter suppresses
it.

A message that names a deprecated constant is a different problem, and the first
guard written for it was wrong. A message naming *another* deprecated constant
reports that one too, and reports it **first**; only a message naming its own
constant must not restart the report. The guard is therefore a set of constants
whose report is under way, not a counter.

### Left as a known difference

When a deprecation is raised while evaluating another constant's message, the
engine attributes it to the **inner constant's declaration line**, not to the
read site. The `.phpt` cases use `%d` there so they pass either way; the
differential case leaves that pairing out rather than guess at the rule.

## 2026-08-25 — the caller's own frame, and what may not be reached by name

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2988 | 3001 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 65.4% | 65.7% |
| `failed` | 1019 | 1022 |
| `unsupported` | 558 | 542 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### A builtin can now see its caller's variables

`extract`, `compact` and `get_defined_vars` were the last big blocked family
that needed no new engine knowledge, only a way to reach the calling frame. A
builtin has none of its own, so `execFrame` now pushes each frame onto
`unit.frames` and pops it on the way out; the top of that stack while a builtin
runs is its caller. Generators resume through `execFrame` too, so a suspended
frame is on the stack exactly while it is executing.

### The overflow symbol table

php2go has compiled variables, not a symbol table: the compiler gives a slot to
every variable the body mentions literally, and nothing else has a home. That
made `extract(["fresh" => 7])` unrepresentable when the body never writes
`$fresh` -- and it had already made `$$n = 5` silently lose the write for a name
with no slot, which nobody had noticed.

`frame.extra map[string]*php.Ref` is where those go, reached through
`namedRef`/`namedValue`/`namedUnset`. `ZEND_FETCH_*` by name, `ZEND_UNSET_VAR`,
`ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_VAR`, `extract`, `compact` and `get_defined_vars` all go
through it, so a variable created under a computed name behaves like any other.
Ordinary variables never touch it.

### Cannot call it dynamically

`extract`, `compact`, `get_defined_vars`, `func_get_args`, `func_num_args` and
`func_get_arg` refuse to be reached through a variable, a callback or
`call_user_func`: what they act on is the frame that *named* them, so the
compiler has to see the name. A probe settled both the membership of that list
and the ordering, which is not obvious: `zend_forbid_dynamic_call` is called
from inside each function *after* it parses its parameters, so a wrong argument
count is reported first. `pendingCall.dynamic` carries the fact to the dispatch
and `Interp.call` checks it right after `verifyBuiltinArgs`, which reproduces
that order without special-casing anything.

`extract` also refuses `"this"` outright -- `Error: Cannot re-assign $this`,
at global scope too, where there is no `$this` to protect -- and the call fails
where it reaches the name rather than skipping it.

### strcasecmp returns a difference, not a sign

`strcasecmp("aef", "dfsgbdf")` is `-3`, not `-1`: `zend_binary_strcasecmp` is
PHP's own loop and returns `c1 - c2` for the first pair of folded bytes that
disagree. Only a common prefix falls through to a three-way length comparison.
The same is true of `strncasecmp` and of `substr_compare` in its
case-insensitive mode.

`strcmp` and `strncmp` look like they should behave the same way and do not:
they go through `memcmp`, whose non-zero return value the C standard leaves to
the implementation. A probe over every (length, position) pair up to 20 bytes
found glibc returning the byte difference only for a comparison of length 1 and
for the last byte of one of length 3, and `+/-1` everywhere else. That is one
library's dispatch table, not a rule, so php2go returns the sign and the
magnitude is recorded as a known difference rather than fitted.

### Also landed

`ob_clean`/`ob_flush` (empty the buffer, keep the level -- `Ctx.ClearBuffer`),
`array_walk` and `array_reduce` on the callback path, `get_called_class`, and
`get_parent_class()` with no argument, which was answering `false` instead of
consulting the calling scope.

## 2026-08-25 — the long tail of missing library functions

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2954 | 2988 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.7% | 65.4% |
| `failed` | 997 | 1019 |
| `unsupported` | 614 | 558 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`. 56 tests stopped being
blocked; 34 of those now pass and 22 fail on something else, which is the
expected shape.

### The lens: the blocking histogram past the top ten

`php2phpt -top 250` past the fourth entry is not lazy objects and fibers -- it
is 80 distinct `call to <function>` lines with one to seven tests each. No
single one is worth a session; together they were 56.

Three new files, all registering into the existing `builtins` map:

- `stringlib.go` -- 40 functions: the case and search family (`ucfirst`,
  `ucwords`, `stripos`, `strncmp`, `strnatcmp`, `strstr`, `strrchr`,
  `strpbrk`), the splice family (`substr_replace`, `substr_compare`,
  `str_split`, `chunk_split`, `wordwrap`, `strtr`), the digests
  (`md5`, `sha1`, `crc32`, `bin2hex`, `base64_*`), the escapers
  (`addslashes`, `quotemeta`, `preg_quote`, `htmlspecialchars`, `strip_tags`)
  and the metrics (`levenshtein`, `similar_text`, `str_word_count`,
  `number_format`).
- `mathlib.go` -- the trigonometric and logarithmic set, `ceil`/`floor`/`round`/
  `pow`, `fdiv`, the NaN predicates, the random family, the path helpers
  (`dirname`, `basename`, `pathinfo`, `realpath`) and the process questions.
- `arraylib.go` -- `array_flip`, `array_reverse`, `array_search`, `array_sum`,
  `array_product`, `array_combine`, `array_pad`, `array_chunk`,
  `array_count_values`, `array_column`, `array_is_list`, the key edges, the six
  set operations and `array_merge_recursive`.
- `introspect.go` -- the ones that need the unit: `get_declared_classes` and its
  siblings, `spl_object_id`/`spl_object_hash`, `get_resource_id`/`_type`,
  `is_subclass_of`/`is_a`, `class_implements`/`class_parents`/`class_uses`,
  `get_defined_functions`.

### The probe found six things reading the manual would not have

Three labelled narrating probes, 84 cases, run before writing a single
differential case. Six disagreements, every one of them a rule I had guessed
wrong:

- **`strnatcmp` has two comparison modes.** A digit run compares by magnitude,
  *unless* either side starts with a zero -- then it compares left to right,
  as a fraction would, so `"x01" < "x1"`. And zeros at the very start of the
  whole string are skipped outright, so `"0001" == "1"`. Both rules are needed:
  either alone gets one of those two cases wrong.
- **`str_split("")` is `[]`**, not `[""]`. PHP 8.2 changed it.
- **`log2()` does not exist in PHP.** `log($x, 2)` is the spelling.
- **INF, -INF and NAN print in capitals** -- Go writes `+Inf`, `-Inf`, `NaN`.
  This was a `var_dump` bug, not a library one, and it was there before this
  session. `printf` is the exception: it spells the last one `NaN`, and that
  inconsistency is PHP's own (`php_sprintf_appenddouble` has the literals).
- **`json_encode(1.0)` is `1`**, not `1.0`.
- **`dirname("a/b/")` is `"a"`.** Trailing separators are stripped first, which
  `filepath.Dir` does not do.

### The one place the engine is deliberately not followed

`php_sapi_name()` answers `"cli"`. The differential harness's own engine says
`"embed"`, because that is the SAPI `php2eval` links. The `.phpt` corpus was
recorded under the CLI, and that is the SAPI php2go stands in for -- the same
reasoning that fixed `firstScriptResource` at 5. It is the only function in
this batch with no differential case, and the reason is written at the call
site.

### Known-wrong, left wrong

`class_implements($subclassInstance)` lists the interfaces in a different order
from the engine when the class inherits them (`I1, I2` where php2go gives
`I2, I1`); the same call on the parent matches. One test uses it. Recorded in
TODO rather than guessed at.

## 2026-08-25 — `function &gen()` yields the slot

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2952 | 2954 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.6% | 64.7% |
| `failed` | 999 | 997 |
| `unsupported` | 614 | 614 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The declaration is what makes the loop legal

`foreach ($gen as &$v)` over a generator is refused unless the generator
function was itself declared `function &gen()`. php2go refused every one of
them, because nothing carried `returns_ref` out of the harvest.

Two pieces: `php2go_fn_returns_ref` reads `op_array->fn_flags & ZEND_ACC_RETURN_REFERENCE`
into `OpArray.returns_ref`, and `ZEND_YIELD` consults it — a by-reference
generator yields `php.MakeRef(slot)` rather than `slot.Copy()`, so the loop
variable in `ZEND_FE_FETCH_RW` binds to the same cell the generator body writes
to. `yield_array_offset_by_ref` and `yield_by_reference` now pass.

### The refusal is an `Exception`, not an `Error`

A differential case caught this: the engine throws a plain `Exception` for
"You can only iterate a generator by-reference…", not the `Error` that most
VM-level refusals are. It comes out of the iterator handler rather than the VM,
and `catch (Error $e)` does not catch it. Nothing in the headers says so; the
case did.

### `finally` is clean

A ten-case narrating probe over `finally` — return-in-finally overriding
return-in-try, `break`/`continue` crossing one, nested finally, an exception
thrown from a finally that is already unwinding another, return-in-finally
inside return-in-finally — matched the engine on all ten. The generator +
`finally` group (`bug71601`, `bug74606`) is not a `finally` bug: those tests
turn on `unset($generator)` destroying a *suspended* generator, which unwinds
its `finally` blocks. That is the refcount family, not this one.

## 2026-08-25 — `yield from` proxies, it does not copy

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2949 | 2952 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.5% | 64.6% |
| `failed` | 1002 | 999 |
| `unsupported` | 614 | 614 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`generators` 91 → 94 of 159.

### Two delegates, one source

`yield_from_multi_tree` builds a *tree* of generators all delegating down to one
source, then round-robins over them. php2go produced repeats -- `0 1 2 3 2 3 6`
where the engine gives `0 1 2 3 4 5 6`.

The cause: a delegating generator was storing the value it pulled from the inner
one in its own `frame.yieldValue`, so `current()` answered with a **snapshot**.
When a second delegate advanced the shared source, the first kept answering with
what it had copied.

The engine proxies instead: a generator suspended inside `yield from` has no
current value of its own -- `current()` and `key()` read the inner generator,
live, however deep the chain goes.

### The fix that hung

Making `current()` recurse into the inner generator overflowed the stack on the
first corpus run. A `yield from` chain can be a *cycle* -- PHP refuses to build
one, but nothing in php2go guarantees the graph is acyclic, and a runtime that
hangs is worse than one that answers oddly.

`innermost()` walks the chain **iteratively** with a hop limit instead. Real
chains are a handful deep; the limit exists only so a cycle cannot run away.

## 2026-08-25 — Destructuring by reference, and a bisect that chased nothing

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2948 | 2949 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.5% | 64.5% |
| `failed` | 1000 | 1002 |
| `unsupported` | 617 | 614 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Three tests unblocked: one passes, two fail honestly.

### `[&$r] = $arr` worked exactly once

The destructuring probe -- 9 sources x 5 forms -- was clean except for the
by-reference form, which failed for every source *after the first*. The minimal
case worked; the loop did not.

The cause is general and was hiding in every reference-producing opcode.
`FETCH_LIST_W`, `FETCH_DIM_W` and their relatives put a **reference** into a
result temporary with `storeResult`, and `storeResult` *writes through* a
reference the slot already holds. The first time an opline runs the temporary is
empty and all is well. The second time it still holds the previous iteration's
reference, so the new reference is written **into the old box** instead of
replacing it -- and the binding keeps pointing at the previous iteration's data.

`bindResult` replaces the slot outright. The distinction is the same one
`ZEND_ASSIGN_REF` already made between `store` and `bindSlot`; the ref-producing
fetches simply had not been told about it.

Also fixed, from the same probe: by reference a non-array source has to *become*
one -- null auto-vivifies, a string is `Cannot create references to/from string
offsets`, and a scalar is `Cannot use a scalar value as an array`. The read form
shrugs and hands out null; the write form cannot.

### The bisect that chased nothing

Three `generators/yield_from_multi_tree*` tests appeared in the "newly failing"
list, so I spent half the round reverting changes one at a time to find which
broke them. None had: they had been **unsupported** all along (`yield from
null`), and my change unblocked them into the failing bucket.

The comparison script only reads the *failure* dump, so a test moving
`unsupported -> failed` is indistinguishable from `passing -> failed` in it. The
counts said so plainly -- unsupported fell by exactly 3 while failed rose by 2
and passed by 1 -- and I did not read them before starting to bisect.

**Check the three counts before believing the set difference.**

## 2026-08-25 — Array keys, and a PHP 8.3 change nobody had applied

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2948 | 2948 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.5% | 64.5% |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### One diff in 27 key shapes

The key-coercion matrix -- 24 key shapes through set, read, isset,
array_key_exists and the stored key's *type* -- was already right everywhere
except one cell, and that cell was not about coercion at all:

```php
$a = [-5 => "a"]; $a[] = "b";   // -4 since PHP 8.3, 0 before it
```

The **first** integer key sets the append slot whatever its sign; afterwards the
slot only rises, so `[-5 => "a", -9 => "b"]` still appends at -4. php2go had the
pre-8.3 rule: `nextFree` started at 0 and only moved for keys at or above it, so
every negative key left it at 0.

This is the second half-applied language change found by probing (the first was
PHP 8's string-to-number comparisons, applied to `==` and not to `<`). Both were
invisible to the corpus.

### Sorting was clean

35 cases -- six sort functions plus `usort` over five arrays including one with
every scalar type in it -- matched exactly. Worth recording as a *negative*
result: the next person does not need to look there.

## 2026-08-25 — Casts and string offsets, by matrix

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2945 | 2948 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.5% | 64.5% |
| `failed` | 1003 | 1000 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Casts: 4 of 138, all one bug

`var_export(INF)` printed `+Inf` and `var_export(NAN)` printed `NaN` -- Go's
formatter rather than PHP's spelling. That matters more than it looks:
`var_export`'s output is supposed to be re-parseable PHP, and `+Inf` is not
anything. `(string) INF` was already right, so only the export path was wrong.

Everything else in the cast matrix -- 23 values x 5 casts plus gettype,
get_debug_type, is_numeric and empty -- already matched.

### String offsets: three operations that disagree

`read`, `isset`/`empty` and `write` on the same index give *different* answers,
and checking them together is what made the rules visible:

| Index | read | isset | write |
|---|---|---|---|
| `2.7` | `Warning: String offset cast occurred` | `Deprecated: Implicit conversion from float 2.7 to int loses precision` | as read |
| `-6` on `"hello"` | `Warning: Uninitialized string offset -6`, `""` | `false` | `Warning: Illegal string offset -6`, **unchanged** |
| `"1abc"` | `Warning: Illegal string offset "1abc"`, then offset 1 | `false` | as read |
| `"1.5"` | TypeError | false | TypeError |

php2go had the negative write as an `Error` (naming the *adjusted* offset, -1,
rather than the one written), refused `"1abc"` outright, and gave isset the
read's cast warning instead of the array-key deprecation.

### A differential case caught the overreach

Fixing `"1abc"` first made `"1.5"` and `"1.0E+121"` work too -- and an existing
differential case failed, correctly. A *wholly* numeric string that is not an
integer is refused; only a string that stops being a number partway through gets
the prefix. The distinction is `is_numeric_string` saying no at all, and I had
skipped straight to "does it start with digits".

## 2026-08-25 — The arithmetic matrix: diagnostics are ordered, and they stop

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2945 | 2945 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.5% | 64.5% |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
No corpus movement again, and 11 of 324 operand pairs were wrong.

### Printing the operands is what makes it a matrix

The first attempt printed only results, and the diff was 1039 lines of noise --
the *diagnostics* have no operands in them, so a one-line shift misaligns
everything after it. Printing a `### a op b` marker before each operation and
diffing **per operation** turned 1039 unusable lines into 11 real differences.

That is the technique, not an incidental fix: a matrix probe needs each cell
labelled, or the first difference destroys the alignment of the rest.

### Operands convert left to right, and the walk stops

All 11 differences were one rule:

| Expression | Engine |
|---|---|
| `2.5 % ""` | the precision-loss deprecation for `2.5`, **then** the TypeError |
| `2.5 % "2abc"` | deprecation for the left, then the non-numeric warning for the right |
| `"" % "2abc"` | a bare TypeError -- **no** warning for `"2abc"` |
| `"abc" + "2abc"` | the same |

php2go converted *both* operands before deciding, so a warning from the second
operand escaped even when the first had already made the operation impossible,
and the int-conversion deprecations were emitted after both rather than
interleaved.

The engine converts strictly left to right and raises at the first operand that
cannot convert. An earlier operand's diagnostic survives the refusal; a later
one never happens.

## 2026-08-25 — 1734 comparisons, and three of them were PHP 7

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2945 | 2945 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.5% | 64.5% |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
**No movement in the corpus**, and two real bugs fixed. `Zend/tests` does not
exercise these corners -- they live in `ext/standard` -- which is exactly why a
probe found them and 53 rounds of clustering did not.

### The matrix probe

The narrating probe finds wrong *routes*. Its complement finds wrong *answers*:
take a representative value set and print every pairing under every operator.
17 values x 17 values x 6 operators = 1734 lines, diffed against the engine in
one run. 26 were wrong.

### PHP 8 compares a number with a non-numeric string *as a string*

The "saner string to number comparisons" RFC. `0 < "abc"` is **true** in PHP 8 --
`"0"` sorts before `"abc"` -- where PHP 7 cast `"abc"` to 0 and answered false.
php2go had the PHP 7 rule for ordering while `==` had already been updated, so
`0 == "abc"` was right and `0 < "abc"` was wrong. A half-applied language change
is harder to notice than an unapplied one.

Also from the same run: an **array is greater than any non-array** (`0 < []` is
true), which php2go answered by comparing numerically and got 0.

### null is a string's equal, not a boolean's

`"0" == null` is **false**. Null beside a *string* compares as `""`, not through
truthiness -- and `"0"` is not `""`. php2go routed every null comparison through
`Bool()`, which makes `"0"` and `null` both false and therefore equal.

And `null === false` is **false**: they are distinct types however alike they
look. `isBoolish` -- one predicate covering null, undef, true and false -- was
being used for both the loose and the strict path, so `===` inherited a
looseness that belongs only to `==`.

## 2026-08-25 — `instanceof` stopped at the first interface

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2943 | 2945 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.4% | 64.5% |
| `failed` | 1004 | 1003 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
A thin round by the metric, and the largest correctness fix in several.

### The narrating probe, again

Second application of the technique from the previous round, this time to the
**iterator protocol**: an `Iterator` whose five methods each echo their name,
driven through `foreach`, `IteratorAggregate`, `iterator_to_array`,
`iterator_count` and `yield from`. The call *sequences* matched the engine
exactly -- and the run still failed, on something the sequences never touched.

### `$obj instanceof Traversable` was false

`class It implements Iterator` is a `Traversable`, because `Iterator` extends
it. `Unit.instanceOf` checked the class's **direct** interfaces and its parent
chain, and never followed an interface's own parents.

Two implementations of the same question had drifted apart: `instanceOfName`,
written later for the signature checks, walks the graph properly through
`abstractSources`. `instanceOf` now does the same, minus traits -- composing a
trait is not a subtype relation, which `abstractSources` includes and
`instanceof` must not.

This is wrong for every interface hierarchy, not only the engine's, and it was
invisible because nothing in the corpus asked `instanceof` about a *grandparent*
interface until the parameter type `Traversable` did.

### iterator_to_array, and calling only what you use

`iterator_to_array` and `iterator_count` were not implemented at all. Adding
them turned up a detail the narrating probe was built to catch: **which
accessors run is observable**.

| Call | Accessors |
|---|---|
| `foreach` | rewind, valid, current, key, next |
| `iterator_to_array($it)` | the same |
| `iterator_to_array($it, false)` | no `key()` -- the keys are discarded |
| `iterator_count($it)` | neither `current()` nor `key()` |

A value-only comparison would have passed all three.

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2934 | 2943 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.2% | 64.4% |
| `failed` | 1013 | 1004 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 9 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### Probing a whole feature at once

The `__toString` hole last round was found by accident, so this round I wrote a
single script exercising **every** magic accessor -- `__get`, `__set`,
`__isset`, `__unset`, `__invoke`, `__clone` -- with an echo in each body, and
diffed it against the engine. Two differences fell out of one run.

That is a cheap technique and worth repeating for other features: a script that
*narrates* what it calls turns "does this work?" into a diff.

### `??` asks __isset first

`$o->p ?? "x"` calls `__isset` and only calls `__get` if it answered true. The
comment in the fetch handler already said so; the code called `__get` directly.
Observable whenever the accessors have side effects, and the reason
`isset($o->p)` can be false on a class whose `__get` would happily answer.

### An overloaded property in write position

`$o->arr[] = 1` where `arr` exists only through `__get`:

```
get(arr)
Notice: Indirect modification of overloaded property M::$arr has no effect
```

with two rules attached, both of which cost a test before they were right:

- The notice belongs to the **modification site**, not to `__get`'s body -- the
  accessor is a call and a call moves the reported location.
- It fires only when what `__get` returned is **not an object**. `$a->p->t =
  "bar"` with `p` an overloaded property holding an object is silent, because
  modifying the object reaches the same instance; the exemption is the same one
  hooked properties get, and `bug34893` exists to check it.

## 2026-08-25 — `__toString` was never called

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2925 | 2934 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 64.0% | 64.2% |
| `failed` | 1022 | 1013 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 9 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### The gap

```php
class S { function __toString(): string { return "S!"; } }
$s = new S;
echo $s;          // printed nothing
echo (string) $s; // printed nothing
echo $s . "x";    // printed "x"
var_dump("$s");   // string(0) ""
```

`stringify` existed and was correct, and had **exactly one caller** --
`checkType`, for parameter and return types. That is why `strlen($s)` worked and
nothing else did: every path that wanted a string called `php.Value.String()`,
which returns `""` for an object because the php package has no way to run a
method.

Echo, the `(string)` cast, `.` and the rope opcodes now go through
`Interp.toString`, which renders through `__toString` and raises
`Object of class N could not be converted to string` for a class without one.

### Two rules that came with it

- **`__toString` has an implicit `string` return type** since PHP 8, so a body
  with no `return` is `Return value must be of type string, none returned`
  rather than an empty string. The compiler emits the `VERIFY_RETURN_TYPE`
  opline for it, and the harvest carries the type -- what was missing was
  running the method at all.
- **A loose comparison renders the object**: `$s == "S!"` is true. `===` does
  not, since it compares types first, and two objects compare as objects rather
  than as strings.

### Why it went unnoticed for so long

`stringify` returned `(value, ok)` and swallowed the error from the method it
called. A caller could not tell "no __toString" from "__toString threw", so the
one caller treated both as "not a string" -- and nothing else called it. A
helper whose failure mode is a bare `false` invites exactly that.

## 2026-08-25 — Attribute targets, and by-reference iteration over an object

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2918 | 2925 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 63.9% | 64.0% |
| `failed` | 1029 | 1022 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 8 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### An attribute may only be written where it says

`#[Attribute(Attribute::TARGET_CLASS)]` means the class may not be written on a
function, and `newInstance()` is where that is discovered:

```
Attribute "MyAttribute" cannot target function (allowed targets: class)
```

Both halves of the message are rendered from flags, and the *target* has to
travel with the reflector -- which declaration produced it is not something the
attribute itself records. `ReflectionMethod` and `ReflectionFunction` share a
reflector, so the bit is chosen by whether the method has a declaring class.

### foreach by reference over an object

Three things were wrong at once, and the readonly test needed all three:

1. **The loop bound the wrong slots.** An object is flattened to an array of its
   visible properties for iteration, and the by-reference form was aliasing
   *that copy* -- so writing through the loop variable never reached the object.
   It now binds `origin.Props` when the keys came from an object.
2. **Uninitialized typed properties were being yielded.** `foreach` skips them;
   php2go handed out the undef and let the loop see it.
3. **A readonly property cannot be aliased at all**, initialized or not:
   `Cannot acquire reference to readonly property Test::$prop`. The test relies
   on (2) to reach the interesting case -- its first loop runs *before* the
   property is initialized and must not raise.

### Illegal array offsets

An object or an array cannot be an array offset, and the refusal is worded twice
over:

```
TypeError: Cannot access offset of type stdClass on array          // read and write
TypeError: Cannot access offset of type stdClass in isset or empty // isset and empty
```

The class is named rather than "object". `arrayKey` has no error path -- it
returns a `php.Key` -- so the check sits at the three opcode sites that take an
offset from user code, which is also where the catch handler is available.

### Iterator and IteratorAggregate

`Class A cannot implement both Iterator and IteratorAggregate at the same time`.
Checked over the whole interface graph rather than the class's own list, since
either can arrive through a parent -- `bug48667_2` reaches it that way.

### A wasted half-hour, worth recording

Three edits looked like they had no effect, and I read the same twenty lines
four times looking for the reason. The reason was the probe: `php2eval` lives in
the job's tmp directory, built with `go build -o`, and **`go build ./...` does
not refresh it**. Every probe after a change has to rebuild it explicitly, or it
silently reports the previous build's behaviour.

The corpus runner is not affected -- `go run ./cmd/php2phpt` compiles each time
-- which is exactly why the discrepancy was confusing: the corpus moved and the
probe did not.

### Result

| metric | before | after |

| `failed` | 1042 | 1034 |

`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 8 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### A better lens than clustering

First-differing-line clustering had stopped separating causes. Two cheaper
questions did better:

- **failures by directory** (last round), which found the trait harvest hole;
- **failures whose output is empty** — this round. **153 of 1042** produce
  *nothing* where PHP produces something, and almost all of them expect a
  link-time fatal php2go does not raise. Grouping those 153 by the first line
  they expect turns a diffuse tail into a list of named checks.

Nothing produces output where PHP produces none, which is worth knowing on its
own: php2go under-reports, it does not invent.

### Three checks off that list

**Property types are invariant.** Unlike a method's, a redeclared property's
type may not narrow or widen — only repeat:

```
Fatal error: Type of B::$prop must be X&Y (as in class A)
```

Comparing in both directions with the DNF machinery gives it for free, and an
undecidable comparison counts as *same* — refusing on a class the program never
declared would invent an error.

**A trait property's signature includes its type and `readonly`.** Exactly the
constant fix from two rounds ago, in the other member table: `public int $prop`
beside `public readonly int $prop` is a conflict, and php2go had compared only
visibility and staticness.

**`class_alias` will not take a reserved word**, and refuses before it looks up
the class being aliased — `Cannot use "int" as a class alias as it is reserved`.

## 2026-08-24 — Enum from(), and a check that could not be made

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2901 | 2905 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 63.5% | 63.6% |
| `failed` | 1046 | 1042 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 4 fixed, 0 newly failing. `enum` 99 → 103 of 139.

### `from()`'s parameter is not the backing type

The obvious implementation checks the argument against the enum's backing type.
`zend_enum_from_base` does not:

| Enum | Declared parameter |
|---|---|
| `enum E: int` | `int` |
| `enum E: string`, weak mode | `string\|int` |
| `enum E: string`, strict mode | `string` |

The `string|int` is deliberate — the comment in php-src says it exists so that
passing an int does not *look* like a coercion to the JIT — and it is
observable, because it is what the TypeError names. An int accepted that way is
then **rendered** with `zend_long_to_str` rather than coerced.

The check also runs before the case table is built, so a call with the wrong
argument type reports that rather than whatever else is wrong with the enum
(`backed-mismatch` asserts exactly that ordering).

### A check I had to take back out

`enum Foo: int implements BackedEnum {}` is a fatal: the engine implements one
of the two enum interfaces for every enum, so naming it is implementing it
twice. I added the check and it refused **every enum** — 102 passing tests in
that directory became 36.

The reason is a property of the harvest, not of the rule: `Class.interfaces`
carries the *linked* interface list, which already includes the engine's
addition, and there is nothing in it to say which entries the source wrote. The
check is not implementable from what is harvested, and pretending otherwise
costs two thirds of the directory. Removed, with the reason written where the
check would have gone.

Kept from the same round: `Serializable` is deprecated for any class that names
it, and an enum naming it is additionally a fatal.

```go
if class.decl.GetKind() == pb.Class_KIND_INTERFACE {
    return nil

```

which is wrong: `interface B extends A` is subject to exactly the same variance

Worth noting how it read: the guard looked like a deliberate exemption and had

### Typed class constants

PHP 8.3's `public const string S = ...` was harvested as far as the name and the
value; the **type** was not read at all. Two consequences, both now fixed:

- The constant is checked against its type **where it is read**, not where it is
  declared, because the initializer may name something that only exists by then
  — `const string BAD = LATE_C;` with `define('LATE_C', new stdClass)` after the
  class. The refusal is `Cannot assign stdClass to class constant A::BAD of type
  string`, and it is raised on *every* read rather than cached.
- The type is part of what makes two trait contributions of the same constant
  compatible. `?array` beside untyped is a conflict, and php2go had compared
  only visibility, finality and value.

## 2026-08-24 — Intersection and DNF types

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2874 | 2886 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 62.9% | 63.2% |
| `failed` | 1073 | 1061 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 12 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### "Not modelled" was a bigger claim than the situation needed

`checkType` had accepted any type containing `&` unchecked, with a defensible
comment: refusing would invent an error the program did not earn. But accepting
is also inventing — `f(X&Y $v)` took a `JustX` without complaint. And the check
does not need anything php2go lacks: a value satisfies `X&Y` when it is an
instance of both, which the class table can answer.

A declared type is a **disjunction of conjunctions**, and PHP nests exactly one
level, so DNF is the whole story:

```
int|string      -> [[int], [string]]
X&Y             -> [[X, Y]]
(X&Y)|(W&Z)     -> [[X, Y], [W, Z]]
?(X&Y)          -> [[X, Y], [null]]
```

A value satisfies the type when it satisfies **every** atom of **some**
alternative. Coercion is only ever reachable through a single-atom alternative —
nothing converts to an intersection.

### Variance too

The same shape settles the variance check that had been reporting these
undecidable. One alternative admits another when every type the *wider* one
names is satisfied by something the *narrower* one names — so `X&Y` narrows
`(X&Y)|W`, and `X` does not narrow `X&Y`.

`signatureCompatible` no longer bails out on `&` or `(`, which was 8 tests in
`type_declarations/*/variance` failing honestly and is now 8 fewer.

## 2026-08-24 — `use T { a as b; }` was never harvested

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2849 | 2874 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 62.4% | 62.9% |
| `failed` | 1098 | 1073 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 25 fixed, 0 newly failing. `traits` 92 → 113 of 165.

### The clue was a directory count

No cluster of failures stood out any more, so I counted them **by directory**
instead: `traits` had 54, the largest coherent one outside the top level. The
cause turned out to be a hole in the harvest rather than in the runtime.

`Class.traits` carried the trait *names* and nothing else. The `as` and
`insteadof` clauses live in `ce->trait_aliases` and `ce->trait_precedences`, and
php2go had never read them — so

```php
class TraitsTest { use THello { a as b; } }
$test->b();
```

simply had no `b`. Both lists survive linking, which is what makes them
harvestable at all: a class using a known trait is linked before the harvest
sees it.

Resolution follows: an alias adds a **name**, not a method — the body stays the
trait's and the original name keeps working — and `A::m insteadof B` takes B's
version out of the running for that name.

### The clauses are validated at link time

A second family, all one-or-two-test messages, is the engine checking the
clauses before it binds anything (`zend_traits_init_trait_structures`):

| Clause | Refusal |
|---|---|
| names something that is not a trait | `Class X is not a trait, Only traits may be used in 'as' and 'insteadof' statements` |
| names a trait the class does not use | `Required Trait T2 wasn't added to C` |
| `A::nonExistent as x` | `An alias was defined for A::nonExistent but this method does not exist` |
| `nonExistent as x` | `An alias (x) was defined for method nonExistent(), but this method does not exist` |
| a modifier clause on a missing method | `The modifiers of the trait method m() are changed, but this method does not exist. Error` — the trailing "Error" is in the engine's string |
| an unqualified alias two traits provide | names both and tells you how to disambiguate |

Ten more tests between them, and worth having for their own sake: an unchecked
`use` clause fails later and less clearly.

## 2026-08-24 — Instantiating a class resolves its initializers

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2837 | 2849 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 62.1% | 62.4% |
| `failed` | 1110 | 1098 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 12 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### `zend_update_class_constants`

The engine resolves a class's deferred initializers -- its constants **and its
property defaults** -- when the class is first *used*, not when each one is
read. php2go resolved a property default only if the compiler had already folded
it, so

```php
class B { public $prop = A::C; }        // A does not exist yet
```

left `prop` as **null** whenever `A::C` had to wait for an autoload. Twelve tests
turned on that alone; the timing was filed as a TODO last round and is worth
more than it looked.

The timing is observable because an initializer naming an undeclared class
autoloads, and an autoloader can print and can throw.

### Marking it done, and when

The obvious guard is wrong. Marking the class resolved *before* the walk --
to stop an initializer re-entering -- breaks `gh10709_2`, where the autoloader
triggered by resolving `B::$prop` itself does `new B()`. The inner
instantiation has to resolve the default itself rather than find a
half-finished class already marked done, so the flag is set only once the walk
*finishes*. A genuine cycle is bounded by `constDepth` and by the call depth,
which is what the engine's own unresolved-constant guard does.

The two remaining `gh10709` variants now differ only in **object handle
numbers**: PHP frees the inner object and reuses handle #2 where php2go hands
out #3. That is the refcounting item, not this one.

## 2026-08-24 — `static` in a callable is the called class

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2833 | 2837 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 62.0% | 62.1% |
| `failed` | 1114 | 1110 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 4 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### The comment said it was wrong, and it was

`callableClass` resolved `static` to the calling *scope*, with a comment saying
so: "the frame that made the call is the closest thing to a called class this
side of the stack". It was not — the frame has `called`, and only the *context*
was missing a way to ask for it.

```php
class Test1 { static function test() { var_dump(is_callable("static::ok")); } }
class Test2 extends Test1 { static function ok() {} }
Test1::test();   // false
Test2::test();   // true
```

`Ctx.CalledScope` now travels beside `Ctx.Scope`, set from `frame.called` on
every frame, so a builtin can ask what `static::` means the same way it already
asks what `self::` does. The same resolution was missing from `defined()` and
`constant()`, which take a `"Class::CONST"` string and never resolved the three
keywords at all.

### Found and filed, not fixed

`gh10709`: **instantiating a class evaluates its class constants**. The engine
calls `zend_update_class_constants` from `new`, so

```php
class B { const C = A::C . "B"; }
spl_autoload_register(function ($c) { class A { const C = "A"; } var_dump(B::C); });
new B();
```

prints `string(2) "AB"` — the autoloader runs *because* `new B()` forced `B::C`.
php2go evaluates constants lazily on read, so the whole script prints nothing.
Recorded in [TODO.md](../TODO.md): `instantiate` has no error path today, and
eager evaluation moves where an initializer's throw appears, so it wants a
round of its own.

`WeakMap` and `WeakReference` had been written off with the GC-timing families,
and that was half right. Reading the directory: `weakmap_basic_map_behavior`,
`weakmap_error_conditions`, `weakmap_nested`, `weakmap_object_reference` and

So the map is implemented and the weakness is not: nothing is ever dropped, and

What the corpus does check about the map:

- **`count()` did not consult Countable for an engine class.** `countOf`
  reached `arrayStoreMethod` and user op_arrays but nothing else, so

  writes `[0]`. Real properties are always named, so the dumper quoted
  everything; whatever a debug-info handler returns is an ordinary array and an
  integer key in one prints unquoted.

### A harness note

The "not contained" message names the object *handle*, and the differential
harness only normalizes `)#N` — anchored on the closing paren so stack-trace
frame numbers stay comparable. A handle inside message text is not covered, so
that probe compares the message's *shape* rather than its text.

## 2026-08-24 — Output buffering, settype, and the object that converts to 1

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2819 | 2823 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 61.7% | 61.8% |
| `failed` | 1085 | 1089 |
| `unsupported` | 661 | 653 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
A thin round: 8 tests unblocked, 4 of which pass.

### Everything that prints has to go through one door

`ob_start` was easy once the mistake it exposed was fixed: `Ctx.Echo` and the
diagnostic writer both went **straight to the output stream**, bypassing
`Ctx.Write`. So the first version buffered nothing an `echo` produced. Both now
route through `Write`, which is also what makes

```php
ob_start(); $x = @something_that_warns(); $warning = ob_get_clean();
```

collect the warning -- a diagnostic is output like any other.

Buffers nest, and only the innermost sees a write. The stack lives on the Ctx,
since it is per-request state.

The oracle cannot grade `ob_get_level()` absolutely: `php2go_eval` captures
through a buffer of its own, so a script that reports level 1 under the CLI
reports 2 there. The differential case compares the level *relative* to
`ob_get_level()` at the top -- the same shape as the resource-id problem from
the previous round.

### settype, and the two conversions that are not casts

`settype($var, $type)` is the one conversion taking its subject **by
reference**, and it spells types the old way (`integer`, `double`, `boolean`).
Two of its answers are not what the cast operators give:

- `settype($x, "resource")` is a **ValueError**: `Cannot convert to resource
  type`. There is no conversion *to* a handle -- one would have to come from
  somewhere.
- an object converted to int or float is a **warning and the number 1**:
  `Object of class stdClass could not be converted to int`. php2go returned 0
  silently, for `(int)$obj` as well as for settype.

### `fopen` was the third-largest blocker, and mostly not about files

36 tests were blocked on `fopen`, and 61 of the 84 calls to it in the corpus are
`fopen(__FILE__, "r")` with nothing read afterwards. They want a **resource** --
a value type php2go did not have -- to cast, compare and print.

`php.Resource` is now that: an id, a type name, and whatever the runtime hangs
off it. Casting is the point of most of these tests:

| Expression | Result |
|---|---|
| `(int)$r` | the id — which is what makes a resource usable as an array key |
| `(string)$r` | `Resource id #5` |
| `(bool)$r` | always true, open or closed |
