| after `fclose` | `resource(5) of type (Unknown)` — the id survives, the type does not |
| `gettype($r)` | `resource`, or `resource (closed)` |
| `get_debug_type($r)` | `resource (stream)` / `resource (closed)` |

`is_resource` is not a builtin call at all: it compiles to `ZEND_TYPE_CHECK`,
and the mask alone is not enough — a closed handle still *is* IS_RESOURCE, so
the check has to ask whether anything is behind it.

A resource used as an array key warns *every time*:
`Resource ID#5 used as offset, casting to integer (5)`. Note the capital `ID#`,
which is not how the string cast spells it.

### The id depends on the SAPI

The first resource a script opens is **#5** under the CLI and **#2** under
embed. The `.phpt` corpus was recorded with the CLI (16 places say
`resource(5)`), while the differential oracle runs embed. php2go numbers from 5
to match the corpus, and the differential case for resources deliberately never
prints an id. Recorded in the LTM, because it will look like a bug otherwise.

`git -C third_party/php-src status` came back dirty: `Zend/tests/bug52508.ini`.
The test writes it with `file_put_contents`, calls `parse_ini_file`, and unlinks
it at the end — and `parse_ini_file` is a gap, so the run stopped before the
unlink. Nothing had ever written a file before, so `file_put_contents` starting
to work turned an ordinary early exit into corpus litter.

`php2phpt` now snapshots each test's directory and removes whatever appeared
while it ran. Only plain files: a new *directory* would be a fixture tree, and
deleting one blind is a bigger promise than the runner should make.

## 2026-08-24 — Attribute filters, the slicing family, and foreach over a scalar

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2788 | 2799 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 61.0% | 61.3% |
| `failed` | 1087 | 1087 |
| `unsupported` | 690 | 679 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 7 previously-failing tests now pass, 4 more came from
`unsupported`, and 7 newly-reached tests fail on other things.

### `getAttributes()` has a filter, and the filter has rules

`getAttributes(?string $name, int $flags)`:

- Without `IS_INSTANCEOF` the name is compared **as written** and nothing is
  resolved -- `getAttributes(A3::class)` is legal where `A3` does not exist.
- With it the *base* has to resolve (`Class "SomeMissingClass" not found`) but
  an **attribute** class that does not is simply not a match.
- Any other flag value is an Error naming the class that declares the method,
  which is `ReflectionFunctionAbstract` for functions and methods.

Also this round: `ReflectionFunction` over an engine function (it has no
op_array, so only its name is answerable and everything else stays an honest
gap), and `newInstance` refusing what has no instances -- `Cannot instantiate
trait foo`, and the interface, enum and abstract wordings beside it.

### array_slice, array_splice, array_unique, array_merge

The rules that are easy to get wrong, all confirmed by probe:

- `array_slice` keeps **string** keys always and integer keys only when asked;
  a negative offset counts back from the end and a negative length stops that
  many short of it.
- `array_splice` renumbers integer keys throughout, and a replacement inserted
  at the very end still lands after everything.
- `array_unique` compares **by string** by default, which is why `1` and `"1"`
  collapse -- and it keeps the first occurrence *with its key*.
- `array_merge` appends integer-keyed values under fresh keys while a later
  string key overwrites an earlier one.

### foreach over a scalar is a warning

```
Warning: foreach() argument must be of type array|object, null given
```

and the loop runs zero times. php2go reported it as an unsupported opcode,
which blocked 3 tests outright and hid whatever came after the loop in several
more. The two it newly reaches both fail on things already in
[TODO.md](../TODO.md) -- by-reference foreach positions, and `var_dump`'s `&`.

### The refcount family, counted again

Clustering the 1087 failures by first differing line: `&` markers 15,
destructor timing 10, object handle numbers 14. **~39 tests now turn on
refcounting**, which makes it the largest single remaining cause. It stays
deferred -- three attempts at pieces of it have been reverted, and a wrong

Emitted for an unqualified call inside a namespace, where the name could mean

## 2026-08-24 — Attributes are harvested, and Reflection starts

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2756 | 2763 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 60.3% | 60.5% |
| `failed` | 1048 | 1062 |
| `unsupported` | 761 | 740 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`attributes` 44 → 48 of 96, with its `unsupported` down from 31 to 21.
Read the two columns together: 21 tests were unblocked, 7 of which now pass and
14 of which now fail honestly instead of reporting a gap.

### Where the 267 ReflectionClass tests actually are

Worth writing down before anyone budgets for Reflection: **223 of them are
`lazy_objects`** -- `newLazyProxy` and `newLazyGhost` alone account for 363 call
sites. Reflection is not the feature those tests need. The rest is 19 in
`attributes`, 5 in `enum`, and a long tail.

### Attributes now travel in the IR

`#[...]` was harvested only as far as `#[\Deprecated]`'s two arguments. The whole
list now travels for classes, methods and functions, properties and class
constants: name, arguments (positional and named), and line.

The arguments stay **unevaluated**, as literals. That is not an optimisation --
it is the semantics. `#[Attr(SOME_CONST)]` is legal above a declaration that
compiles before the constant exists, because the engine keeps the argument as an
AST and only evaluates it when something reflects on it.

The engine's attribute table is a packed hash of variable-length structs, so
every field needs a C shim; `zend_attribute` cannot be mirrored in Go.

### ReflectionClass, ReflectionAttribute, Attribute

Enough to answer what the corpus asks: `getName`, `getShortName`, `isInterface`,
`isEnum`, `isAbstract`, `isFinal`, `hasMethod`, `hasProperty`,
`getInterfaceNames`, `implementsInterface`, `getAttributes`; and on the
attribute side `getName`, `getArguments`, `newInstance`.

Two placement rules, both settled by a probe rather than by reading the header:

- `new ReflectionClass("NoSuch")` throws **ReflectionException**, not the Error
  a missing class usually earns.
- `new Attribute(-1)` is **accepted**. The flags value is only refused where an
  attribute of that class is instantiated, which is also where an argument
  naming something undefined (`#[Attribute(Foo::BAR)]`) produces
  `Class "Foo" not found`. I had implemented the check in the constructor; the
  differential case caught it.

A reflection constructor needs the class table, which the `builtinCtor` hook has
no way to reach, so these classes route `__construct` through the
`builtinMethod` path instead.

## 2026-08-24 — Magic forwarders, and the array functions that change a length

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2726 | 2756 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 59.7% | 60.3% |
| `failed` | 1066 | 1048 |
| `unsupported` | 773 | 761 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
The first pass rate over 60%.

### Which forwarder answers is decided by `$this`, not by the syntax

`__call` and `__callStatic` are not "the instance one and the static one".
`zend_std_get_static_method` prefers **`__call`** whenever there is a `$this`
that is an instance of the class being named:

```php
class bar {
    public function __call($a, $b) { ... }
    public function test() {
        self::ABC();                       // __call
        bar::ABC();                        // __call
        call_user_func(['BAR', 'xyz']);    // __call
    }
}
call_user_func(['BAR', 'x']);              // __callStatic, from outside
```

So the decision needs the *bound object of the innermost call*, not the calling
scope. `Unit.callingThis` reads it off the stack the backtrace already keeps,
and `forwarderFor` makes the choice in one place for the three paths that need
it: `ZEND_INIT_STATIC_METHOD_CALL`, `staticTarget`, and the validity check.

This started as a two-test TODO item and fixed **21**. The array-callable path
had never forwarded at all, and `is_callable` had its own copy of the rule.

### array_pop and friends

`array_pop`, `array_shift`, `array_push`, `array_unshift`, `array_fill` and
`array_fill_keys` were all missing -- 13 tests were blocked on them. The
mutating four take their first argument by reference, which here means the same
`*php.Array` every holder has, the way the sorts already worked.

Two details that are not obvious from the name:

- **`array_pop` takes the next-free key down with it.** `[1,2,3]`, popped and
  then appended, gives back key 2 rather than 3.
- **`array_shift` renumbers**: integer keys are rewritten from zero and string
  keys keep both their names and their places. `array_unshift` does the same.

### A hang, caught and reverted

By-reference `foreach` iterates the array rather than a snapshot, so an element
appended inside the loop is visited (`foreach_013`). Implementing that by
extending the snapshot with whatever the array grew made `foreach_016` **loop
forever**: it calls `array_unshift` inside the loop, and since unshifting
renumbers, the value that triggered it comes round again under a new key.

PHP is immune because a by-reference loop holds a *bucket position*, which
renumbering moves along with the data. Modelling that needs positions the array
type does not have. Reverted -- a corpus hang is much worse than four failing
tests -- and recorded in [TODO.md](../TODO.md).

## 2026-08-24 — Compound callables, and what makes a callback invalid

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2719 | 2726 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 59.5% | 59.7% |
| `failed` | 1073 | 1066 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 8 fixed, 0 newly failing.

### `[$obj, "parent::m"]`

A callable's method half may name a scope. The scope is resolved against the
**class the callable named** -- the object's class -- and not against the
calling function's scope, which is why `bug48770` calls `B::func` from inside
`B` when `$this` is a `C`: parent-of-C, not parent-of-B. The form is deprecated
rather than refused:

```
Deprecated: Callables of the form ["C", "parent::func"] are deprecated
```

and the first name in it is the class *written down*, not the one the scope
resolved to.

### A bad callback has a reason

`call_user_func` and friends validate before calling anything, and the
diagnostic is a TypeError naming both the argument and a specific reason:

```
call_user_func_array(): Argument #1 ($callback) must be a valid callback, class B does not have a method "inexistent"
                                                                          cannot access private method B::func22()
                                                                          first array member is not a valid class name or object
                                                                          cannot access "self" when no class scope is active
                                                                          class "foo" not found
```

`callableReason` produces these; `ZEND_INIT_USER_CALL` raises them. The plain
dynamic call (`$f(...)`) keeps the bare `Error` it always had -- the wording
belongs to the builtin, not to calling.

Two details cost a round each:

- The deprecation is reported by `zend_is_callable_ex`, which is *also* the
  validity check -- so it appears even when the answer is "not callable", and
  before the method is looked up. Here validation and resolution are two calls,
  so the second takes a `quiet` flag rather than reporting again.
- Resolving the class half **autoloads**. `call_user_func_002` asserts on the
  autoloader printing the name it was asked for -- and on it *not* being asked
  for the empty string.

The class named in the reason is the one the callable resolved to, not the one
that declared the method: a private `A::func22` reached through `parent::` from
a `C` is reported as `B::func22`.

### Left on the table

`[$obj, "m"]` where the class has `__call` is a valid callable that forwards.
php2go resolves the method or fails, so `bug45186`/`bug45186_2` still fail. The
machinery is `methodCallable`'s magic-forwarder logic, which `is_callable`
already uses; the array-callable path does not.

## 2026-08-24 — Linking asks for classes, and asking runs the autoloaders

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2711 | 2719 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 59.3% | 59.5% |
| `failed` | 1082 | 1073 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison: 9 fixed, 1 newly failing, then that one fixed too.
`type_declarations/variance` 19 → 23 of 43.

### Declaring a class did not ask for its parent

```php
spl_autoload_register(function($c) { echo "load $c\n"; });
class B extends A {}
```

printed nothing and carried on. The engine prints `load A` and then
`Uncaught Error: Class "A" not found`. Linking is exactly where the engine finds
out it has not seen a class, and php2go never asked -- not for the parent, not
for the interfaces, not for the traits, and not for the classes a variance check
needs. `resolveDependencies` at `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` and
`ZEND_DECLARE_ANON_CLASS` now asks for all of them.

### `findClass` is not "available"

The first attempt still printed nothing, because the harvest *has* class A --
declared inside the autoloader's closure, which the harvester walks. Being in
the harvest is not being declared. `classDeclared` answers the second half, but
returns **true** for a name it has never heard of ("no opline to wait for",
which is the right answer for `class_exists` and the wrong one for linking).
`classAvailable` is the conjunction, and it is what the linking paths want.

`resolveClass` -- what `new` and `FETCH_CLASS` go through -- now uses it too, so
a harvested-but-undeclared class is autoloaded first. If no autoloader produces
it the harvested declaration is still used: deciding that a program may not
reach its own class is a bigger claim than this needed to make.

### `Could not check compatibility`

The signature checker's undecidable verdict has a wording of its own when the
reason is a missing class:

```
Could not check compatibility between ns\Foo::method(ns\stdClass $o) and Iface::method(stdClass $o),
because class ns\stdClass is not available
```

Which class gets named is decided by the *order of lookup*, and that order is
observable because a lookup can autoload and an autoloader can print. The engine
resolves the **child's** class first and never asks for the parent's if the
child is unavailable. Doing it the other way round printed an extra `X` in
`exception_during_variance_autoload`.

Two more rules fell out:

- A prototype's `static` names no class, so nothing is looked up -- it was being
  autoloaded as if `static` were a class name.
- `self` in a **trait** method is the *using* class, not the trait. The trait is
  still what the diagnostic names, so the resolution scope and the display scope
  had to be separated (`selfScope`).

## 2026-08-24 — Destructors at the end of the request, and an oracle that runs them

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2704 | 2711 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 59.2% | 59.3% |
| `failed` | 1089 | 1082 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
Set comparison against the previous run: 8 fixed, 1 newly failing.

### `__destruct` was not called at all

44 failing tests expected destructor output. PHP destroys an object the moment
its last holder goes away, which php2go cannot reproduce without refcounts --
but the *shutdown* half of that is exact and was simply missing. `Unit.live`
now remembers every object whose class has a `__destruct`, and `RunUnit` runs
`shutdown_destructors` after the registered shutdown functions:

1. `zend_hash_graceful_reverse_destroy(&EG(symbol_table))` -- globals in
   **reverse** insertion order;
2. whatever objects remain, in creation order.

An object PHP destroyed mid-script is destroyed here instead: late rather than
never. That is a real limitation and it costs `bug73338`, where a destructor
throws and PHP's `catch` is still on the stack when it does.

### PHP does not destruct what it did not construct

The first version regressed 7 tests, all the same rule. `new Foo` where the
constructor throws, and `new Foo(bang())` where an *argument* throws so the
constructor is never entered, both leave an object that is never destructed.
Modelled by blocking destruction at `ZEND_NEW` when a constructor is going to
run and releasing it when that call returns -- which covers both, where
marking on the error path only covered the first.

### The oracle was crashing on this, and nobody had noticed

`php2eval` segfaulted in `php2go_reset_user_symbols` for any script leaving a
live object of a user class *with a destructor*: the class table was reset
first, and destroying the object then called `__destruct` through a freed
`zend_class_entry`. Without a destructor the free needs nothing from the class
entry, which is why every earlier case got away with it.

The fix is also what makes the oracle honest: `php2go_eval` now performs the
same two shutdown steps inside the output capture, so the engine's answer
includes the destructor output a real script prints. Before this, the oracle
would have graded correct destructor output as a mismatch.

## 2026-08-24 — Signature compatibility

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2682 | 2704 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 58.7% | 59.2% |
| `failed` | 1111 | 1089 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`traits` 85 → 92 of 165; the rest is spread over `type_declarations`,
`return_types` and the top-level directory.

### The largest coherent family left

124 tests in `Zend/tests` quote `must be compatible with`. Nothing checked
signatures at all, so every one of them ran the program the engine refuses to
link. `runtime/interp/signature.go` now implements
`zend_do_perform_implementation_check` at `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS`, next to the
abstract and trait checks that were already there.

The rule is short and worth having exactly:

- the number of **required** arguments may not increase, and a declared
  argument may not be removed (arity is checked against the declaration, not
  against what is passed);
- a by-reference **return** is covariant -- dropping it is a refusal -- while a
  by-reference **argument** is invariant;
- a variadic function may not become non-variadic, and past the end of a
  variadic declaration every further position is that same parameter again;
- parameter types are contravariant, return types covariant, and a return type
  may not be removed.

### Rendering is half the feature

The message prints both declarations through `zend_get_function_declaration`,
which has a shape of its own: `& ` for a by-reference return, the type before
the `&`/`...`/`$name`, and a default rendered from the `RECV_INIT` opline rather
than from the argument -- `'ten chars…'` cut at ten bytes with `...`, `[]` or
`[...]` for an array, a bare constant name for `PHP_EOL`, `<expression>` for
anything else. Getting the rule right and the rendering wrong fails the test
just the same.

### Four ways to invent an error that is not there

A check that can refuse a program has to be wrong in the safe direction, so the
verdict is a pair: compatible, and *decidable*. A full corpus run found five
spurious fatals on the first version, each a real rule:

1. `class_alias` -- both sides of a class-type comparison have to go through the
   class table, or `Bar` and `Foo` look like different classes.
2. `never` is the bottom type: `__toString(): never` satisfies `: string`.
3. A **concrete** trait method is not a prototype. Composing a trait copies its
   methods in; a method the class writes itself replaces one outright rather
   than overriding it. Only an *abstract* trait method constrains.
4. `static` on the prototype side is a promise about the called class, and only
   `static` keeps it -- `A::duplicate(): static` is not satisfied by
   `B::duplicate(): A`. On the child side it resolves to the child.

Intersection and DNF types are reported undecidable rather than guessed, which
leaves 8 tests in `type_declarations/*/variance` failing honestly.

### A trait's method is checked, and named, as the trait's

`traits/inheritance003` links `class MyHelloWorld extends Base { use SayWorld; }`
and the refusal names `SayWorld::sayHello(Base $d)` against
`Base::sayHello(array $a)`. The engine copies a trait function in without
rewriting its scope, so the check has to run over what the declaration
*contributes*, not over what it declares, and the diagnostic names the trait.
That one change took `traits` from 88 to 92.

## 2026-08-24 — Indirect modification, `&get`, and typed references

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2670 | 2682 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 58.4% | 58.7% |
| `failed` | 1123 | 1111 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.
`property_hooks` 139 → 145 of 198; `type_declarations` picked up the rest.

### Writing *through* a hooked property

`FETCH_OBJ_W`/`_RW`/`_UNSET` on a hooked property had never been wired, so
`$o->hooked[] = 1` quietly wrote a slot that does not exist.
`zend_std_read_property` gives the rule verbatim: in write mode, what the get
hook returned must be a reference or an object, and otherwise

```
Indirect modification of C::$p is not allowed
```

The object case is not an exception the engine makes reluctantly -- an object
can be mutated without writing the property back, so the fetch hands out a copy
of the handle and everything works. That is the same `copyOnly` shape the
readonly and asymmetric-visibility refusals already used.

A `&get` hook is the other way through: it returns a slot, and a write reaches
it. `ZEND_ACC_RETURN_REFERENCE` on the hook's op_array is what says so, now
harvested as `OpArray.returns_ref` (it is the same flag `function &f()` sets, so
it is worth having for its own sake). Our `ZEND_RETURN_BY_REF` already yields a
`php.MakeRef`, so honouring `&get` was reading the flag and skipping the deref.

### A reference to a typed property is itself typed

`typed_properties_062/063/064` are the same script three ways -- the reference
held in an object property, in a variable, in an array element -- and all three
say things like

```
Cannot assign string to reference held by property class@anonymous::$foo of type int
Cannot increment a reference held by property class@anonymous::$foo of type int past its maximal value
```

The constraint belongs to the *box*, not to the name. `php.Ref` now carries
`sources []RefSource`, added when `elementRef` hands out a slot of a declared,
typed, non-dynamic property, and every write path that can reach a shared box
checks them: the CV store, compound assignment, `++`/`--`, and the object and
array element forms of each. 29 tests in the corpus quote that wording.

`zend_incdec_typed_ref` decides the increment case on the *shape of the step*
rather than on the resulting value: an int that became a float, held by a source
that does not accept floats, is "past its maximal value". Reading that mattered
-- I had first written a range check, which gets `PHP_INT_MIN--` wrong because
`(double)PHP_INT_MIN` is exactly representable and passes a range test.

### Out-of-range floats do not coerce to int

Falling out of the above: `ZEND_DOUBLE_FITS_LONG` is a *refusal*, not a
truncation. `zend_parse_arg_long_weak` returns failure for NaN and for anything
outside `[-2^63, 2^63)`; only a float that fits but has a fraction gets the
"loses precision" deprecation. `coerceScalar` truncated everything, so
`$typedInt = "21e50"` silently became `PHP_INT_MAX` instead of raising. This is
a shared path, so it corrects parameters and return values too.

### Measured and not done

Clustering all 1117 failure diffs with the EXPECTF placeholder rules applied:
exactly **13** tests differ from expected *only* by `var_dump`'s `&` markers.
That is the whole remaining payoff of holder counts, which two rounds ago I
recorded as needing real refcounting. It stays deferred, and now with a number
against it.

### Result

A thin round: one harness fix, and a negative result on the largest deferred
item.

### A test whose diff showed nothing

`flexible-heredoc-nowdoc` failed while `-diff` printed two blocks that were
byte-identical -- I compared them and they were. The difference was `\r\n`
against `\n` inside a heredoc body, which `cat -A` renders the same as the
surrounding lines because the CR sits before a newline either way.

`run-tests.php` normalizes CRLF to LF on **both** sides before comparing.
`internal/phpt` trimmed but never normalized. The LTM entry on harness fidelity
already listed this as something run-tests.php does; it was written down and not
implemented, which is its own lesson about writing the note before the code.

### The `&` marker cannot be a flag, confirmed by measurement

Two rounds ago I recorded that `var_dump`'s `&` tracks a *live* second holder
and so needs holder counts. This round I built the flag version anyway, because
the `list/` directory is 6-of-9 blocked on it and array references had since
started working -- worth re-testing an old conclusion against a changed
codebase.

Marking only the deliberate aliasing sites (`$r = &$x`, `[&$x]`, `foreach as
&$v`, `MAKE_REF`) and not the write-path boxes avoids the over-marking that
sank the first attempt, and measured **+3**: 2670 to 2673.

It also broke a differential case, and correctly: after `f(&$x)` returns, PHP
stops marking and the flag does not. Withdrawing the marking at the argument
sites did not help, because the callee's own `foreach ($args as &$a)` marks the
caller's boxes from the inside -- correct while the loop runs, stale afterwards.

Three `.phpt` tests against a divergence the differential oracle catches is a bad
trade, so this is reverted. The conclusion is now measured rather than reasoned:
a flag buys +3 and costs correctness; only holder counts that decrement will do.

## 2026-08-24 — References that arrive through arrays

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2663 | 2669 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 58.3% | 58.4% |
| `failed` | 1131 | 1124 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 593 | 595 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### `[&$x]` did not store a reference

`ZEND_INIT_ARRAY` and `ZEND_ADD_ARRAY_ELEMENT` carry `ZEND_ARRAY_ELEMENT_REF` in
their extended_value, which php2go ignored: `$arr = array(&$a); $arr[0] = 5;`
left `$a` alone. Everything downstream of that was unreachable, which is why
three separate by-reference bugs were really one.

With it fixed, three more followed:

- **`&...$args`** collects the caller's slots. `RECV_VARIADIC` was dereferencing
  and copying every argument into the variadic array, so `foreach ($args as
  &$a) { $a++; }` wrote into copies. The same for `f(...$array)` on a by-ref
  variadic, where the *elements* of the unpacked array have to be passed as
  slots.
- **`call_user_func_array`** is not a call to a builtin at all: the compiler
  specialises it into `ZEND_SEND_ARRAY`. That opcode passes an element that is
  already a reference as one, and warns -- `Argument #1 ($x) must be passed by
  reference, value given` -- when the callee wants a slot and the element is not
  one. Fixing the builtin instead does nothing, which cost a detour.
- **A by-value parameter never shares the caller's slot**, even when the
  argument arrives as a reference from such an array. `verifyArgument` returned
  the value untouched when no type was declared, so a reference passed to a
  by-value parameter wrote back.

`Array.Each` dereferences, so telling whether an element *is* a reference needs
a raw read; `Array.Raw` is new for that.

### A hang, again from making something work

`$a = [&$a]` was previously impossible to build, so a recursive array never
existed and comparing one never came up. Now it does, and `===` walked forever.
Two guards: the same array is identical to itself without looking inside -- which
is what makes `$a === $a` answer at all -- and a depth bound below that. PHP
reports "Nesting level too deep - recursive dependency?" where this stops
silently; that is a gap in the diagnostic, recorded, but not a hang.

That is the second time this week a fix has exposed a latent infinite loop
downstream. Making something possible for the first time is worth a corpus run
on its own.

## 2026-08-24 — Where a generator says it was called from

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2654 | 2663 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 58.1% | 58.3% |
| `Zend/tests/generators` passing | 81 | 90 (of 156) |
| `failed` | 1140 | 1131 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 592 | 593 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### A generator body has a frame, and it depends on what resumed it

php2go put no frame on the stack for a generator body at all, so a backtrace
taken inside one skipped straight to whoever pulled on it. PHP shows the body,
and what it says about *where it was called from* is not fixed:

```
#0 file(4): f1()                        <- called from the body
#1 [internal function]: f2('foo','bar') <- the body, resumed by Generator->rewind()
#2 file(13): Generator->rewind()
```

versus, for a `foreach`:

```
#0 file(8): gen()                       <- the body, resumed by foreach
```

The difference is whether the resume already contributed a frame of its own. An
explicit `Generator->rewind()` is a call and gets one, so the body below it has
no call site left to name and reads `[internal function]`. A `foreach` resumes
without any such frame, and the body is reported at the foreach's own line.

`php.InternalFrameFile` marks the first case, and the renderer drops the `(line)`
for it -- `#1 [internal function]: f2(...)`, not `#1 [internal function](0): ...`.

### getReturn primes

`(function () { return 42; yield; })()->getReturn()` is `int(42)`: asking a
generator that has not started runs it, and for a body that returns before its
first yield that is enough to answer. php2go threw "hasn't returned" without
starting it.

## 2026-08-24 — Two conversions where there looked like one

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2645 | 2654 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 57.9% | 58.1% |
| `failed` | 1149 | 1140 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 589 | 592 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### `(int)$float` and `(int)"$float"` are different conversions

```php
(int) 1.0E+121    // 0
(int) "1.0E+121"  // 9223372036854775807
```

The engine has two functions for this, and the difference is deliberate:
`zend_dval_to_lval` yields 0 for an out-of-range double, while
`zend_dval_to_lval_cap` -- "used to convert a string float to integer during an
(int) cast", says the comment -- saturates to the nearest bound. php2go used one
conversion for both.

### A hang, and the rule behind it

Fixing that turned a corpus run into a hang: `$string[(string) 10e120] = 'E'`
now converted the offset to `PHP_INT_MAX` and the string-offset write padded
towards it. The engine never gets there, because a *string* used as a string
offset must be an **integer** numeric string -- `"007"` is fine, `"1.5"` and
`"1.0E+121"` are `TypeError: Cannot access offset of type string on string`. A
float offset is allowed only as an actual float, which warns and truncates.

php2go accepted any numeric string. Worth noting how the two bugs interacted:
the offset rule had been wrong all along, and only became *visible* once the
conversion beneath it started producing a large number instead of zero. A
plausible-looking wrong value can hide a second wrong rule indefinitely.

An exact integer string is also not a cast, so it produces no "String offset
cast occurred" warning -- which the old code emitted for every string offset.

### VERIFY_RETURN_TYPE converts in place

`function f(): string { $int = 42; $ref =& $int; return $int; }` returned
`int(42)`. When the opcode has no result slot -- which is the shape the compiler
emits here -- the conversion happens in **op1**, which the following `RETURN`
reads; php2go stored it into a result slot that was not there. The engine
separates first, so a variable that was a reference does not carry the converted
value back to whatever it aliased.

## 2026-08-24 — The rest of the type checks

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2637 | 2645 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 57.7% | 57.9% |

Following last round's observation -- that the machinery for a rule can exist
and simply not be called from everywhere the rule applies -- three more sites.

### Static properties and compound assignment

`C::$typed = "42"` and `$o->typedInt .= "abc"` were both unchecked. The static
form takes its declaration from the class rather than the object but is
otherwise identical; the compound form had to route the *result* of the
operation through the check, which meant giving the write closure somewhere to
report a refusal from.

### strict_types belongs to the caller

`declare(strict_types=1)` decides whether an **argument** is coerced, and the
file that decides is the one containing the *call*, not the one containing the
function. Only the return type uses the callee's own setting. php2go read the
callee's flag for both, which is indistinguishable within one file and wrong
across an `include`.

`pendingFrame` now carries the call site's setting to the frame -- the same
one-slot hand-off the variadic's named arguments already used, generalised so
there is one of them rather than two.

### A float in a stack trace is not a string cast

`t(1.0)` renders as `t(1.0)`, and `1.0e100` as `t(1.0E+100)`. php2go fell
through to `Value.String()`, which gives `1`. The rendering is var_export's, not
the string cast's -- a trace argument has to read back as the type it was.

`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### `$t->i = "42"` on `public int $i`

Parameters and return values were type-checked; **properties were not**, at all.
`$t->i = "42"` stored the string. The declared type is already on the object's
`Declared` map -- it has to be, for the uninitialized diagnostic -- so the check
is `checkType` with the same weak/strict rule arguments use, and the failure is
`Cannot assign string to property T::$i of type int`.

Worth 22 tests, and cheap because everything it needed was already there. Places
like this are worth looking for: the machinery for a rule can exist and simply
never be called from one of the places the rule applies.

### Exception chaining in a finally, done properly

Last round's attempt chained where the new exception was *raised*, which also
chained one that gets caught inside the same finally. The distinction is whether
the new exception **escapes** the finally block, and that is knowable at raise
time after all -- `catchTarget` picks the handler, so comparing it against the
pending entry's finally bounds answers it.

`unwind` now records those bounds when it is pushed for a finally, and `raise`
chains only when the new handler lies outside them (or there is no handler at
all). Both directions pass: `try_finally_002` and `catch_finally_004` chain,
`bug65784` and `bug72213_2` do not.

### A trait's abstract method belongs to the using class

`abstract class C { use T; }` where `T` declares `abstract private function m()`
reports `C::m`, not `T::m` -- the trait's members are flattened into the class.
And a declaration the class makes itself replaces the trait's requirement, even
when that declaration is *also* abstract, which is what makes `abstract_method_7`
legal.

## 2026-08-24 — A catch that does not match is not the end of the frame

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2606 | 2610 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 57.0% | 57.1% |
| `Zend/tests/try` passing | 50 | 54 (of 74) |
| `failed` | 1187 | 1183 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 583 | 584 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### One line, four tests

```php
try {
    try { throw new Exception("x"); }
    catch (TypeError $e) {}      // does not match
    finally { echo "1"; }
} catch (Exception $e) { echo "c"; }
```

`ZEND_CATCH` with the last-in-chain flag and no match was doing

```go
return php.Undef(), &thrown{object: top.object}
```

-- leaving the frame outright. But the exception has not finished with this
frame: this try may still have a `finally`, and so may an enclosing one. Raising
it from the catch position instead lets the ordinary search find them, and
`catchTarget` already resolves a region to its finally once `pc` is past the
catch. A plain `try/finally` worked; it took *both* a non-matching catch and a
finally to expose it.

### Exception chaining in a finally: attempted and backed out

An exception thrown inside a `finally` while another is in flight becomes the
new one's `previous`, which `try_finally_002` and `catch_finally_004` check.
Chaining at the point the new exception is raised fixed those two and broke two
others (`bug65784`, `bug72213_2`): a throw inside a finally that is **caught
within that finally** must not chain, and must leave the original still in
flight. At raise time it is not yet known which it will be.

Doing it properly means chaining where the finally *completes* -- when the
fast-return would resume the pending unwind and finds a different exception in
flight -- rather than where the new one is thrown. Backed out at no net change;
the measurement was 2610 either way, with two tests traded for two.

## 2026-08-24 — #[\Deprecated]

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2593 | 2606 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 56.8% | 57.0% |
| `Zend/tests/attributes/deprecated` passing | 0 | 13 (of 31) |
| `failed` | 1200 | 1187 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 582 | 583 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The first attribute the IR carries

Nothing in the harvest carried attributes at all. `#[\Deprecated]` needed three
things: the flag, and the two optional arguments -- which may be positional or
named, and may be *expressions* rather than literals. One of the tests uses a
deprecated constant as another's deprecation message, which is why they travel
as `Literal` and go through `constantLiteral` like any other deferred
initializer.

`zend_get_attribute_str(attributes, "deprecated", ...)` reads it, and the
argument walk has to handle both forms: a named argument matches by name, and a
positional one is `message` then `since`.

### The wording, and the level

```
Function f() is deprecated[ since X][, message]
Method C::m() is deprecated…
Constant C::K is deprecated…
Enum case E::A is deprecated…
```

The suffix is built in that order -- `since` first, then the message -- and
either half may be absent.

The level is `E_USER_DEPRECATED`, not `E_DEPRECATED`: an error handler is told
16384. Both print under the label "Deprecated", so `Ctx` gained a level whose
printed name differs from its selector, which is the first time that
distinction has mattered. The E_USER_* family will need the same treatment if
`trigger_error` ever grows a test.

### Also

A plain function call names its target and resolves it at `DO_FCALL`, so the
deprecation lookup happens there rather than at the pending call -- the same
place `argumentByRef` and named-argument resolution had to look.

Twelve failures remain in that directory: the interaction between a deprecated
function and a *deprecated error handler* (which must not recurse), and the
naming of a method reached through `__call`.

## 2026-08-24 — What an enum may not be

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2570 | 2593 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 56.2% | 56.8% |
| `Zend/tests/enum` passing | 73 | 92 (of 131) |
| `failed` | 1223 | 1200 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 581 | 582 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Eleven tests, one list

`Fatal error: Enum Foo cannot include magic method __get` and ten siblings.
`zend_verify_enum_magic_methods` has the list, and it is shorter to say what is
*allowed*: `__call`, `__callStatic`, `__invoke`. Everything else --
`__construct`, `__destruct`, `__clone`, `__get`, `__set`, `__unset`, `__isset`,
`__toString`, `__debugInfo`, `__serialize`, `__unserialize`, `__sleep`,
`__wakeup`, `__set_state` -- is refused.

The engine raises this as `E_COMPILE_ERROR`, but the harvest does not see it:
an enum implements `UnitEnum`, so its declaration is deferred to
`ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` and the check runs while linking. That is where php2go
does it, next to the trait and abstract checks.

Four more link-time refusals came with it: an enum redeclaring `cases()`,
`from()` or `tryFrom()`; a non-enum implementing `UnitEnum` or `BackedEnum`; and
extending a final class. And two catchable ones: cloning an enum case
(`Trying to clone an uncloneable object of class Foo`) and giving one a dynamic
property, which is an `Error` rather than the deprecation every other class
gets.

### Duplicate backing values are noticed by the *table*

`enum Foo: int { case Bar = 0; case Baz = 0; }` is not a fatal at declaration.
It is a catchable `Error: Duplicate value in enum Foo for cases Bar and Baz`,
raised when the **backed value table** is built -- so reaching a case by name
and calling `from()` both raise it, and `cases()` does **not**, because that
walks the declarations directly and needs no table.

It also raises *every* time, not once: the table is never successfully built, so
the verdict is remembered rather than the fact of having asked. Memoising "we
already checked" silently passed the second access.

Both of those came from the differential run disagreeing, not from reading the
source -- the `cases()` exemption in particular is not something the code makes
obvious.

`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Which refusal applies depends on *when*

Last round I disabled the asymmetric-visibility check for readonly properties
because it relabelled every readonly error. That was too broad, and the corpus
said so: `initialization_scope.phpt` wants exactly the asymmetric wording. One
probe settled it:

| state | write from outside | write from the declaring scope |
|---|---|---|
| uninitialized | `Cannot modify protected(set) readonly property A::$p from global scope` | allowed |
| initialized | `Cannot modify readonly property A::$p` | `Cannot modify readonly property A::$p` |

Before it holds a value, writing a readonly property is an *initialization*, and
what governs that is the set-visibility a `readonly` declaration implies -- which
is why the message names it. Once it holds one, readonly's own rule takes over
and applies to every scope, including the one that wrote it.

The declaring class is what both messages name, not the class the object is:
`B extends A` reports `A::$p`. `checkReadonlyWrite` had its own copy of the
asymmetric wording using the object's class, which is where the wrong name came
from; that copy is gone and the single check owns the case.

`public readonly` and `public protected(set) readonly` are indistinguishable in
the flags -- both harvest as `readonly protected(set)` -- so the distinction had
to be the initialization state rather than anything the declaration records.

### __clone may reinitialize

PHP 8.3 lets `__clone` write the clone's readonly properties, **once each**, and
only while it runs. A second write to the same property is refused, another
object is unaffected, and the permission does not survive `__clone` returning.
`php.Object.Reinitable` grants it per property and the first write spends it.

## 2026-08-24 — ++ and -- are not + 1 and - 1

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2541 | 2566 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 55.6% | 56.2% |
| `Zend/tests/in-de-crement` passing | 8 | 25 (of 30) |
| `failed` | 1253 | 1228 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 577 | 579 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The increment table

php2go implemented `++` as `+ 1` and `--` as `- 1`. Neither is right, and the
two are not even symmetric. One probe against the engine over every scalar shape
produced the whole table:

| value | `++` | `--` |
|---|---|---|
| null | `int(1)`, silently | **no effect**, Warning "Decrement on type null has no effect, this will change in the next major version of PHP" |
| bool | no effect, Warning | no effect, Warning |
| int / float | +1 | -1 |
| numeric string | numeric ±1, int or float | same |
| alphanumeric string | Perl increment: `"z"`→`"aa"`, `"Az"`→`"Ba"`, `"a9"`→`"b0"` | **no effect**, Deprecated "Decrement on non-numeric string has no effect and is deprecated" |
| string with anything outside `[0-9A-Za-z]` | Deprecated, then incremented anyway (`"0x1A"`→`"0x1B"`) | as above |
| `""` | Deprecated, becomes `"1"` | Deprecated "Decrement on empty string is deprecated as non-numeric", becomes `int(-1)` |
| array / object | TypeError "Cannot increment array" / "Cannot increment Foo" | same |

The Perl increment carries leftwards within a character's own class and, on a
carry off the front, prepends a digit or a letter of the class that *last*
carried -- which is why `"a9"` is `"b0"` and not `"b:"`. `increment_string` in
`zend_operators.c` is the authority; the deprecation for a non-alphanumeric
string is emitted and then the increment happens regardless.

Reading this out of the engine rather than inferring it was worth 17 tests in
one directory.

### A closure's name in a stack trace

Since PHP 8.4 a trace calls a closure `{closure:file:line}`, not `{closure}`.
The compiler already puts that name on the op_array -- the same one `var_dump`
shows -- and the trace was using a literal instead.

## 2026-08-24 — Named arguments

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2533 | 2541 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 55.4% | 55.6% |
| `Zend/tests/named_params` passing | 5 | 10 (of 32) |
| `failed` | 1263 | 1253 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 575 | 577 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Choosing the target

Measuring failures per directory rather than clustering by diff put
`named_params` at 5 of 32 passing -- one PHP 8.0 feature, entirely missing, and
one whose absence also costs tests in `attributes`, `function_arguments` and
elsewhere. That is a better shape than the three-test clusters the diff view has
been surfacing.

### How a named argument arrives

`f(b: 2, a: 1)` compiles to ordinary `SEND_VAL`/`SEND_VAR` oplines whose **op2
is a CONST holding the parameter name** where a positional argument carries its
number. Nothing else marks them.

Which slot a name fills is not known until the callee is, and for a call by name
the callee is not resolved until `DO_FCALL` -- so the resolution happens there,
against `method` / `closure.op` / the unit's function table / the harvested
builtin signature.

Rules the engine settled:

- An unknown name is `Error: Unknown named parameter $x`, *unless* the callee is
  variadic, which takes any name and keeps it as a string key in the variadic
  array.
- A name landing on a position the caller already filled positionally is
  `Error: Named parameter $a overwrites previous argument`.
- A **hole** -- a position skipped by a later named argument -- is
  `ArgumentCountError: f(): Argument #2 ($b) not passed`, which is a different
  diagnostic from passing too few. A hole whose parameter has a default is
  filled with it, and `func_get_args()` then shows the default rather than
  nothing.
- `__call` and `__callStatic` do not resolve names against their own two
  parameters: a named argument keeps its name as a string key inside the array
  they receive.

`Unit.pendingExtraNamed` carries the names a variadic collects from the call
site to the frame about to be created. One slot is enough because nothing else
creates a frame in between, and `runFrame` clears it whether or not it uses it.

Eleven failures remain in that directory, now mostly internal functions --
`array_merge` and friends have their own refusal wording for unknown names, and
several tests need `array_slice`/`array_merge` implemented at all.

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2530 | 2533 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 55.4% | 55.4% |
| `Zend/tests/asymmetric_visibility` passing | 30 | 32 (of 38) |
| `failed` | 1266 | 1263 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 573 | 575 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Two ways for a typed property to hold nothing

Finishing the asymmetric-visibility tail turned into a distinction php2go did
not have. A declared typed property can be empty for two different reasons, and
PHP treats them differently:

| State | `var_dump` | `__get`/`__set`/`__isset` | Reading it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Never assigned | `uninitialized(int)` | not consulted | Error: must not be accessed before initialization |
| `unset()` | `uninitialized(int)` | **consulted** | whatever `__get` returns |

The engine distinguishes them with `IS_PROP_UNINIT` on a slot that exists in
both cases. php2go removed the slot on `unset`, which got the accessors right
and lost the dump. `php.Object.Cleared` now records the removal while the slot
survives holding undef, and the read, isset and write paths ask which state it
is in.

Only a *typed* declared property behaves this way. An untyped one disappears
entirely, as it always did.

Along the way: `instantiate` recorded a property's declared type only when there
was no initializer, so `public int $a = 1` dumped as `uninitialized()` once
unset. The type travels unconditionally now.

### The rest of the asymmetric tail

`__set` answers for a write the set-visibility refused **only** when the slot is
absent -- which, after the above, means explicitly unset rather than merely
uninitialized. And the forward has to consult the magic re-entry guard: without
it, `$this->a = $value` inside `__set` forwards to `__set` again and ends up
creating a dynamic property instead of raising with the inner scope.

Six failures remain in that directory, now mostly about the RW fetch of an
uninitialized typed property.

### Result

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Choosing what to work on

Two candidates were measured before picking. The `var_dump` `&` marker is the
largest-sounding item left, but counting the diffs showed only **10** tests
differ *purely* by `&` -- the other 67 that mention one fail for other reasons
too. Against the invasiveness of holder-counted references, that is a bad trade,
and it stays deferred.

The `offsets/` family (11 tests) needs a resource value kind *and* Reflection,
so it is blocked twice over.

PHP 8.4 asymmetric visibility was the better target: 17 failures in one
directory, one missing concept.

### `public private(set)`

The write half of a property's visibility is a separate pair of flags
(`ZEND_ACC_PRIVATE_SET`, `ZEND_ACC_PROTECTED_SET`), harvested onto
`Property.set_visibility`. A write is allowed from the declaring class exactly,
or -- for `protected(set)` -- from anywhere in its hierarchy.

Three details that had to come from the engine rather than from the feature
description:

- **`readonly` implies `protected(set)`.** Every readonly property carries the
  flag whether or not the source wrote one, so an unconditional asymmetric check
  relabels every readonly error. Readonly's own rule is stricter and runs first.
- **An object-valued property is exempt from the indirect check.**
  `$o->prop->field = x` and even `$r = &$o->prop` are allowed when `prop` holds
  an object: the fetch cannot modify the property itself, so the engine hands
  back a *copy* rather than refusing. The comment in
  `zend_fetch_property_address` says so outright, and this applies to readonly
  as well -- which corrected a check added last round that was too strict.
- **`__set` is not offered a write the set-visibility refused** when the
  property currently holds a value. Forwarding unconditionally passed nothing
  and broke two tests.

Eight failures remain in that directory: the message names the *called* scope
rather than the executing one in two of them, and the interaction with `__set`
on an unset property needs the same "is the slot occupied" distinction the read
path already makes.

### The same builtin, two rules

Last round's `method_exists` fix -- "a private method belongs to the class that
wrote it" -- was right for `method_exists_002` and wrong for `bug50810`, which
expects `method_exists($this, 'privateParentMethod')` to be **true**. Reading
`zend_builtin_functions.c` rather than reasoning about it:

```c
RETURN_BOOL(Z_TYPE_P(klass) == IS_OBJECT
    || !(func->common.fn_flags & ZEND_ACC_PRIVATE) || func->common.scope == ce);
```

Asked about an **object**, visibility is ignored entirely. Asked about a class
**name**, a private method the class inherited rather than declared is excluded.
The engine's own comment calls the second case "shadow properties" and notes the
inconsistency as a TODO -- it is not a rule anyone would derive.

A middle attempt using `zend_check_protected` (which is what the *scope*-aware
branch of `is_callable` uses) passed `bug50810` and broke `method_exists_002` in
three places. The two builtins genuinely differ.

### Unpacking a Traversable into a by-reference parameter

`f(...$generator)` cannot bind a reference -- a Traversable yields values, not
slots -- so PHP passes by value and warns, naming the argument position and the
callee. Wiring it exposed a second gap: `argumentByRef` could not answer for a
plain function call at all, because `ZEND_INIT_FCALL` leaves the callee as a
name and resolves it at `DO_FCALL`. It now consults the unit's function table,
which is also what a first-class callable needed.

### There is no key after PHP_INT_MAX

`[PHP_INT_MAX => 42, "next"]` and `$a[] = x` on such an array are
`Error: Cannot add element to the array as the next element is already
occupied`. php2go wrapped to the negative end instead, producing an element at
`PHP_INT_MIN`. `Array` now records that the append slot is saturated rather than
letting `nextFree` overflow.
