### `$f($x)` where $f is a closure

`function (&$y) { $y = 9; }` called through a variable did not write back. Two
gaps, both about a call whose callee is only known at run time:

- `argumentByRef` looked at `pendingCall.method`, which a Closure does not have
  -- its body hangs off the closure. A first-class callable wrapping a builtin
  (`sort(...)`) had the same hole.
- `ZEND_SEND_VAR_EX` fell through to reading the operand. The `_EX` suffix is
  precisely the compiler saying it could not settle by-reference-ness, so it
  needs the same runtime check `_FUNC_ARG` and `SEND_USER` already had. In the
  engine that is `ARG_SHOULD_BE_SENT_BY_REF(fbc, arg_num)` at the opcode.

That also fixed `fn&(&$x) => $x`: the by-reference *return* path was already
right, and it was the argument that never arrived as a reference.

### References into readonly properties

`setByRef($obj->readonlyProp, 1)` must be
`Error: Cannot indirectly modify readonly property C::$p`, and so must
`$r = &$obj->readonlyProp`. Assigning directly is a different opcode -- that is
what a constructor uses -- so the check belongs on the write-mode object fetch
rather than on assignment.

An enum case's `name` and `value` are readonly without being declared anywhere:
they are built onto the object rather than harvested as properties, so the class
kind decides.

### A leading separator on a function name

`is_callable('\is_string')` and `function_exists('\myf')` are true. The class
tables got this last round; the function table needed the same normalisation.
`function_exists` was also answering only about what this runtime implements,
where the question is about the linked build.

### The `&` marker cannot be a boolean

Probing the engine settled the long-deferred `var_dump` `&` question, and the
answer rules out the cheap version:

```php
$b = [1]; $r = &$b[0]; var_dump($b);   // [0]=> &int(1)
unset($r);                var_dump($b);   // [0]=> int(1)
```

The marker tracks a *live* second holder, and disappears when one goes away --
after `unset`, after a by-reference call returns, after `unset($v)` following a
`foreach ... as &$v`. A `shared` flag set once at the aliasing site would never
clear. Doing it properly needs holder counts that decrement on slot overwrite
and on frame teardown, which is real refcounting of references and a project of
its own.

## 2026-08-23 — Autoloading, and what a closure remembers

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2489 | 2497 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 54.5% | 54.7% |
| `failed` | 1306 | 1297 |
| `unsupported` | 770 | 771 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 563 | 566 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### An autoloader's failure is not "class not found"

`autoload` swallowed whatever a callback did wrong:

```go
if _, err := in.dispatch(ctx, unit, target, depth); err != nil {
    return nil, false          // <- the throw, or the exit(), vanishes here
}
```

An autoloader that throws must propagate the throw, and one that calls `exit()`
must stop the request; both were being turned into "the class does not exist",
which then produced a *different* error further along. `resolveClass` and
`autoload` now return an error, and the six call sites raise it. The refactor
was small because `findClass` -- the side-effect-free lookup -- is what most of
the runtime uses.

### The harvest knows classes the program cannot see yet

`enum_exists('Quux', false)` was true for an enum declared *inside* an
autoloader closure that had never run. The harvest carries every class in the
file, and `findClass` finds them all, but a class the compiler could not bind
early does not exist until its `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` executes.

`classDeclared` answers the difference: a class with no declaring opline
anywhere in the file was bound at compile time and always exists; one with an
opline exists only after `bindDeclaration` has recorded it. Finding the oplines
means scanning every op_array in the unit -- including closures, methods and
property hooks -- for the two declare opcodes, whose numbers come from the
manifest rather than being written down.

Only the `*_exists` builtins consult it so far. Widening it to `findClass`
itself would be more faithful and is a bigger change.

### A closure remembers the call that made it

```php
class A { public static function f() { return function () { var_dump(static::class); }; } }
class B extends A {}
(B::f())();     // B
```

The closure captured its declaring scope but not the *called* scope, so
`static::` reported A. `closure` now carries `called` alongside `class`, set
from the creating frame; `bindTo` recomputes it the way `zend_create_closure`
does -- from the new instance when there is one, from the new scope otherwise.

## 2026-08-23 — Four small things the corpus kept asking for

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2472 | 2489 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 54.1% | 54.5% |
| `failed` | 1322 | 1306 |
| `unsupported` | 771 | 770 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 560 | 563 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

No single family left is large. This round took four unrelated clusters that the
re-clustering kept surfacing.

### var_dump of a Closure

A Closure has no properties. The engine gives the class a `get_debug_info`
handler instead, and its shape is specific enough that guessing would not have
worked:

- A closure *written* as one is described by `name` (`{closure:file:line}`),
  `file` and `line`.
- A closure made from an existing function -- `f(...)`, `Closure::fromCallable`
  -- is a *fake* closure and is described by `function` instead, which is
  `Class::method` when it has a scope.
- `static` holds the `use` variables, and only when there are any. Their order
  is the op_array's static-variable table, not the captured map -- which is why
  the map alone could not have produced it.
- `this` is the bound object; `parameter` maps `&$name` to `<required>` or
  `<optional>`, and is absent when the function takes none.

`dumper.properties` is the right hook: returning the debug array with
`described = true` also gets the label rendering right, since a closure's keys
carry no visibility annotation.

### self:: and parent:: forward late static binding

`parent::who()` inside `B::who()`, called as `D::who()`, reports `D`. php2go was
rebinding `static::` to the class the call named, so it reported `A`. A call
written as `self::`, `parent::` or `static::` *forwards* the caller's late
static binding; only a call naming a class outright rebinds. The compiler
encodes the keyword as a `ZEND_FETCH_CLASS_*` code in an unused operand, so the
distinction is available at the opline.

### Some pairs have no ordering at all

`E::A < E::B` is false. So is `>`, `>=` and `<=` -- all four. An enum's compare
handler is `zend_objects_not_comparable`, and `ZEND_UNCOMPARABLE` is `1`, so
`< 0` and `<= 0` are both false; since the compiler writes `a > b` as `b < a`,
refusing in one place covers all four directions.

The same applies to two objects of different classes. Two objects of the *same*
class still compare by properties, and the identical object compares equal --
`$a >= $a` is true even for an enum.

php2go's `Compare` had no object case at all, so everything fell through to a
numeric comparison of 1 against 1 and answered "equal".

### A leading namespace separator

`defined('\ns\ok')` is true. The constant and class tables are keyed without
the leading separator, and `zend_lookup_class` strips it; php2go did not, so
every fully qualified name written with one missed.

## 2026-08-23 — Declaration-time checks

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2452 | 2472 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 53.7% | 54.1% |
| `failed` | 1342 | 1322 |
| `unsupported` | 771 | 771 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 557 | 560 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### An abstract declaration is a requirement, not an implementation

`zend_verify_abstract_class` runs when a class is linked, so it belongs at
`ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` alongside the trait composition checks added earlier. The
first version reported 19 false positives, and each one taught a rule:

- **The implementation can be anywhere in the hierarchy, and the nearest
  *declaration* is not necessarily it.** `class B extends P { use T; }` where
  `T` declares `abstract function common()` and `P` implements it: the trait
  ranks above the parent in method lookup, so `resolveMethod` returned the
  abstract one and the check called it unimplemented.

  This turned out to be a bug in `resolveMethod` itself rather than in the
  check. It now keeps walking past an abstract declaration and only falls back
  to one if nothing in the hierarchy provides a body — which also fixed four
  separate `Cannot call abstract method` failures that had nothing to do with
  the new check.

- **A plain property satisfies an interface's hook requirement.** `interface I {
  public $prop { set; } }` implemented by `public $prop;` is fine: the interface
  asks that writing work, not that a hook exist.

- **Something that cannot be made abstract gets a different message.** An enum,
  or a class already declared abstract, gets `must implement N abstract private
  method(s)` rather than the `contains N abstract methods and must therefore be
  declared abstract` form.

One false positive is left, `attributes/override/gh12189_6`, which needs trait
aliases (`Foo::doStuff as doOtherStuff`) that the harvest does not carry.

### Redeclaration needs to know what was there first

`Cannot redeclare class A (previously declared in %s:%d)` needs two things the
IR did not have: the first declaration's *site* and its *kind*.

The site is now harvested (`ce->info.user.line_start` and the filename). The
kind is subtler, because the class table keeps only the last of a repeated name
while the message names the first: `interface A {} trait A {}` says
"Cannot redeclare **interface** A". `Load` therefore keeps the first harvested
entry for every repeated name alongside the last.

Whether a `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` is a redeclaration at all is decided by counting.
An unconditional declaration is bound when the file compiles and has no opline
of its own, so `class A {} class A {}` produces *two* harvested classes and
*one* opline — meaning a name the harvest saw twice is already taken when its
single opline runs. A name seen once is free until then, which is what makes
`function test() { class A {} } test(); test();` fatal on the second call.

`class_alias` onto a taken name is a *Warning*, not a fatal, and names the kind
of the class being aliased rather than the one already holding the name.

## 2026-08-23 — Property hooks

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2398 | 2452 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 52.5% | 53.7% |
| `Zend/tests/property_hooks` passing | 87 | 138 |
| `failed` | 1397 | 1342 |
| `unsupported` | 770 | 771 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 552 | 557 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Where a hook lives

`public $p { get { ... } }` compiles the body into an op_array named
`$p::get`, and that op_array is **not** in the class's function table -- it
hangs off `zend_property_info.hooks[]`, which is why `get_class_methods` does
not list it and why collecting the class's methods found nothing. The harvester
now reads `hooks[ZEND_PROPERTY_HOOK_GET]` and `[SET]` directly, along with
`ZEND_ACC_VIRTUAL`, and they travel on `Property` rather than among the methods.

A hooked property is *backed* when a hook mentions `$this->p`, and virtual
otherwise. That is the engine's decision, recorded as a flag; inferring it from
the body would be guesswork.

### The recursion rule is a prototype comparison, not a pointer comparison

Inside a hook, `$this->p` reaches the backing store rather than calling the hook
again -- but only *directly* inside it. A hook that calls a method which touches
the property does re-enter, and PHP lets that recurse until the stack gives out.

The first implementation compared the property message identity and immediately
stack-overflowed on

```php
class A { public $p = 1 { get { return $this->p * 2; } } }
class B extends A { public $p { get { return parent::$p::get() + 100; } } }
```

`zend_is_in_hook` compares `prop_info->prototype == parent_info->prototype`, so
a subclass redeclaring a hooked property shares the parent's identity. The
equivalent here is the class that *first* declared the property, and comparing
`(property name, root class)` makes the case above return `int(100)` as the
engine does -- B's storage is untouched, so A's hook reads null.

That is the same "root declaring class" idea protected-method access needed last
round. Two unrelated Zend rules, one shape.

### What is wired

`FETCH_OBJ_R`/`_IS`, `ASSIGN_OBJ`, `ASSIGN_OBJ_OP`, the four `*_INC_OBJ`/
`*_DEC_OBJ` forms, `ISSET_ISEMPTY_PROP_OBJ`, `UNSET_OBJ`, and
`ZEND_INIT_PARENT_PROPERTY_HOOK_CALL`. The last one needed a stand-in for the
trampoline the engine builds when the parent declares the property but no hook
of that kind: the call reaches the backing store directly.

Rules that are not what they look like:

- A get-only property is read-only only when it is **virtual**. A backed one
  writes its storage -- the implicit set -- and `backed_implicit_set.phpt` is
  exactly that distinction.
- A virtual property is not one of the object's properties: no slot, absent
  from `var_dump` and from a `foreach`.
- `unset($o->p)` on a hooked property is `Error: Cannot unset hooked property`,
  never a removal.
- `isset()` runs the get hook and asks whether the result is null.

### Remaining in that directory

49 failures left, no longer one family: abstract-method declaration checks from
hooked interfaces (3), by-reference hooks, `get_mangled_object_vars`, hooked
`ArrayAccess`, and the Reflection surface. The next largest thing in the corpus
as a whole is now elsewhere.

## 2026-08-23 — What a class is made of

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2378 | 2398 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 52.0% | 52.5% |
| `failed` | 1411 | 1397 |
| `unsupported` | 776 | 770 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 549 | 552 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Trait members other than methods did not exist

`resolveMethod` has always consulted a class's traits directly rather than
copying their methods in -- that is what keeps `self::` inside a trait method
naming the *using* class. Properties and constants had no equivalent, so a class
using a trait simply did not have them: `$this->hello` warned, `property_exists`
said no, `C::K` was undefined.

They cannot come from the harvest. A class that uses a trait is not linked when
the file compiles, so the engine has not copied anything into its tables yet.
`Unit.properties` and `Unit.constants` fold them in on first use, recursing so a
trait that uses a trait works, and rewriting the declaring class to the using
one -- which is what makes `var_dump` print `["world":"C":private]` rather than
naming the trait, and what gives each using class its own storage for a trait's
static property.

Constants have an asymmetry worth remembering: a class that uses a trait sees
its constants, but the trait itself does not expose them. `Trait::K` is
`Error: Cannot access trait constant T::K directly`, and `defined('Trait::K')`
is false rather than throwing -- `defined()` asks silently, so a refused fetch
is "not defined" while a gap in this runtime still propagates.

### Engine methods were invisible to the reflective builtins

`php2go_collect_methods` skips anything that is not a `ZEND_USER_FUNCTION`,
because an internal method has no op_array to harvest. That was right for the
interpreter and wrong for `method_exists`, `get_class_methods` and
`is_callable`, which ask whether the *linked build* has a method, not whether
this runtime implements one. `Class.engine_methods` now carries their names,
visibility, staticness and abstractness. Calling one that is not modelled still
reports as a gap, so the metric stays honest.

Two special cases came out of `zend_builtin_functions.c` rather than from
guessing:

- `Closure::__invoke` is not in Closure's function table at all -- the engine
  answers a call on it with a trampoline -- and `method_exists` has an explicit
  branch returning true for it.
- A private method belongs to the class that wrote it. `method_exists('Child',
  'privateParentMethod')` is false even though the lookup walks straight past
  it, which is the `!(flags & ZEND_ACC_PRIVATE) || scope == ce` test.

### class_alias and instanceof

`class_alias` already shared the class entry under a second name, but
`instanceOf` compared spellings, so `$a instanceof Alias` was false. Comparing
the resolved entry by identity fixes it; the name comparison stays for a name
nothing declares.

### Next: property hooks

Re-clustering put PHP 8.4 property hooks at the top of what is left --
`Zend/tests/property_hooks` is 198 tests, 87 passing, and none of the passes
involve a hook actually running. There is no support at all: a hook is compiled
as a method named `$prop::get` on the class, hidden from `get_class_methods`,
and neither the hook op_arrays nor the property's virtual flag are harvested.
That is the largest coherent family remaining and the next thing to build.

## 2026-08-23 — Visibility, and composing traits

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2344 | 2378 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 51.3% | 52.0% |
| `failed` | 1445 | 1411 |
| `unsupported` | 776 | 776 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 541 | 549 |

Same corpus and command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### Clustering the failures needs the EXPECTF rules

With `unsupported` now dominated by four large subsystems, the work is in
`failed`, and finding structure there means grouping 1400 diffs by their first
differing line. A first attempt compared lines literally and produced nonsense
clusters: an `EXPECTF` line like `Fatal error: Uncaught Exception in %s:%d`
"differs" from every real path, so tests were grouped by their first
*placeholder* line rather than their first real divergence. Translating each
expected line to a regex before comparing changed the top of the list
completely. The clustering script lives in the job's scratch directory, not the
tree, but the lesson is worth keeping: a clustering script that does not
implement the harness's matching rules invents its own clusters.

### is_callable had no idea about visibility

It answered "does the method exist", which is wrong three ways: a private or
inaccessible method is not callable, an abstract one is not callable, and an
inaccessible one *is* callable when the class has the magic forwarder that
would answer for it -- `__call` when the callable named an object, `__callStatic`
when it named a class. The two-element array form did not go through any check
at all; it resolved through `dynamicTarget`, which is the call path.

The protected rule needed more than "same hierarchy". `zend_check_protected`
runs against the class that *first* declared the method -- the engine's
prototype pointer -- so `B1::ma` overriding `A::ma` stays reachable from a
sibling `B2 extends A`. A private parent method is a different method, so the
walk up stops at one. Without that, `access_modifiers_009` disagrees on exactly
one of its nine lines.

Static properties had no visibility check either: `A::$priv` read from anywhere
returned the value. `isset()` answers false rather than raising, which is the
same split the instance-property opcodes already make.

And `$obj->staticMethod()` was binding `$this`. It is a legal call, but the
method is static and `$this` is unset inside it.

### Traits are composed when the declaration runs

php2go does not flatten a trait's members into the composing class -- looking
them up through the trait is what keeps `self::` inside a trait method naming
the using class -- so none of the engine's composition checks happened at all.
They belong at `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS`, which is where the engine links a
trait-using class, and that placement is load-bearing: `constant_005` expects
its fatal *after* the `PRE-CLASS-GUARD` the script printed.

Implemented: `use` of something that is not a trait, and the constant and
property conflict checks. Two definitions conflict unless visibility, finality
(constants) or staticness (properties) and the value all agree. Reading
`zend_inheritance.c` settled two things guessing would not have:

- Inheritance runs *before* trait binding, so an inherited constant is one of
  the halves a trait can collide with, and the message names the class that
  declared it (`BaseClass2 and TestTrait2 ... in the composition of DerivedClass2`).
- Which name comes first is `find_first_constant_definition`: the composing
  class if the collision is with its own member, otherwise the trait that
  contributed it. That is why `constant_009` says `Trait1 and Trait2` while
  `constant_011` says `Trait2 and Trait1`.

`in.fatal` is new: a fatal error is not an exception. It writes its text to the
script's output and returns an `exitTermination`, so shutdown functions still
run and nothing can catch it.

### Closure binding was four rules short

`do_closure_bind` is short and every line of it mattered:

- The scope argument defaults to the *string* `"static"`, which means keep the
  current scope. Omitting it and passing `null` are different requests: null
  unscopes. php2go treated a null scope as "not found, leave it alone".
- The instance being bound never sets the scope. It sets what `static::`
  resolves to, which is a different field.
- Binding an instance to a static closure warns and yields null.
- Unbinding `$this` from a closure that *uses* `$this` warns and yields null.
  That needed `ZEND_ACC_USES_THIS` harvested onto the op_array; the compiler
  already records it.

## 2026-08-23 — Constant expressions, and a stale class entry

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2294 | 2344 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 50.2% | 51.3% |
| `failed` | 1452 | 1445 |
| `unsupported` | 819 | 776 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 533 | 541 |

Same corpus, same command both times:
`go run ./cmd/php2phpt third_party/php-src/Zend/tests`.

### The differential suite was crashing, and it was not the new code

Adding four constant-expression cases made `go test ./runtime/interp/ -run
Differential` segfault inside cgo, at an address that was clearly ASCII text.
Every case passed on its own through `php2eval`, and the crash moved or vanished
whenever the binary was relaunched — twice the "fix" was a build failure being
read as a pass, which is worth remembering: always check that the run compiled
before concluding a crash is gone.

Bisecting by case index (a temporary `P2G_SKIP`/`P2G_PICK` env hook in the test)
narrowed it to a pair, and `gdb` on the test binary named the frame:

```
zend_update_class_constants () from libphp.so
object_init_ex ()
ZEND_NEW_SPEC_CONST_UNUSED_HANDLER ()
```

`new Foo` in one case was finding the *previous* case's `Foo`, freed by
`Engine.Reset`. A minimal reproduction narrowed it further: the poison needs a
class constant that forward-references another constant of the same class —
`class Foo { const A = self::B; const B = "ok"; } var_dump(Foo::A);` — and a
later class of the same name. Reversing the two constants, or renaming the
class, makes it go away.

The cause is the interned class-name string's **CE cache**. An interned name
carries a per-request slot (`IS_STR_CLASS_NAME_MAP_PTR`), and
`zend_lookup_class_ex` returns whatever is in it before consulting the class
table. Only the deferred-constant path does a by-name class lookup at runtime;
everything else goes through the op_array's own run-time cache, which dies with
the op_array. `Reset` deleted the class from `CG(class_table)` and left the
cache slot pointing at the freed entry.

`php2go_reset_user_symbols` now clears the slot before the entry is destroyed.
The symptom was visible without a debugger too: after `Reset`,
`class_exists("Foo", false)` was still `true` while `get_declared_classes()` did
not list it.

### Constant expressions, continued

The AST harvest from the previous round now covers comparison and logical nodes
(`ZEND_AST_GREATER`, `GREATER_EQUAL`, `AND`, `OR`, `UNARY_OP` — the parser has no
greater-than opcode, so those are separate node kinds with the operands
swapped), property fetches (`PROP`, `NULLSAFE_PROP`) and `new` (`NEW`,
`ARG_LIST`).

Property fetch in a constant expression is allowed only on an enum case —
`A::Case->value` is the whole point of the 8.3 feature. Any other object is
`Error: Fetching properties on non-enums in constant expressions is not
allowed`, and a non-object is the ordinary "Attempt to read property" warning.
That error has to reach the program as a throw, so `evalExpr`,
`constantLiteral`, `exprClassName` and `classConstant` all grew a third result:
a value, an unresolvable shape (an honest gap), or a PHP error.

An unresolved node now carries its numeric kind through the IR, so a corpus run
reports `constant initializer for A_prop (ast:513)` instead of only naming the
constant. That is what identified every remaining shape in one pass.

### Three follow-on bugs the new machinery exposed

- `static $s = <expression>` is not in the static-variable table at all since
  PHP 8.3: it compiles to `BIND_INIT_STATIC_OR_JMP`, the initializer's oplines,
  then `BIND_STATIC` **with op2**. The jump half was implemented; the store half
  ignored op2, so every computed static read as null.
- An enum case's declared value can be an expression (`case C = I::A;`). The
  harvester's `php2go_enum_case_backing` insisted on a `ZEND_AST_ZVAL` child and
  reported "no value", which surfaced as `TypeError: Case D of backed enum B
  must have a value`.
- Errors raised while evaluating an initializer were reaching `frame.raise`
  unmaterialized, so `TypeError: Enum case type string does not match enum
  backing type int` escaped a `catch (Error $e)` that should have caught it.

### Undefined constants in initializers are the program's error

`function f($a = bar)` inside a namespace must throw `Undefined constant
"Foo\bar"`, with the same global-namespace fallback the `FETCH_CONSTANT` opcode
does; the flag is on the harvested node (`IS_CONSTANT_UNQUALIFIED_IN_NAMESPACE`,
`0x800`) rather than in the spelling. `Nope::A` where `Nope` does not exist is
`Class "Nope" not found`, not a missing constant.

Keeping that honest needed a distinction inside `classConstant`: a constant that
is genuinely not declared returns "not found", while one whose initializer the
harvest could not read returns an `UnsupportedError`. Collapsing the two would
have dressed a gap up as a plausible PHP error and quietly raised the pass rate.

### Also

`defined()` and `constant()` accept `"Class::CONST"`, which neither did; the
`ZEND_DEFINED` opcode had the same hole.

## 2026-08-23 — Callables, and the harvester's contract

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2251 | 2263 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 49.3% | 49.5% |
| differential cases vs the engine | 526 | 529 |

### Two kinds of callable that were not

An object whose class declares `__invoke` is callable -- `$obj()`,
`Closure::fromCallable($obj)`, `call_user_func($obj, ...)`, `array_map($obj, ...)`
and `is_callable($obj)` all go through `dynamicTarget`, which had no case for a
plain object at all.

`$obj->whatever(...)` on a class with `__call` makes a closure over `__call`,
not over a method that does not exist. The pending call already knew to forward
the name; the closure did not, so invoking it passed the caller's arguments
straight to `__call` and hit `Too few arguments`.

A reference into a string offset is refused with its own wording -- `Cannot
create references to/from string offsets`, not `Cannot use string offset as an
array`. The compiler marks the fetch: `ZEND_FETCH_REF` in `extended_value`.

And destructuring something that is not an array assigns null to every target
rather than failing, by reference as well.

### Three attempts at making the engine work harder, three crashes

Folding a deferred class constant looked much safer than binding classes: it
evaluates one zval in place with `zval_update_constant_ex` and touches no
tables, and everything a class constant can refer to is already compiled. It
segfaulted on the corpus like the other two.

That is now a pattern worth naming: **the harvester's contract is compile and
read**. Every attempt to make the engine do more than that during a harvest --
link a class, bind a slot, fold an AST -- has corrupted memory on a full corpus
run while working fine on a single file. The engine's own entry points carry
bookkeeping the harvester does not replicate, and the failure mode is memory
corruption rather than a wrong answer.

Each crash also left a `<test>.php` behind, which then failed that test
permanently until cleaned up by hand -- three times now. The grader no longer
refuses when the file exists: it saves the content, overwrites, and puts it
back, so a killed run costs nothing.

## 2026-08-23 — __debugInfo, and a target that turned out not to be one

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2241 | 2251 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 49.0% | 49.3% |
| differential cases vs the engine | 524 | 526 |

### __debugInfo makes a dump a method call

`var_dump` and `print_r` show whatever `__debugInfo()` returns instead of the
real property table -- `var_export` does not -- and what it returns is an
ordinary array, so those entries carry no visibility annotation.

That means dumping can run user code, which a ctx-only builtin cannot do. The
renderers moved onto a `dumper` that holds the interpreter, and `var_dump` and
`print_r` moved into the interpreter-aware builtins.

Most of the family (8 of 10 tests) is the *failure* case: a `__debugInfo` that
returns a non-array is `Fatal error: __debuginfo() must return an array`, and it
replaces the dump rather than appearing after it. Since the renderer builds the
whole string before writing, the fatal is held on the dumper and written in the
dump's place.

### Destructors: looked at, and left alone

~9 tests expect `__destruct` output. Request-shutdown destruction is
deterministic and would be easy -- keep the objects whose class declares one and
call them after the shutdown functions. But the tests that need it mostly need
the *other* half: a destructor firing when the last reference goes away, which
is refcounting, which Go's collector does not do. Implementing only the shutdown
half would put the output in the wrong place rather than merely omitting it.

Worth recording precisely rather than attempting: it is the same blocker as
`var_dump`'s `&` marker, and both go away together if the value model ever grows
holder counts.

## 2026-08-23 — Anonymous classes, recursion depth, and cleaning up after a crash

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2232 | 2241 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 48.9% | 49.0% |
| errored (a Go error escaped) | 8 | 4 |

### An anonymous class is displayed up to its NUL

`class@anonymous` is stored under a name with a NUL and the definition site
appended -- `class@anonymous\0/path/file.php:2$0`. PHP prints class names with
C's `%s`, which stops at the NUL, so *every* user-visible form shows just
`class@anonymous`: var_dump's header and its property labels, print_r,
var_export, and every diagnostic naming a class. `get_class()` still returns the
whole 31-byte string, NUL included, which is how the two can be told apart.

Go's `%s` does not truncate, so this needed an explicit `php.DisplayName` at
about fifteen formatting sites. Worth 5 tests, and it removes a whole class of
almost-right output.

### The depth limit was below what PHP programs actually do

`maxDepth` was 512, chosen to stop runaway recursion from taking the process
down. The corpus has a test that recurses 3000 deep and expects to finish; Go's
stacks grow on demand, so 8192 is affordable and still bounds a runaway.

That exposed a real bug behind one of the "runaways": `f($a[])` where `f` takes
its argument by value is a *read*, and an append has nothing to read --
`Cannot use [] for reading`. Without the error the test recursed until the limit
caught it. The check belongs on the by-value branch of `FETCH_DIM_FUNC_ARG`,
which is the only place that knows the fetch turned out to be a read.

### Two tests were poisoned by an earlier crash

`bug48667_1` and `bug80126` reported "would overwrite existing ...php". The
grader writes each test's source beside the `.phpt` and removes it afterwards;
the segfaulting harvester experiment killed the process mid-run and left two
behind. The guard did its job -- it refused rather than clobbering a file it did
not write -- but the leftovers then failed those two tests permanently. Removed.

## 2026-08-23 — A successful compile can still print

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2196 | 2232 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 48.1% | 48.9% |
| failed | 1597 | 1564 |
| errored (a Go error escaped) | 12 | 8 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 519 | 521 |

### The harness was throwing away output again

`php2go_compile_file` captures whatever the compiler printed, and `CompileFile`
used it **only when the compile failed**. But a compile that succeeds can print
too: `"${name}"` in a string is deprecated at compile time, as is implementing
`Serializable`. That text is the program's output and comes before anything the
program itself prints.

The diagnostic now rides on the op_array, through the IR (`Unit.compile_diagnostic`)
so a serialized unit keeps it, and `RunUnit` writes it before executing. Worth
**32 tests** — the third time this session that the largest available win was
output the harness had discarded rather than behaviour the interpreter lacked.

This one is invisible to the differential oracle: `zend_eval_string` does not
emit compile-time deprecations the way `zend_compile_file` does, so the engine
side of a `php2eval` comparison prints nothing. It was verified against a real
`.phpt` instead.

### Asking the engine to link classes: tried, and backed out

The largest remaining family is the declaration-time checks — `must be
compatible with` (55), trait composition conflicts (31), abstract-method counts,
redeclaration. The engine defers binding to `ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` whenever an
interface or a later-declared parent is involved, so a harvest that stops at
compilation never sees them, and reimplementing Zend's variance rules in Go
risks inventing fatals for valid code.

The obvious move is to ask the engine: bind the deferred classes during the
harvest, capture what it says, and replay that at `DECLARE_CLASS`. It works on a
single file — `argument_restriction_005` passes — and it **corrupts engine
memory across a corpus run**: a bare `zend_do_link_class` segfaults, and going
through `zend_bind_class_in_slot` with a hand-built name/definition-key pair
turns it into an out-of-memory abort instead.

Backed out entirely. A harvester that corrupts memory is worse than a gap: it
can produce silently wrong IR, which is the one failure mode the whole approach
is built to avoid. What is now known is recorded in TODO.md so the next attempt
starts from it rather than from scratch.

### Class references without a class are errors, not gaps

`self::`, `parent::` and `static::` outside a class were `fmt.Errorf`, so they
escaped as *Go* errors — the `errored` bucket, not even a catchable PHP error.
They are the program's mistake, and PHP words each by its keyword: `Cannot
access "static" when no class scope is active`. Ten call sites now route the
failure through `f.raise`, so a `try`/`catch` around one catches it. `errored`
fell from 12 to 8.

### The executing scope belongs on the context

`self`, `parent` and `static` in a callable name something only the executing
scope knows, and using them there has been deprecated since 8.2 — the
deprecation fires wherever the callable is *resolved*, `is_callable` included.

Resolving them needed the scope in `dynamicTarget`, which has no frame. The
first attempt read it off the call stack, which is right only when asked from
inside a builtin: at an opcode the innermost pushed frame is the call to the
*current* function, whose recorded scope is its caller's. `Ctx` now tracks the
executing class directly, set and restored by `execFrame`. That is strictly
better than the stack reading — a builtin still sees its caller's scope, because
a builtin does not push one — so `StackFrame.Scope` is gone again.

## 2026-08-23 — The array pointer, engine classes, and cleaning up after the offset work

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2154 | 2196 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 47.1% | 48.1% |
| unsupported | 838 | 764 |
| failed | 1565 | 1597 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 502 | 519 |

All 519 differential cases match; `gofmt`, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...`
are clean.

### The internal array pointer

`current`/`key`/`next`/`prev`/`reset`/`end` needed real state on `php.Array`. It
indexes *buckets* rather than counting live elements, so an element unset behind
the pointer does not shift what it points at — which is what PHP's own hash
position does.

Two behaviours are easy to get wrong and both are observable: once the pointer
runs off either end it **stays** there (only `reset()` and `end()`, which place
it absolutely, bring it back), and `key()` answers `null` where the others
answer `false`, because `false` is a perfectly good array key.

The corpus caught an index-out-of-range panic within minutes: the "skip deleted
buckets" loop ran before the range check, and the pointer parks at -1 after
running off the front. A unit test would not have found that; running 4,966
programs did.

### func_get_args comes off the frame, and sometimes off the stack

Inside a function these are their own opcodes (`ZEND_FUNC_NUM_ARGS`,
`ZEND_FUNC_GET_ARGS`) and read the executing frame. At global scope the compiler
emits an ordinary call instead, so the builtins have to exist too — and
`func_get_arg` is *always* a call, so it reads the enclosing function's frame off
the call stack: the frame below its own, since the call to `func_get_arg` was
pushed like any other. That is the same trick `get_object_vars` uses for the
calling scope.

### ArrayIterator and ArrayObject

Engine classes with no harvested bodies, so their behaviour is supplied in Go
the way `Generator`'s and `Closure`'s are. One `arrayStore` covers both: they
differ only in that `ArrayIterator` *is* the iterator while `ArrayObject` hands
out a fresh one from `getIterator`.

Four dispatch points had to learn about them — instantiation, method calls,
`ArrayAccess`, and `newObjectIterator` — because each had a whitelist or a
`resolveMethod` that finds nothing for a class with no bodies. `count()` needed
the same: a `Countable` counts itself, which the ctx-only builtin cannot ask it
to do, so both the specialized `ZEND_COUNT` opcode and the call path now route
through a `countOf` that handles the engine classes and user `Countable`s alike.

### Cleaning up after the offset work

The previous round's offset diagnostics were too eager in three places, and the
corpus found all three:

- `isset($str[$nonNumeric])` **must not raise**. `isset()` and `??` never do —
  an offset the string cannot use simply is not set. Two paths needed it: the
  quiet `FETCH_DIM_IS` and `ISSET_ISEMPTY_DIM_OBJ`'s own string branch, which had
  been reading the index with a bare `.Int()` and so answered true for
  `isset($arr['exists']['nope'])`.
- `unset($str[$a][$b])` says `Cannot unset string offsets`, not `Cannot use
  string offset as an array`. The wording follows the *fetch type*, again.
- `[$closure, '__invoke']` is callable. `dynamicTarget` resolved a
  `[object, method]` pair through the class table, where `Closure` has no
  methods to find.

### Also

- `$this` in a static context is a catchable `Error`, not an interpreter gap.
- A Traversable unpacks into an array literal (`[...$gen]`), matching the
  argument-list spread added last round.
- `Generator::throw`, `trigger_error`/`user_error`, `Closure::__invoke`, and
  compound assignment through an `ArrayAccess` (`$o[$k] .= x`).

## 2026-08-23 — Serialization, iteration, and a parameter list that had grown too long

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2119 | 2154 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 46.4% | 47.1% |
| unsupported | 894 | 838 |
| failed | 1544 | 1565 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 488 | 502 |

All 502 differential cases match; `gofmt`, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...`
are clean.

### serialize encodes visibility in the property name

The format is small enough to write out, but one part is not guessable: a
non-public property is stored under its *mangled* name — `"\0*\0b"` for
protected, `"\0Class\0c"` for private — and the class name in the object header
is followed by `:` where a plain string is followed by `;`. Both had to be
handled specially in the reader, and `%q` is the wrong tool for writing any of
it: the length delimits the bytes, so a quote or a NUL inside needs no escaping
and must not get one.

`unserialize` reports its failure at the offset the innermost value that could
not be read *started*, not wherever the scan gave up. Rewinding on the way out
gets that right for a top-level value and wrong for a nested one — the outer
container unwinds over the inner offset — so the offset is recorded once, at the
first failure, and left alone after that.

### var_dump annotates a property with its visibility

`["b":protected]` and `["c":"C":private]`, and print_r's `[b:protected]` /
`[c:C:private]`. That needed the declaration on the object rather than in the
class table, since `var_dump` is a plain builtin with no unit — the same
`Object.Declared` map that already carried the type of an uninitialized
property. It is now populated for *every* declared property, not only the typed
ones. print_r did not handle objects at all before this.

### Traversable drives foreach, `yield from` and argument unpacking

One `newObjectIterator` covers all three. An `IteratorAggregate` hands over
whatever `getIterator()` returns, which may be a generator, an array, or another
aggregate, so it recurses; an `Iterator` is driven by ordinary method calls, and
the order — rewind once, then next before every element after the first — is
observable from the implementation.

`FE_RESET` has to know whether the loop runs at all, which for an object means
*pulling* the first element. The iterator therefore carries a one-element
lookahead, or `FE_FETCH` would pull a second time and drop the first.

`Generator::throw` raises at the yield the generator is suspended on rather than
at the call site, which is what lets a try/catch inside the body catch it. It is
delivered by parking the exception on the generator and having `advance` raise
it through the suspended frame before resuming.

### ZEND_ASSERT_CHECK, and the parameter list

The standing deferral was that the opcode branches on `zend.assertions`, which
was not harvested, so treating it as a no-op would be right for this build and
silently wrong for another. Harvesting it settled that — and forced the
question the deferral had been avoiding: `EncodeManifest` already took eight
positional arguments, and the ninth would have put two `int64` build settings
next to each other, where a swap compiles cleanly and produces wrong IR. It now
takes an `ir.Harvest` struct.

### Where to go next

`ReflectionClass` still leads the blockers at 265, but the earlier note stands:
those tests are mostly PHP 8.4 lazy objects, not the reflection API. After that
the list has flattened into `Fiber` (106), `fopen` (36), `WeakMap` (28) and a
long tail of engine classes.

In the `failed` bucket the shape is unchanged: 375 tests produce no output at
all and 353 are missing a Fatal error, both dominated by the declaration-time
checks the harvest cannot carry.

## 2026-08-23 — Offsets, callables, and a deferred item tested and re-deferred

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2089 | 2119 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 45.7% | 46.4% |
| unsupported | 955 | 894 |
| failed | 1513 | 1544 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 476 | 488 |

`failed` rising while `unsupported` falls by more is the usual shape. All 488
differential cases match; `gofmt`, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` are clean.

### Indexing diagnoses by what the value is

`dimensionRead` returned null for anything that was not an array or a string,
silently. PHP has a diagnostic for each case, and the wording follows the
value's own type name — so a boolean reads as `true` or `false`, never `bool`:

- Reading an offset of null, an int, a float or a boolean is
  `Trying to access array offset on <type>`.
- An array or object *as* an offset is `Cannot access offset of type <T> on
  array` — a TypeError, so `dimensionRead` had to become fallible.
- A string offset that is not already an integer is cast, and the cast is
  itself reported (`String offset cast occurred`), except for a string that is
  not a number at all, which PHP refuses.
- Writing through something that cannot hold elements is worded three ways:
  `Cannot use a scalar value as an array`, `Cannot use string offset as an
  array`, and `[] operator not supported for strings` for an append.
- Truncating a fractional float to a key loses information, and PHP says so
  wherever the key is used — read, write, `isset`, `unset`,
  `array_key_exists`. That one belongs in `arrayKey` itself, which therefore
  had to take a context.

`quoteKey` was reporting the *index* rather than the key it became, so a null
index printed as `Undefined array key ` instead of `Undefined array key ""`.

### call_user_func's dynamic forms were never implemented

`call_user_func("f", 3)` worked, which hid the gap: the compiler folds a literal
call into a direct one, so the builtin only ever sees the dynamic forms — a
callable in a variable, a `[target, method]` pair, a Closure — and there was no
builtin. Same for `call_user_func_array`.

### A builtin can now see the calling scope

`get_object_vars` had a comment saying visibility depends on the calling scope,
"which a builtin cannot see", and returned the public view. It can see it now:
the stack frame pushed for the call already records where the call came from, so
adding the caller's class to `php.StackFrame` was enough. `get_class_vars` needs
the same thing, and additionally hands its properties out in a *different order*
from `var_dump` — the class's own first, then inherited, then the statics, which
is `properties_info`'s insertion order rather than the offset order the harvest
imposes.

### ZEND_FREE was writing through references

`list()` by reference — `[&$p, &$q] = $a` — compiles to `MAKE_REF` of the array,
a `FETCH_LIST_W` per target, and a `FREE` of the temporary holding the alias.
`ZEND_FREE` cleared its operand with `store`, which writes *through* a
reference, so freeing that temporary destroyed `$a` itself. It has to unbind the
slot, not write through it. The bug was invisible until `FETCH_LIST_W` existed
to create the situation.

### The `&` marker: measured, and still deferred

`var_dump` not printing `&` for a shared slot is the largest single mechanical
item left (48 tests). The standing note said approximating it — printing `&`
whenever the slot holds a `Ref` — would be spuriously wrong after `unset`. It
was worth measuring rather than assuming, so it was implemented and graded:
**2119 → 2115**, a net loss of four.

The reason is sharper than the old note, and worth recording so nobody tries
again: `Array.RefAt` boxes an element whenever a *write descends through it*, so
`$b[0][1] = 2` leaves `$b[0]` holding a box with exactly one holder. "Holds a
reference" is not close to "is shared" in this value model, and the false
positives outnumber the true ones. Doing it properly needs holder counts, or an
`elementRef` that unboxes once the write completes.

### Also

- `json_encode`, including the list-versus-object rule, `JsonSerializable`, the
  `\u` escaping and the `/` escape, and returning `false` for a value JSON
  cannot hold.
- An `ArrayAccess` on a write path descends through `offsetGet`, which is what
  `$o[$k][$j] = x` needs.
- `get_class()` with no argument names the class whose *body* is running.

## 2026-08-23 — Diagnostics that route through PHP, and the type system

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 2012 | 2089 |
| pass rate (of 4569 attempted) | 44.0% | 45.7% |
| unsupported | 957 | 955 |
| failed | 1588 | 1513 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 445 | 476 |

The denominator did not move this round, so the two rates are comparable.
All 476 differential cases match. `gofmt`, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...`
are clean.

### set_error_handler was accepted and then ignored

`set_error_handler` returned null and did nothing. Every diagnostic went
straight to the output, so a program that installs a handler — a common shape
in the corpus — diverged from the first warning onwards.

Wiring it up needed a way back into PHP from `Ctx.raise`, which is called from
places that cannot call anything: deep inside the value model, with no unit and
no interpreter. The shape that worked is a hook (`Ctx.SetErrorHandler`) plus a
parked exception (`Ctx.TakePendingError`) that the main loop picks up at the
next opcode boundary. That is one opcode later than PHP, which throws from the
diagnostic itself, but nothing in the corpus can tell.

The engine settled four rules that guesswork would have got wrong:

- The handler is called even when `error_reporting` would hide the level, and
  even under `@`. The mask gates the *default* handler, not the callback.
- Only an explicit `false` asks for the default text as well; returning nothing
  counts as handled.
- A diagnostic raised *inside* the handler is not fed back to it.
- `restore_error_handler` pops to the previous one, so the handlers are a stack.

One further thing only showed up in the suite: the location has to be
snapshotted before the handler runs. The handler's own body moves `Ctx`'s idea
of where execution is, so a diagnostic that falls through to the default printer
reported the line of the *closure* instead of the site that raised it.

And installing a throwing handler in one differential case turned every later
case's warning into a fatal — `EG(user_error_handler)` survives an eval, and
`Engine.Reset` did not clear it. Nor did it clear the exception handler, which
had been leaking silently the whole time.

### The by-name variable opcodes carry the name, not the variable

`ZEND_UNSET_VAR` and `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_VAR` were being treated as though op1
were the variable. It is the *name holder*: `unset($$n)` was unsetting `$n`
itself, and `isset($$n)` was asking whether `$n` was set. The CV forms
(`ZEND_UNSET_CV`, `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_CV`) are the direct ones; the VAR forms
never are. This is the same family as the `$GLOBALS` fetch, and the flag in
`extended_value` picks the symbol table for all of them.

While there: the fetch diagnostics follow the fetch *type*, and two were wrong.
`ZEND_FETCH_IS` and `ZEND_FETCH_UNSET` were complaining about an undefined
variable — the question already admits the answer may be "not set" — while
`ZEND_FETCH_RW` was not, although a read-modify-write reads before it writes.

### Type declarations

`ZEND_RECV` bound its argument without looking at the declared type, and
`ZEND_VERIFY_RETURN_TYPE` passed the value straight through with a comment
saying a mismatch is a TypeError and there is no machinery for it. There is now.

The declared type arrives as the engine's own rendering — `?string`,
`string|int` in the normalized order it chose, `Foo` — so the wording of every
TypeError comes from the harvest rather than from anything reconstructed. What
had to be learned from the engine rather than assumed:

- An int satisfies a `float` declaration in *both* modes, but as a float: the
  value widens. Treating it as an exact match left `float(1)` printing as
  `int(1)`.
- A boolean is reported by its singleton type in a TypeError — `true given`,
  not `bool given`.
- `__toString` is part of the string type rather than a coercion: it applies in
  strict mode too.
- Passing null to a non-nullable parameter of an *internal* function is
  deprecated; the same value to a user function throws. That one rule accounted
  for most of the spurious TypeErrors the first attempt introduced.
- An implicit end-of-body is `VERIFY_RETURN_TYPE` with an unused op1, which for
  anything but `void` and `never` is itself the error: "none returned".
- `declare(strict_types=1)` is decided by the *caller's* file. `OpArray` now
  carries the flag, but the check uses the callee's, which is the same thing
  in a single file and wrong across files. Recorded in TODO.md.

Argument checking also applies to engine functions, from the harvested
signatures — including the handful the compiler specializes into their own
opcode (`ZEND_STRLEN`, `ZEND_COUNT`, `ZEND_GET_TYPE`, `ZEND_GET_CLASS`), which
never reach the call path and so needed the check repeated. `get_class()` with
no argument is one of those: it names the class whose *body* is running, not the
object's, and reading its unused operand as an argument produced a TypeError
about a null that was never passed.

### Property visibility, readonly, and dynamic properties

With `visibility`, `readonly` and `declaring_class` all harvested, the property
paths could enforce what they describe. The rules are less symmetric than the
method ones:

- A private property of an *ancestor* is not merely out of reach, it is
  **invisible**: the diagnostic is about an undefined property, and writing the
  name creates a dynamic one beside it. Only a private property of the object's
  own class produces "Cannot access private property".
- Protected always produces the error, and it names the *object's* class, not
  the class that declared the property.
- `__get` / `__set` / `__unset` answer for a property the caller may not reach,
  exactly as they do for one that does not exist. The error is what happens when
  the class has no accessor.
- `isset()` never raises: an unreachable property simply reads as not set.
- readonly refuses a second write from every scope including the declaring one,
  and the "already initialized" check comes first — the message stops mentioning
  visibility once visibility is no longer the reason.

Creating an undeclared property is deprecated since PHP 8.2 unless the class
opted back in. The opt-in is a class flag (`ZEND_ACC_ALLOW_DYNAMIC_PROPERTIES`),
not an attribute to re-read, so it harvests like everything else.

Modelling that exposed a gap in the object model: PHP keeps a private property
and a dynamic property of the same name in *separate* slots, because the
declared one is mangled per class. One map holds both here, so which is which
is recorded on the object (`Object.Dynamic`).

### Assorted

- `usort` had a comment claiming it lived "alongside the other
  interpreter-aware functions". It did not, as noted last entry; it and
  `uasort`/`uksort`/`array_map`/`array_filter` now do.
- Both by-reference notices depend on what the value turns out to be at run
  time rather than on how it was written. `Only variables should be assigned by
  reference` fires when `ASSIGN_REF`'s source is a call result that is not a
  reference; making `RETURN_BY_REF` actually return one — inventing a fresh
  reference for a literal, after its own notice — is what keeps the caller
  quiet in the cases PHP keeps quiet.

### Milestones

```
2012  start of this round
2032  set_error_handler, and the by-name variable opcodes
2064  parameter and return type checking
2069  engine-function argument types, "none returned"
2074  property visibility, readonly, dynamic-property deprecation
2081  the by-reference notices
2089  null-to-internal deprecation, __toString, get_class()
```

### Where to go next

The largest remaining family is `must be compatible with` (55) — inheritance
signature variance, checked at class-link time. The engine defers linking to
`ZEND_DECLARE_CLASS` whenever an interface or an unresolved parent is involved,
so compiling the file does not raise it and the harvest cannot carry it. Doing
it properly means implementing Zend's variance rules in Go, where a *wrong*
check invents fatals in valid code; doing it partially means arity only. It also
needs internal classes' method signatures, which are not harvested today —
`ArrayAccess::offsetSet(mixed $offset, mixed $value): void` has to be rendered
to match the message.

After that: trait composition conflicts (31), `Cannot redeclare` (16), and the
remaining 386 tests that produce no output at all, which are the same
declaration-time checks in other clothes.

## 2026-08-23 — The harness was still lying, and then a batch of semantics

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 1022 | 2012 |
| pass rate | 26.5% of 3860 attempted | 44.0% of 4569 attempted |
| unsupported | 1118 | 957 |
| failed (runs, output differs) | 1708 | 1588 |
| compile-error (excluded from the rate) | 710 | 1 |
| errored (Go error escaped the harness) | 12 | 12 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 372 | 445 |

The `attempted` denominator moved because `compile-error` is excluded from it,
and that bucket went from 710 to 1. Both numbers have to be quoted together or
the rate looks better than it is: 1022/3860 and 2012/4569 are the honest pair.

All 445 differential cases match the engine. `gofmt`, `go vet ./...` and
`go test ./...` are clean.

### The harness was wrong twice more, and it was worth 799 tests

The previous entry's first finding was that the harness was wrong before the
interpreter was. It still was, in two more places, and between them they
account for 799 of the 990 tests gained.

**1. The test file has to be named after the test (668 tests).** `run-tests.php`
writes the `--FILE--` body to `<test>.php` beside the `.phpt`
(`$main_file_name = basename($file, 'phpt')`). The grader was writing it to
`php2phpt-<random>.php`. Any expectation of the form
`Fatal error: ... in %sfoo.php on line 3` — and there are hundreds — cannot match
a randomly named file. Worse, the failures did not look like a naming problem;
they looked like hundreds of unrelated diagnostics being subtly wrong.

Comparison also has to trim **both** ends. `run-tests.php` does
`$output = preg_replace("/\r\n/", "\n", trim($out))` and `$wanted = trim(...)`.
The grader trimmed only trailing whitespace, and the engine prints a leading
newline before every fatal error, so every single-diagnostic test failed on a
blank first line.

**2. Most compile-time diagnostics are never printed (131 tests).** A syntax
error is a thrown `ParseError` and a bad modifier is a thrown `CompileError`;
neither reaches the output on its own. `php2go_compile_file` was reading the
exception's `message` property, which produced nothing useful — and in fact
produced nothing at all, because `zend_read_property_ex` *returns* the zval
rather than filling the `rv` it is handed, so the check on `rv` never fired.
The fix is not to read the property but to call `zend_exception_error(ex,
E_ERROR)` inside the output buffer, which is what the CLI does and the only way
to get the exact `Parse error: <msg> in FILE on line N` wording. It also drains
the exception, which had to happen anyway.

Rule, again: before attributing a `.phpt` failure to the runtime, check what
`run-tests.php` actually does. Two sessions running, the largest single cluster
was the harness.

### Namespaces fall back for functions and constants, and the compiler says so

`foo\strlen()` means `foo\strlen` if that exists and the global `strlen`
otherwise. Only functions and constants do this; classes never do. The
temptation is to check whether the name contains a backslash, which is wrong —
a written-out `Foo\BAR` does not fall back. The compiler marks the sites:
`ZEND_INIT_NS_FCALL_BY_NAME` is emitted only for the unqualified form, and
`ZEND_FETCH_CONSTANT` carries `IS_CONSTANT_UNQUALIFIED_IN_NAMESPACE` (0x800) in
its op1. Both were confirmed by harvesting rather than by reading the header:
`php2harvest` showed `UNUSED:2048` for `PHP_EOL` inside a namespace and
`UNUSED:0` for `Other\THING`.

Relatedly, PHP resolves a function name at `INIT`, not at `DO_FCALL`, so
`Call to undefined function f()` is thrown at the call site and its trace has no
frame for the callee. Raising it after pushing the frame invented a `#0 f()`
line that PHP never prints.

### Method modifiers are not in the op_array unless you harvest them

`Class.methods` was `repeated OpArray` with no flags, so nothing downstream
could tell a static method from an instance one. That single gap was behind a
family of wrong behaviours: `self::s()` from an instance method kept `$this`
bound, so traces said `A->s` where PHP says `A::s`; no visibility could be
enforced; `Cannot call abstract method` could not be raised at all.

`OpArray` now carries `visibility`, `static`, `abstract` and `final`. They are
decided in the cgo shim — `php2go_fn_is_static` and friends — rather than by
masking `fn_flags` in Go, because a shifted constant transcribed into another
language is exactly the kind of thing that goes quietly wrong, and the
`ZEND_ACC_*` macros are already in scope on the C side.

With that in hand, visibility is enforced against the **declaring** class rather
than the one the call site named, and an inaccessible method falls through to
`__call`/`__callStatic` before erroring — PHP treats "you may not call this" and
"this does not exist" identically at that point.

### Assorted things the engine had to be asked about

- **`parent::__construct()` has no method name.** `INIT_STATIC_METHOD_CALL` with
  an UNUSED op2 means the constructor; the engine takes it from the class entry.
  Reading op2 anyway produced `Call to undefined method A::()` — the empty name
  in that message was the whole clue. A parent with no constructor gives
  `Cannot call constructor`, naming no method because the source named none.
- **A class reference can be an object.** `new $obj`, `$obj::CONST` and
  `$obj::m()` name the object's class. Converting it to a string instead asks
  for `__toString` and, on a class without one, yields `Class "" not found`.
- **A typed property with no initializer is uninitialized**, which is a third
  state distinct from null: it is listed by `var_dump` but not counted, `isset()`
  is false *without* consulting `__isset` (only `unset()` reaches that), and
  reading it is `Error: Typed property C::$p must not be accessed before
  initialization` naming the declaring class.
- **`$GLOBALS["x"]` is not an array access.** The compiler rewrites it into a
  by-name fetch against the global symbol table, flagged in `extended_value`,
  and the diagnostic even has different wording: `Undefined global variable $x`.
  `$GLOBALS` as a whole is a separate opcode and, since 8.1, a snapshot.
- **`%g` keeps a fractional digit in the exponential form.** PHP prints
  `1.0e+20` where trailing-zero stripping alone gives `1e+20`. Left-aligned
  padding uses a custom `'x` padding character but not a `0` from the zero flag.
  Both were found by running the format cases against the engine, not by
  reasoning about C.
- **`usort` was never implemented.** `builtins.go` had a comment saying it lived
  "alongside the other interpreter-aware functions"; it did not, and calling it
  reported unsupported. A comment describing an intention read as a description
  of the code.

### What was added

Opcodes: `ZEND_SPACESHIP`, `ZEND_CASE`, `ZEND_CASE_STRICT`, `ZEND_JMP_SET`,
`ZEND_COPY_TMP`, `ZEND_GET_CALLED_CLASS`, `ZEND_ISSET_ISEMPTY_THIS`,
`ZEND_FETCH_GLOBALS`, `ZEND_DECLARE_FUNCTION`, `ZEND_SEND_ARRAY`,
`ZEND_ADD_ARRAY_UNPACK`.

Builtins: the `sprintf` family, `var_export`, `usort`/`uasort`/`uksort`,
`array_map`, `array_filter`, `chr`, `ord`, `range`, `exit`/`die`,
`debug_backtrace`, `debug_print_backtrace`, `get_debug_type`, and a first set of
string functions (`strtoupper`, `strtolower`, `trim` family, `strcmp`,
`strcasecmp`, `strpos`, `strrpos`, `str_contains`, `str_starts_with`,
`str_ends_with`, `substr`, `str_replace`, `strrev`, `str_pad`).

Features: `ArrayAccess` (all four methods, in the order the engine calls them),
enum cases printing as `enum(Suit::Hearts)`, uninitialized typed properties, and
method visibility.

```
1821  compile-time diagnostics reported through zend_exception_error
1862  namespaced function fallback
1866  undefined function thrown at the call site, not inside a pushed frame
```

### Where to go next

The `failed` bucket no longer has a dominant cluster; the top signals are

```

394  missing a Fatal error the engine raises
201  missing the Stack trace: block (because the error was not raised at all)
```

## 2026-08-23 — Grading against `Zend/tests`, and what it turned up

### Result

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Zend/tests` passing | 823 | 1022 |
| pass rate (of 3860 attempted) | 21.3% | 26.5% |
| unsupported | 1574 | 1118 |
| failed (runs, output differs) | 1433 | 1708 |
| errored (Go error escaped the harness) | 30 | 12 |
| differential cases vs the engine | 314 | 372 |

`failed` rising while `unsupported` falls is the expected shape: tests that used
to stop at a missing opcode now run to completion and diverge somewhere later.
The two numbers only make sense read together.

Every differential case matches the engine exactly. `go test ./...`,
`go vet ./...` and `gofmt` are clean.

### Method

The session was a loop: dump every failing test's expected-vs-actual, cluster
the diffs by which diagnostic is missing or spurious, fix the largest cluster,
re-measure. Two pieces of tooling made that possible and are worth keeping:

- **`php2phpt -diff N`** prints expected against actual for the first N
  mismatches. Before this the only signal was a 60-character truncated string,
  which is not enough to tell a wrong warning from a wrong value.
- **`cmd/php2eval`** runs a snippet through the linked engine and the
  interpreter side by side (`php2eval -c '<php>'`, or `-engine` for the engine
  alone). Nearly every behavioural question below was settled by asking it
  rather than by reading `zend_vm_def.h`.

Clustering was done with a throwaway script over the `-diff` dump: normalise
paths and line numbers, then count, per test, which diagnostic lines appear in
the expectation but not the output and vice versa. That ranking drove the whole
session and was right every time about where the mass was.

### Findings

#### 1. The harness was wrong before the interpreter was

`php2phpt` wrote the `--FILE--` body to `/tmp`. PHP resolves an `include`
against the directory of the *including* file, so every test requiring a sibling
`.inc` failed through no fault of the interpreter. Writing the file next to the
`.phpt` — which is exactly what `run-tests.php` does — was worth ~47 tests on
its own.

Lesson: before attributing a `.phpt` failure to the runtime, check what the real
runner does.

#### 2. The oracle only answers questions it is asked

Four separate leaks made the differential harness compare unequal states:

- `EG(symbol_table)` survived `Reset`, so a leftover `$arr` from an earlier case
  made a *correct* interpreter look wrong.
- `EG(error_reporting)` survived, so one case calling `error_reporting(0)`
  silenced later ones.
- The SPL autoload registry survived — and it is a file-static in `ext/spl`,
  unreachable from C, so `Reset` now asks PHP:
  `foreach (spl_autoload_functions() as $f) spl_autoload_unregister($f);`
  (only when PHP has actually executed, tracked by `Engine.executed`).
- `zend_eval_string` leaves an escaping exception merely *pending*: the
  "Fatal error: Uncaught …" text is produced at request shutdown, which never
  happens under embed. `Eval` now calls `zend_exception_error` itself. Until it
  did, the single most common shape of expected output in the whole `.phpt`
  corpus was invisible to the oracle.

Both sides also need the same *capabilities*: the differential harness and
`php2eval` now install `ir.EngineLoader` (or a case using `eval`/`include`
compares working PHP against a missing-compiler error) and pass the harvested
builtins into the manifest (or every undefined-function case reads as a gap).

The symptom of this family is always the same — a case that passes alone and
fails in the suite, or the reverse.

#### 3. Write fetches are silent; read-modify-write fetches are not

The largest single cluster (~100 tests) was spurious `Undefined variable`
warnings. PHP's diagnostics follow the *fetch type*, not the syntax:

- `BP_VAR_W` is silent and creates: `$a[0] = 1`, `$this->p[] = x`,
  `f($arr[])`, `$u->p = 1`. The only error a write raises is about the
  assignment (`Attempt to assign property "p" on null`), never about the read.
- `BP_VAR_RW` warns, then creates: `$c[0] .= "x"` emits both
  `Undefined variable $c` and `Undefined array key 0`.
- Taking a reference *defines* the target as null — `$c = &$undef`, a by-ref
  argument, `use (&$j)` — and says nothing. In `frame.slotRef` this has to
  normalise an *existing* box holding undef too: at global scope every CV slot
  is already a reference into `Ctx.Globals`, so the make-a-new-box path is never
  taken there.
- A by-value `use ($i)` warns once, at capture, and captures the null the read
  produced. Storing undef instead re-warns on every read inside the body.
- `false` still grows into an array, with
  `Deprecated: Automatic conversion of false to array is deprecated`.

Read diagnostics also name the type they found — `Attempt to read property "q"
on null` / `on string` / `on int` — never "on non-object".

#### 4. `$this` is an unused operand, not a variable

`$this->m()`, `$this->p++`, `$this->p[] = x`, `$this->p .= "y"`,
`isset($this->p)`, `unset($this->p)` and `$this->p = &$x` all encode `$this` as
`op1_type == IS_UNUSED`. Reading op1 with the ordinary fetch yields undef, so
every one of these reported "on null". `$this->f()` inside a method was broken
across the board — a large, quiet correctness hole that only surfaced once the
error paths started printing real messages.

All of them now go through `frame.objectOperand`, which falls back to `f.this`.

#### 5. Zend class tables are flattened

`ce->function_table` contains everything the class inherited, and
`ce->properties_info` likewise. Harvesting them wholesale looks right and is
wrong:

- **Methods** must be filtered on `fn->common.scope == ce`. Without it a
  subclass carries its own copy of a parent's method, so the resolved declaring
  scope is the subclass and `self::` inside an inherited method names the wrong
  class. Trait methods keep the *trait* as their scope, so they are filtered out
  too and `resolveMethod` now consults `decl.GetTraits()`, ranking traits above
  the parent — the precedence PHP applies when flattening.
- **Properties** must be sorted by `info->offset`, which the engine hands out in
  declaration order with a parent's first. The harvester sorted by *name*, which
  made every `var_dump` of a two-property object wrong, along with `foreach`
  over an object and `get_object_vars`.

Late static binding was threaded through at the same time: `pendingCall` and
`frame` now carry a `called` class distinct from the declaring `class`, so
`static::` sees the subclass a call site named while `self::` sees the body's
own class.

#### 6. A program's mistake is a PHP error, not a gap

Several failures escaped as bare Go errors, which meant tests *expecting* those
messages could never pass: `can only throw objects`, `__clone method called on
non-object`, `too few arguments`, undefined constants and undefined classes.
Each is now a catchable PHP error with the engine's exact wording (including
`ArgumentCountError`'s "exactly N" vs "at least N", and the caller's file and
line, which comes off the new call stack).

The rule for telling an error from a gap is answered from harvested data, never
guessed:

- Function in `Manifest.builtins` but unimplemented → gap. Absent from the
  linked build → `Error: Call to undefined function f()`.
- Class where `isBuiltinOnly` holds → gap. Declared by the program → its missing
  method is `Error: Call to undefined method C::m()`.
- Name resolving to nothing after autoloading → `Error: Class "X" not found`.

This is what keeps the pass rate meaningful; `php2phpt` counts `unsupported`
separately from `failed` for the same reason.

#### 7. Everything else

- **Stack traces.** `Ctx` now carries the call stack; an exception snapshots it
  at *creation* (which is also when PHP records `file` and `line`, not at
  throw). Argument rendering matches the engine exactly, elision included:
  `C->m('a-very-long-str...', Array, Object(stdClass), true, NULL, 1.5)`.
- **`error_reporting()`** is now a real mask on `Ctx`, filtering by level.
  The default is harvested (`Manifest.default_error_reporting`) rather than
  transcribed — it is 30719 on this build, not `E_ALL`, because it is an ini
  default. This removed the last hard-coded `errorReportingAll = 32767`.
- **PHP 8 operand rules.** A wholly numeric string converts silently, one that
  merely starts with a number warns (`A non-numeric value encountered`), and
  anything else is `TypeError: Unsupported operand types: …`. Integer operators
  additionally deprecate a lossy float or float-string conversion. Two arrays
  under `+` union; two strings under `& | ^` combine bytewise.
- **Magic accessors.** `__get`, `__set`, `__isset`, `__unset`, `__call`,
  `__callStatic`, with a re-entry guard so `return $this->$name` inside `__get`
  does not loop. Note `isset()` is answered by `__isset` alone while `empty()`
  goes on to ask `__get` — conflating them is observable.
- **Autoloading.** `spl_autoload_register` and friends; `resolveClass` consults
  the callbacks from `new`, static calls and class-constant fetches.
- **`FETCH_*_FUNC_ARG` / `SEND_FUNC_ARG`.** The argument position comes from the
  preceding `ZEND_CHECK_FUNC_ARG`'s op2, *not* from the fetch's
  `extended_value`; the callee's arg-info (user function, or harvested builtin
  by-ref flags) then decides read vs write.
- `Array to string conversion` is an `E_WARNING` in PHP 8, not a notice. A
  hand-written unit test asserted the PHP 7 level and had to be corrected —
  which is the argument for the differential oracle in one line.

### Where to go next

Ranked by tests currently blocked:

```
257  instantiation of ReflectionClass
102  instantiation of Fiber
 37  call to fopen
 28  instantiation of WeakMap
 23  instantiation of ReflectionFunction
 18  call to debug_print_backtrace
 17  call to serialize
 16  index assignment on object        (ArrayAccess)
 14  call to array_map
 14  call to printf
 13  ZEND_SEND_ARRAY
 13  call to exit
```

Blocked ≠ would-pass: unblocking moves a test from `unsupported` into `failed`,
and it still has to produce the right output. The remaining diagnostic clusters
in the `failed` bucket are smaller and more scattered than at the start of the
session — the largest is still spurious `Undefined variable` at ~61 tests, whose
causes are now individually distinct rather than one systematic rule.

Two known-wrong things deliberately left alone:

- `var_dump` does not print the `&` marker for a referenced slot. Getting it
  right needs refcounts, and approximating it ("print `&` whenever the slot
  holds a Ref") would be spuriously wrong after `unset`. ~37 tests expect one.
- Class constants whose initializer the compiler defers (e.g. a spread of
  another constant) have no harvested value and report as undefined.

### Environment note

`bazel` is not on `PATH`; `hack/cgoenv.sh` needs both it and the output root
that produced `bazel-bin`:

```sh
export BAZEL=~/.cache/bazelisk/downloads/sha256/<hash>/bin/bazel
export BAZEL_STARTUP="--output_user_root=<the root bazel-bin points into>"
eval "$(hack/cgoenv.sh)" && go build ./...
```

Regenerating the IR bindings after a `.proto` change needs `buf` and
`protoc-gen-go`, both present under the mise Go install:
`(cd proto && buf generate)`.
